en: The *Pramāṇavārttika-svavṛtti-ṭīkā*:
He whose movement has destroyed all bonds, who stands in perfect mastery,
and in whom there arises a continuous stream of most pure knowledge extending over all objects of cognition.
Having bowed many times to the glorious Lord Mañjunātha, the all-pervading one whose mind has long been intent on the welfare of sentient beings,

I now wish to state something from the *Vārttika* regarding the author of this commentary; for he possesses every excellence, such that even in this profound subject matter, he speaks in a manner accessible to those like us.
When the obstacles have been removed by the tusks of the noble elephant, the young elephants proceed happily once the paths are found.
If there is anyone who disregards me out of pride in their own virtues, let him know that this effort is not directed toward him at all.
There may be someone at some time who seeks this [work], for there is no end to the diversity of intellects among living beings in the world.

Although the completion of a treatise without hindrance occurs through the accumulation of merit by performing salutations to one’s chosen deity with body, speech, and mind— even without introducing a verse of homage at the beginning of the work— nevertheless,

the Teacher introduced a verse of worship to a specific deity after considering that the activity of the commentator and the listeners preceded by such praise generates an excellence of merit, serves the welfare of others, and maintains the tradition of the virtuous.

Regarding the passage beginning with "shaken free from conceptual construction" (*vidhūtakalpanā*), when the term "Samantabhadra" is not understood through conventional usage as referring to a Bodhisattva, then this constitutes worship of the Blessed Buddha;
and that worship is twofold: by way of praise and by way of prostration.
By the word *namaḥ* [homage], there is praise through prostration; by the remaining [words], there is praise through eulogy.

Furthermore, that eulogy is threefold: by way of the perfection of one's own welfare (*svārthasampatti*), by way of the perfection of the welfare of others (*parārthasampatti*), and by way of the means for the perfection of the welfare of others.
One who has perfected their own welfare becomes capable with respect to the welfare of others. (Note: The reading in brackets is from PVb.)
First, the fulfillment of one’s own welfare (*svārthasaṃpat*) was stated by means of the first half [of the verse];
and this fulfillment of one’s own welfare, characterized by the three bodies (*kāya*), is manifested as being distinguished by three specific qualities.
By way of the excellence of the abandonment of obscurations, the excellence of profundity,
and the excellence of vastness.

In that regard, "conceptualization" refers to the minds and mental factors belonging to the three realms, which function in the forms of "self" and "mine," and so forth, as well as in the forms of "grasped object" and "grasping subject. Because these are of the nature of being bound by a net, they are "shaken off"—that is, destroyed along with their latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) and brought to a state where they will never arise again. Those physical forms whose nature it is to have achieved this are described as such.
By this, the excellence regarding the abandonment of obscurations has been stated;
however, the excellences of profundity and vastness are expressed by the two terms "profound" and "vast.
They are profound because they have shaken off the web of conceptual construction and because they are not within the domain of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others.
The three bodies— svābhāvika, sāmbhogika, and nairmāṇika— are sublime because they pervade all objects of knowledge and the welfare of all sentient beings; that Blessed One,
whose forms are profound and sublime, has shaken off the web of conceptual construction.

"Bhadra" means auspiciousness, characterized by worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Because he brings about that [auspiciousness] completely and without remainder for those who seek it, according to their spiritual capacity (*yathābhavyam*), he is "Samantabhadra. By this, the perfection of the welfare of others (*parārthasampad*) is stated.

By the phrase "of this perfection of the welfare of others, whose radiance flashes everywhere," the means for its accomplishment is stated. Here, "radiance" (*tviṣ*) refers to rays; however, by way of analogy, the teaching of the Dharma—which concerns the means for achieving both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)—is called "radiance" because it perceives things exactly as they are.

"Samantaspharaṇatviṭ" means he whose light—consisting of the teachings of the Dharma—is "samantaspharaṇa," that is, it radiates and pervades all directions without remainder as a means for accomplishing the welfare of others, because these [teachings] are explained in their entirety to those to be trained (*vinaya*). Due to the connection with the word "namaḥ," the dative case is used here in every instance. However, when conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is considered, this term "Samantabhadra" is conventionally established in the Mahāyāna as referring to a specific Bodhisattva; thus, this is an act of worship to that Bodhisattva.
The meaning of the terms, however, should be applied as before;

this, moreover, is the distinction: the state of having shaken off the web of conceptual construction is to be understood from the abandonment of the obscurations of the bodhisattva stages, and its profundity is due to its being beyond the sphere of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary worldlings.

As for magnanimity, however, it exists indeed among Bodhisattvas in accordance with their own nature, even in relation to the three bodies (*kāyatraya*); yet, because they have reached the ultimate excellence, it is established as belonging to the Buddhas.
The missing portion is found in the margin in a different hand.
The missing portion is found in the margin in a different hand.
The missing portion is found in the margin in a different hand.

Indeed, there certainly are those who will grasp this treatise known as *Santosa-vārttika*; nevertheless, because of the abundance of defects in listeners, one might render even an existing benefit as if it were non-existent. Thus, showing that the very state of having a mind cultivated by the practice of well-spoken words is the cause for undertaking the treatise—and that this defect of the listener’s fault is a cause for the loss of its great purpose and ought to be abandoned—he speaks the second verse beginning with "prāyaḥ-prākṛta... by way of an indirect expression (*vakrokti*).
Here, four kinds of defects of the listener are revealed: faulty wisdom, ignorance, lack of desire [to hear], and lack of impartiality;
the word *prāyas* generally ends in the vowel *o* and signifies abundance or multiplicity.

"Most people" means the majority of people; "attached to the vulgar" (*prākṛtāsakta*) is a *vyadhikaraṇa* (non-co-locative) *bahuvrīhi* compound, meaning one whose attachment (*sakti*) is directed toward "vulgar treatises" (*prākṛtāni*), that is, external scriptures (*bahiḥśāstrāṇi*), since the compound is formed through its expressive power (*gamakatvāt*).
Or, it is a coordinate (samānādhikaraṇa) compound meaning "one whose attachment is natural" (*prākṛta*); and because its object is the natural, the attachment itself is called "natural."
By this, the fault of the listener—namely, defective wisdom—is stated.
"One of weak intellect" (*apratibalaprajña*) refers to one whose wisdom lacks the capacity to grasp the treatise; the connection is that such a person is generally [the case].
By this, ignorance is expressed.
It is not only that one who lacks the desire for [hearing] well-spoken words [does not listen], but rather, being possessed by the impurity of envy, he even hates the speaker of well-spoken words;
the meaning is that he both lacks the desire and harbors hatred.
By this, "lack of desire" and "lack of neutrality" are stated respectively.
In this case as well, "people" (*jana*) should generally be connected [with the preceding word];
however, others explain that there is also a particle ending in the vowel *ā* for the word *prāyas*,
and that it naturally occurs in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārtha*) meaning "in abundance" (*bāhulyena*).
Envy is the resentment of the mind toward the prosperity of others; that very thing is a "stain" because it defiles the mind.
The plural number is used due to the diversity of individual instances.
For this reason, this work entitled *Vārttika*, which is now being undertaken,
is a "benefit for others" (*paropakāra*); it is so called because others are benefited by it, the suffix *ghañ* being used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).
"Paropakāraḥ" means "one who benefits others"; the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.1.
"We have not even the thought of helping others"—if this is so, how then is there an engagement in composing a treatise? To this he says:
"The mind for a long time," and so forth.

Some explain it as follows: "A *vyasana* is an addiction, an attachment, or a state of being devoted to something; that whose mind has had such an addiction increased by the long-term practice of the *sūktas* is described thus. For this reason, the mind has become bound by longing—that is, desire has arisen—for the composition of the commentary (*vārttika*) here."

Others, however, raise a different question: "Why does this teacher Dharmakīrti explain the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* according to the method of a *vārttika*, rather than composing an independent treatise (*śāstra*)? On this occasion of inquiry, he says "mostly," and so forth.
The summarized meaning of this verse is as follows:

my mind has conceived a longing for the commentary on the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* due to both reflection and compassion; here, "reflection" and "compassion" refer to [the concern] that the treatise composed by the teacher Dignāga provides only limited benefit.
And the fact that [the teaching] is of little benefit is stated by way of an illustration through the offense of one's own kinsmen;
the connection is that "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*) means for the most part, and "people" refers to those whose attachment is to the worldly (*prākṛta*).
In the world, a "prākṛta" is said to be a base person whose lineage is wicked;
likewise, the treatises of non-Buddhist sectarians are composed by others and serve to subvert the teacher’s treatise on ethics.
Because they originate from perverted knowledge and because their lineage is corrupt, those [objects] are called "prākṛta" (ordinary/vulgar);
he who has attachment—that is, passion—for them is so described.
But why does he have attachment to the ordinary? To this he says:
One of weak intelligence,
because of this, takes even what is poorly spoken to be well-spoken and becomes attached to the vulgar;

and precisely because of his weak intelligence, being unable to understand the well-spoken words of the Teacher as they truly are, he perceives them as faulty and finds no benefit in those well-spoken words of the Teacher.
And he says that one becomes hostile toward the teacher as well,
in the passage beginning with "merely," etc.;
not only is such a person devoid of benefit from the teacher’s well-spoken words, but being overwhelmed by the impurities of envy, he even feels hatred toward the teacher.

What has come to pass? An addiction increased by the practice of well-spoken verses indeed establishes a connection even with that which is remote, according to the maxim: "Whatever is related to something, it belongs to that [thing] even if it stands at a distance."

"Well-spoken" means excellent; "well-uttered" refers to the teaching of the Blessed One. He for whom there was practice in that [teaching], an increased passion for it, and an extreme attachment to it—namely, the master Dignāga—is thus described.

By this, he states that the master Dignāga had accumulated merit and knowledge, for only those who have accumulated merit and knowledge develop a passion intensified by the practice of well-spoken words.

Because he possesses weak intellect, is indifferent to the well-spoken words of the masters, and is attached to the vulgar, for that reason this compendium of valid cognition (*pramāṇasamuccaya*) is not a service to others;
"service" (*upakāra*) means an instrument (*upakaraṇa*), derived from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of action, according to Pāṇini 3.3.18.

Thinking that no superior benefit for others arises from this, one might suppose that benefiting others is not even a minor benefit; however, such a benefit certainly does exist, and it is precisely indicated by the word "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*),
where the word "iti" functions as a causal particle.
For this reason, we have a concern:

"Even though this treatise possesses great significance, it has not become beneficial to many; how then may I bring about its complete success? Furthermore, even a slight hostility toward the Teacher, who is like a Bodhisattva, is a cause of harm. Therefore, by correctly elucidating the Teacher’s system and thereby generating great respect for the Teacher, I shall turn people away from that cause of harm. Thus, there is also compassion, characterized by the desire for their separation from suffering, as indicated by the word "also" (api).

In this context, by the second word "with longing" (*anubaddhaspṛham*), he states that reflection (*cintā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) are the causes [of his undertaking]. Thus, by means of these two—reflection and compassion—his mind has for a long time, over a vast duration, possessed a continuous desire (*anubaddhaspṛham*) for the composition of this *Pramāṇavārttika*, which serves as a commentary on the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*. Anticipating the objection—"If the Master Dharmakīrti intends to compose a commentary on the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, why does he establish inference (*anumāna*) independently?"—he speaks as follows to dispel that doubt.

Regarding the phrase "benefit and harm" (*arthānartha*) and so forth: "benefit" (*artha*) is that which is conducive to welfare, while "harm" (*anartha*) is its opposite; "discernment" (*vivecana*) refers to the differentiation between these two. The analysis of the compound is as follows: it is that whose basis (*āśraya*) is inference (*anumāna*), because that discernment relies upon inference. For, having ascertained benefit and harm through inference, one establishes them in their respective categories—namely, for the sake of attainment or avoidance—by means of a continuous stream of cognition that follows in the wake of inference.
Therefore, some explain it as follows: "The discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful is based upon inference;
because there is disagreement regarding that [inference], [this treatise] is for the purpose of establishing it. This is said because there are conflicting views concerning that inference.
In this regard, however, the following must be considered:
if it is determined that the discernment between what is beneficial and what is harmful rests solely upon inference,
that is not correct.

Since the discernment of a third object, which is neither beneficial nor harmful but to be disregarded, also relies upon inference— and since the discernment of what is beneficial and harmful is not restricted to inference alone,
its reliance upon perception is not excluded— what excellence is proclaimed of inference such that it is explained first?
Or rather, let it be determined thus:
"Because the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful is based solely on inference"—
this restriction is likewise incorrect,
because the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful is also based on perception.
For in this way, benefit (*artha*) and harm (*anartha*), having distinct forms, appear in perception itself;

and that perception, having attained proficiency through the excellence of repeated practice, eliminates the causes of error and generates a subsequent conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that discriminates between benefit and harm.

Indeed, this alone is the basis for perception’s role as the ground for discriminating between benefit and harm: namely, having experienced benefit and harm in their distinction, it produces a certainty (*niścaya*) therein according to that experience.
In the margin.
In the margin:
"And it cannot be said that benefit and harm are distinguished by the latter alone."

Because a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not grasp the true nature of an object, or because its status as a conceptual construction would be lost if it did, there is a contradiction in the fact that for a cognizer bound by conceptualization, the object appears clearly. However, when perception—due to a lack of intensity regarding a certain object—is unable to remove the causes of error, a certainty is sought through inference; this is not the case everywhere.
Therefore, the determination of the validity of perception occurs both intrinsically (*svataḥ*) and extrinsically (*parataḥ*).
This point will be established in the second chapter, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.

Furthermore, it must be accepted that perception, by the force of repeated practice, removes the causes of error and thereby produces a certainty that accords with experience; otherwise, it would serve as the basis for distinguishing between what is beneficial and what is harmful. Otherwise, even inference could not be established, because the mark (*liṅga*), such as smoke, would not be certain.
If one were to understand smoke and so forth through another inference, there would be an infinite regress.

In that case as well, [the reason] would have to be established by another inference from another mark (*liṅga*). Furthermore, if perception were not the basis for discriminating between what is beneficial and what is harmful, then that which was stated by the author of the treatise in another section— namely,
that "the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful are invariably preceded by correct knowledge," and so forth— would be contradicted.
Likewise, others maintain that because it has been stated [elsewhere], "for one does not determine the object in this [state]," and so forth,
and further stated, "recollection and so on arise from the power of consciousness regarding things already seen," and so forth,
it must therefore be explained otherwise.

The definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth composed by the master Dignāga are the "meaning" because they are logical; those composed by the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) are not the "meaning" because they are illogical. The discernment between these two—their establishment as being logical or illogical—is based upon inference (*anumāna*).
For it is precisely by relying on inference that the logicality or illogicality of definitional statements is established, since perception (*pratyakṣa*) is non-discursive (*avicāraka*).
That too is incorrect,
because the validity or invalidity of definitional statements does not reside in their own form, but rather through their meaning;
and that meaning is perceived as being consistent with inference just as it is perceived through direct perception.
And so he will say:
"Perception is free from conceptual construction; it is established by perception itself" (Pramāṇavārttika 3).
123. Likewise, there is also the view held by some that the ascertainment of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) occurs through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and so forth.
It is true that the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful is indeed accomplished through perception and inference;

however, as for the claim that this discernment of benefit and harm relies exclusively upon inference—that is incorrect. For even regarding objects of perception, when a dispute arises, there exists no basis for a definitive resolution other than inference. Therefore, because of its preeminence, it was stated that inference is the basis for such discernment.
This too is untenable.
Since that alone is established as the object of perception which is certain, and no dispute is possible regarding what is certain, this [objection] is untenable.
However, another says:
"The discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful arises from inference alone, not from perception."

Since those objects and non-objects whose results have already been experienced, or are currently being experienced, are not the objects of purposeful activity because their result has already been accomplished, one therefore engages with those objects and non-objects capable of future causal efficacy for the sake of that future efficacy. Furthermore, that capacity is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) among them, by virtue of which they would become objects of purposeful activity.
Since the purposeful activity (arthakriyā) to be accomplished by engagement is yet to occur, its capacity—the state of being "kuru-rūpa" (performing its function)—is also yet to occur.

Therefore, because of the similarity between present objects and those things that previously accomplished purposeful activity, the determination of suitability for future results regarding even perceptible objects does not arise from perception itself; thus, the discernment of what is beneficial and harmful proceeds only through inference.
This too is incorrect.

For if that capacity, which is the state of being "producing" (*kurvadrūpatā*), exists in objects as something belonging to the present time, then it would be determined by perception— even for one possessing an excellence of practice— just like a logical mark (*liṅga*).
On the other hand, if that capacity were only future, then it could not be determined even by inference, because, as he will state later, there is no inference regarding what is yet to come.

By this, that which is said—that the attainment of an object that is the locus of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) is indistinguishable for perception and inference—should also be regarded as refuted. For the locus of purposeful activity is that which is capable of future causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), and it has been stated that such capacity is not ascertained by perception or inference. Furthermore, the locus of purposeful activity is held to be something delimited, and since a continuum (*santāna*) is not delimited by a single moment of perception or the like, how could it be the locus of purposeful activity?

Now, it is argued that even though perception functions at a single moment, it is incorrect to say that it has a single continuum as its object by virtue of having the generality of moments as its object through the power of conceptual determination (*niścaya*).

For it is only by virtue of conceptual determination that perception is established as having a generality as its object based on the very object that appears; in ultimate reality, however, perception has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.
Just as perception has a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object,

so too this appearing particular characteristic of smoke— whether it be produced from grass, from leaves, or something else— is established as a perception having a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, because, despite having the particular characteristic as its object, there is no ascertainment of its specific qualities and there is only a momentary determination.

Since the determination (*niścaya*) that arises subsequent to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) conforms to the object of that perception, it is not possible to establish direct perception as having a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) as its object. For the moment that appears in direct perception is not determined; nor is it possible for it to have the form of either a preceding or a succeeding moment, because they exist at different times.

Therefore, how could direct perception be established as having the generality of moments (*kṣaṇasāmānya*) as its object, given that there is no ascertainment of particulars and only a determination of the mere moment?

Although the certainty "this is that very same [thing]" which arises subsequent to direct perception has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, it does not have the continuum (*saṃtāna*) as its object; for, by taking both the previously perceived and the presently perceived [moments] as its objects, it does not ascertain future moments, and because its object is a form excluded from those of a different class (*vijātīya*). For this very reason, even when a moment appears, there is the certainty of the cognition "this is a jar.
Now, if the continuum of things capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samartha*) is not determined by either direct perception or inference...
How, then, do these two possess the capacity to initiate [action]?
We reply: it is because they determine the mere essential nature of the thing.

For instance, when one ascertains through perception that a thing such as fire is capable of performing a purposeful action like burning by way of continuous occurrence in one place, one determines that this same thing, when perceived in another location and so forth, must likewise perform such an action by way of continuous occurrence.

Furthermore, at another time, that same person, seeking the result and investigating its nature, perceives fire and so forth through perception and inference; having first reached the certainty that "this is that very thing," he acts. Therefore, the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in the determination of the mere nature of that object, not in the determination of its continuous existence, nor in the determination of its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), because all of these have already been determined previously.
Therefore, it is indeed logical that perception and inference are the motivators [of action].
How then was it stated that the discernment between what is beneficial and what is harmful depends upon inference?
there is neither meaning nor even intention here; rather, it is the Four Noble Truths.
Since we are seekers of liberation, and the Blessed One has stated that liberation arises from the vision of the Four Noble Truths,
and that such vision is accomplished through the practice of cultivation (*bhāvanā*),
and engagement in cultivation occurs through certainty regarding the Four Noble Truths;
And because that ascertainment is beyond direct perception, it arises from inference alone; thus, inference alone is the basis for the discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful.
Here, "beneficial" refers to cessation and the path because they are to be adopted, while "harmful" refers to suffering and its origin because they are to be abandoned.

Alternatively, "beneficial" is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) and "harmful" is conventional truth (*saṃvṛttisatya*); since the discrimination between these two—their establishment according to their respective natures—is based upon inference, inference is the foundation.

Furthermore, all cognition that effects the discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful does not apprehend the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), but rather determines it; thus, it is indeed erroneous.
Therefore, if the cognition of words and so forth is held to be the basis for the discrimination between the beneficial and the harmful, it too is invalid due to its erroneous nature.
For this very reason, there is no possibility of its being explained here.
Even though inference is erroneous, its validity exists by virtue of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*);

however, if the validity of verbal cognition and the like were accepted in this same way, they would be included within inference. Since that which is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) cannot be a means of proof, it is inference alone that serves as the basis for discerning what is beneficial and what is harmful.

Now, if the validity of inference is due to the force of the necessary connection, would not conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "eternal" and so forth also possess validity? For there is a necessary connection between them and objects such as momentary things.
Now, if validity were based on a connection with the determined object, then the cognition of a gem in the luster of a gem would be valid;

for that too is connected with the gem as it was determined. Therefore, even when there is a connection, inferential cognition is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only when it causes one to obtain that object which was determined as being connected to a certain place and so forth—due to the determination of the identity of the continuum (*santāna*) with respect to that place and so forth—but not every cognition.
The discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful is of the nature of comprehension; its form is inference because it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Alternatively, the inferential mark (*liṅga*) itself is the inference; therefore, the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful has inference as its basis.
This is because there is confusion regarding that inference.

In order to establish that [inference]—that is, to establish that inference by removing misconceptions regarding it—the author of the Sūtra says "the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth.
If it is asked: "If inference is what is to be established, why does he establish only the logical reason (*hetu*) by means of 'the property of the subject' and so forth?"
This is not a fault;
for since the misconception regarding inference occurs through a misconception regarding the logical reason (*hetu*), its establishment is achieved precisely by means of explaining that [reason].

Furthermore, inferential cognition arising from a mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics is well-known in the world; therefore, the misconception is refuted by means of that very common understanding.

Alternatively, when the word "inference" (*anumāna*) refers specifically to the inferential mark (*liṅga*), then it establishes the reason itself for the removal of that misconception; thus there is no fault. In this verse, the definition of the inferential mark, the restriction of its number, the cause for that restriction of number, and the exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) are stated.
The definition is: "The property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) which is pervaded by a part of that [subject]."

The property intended to be proven is that which is a part of that [subject's] side; it is pervaded by that [reason]— this restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) constitutes the determination of the number as "only three" (*tridhaiva*),
while "because of the necessity of inseparable connection" (*avinābhāvaniyamāt*) is the cause for that determination of the number.

The meaning is that invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is restricted to these three [types of reasons] alone. "Fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are other than those" means they are excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*);
therefore, fallacious reasons are those other than the three types of valid reasons.
Now, if the pervasion by that part [of the reason] were grasped only in the example,
then inference would not arise at all,
because the pervasion of the reason by the property to be proved would not have been grasped in the subject of the inference (*sādhyadharmin*).
And at that time, the definition "the reason is a property of the subject" would be useless because it lacks probative force;
furthermore, even if pervasion were grasped through universal inclusion (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), there would be no validity for inference,
as it would be of the nature of a memory (*smṛti*) since its object is already apprehended by the means of valid cognition that grasps the pervasion.

Furthermore, it should not be stated that "the reason is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*), because this is already understood by the statement of its pervasion by that [subject's] part; and it is by virtue of its pervasion by that part that the property of the subject is a prover, not merely by its existence in the subject, since a donkey or similar thing residing therein is not a prover.
Therefore, "the reason is a property of the subject" should not be stated as a separate definition.
As it has been said:
"Where there is the condition of being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapannatva*), what is the use of the three [criteria]?
Where there is not the condition of being otherwise impossible, what is the use of the three?"
Furthermore, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) cannot be a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), because the apprehension of something else is a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*).

A reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) has the subject itself as its form, and a reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*) does not depend on a subject independently. Moreover, a constructed (*kalpita*) property of the subject cannot function as a reason based on effect or essential nature, nor can it possess the pervasion by the probandum (*sādhyavyāpti*). Therefore, it must be stated that a reason is not merely a property of the subject.

Likewise, if the state of being a cause (*hetutva*) were pervaded by the number three, then because the state of being a cause is not restricted [to those three], its existence as a cause in other instances—such as in the case of the "conjoined" (*saṃyogin*) and so forth—would remain unavoidable; thus, the restriction "only threefold" would be illogical.

Alternatively, if the state of being a cause were pervaded by the number three, then because the number three is not restricted to causes, even effects (*kārya*) and so forth would lack the status of being a cause; consequently, it would not be tenable that only effects and the like possess causality.
Furthermore:

If there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) and the probandum, then even an unconnected reason would be a means of cognition; thus, the restriction that "the reason is of only three kinds" would not hold. If, on the other hand, such a connection does exist, then because it is necessarily included within either the effect (*kārya*) or the essential nature (*svabhāva*), the reason would still be of only three kinds. Even so, it is not tenable [to claim] that "fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are other than those," for it is incorrect to say that their absence is established by perception and the like, since another type of reason is absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*). Thus, what was stated is improper.

"The reason is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) that is pervaded by a portion of it; it is of only three kinds because of the restriction of inseparable connection (avinābhāva); other than these are fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa).
Regarding this, it is said:

although the pervasion between the probandum (sādhya) and the probans (sādhana) is apprehended through a universal induction (sarvopasaṃhāreṇa), nevertheless, the mere grasping of pervasion does not produce a specific determination here that "the property to be proved now exists in the subject of the inference" (sādhyadharmiṇi). This [specific determination] must come from inference itself.

Therefore, inference is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it establishes the object to be proven (*sādhya*) as connected with a specific place and so forth that have been apprehended; and this [inference] occurs only when there is the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), and not otherwise. Since a probans (*sādhana-dharma*) located in one place cannot be connected with a locus of the probandum (*sādhya-dharmin*) located in another place, the cognition of the probandum as delimited by a specific place and so forth arises solely through the power of the cognition of the probans as delimited by a specific place and so forth. Thus, inference is the very cognition of the probandum as delimited by a specific place and so forth, and not the mere cognition of fire from the mere [presence of] a property, for the latter is the fruit of the means of valid cognition that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Nor does the property of being a "property of the subject" (pakṣadharmatva) of the probans become established merely by the general understanding that "wherever there is the property of the probans, there is the property to be proven," because the specific nature [of the probans] as a property of the locus of the property to be proven (sādhyadharmin) is not perceived; this is due to the statement being made in a general sense.
Therefore, in order to bring about the cognition of the property to be proven as delimited by a specific location and so forth, the property-of-the-subject status must be demonstrated.

Consequently, the following argument is refuted: "Since the property-of-the-subject has already been stated by the very formula 'wherever there is smoke, there is fire,' one need not say 'and here there is smoke' for the sake of establishing fire in a particular location, because the meaning has already been expressed."

Now, if inference were thus to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then even an inference that does not have the property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) would be a valid cognition, because it apprehends what was previously unapprehended;
for example, just as one infers rain above by seeing a swelling of the river below, so too [one might infer]: "This child is a Brahmin, because his mother and father are Brahmins."
As it has been said:
"Just as the swelling of a river, being observed downstream, necessarily leads one to infer the rain that caused it upstream. Thus, the effect serves as the regulator for the cause.
In the margin:
"Thus, the state of having dharma as direct perception is accepted as the primary member of the reason.
In the margin.
That [inference] is rendered inconclusive because of the observation that the aforementioned properties belong to something else;
furthermore, the inference of a son’s Brahminhood from the Brahminhood of his parents is well-known to all the world and does not depend upon the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

If one were to imagine that the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) exists even there [in the case of a fallacy] due to a flaw (*kleśa*), then for such a person, this definition would not accord with the object to be defined (*lakṣya*);
for it is by means of definitions that [an object] is understood in accordance with what is well-known in the world.
If it is argued that the definition of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) would thus be something not previously established and therefore cannot be proven,
it is replied: why is it that the inference of rain occurs only above [the clouds] and not elsewhere?

If it is argued that [the flood] indicates rain because it is related to it, then if this is so, the inference of rain must be made at the place from which this river-flood has come, and not elsewhere, due to the possibility of deviation (vyabhicāra). Furthermore, for the flood to be a probans (gamaka), its relationship to the rain must be ascertained; otherwise, it would be inconclusive (anaikāntika).

Likewise, in the case of the argument "this child is a Brahmin because his parents are Brahmins," it is the very Brahminhood of that specific child which is the probandum (*sādhya*), and it is the property characterized by the Brahminhood of his parents—standing in a relation to him—that serves as the indicator (*gamaka*), not the mere Brahminhood of the parents in general. This is because the Brahminhood of parents related to someone else cannot indicate [the status of this child]. Therefore, since this too possesses the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) while functioning as an indicator, there is no need for the laborious conceptualization of *pakṣadharmatva*.

Alternatively, that which is the very cause of non-deviation is itself the logical reason (*hetu*). For example, smoke’s being an effect of fire, and a child’s being born of a Brāhmaṇa mother and father, are the causes for the child’s Brāhmaṇahood; thus, these alone are rightly considered the reasons, as the postulation of anything else would involve unnecessary complexity.
Likewise, there is no inference of ocean-tide rise from the rising of the moon, because it would follow that such an inference could be made even before or after the moonrise.
If it is argued that the inference of that [moonrise] occurs at the very time of the moon's rising, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been apprehended at that very moment;
In the margin:
If it is thus, then the connection with that very time is what constitutes the relationship between the probandum and the probans;

and in that case, that same time is the locus (*dharmin*), and the inference of the probandum occurs in relation to that very [time], since the rising of the moon is connected to it—how then can there be a lack of the property of being a characteristic of the locus (*apakṣadharmatva*)?
Now, if time is not accepted, then this inference is fallacious due to deviation;
or if it is argued that for Buddhists this inference does not exist because of the non-existence of time,
that is incorrect.

Since it is accepted that "time" is the designation for a particular great element (*mahābhūta*) which is the object of cognitions such as "forenoon" and so forth, the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) should be applied in the same way elsewhere as well.

Now, one might argue: "Granted that inference possesses validity when the property of the subject is present, nevertheless, the 'property of the subject' should not be defined as a separate characteristic, because it is already included within the statement regarding the pervasion of its [the subject's] part."
This is true;
however, it was stated for the purpose of excluding as a logical reason (hetu) that which, though pervaded by the probandum, does not reside in the subject (apakṣadharma),
such as the smoke observed in a kitchen or elsewhere when inferring fire in the ocean.
Is it not the case that a logical mark (*liṅga*) must be pervaded [by the probandum], yet the smoke found in a kitchen and such places is not pervaded by fire—the probandum—in the ocean?
True;

however, by the mere statement of the definition that "the reason is that which is pervaded," one does not obtain the result that inference of the pervading property occurs only where the pervaded property exists.
Furthermore, in order to eliminate the suspicion that [the reason] might be inferable elsewhere as well, the statement of the "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) is necessary.
For even in the case of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), there is indeed the property of being a property of the subject.

When the non-perception of one thing is precisely the capacity of another thing—such as the ground—to produce a perception, then since that capacity is the very nature of that other thing (the ground), how could non-perception not possess the property of being a property of the subject?
In this same way, properties such as "being produced" (kṛtakatva) belong to sound and so forth;

likewise, although non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) is of the nature of a property of the person [who perceives], it is in reality a product of another thing, such as the bare ground, and thus belongs to that [ground] because it is dependent upon it.

Similarly, for an effect such as smoke, its status as a property of a particular location and so forth is established by conceptual construction (vikalpa) alone, as being "this property of the subject" (pakṣadharma), even though it is in fact merely the essential nature of those related things themselves.

The state of being a reason (*hetutva*) is pervaded by invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), because that which lacks known invariable concomitance is not a reason, as it does not produce cognition. Furthermore, invariable concomitance is pervaded by both effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and essence-reason (*svabhāvahetu*);

for when there is a positive or negative probandum (*sādhya*), an effect-reason functions when another entity is affirmed, while an essence-reason and a non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) function when there is a negation. Thus, since the state of being a reason is pervaded by these three types, it is of exactly three kinds.

But it is not the case that only the threefold reason [is a prover], because even the non-perception of an effect and so forth would not be a reason if [the relationship] were unknown; furthermore, the capacity of the non-perception of the cause and the pervader to convey knowledge arises precisely from their necessary connection (*pratibandha*), as follows:
By the very same connection through which [the non-perception of] the effect and the pervaded lead to the cognition of the cause and the pervader,
by that same connection the non-perception of the cause and the pervader leads to the cognition of the absence of the effect and the pervaded.

Even in the case of the non-perception of an essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), when the self of a jar or similar object— which is capable of producing its perception— is called "perception," and when existence itself is "perception" because it is never deviant from perception provided all other causes are present, then here too, in this position, the capacity to make [the probandum] known is based solely on the connection of identity (*tādātmya*).

Furthermore, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is not included within [the categories of] effects and so forth as a logical reason (*hetu*), because it does not depend upon a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with respect to its own probandum (*sādhya*).
Moreover, the cognition of the probandum from the reason would only occur if it were dependent upon that [reason];
however, there is no such dependence when there is conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because those things which are not conjoined lack conjunction.
Even for conjoined things (*saṃyukta*), there is no dependence on conjunction, because conjoined things arise from something else entirely;
the same should be said regarding inherence (*samavāya*).

Therefore, dependence arises only through identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*); consequently, for conjoined things and the like—which fall outside the scope of the non-perception of the nature of the effect—there is no status as a cause, because in the absence of dependence, there is an absence of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).
Now, if it is dependent on that [invariable concomitance], then that alone is the cause for its being a means of cognition; thus it is established that the reason (hetu) is indeed of three kinds.

But even so, how can inference arise, given that non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) does not grasp the property (*dharma*), the locus (*dharmin*), or their relation, since it apprehends two things independently?
It is said in reply:

Even by means of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), the apprehension of the relationship between property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*) regarding smoke, location, and so forth, is nothing but the manifestation of a successive sequence;

and that [successive manifestation] exists even in non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*). The only distinction between conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions consists in the fact that the former involves verbal delineation (*ullekha*) while the latter does not. Furthermore, that non-conceptual cognition is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it produces affirmation and negation—such as "this is here" or "this is not here"—precisely with respect to the object as it was apprehended.
Therefore, the determination of the essential natures of the property and the property-bearer is produced solely by the perception that establishes their relationship;
thus it is said [in the verse] that "it is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*).

In the Sūtra, the "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) is defined as the aggregate of the property and the property-possessor; however, since the opponent does not accept that the reason (*hetu*) possesses the status of being a property of such an aggregate, every such reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*). Alternatively, if it were established for him, inference would be redundant. Thus he says:

The "subject" (pakṣa) is the locus of the property (dharmin), because the term for the whole is applied metaphorically to its part; and this application of the term for the whole to a single part is the basis for the metaphorical usage. Therefore, the subject of the example (dṛṣṭāntadharmin) is not called the "subject" (pakṣa).
Īśvarasena said:
"One should state only that 'the property-possessor (dharmin) is the reason' (hetu); because there is no purpose [for more], there is no metaphorical usage.
Thus he says.
He refutes [the objection] beginning with "purpose" and so forth by means of the words beginning with "no," [stating that] it is not the case that there is an absence of purpose.
How is it that this is expected because the figurative designation (upacāra) has the purpose of negating both the subject (dharmin) and its properties (dharma)?
For in the absence of such a figurative designation, one would have to provide the instruction "the subject and its properties."

And thus, even a property of the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) would become the reason (*hetu*). But if [the term "property"] is used figuratively (*upacāra*), then the property of every subject is precluded.
If one asks how so, he says:
The status of being a part of that [whole] and so forth is as follows: for there is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the whole to its parts;
however, this metaphorical application does not occur everywhere, as it is based specifically on the fact of being a part of that [whole].

And because the subject (*sādhyadharmin*) is a part of the thesis (*pakṣa*), it is fit for the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of "thesis" due to being a constituent member thereof; the application of this metaphor is for the sake of understanding its property.
Thus, in the comprehension of the subject fit for such metaphorical designation, there is the exclusion of [properties] such as visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*);
by the word "etc. (*ādi*), examples such as "because of the blackness of a crow" and so forth are included.

Now, if the meaning of the reason "because of being visual" (*cākṣuṣatvāt*) is "because of being an object of visual consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñānaviṣayatvāt*), then this reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and is already refuted by the statement regarding the pervasion of its own part; so what is the use of this figurative expression?

Alternatively, if the meaning of the reason is "because of being a producer of visual consciousness," even then, that capacity for production is simply existence (*sattva*), and since that exists in sound as well, this [reason] is not a property belonging only to the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmidharma*). So says someone.
In the margin. In the margin. In the margin.
That is incorrect;

for the capacity to produce visual consciousness is a specific property of existence (*sattvaviśeṣa*), and that belongs only to jars and the like, not to sound. Therefore, the employment of figurative designation (*upacāra*) is for the purpose of excluding that [capacity], but even in the absence of such a designation, that which is pervaded [by the probandum] possesses the status of a logical mark (*liṅgatva*).
Furthermore, since visibility is not pervaded by the non-eternality of sound, how can it serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*)?
This is not a fault.
For it is pervaded by impermanence alone, and since that [impermanence] exists in sound as well, how could it be a non-reason (*ahetu*)?
Regarding the phrase "by the statement of the property" (*dharmavacanena*) and so forth:

since the property (*dharma*) is pervaded by its own locus (*tadaṃśa*), even by the mere statement of the property, the property—being dependent upon the locus (*dharmiparatantra*)—necessarily implies that locus.

The "basis" (*āśraya*) is the resorting to or the grasping of that subject (*dharmin*). When that [basis] is established, it is understood from the force of the mention of the "subject" (*dharmin*) in the phrase "the property of the subject" (*dharmidharma*) that "proximity" (*pratyāsatti*) is intended here;
for if pervasion (*vyāpti*) were intended, the mention of the subject would be purposeless.
Therefore, by the force of the expression of the subject, proximity is established.
And proximity belongs to the subject (*sādhyadharmin*) itself, because the reason is presented there first;
by that proximity, the inclusion of the subject will occur, for how could the inclusion of the subject arise from proximity [to something else]?
Not only in the case of the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), but also in the case of the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), because—

when a syllogism preceded by the observation of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is employed— the existence of the reason (*hetu*) is first demonstrated even in the subject of the example due to its proximity [to the reason].
If the property-bearer of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*) is not established through proximity, then it must be established by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*);
for, by means of the pervasion of that part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*) which serves as the reason, the existence of the property in the example-bearer (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) is established.
He thinks that without an example, the pervasion of the reason by the probandum cannot be demonstrated.
Therefore, since the subject (*dharmin*) is already included by virtue of being distinguished from [other] subjects through the mention of the property (*dharma*),

and because the word "its part" (*tadaṃśena*) connects the subject— implied by the mention of the property— with that [property], one should not even suspect that the mention of the subject is for the sake of establishing that connection;
for where no other purpose is possible, that is the domain of the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*).

Thinking that there might be another purpose for the statement of the subject (*dharmī*), the proponent of the established tenet (*siddhāntavādin*) says: [the notes marked 13-1 and 13-2 belong to the base text, which was not keyboarded]. "It is stated" (*smos-pa*). "It is" (*yin-pa*). [End of notes]. Thinking that another purpose is possible, the proponent of the established tenet says:

Once it has been established that [the probans] exists in the subject of the example by way of pervading its constituent parts, the further mention of the "subject" (dharmin) might be suspected of having the restrictive purpose of implying: "only that property which belongs to the subject of the example is the logical reason.
Consequently, only properties such as visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) would be valid reasons, and not properties such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*), which would lead to an undesirable result.
Therefore, a figurative usage (*upacāra*) must be employed.
Furthermore, since it might be asked whether a statement for the sake of restriction is seen anywhere in the *Tarkaśāstra*, he says:

"Only in that which is of the same class," and so forth. In that regard, according to the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*) given by the Teacher [Dignāga]: "That which exists in the similar class (*sajātīya*), and is of two kinds [present and absent] in the absence of that [similar class], is the reason."

Although it is established by the restriction "existence [of the reason] only in the similar class" (*sajātīya eva sattvam*) that the reason is absent from the dissimilar class (*vijātīya*, i.e., the *vipakṣa*), the Master has explained the statement "its non-existence there"—meaning its non-existence when the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is absent—as being for the sake of a restriction (*niyamārtha*). He did so so that non-existence might occur only where [the *sādhya*] is absent, and not elsewhere, nor in the contradictory;
likewise here, the mention of the locus (*dharmin*) is suspected of being for the sake of a restriction regarding existence.
But surely, since that which is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) cannot be a valid reason, there can be no suspicion of it being for the sake of a restriction?

Since the probans (*hetu*) must be pervaded [by the probandum], and a property residing in one locus (*dharmī*) is not pervaded by a property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) residing in another locus, it follows that the inclusion of the subject (*sādhyadharmin*) will occur solely through the force of stating a probans whose pervasion is restricted to that portion [of the subject]. To this, he says:
"By the force," and so on.

From the force just mentioned, there arises a cognition—characterized by the inclusion of the subject—for listeners of keen intellect; however, for those who pursue an unexpressed meaning on their own, there would be a burden of comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*).

Therefore, by this mere metaphorical designation—which is itself devoid of the need to infer a meaning not explicitly stated by the word—the cumbersome nature of understanding [the definition] is avoided through the use of the term *pakṣadharma* (property of the subject) as a synonym for *dharmidharma* (property of the locus).
Furthermore, by the word *ca* (and), he says this:
"This meaning should be understood from the statement of the definition by those who require instruction from another."
Since it is understood according to its own definition, why is there this suspicion that "that which is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) is not a logical reason" (*hetu*)?
Furthermore, the employment of figurative usage (*upacāra*) is for the purpose of removing the suspicion regarding the necessity of those [reasons] that follow the definition.
In this context, because the application of words necessarily has the result of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), it must certainly be determined [as follows].

Furthermore, since the term *pakṣadharma* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), no other type of compound is possible; thus, by the restriction that it is "the property of the subject alone" (*pakṣasya eva dharmaḥ*), its pervasion by a portion of that [subject] (*tadaṃśavyāpti*) is contradicted. Pointing out this contradiction with the definition of a contradictory reason (*viruddha*), he says:
"Insofar as it is a property of the subject, the subject must function as a qualifier, which requires the exclusion [of the property] from everything else."

The non-occurrence of a property that depends on a qualification of that [subject] elsewhere— in other words, in a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) other than the subject (*pakṣa*)— is as follows: for whatever is qualified by the subject belongs to the subject alone.
Just as Devadatta’s son [is unique] because he does not persist elsewhere than in him, so too there would be uniqueness (asādhāraṇatā) and no commonality (sādhāraṇatā);
the meaning is that this would contradict the pervasion by its own part (tadaṃśavyāpti).
Because it is established that there is a pervasion by that [probandum] in a general sense, [the opponent objects]:

"If it is not a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), then there is no pervasion by its part; if there is pervasion by its part, then it is not a property of the subject. Thus, the definition is contradictory. [The author replies: Well then, if the pervasion of the probans (*sādhana*) by the probandum (*sādhya*) is not apprehended in the locus of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*), then the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). But if it is apprehended, what is the use of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the reason in the example? Furthermore, how is the pervasion by its part of the property of the subject contradicted, since pervasion is also understood in the locus of the probandum?
When the momentariness of all entities is to be proven, what positive concomitance (*anvaya*) could there be for the reason characterized by existence?

Therefore, a reason is established as being pervaded by its probandum through an essential connection (*pratibandha*); and since that [pervasion] is established even in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) by the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the opposite case, there is no need whatsoever for reliance on positive concomitance elsewhere.

How, then, can this doubt be raised—that [the reason] is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) because it does not occur elsewhere? True; although inference cannot arise with respect to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) without the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason by the probandum, nevertheless, without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probandum and the probans in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), pervasion cannot be established even for the subject of the thesis. It is for this purpose that this doubt is raised.
In the margin:

As for what was stated—that this [objection] was raised with respect to the distinction between the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) and the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*)—that was said with reference to existence (*sattva*) in the inference of momentariness, because that [existence] is a means of cognition precisely through the operation of the valid cognition that sublates the counter-example (*vipakṣabādhakapramāṇa*). We shall examine this further below.

Therefore, for the sake of recollecting the means of valid cognition that established the necessary connection previously apprehended, the occurrence of the reason elsewhere must be taken into account. [The author] refutes this with the words beginning "no," and so forth.
It is not that there is no non-occurrence elsewhere; rather, how could there be non-connection? For the subject is qualified by the exclusion of that [other], which constitutes the relation.
For a qualifier does not function solely by excluding connection with another; it also functions by excluding non-connection.
This is because where the existence of a property in a given subject is doubted, the exclusion of non-connection is logically required.
An example of this is: "Caitra is an archer."
For, regarding Caitra, there is doubt as to whether he possesses archery or not;

thus, when it is said "Caitra is an archer," this exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*)—which eliminates the alternative possibility of non-archery raised by the listener's expectation—is logically established.
Desiring to refute the exclusion [of others] as intended by opponents, he says:
The connection [of the terms] is as follows: because it does not apply elsewhere, the qualification by means of the exclusion of connection with others results in its being "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa).

Here too, there is an example: "Pārtha is the archer. Although this word "archer" is a general term, through the force of the context and so forth, it functions here to denote one of preeminent quality; for since the status of being an archer is already established in Pārtha, there is no suspicion of non-connection (ayoga).

When there is a doubt regarding the possibility of connection with another—that is, whether such a thing possessing excellence exists elsewhere or not—and one says, "Pārtha is the archer," then it is understood that Pārtha alone is the archer possessing excellence and no other;
therefore, in this case, the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is logically established.

Similarly, when there is a doubt as to whether this property exists in the subject (*pakṣa*) or not, and one says, "It is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*), it is understood that it is indeed a property of the subject and not a non-property.
And because the property (*dharma*) is dependent [on the subject], it functions as a qualifier; thus, non-connection is excluded, but connection with another is not.
Since the exclusion of connection with another is established through the pervasion of its own part, there is no doubt regarding the example.
We shall explain this and demonstrate it in the fourth chapter. 4.
