In the margin.
"In that part there is that property"— here, by the word "that" (tat), the subject (*pakṣa*) is referred to, not the property (*dharma*),
because it is impossible for a property to possess another property; thus, the "part of that subject" is the very property to be proven (*sādhya*).
If it is asked how the word *aṃśa* (part), when applied to a single portion [of a whole], can convey the property (*dharma*), he replies:

"By virtue of the speaker’s intention. The denotative power of words does not arise from the force of the objective reality itself, but rather from the speaker’s desire to speak (*vivakṣā*). Thus, the connection with the subject at hand is that "that part" is called "a portion of it" by virtue of the speaker's intention.
If it is asked, "Why is it so?
he replies: "Because the word 'pakṣa' does not denote a composite whole.

For if the word 'pakṣa' were to denote a composite whole, then a part consisting of the property (*dharma*) would be a portion of the 'pakṣa' which is essentially a composite of both the property and the property-possessor (*dharmin*).
However, by the term *pakṣa* used in a figurative sense, it is the locus (*dharmin*) itself that is denoted;
and since that [locus] is a single entity, how could there be a "part" of it?
He explains this with the words beginning, "the pervaded term is the pervasion," and so forth.

The pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that which exists as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) consists in that which pervades and that which is pervaded, based on their being cognized as the pervading and the pervaded properties respectively. When it is intended as the state of being the pervader, the connection is: "the existence of the pervader, which is the object to be known, [occurs] therein. Here, the locative case in the word *tatra* primarily signifies the sense of "in relation to" rather than primarily signifying a physical substratum (*ādhāra*), because one property cannot be a separate entity from another property.
Therefore, this is the meaning:

wherever the pervaded exists in a given subject (dharmin), there the pervader necessarily exists; thus, pervasion is the property of the pervader, but it is not determined in this way that the pervader exists *only* there.
Because it would follow that there is an absence of a logical reason (hetvabhāva),
since even non-pervasive properties such as corporeality (mūrtatva) exist therein;
nor can it be restricted by the phrase "only in that [locus]."
Otherwise, [characteristics] such as "being produced immediately after an effort" would result in being non-reasons (ahetu),
and the reason would become "common" (sādhāraṇa) because it exists only among knowable objects (prameya) while [the property of] permanence exists [only] among eternal things.

However, when the intended meaning of pervasion (vyāpti) is that the state of being the pervaded (vyāpya-dharmatā) [is defined by the pervader], then the existence of the pervaded occurs only where the pervader exists in the subject (dharmin), and not elsewhere.

In this case as well, the restriction that "only the pervaded exists there" is not adopted because it would entail the non-existence of the reason; for even that which is not pervaded may exist there,
nor is it restricted such that "only the pervaded exists there."
Because that which exists in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣaikadeśavṛtti*) would result in being a non-reason (*ahetu*),
and because the common reason (*sādhāraṇa*)— such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*)— would become a valid reason due to its necessary presence among eternal things,

the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is implied by the phrase "the presence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) therein," or the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is implied by the phrase "the presence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) only therein."

Alternatively, the description of the pervaded (vyāpya) and the pervader (vyāpaka) properties within the context of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is for the purpose of demonstrating their respective necessity and non-necessity; thus, the reason (*hetu*) is that which is pervaded, but not the pervader, because the latter is non-necessary. [Objection: But how can a property that exists without the pervaded be considered a pervader? For it would not be a pervader due to its lack of connection with the pervaded.
It is true that the relationship of pervaded and pervader between two properties is determined only in a general sense; however,

since the generality of impermanence— which has been ascertained as the pervader of the property of being produced immediately after an effort— is also observed in that which is not produced immediately after an effort, the pervader is said to be non-exclusive.

If, however, impermanence can be ascertained as having a nature that follows immediately upon effort, then these two are mutually pervaded, and thus the reason becomes truly pervaded. And this is the logical rule: where there is a dispute, that very point is the probandum (*sādhya*), and the other is the probans (*sādhana*).

If, then, the definition of a reason is merely that it is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and is pervaded by a part of it, then the reason would have only two forms—being a property of the subject and being pervaded by a part of it—whereas elsewhere it is said to have three forms; how then is there no contradiction? To this he says:
By this statement regarding the pervasion of that part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*), both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are expressed;
the sense is that pervasion consists in the nature of positive and negative concomitance. To explain:

When that which is indeed concomitant with another, and which ceases upon the cessation of that other, is said to be pervaded by it—since pervasion consists in being of that very nature—the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) are expressed by the statement of pervasion. Therefore, because the two aspects are expressed by the statement of pervasion, there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, since these two [aspects] fall under the category of the "indicative reason" (jñāpaka-hetu), they must be ascertained;
and their ascertainment does not occur through a single means of valid cognition alone, but rather through whichever specific means of valid cognition is the appropriate determiner for each.
Furthermore, its specific measure will be explained later.

Now, one might object: since the logical mark (*liṅga*) is positive in nature, how can it have "negative concomitance" (*vyatireka*), defined as its absence when the probandum is absent? To this, [the author replies]: "its nature is such."
For that very existence of the mark which constitutes the probandum is itself the negative concomitance (vyatireka) when the probandum is absent;
thus, there is identity between positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance, while their distinction is merely constructed by conceptual thought.
Others maintain that *vyatireka* (negative concomitance) is the property of the absence of the probans (*liṅga*) when the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent;
whereas *anvaya* (positive concomitance) consists in the form: "wherever there is the property of the means of proof (*sādhana*), there is the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
Therefore, as for what was stated by the venerable Kumārila Bhaṭṭa:
In the margin:
That sunrise which is yet to be is not accompanied by today’s sunrise;
nevertheless, from today’s sunrise, it is inferred that it will also occur tomorrow.
The tip of smoke is seen in the sky, yet fire is perceived on the ground;
the tip of smoke follows the fire, but it does not rest upon the ground.
Thus, it has been refuted that the mark (liṅga) follows the marked (liṅgin) by way of space and time,
and therefore no relational part called "inherence" (anvaya) is perceived in it.
And since the reason, as previously described, exists as being concomitant with the probandum, this [objection] is thereby refuted;
thus, in this case as well, the postulation of a relation of pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be rejected.
For how could that which is not followed by something else be pervaded by it?

Precisely for this reason, in order to refute such a pervasion (vyāpti) imagined by others, the Master [Dharmakīrti] demonstrated the worldly pervasion through the statement "the presence there of the pervader" (*vyāpakasya tatra bhāvaḥ*), etc., [showing] the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the relationship, which grasps the dependence of the mark (*liṅga*) upon the probandum (*sādhya*).

And that which apprehends this dependence is precisely what grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*) consisting of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), because dependence upon the probandum (*sādhya*) is itself the nature of pervasion.

Therefore, from that very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which grasps the pervasion, there arises certainty even regarding non-existence: "wherever the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is absent, there the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is absent; wherever the pervader is absent, there the pervaded is absent."
Therefore, as for that which was stated by Kumārila Bhaṭṭa— [in the margin].
In the margin.
Furthermore,
because its object is a universal, there can be no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in perception;
nor is it inferred, since no prior concomitance has been cognized.
Now, if there were an inference based on positive concomitance (anvaya) devoid of any other positive concomitance,
then since this [inference] would be established independently of it, what would be the use of positive concomitance elsewhere?
Furthermore, even negative concomitance (vyatireka) of the mark (liṅga) cannot be obtained from the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa).

In the absence [of such knowledge], that [non-occurrence] could not be understood, because it is not known even by those who have exerted effort; for as long as the limit of all opposing factors has not been determined, who is able to know from that [evidence] the non-occurrence of the reason?
That too has been refuted.

[The text written in the margin was enclosed in brackets, but there is no opening bracket here. The connection is as follows: it should be understood that "dharma" is stated as being ascertained by its respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, by the very statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is indeed expressed; therefore, there is no contradiction.
In the margin:

Therefore, that which was stated by Vidhakarṇa—namely, "We do indeed accept inference as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is recognized by the world; however, the definition of its logical mark (*liṅga*) is incorrect"—is thereby refuted.
Since the three-fold nature of the mark (*liṅga*) is well-known in the world, just as in the case of smoke and so forth,

one might ask: how is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) ascertained by its respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), given that the mark is a universal (*sāmānya*) and that universal is not apprehended by perception because the latter has only the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object?
Furthermore, that which is ungrasped cannot be a probans (*liṅga*);
nor can that which is grasped as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) be a probans, because it lacks concomitance (*anvaya*).

Nor is there a grasping of a universal (*sāmānya*) by means of inference, because its probans would itself have to be a universal, and since such a probans is not grasped by perception, its grasping by inference would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
In the margin:

"Therefore it is said: because the marks (liṅga), the objects possessing the marks (liṅgin), and the inferences (anumāna) are infinite, [there is no single means] for a single object possessing a mark."
"Even over many thousands of yugas, no such course of existence is found. (Ślokavārttika, marginal note).
Now,

it may be argued that the universal (sāmānya), which appears as a conceptual construction of the nature of the effect and so forth, is called the "reason" (hetu) for the effect and so on because it serves as the basis for the perception of the effect and because of the subsequent determination (adhyavasāya) of it;
however, this is incorrect.

Since that [exclusion] is also not distinct from conceptual construction, it—like the conceptual construction itself—does not persist in another [instance], namely, in a different conceptual construction; how then could it be a universal or a logical mark (*liṅga*)?

Therefore, it is only the nature of smoke and so forth as excluded from what is of a different class (*vijātīya-vyāvṛtta*) that is the indicator, because we are here concerned with the cause of cognition. This is ascertained by perception, and while its specific features are not determined, it is called a "logical mark characterized as a universal" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-liṅga*).
It is not, however, the exclusion from the dissimilar or the form of the conceptual construction, because these are non-entities (*avastu*).
Therefore, the meaning is as follows:

by means of a determination (*niścaya*) arising in the wake of perception—which determines the form of smoke as excluded from non-smoke—and by means of not determining specific differences such as whether this appearing particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of smoke is made of grass, made of leaves, or something else, the inferential mark (*liṅga*), which is a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) consisting of multiple particular characteristics, is established within the domain of perception.
And just as the inferential mark possesses a universal nature due to the non-determination of its specific differences, so too does the probandum (*sādhya*).
Thus it is said:

"Because it establishes merely the thing as excluded from what is not that [thing], the logical mark (liṅga) is declared to have the universal (sāmānya) as its object, since it does not rest upon particulars (bheda)."

And for such a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) which serves as a logical mark (*liṅga*), its being an effect of the probandum (*sādhyakāryatva*) and its being of the same nature as the probandum (*sādhyasvabhāvatva*) are not contradictory because it is a real entity (*vastu*); furthermore, since that logical mark is ascertained by perception and other means of knowledge, everything is well-established.
With the words "ta ete" and so forth, he explains the phrase "it is indeed threefold."

"These very [reasons]," being endowed with the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and with the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*), are "those whose characteristic nature" (*lakṣaṇa-svabhāva*) consists of effect, essential nature, and non-perception; thus they are so described.
"From smoke" is the statement of the reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*).

In the formulation "there is fire here," the probandum (sādhya) is the result; however, this is not a formal application of the thesis (pakṣaprayoga). Now, one might object: "Is not that location which is connected with fire beyond direct perception (pratyakṣa)?"

Furthermore, that which is perceptible as a portion of space, consisting of light and so forth, and appearing as possessing smoke, does not possess fire; therefore, how could the existence of smoke be established through perception in that location? Consequently, Uddyotakara maintains that smoke alone is the proper subject (*dharmin*), and the relationship between the probandum and the probans is such that "this smoke possesses fire because it is smoke.
However, even for him, a portion of the smoke that possesses fire is not perceptible.

Furthermore, since the visible portion situated above [the fire] occurs simultaneously with the fire, how can there be a perceptual ascertainment of the universal "smoke" (dhūmasāmānya) in the subject of the inference?
If it is argued that the composite whole (avayavin) consisting of smoke is perceived, we say no.

Since it does not exist apart from its constituent parts, there is a worldly determination [of it as a whole]; or, if it were a single entity, one could not prevent even a spatial region from being conceptually regarded as having a unitary nature. Furthermore, it is the spatial region itself that people perceive as fire, and not the smoke which serves as the locus (*dharmin*).
Therefore, if the inference of fire is intended by that [statement], let the inference be of the fire in the very locus (pradeśa) which is the subject (dharmin); this is the purport of the passage.
(Cf.
Nyāyavārttika 1:1:5).
However, some maintain that the previously mentioned refutation of the fault does not apply here;

for either the observed location is the subject (*dharmin*) and "possessing fire below" is the probandum property (*sādhyadharma*), rather than "fire alone," and by means of such a probandum property, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has already been established.
Furthermore, since smoke is established here through direct perception, how could it not be a basis for inference?

As for the claim that the probative power of an effect-reason depends on considerations of place and so forth, that is entirely inconsistent, because the qualifying attributes such as "place" and so on are themselves unestablished.
Furthermore, because this probandum is established merely by the sight of smoke;

or rather, this should be viewed as an illustration when, having seen fire in a particular location, one dispels a doubt regarding its specific nature— such as whether it is *kiṃśuka* wood or something else— by means of seeing smoke.
For at that time, both the subject (*dharmī*) and the probans (*sādhanadharma*) are established by perception;
as for what is said—
that inference occurs only when the subject consists of both perceptible and imperceptible aspects— [that is not the case].
That is incorrect;

for although the reason (*hetu*) is established with respect to the perceptible portion, there can nevertheless be no inference of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) therein, because it is sublated by perception (*pratyakṣabādhitatvāt*).
As for the imperceptible portion, there might indeed be an inference, but in that case, the reason itself is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, a property of a subject (*dharmin*) that possesses both perceptible and imperceptible aspects cannot be established by perception alone, because perception does not operate upon the imperceptible portion. Or, when there is an inference of impermanence regarding sound—which is grasped by hearing—how could the subject possess both perceptible and imperceptible forms? This [objection] is trivial. As for the example of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), "because it is a *śiṃśapā*": [The opponent objects: "In that case, since the *śiṃśapā* is not perceived as distinct from the tree, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) would not be established. For it is impossible to state the pervasion as 'whatever is a *śiṃśapā* is a tree,' because the *śiṃśapā* is not perceived apart from the tree. Nor can one say 'whatever is a tree is a *śiṃśapā*,' because trees such as the *palāśa* are perceived as distinct from the *śiṃśapā*. Therefore, since the pervasion is not established, how can this be an essential reason? [The author replies: This is not so. It is indeed possible to state the pervasion as "whatever is a *śiṃśapā* is a tree. Even if the *śiṃśapā* is not perceived apart from the tree, its existence is nonetheless established through the cognition of the tree itself; thus, the pervasion is established. Furthermore, the cognition of the tree is not necessarily dependent on the cognition of the *śiṃśapā*, whereas the cognition of the *śiṃśapā* is necessarily dependent on the cognition of the tree. Therefore, the pervasion is established. Moreover, even if the *śiṃśapā* is not perceived apart from the tree, the pervasion is established by means of the cognition of the tree, which is the substratum (*dharmin*) of the *śiṃśapā*. Consequently, the objection that the pervasion is not established is baseless. Thus, the example of the essential reason is valid.

Thus, in this case, the capacity of the essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) to serve as a means of proof is utterly discarded, because the relationship between the signified and the signifier is based upon a distinction (*bheda*).
For there is no such thing as a necessary connection between non-different things; a *śiṃśapā* tree is not identical with the nature of "tree," because it would otherwise be excluded from it.
For that which is excluded from something else is not of the nature of that thing,
just as a cloth is not of the nature of a jar;
and since the *śiṃśapā* tree is excluded from *khadira* trees and the like, it is not of their nature.

Furthermore, if there were identity (*tadātmatva*), then at the very moment the logical mark (*liṅga*) is perceived, because there is no distinction [between them], the probandum (*sādhya*) would be as unperceived as the mark itself; yet since the nature of the probandum would already have been grasped, its status as an object of inference (*anumeya*) would be lost. Moreover, if *śiṃśapā*-ness functions as a signifier (*gamaka*) by virtue of identity, then—since identity is equally present in both—it would follow that "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*) is also a signifier with respect to *śiṃśapā*-ness. If it is argued that tree-ness is not a signifier because it is not invariably concomitant (*aniyata*), then necessary concomitance (*niyatatā*) alone must be the cause of being a signifier, and not identity; for identity is observed even in the case of "tree-ness," which is deviant (*vyabhicārin*).
Now, [if one argues that] the *śiṃśapā* does not exist in the tree by virtue of its own self...

...then they would be identical in every respect; by that [identity], there could be the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*), whereas in the case of difference, there is an absence of identity.
Thus, the relationship of the signified and the signifier between the exclusions (*apoha*) of "non-śiṃśapā" and "non-tree," or between the cognitions (*buddhi*) of those exclusions, must be rejected.
In the margin. In the margin. In the margin.
That is incorrect;
for the *śiṃśapā* has the nature of being a particular kind of tree, and that particular kind of tree also has the very nature of the *śiṃśapā*; thus, identity (*tādātmya*) pertains to both.

Furthermore, even though there is identity (*tādātmya*), someone might be somewhat confused regarding the nature that is excluded from non-trees, [failing to see] how it is also excluded from non-śiṃśapās;
therefore, because the sign (*liṅga*) such as the śiṃśapā is apprehended, there is no loss of its status as an object of inference (*anumeya*).
And this is because the śiṃśapā does not have the nature of being merely a tree.
Therefore, it is not the case that "treeness" (vṛkṣatva) possesses the quality of being an indicator (*gamaka*) with respect to "śiṃśapā-ness"; furthermore,
the author of the treatise himself will refute the fault of the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*), the probans (*sādhana*), and so forth— thus, this [objection] is trivial.
The term "location" (*pradeśa*) is a statement of non-perception;
"in a specific location" refers to a particular place that has been indicated as "somewhere" and is well-known to both the proponent and the opponent.

The conventional usage of the absence of a jar, expressed as "there is no jar," is what is to be proven; the statement beginning with "because of perception" is the indication of the reason; and the "characteristics of perception" refers to the instruments of perception, such as the eyes, whose capacities are unimpeded and which thus constitute the characteristics of perception.

The meaning is this: that object which, having been reached, possesses a specific nature capable of generating a cognition appearing as itself, and is thus included within the causal complex for the production of its own cognition—
due to the non-apprehension of such an object, the conventional designation of its non-existence is established.
In the margin:

But how can that which does not exist in a certain place be characterized by the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) there? For being characterized by the conditions for perception means being an object of cognition; and if that is the case, how can there be non-existence?
It is said:

when a certain collection of conditions is present, if a thing that was previously established were to exist under that very same collection of conditions, it would be perceived just as it was in the previous time. Thus, having mentally reflected upon the fact that the thing has attained the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāptatva*), a negation is made on the grounds that it does not appear;
however, this does not apply to that which is imperceptible.
Because there is no means for the conceptual determination of appearances,
[the object] is never apprehended.
(Marginal note)
If it is asked, "In the absence of the object of perception, how is that very causal complex (sāmagrī) apprehended?",
we reply: "Because of the apprehension of one [of two] entities that are objects of a single cognition."
And it is determined that what is being negated by its very nature possesses the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*).
To demonstrate that this very thing constitutes the possession of the conditions for perception by virtue of its fitness for producing a single cognition, he says: [in the margin].

If an object such as a jar were to possess existence as something perceivable, it would necessarily be of that very nature and not otherwise; thus, being of such a nature, it would never be ungraspable, meaning it would invariably not deviate from cognition.
For this reason, by that cause...

Regarding the qualification "of that which has reached the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasya*) which was stated, it follows by implication that it means "of an existent that has reached the conditions for perception.
Here, however, the external object is [meant];
"condition" (*lakṣaṇa*) is so called because it is characterized (*lakṣyate*) by this.

The meaning is as follows: "attainment of the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*) refers to that which has reached the characteristic of being perceived; that is to say, it is that which possesses an invariable connection with cognition.
A "being" (*sattva*) characterized by such [perceptibility] is what is so described.
The underlying idea is that when a being is of such a nature, its cognition necessarily ceases upon the cessation [of the object].
Since all proof is pervaded by affirmation and negation,

and the probandum being affirmed is divided by the two types of logical connection, [the author] says "In that regard," etc., demonstrating that affirmation and negation depend upon the three types of reasons.

In that regard, among the three types of reasons, it is restricted that two— the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) and the reason of effect (*kāryahetu*)— are the two alone that establish a real entity (*vastusādhana*) and establish an affirmation (*vidhisādhana*); however, it is not restricted that they are "only" those that establish a real entity,
because by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is also established through these two.
"One [is] the probans for negation" means that non-apprehension, as defined above, is indeed a probans for negation; however,
it is not restricted to being the *only* one, because exclusion is understood through the two preceding [probans] as well.
Someone says:

"Exclusion (vyavaccheda) is established by means of words and logical marks; whatever exclusion there may be, all of it arises solely from non-apprehension (anupalambha). Therefore, non-apprehension alone is the single probans.
This is incorrect.

Since this is not stated with reference to the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the operation of the means of valid cognition pertains precisely to the real entity (*vastu*); therefore, it is said:
"For that very reason, the validity of both [perception and inference] has the real entity as its object."

Nor is this stated on the basis of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), because the object itself is what is determined; furthermore, there is no connection between the logical mark (*liṅga*) and exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).
As for the one who thinks that in non-perception (*anupalambha*), what is being proven is the fitness for the conventional usage of "non-existent," and not a negation (*pratiṣedha*):
Furthermore, fitness (*yogyatā*) is indeed of the very nature (*svabhāva*) [of the thing].

Thus, when a location possessing fire is to be proven, the fact that the location possesses fire is itself the property to be proven (*sādhya*), and since the reason (*hetu*)— namely, "because it possesses smoke"—
is non-different from the location, every reason is exclusively a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*).
That is incorrect;
for if it were so, even donkey-ness and the like would be indicative [of fire].
If you argue that this does not happen because the donkey lacks the property of being an effect of fire, [we reply:]...
If this is so, since the fact that smoke is an effect of fire is the very basis for its being a signifier, why is it not an "effect-reason" (*kāryahetu*)?
Another, however, thinks: "Non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), moreover, is the effect of a location; thus, when the non-existent conventional usage is to be proven, it is indeed an effect-reason.
Furthermore, the conceptualization of 'being produced' is the effect of the word 'impermanent'; therefore, every reason is an effect-reason."

That too is incorrect; for if the conceptualization of "produced" were to indicate that very thing because it is the cause of being produced, one might as well argue that it establishes impermanence—on the grounds that the produced is of the nature of the impermanent. If you say this, [we reply: no.

If this were so, the cognition of impermanence would arise from the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) alone, and not from the conceptualization of "being produced," because [the reason] indicates impermanence precisely by way of its nature as something produced;
otherwise, there would be an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) argument, such that something could be a conceptualization of "being produced" and yet not be impermanent.

The capacity to produce a conceptual construction of something produced is not distinct from that which is produced; therefore, it does not exist prior to or subsequent to it. Consequently, since this [capacity] is impermanent, and since the capacity is non-distinct [from the thing itself], it establishes the impermanence [of the thing]. Thus, how could this not be a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*)? This objection is trivial. Furthermore, why are there only two means of establishing a real entity? He says:
"The proof is the connection by way of essential nature" (*svabhāvena pratibandhaḥ sādhanam kṛteḥ*); such is the compound.

Being bound by its own nature means, in other words, having a nature that is necessarily connected; when that [nature] exists, the object— the mark (*liṅga*)— does not deviate from the object— the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*).
And from what does that essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) arise? He says:
"Because of being of that nature" (*tadātmatvāt*), meaning because [the probans] has the nature of the probandum;
that is, when the probans has the nature of the probandum, it possesses the nature of the probandum's essence.

Thinking that there might be the objection that "the probandum itself is the probans," and thus there is no distinction between the probandum and the probans— such that the reason would be a part of the meaning of the proposition itself—
he says "no" and so forth;
for the various properties constituting the probandum and the probans are conceptually constructed through the differentiation of their exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) by way of superimposition (*āropa*).
In the margin:
this is what is meant; a distinction between properties is superimposed, and by that, a distinction between the probandum and the probans [is established].
Since that which is ascertained is called the "indicator" (*gamaka*) and that which is to be ascertained is called the "indicated" (*gamya*),
and since the object of ascertainment is indeed merely superimposed, the distinction between properties (*dharmabheda*) is superimposed upon the distinction of ascertainment;
and this we shall explain in the section on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
In the margin:
Ācārya Dignāga also stated this; thus he says [the following], *Pramāṇavārttika* 3:163–73.

And so it is with the phrase "all [this]" and so forth: even in cases where there is a real distinction between the probandum and the probans, such as fire and smoke, because conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is not possible through the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is inference—namely, that by which one infers (*anumīyate*). This consists of the inferential mark (*liṅga*), the object of inference (*anumeya*), which is the subject of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*), and the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Their conventional usage takes the form of diversity;

that is to say, the distinction between the property and the subject is established by means of a distinct form that has ascended into the intellect (*buddhi*), appearing within the manifestation of the intellect. This is what is meant by the conventional usage of distinction.
If, then, the convention of property and property-bearer is merely imagined by the intellect, then it follows that the establishment of the probandum is achieved from an imagined reason;
consequently, every fault that is attributed to a reason would apply here. Thus says Bhaṭṭa:
In the margin:
*Ślokavārttika*, *Nirālamba* 171–72:
"Or alternatively, even if difference exists, it is conceptually constructed by the intellect."
The properties of the probandum and the probans, and so forth, are postulated for the sake of conventional discourse;
therefore, regarding this means of proof employed by you, as long as it is stated,
the fault would arise that a cognition is produced in every instance.
In the margin:
here he says,
"Difference," and so forth.

It is precisely this [conceptual] meaning that causes the object to be understood; however, the distinction—the diversity consisting of "this is a property" (dharma) and "this is a substratum" (dharmin)—is created by the form of the intellect and is merely imagined by the intellect. It is neither the object nor the logical mark (liṅga), for both are produced by the form of the intellect.
To the question, "Why does the comprehension of the object not arise from a logical mark that is itself constructed by conceptualization?
he says, beginning with the words "vikalpa... (conceptualization...).

The meaning is as follows: because conceptual distinctions—that is, specific types of conceptualization—are independent insofar as they follow merely one’s own will, they do not have objects as their basis; since they are not connected to actual objects, they do not arise directly from them, and thus they do not have objects as their objective support (*ālambana*). Therefore, if it is admitted that there is a cognition of an object based on those conceptualizations—which are themselves imagined by those [conceptualizations] that lack an object as their basis—then there would be only the attainment of what is not an object, and never the attainment of an actual object.
In the margin:
he states the second definition of the relation of invariable concomitance (*pratibandha-lakṣaṇa*) with the words "of the effect as well," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of that nature" (*tatsvabhāvasya*), it refers to the nature of the effect (*kāryasvabhāva*). Because it arises from that [cause]—that is, because it arises from the cause—one addresses those who do not accept the validity of inference (*anumāna*) by stating:
"These two cognitions of the inferable are valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*); this is the connection.
"These two" (*etāv*) refers to the two logical marks (*liṅga*), namely essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*).

Since non-apprehension is included within the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), he says "two"; or rather, he says "two" with reference to what was previously introduced—the two cognitions of the inferable objects, namely essential nature and cause. Regarding the phrase "even though it does not manifest that," it means even though it does not manifest the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the inferable object.
If one asks, "Since [the object] does not appear [in the cognition] and since there is no direct production [of the cognition from the object],
how then can there be non-deviation? he says,

"Because of being produced from that," meaning because of being produced through a lineage of succession from the two inferable things, namely the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the cause (*kāraṇa*).
"Those two are non-deviating" means they are non-deviating with respect to the object of inference;
thus, the reason is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) just like perception.

Therefore, the argument stated by Vidhakarṇa—that "a valid means of knowledge is the determination of an object not yet apprehended, and consequently inference is not a valid means of knowledge because it lacks the capacity to determine an object"—is refuted.

Since every discerning person desiring action seeks a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) precisely because it reveals an object that serves as the goal of that action— and since the object that is the goal of action must be capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samartha*), and it has already been stated that perception does not determine the capacity for future causal efficiency in an entity— how, then, can this [perception] possess validity merely through the determination of the object?

Therefore, with respect to its own object, perception is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it induces activity by producing a certainty—such as "this is that very same thing"—regarding what was previously apprehended through a continuous series as being capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*). Likewise, inference is also [a means of valid cognition].
By the words "of perception as well" and so forth, he states the pervasion (*vyāpti*), namely:
"only in the non-deviation from the object."

When an object previously determined to be capable of performing a desired function is actually present, it is only in that case that perception possesses validity; otherwise, in the absence of that [function], there being an absence of the object, the perception that arises would be deceptive because it does not correspond to the determined object.
What is meant is this:
when perception does not discern an entity capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samartha*).
And if even such a thing were to deviate [from its cause], then there would be no valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) at all.

Furthermore, what else could non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of one thing from another be, if not arising from that (*tadutpatti*)? That non-deviation of one thing which exists as a distinct entity from another, in relation to that other—what else could it be than arising from that?
It means that arising from that itself is non-deviation.
Why?
Because for things whose forms are not dependent and whose natures are not connected, there is no necessity of coexistence, and consequently no necessity of non-deviation.

Therefore, since perception arises from an object that is ascertained by its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), its non-deviation consists precisely in this arising; and since this [capacity] also exists in inference, the two are equal—this is the intended meaning.

By this, the following [objection] is also refuted: that because a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-figurative (*agauṇatva*), the ascertainment of an object through inference is difficult to obtain.
If "non-figurative" is said to mean being non-metaphorical (*anupacarita*), then inference is likewise non-metaphorical, since its nature consists in an unerring cognition.

Alternatively, if it is argued that when the composite of the property (*dharma*) and the locus (*dharmin*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), it is impossible for the reason (*hetu*) to possess the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) or positive concomitance (*anvaya*); therefore, in order to establish the property-of-the-subject, the locus must be treated as the probandum in a figurative sense, and in order to establish positive concomitance, the property must be so treated—thus, because its object is figurative, inference is itself figurative.

That is incorrect because, in the world, when mere smoke is seen in a subject (*dharmin*) as being pervaded by mere fire, it is precisely there that the cognition of fire arises; thus, what here is metaphorical? In this way, the status of the whole (*samudāya*) as the probandum (*sādhya*) is established, as it has been said: "When the property alone is to be proved in the subject, the establishment of the intended whole is thereby accomplished."
Nor is it the case that when the term "probandum" (sādhya) is used metaphorically regarding the object of inference, inference itself becomes metaphorical. Furthermore,

if it is argued that because a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-figurative and non-erroneous, whereas inference is erroneous, inference lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge— that is incorrect.

Even though the inference of fire is erroneous, it is observed in the world to possess validity because it arises from that [perception] and results in the determination of external fire, just like perception. Now, if even perception were not accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there would be a contradiction with worldly consensus,
since both perception and inference are recognized as valid means of knowledge by the world.
Now, if it is not the case that the validity of perception and inference is being denied,

but rather that the logical mark (*liṅga*)— whether characterized by three features or four— is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then in response to such an inquiry, if inference is stated as the proof,
the same inquiry applies there as well; thus, in every instance, the sūtras are merely devoted to such inquiries.

And thus the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* states: "In the case of a specific [property], there is a lack of a corresponding [reason]; in the case of a general [property], it is a proof of what is already established."
That too is incorrect,
because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the three features (*trairūpya*) has already been implied by the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*);
furthermore, one cannot be challenged by another by means of what is not a valid cognition, since such a thing would be unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent.
In the margin:

Now, [the opponent claims] that inference consisting of speech is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the speaker; yet, if one conveys [the meaning] to another by means of speech, then an interrogation is conducted by means of what is not a *pramāṇa*.
This too is untenable.

For from the speech of both [the speaker and the listener], the cognition of the object arises as something possessing the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it delimits the object. However, since the speaker’s own realization has already been accomplished, it is not a valid cognition for him; yet, if it were invalid for him, it would be invalid for both. How, then, could there be a cognition of the object from that?

As for what is also said:
The claim that an inference is refuted by means of an inference established for the opponent is also refuted by this very [argument]:
if [fire] were to indicate [its presence] by virtue of conjunction,
then fire would not be conjoined with any of its constituent parts.
Or rather, smoke would in every respect lead to the manifestation [of fire] by means of itself;

thus, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the relationship of signifier and signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*) would exist in all respects—a point raised by the Master Dignāga against his opponent—is here also suspected regarding the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), beginning with the words "If... and so forth. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Because it arises from the probandum (*sādhya*), the effect is the signifier of the cause. Consequently, the relationship of signifier and signified would obtain in every respect;
even the specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*) such as being produced from grass or wood, which are like the general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) of fire, would become signified.
Just as specific properties [of smoke] are indicators, so too would general properties such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and earthiness (*pārthivatva*) be indicators for fire;
why?
Because there is a relationship of produced and producer in every respect.

For instance, just as fire is a producer by means of general properties such as being fire (*agnitva*), being a substance (*dravyatva*), and existence (*sattva*), so too is it [a producer] by means of specific properties such as being produced from grass (*tārṇṇa*) or wood (*pārṇṇa*). And just as smoke is produced as something endowed with its own restricted specific properties such as being smoke (*dhūmatva*) and being white (*pāṇḍutva*), so too is it [produced] by means of general properties such as existence and being a substance. Consequently, just as there is a relationship of cause and effect between these two, there would likewise be a relationship of the signifier and the signified; therefore, he says:
[in the margin].
In the margin:
"No," and so forth;
there is not a relationship of produced and producer in every respect, and therefore, how could there be a relationship of the signified and the signifier?

If it is asked why, it is because in the absence of that— namely, in the absence of those specific properties such as being produced from wet fuel (*tārṇa*) or dry fuel (*pārṇa*)— there would be no such rule of origination for mere smoke (*dhūmamātra*) characterized by the thought, "it arises from those very specific properties. Likewise, in the absence of that— namely, in the absence of fire— there would be no such rule of origination for general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), characterized by the thought, "this [substantiality] arises from fire alone."
Why [is this so]? Because the relationship of producer and produced would exist in every respect, whereby the relationship of signifier and signified would also exist in every respect.

Therefore, for this reason, the effect—such as smoke—is characterized by its own inherent properties, such as "smokeness" and so forth; the third case ending (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇā*) is used here in the sense of characterization.
That which is invariably concomitant does not exist without [the other]; where is that which is invariably concomitant?
In the phrase "kāraṇe," it refers either to the cause itself as the object, or else "kāraṇe" is the locative case denoting location (adhikaraṇa-saptamī).

The meaning is that the effect is the indicator (*gamaka*) of those general properties residing in the cause— such as "fire-ness," "substance-ness," and so forth— which are invariably concomitant with as many essential natures as exist within the cause.
What is the reason for this?
Because of the rule of being its effect— that is,
because of the existence of a rule in the form "only those general properties residing in the causes produce that effect"—
the effect never deviates from those general properties at any time.
Thus far, it has been explained that the general properties residing in the cause are to be understood.
Showing that the specific properties residing in the effect are the indicators [of the cause],
he says "by those very [properties]" and so forth;
the effect, too, is an indicator of the properties residing in the cause by means of those very properties residing within itself.
Specific forms such as "smokiness" and "pale-whiteness," which cannot exist elsewhere, do not occur without those general properties residing in the cause;
for here too, it is required that there be a necessary rule of being an effect [of them],
because there is a necessary rule of being an effect for those very specific properties residing in the effect with respect to the general properties residing in the cause.

If the relationship of the signifier and the signified exists because there is an inseparable connection (avinābhāva) only between general properties residing in the cause and specific properties residing in the effect, then there would be a partial relationship of produced and producer;
that is, only the general properties of fire would be the producers,
and only the specific properties of smoke would be the produced.
In every respect, the relationship of producer and produced is intended [to be established], which contradicts your own admission; he resolves this by stating:
"There is no consequence of a producer-produced relationship occurring through parts."

Since a real entity is partless, it must be admitted that it is in every respect both produced and productive; and since the relationship of the signified and the signifier is likewise accepted in its entirety, he says this:
Regarding the phrase "produced by that" (*tajjanya*) and so forth:

for if the specific quality (*viśeṣa*) produced in the effect by those specific properties residing in the causes can be apprehended— since this discussion concerns inferential reasons as indicators (*jñāpaka-hetu*)—
then, because the apprehension of the specific quality produced by them is intended, the specific properties residing in the causes possess the status of being the objects of inference (*gamya*).
For instance, when there is the perception of the smoke of *aguru*, there certainly occurs an inference of that fire;

likewise, a "particularized mark" (*liṅgaviśeṣa*) means that the particularity (*viśeṣa*)—namely, the specific characteristic of smoke—is the "limiting condition" (*upādhi*) or qualifier for those [universals] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth. Since it is accepted that the capacity to indicate [the probandum] resides in the perception of these [particularized universals], substances and the like, as qualified by smoke, do not deviate from fire.
Is it not the case that smoke alone is the indicator there, and not its qualifiers such as substantiality and so forth—
just as in the argument "because of being knowable while being produced," it is being produced alone that is the indicator, not being knowable?
This is true.
Some maintain that this formulation is intended merely to demonstrate non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*).
However, another says:

it is not because smoke deviates [from fire] that the universal (*sāmānya*) is mentioned here; rather, for all cognizers, there is first a cognition of the object in its universal form when it is perceived, and only subsequently does the determination of its specific features (*viśeṣa*) occur.
And in that case, the universal which has been apprehended is not at all abandoned;

therefore, by virtue of the cognizer's conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), it is the universal as qualified by the particular that becomes the probans, and not the particular, because of its variability.
This is logical.
If this rule holds— that the cognition of a particular must be preceded by the cognition of a universal—
then how is it that there is a cognition of mere smoke devoid of [universals] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*)?
Furthermore, the objection previously stated remains exactly as it was.

Therefore, it is well said here that because a specific property of the mark (*liṅga*) is taken only as a qualifier of the general [property], it lacks the status of being a reason (*ahetutva*); for if it were taken as a reason, it would indeed possess the status of a reason, and not otherwise. When, then, do the general properties residing in the mark fail to be indicative? To this he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "aviśiṣṭa" (undifferentiated):
when substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and so forth are intended as undifferentiated, their status as indicators (*gamaka*) is not accepted because they are deviant (*vyabhicāra*).
This is stated with reference to the essential nature as a logical reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
The phrase "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) and so forth continues as "the reason" (*hetu*); therefore, [it means] "the reason for those.

Thus, when intrinsic nature is the probandum (*sādhya*), of what kind is it? It is that which follows from the mere existence [of the subject]; that is, it follows from the mere presence of the reason. In this case, the entity (*bhāva*) is the reason; the intrinsic nature is the reason.
The inclusion of the word "only" (*mātra*) is intended to demonstrate that [the nature of the reason] does not depend on any other factor;
for why is it said that the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the reason conforms to that alone?
He says: "For the identity (*tādātmya*) of the object conforms to that alone."
That which is the essence of the object to be established (the probandum) exists only as that [essence];
it does not depend on anything else, nor is it contingent upon other causes, and it possesses identity (tādātmya) with that which arises subsequently.
If one asks why, he says:
"Because of its existence," and so forth;
because there is no necessity regarding the subsequent existence of that property which, having been non-existent in the future, depends upon other causes.
For it is not necessarily the case that something which occurs later and is dependent on other causes must come to be;
why?
Because causes can deviate from their effects.
Since there is the possibility of obstacles to causes, how can the effect be necessarily produced from them?

But surely, the identity of the probans with the probandum is not accepted by anyone; so how can it be said that "identity consists in following the mere existence of that [probandum]"? The intention is as follows: even by those who accept the two properties called "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) as distinct, it must necessarily be admitted that [the object] comes into being after having not existed and ceases to exist after having existed; otherwise, producedness and impermanence would not belong to cloth and the like, just as they do not belong to the self (*ātman*) and other such things.

Therefore, let that very coming-into-being of an entity which did not previously exist be its "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*), and let that very non-persistence which is the ceasing-to-be after having existed be its "impermanence" (*anityatva*); what is the use of postulating another universal (*sāmānya*)?
Thus he says: "because it is unperceived...
(in the margin).
Regarding the passage beginning with "non-occurrence" (*apravṛtti*), for what is there non-occurrence? It is for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The plural number is used because there is a multiplicity of means of valid cognition due to the distinction between individual instances.
Dependent upon scripture...
[in the margin]
The twelfth leaf is missing.
It is said that "it is accomplished";
thus it is considered.
There is no sublation of the knowledge and the object of knowledge because they are distinguished by their nature as consciousness;
thus, the means of valid cognition, such as perception, which are of the nature of consciousness, are established intrinsically (*svataḥ*),
whereas objects of knowledge such as pots, being insentient in nature, depend upon a means of valid cognition.

Since there is no distinction between the absence of knowledge and the absence of the object of knowledge due to both being formless (*nīrūpa*), how can it be said that the absence of knowledge is established by itself, while the absence of the object of knowledge is established through the absence of knowledge?
Furthermore, the absence of knowledge is not established by another [cognition],
because cognitions, having the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedita*), lack the property of being associated with a single [simultaneous] cognition.

If it is claimed that knowledge would be perceived were it to exist solely within one's own continuum, yet because it is not perceived, its non-existence is established by itself as being simply non-existent—and thus the absence of knowledge is proven—then in that case, the absence of existence (sattā) would likewise be proven.

For in that instance too, if existence were present, it would be perceived; since it is not perceived, it is determined that it does not exist. Consequently, non-perception would be redundant for establishing non-existence.
In order to refute the position that consciousness itself is the other object, he says "atha" and so forth:

"The establishment of the non-apprehension of a jar through the apprehension of the ground as distinct from the jar and so forth is non-apprehension established by direct perception (*pratyakṣasiddhānupalabdhi*)."
This is what is meant:

because the state of being a grasper of a jar and the state of being a grasper of the ground are conjoined within a single cognition, when that cognition occurs as a grasper of the ground alone, it determines the absence of the state of being a grasper of a jar; thus, the non-apprehension of the jar is established by the very perception of the cognition itself.
In that same way, why is non-existence not established by the existence of another?
[The answer is] "in that same way," just like non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*);
for both the jar and the location are associated with a single cognition—this is the intended meaning.
If the existence of something else, such as the ground as distinct from the jar, is established by its presence, why is the existence of the object to be negated not also established?
[Objection: But surely non-existence is of the nature of the cessation of an entity; how then can it be said to be established by perception?
[Reply: It is thought thus.

That which is called "non-existence" does not exist at all; rather, it is simply that the perception of an existing object causes the fool to engage in the conventional usage of another's non-existence.
Therefore, what was stated—that non-existence is cognized through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—is incorrect.

For, first of all, the mutual non-existence of things such as jars and so forth is not identical [to those things], because if it were, it would follow that when a jar is destroyed, a cloth or some other object would arise.
Since the absence of cloth and so forth has perished,
if the absence were distinct [from the entity], then there would be no mutual difference between jars and the like;
for when the cloth, which is of the nature of the absence of a jar, does not exist, then the cloth would be the jar itself.

Or, just as a jar possesses the nature of a jar because it is distinct from the absence of a cloth, so too would a cloth and other such things possess that nature simply because they are distinct from the absence of a jar;
furthermore, in the case of these [entities] which are not mutually distinct, no differentiation can be established in their absence.
Since it is incapable of effecting either the differentiation or the non-differentiation of that [entity], mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is not possible among things that are non-different;
nor is difference produced by the non-existence of mutually distinct things, because those things arise as distinct from their own respective causes.
Nor is a conventional usage of difference established [by inference],
because the very arising of entities in their respective individual forms is difference per se,
and that, by virtue of appearing directly in perception, is the cause for the conventional usage of difference.
Therefore, that which was asserted— that the establishment of the non-confusion of entities depends upon the means of valid cognition consisting in non-existence— is refuted. Furthermore,
the distinction between existence and non-existence is not based on non-existence, for that would lead to an infinite regress.
Now, if difference exists by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), then that would also apply to absences (*abhāva*); so what is the point of postulating an absence?
Nor does the non-existence of prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) entail the consequence of the effect being beginningless, because [the effect] does not arise due to the absence of its cause.

Now, if prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) exists, there would be production from a cause; but if prior non-existence does not exist, there can be no production because [the effect] would already be present.
If this were so, the effect would never be produced, because its contradictory, prior non-existence, would be ever-present.

Nor can it be argued that the effect is produced upon the destruction of that [non-existence], for that would entail the absurd consequence of admitting the production of an effect even in the absence of prior non-existence.
Nor is the very arising of the effect the destruction of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), because that [arising] is impossible due to the presence of its opposite;
for prior non-existence is not destroyed at the time the cause exists,
whereas it is destroyed at the time the effect arises, just like the destruction of the cause.
Therefore, prior to its production, the effect possesses neither existence nor non-existence, because a thing lacks the property of [inherent] existence and because a real entity is partless;
rather, when it is produced, it is conventionally designated as "existent," and at other times, it is said that it "does not exist."
Therefore, it is said that "the non-existent arises"; furthermore, the Master himself will later state that the nature of destruction is non-existence.
And whatever arises from something is called the effect of that thing, and [that thing] is called its cause.

Furthermore, because they arise as persisting for only a single moment, their perishability is established; and because they arise in their own respective natures, their mutual distinctness is also established.
Consequently, even in the absence of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the rest, conventional usage regarding causes and so forth certainly occurs.
Moreover, no mutual distinction between antecedent non-existence and the others ever appears [as a separate entity].
Because, in the case of a jar or the like, only its cessation— whether prior, posterior, or elsewhere— is perceived as undifferentiated;
even if a difference in time is indeed cognized,
the universal "cowness" does not become manifold simply because it is perceived as related to multiple times and so forth.
Furthermore, since cessation is formless, how can there be multiplicity in non-existence? For non-existence consists simply in the cessation of existence.

Therefore, this statement—"the effect is non-existent before, after, and elsewhere"—is made merely to negate the superimposition of existence upon one who is deluded enough to desire the existence of an effect prior to its production, after its destruction, or in another location. It is a mere negation of the attribution of being.
Therefore, what was stated—that these forms cannot belong to a non-entity—is refuted.

Furthermore, this should be seen as refuted for another reason: because there is no connection between an entity and its prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) or its posterior non-existence (pradhvaṃsābhāva), whether characterized by origination from it or characterized by opposition, since they do not coexist and thus lack a dual substratum.
For this very reason, the relation of qualifier and qualified is not possible;
nor is there a relation of qualifier and qualified because of their non-simultaneity, as well as due to the absence of the nature of a qualifier and a qualified in any real entity.
This [relation] is merely postulated by way of another connection, like that between a staff and a staff-bearer.

Furthermore, if the cognition "the prior non-existence of an entity" occurs by virtue of the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*), then there would likewise be a cognition "the existence of prior non-existence and so forth," since the relation is no different.
Therefore, the cognition of prior non-existence and the like as being related to an entity, when they are actually unrelated, is nothing but an error.
Furthermore, there is no mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) among entities.
For the cessation of a jar is not the cessation of a cloth, as this is not perceived. Nor is it logical that such cessation belongs to the cloth simply because it abides in it;
for if that were so, even antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the rest would be mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), since they abide in their causes and so forth.

Therefore, there exists only non-existence (*abhāva*) and not mutual non-existence; thus, since antecedent non-existence and the others are not distinct from non-existence, how can it be said that non-existence is fourfold?
In the margin:
Since the refutation of the non-existence of perception has already been stated in the *Nairātmyasiddhi*, it is not discussed here.
However, [an objection may be raised]: "If non-existence is experienced as being non-existent, how can there be a determination by means of perception?"

This is not a fault, because when two things are conjoined within a single cognition, the perception of one is itself the non-perception of the other; and that very non-perception is the apprehension of its absence. For if it were present, its non-perception would be impossible. As it has been said: "When all other causes are complete and there is no deviation from them, perception is existence;
non-perception is non-existence; and the perception of something else is non-perception."
In the margin:
"Therefore, this meaning—
that perception determines non-existence— does not mean that it determines [it] at all."
And that ascertainment of the non-existence of the perceptible object is indeed the very ascertainment of its absence;
thus, it is established that the conceptual construction (vikalpa) arising subsequent to perception follows the object of that perception.

Therefore, since the conventional usage regarding the absence of an object—just like the conventional usage regarding the absence of a perception—is itself established by perception, it is not to be proved by means of a logical mark (liṅga).

Thus, for one who is not deluded, the non-perception of the perceptible does not deviate from absence; therefore, the conventional usage of "absence" is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, it is not reasonable to say that because things may exist even when unperceived, the non-perception of what is capable of being perceived is always subject to deviation, and thus the conventional usage [of absence] is impossible.

For in this way, even perception would not be a determiner of non-existence because of doubt; nor is it logical that one thing which determines [an object] should be a different factor for conventional usage than another.
Therefore, because perception is a determiner, it brings about the conventional usage of the non-existence of a perceptible object just as it does for its existence.
Regarding the absence of a middle term (*roṅ-du-med-pa*), he asks: "How then can there be the status of a probandum for a conventional expression of a non-existent?
and replies with the words beginning "But when... (*yadā punar* etc.).
For in such a case, the non-existence of non-existent objects is simply their non-perception despite being perceptible, and nothing else;

for even though you have established through perception the object of the conventional usage of "absence," there is still a cognition of the non-existent— of that which is absent— as the subject [of that cognition], due to delusion.
The form "it does not exist," the word "it does not exist" of such a nature, and the activity of a person characterized by unhesitating coming and going— these constitute worldly discourse;
a person who does not comprehend them [would not engage in such discourse].

By demonstrating the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent"— namely, the perception of a location devoid of a jar— he provides an example to show how, at that time, one is prompted to engage in the conventional usage of "absence."
Regarding the passage beginning with "yathā" (just as),
the cow is precisely that which consists of the collection of the dewlap and so forth;
therefore, it is not "cowness" (*gotva*) that is being proven in that case, but rather the conventional usage of the term "cow."

When this person of dull intellect, having applied the conventional usage of "cow" to a *śābaleya* (a brindled cow), does not apply that same usage to a *bāhuleya* (a black cow) because it lacks the form of a *śābaleya*, he is then led to apply the usage of "cow" by being shown the underlying cause:
for the usage of "cow" is based on the collection of features such as the dewlap and so forth, and not on the specific form of a *śābaleya*.
Since that same basis exists in the *bāhuleya* as well, why should the usage not be applied there?
In the same way, even with respect to a location devoid of a jar, one is led to engage in the conventional usage of "non-existent" by demonstrating the grounds for its non-perception.

And likewise, by that very [means] through which this conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is established, the objection regarding the non-establishment of the example (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*) is also refuted and rejected.

For when non-existence is to be proven by means of the mark (*liṅga*) of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), if the absence of the mark in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) were itself to be proven by another mark, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), since one would require yet another example for that [second] case as well.
However, when conventional usage is what is to be proven, there is no infinite regress.
Since the very linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) that was previously set in motion is set in motion again at a later time, one might ask:
"Is it not the case that whoever apprehends the object also apprehends the subject; how then can the linguistic convention itself be something to be established?
To this, he says "viṣaya... and so forth.
For such people are indeed seen in the world who, even while engaging with an object, do not engage with the subject [of that engagement].

For example, a Sāṃkhya, although he has initiated the conventional usage "there is no *rajas* in *sattva*," does not apply it to a lump of clay due to the absence of a certain cognition of the cause. He is made to apply the conventional usage regarding the absence of a jar only when the cause for its non-perception is demonstrated.
Such is the conclusion, beginning with the words "in this way" (*evam*).
In the manner thus stated, the two non-apprehensions—the apprehensible and the non-apprehensible—have an equal result, namely the negation of the conventional usage of "existence.
How so? By means of the presence or absence of their respective opposites as causes:

by the word *sva* (self), the essential nature of the conventional usage of existence is grasped; and by the word *viparyaya* (opposite), the conventional usage of "non-existence," which is contrary to the conventional usage of existence, is grasped.
The causes of those two are their respective contradictory causes;
therein, the cause of [the object] itself is perception, while the cause of its contradiction is the non-perception of the perceptible.
The non-existence and existence of those two are the non-existence and existence of their respective causes of error; by means of these two...
This is what is meant:

in the case of the non-apprehension of the imperceptible (*adṛśyānupalabdhi*), since apprehension—which is the cause for the conventional usage of "existent"—is absent when perception and inference have ceased, there is a cessation of the conventional usage of "existent. In the case of the non-apprehension of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*), however, because the cause for the conventional usage of "non-existent"—which is opposed to the conventional usage of "existent"—is present, that [usage] proceeds; thus, by that means, there is a cessation of the conventional usage of "existent. Therefore, the result of negating the conventional usage of "existent" is the same in both cases.
[Objection: But even when perception has ceased, since there is doubt regarding the object, how can the conventional usage of "existence" (*sadvyavahāra*) be precluded? [Response: He says:

"In one case... Because there is doubt regarding existence in the case of non-perception whose object is invisible, the conventional usage of existence—which consists of certainty—is indeed precluded;
however, the conventional usage of existence that is merely doubtful is not precluded.
But in other cases, regarding the non-perception of the perceptible, there is the opposite; thus, "certainty" refers to the reversal of doubt and error, meaning it is a certainty of non-existence.
[The opponent asks: "If there is doubt regarding the non-perception of the imperceptible, how can that be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? To this, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "tatrādyā" and so forth:

among those two types of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), the first—namely, the non-apprehension of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*)—is stated to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is useful for, that is, functions in, the negation of the conventional usage of existence (*sadvyavahāra*).
To the question, "In what case, then, is it not a means of valid cognition? he says:
"But not," and so forth;
this refers to the observation and ascertainment of the absence of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), both verbal expression and conventional usage are understood.
Since certainty regarding non-existence does not arise from doubt,
the second [type of cognition] is therefore not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The non-perception of a perceptible object is the result of this [non-apprehension] because it has certainty as its fruit, since certainty arises from the observation of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and so forth;

thus, taking it that certainty alone is its fruit, that non-perception of a perceptible object is fourfold according to the differences in its formal application (*prayoga*). This is the connection [of the sentence].
The term *virūpaikaśeṣa* (an elliptical compound consisting of dissimilar members) refers to both "the contradictory" (*viruddha*) and "the body of the contradictory" (*viruddhakāya*). Furthermore,
the word "establishment" (*siddhi*), which means "perception," should also be connected here with the phrase "of the perceptible nature" (*dṛśyātmanoḥ*).

By this, two [types of non-apprehension] are indicated: the apprehension of what is incompatible with the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*) and the apprehension of the effect of the incompatible (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*).

"Non-establishment of the cause and the essential nature" means the non-apprehension of the cause and the essential nature when they have reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), that is, when they possess a perceptible nature.
By this [verse], two [types of non-perception]—the non-perception of the cause and the non-perception of the essential nature—are also indicated; thus, there are four [types].

It is "for the purpose of non-existence" (*abhāvārtha*), meaning that its object (*artha*) is both non-existence (*abhāva*) and the conventional expression of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*), which constitutes its function (*prayojana*). (Note in the margin)

Now, one might object: "In the case of the establishment of two contradictory effects, it is not stated that it is 'non-apprehension' (anupalabdhi); so how can these two be considered non-apprehensions? To this, he says:
"Whatever [is the case]... and so forth.
If it were stated that "whatever there may be" implies universal pervasion,
then no inferential linguistic usage of negation could exist without non-apprehension;
however, this does not mean that the linguistic usage of absence is established by perception.

This has already been refuted and previously stated; however, in order to demonstrate that very pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says "for thus" (*tathā hi*); here, "that" (*sa*) refers to the negation (*pratiṣedha*).
It would be divided—that is, it would be subject to linguistic convention—either by the affirmation or the negation of some object;

and even when the affirmation of one [object] is being performed, either a contradictory [affirmation] or a non-contradictory [affirmation] would be established. In the case of a non-contradictory affirmation, since there is no contradiction between the coexistence of that which is being negated and that which is being affirmed, there is no negation of what is intended to be negated.
"Even of the contradictory," and so forth;
for it would be contradictory only if there were a non-perception of its own contradictory therein. He states this very point with the words "for thus," and so on.

Regarding the phrase "of that which has an unlimited cause," this refers to you [the opponent] for whom cold touch and so forth arise in a continuum as long as their cause is not exhausted; it should be understood as occurring prior to the proximity of fire and other such factors.
The understanding of contradiction arises because there is an absence—meaning non-arising—when another factor, such as fire, is present;
it does not, however, arise from the absence [of the cause], since destruction would otherwise be causeless.
In the margin. In the margin.
This is what is meant:

When each preceding cold touch ceases by its own nature, there arises a subsequent one characterized by a progressive diminution of the cold touch according to the degree of the fire; this occurs sequentially until, through the total non-arising of all [cold touches], it becomes characterized by hot touch.

Therefore, even though destruction is causeless, when fire is present, the tactile sensation of cold—which had been proceeding in a continuous stream—ceases by its own nature; and since another [sensation] that was about to arise in a continuous stream does not arise when fire is present, the opposition between fire and cold is understood in the world. However, there is no opposition in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).
