For this very reason, he says that it is merely the "cognition of opposition.
Furthermore, as for what is said:
Without the cessation of the cause, nothing can be called a "cessator" of something such as fire.
That is incorrect, because destruction is causeless; how could it be the remover of a cause?
If, on the other hand, you speak thus while accepting that destruction has a cause, then why does it not remove the effect just as it removes the cause?

Furthermore, if it were impossible to eliminate an effect without eliminating its cause, then how could that [cause] itself be eliminated as long as its own cause has not been eliminated? If the same logic applied to that cause as well, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and nothing whatsoever would be the eliminator of anything.

Nor is it appropriate to speak of this in terms of a "continuum" (*saṃtāna*), because when destruction possesses a cause, the continuum itself does not exist; thus, this argument is trivial. Moreover, that contradiction characterized by non-arising—the absence [of one thing] when another exists—is designated on the basis of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
By this, contradiction characterized by non-coexistence has been explained.
Showing the second type of contradiction, he says:
"Mutual perception," and so forth.

Mutual apprehension is reciprocal cognition; its exclusion is "separation" (*viveka*). Those two whose characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), that is, their own nature (*svarūpa*), is established by means of that [separation], are so described.
The state of those two is "the state of having characteristics established through the exclusion of mutual apprehension," or that very state is contradiction (*virodha*).
The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of conjunction;
"like permanence and impermanence" is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
[Objection: But surely, even in the case of the first contradiction, there is indeed mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*).
In the second case as well, there is non-coexistence;
for this second type of contradiction pertains precisely to those two phenomena that cannot abide together in one place,
as is not accepted in the case of color and taste.
If it is asked why these two contradictions were stated, the answer is: true; however, they were stated for the sake of distinguishing their respective domains.
The former contradiction pertains exclusively to the domain of perceptible objects.
However, some maintain that the second [type of non-apprehension] has as its object not only a non-entity but also something invisible;
alternatively, the first consists in the apprehension of the absence of one thing through another, and thus involves a contradiction with that other,
whereas the second concerns the essential nature itself by means of the absence of identity with another— thus there is a great difference between these two types of contradiction.

For instance, impermanence consists in the cessation of permanence, and permanence consists in the cessation of impermanence; thus, contradiction is established by their very nature as mutual exclusion.

However, yellow does not consist in the cessation of blue, nor does blue consist in the cessation of yellow. Since these two are positive entities, and because it would follow that yellow exists in the absence of blue, this is not a case of contradiction between them.
Nor is this contradiction [between blue and non-blue] due to their being invariably concomitant with mutual exclusion, because such a relationship is not perceived;
for this very reason, it is said that there is the affirmation of what is non-contradictory.

Furthermore, this contradiction of blue is with a non-blue in the form of the cessation of blue, not with a non-blue necessarily determined by the absence of blue, since there exists no such non-blue entity distinct from yellow and other colors.
How, then, is there a negation of identity with yellow and so forth while blue and so forth are being perceived?

This is not a fault, because when a single [thing], such as blue, is perceived, if another [thing]—though unperceived—were of a nature that is being perceived, it would be perceived in that very same way. Thus, having considered its fulfillment of the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*), identity is negated through the non-perception of its nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*).
And here too, regarding contradiction, the phrase "and that [is established] from non-apprehension" (sa cānupalabdheḥ) must be supplied; thus, the meaning is this:
that contradiction consisting of mutual exclusion is to be ascertained solely through non-apprehension.
For instance:
The contradiction between contradictory things is said to be precisely the non-appearance of one when there is the appearance of the other;
and when the form of an entity appears, its absence does not appear.
Therefore, because existence and non-existence do not appear as identical, their contradiction is determined.
In this way, [the distinction between] the permanent and the impermanent and so forth must be ascertained;
and the non-appearance [of one] is said to be precisely the appearance of the other.
Thus he says:
"In that case as well," and so forth;
there too, in the contradiction just mentioned,
by means of the apprehension of one [of the two].
The non-apprehension of one thing that is contradictory [to another] is itself called the non-apprehension of the object to be negated;
otherwise, if the non-apprehension of the other were not stated by means of the apprehension of one,
then for that object of negation whose [apprehension] has not been negated, its absence would remain unestablished even when the one is apprehended.
Furthermore, that which is being perceived could not possibly be contradictory;

therefore, since both types of contradiction are produced by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), even those [reasons] such as the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) which are formulated in a positive manner (*vidhimukhena*), are in their essential nature non-perceptions.
Now, is it not the case that in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), non-perception is what grasps the relationship characterized by contradiction between two contradictory things?
Furthermore, the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends a relationship does not belong to the two related entities themselves;
for the nature of the perception (*pratyakṣa*) that apprehends the relationship between fire and smoke belongs neither to the smoke nor to the fire.
How then can the "perception of the contradictory" (*viruddhopalabdhi*) be a non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), given that it manifests in the form of a perception?

Therefore, having perceived fire and so forth— which are known to be incompatible with cold— in one instance within the example, the absence of cold and so forth is inferred upon seeing them in another location.
To this, it is replied:

If the relationship of the signifier and the signified were established through the relation of contradiction, then from the perception of fire there would ultimately follow the cognition of cold, because that [cognition] arises precisely through the relation of contradiction between those two;
it would not follow from the absence of cold, as that is not related [to fire].
Furthermore, when the cold is eliminated by the fire, how could there be a relation of contradiction, given that [a relation] cannot reside in only one of the two?
Furthermore, there is no contradiction between fire and the absence of cold, because they can coexist;
nor can the absence of cold be inferred from fire, since the absence of cold is not invariably concomitant with fire,
as cold is observed even when fire is present.

Therefore, just as the non-perception of cold occurs wherever fire is present, and since its absence has been established in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the absence of cold in other instances of fire is likewise inferred; thus,
this is the meaning.
When cold is not perceived even though fire exists in the subject (*sādhyadharmin*), only then does fire possess the quality of being an opponent; it is not at other times.
Since its status as a prover (*gamakatva*) depends on this opposition, it follows that its function as a prover is through the non-perception of something else.
Therefore, the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) is essentially a form of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), because it is invariably determined by non-perception.
Just as the perception of the bare ground is of the nature of the non-perception of a jar,
so too, even in the case of mutual exclusion, the perception of the contradictory is indeed non-perception itself,
as it would be for the Jains.

If one were to say that an impermanent jar is permanent, the non-perception of permanence is indeed nothing other than the perception of impermanence; therefore, there is no entity that possesses both permanent and impermanent forms.
In the margin:

Having thus established that non-apprehension is the means of cognition for the negation of a thing even when another thing is being affirmed, he says "of one," etc., in order to establish it also for the negation of another thing.
Why?
Because of the negation, and so forth;
nor does the over-extension [of negation] to other objects follow from the absence of other objects, in the case of the negation of another object.
Because, even in that case, if the negation of "other" were the probandum (*sādhya*),

the reason (*hetu*) would have to be either the negation of both cause and effect, or the negation of that which is neither [cause nor effect], namely, that which is neither an effect nor a cause; such being the case among those [options].

Since that which is neither [cause nor effect]— being devoid of the nature of cause and effect— lacks any necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with the object of negation, how can it be established that "in the absence of that [object],
there must not be the other"— namely, that which is intended as the object of negation— given that the former is unconnected to the latter?
The connection [of the argument] is: "Even in the case of the non-perception of the effect, how is there the absence of that?"—that is, the absence of the cause.
This is because causes are manifold, and it is possible for them to be deficient or obstructed, even though they possess the capacity to produce the effect.
And this was stated merely by taking the cause into account: the absence of a cause whose capacity is unimpeded is indeed understood from the absence of the effect;

since it is the non-perception of both [the cause and] the effect that serves as the means of cognition, therefore it is the non-perception of the cause alone that makes known the absence [of the effect].
[The word] "of the effect" is understood from the context [in the preceding verse].
If it is argued that the restriction [implied by the previous statement] is improper because non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is also a reason for non-existence, he says:
The non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), however, is simply its own non-existence;
it does not establish the absence of some other entity here.

Furthermore, when the negation of another intrinsic nature is to be proven, it is precisely the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) that is intended—this is the restriction [of the definition]. Therefore, there is no contradiction.
But what is established there? He says "only," etc.;
"there" refers to the non-apprehension of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), and the object is the cognition of non-existence and so forth.

In this case as well— that is, in the non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*)— when one states the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) through the non-perception of a pervading property (*vyāpaka*),
as in "there is no *śiṃśapā* tree here because of the absence of trees," then even the identity (*abheda*) of the pervaded is established.
By the force of the word "also" (*api*), conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is also included.

For instance, when a forest of trees is seen on one area of two elevated mountain regions, and because of its extreme density the specific species of the trees cannot be determined, then the absence of *śiṃśapā* trees cannot be ascertained on the other part of the mountain, since the *śiṃśapā* is not visible. However, in the case of a tree that has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), it is possible to ascertain its absence.
At that time, due to the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is established;
cf.
"then there is also non-existence."
With the words "this," etc., he explains the portion of the verse beginning with "for the purpose of non-existence" (*abhāvārtha*),
[interpreting] "by the establishment of the contradictory" (*viruddhasiddhyā*) as "by the perception of what is contradictory to the intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhyā*).
"Yathā" and so forth:
in a case where the cold touch is imperceptible in a given substratum (*dharmin*) and fire is perceived.
In this distant context,

this usage— "by this"— should be understood as stating the establishment of the contradictory of the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddha-siddhi*) by means of the example of the perception of what is incompatible with the essential nature (*svabhāva-viruddhopalabdhi*);
"just as," etc., is the illustrative example.
A specific cold touch accompanied by frost is *tuṣāra*; its pervader is coldness, and fire is the contradictory of that [coldness].

In this case, fire, by excluding its contradictory—coldness—also excludes *tuṣāra*-touch, which is pervaded by it. Thus, this [inference] is included within the perception of what is contradictory to an essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*) by implication.
And where fire is perceived and the touch of cold or the touch of frost is unperceived, there this formulation should also be seen:
"By the non-establishment of the effect of that which is contradictory," and so forth.

"There is no sensation of cold here because of smoke"—this means that fire, which is the opposite of cold, has smoke as its effect; that [fire] brings about the presence of itself, and it removes the cold.
Where the sensation of cold is imperceptible, yet both fire and smoke are perceptible, this formal argument (*prayoga*) is to be seen.
Thus, the establishment of the effect of what is contradictory (*viruddha-kārya*) has been explained.
Now,
he explains this by means of the narration of the example [beginning with] "by the non-establishment of the reason," that is, through the non-perception of the cause.
Regarding the phrase "yathā" and so forth:
when there is doubt as to whether the vapor and such above a great lake are actually smoke and the like, then this formal argument (*prayoga*) is to be observed.
For in that case, if there were fire in the motionless great lake, it would certainly be perceived due to its luminosity.

Precisely because fire is not perceived, the absence of its effect is established through the non-establishment of its own nature; thus, by means of the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), it is understood that "there is no smoke there because [fire] is not perceived," provided that [the object] meets the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). This is how it should be understood.

By this— that is, by the formal argument consisting in the non-perception of intrinsic nature— it is stated that there is the non-establishment, i.e., the non-perception, of that which is both a pervader and an intrinsic nature, as in: "There is no *śiṃśapā* tree here, because of the absence of trees."
The very nature of being a *śiṃśapā* is tree-ness; therefore, a *śiṃśapā* is pervaded by tree-ness.

Now, it is indeed only through the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) that there is the negation of a perceptible object, and not through the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) and so forth.
For it is precisely the imperceptible cold touch and its imperceptible effect that are established as being negated.
For if [the object] were perceptible, it would simply be a case of the non-perception of its own nature;
therefore, just as there is a negation of imperceptible things such as cold touch and so forth, so too would there be a negation of things like *piśācas*.
To this, he says "in all cases," and so on.
This is what is meant:

just as in the case of the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), the absence of a jar or similar object—which has been perceived elsewhere—is established in a particular location, so too the absence of a cold touch whose opposition is known elsewhere, or of an effect whose causal status is known, is established in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) through the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) and other such means; it is not, however, [established] for that which is always invisible. Thus, the term "non-existence" (*abhāva*) refers to both non-existence itself and the linguistic convention of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) when non-existence is being proved by means of either affirmation or negation applied in all cases.

Furthermore, regarding those causes and so forth whose absence establishes the non-existence [of the probandum], their non-establishment—namely, their non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*)—is understood as being only insofar as they possess a perceptible nature (*dṛśyātman*).

Likewise, the establishment of things contrary to them—that is, of things contrary to the object to be negated, such as those whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is contradictory [to it] and so forth—is to be known as having apprehension (*upalabdhi*) as its logical mark (*liṅga*).

And in this context, the phrase "establishment as having a perceptible nature" is not to be connected [to the non-apprehension], because the state of having a perceptible nature is already obtained from the very word "apprehension."
However, the connection should be formulated in this way:
"the establishment of those things which are contradictory to the objects intended to be negated by means of the perceived nature.
What is the reason for this?
Because the non-existence of other imperceptible entities such as causes and so forth is not established,
there is no proof of contradiction— such as through a nature that is incompatible (svabhāvaviruddha)— with respect to those imperceptible things intended to be negated;
this is what the opponent [means] by the words "if" and so forth.
If the absence of cold is established by the perception of smoke— the effect of fire which is opposed to cold—

then why is the absence of cold not also established by the perception of the cause of that fire opposed to cold, namely wood and so forth? Why does it not succeed through the perception of its cause?
In the margin. 1 In the margin.
The Master [says]: "Of that which is contrary to it," and so forth.
The perception of wood or the like, which serves as the cause for fire that is incompatible with that cold touch,
is fallacious when there is sometimes an absence of incompatibility between the two causes.
Since there is no contradiction between fire and cold as their respective causes, he provides an illustration,
beginning with "for example" (yathā), and so forth.
For in this case, since there is no contradiction between mere wood as the cause of burning and frost or the like as the cause of cold,

even though there is a contradiction between that wood which possesses unimpeded power to produce fire and the cause of cold, nevertheless, because such wood is ascertained precisely through the observation of its effect, there would be a contradiction with respect to the effect itself. Furthermore, when there is a contradiction between two causes, the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) is indeed what indicates [the absence].
Just as this man has no specific effects such as horripilation—
the word "etc. including [effects like] the lute of the teeth and trembling— the use of the term "specific" is for the purpose of excluding the effects of cold.
For those [effects] can also arise from transformations caused by piśācas and the like; "one for whom a particular fire is present" refers to such a person, and the state of being so is "tadbhāva.

Therefore, even here, the inclusion of the term "particular" (viśeṣa) is for the purpose of grasping that specific kind of fire which is capable of removing the bristling of hair and other such symptoms.
For here, there is a contradiction between the burning heat, which is the cause of torment, and the cold, which is indicated by such signs as horripilation;
therefore, the fire, by removing its own opposite—cold—also removes its effect, namely horripilation and the like.

Thus, when both the sensation of cold and its effect, horripilation and so forth, are imperceptible, this formal argument (*prayoga*) is to be understood as intended to establish the cessation of horripilation and the rest through the cessation of the cause of cold upon seeing the fire.
In the margin:

By this example of the contradictory cause (*kāraṇaviruddha*), it is stated that from its effect as well— that is, from the effect of that which is contradictory, one attains the understanding of the absence of the effect of that [contradictory thing].

When the effect of a certain contrary thing is perceived, that which is the second contrary counter-positive is "contrary to it"; the cognition of the absence of its effect is what has been stated. For example, as an illustration:
a person who possesses specific symptoms such as horripilation caused by cold, in whatever place he may be found, is [described] in that manner.
The mention of "a particular location" (*pradeśa*) in the statement "because of smoke" (*dhūmāt*) is for the purpose of establishing the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatva*);
for if the subject were merely "the person," the reason would not be a property of the subject, since smoke is a property of the location.
And this is the formal argument (*prayoga*).
Where fire is present, but the sensation of cold touch and specific effects such as horripilation are imperceptible, that case should be understood as one for establishing non-existence (*abhāva*).

For in such a case, by the perception of smoke—which is the effect of fire, the opposite of cold—one intends to establish the absence of horripilation and the like, which are the effects of cold, the opposite of fire. Therefore, it is precisely such a thing that is the probandum (*sādhya*).
Indeed, smoke brings fire into proximity and thereby eliminates the cold.

The meaning is that as it ceases, it causes its own effects, such as the bristling of the hair, to cease; therefore, this is by implication an "apprehension of what is incompatible with the cause" (kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi),
The meaning is "perception of what is incompatible with the cause.
Because this very non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) was already indicated previously by the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*),

and because in these two applications as well, the understanding of the absence of the effect is derived solely from the non-perception of the cause, therefore this is stated as being simply the non-perception of the cause.

Thus, although this [non-apprehension] is fourfold by way of its primary divisions— as in the passage beginning "it is thus"— it becomes eightfold through the further distinction of its intermediate applications (prayoga).

For instance, the apprehension of what is incompatible with the pervader (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi) is stated to be a sub-division of the apprehension of what is incompatible with the essential nature (svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi).

The non-perception of the nature [of the object], the non-perception of the pervader, the non-perception of the cause, the perception of that which is contradictory to the cause, and the perception of the effect of that which is contradictory to the cause—
while the perception of the contradictory effect is of one kind— thus there are eight types [of non-apprehension].

Now, one might object: "Since smoke is present even when fire has long since perished in a dwelling house or similar location, how is there no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the perception of a contradictory effect? To this, he says:
"In that case," and so forth;
"even in the case of a contradictory effect, dependence on place, time, and other factors is required."

In this case, there is no cold at any time when fire has become present; thus, there is a dependence on time. Regarding space, there is no cold in any location where smoke arises from fire; thus, there is a dependence on place.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), one should understand dependence on specific states.
A specific state of smoke that has been observed in proximity to fire is taken into account to infer the absence of cold even at the present time;
thus, even in the case of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), such as "there is fire here because of smoke," dependence on place, time, and so forth is accepted.
The word "also" (*api*) serves to include this very point.

If it is argued that the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*) because the locus (*dharmin*) would be absent if dependence on place, time, and so forth were a qualification of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), we say no;
for it has already been stated that the place itself serves as the locus, since [the reason] functions as a means of cognition by virtue of its dependence on place, time, and so forth.
"Otherwise" means that if there were no dependence on place and so forth, then the contradictory effect would be fallacious (*vyabhicārin*).
For example, ash that does not depend on a specific place or time is fallacious when used to prove the absence of cold as the probandum (*sādhya*) in the proof of non-cold; it is just like that.
Thus far, it has been established that the perception of the contradictory and so forth is [in fact] non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "But then," the opponent argues:
when one infers an effect— such as a sprout— upon seeing a collection of causes such as earth, seed, and water, which are present and unimpeded,
how does that cause known as the "cause" (kāraṇa-hetu) fit within the threefold classification of reasons consisting of essential nature (svabhāva), effect (kārya), and non-perception (anupalambha)?

It cannot be [a case of] non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), because it functions as a proof by affirmation; nor can it be a reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*), because an entity is not inferred from another distinct entity; nor can it be a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*).

He states the inclusion [of the effect] by means of the cause, and so forth, up to the word "by the complete [assemblage]. This is because an effect is seen to arise from as many a collection of causes as is required; it does not arise from that which has reached its final state, since the effect is already perceptible even before the apprehension of the probans (*liṅgin*) therein.

Alternatively, if [the final state] were not perceptible, it would be impossible to ascertain that final state; thus, there can be no inference. Furthermore, no one will be able to ascertain them, because for one who perceives only what is proximate (*arvāgdarśana*), the final moments cannot be ascertained.
That which is inferred from the production of an effect has been described as the nature (*svabhāva*) of the cause.
Why? Because it does not depend on anything else.
Therefore, the meaning is as follows: since [the capacity] is invariably concomitant with the mere fitness for producing the effect, it is indeed of the nature of the thing itself (*svabhāva*).
Now, one might ask: "If the production of the effect depends upon the final state, how can it be independent of anything else? To this, he says:
"That too" refers to the production of the effect; it is according to how the collection of causes is present— that is, of whatever nature the collection of causes is present.
Since it does not depend on any object other than such a proximate [cause], the nature that is invariably concomitant with just that belongs to what?
It belongs to the entire complex of causes.

This is stated with reference to the continuum (*santāna*), not with reference to the moment (*kṣaṇa*); the meaning is that the causal complex (*kāraṇakalāpa*) as a continuum is independent in its production [of the effect]. Even though the arising of the effect is independent, he asks: "How can it be the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) since it is a different entity? and answers:
Regarding the passage beginning with "tatra" and so forth:
because, in that case, when all causes are present, the possibility of the production of an effect from the complete set of causes is inferred;
thus, "sambhava" (possibility) means that which arises from this [complete cause].
The meaning is that the capacity for producing an effect is inferred; he clarifies this very point by stating,
"because of the inference of the capacity for producing an effect in those things that are complete."
And this capacity (yogyatā) is invariably concomitant with the mere collection of causes (sāmagrīmātrānuvandhinī), because it does not depend on any other cause.

If, then, the power to produce an effect is necessarily concomitant with that [collection] alone, then the production of the effect is certain; why, then, is that [production] itself not inferred? Thus the opponent asks:
"But why is the effect itself inferred from the collection? To this, he replies:
Regarding the phrase "the causal complex" (*sāmagrī*) and so forth:
the result of the causal complex and those very potencies are called "the potencies that are the results of the causal complex" (*sāmagrī-phala-śaktayaḥ*).

For instance, from a preceding complete complex, there arises a subsequent moment that is capable; its own excellence (*ātmātiśaya*) is the potency. Thus, the causal complex is the result, and the potency is the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of these [moments].
When an effect that arises through a continuous succession and depends upon that [preceding cause] is to be inferred from its cause, why is there inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā)?
Because an obstruction is impossible,
he explains that [point] with the words "for not," and so forth.
The causal substances produce their own effect only when they are complete, that is, when they are present together;
for what reason?
Because of the totality (*sāmagrī*), and so forth.
The successive transformation of those potencies which arise from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*)— that is, the production of each subsequent,
more distinguished moment from each preceding moment— is due to the dependence of the arising of the effect upon that [transformation];
and "in the meantime" refers to the period during which the continuum undergoes this transformation.

[Objection: "But surely even *yogyatā* (capacity) is obstructed by the successive transformations of subsequent moments, and since obstruction is possible there as well, how can there be an inference of that [capacity] either? To this, he says:
"But of *yogyatā*, etc."
Because it does not depend on a separate substance— that is, because it does not depend on any other cause apart from the collection of causes already present— inference is not contradicted;
he states that very inference in the verse beginning with "uttarottara," etc.
The production of a subsequent capable moment based upon each preceding moment is the "transformation of successive potencies.
With that as the reason, the statement of the thesis is: "it is capable of producing an effect";
this causal totality is the subject (*dharmin*).

The reason is "because there is no other requisite condition for the transformation of the capacity. Since there is no other auxiliary condition (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) for the transformation of the capacity that must be depended upon, [the opponent asks] from where, then, does the production of the capacity arise?
To this, he says "pūrva... and so forth.
That which has a prior homogeneous cause—that is, a preceding causal complex of exactly that magnitude—is "produced by such power";
the state of being so is "therefrom.
For this reason, that capacity is said to be independent of anything else.
Now, if the capacity of a cause with respect to its effect is called "power" (*śakti*), then when the effect is absent, the capacity would also be absent; how then could this be an inference?
If, on the other hand, it is said that there is the possibility of capacity, then the meaning would be: "the effect may or may not exist.
Even so, how can this be an inference? Because of doubt.
To this it is replied:
how can the opponent challenge whether this inference is produced by the three types of reasons?
For if this inference is established by the opponent, then the Teacher demonstrates that it is indeed produced by the threefold logical mark (liṅga).
Some maintain that this is intended to show that this is not an inference regarding ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Alternatively, if one were to infer the capacity for the production of an effect as being absolute,
then the inference would be invalid due to fallibility (*vyabhicāra*).
But when a possibility (*sambhava*) is inferred in the form "it might happen at some time or other," how could there be any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case?
Therefore, the meaning is this: if, in the course of successive transformations, there is an absence of continuity (*prabandha*), then an effect may occur; otherwise, it does not.
However, regarding the opponent's claim of an absolute inference of an effect, there is indeed a deviation.

Others, however, hold that when there is no obstacle to a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) possessing the capacity for transformation, there arises an absolute fitness for the production of the effect; it is this very fitness that is inferred. Furthermore, since the cognition of this fitness implies the effect as its own qualifier, a separate inference of the effect is not performed. They maintain that the charge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is raised only against the inference of an effect from the mere causal complex alone. If it is asked, "How is the absence of obstacles known? [the answer follows].
This is true:

for he who is able to know that [invariable concomitance] possesses this inference; just as he who is able to know that smoke is produced by fire possesses the inference of fire from smoke, and no one else does.
With the words "But then... and so forth, he again states the contradiction of the claim that "it is of three kinds only."

The cognition of color and so forth through taste and so forth— where "and so forth" includes smell and so forth— is by means of a non-essential property (asvabhāva) that is neither the cause nor the effect of the object to be inferred.
Here too, by the word "etcetera," touch and so forth are included;
for in the dark, having tasted the juice of a citron or similar fruit, and having smelled the fragrance of a campaka flower, [one perceives them].
Having experienced the touch of fire,
their common property of form is inferred;
likewise, having seen the form of fire, its touch is inferred.
Regarding the question of how that [non-apprehension] is included within the threefold cause under discussion,

and given that it is not itself a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), he says "that too" and so forth, lest there follow the undesirable consequence of having yet another logical mark (*liṅgāntara*).
The connection is that "that too is an inference.

Of what kind [of form and so forth]? It is the cognition [of form] from taste as a mark (*liṅga*), which is dependent upon that very same causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces the taste, [the form] being itself subject to that same causal complex.
This is by means of the inference of the property of the cause:

that which is the cause of taste—its prior substrate—and its property, namely, the capacity to produce color; by means of that inference, this meaning is determined from the taste itself: that the cause of that [color] possesses the capacity to produce color at a time simultaneous with the taste.

For in this way, its capacity to produce a color that exists at the same time as the taste is ascertained only if there were also an ascertainment of the color existing at that same time; therefore, for past things belonging to the same moment, there is only one mode of cognition, namely that born from the mark of an effect. Indeed, an inference of a simultaneous color subsequent to a cause of taste that has not been explicitly stated would involve a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the inference of a cause from an effect.
Furthermore, in the inference of the capacity to produce an effect, there would be no inference of the color that exists at the same time as the taste,
because there is no cognition resulting from an inference based on another inference;
therefore, as for what is said:

When the [inference] concerns past things, it arises from an effect which is its mark (*liṅga*), because [the thing] was born from that; thus it is "born from an effect as a mark" (*kāryaliṅgaja*). But when the [inference] concerns simultaneous things, then the effect is the mark for that inference of the property of the cause; that is "an effect as a mark," and what is born from that is "born from an effect as a mark. That [explanation] is refuted.

In this regard, others [hold that] the qualities such as color (rūpa) are established in a composite substance (avayavidravya); therefore, it is logical that there is a movement of color and so forth which were previously absent there. This is not the case for the Buddhists, because they do not admit a composite whole distinct from color and the other qualities, and thus, due to the absence of a substratum (dharmin), [movement is impossible].
Furthermore, if inference were possible without a subject (dharmin), it would follow that one could infer color and so forth from taste everywhere; moreover,
the collection [of properties] would become the probandum (sādhya), and the logical reason (hetu) would not be a property of the subject (apakṣadharma).

Nor is inference from the property of a cause tenable, because taste and so forth are not perceived as effects of visible form and so forth. Furthermore, this is not stated without first determining the position of momentariness;

for if there were momentariness, visible form and so forth would be the effect of something of their own kind, and not the effect of taste and so forth, due to the absence of any apprehended necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
There can be no conventional usage of inference and the object of inference regarding momentary entities because their relationship cannot be ascertained.

However, if one were to base such usage on a continuum (*santāna*), since a causal relationship has not been established between the continua of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, how could there be a conventional usage of inference and the object of inference?
This is what [the opponent] intends.

It is not the case that there is an inference of color and so forth from taste and so forth in all instances; rather, in a locus such as a mango, the mutual inseparability of color and the other qualities is indeed perceived.
And that [inseparability] is caused by a necessary connection (*pratibandha*); otherwise, there would be a mutual inseparability even among things like jars and cloths.

Furthermore, there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between them; it cannot be identity (*tādātmya*), because they are perceived as distinct, nor can it be origination from that (*tadutpatti*), because they exist simultaneously.

Nor is there inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*) for them, since there can be no inherence in a single object for things that do not themselves inhere [in anything], precisely because inherence itself does not exist.
Furthermore, this would lead to an over-extension: why would even those things that are already inherent require inherence, since they are produced as such from their own causes?
It is precisely because they are produced in that way that they possess the capacity to signify through their denotation.

Therefore, dependence upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*) constitutes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*). And for one who has ascertained this connection, there is inference regarding another time.

Even though, in this case, no "whole" (*avayavin*) exists, nevertheless, because the object of the cognition of the mango and so forth serves as the subject (*dharmin*), there is the apprehension of color and other qualities from the taste.
But even so, how can these [causes] be dependent on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*),

given that the very nature by which a form (*rūpa*) produces another form does not produce taste (*rasa*) and so forth by that same [nature], for otherwise there would be the consequence of their mutual non-difference;
nor does it produce another [effect] by a different [nature], for that would entail a difference in its own nature (*svabhāvabheda*).
This is not a fault, because in that case, form does not first produce a single effect— by which this fault would arise—
but rather produces multiple effects simultaneously.
Since its production is observed from that very [cause],

the causality of a cause does not consist in the mere absence of the effect— which would entail the absurdity that a single effect produced from multiple causes must itself be singular— but rather, its causality consists in its prior existence at the time of the effect's production. For just as its prior existence is seen to be the cause for the production of a single effect, so too is it observed to be the cause for the production of a complex aggregate (*kalāpa*).

Alternatively, by whichever very same intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) form produces form, by that very same [nature] it also produces taste and so forth; however, the difference in their own natures (*svarūpabheda*) is caused by a difference in their material causes (*upādāna*), not by auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*).
For instance, although touch exists in wind, form and the rest do not arise because of the absence of form and so forth;
and although form and the rest exist in fire, taste does not arise because of the absence of taste.

Even though water possesses qualities such as taste, it lacks odor; therefore, odor does not arise [therein]. Consequently, it is determined that for taste and the other qualities, their respective causes are necessarily taste and so forth themselves.
A necessary cause is an *upādāna-kāraṇa* (material cause), which is of the same genus or exists within an undifferentiated continuum.
Therefore, due to the difference in their material causes, there is a difference in the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of visible form and the other qualities.
Furthermore, as for what is said there— that there is a conjunction of multiple powers,
whereby one power produces form while another produces taste and so forth— this is incorrect.

That is incorrect; for even if one accepts that a single entity produces multiple effects by means of multiple powers, the consequence of its being multiple remains unavoidable, since the entity would possess as many natures as there are powers.
Furthermore, because the powers are non-different from the entity, if the powers were distinct, it would follow that the nature [of the entity] itself must be distinct.
Alternatively, if there were a distinction between the powers (*śakti*), it would follow that the nature [of the entity] itself is not the causal agent;
nor does an incapable thing become a causal agent through the connection with power, because an incapable thing lacks such a connection.

Furthermore, what is the use of a connection with power for that which is already capable, since its status as a causal agent exists by its very own nature? Moreover, the power itself would not be a causal agent, as it lacks a connection with another power.
Now, if it is argued that because it is a power (*śakti*), it does not depend on another power,
then why should an entity (*bhāva*) also depend on a power, given that it too is a power? This is what the Mīmāṃsaka thinks.
Power (*śakti*) is simply an excellence of the essential nature (*svarūpātiśaya*) of an entity (*bhāva*); and it is both distinct and non-distinct from that entity.
It is distinct from the entity because when the entity is perceived, its power is not perceived;
yet it is non-distinct from the entity because of the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the effect. Otherwise, the entity would lack the status of being an agent (*kārakatva*).
Thus, that [argument] which states, "The powers of all entities are postulated through the presumption based on their effects" (kāryārthāpatti),
has also been refuted.
Because it is contradictory for a single power to possess both distinct and non-distinct natures,

and because— by means of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)— one must postulate that the non-distinct power belongs only to that entity which exists prior to the effect, it follows that power is simply prior existence;
and since that is established by direct perception, how can power not be perceptible?
That [cause] is determined solely through the observation of its effect;

therefore, because one infers the properties of the cause from that effect— such as rasa and so forth— it is included within the category of "effect-reason" (*kāryahetu*), just like the inference of fire from smoke.
Just as, from the inference of a causal complex such as fire and so forth from smoke, there is an inference of transformations in the fuel such as ashes and embers; similarly [in this case].
Now, one might object: "This is an inference of a contemporaneous effect from a cause inferred through its effect, namely taste, and not an inference of a property of the cause"; to this he says:
"In that case... (tatra).
Since the cause [of taste] is of such a nature that it leads to the cognition of color, the relation of producing color is inferred;
when this is being inferred, another effect—which serves as its qualification—also becomes ascertained.
However, another effect is not to be inferred subsequently from the cause once it has already been inferred.
Why is this so? He says:
because that whose power has proceeded and is unobstructed is "one whose power has proceeded."
And since that material cause of color is of such a nature, it is so described;
being its cooperative condition (*sahakāri-pratyaya*), it produces taste by means of the cause of taste.
And when such a cause exists, the inference of color follows from the [inference of] taste by implication, because color and taste are dependent upon the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatvāt*).
For example, ash, charcoal, and so forth are specific transformations of fuel;
the material cause (*upādāna*) of that is wood, and its cooperative condition (*sahakāripratyaya*) is fire.

Just as smoke is produced by that [fire], in the same way, the dependence of color and taste upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*) is established by the passage beginning with "for thus" (*tathā hi*). The aphorism (*sūtra*) "the manifestation of capacity" (*śaktipravṛtta*) is explained by the passage beginning with "of its own cause" (*svakāraṇasya*).

Regarding the phrase "of its own cause": the production of the fruit from that which is the cause of the *rasa*—namely, the production of the *rasa* itself—is impossible without the presence and suitability [of the cause] directed toward that production; this very thing is the "activation of power" (*śaktipravṛtti*).
The explanation of the term "another cause" (*anyakāraṇa*) begins with the words "the material cause of form" (*rūpopādāna*), and so forth.

The material causes (*upādāna-hetu*) of form (*rūpa*) are those atoms of form (*rūpa-paramāṇu*) comprised within the preceding characteristics; their "activity" (*pravṛtti*) is their orientation toward the production of form. The cause of that [activity] is the activity of the material cause of form being oriented toward its own effect, by means of the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) which is precisely the cause of taste. That activity of the cause of taste is so described because it has the nature of acting together with the activity of the cause of form toward the production of form.

Therefore, since it is so, just as the taste—which is intended to serve as the logical mark (*liṅga*)—arises from a cause that is exactly as it is, namely from the preceding moment’s collection [of factors] accompanied by the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) whose capacity has been activated, so too, while making known that very same cause, it makes known the color which exists at the same time.
Thus, the meaning is this: such a determination of the reason (*hetu-niścaya*) itself is [the means of knowledge], and nothing else.
— *Pramāṇasamuccaya* [V.10].
Furthermore, there is no inference of an effect subsequent to an inferred cause;
and since the determination of the property of the reason (*hetu*) occurs solely through its being a producer of the effect and not otherwise,
he says "there too" and so forth.
Thus,
by this means, even in the inference of color and so forth from taste and so forth, there is the apprehension of past and simultaneous [objects];
for those [past objects] are co-existent with the time of the material cause of the taste and are themselves past.

The movement of those [elements] which coexist with the manifested rasa at one and the same time cannot be an inference of future states by means of a present sign (*liṅga*), because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*);
for a future state may indeed not occur if it is obstructed by other causes, since a deficiency in those causal conditions is possible.
Furthermore, the inference of tomorrow’s sunrise from today’s sunrise is not a valid inference because it lacks a determining mark (*niyāmaka-liṅga*);
it would be like inferring tomorrow’s sunrise from seeing a donkey today.
Therefore, this cognition of color and so forth from taste and so forth is also an inference based on an effect as its mark (*kārya-liṅga*).

And because a reason is a means of cognition only insofar as it is dependent upon the probandum, for that reason there is no other reason—such as a "conjoined" (saṃyogin) reason—that can produce cognition, apart from the three types of reasons.
Why? Because there is no rule of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) for a nature that is not tied to the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) through identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*).
This is what is meant.
First of all, there is no conjunction of things that are not already joined;
nor is there any need for conjunction even in the case of those that are joined, since they arise from their own causes already joined.
Therefore, the capacity to convey meaning does not depend on conjunction, because [the relationship] is not obstructed [by it].
Just as there is no inherence (*samavāya*) between two distinct jars, so too there is no inherence among things that are separately established (*pṛthaksiddha*).

Furthermore, even for those things that are inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*), what is the need for inherence? Since they arise from their own causes in a successive sequence of one upon another, they do not possess the capacity to indicate [the whole] by means of inherence either.
Furthermore, because it does not depend on the probandum (*sādhya*), there is no inherence (*samavāya*); this will be stated later.
For this very reason, it was previously stated that there is an absence of [inherence] in the case of two things inhering in a single substrate.
Moreover, the contradictory [reason] is included within non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).

And as for that which is stated by the Naiyāyikas—namely, that inference (*anumāna*) is of three kinds: "prior" (*pūrvavat*), "residual" (*śeṣavat*), and "generally observed" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*)—as found in the *Nyāyasūtra* (1.1.5): The translation of the sūtra is as follows: "Inference, moreover, is of three kinds: that which possesses a prior [cause], that which possesses a residue, and that which is generally observed.
In this regard, as before, inference from cause to effect has been established as fallacious; however,
the *śeṣavat* inference— inference from effect to cause— is precisely what is accepted by the author of the treatise.

Inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭam anumānam*), however, is that which, having observed the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans in one locus (*dharmin*), performs an inference regarding another;
for example, having observed Devadatta’s arrival at another location to be preceded by motion, one infers motion in the sun as well from its arrival at another location.
This too is indeed produced from the mark of an effect (*kārya-liṅga*).
Since reaching another location is an effect of motion,
the Master himself will state in the third chapter that all inference is indeed "based on general observation" (sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa);
this is also what was illustrated by Udyotakara as an example of sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa.

As it has been stated in the *Nyāyavārttika* (1.1.5) regarding the determination of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-viniścaya*): "The inference from the crane's nest is likewise based solely on the mark of an effect (*kāryaliṅgaja*).
Therefore, it is established that there is no other probans (*hetu*) capable of conveying knowledge apart from these three types of reasons.
By this— namely, by stating that the inference of color and other qualities from taste and other qualities arises from an effect as its logical mark (kāryaliṅga)— [the following are included]:
the emergence of ants with their eggs carried elsewhere,
and the agitation and transformation of fish.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the expansion of lightning, the croaking of frogs, and so forth are included.

In the phrase "inference of rain, etc.," the word "etc. also indicates the inference of wind and so forth, as that too arises from the inference of the property of a cause based on its effect as a logical mark (*kāryaliṅgaja-hetudharmānumāna*).
He says this very thing with the words "tatrāpi" and so forth;
"tatrāpi" refers to such instances as the swarming of ants and the like.
"The transformation of the elements alone is the cause of rain"— here, the particle "alone" (eva) is displaced [in its logical order],
meaning that the transformation of the elements is indeed the cause of rain.
The cause of such phenomena as the agitation of ants and their subsequent migration is a specific transformation of the elements;
from that causal transformation of the elements as it actually occurs, the alteration of the ants and other creatures arises.
Thus, by inferring the cause as it truly is, one infers the rain and so forth occurring at the same time.
In other cases, however, it is the capacity (*yogyatā*) that is inferred, and not the effect itself, because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the possibility of an obstruction;

therefore, even from a complete collection of causes, there is no inference of the effect, but only an inference of the capacity. As for those such as the Mīmāṃsakas who infer the effect even from an incomplete cause—
Showing that they are utterly excluded from logic, he says:
"But by an incomplete reason," and so forth;
"incomplete" means deficient.
The meaning is that inference based on the remainder (*śeṣavat-anumāna*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Why? Because of its lack of capacity.
The explanation of this is: "For indeed, only those [causes] which are complete," and so forth.
First of all, there is no inference whatsoever of the effect;
for even when [the causes] infer their own capacity (*yogyatā*), they infer only themselves as being complete—this is what is indicated by the word "even" (*api*).
Since that which is incomplete is absolutely incapable, and since it is also incapable through the process of successive transformation, there is not even an occasional inference of the effect.
The explanation of the example "like the inference of passion from the body" begins with "yathā" and so forth;
"dehaś cendriyāṇi ca buddhayaś ca" is a *dvandva* compound [meaning: the body, the sense organs, and the cognitions].

This person possesses passion and so forth, because he possesses a body, because he possesses sense organs, and because he possesses intellect; thus, from the body and other such factors, passion and so forth are inferred—
the word "and so forth" (ādi) including hatred, delusion, and the rest.
In the Sūtra, however, the mention of "attachment to the body" is an elliptical indication; for it is not the sense faculties and so forth alone that are the cause of attachment and the like,
since attachment and the rest are preceded by the deep-seated clinging to a self and what belongs to a self.
The attachment consisting of "I" and "mine" toward the self and what belongs to the self is the primary cause of passion and the other afflictions; for that reason, they are so described.
The phrase "unreasonably" (*ayoniśas*) and so forth is a further elaboration of that very point:
the "source" (*yoni*) of things is their impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and so on.
Because it is the cause for the arising of right view,

one praises it as "ālambate" (it takes hold); "yoniśaḥ" means "one attends to each basis (yoniṃ yoniṃ manaskaroti)," or alternatively, the suffix -śas is used in the sense of repetition (vīpsā) from the singular number.

And that mental attention (*manaskāra*) being of such a nature is "proper mental attention" (*yoniśomanaskāra*). Knowledge of selflessness (*nairātmyajñāna*) is this [proper attention], whereas knowledge of a self and so forth, which is its opposite, is "improper mental attention" (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), because all defects such as passion arise preceded by that [improper attention].
(Pāṇini 5.4.43)

"Is it not the case that the body, the sense faculties, and the intellect are also causes of attachment and so forth, since attachment and so forth are not observed in those who lack them? To this he replies:

"Even though the body and so forth are causes," [meaning] "of those that are alone," that is, of those devoid of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), with respect to the probandum, which is attachment and so forth.

Objects such as pebbles, which are devoid of passion and so forth, constitute the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). In this case, even though the presence of the reason—namely, "possessing a body" and so on—is not observed [in the counter-example], there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding its absence in the opposite case; therefore, this is an inference *śeṣavat* (by elimination). From this, doubt arises rather than certainty.

Just as what was just mentioned is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), so too [the inference] based merely on the non-observation of the reason in the counter-example is not valid, because one observes the general class of effects (*kāryasāmānya*) or the mere effect itself.
Inference based on a specific cause (*hetujñāna*) is a semblance of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*), meaning it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*);
for example,
just as passion and so forth [are inferred] from speech.
Now, one might object: "Since every speech is an effect of passion and so forth, how can it be a general effect [of those causes]?
To this he says, "For not... and so on;
for at the time of speaking, there is necessarily a movement or vibration of the lips.

If it is argued that—by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), other factors such as facial expressions occurring at the time of speaking are also included—and that the mere desire to speak, which is the general intention without distinction, is the cause of those [actions] such as movement, and therefore that very desire to speak is "attachment" (*rāga*): [Response: No, because there is no difference between the two. For the desire to speak is not distinct from attachment; rather, it is simply a specific manifestation of attachment. Furthermore, since the desire to speak is observed even in one who is free from attachment, it cannot be the cause of those [actions]. Moreover, if the desire to speak were the cause, then all actions would have to occur simultaneously, because the desire to speak is present at all times. The Master thinks that because passion (*rāga*) consists of attachment (*āsakti*), nothing is contradicted, since it is [already] accepted [by us]. Thus he says:
"Because it is desired, nothing is sublated."
The desire to speak arises from the wish for the expression of the matter; thus, it is not something undesirable.

Furthermore, the desire to speak is not itself passion (*rāga*); rather, the wise declare that passion is the mental attachment directed toward the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), which has as its object the phenomena associated with outflows (*sāsrava*). This attachment is projected and produced by a view characterized by the adherence to a permanent self, pleasure, and what belongs to a self.
It might be thought:

"Loving-kindness, compassion, and so forth are accepted for those considered to be free from passion (*vītarāga*); yet, because they have sentient beings as their object, they proceed from the view of a self and so on, and by proceeding through attachment to sentient beings, they are by nature characterized by clinging. Therefore, even those free from passion would consequently become possessed of passion. To this, he says:
Compassion and the like are not thus; therefore,
the compassion and other [virtues] of those free from passion do not have sentient beings as their object,
because they can occur in another way as well.

Since it is also possible for [words] to have phenomena (*dharma*) as their objective referent, we shall explain this immediately hereafter. In this context, the connection is as follows: when an inference of passion is being made from speech, there is no comprehension from speech alone, because just as one who is impassioned speaks, so too does one who is dispassionate—even one whose passion has been extinguished.
Inference of passion does not arise from speech in general, but rather from a specific kind of speech that is produced by passion alone; thus he says,
"Nor from a specific [speech]."
What is the reason?
Because intention is difficult to understand;
for one who is dispassionate may behave as if he were passionate.
The intention that "one who is impassioned appears as if dispassionate" is difficult to comprehend;

consequently, due to the confusion of conventional usage, there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in all such statements— whether they be mere utterances or specific utterances— since these are presented as indicators (*liṅga*) of passion and the like.
Regarding what was stated— that even from a distinction one can infer passion and so forth, such as when someone speaks while being detached— an objection is anticipated there,
beginning with the words "prayojana" (purpose), etc.
The utterance of speech constitutes conventional usage (*vyavahāra*);

for there is no purpose in the utterance of speech for one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*). Thus, the point is that there is an invariable concomitance (*avyabhicāra*) between passion and speech.
To this, the Teacher says "no."
There is no lack of purpose, because speech is for the sake of others.

"It is not logical," and so forth; for one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) cannot be attached to others, and there is no engagement in the welfare of others without attachment—this is the sense.
This is not so.
If it is argued that because [the Buddha] acts out of compassion,
that very compassion is attachment (*rāga*), then this is acceptable; for we agree that compassion is given the name "attachment."
If it is argued that compassion is also a fault consisting of passion because it arises from the perversion of viewing sentient beings [as real],
he says "not from perversion," and so forth;
this explains precisely how it arises from non-perversion.
Even in the absence of grasping at a self, and so forth—
merely by perceiving specific forms of suffering, that is, merely by defining the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā)—
compassion indeed arises, produced by the power of habituation; it is generated by successive moments of a similar nature.
Corroborating this also with scripture (*āgama*),
he says "for thus," and so forth; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), those [teachings] that are without an object (*anālambana*) are included.
It has sentient beings as its object for ordinary persons;
it has phenomena as its object for noble ones;
and it is without an object for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who are free from the attachment to grasped and grasper.
Loving-kindness and the others—namely, loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—are accepted in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

But surely these are practiced by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) as having only sentient beings as their object; so how can they be said to have phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth as their objects? To this he says:
"And these [four], loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity..."
Their modes of activity consist in the repeated practice of their own kind, because they arise by the power of preceding similar moments;

however, there is this distinction: as long as one perceives a sentient being, they have a sentient being as their object, and as long as one perceives a phenomenon, they have a phenomenon as their object.
"Not dependent on passion" means that they do not function toward sentient beings by way of a latent tendency (*anuśaya*).

[Objection: But was this meaning not already stated immediately before, namely, that [compassion] is produced by the power of cultivation merely through the perception of specific suffering? [Response:
True.
The distinction is that now [the yogi] relies on compassion alone for all [actions]. [Objection:
"In that case, even when the view of self has ceased, passion and the like would still arise through habituation, just as compassion does. [Reply:
It is not so; passion and the like do not function through habituation to their own kind, such that they would continue to arise even when the view of self has ceased.

If one argues that for a compassionate person, the undertaking for the sake of others would be fruitless because it does not exist in the absence of errors such as [the belief in] a self— since there is no self-interest due to the absence of adherence to a self and so forth resulting from the absence of error—
this is not a fault, because the welfare of others alone is intended to be the fruit.
If it is asked, "The beloved is indeed for the sake of another; how then can it be the result?", he says:
"Desire," and so forth.
"It is characterized by desire" means that it is defined by desire;
the sense is that it is the object of desire, which is to say, whatever is desired is the fruit [of action].
If it is asked: "How can there be activity even for the sake of another in one who lacks the cognition 'I'?"
Some say that the activity [of the mind] is not undefiled because of the presence of knowledge;
others say it is because of the manifestation of pure mundane consciousness through the power of yoga.
Others say that [the Buddha appears] in such a way because he manifests thus to those to be trained;
"in every respect" is the conclusion.
If the desire to speak is proven for one free from passion (*vītarāga*) by means of his speech, then, if that [desire to speak] is compassion (*karuṇā*), he is said to possess passion (*sarāga*).
Since there is no superimposition of what is non-existent in any way, one who is free from passion and so forth is faultless;
for since passion and the like, which are of the nature of faults, necessarily exist,
proving that one free from passion possesses faults by means of something other than those— namely, the desire to speak and so forth— is not at all undesirable.

One might think: "Since attachment and other such qualities are observed in the speaker himself, an inference will occur even regarding those regarded as free from passion, merely by seeing their presence in the similar class (sapakṣa). To this, he says:
"In the speaker himself," and so forth.
Otherwise, there would be the over-extension [of the principle] to the inference of passion and so forth in one who is considered free from passion;
for it would follow that whatever specific quality is observed in the speaker’s own self must be inferred elsewhere as well,
since specific qualities such as being dark or fair observed in the self are subject to deviation.
Regarding the phrase "inference of something other [than passion]": if one infers some specific quality residing in the self that is distinct from passion,
there is no certainty whatsoever as to why there would be no deviation even in the case of passion and the like, which are the very things intended as the probandum here.

Because there is no necessary connection between passion and speech, inference does not follow from the observation of a self; therefore, speech would have to infer both the excellence of the instrument and the desire to speak.
"Excellence of the instrument" refers to the proficiency of the palate and other vocal organs, and "desire to speak" is the wish to utter; these two form a copulative compound (*dvandva*).
This is indeed the dual number of the second case;
for since speech is not observed in relation to stones and the like, which lack the capacity to arouse passion, it is that very capacity which is determined from the speech— thus he says.
Regarding the passage beginning with "rāge" (passion) and ending with "tadanumāne," there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of inferring capacity (*yogyatā*).

To explain: just as there is an absence of the capacity to produce passion in stones and the like, so too there is an absence of all human attributes [in them]. Therefore, if one were to infer the capacity to produce passion simply because such speech is not observed in those things, then by that same logic, one would have to infer all human attributes [in them].

Now, if it is thought that the capacity for the production of passion is indeed the single cause of both passion and speech, and that when this [capacity] is inferred, passion is also inferred by implication— therefore, the inference is only of the capacity and not of all the attributes of a person— to this he says "of passion," and so forth.
If passion (*rāga*) has no utility with respect to speech, since sound is produced solely from the activity of the palate and other organs, how could it have such a capacity?
How then is the capacity of passion utilized for speech?
Or, if it is maintained that at the time of the activity of the palate and other organs, the capacity of passion is also considered to be utilized for speech—

Consequently, at the time of the production of the first letter, passion (*rāga*) is also produced, because it depends upon the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*); and since that passion continues as a stream (*santāna*), it would be exhausted during the production of the second and subsequent letters. Thus he says:
For if it were employed by its own power, it would be that very [power] which is employed;
however, it has already been stated previously that there is no employment of passion (*rāga*) [in this regard].
Alternatively, for those who are free from the attachment to self and what belongs to self (*ātmātmīyābhiniveśa*), there is no employment of passion with respect to speech.
How can that power—the power of attachment known as latent predisposition (*vāsanā*), characterized by the clinging to "self" and "mine"—be applicable to speech?
For among those free from passion, there is an absence of clinging to a self and so forth;
indeed, it is only when such a power is operative that [clinging] occurs with respect to speech.
That very passion would be applicable [to all], because everyone who possesses an adherence to a self and so forth is passionate;
and it has been stated in this context that such passion lacks utility for speech,
because the desire to speak is a general cause.
Therefore, the conclusion beginning with "therefore" (tasmāt) is necessarily inseparable; it is indeed invariably concomitant with the reason,
because of that [logical] connection.
In that case, because [the probandum] is dependent upon the cause, there is nothing else unobstructed; for even if the reason is not observed in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*),
there is no certainty [of its absence] for one of limited vision based on mere non-observation.
However, for the All-Seeing One, certainty arises through the cessation of [ordinary] seeing; for his knowledge pervades all that is knowable.
This very point is stated in the verse beginning with "sarvadarśana" and so forth.
How much less, then, can there be a certainty of non-existence based on mere non-perception?
To this he says: "In some cases it is so," and so forth; [this refers to] those things previously seen in that manner.
Furthermore, the word "distinction" (bheda) is connected with each term in the phrase "by the distinction of place, time, and processing" (deśakālasaṃskārabhedena).
"Processing" (saṃskāra) refers to such things as sprinkling with milk;
it would result in something different from the manner previously observed.
To the question "What is it like?", he says: "Just as with the *āmalaka* fruits.

This is an illustration of the difference in processing (*saṃskāra*), and it is not the case that [sweet fruits] are frequently seen in such abundance; indeed, sweet fruits are not commonly observed in great numbers.
Because astringent fruits are frequently observed,
one does not now— due to the non-observation of sweet fruits in abundance— reject the possibility of a sweet fruit that might occur in some instances.

Likewise, he states this by means of the example of the *āmalakī* fruit: that the production of the date palm (*piṇḍakharjūra*) occurs through difference of place, and that of flowers and so forth occurs through difference of time.
Just as *āmalaka* fruits change through processing with milk and other substances,
so too the mental continuum, which is predisposed toward passion and the like, becomes predisposed through the formative influence (*abhisaṃskāra*) of the practice of reality.
And from such practice, consciousness that has selflessness as its sole object of focus, appearing with clarity, is called dispassion (*vairāgya*).
Because, through the vision of selflessness, attachment and other afflictions do not arise due to the disappearance of clinging to a self and so forth,
and because knowledge that takes the momentariness of all phenomena and such as its object becomes clearly manifest, it is called omniscience,
owing to the total removal of all ignorance.

Therefore, it is precisely the increase in clarity resulting from the practice of reality (*tattva*) that, by means of the direct perception of reality, brings about its manifestation as direct perception and subverts the nature of cognition that is susceptible to passion and the like.
Consequently, even if something has been observed otherwise, it may yet become otherwise through the force of causes;
thus, even if no speech is observed in someone devoid of passion in a particular instance, there is no certainty that one cannot expect speech from a person free of passion in every case.
Furthermore, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not ascertained, there can be no inference of passion and so forth from mere speech;
for this reason, it is improper to say that a speaker like me— who, like you, possesses improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*)— is such a speaker.
He says that very thing in the passage beginning with "rāgotpatti" (the arising of passion), and then asks: "But who is this? and provides the answer.

The view of a self and so forth refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); it is the inversion of permanence, pleasure, and so on, which constitutes improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*).

This is a *dvandva* compound, meaning "unwise attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) is indeed the view of self (*ātmadarśana*"); or it is a descriptive (*viśeṣaṇa*) compound, meaning "at that time, one like me speaks. Even with such a qualification, the citation of the statement is purposeless.
The meaning is that the example for the reason "because of speech" is purposeless;
for in that case, the reason would simply be: "Whoever is like me, being endowed with a specific condition for the arising of passion, is passionate, just as I am."

Since there is no certainty [of absence] based merely on such non-perception, one might think that the non-observation of the reason in the counter-example—that is, its not being seen in the *vipakṣa*—would constitute the ascertainment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the logical mark. One might further think: "The reason would be fallacious if it were observed in the counter-example; however, speech is not observed in those free from passion (*vītarāga*). Therefore, due to this non-observation, the negative concomitance is established in the absence of the probandum. To this, he says:
Nor is there non-deviation of the reason from the counter-example (vipakṣa) by mere non-perception;
why?
Because deviation is possible.

That for which deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is possible is "one in whom it is possible"; the state of being such is "possibility of deviation. Even if [the reason] has not been observed in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), nevertheless, its presence there is not contradictory; thus, deviation is considered possible, just like the cooking of rice grains contained within a pot (*sthālītaṇḍula*).
In order to support this very illustration,
he says "for not," and so forth:
even when those things inside a pot are seen to have been cooked in abundance, cooking is not established by the mere fact of being inside the pot.
The inclusion of the word "only" (mātra), however, is for the purpose of excluding specific cases;
for as he will say, "let it be thus," how could there be a lack of proof, since deviation is observed?
"Having such a nature" means that those which are seen to be ripe possess a nature identical to them;
those whose cause of ripening is the same as these very ripe ones are "ripe.
Otherwise, however—if this qualification were not present—[the definition would be flawed].

"Remainder exists" (*śeṣosti*) means that there is an unascertained object; and since that is fallacious, he asks: "Is the *śeṣavat* inference intended here—the one described by the Naiyāyikas as the inference of a cause from an effect—or is it something else entirely?"
"What more," and so forth,
he states the nature of the *śeṣavat* [inference] with the words "of which," and so forth.
