When the absence [of a reason] from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is established by the mere non-perception of that reason—which lacks any means of valid cognition—that inference is illustrated as being "like the remainder" (*śeṣavat*), because that reason is a cause for doubt, meaning it produces uncertainty. Why is this so? Because since that exclusion (*vyatireka*) of the reason is not certain, its presence in the dissimilar class might still be suspected.
Why, then, is it not certain? He says: "The absence... and so forth. To the question, "How can there be doubt even when there is non-perception? he says:
"Not all," and so forth:
it is not merely the non-perception of the perceptible that establishes [the absence];

for since the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) does not follow from mere non-observation, one who desires the exclusion of the probandum through the exclusion of the probans—that is, the exclusion of the other—must accept some essential connection (*pratibandha*) between those two, the probandum and the probans, characterized by either identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*).
It is not merely non-perception;
otherwise, the reason would fail to establish the undesired state of the connection, because the pervasion (vyāpti) would remain unascertained.

For this very reason, for that cause, the determination [of the logical mark] in all three forms— the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)— has been described by the Master Dignāga in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* and other works,
starting with the passage: "But that which is unestablished for both [parties] is not a means of proof," and so forth.
To the question "By the exclusion of what?", he says "asiddha," etc.;
because it belongs to the group beginning with *ādi*, the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the instrumental case, meaning "by the counter-example" (*vipakṣeṇa*).

In this context, the determination of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is described by means of its opposite, the unestablished (*asiddha*); the determination of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is described by means of its opposite, the contradictory (*viruddha*), which has a contrary meaning;
and the determination of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is described by means of its opposite, the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), which is characterized by deviation.
Furthermore, by describing the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is indeed shown implicitly;
for when there is no necessary connection, there can be no ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance.
Therefore, by demonstrating that very connection—characterized as identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*)—the author states the ascertainment while implying it.
He explains that certainty which was stated regarding the non-expectation of a particular fault with the words "In that case," and so forth;
[the phrase] "of those that are contradictory and those belonging to the side of the contradictory" refers to both the contradictory [reasons] and those belonging to the side of the contradictory.

Those [reasons] which possess presence in the contradictory class (*viruddhapakṣya*)—where their presence in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is certain, but their presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) is doubtful—are indeed "doubtful inconclusives" (*sandigdhānaikāntika*). This statement is made according to what is established by others; however, the connection with the subject at hand is that this is so because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not certain.
The connection is "the exclusion of the inconclusive [reason].
By this, the meaning is as follows: [it refers] to the common inconclusive [reason] and to that position.
And by the term "anaikāntika" (inconclusive),
there is the exclusion of the "śeṣavat" type [of inference] and others;
by the word "ādi" (etc.), there is the exclusion of that which is doubtful regarding both the similar instance (sapakṣa) and the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa).

Now he explains the passage from the Master’s treatise beginning with “of the two,” which states: “That [reason] for which there is presence in the similar class (sapakṣa) and for which there is negative concomitance (vyatireka) merely through non-observation in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) is ‘with remainder’ (śeṣavat); however, it is well-known as being of two kinds.
This is the text beginning with “of the two” and so forth.

By the phrase "of the two," the connection is as follows: the negation of that which is established for either the proponent or the opponent by the statement of what is well-known [is the subject]; and the negation of the two types of [reasons]—those that are doubtful and those that are uncommon (asādhāraṇa), like the *śeṣavat*—is [the predicate].
To the question "Of which two doubtful ones? he says:
The phrase "also in the case of the similar and dissimilar instances" implies that for the *śeṣavat* [reason], there is doubt regarding the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*),
whereas for the *asādhāraṇa* [reason], there is doubt regarding both the similar and dissimilar instances.
Therefore, by his statement regarding certainty, the Master [Dignāga] also accepts the necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

Otherwise, if the teacher were to accept a negative concomitance (vyatireka) based merely on the non-observation [of the reason] in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa), while there exists no other obstacle to the relationship between the probandum and the probans,

then the statement of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-vacana)— which was asserted as the counter-argument against the inconclusive (anaikāntika) due to its deviant dissimilar instance— would be purposeless; this is the intended meaning.
But where was it promised by the Teacher? He says:
"When," and so forth; this was stated in the *Nyāyamukha*.

Regarding the statement that "both must be stated," namely similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), he says "contradictory" (*viruddha*) and so forth, to explain what has been said as a counter-argument to what.

The statement of the proof (*sādhana*) serves as the counter-position to the contradictory; the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-vacana*) serves as the counter-position to the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, that which has non-perception as its result is merely a result of non-perception; such is the statement of dissimilarity.
He explains this very point with the words "If," and so forth;
by that statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the non-observation of the reason (*hetu*) in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is made known.

Thus, even when dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is not explicitly stated, non-perception (*adarśana*) is understood; since non-perception, characterized by the absence of perception, is established even prior to the statement of dissimilarity,
the statement of dissimilarity is therefore redundant.

If it is argued that there exists a misconception regarding the reason in the counter-example (vipakṣa), and that the statement of dissimilar instance (vaidharmya) is for the purpose of removing that [misconception],
he replies with "na hi" and so forth;
[the meaning is] "of that," i.e., of the person to be instructed, prior to the statement of the dissimilar instance.
If it is argued that there exists a mistaken perception regarding the reason's presence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), which is removed by the statement of its absence (*vaidharmya-vacana*);

therefore, just as there is no error in perceiving the reason in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) but it has been forgotten, and thus it is recalled by the statement of similarity (*sādharmya-vacana*),
so too the recollection of its non-perception in the dissimilar instance is produced by the verbal statement of dissimilarity.
In order to refute the very example [adduced by the opponent], he says "darśanam" and so forth:

it is logical that a perception (*darśana*) which is not being experienced and is not being remembered is not a factor for the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhyapratipatti*); thus, in that case of perception, there is the "instilling of memory" (*smaraṇādhāna*), which is the production of a memory (*smṛtijanana*), by means of speech.
However, non-perception as a [valid] means of knowledge is not tenable,
because non-perception is simply the absence of perception; and that [absence] in the counter-example (vipakṣa) is sublated by perception.

In the absence of that—that is, in the absence of seeing the counter-example—the absence of seeing is already established; therefore, the statement of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) for the sake of establishing that, i.e., for the sake of establishing the absence of seeing, is redundant.
The intention [behind this objection] is that since seeing is beyond the senses (parokṣa), it might be forgotten, and thus a statement is appropriate for the purpose of remembering it.
However, the absence of seeing consists in the cessation of seeing, and that manifests precisely from the absence of the experience of seeing.
And what is the use of memory for that which is already appearing?
To establish it, such a statement is purposeless.

Indeed, for a person who does not perceive [an object], there can be no certainty that "the reason is absent in the counter-example" based on mere non-perception alone; for even when things are remote in space and so forth, they may still exist despite being unperceived.
If it is argued that the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is for the purpose of producing the certainty that "it does not exist," that is not so;
because that which is being negated does not simply cease to exist merely by a word such as "it does not exist" which lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).
How, then, is it understood that "it does not exist"? To this he says:
"Such as" (*yathā*) and so forth;
this is what is meant:

the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of the reason with its own probandum is that which apprehends its dependence upon the probandum, and it is this "observation" (*darśana*) that is intended here. And that observation of the reason only in the presence of the probandum is itself the non-observation of it in every instance of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).

The meaning is this: for that very person whose perception grasping the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) has occurred but been forgotten, the recollection is produced by means of the statements of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) once the [respective] perceptions and non-perceptions have been cognized; it is not so for anyone else.
As it has been said: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is demonstrated by means of the two examples (*dṛṣṭānta*)."
"Just as it is said that 'if it does not exist, it is made known'— that is,

by whatever means or in whatever manner the reason (*hetu*) does not exist in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) due to its necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with its own probandum (*sādhya*), if that principle— the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which apprehends that connection— is made known or remembered, then it is understood that [the reason] does not exist;
but this is not so without the connection."
He states the first portion of the verse beginning with "yadi" (*if*,

etc.): if one, not perceiving [something], does not conclude that it is non-existent based on mere non-perception, then one will likewise not conclude [its non-existence] from a statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) that lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*),
because that statement of dissimilarity is also [of that nature].

By that [statement], he indicates precisely non-apprehension and nothing more; it would not be a further distinction. It is held that the absence of the reason caused by the absence of the probandum is indicated by the statement of dissimilar instance (vaidharmya).
Since there is a distinction [between these cases], he says "nor is it one," and so forth;
"non-apprehension of one" refers to the non-apprehension of the probandum (*sādhyānupalambha*).
The meaning is that the absence of another [thing] and the absence of the means of proof [do not follow] when there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*),

because of the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For if cessation occurred without a necessary connection, then by the cessation of a cow, there would necessarily be the cessation of a horse as well.

Now, if it is thought that because the Master [Dignāga] stated that the reason does not exist in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa), certainty arises for that very reason, he says "na ca" and so forth.

Therefore, because that noble one has made the statement regarding dissimilarity (vaidharmya) that "it does not exist," it follows that the non-existence of the entity itself would occur, due to the consequence of over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

For if that statement were authoritative, the proof of the probandum (sādhya) would result from the mere thesis (pratijñāmātra). Thus, how can the exclusion of the inconclusive (anaikāntika) be achieved by means of a statement of dissimilarity?
Therefore, one who desires the exclusion [of the reason] from that counter-example must state the logical principle regarding that exclusion;
for according to the rule: "The logical principle is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which apprehends the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probandum and the probans."
"Is this not so? and so forth is the opponent's objection, [intending] that there is a certainty regarding the proof of what is to be established— that it is an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
In the absence of that [the probandum], because of its non-perception when the probandum is absent, the exclusion of the reason is established; this very logic is what is intended.
If the exclusion of the reason from the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) were based merely on non-observation, then why would inference *śeṣavat* not be fallacious? It would indeed be fallacious.
He asks, "What, then, is that like? and says "Just as," etc.; these fruits are those other than what has been consumed.
And this is the statement of the subject (*dharmin*):
"these fruits"; and "if they have such tastes" is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), namely, that they have such tastes as being sweet or sour.
The reason is "because there is no difference in form," meaning because it is identical to the form— such as redness and so forth— of the fruit that has already been consumed.
"Or because it originates from a single branch" is the reason (*hetu*);
"like that which has been consumed" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

He states [the following] because, if a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) were desired based on mere non-perception, there would be a lack of invariable concomitance (*avyabhicāritva*) in the case of the *śeṣavat* inference.
Regarding the passage beginning with "atrāpi" and so forth:

here, in the case of the *śeṣavat* inference, when the entire remainder of the fruit—other than that which has been consumed and endowed with specific characteristics such as its particular form—is made the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no non-perception of the reason (the remaining form, etc. in the absence of the probandum. Consequently, because it is excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), there would be non-deviation (*avyabhicāritā*).

For instance, apart from that which has been made the subject (*pakṣa*), namely the fruit, and that which is employed as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), there is no occurrence of the aforementioned reason in a third category consisting of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). [Objection:

There is a suspicion of sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) and so forth, because it is possible to perceive through direct experience a fruit produced on a single branch that is either unripe or lacks that specific taste; thus, some, such as Īśvarasena and others, maintain that the "residual" (*śeṣavat*) inference is fallacious due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Thus, the meaning is this: a reason is not a means of cognition through mere positive and negative concomitance alone, but rather when its object is uncontradicted;
he refutes [the objection] with the words "not," etc., because there is an absence of contradiction by perception regarding that hidden object which has been made the subject of the thesis.
If it is argued that there is no suspicion of sublation by an active perception, but rather a possibility of sublation by the perception of odor at some time,
[the author] replies with "tathā" and so forth;
for if there were such a suspicion that sublation by perception might occur at some time, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
The point is that because there is no rule that perception cannot subvert a reason accepted by another party—
since, upon accepting a [logical] connection, the suspicion of subversion by the opponent does not cease—
one who does not accept an essential connection (pratibandha) must admit that an established means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) serves as the subverting factor.

If sublation were to occur through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that has not itself been established, there would be a lack of confidence in all cases; that is, there would be no assurance—no certainty regarding the capacity to prove—the reason (*hetu*), because a sublater might always be suspected.

However, this is not so for one who maintains the theory of essential connection (*pratibandha*); for when a reason is essentially connected to the probandum (*sādhya*), there is no suspicion of sublation whatsoever in any case.
However, prior to the application of the reason (*hetu*), there might be a suspicion of sublation;
for this very reason, the statement of the reason is said to be made when [the matter] is doubtful.
And there is no established means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates the inference based on the remainder (*śeṣavat*).

Therefore, it remains established that if there is a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based on mere non-perception, there would be non-deviation even for the "remainder-like" (*śeṣavat*) inference.

Now, one might object: "By the force of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), when there is a negative concomitance of the reason in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*), the negative concomitance would be indicative by its mere existence. To this, he says:
"But as for the negative concomitance," and so forth.
That exclusion of the reason from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is indeed established and certain as the means of proof;

thus, it requires the ascertainment that the reason exists in such a manner [in the similar class], namely, the ascertainment that the absence of the reason follows upon the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*). This is what he says.
For us, as for you, exclusion is not merely due to the absence of perception;

rather, when there is a necessary connection between the probandum and the probans, the property inherent in the reason is its exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) upon the absence of the probandum.
Furthermore, whatever is the nature of the reason necessarily depends upon its own ascertainment, because it is a means of cognition.
If it is asked, "How is the *śeṣavat* [reason] fallacious according to your view?", he says:
"But because of non-perception," and so forth;
for even if the absence of the reason in some part of the heterologue (*vipakṣa*) is established, the reason remains unconnected to the probandum (*sādhya*).

In the absence of that [the reason], because its non-existence in all instances of the counter-example (vipakṣa)—that is, in the absence of the probandum—is not established, there arises doubt. Consequently, that very lack of exclusion from the counter-example constitutes the fallacy of "deviation" (vyabhicāra) for the *śeṣavat* inference; the particle "ca" (and) serves to aggregate this with other defects. Furthermore, if exclusion were based merely on non-observation, then even a purely negative (*vyatirekin*) reason would become a valid logical mark.

This was stated by way of a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga), beginning with the question "Of what kind would this be if it were soulless? and so forth; for [if it were soulless], it would follow that it lacks breath and other such functions, whereas because it possesses breath and other such functions, it is endowed with a soul.

And this reason (hetu) is not observed anywhere among things possessing a self (sātmaka), yet it is excluded from things devoid of a self (nirātmaka); thus, because it possesses the property of being absent when the probandum is absent, it is said to be non-deviant (avyatirekin).

For instance, since breath and so forth—namely, the inhalation, exhalation, opening, and closing of the eyes—are not observed in jars and other objects that are devoid of a self and lack a soul, whether those objects are perceived or unperceived;

and in the case of those that are perceived, their non-observation is due solely to the non-apprehension of their own nature, because breath and the like meet the conditions for perceptibility (upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta).
Even regarding those [objects] not yet perceived, because they belong to that same class,
selflessness is pervaded by the absence of breath and so forth;

however, in the case of a living body, through the cessation of that [absence], there is the cessation of the absence of possessing breath and so forth, and thus the cessation of selflessness would result in the cognition of a self.
If it is asked, "In that case, how is it a cause for doubt? he says:
"Because the self is invisible," and so forth.

Since the nature of jars and the like is not established due to the non-perception of the invisible self, and because the absence of self (nairātmya) in jars and the like is therefore unestablished, there is no exclusion of breath and so forth from that which is devoid of self.
The meaning is that because the absence of breath and so forth is doubtful, the selflessness (*nairātmya*) is likewise unestablished.
If it is argued that since selflessness has been accepted by the Buddhist, the lack of a self in jars and other things is established by virtue of that acceptance—
then if the Buddhist’s own acceptance were a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how could the existence of a self in a living body be established now?
Even that [body] is accepted by the Buddhist as being without self;
since the acceptance of selflessness regarding the living body lacks authoritative means of knowledge (*apramāṇaka*), if you therefore seek to prove a self for it,
then how could the proof of selflessness for anything other than the living body— such as a jar and the like— not also lack authoritative means of knowledge?
For a Buddhist does not maintain that his own assertion is a valid means of knowledge in some cases and not in others;

moreover, by mere assertion alone, one distinguishes between things with a self and those without a self, and since jars and the like are asserted as being without a self both by the opponent and by us,
they are therefore without a self.

The living body has been accepted by us as having a self (*sātmaka*), whereas you have maintained it to be without a self (*nirātmaka*). Thus, by distinguishing between the two and asserting that vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth serve as indicators for the existence of a self only when they are absent from those things lacking a self, the opponent has admitted that the self is known through scripture (*āgamika*) and not through inference (*anumeya*). Therefore, even though the self is not observed in objects such as jars, its absence is not established because its nature is inherently unobservable; consequently, there is no exclusion of vital breaths and the like from anything that is soulless, and thus these are not indicators [of the self]. In this way, the exclusion of the self from anything whatsoever is certainly not established.
However, even granting [the opponent's position], it is said:

"Even when that [breath] ceases, and even when the self ceases, in some cases"—that is, although breath and so forth cease in observed objects such as jars, because there is no obstruction [to their cessation] and because there is no necessary connection with the self, the cessation of breath and so forth is not established by the cessation of the self even in all unobserved cases such as jars; therefore, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful, [the reason] is non-probative.
If one accepts a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based on mere non-perception, there is this further fault; thus he says "yāpi" and so forth.
To the question "What, then, is that [fault]?", he says:

Likewise, regarding the statement "present in the similar class" (*sapakṣe san*) and so forth, this is the text of the Master (*Ācārya*); therein, it was stated that the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is understood as being ascertained by both the proponent (*vādin*) and the opponent (*prativādin*).
Therefore, this excludes both types of unestablished [reasons]: the unestablished in itself (*svarūpāsiddha*) and the unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).

Just as the fourfold unestablished is excluded by the ascertainment of the reason’s presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), so too is the entire class of unestablished reasons—such as those that are "present in the similar instances" (*sapakṣe san*) or "absent from the similar instances" (*sapakṣe asan*)—eliminated by the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). This is because the various forms of unestablished reasons, such as the "unestablished for one party" (*anyatarāsiddha*), cannot possibly exist within the similar instances and so forth;
he says that these should be illustrated accordingly.
Nor should it be said that this is an application of non-establishment (*asiddhi*);
for he explains that very point with the words "it is simply non-perception," and so forth,
because when there is non-perception lacking a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*), there remains doubt regarding the presence of the reason (*hetu*) in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
How so? Because that [doubt] is impossible upon perception;
for when the reason (*hetu*) is perceived in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), that doubt does not exist.
Therefore, by virtue of this reason of non-perception, there is exclusion from the counter-example; thus, in effect, a reason with a doubtful exclusion (*sandigdhavyatireka*) is indeed accepted.

If it is argued that, therefore, a doubtful negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—rendered doubtful by uncertainty—is unavoidable and cannot be excluded, and that because of the phrase "as the case may be" (*yathāyogam*), such a doubtful instance is indeed not prohibited, and should be cited accordingly; [Response: [This is not so.]...
This is not so;
for immediately following that, there is the statement beginning with "But that very [term] which expresses what is certain for both," and so forth.

That very word which denotes the three-fold nature (trairūpya) as ascertained by both parties, or [the fallacies such as] unestablishedness (asiddhatva), is the proof (sādhana) or the refutation (dūṣaṇa); it is not, however, that which expresses what is established or doubtful for only one of the two, because that would require further proof. This passage is the illustration here.
Whatever one of the two—either the proponent or the opponent—states that is unestablished (*asiddha*) or doubtful (*sandigdha*), that is neither a proof (*sādhana*) nor a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).

A reason whose negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful cannot be a certain cause [of knowledge] for either party, because it remains doubtful in both the heterologue (*vipakṣa*). Therefore, the statement of such [a reason] is not a proof.

Since it has been stated that only a reason (hetu) certain in both respects [in its presence and absence] is valid, one who— despite non-perception— suspects the non-exclusion of the reason from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) due to doubt regarding its cessation, declares the invalidity of such a reason whose negative concomitance (vyatireka) is doubtful by way of demonstrating its lack of proof. Furthermore, if cessation were intended to be established merely through non-observation, then specific properties such as audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*), which are unique to the subject, would become reasons for exclusion.
What is the reason?
Because of the non-perception of the eternal and the non-eternal;
he explains that as follows.
"Of audibility as well," and so forth;
for it is held that exclusion [from a locus] occurs merely through non-perception,
and there is indeed a non-perception of [the property] in both the permanent and the impermanent.

The property of audibility would be the cause for its exclusion [from the class of impermanent things], and it would thus become the cause for the negation of both permanence and impermanence; for if audibility were indeed excluded from that [class of impermanent things] due to non-perception, one might ask: "From where does it derive the status of being the cause for that exclusion? To this, he says:
"No," [he replies].
For there is no exclusion other than the exclusion of that; thus, the exclusion of the eternal and the non-eternal is [the same as] the exclusion of that.
If it is asked, "How then is audibility not the cause of exclusion for you either? he says:
Because there is no exclusion—

since, from the mere fact of non-perception, one cannot ascertain the exclusion [of a thing] from anything permanent or impermanent, as expressed in the passage beginning with "adṛṣṭatvāt" and so forth.
And there is uncertainty because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with either one [of the two] is not established.

This must necessarily be so; otherwise, if a property (*dharma*) is ascertained to be absent in a certain locus (*dharmin*), how could that same property, when it exists, not indicate the absence of that [other] property which was ascertained to be absent? Even in the case of audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*), which is excluded from both the eternal and the non-eternal, if one were to suspect a contradiction by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-bādhā*) regarding the proof of the exclusion of both, [it would be untenable].
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "athāpi" is an explanation of this very point:

if there exists another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates [the argument] when one intends to prove the exclusion of both [eternal and non-eternal] through the property of being audible (*śrāvaṇatvena*),
then he states it as follows.
"Mutually," and so forth:
those whose nature consists in mutual exclusion are "such";

for indeed, impermanence is simply the exclusion of permanence, and permanence is simply the exclusion of that [impermanence]; likewise, non-existence is simply the exclusion of existence, and existence is simply the exclusion of non-existence.
Because one [of the two] is excluded while the other is affirmed, and because the second is the affirmation of a contradictory [term], there is no negation;
this is what is meant.
For when audibility is excluded from the eternal— meaning it would differentiate itself from that— it would thereby establish impermanence;
and since that very same [audibility] is excluded from the impermanent, it would thereby differentiate the impermanent.

And since [the opponent] maintains that [the self] exists eternally, there would have to be both injunction and prohibition for the same thing at the very same time; and that is illogical. Because injunction and prohibition are mutually contradictory, there can be no prohibition of anything whatsoever.

For an injunction is characterized by the cessation of a prohibition, while a prohibition is simply the cessation of an injunction. How could these two, being mutually opposed, exist simultaneously in one and the same thing?
Therefore, there is no certainty regarding exclusion from anything whatsoever on account of audibility;
thus says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) when there is no possibility of sublation by the term "now."
If it is argued: "Because [the reason] is not seen, its non-existence in the counter-example (vipakṣa) is established;
therefore, when this is the case, non-perception is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), since there is no possibility of sublation (bādhā).
Let it be that audibility alone is not a valid cognition, but not so for others, because there is no sublation [in their cases]," to this he says:
"In the same way," and so forth;

elsewhere too, why should there be the possibility of sublation by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the non-perception that establishes the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason?
Regarding the passage beginning with *lakṣaṇa*:

the definition of the reason (*hetu*) is that it is based on the exclusion [of the reason] from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). When there is no possibility of sublation (*bādhā*) regarding the non-perception of audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) as characterized by that definition, then that very definition of such non-perception—which serves as the means for establishing the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—would have its universal scope and essential nature (*svarūpa*) undermined. Consequently, there would be no confidence in non-perception everywhere as a means of establishing negative concomitance, nor any certainty regarding its capacity to prove [the conclusion].
If this is so, then even in the domain of inference, contradictions between perception and inference are observed in certain cases;

for instance, when it is argued that "sound is eternal because it is audible, like the nature of sound (*śabdatva*)," its eternity is sublated by inference. Likewise, [the claim] that "sound is inaudible because it exists, like a jar," is sublated by perception.
And if it is argued that, consequently, there would be a lack of confidence even in inference based on the remaining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in all cases,

this is not so; for, as has been stated, in an inference produced by a logical mark (*liṅga*) consisting of effect, essential nature, or non-perception (*anupalambha*), there is no contradiction with perception or inference.

Since that which is subject to contradiction by perception and so forth cannot possess the definition [of a valid reason], and since such [contradiction] is not a defining characteristic of inference,

if there were no sublation (*bādhā*) in an inference possessing the aforementioned definition, then two reasons endowed with the characteristics of a reason (*hetu-lakṣaṇa-yukta*) that establish mutually contradictory objects would descend upon a single locus (*dharmin*). If it is argued that the Master [Dignāga] did not mention this [type of reason called] "the non-deviant contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*), [the author] states by this [passage] that [such an argument] results in the abandonment of one's own accepted position (*abhyupetahāni*).

Since the mention of the "contradictory-vague" (*viruddhavyabhicārin*) fallacy and so forth regarding the object of inference is indeed accepted [by us], how could there be an abandonment of what was previously asserted?
To the question, "Where then did the Teacher say this?", he replies with the words "And the object," and so on.

Regarding this "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) reason, [the author] says "kiṃca" and so forth; here, indeed, the Vaiśeṣika has stated the sūtra, "And touch, and [the fact that it is] not seen among [visible] things," for the purpose of proving the existence of air (*vāyu*).
This is its meaning:

whatever is a quality (guṇa) is that which resides in a substance (dravyāśrayī), such as color-form (rūpa) and so forth, as well as touch that is not produced by heat and is neither hot nor cold; since these are qualities, there must therefore exist a substance that serves as their substratum.
Nor is this a quality of the perceived elements such as earth and the rest, because they possess qualities such as touch that is produced by heating and is neither hot nor cold;
therefore, when it was stated by the Vaiśeṣika that "that which possesses this quality must be air," the Master Diṅnāga replied to that effect.

The author of the *Vārttika*, demonstrating that the statement "if a negation is made based on mere non-perception regarding things that have been seen, that too is not tenable" is contradictory, says: "dṛṣṭa... and so forth.

If cessation were to occur through non-perception, then because of that non-perception— due to the cause of not seeing it— the previously described "inconsistency of what is not produced by cooking," namely the lack of connection with the tangible qualities of neither-hot-nor-cold in earth and the other [elements] as asserted by the Vaiśeṣikas, would be "not inconsistent"; that is to say, it would indeed be logical.

As for what the Teacher [Vātsyāyana] stated in the section on Air (*vāyu-prakaraṇa*): "If the Vaiśeṣika were to negate touch in earth and the other elements merely because it is not perceived, that too would not be logical"—if the Teacher also intended a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based on mere non-perception, then how could the negation of touch be improper? It would indeed be perfectly logical.
"What is the reason?
Because here too, since non-existence is established through the non-perception of a cause, [non-existence] is accepted.
Thus begins the objection of the opponent with the words "nanu" and so forth.

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) asks: "Is the negation of a touch that is neither hot nor cold—which is not perceived and which, being produced by causes, meets the conditions for perception (upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta)—in earth and the other elements logical? Or is it not logical? What is the reason?"
That which is perceptible, such as earth and so forth, when endowed with a touch other than hot or cold, is visible;
and even where it is not perceptible, such as in another location, earth and so forth are likewise endowed with that same kind of touch and possess that nature.
This is a *dvandva* compound meaning "both visible and possessing that nature."

"That very [object] is the object; that alone is 'tanmātra'—this is a *sup-supā* compound. Since there is no prohibition regarding that, if there were a prohibition of touch (*sparśa*) therein, then certainty would indeed arise. However, this Vaiśeṣika states the prohibition of touch by grasping the substratum, such as earth and so forth, in a general and undifferentiated manner."
Whatever exists, such as earth and so forth, all that is devoid of a touch that is neither hot nor cold;
furthermore, there is no attainment of the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpti*) of touch in earth and the other elements alone,
nor is there a restriction to a single touch in earth and the others.

Because, in that case, although the generalities such as earth and so forth persist in their particulars—such as cotton, stones, and sprouts—and although the nature of earth and so forth remains present, a difference in touch is observed;
for instance, the touch of cotton is of one kind, characterized by smoothness, while that of stones and the like is of another kind, characterized by roughness and so forth.

Regarding this [touch] as well—namely, the touch that is neither hot nor cold—one must consider that it might possibly exist in some particular kind of earth-substance; therefore, a negation of the touch that is neither hot nor cold based merely on its non-perception in all instances of earth and so forth is improper.
As for what is said:

Since earth and the other elements are uniform everywhere, the touch that is neither hot nor cold must likewise be uniform; as for the variation in smoothness and so forth that occurs despite the presence of earth and the others, that is caused by the density or lack of density of the conjunctions of the atoms of earth and the others—
this is incorrect, for in the case of non-dense [atoms], there is an absence of conjunction due to the absence of immediate contiguity (*nairantarya*).

Therefore, just as there is density in the conjunction of stone-atoms (*upalaparamāṇu*), so too would there be in cotton-atoms (*tūlaparamāṇu*); how then could there be a distinction such as smoothness and so forth?

Consequently, even though conjunction exists, stone-atoms are by their very nature different from cotton-atoms, and it is precisely this [difference in nature] that causes the distinction of smoothness and so forth, not the density or lack of density of the conjunction.

And thus, just as there is a distinction in touch—such as smoothness and so forth—due to the distinctions of earth and the other elements, so too a distinction of "neither-hot-nor-cold" might be possible. [Objection: Let it not be so in the case of the unperceived object; however, in the case of the perceived object, since the neither-hot-nor-cold touch that is actually observed is not found to belong to earth and the other elements, the inference of air (*vāyu*) would proceed from that. This is what is being thought.

If the quality-nature of touch and so forth were established, then there would be an inference of the substance air; however, that very [quality-nature] is unestablished because [touch] is perceived independently. Moreover, for us, air is said to be merely a particular kind of touch.
However, the Master Dignāga, having accepted that air is distinct from touch, stated that the inference of another [opponent] regarding it is untenable; thus, there is no fault.

Therefore, this remains established: by stating that there is an absence of negation based merely on the non-observation of positive and negative concomitance, the Master intended a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
If it is asked, "Who then is being thus reproached?", he says "evam" and so forth;
"evam" means by means of the arguments just stated.
A certain disciple of the Teacher, who was ignorant of the Teacher’s treatises, was rebuked for asserting non-existence on the grounds of non-perception.
Furthermore, in order to demonstrate the contradiction with direct perception that would arise if one were to accept non-existence based merely on the failure to observe something, [the author] says:
"Because of differences in location and so forth..."
Due to differences in time and processing (saṃskāra), as indicated by the word "etcetera" (ādi),
various potencies characterized by taste, potency (vīrya), post-digestive transformation (vipāka), and so forth, are seen to be distinct and manifold even among substances of a single genus.

In that case— among substances possessing multiple potencies— it is not logical to determine the existence of a certain property in another place and so on, based on the observation of a single nature in a substance through a single perception.
The determination of the nature of a thing as it has been observed is explained by the passage beginning with "yadi" (if).

If, merely because the reason is not observed in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), its non-deviation from its own probandum— that is, its non-deviation from the probandum— is accepted for that which is unconnected [to it], [then there would be an over-extension].
In that case, the form of a substance perceived in one place would have to be inferable from the commonality of the substance in another place as well;
for at that time, there is likewise merely the non-perception of the reason in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) there too,
and this is not tenable.

He states the subject matter with the words "yathā" and so forth: because in a certain place some substances are seen in a certain way by virtue of having specific tastes and other qualities, yet they are seen elsewhere in a different way, that is, contrary to the form as previously observed.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: *pariṇāma* (transformation) is the power to eliminate the defects of potency (*vīrya*); those [substances] which possess specific potencies, potencies, and transformations are [referred to by this term].
"Not elsewhere" means other than in that specific field;
just as [qualities differ] due to a specific location, so too do they possess distinct tastes, potencies, and post-digestive transformations due to differences in time and processing (*saṃskāra*).
"Processing" refers to the application of substances such as milk and the like.

Nor can it be established that all things—even those not located in that same place—are identical in their true nature by virtue of having the same form and so forth, on the grounds that they have been seen to possess such specific tastes and qualities as those found in the persons residing in that region.
Why? Because other qualities, namely the specific variations of taste and so forth, depend upon other causes.
In the absence of a specific reason [to the contrary], however, there would be an inference of a single nature:
that which has an unseen author, such as the Veda, is likewise preceded by human refinement and caused by human effort.
And this result to be proven—the fact that there is no distinction between sentences intended to be of human origin and those not of human origin—is stated here as the reason (*hetu*).
The formal application (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever entity has a nature non-different from another, that must have the same causes.

Just as a single instance of smoke belongs to the same class as other instances of smoke, so too do those sentences regarded as non-human (apauruṣeya) possess a nature that is not distinct from human-authored sentences; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu),
and the reason is not unestablished (asiddha).
For instance, since all those various methods by which the removal of poison and so forth is achieved— through which the Vaidikas claim their superiority— are observed to be produced by human agents;
for even in the case of mantras such as those of the Śabaras, the removal of poison and other such effects are seen to occur.

If, on the grounds of the similarity in the nature of sound, it is inferred that even that which has no visible author is of human origin, then, by observing the continuum of one's own mind, all mental phenomena (*cittadharma*) are known. Therefore, as long as there is the nature of consciousness, so long is everything dependent upon the five sense faculties and conceptual; and as everything now contains within it the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that generate passion and the like, so it will be in the future state as well. And just as it is for me, so it is for others too.

Anticipating the objection—"Since it is spoken of as being of the nature of consciousness (*cittatva*), as being dependent on the sense faculties (*indriyāśritatva*), and as being the cause of speech and so forth, why is it not inferred that the mind of every person is always associated with passion (*rāga*) and the like, and that, because it apprehends only specific objects, it does not have all things as its domain?"—he says "not so" (*naivam*) and so forth:
"Just as sentences do not lack specific reasons for their occurrence, so too persons do not lack specific reasons; for, by virtue of the absence of such specific reasons..."

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "speech etcetera," there is the inclusion of [properties] such as being dependent on sense faculties (*indriyāśritatva*) and being mental (*cittatva*).

From that mark (*liṅga*), which possesses a partial similarity (*sādharmya*) with speech etcetera alone in some respect or in one part, one might infer a complete identity (*sāmya*) among men in every aspect—whether by their possessing passion and so forth, by their having restricted objects, or by something else. He asks: "How can there even be the possibility of a specific reason (*viśeṣahetu*)? [and answers:]...
Because a specific distinction is observed among all mental qualities,
for even those such as passion and wisdom, though their functioning toward the apprehension of their respective objects may be very slow at first, they become more acute over time,
and their respective objects become clearer; thus, a specific distinction is observed.
He asks, "From what does that [excellence] arise? and replies:
"From *saṃskāra*, which is practice (*abhyāsa*); for it is through its specific excellence that the excellence of wisdom and the other [faculties] is perceived.
Let it be granted that there is a pre-eminence of wisdom and the other qualities of the mind resulting from practice, since this is observed.
But since omniscience and the like have not been perceived, how can their existence be established? To this he says "tadvat" (in the same way), etc.,
because other specific qualities such as omniscience are also possible.

Furthermore, through the power of cultivation, the clarity that arises regarding the conceptual construction of selflessness— which apprehends all things— and the conceptual construction of universals is itself detachment and the state of omniscience.
Therefore, by these three modes, there would be an inference of the impossibility of any distinction between detachment and omniscience,
provided that a conceptual construction having selflessness as its object or having all things as its object were impossible.
Or, even if conceptual cognitions were possible, if there were no distinction [between them],
or if a distinction existed but its cause were not known; however,
since conceptual cognitions having objects such as selflessness are possible, and their cause— the repeated practice— is well known.

Therefore, just as there is an inference of capacity based on the fact that this causal complex of seeds is capable of producing a sprout when there is no obstruction or deficiency, so too—in the absence of obstructions or deficiencies, and due to a specific kind of practice that is continuous over a long period—it is possible for knowledge regarding the object of selflessness and all things to attain clarity. Thus, there is an inference of the possibility of dispassion and omniscience;
such, then, is our inference of possibility.

But when non-existence is to be inferred, there exists for you no probans that sublates that property; and because of its absence, the connection is that "men do not possess the cause for the impossibility of [certain] specific qualities. He asks: "How, then, is there an absence of a sublater? and replies:
This is an indicative mark because dispassion is unperceived; it is also an indicative mark because even an omniscient being is unperceived.
And by means of what is unperceived, [dispassion] is not harmed. (Note 70-1: "Even that which is unperceived is not to be invalidated.")
Since the relationship of sublated and sublator between the reason and the [thesis] is not established,
it might be thought:
"It is not inferred from speech and so forth that dispassion and the like are directly impossible, such that a subverting reason would have to be sought."
However, passion and other such qualities are inferred in those who are considered to be free from passion;
once these have been inferred, it follows by implication that their state of being free from passion is negated, because passion is incompatible even with unseen dispassion.
To this, he says "rāga... and so forth.
For there is no effect that is invariably concomitant with passion and the like;
by the inclusion of the word "and the like," the non-omniscient is also included.

That is to say, starting from the acquisition of linguistic convention, to the extent that one’s thorough knowledge of an object increases, to that same extent does one’s capacity to speak regarding that object arise. Therefore, if someone were to possess a cognition whose object is everything, who could prevent their capacity to speak regarding those objects as well?
One might object: "If he possesses such distinctions characterized by dispassion and so forth, why are they not perceived by us? To this he replies:
"Even though those specific qualities characterized by dispassion and so forth may exist, they cannot be seen in the mental continuum of another."
Nor is there a rejection [of such things] because they are not perceived;
for he says that such things, being remote, are not fit for rejection.
This might be so.
Just as persons are not to be rejected, so too are their statements;
thus he says "not so," and so forth.
What is the reason?
Because it is a specific instance of what is perceived;
for indeed, the specific nature of Vedic sentences is held to be perceived,
or else it is not so held.
Even if such an imperceptible distinction is admitted,
there would be a contradiction in asserting that Vedic sentences— which possess distinctions not perceived through that imperceptible distinction— are of a different genus from worldly sentences;
this might be the thought.

The specific characteristics of Vedic texts—such as being difficult to hear and difficult to pronounce—are indeed perceptible; [the opponent might argue] that because of these, they must be distinct from human compositions.
To this, he says "of those specific characteristics," and so forth;
"elsewhere" refers to human compositions.

Not only is it untenable that particulars (*viśeṣa*) are imperceptible because it contradicts the admission of their being of a different class from those things whose specific qualities are not seen, but for this further reason as well: it contradicts the nature of what is perceptible to be imperceptible.
Indeed, two contradictory natures cannot coexist in a single thing;
the particulars are simply perceptible, though they appear otherwise due to the presence of causes of error.
If it is argued that [the universals] are not apprehended because they are like the potency of poison and so forth, he replies:
"Because there is no cause for error.
For the perception of similarity in form is indeed the cause of error in the case of poisons and the like.
If it is asked how this is known to be so regarding Vedic matters, he says: "Because there is no sublation and because error is not established."

If, while no specific distinction among Vedic words is perceived through error, a further means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were to arise that relies upon such a distinction and serves as a sublater (*bādhaka*) of the error, then there would be certainty regarding that error and its cause; however, that does not exist. Therefore, when it is to be proven that Vedic words are non-distinct from worldly words, there is no proving evidence. [The opponent asks: "In that case, what is the sublater by which there is a fault in attempting to prove the equality of all qualities in persons? To this, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "among men" and so forth:

if the mind of a person were such that detachment were impossible, then the very observation of excellence— such as wisdom and other qualities— which is preceded by practice, would serve as the subverting proof [of the possibility of detachment].
It cannot be that there is no excellence to be produced through practice;
for if there were,
then the observation of such excellence would constitute a sublation [of the opposing view], and thus it is not the same.
Regarding the inference from Vedic statements, as for what was said— that there is an absence of a non-perceptible nature in perceptible words—
this fault would indeed arise if the particular were an intrinsic nature; however, he says that it is rather an extrinsic nature.

Regarding the phrase "of that which has become another nature" (*parabhāvabhūtasya*): having gone to another nature is "become another nature," meaning it has a different intrinsic nature (*anyasvabhāva*).
"Because they do not possess that distinction" means because they do not possess the distinction of being sentences;

since there is no distinction among sentences, therefore, for all of them— whether considered human or non-human— the "human action" (*puruṣakriyā*), that is, their production by persons, [is the same].
The meaning is that it is not the human action of anyone, not even of a worldly person.

Thus, having stated both the contradiction with the text and the contradiction with valid cognition for one who desires the exclusion of the reason from the counter-example based merely on the non-perception of the Teacher’s [work], he now states the mutual inconsistency among the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
"Furthermore," and so forth; that "clay is sentient" is the Lokāyata view.
The term "self and earth-consciousness" (*ātmā ca mṛccetanā ca*) is a copulative compound (*dvandva*).

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), substances such as milk and so forth are included. Non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), though stated by the opponent as a means to establish the non-existence of these things, is held by the proponents of the self and other [entities] not to be a prover of that non-existence, because mere non-apprehension is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatvāt*).

That very non-perception (*anupalambha*), which is not accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the negation of a self (*ātman*) and so forth, would nonetheless establish the absence of a reason— that is, the exclusion of the reason from its opposite (*vipakṣa*). Furthermore, for one who employs this non-perception as a means of valid cognition to prove the absence of a reason— such as the Vaiśeṣika and others— the doctrine of a self (*ātmavāda*) would become baseless and unsupported,
because in that case, non-perception is possible as a proof of non-existence.
For indeed, there is no perception of the self through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because its eternal transcendence (*nityaparokṣatva*) is accepted.
Now, it might be argued that there is indeed perception of the self through inference (*anumāna*); to this, he says "tatkārya" and so forth.

Precisely because the self is not perceptible, there is no apprehension through inference, since its logical mark (*liṅga*)— consisting of its effects or its essential nature— is not ascertained. If it is argued that, just as there is inference for the sense faculties and so forth even though they are eternally beyond perception, the same will hold for the self, [the author] says "of the sense faculties," etc.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the seeds of memory and so forth are included; consciousness alone is their effect, because it occurs only occasionally.
For instance, even when form, light, and mental attention are present, consciousness is absent in states such as when the eyes are closed.

Furthermore, because consciousness exists during states when the eyes are open, it is established that the effect—consciousness—is dependent upon other causes; thus, through the establishment of this dependence, the existence of the sense faculties and so forth is asserted.
This is what is meant:
Since this occasional cognition is dependent upon something else, it is inferred that there exists some cause for this cognition;
and that very cause is conventionally designated as the "sense faculty" (indriya).
The meaning is that the sense faculty is not inferred as being endowed with such a specific form, such as corporeality (*mūrtatva*) and so forth.
"In this way" means that just as the inference of the sense faculty is based on the fact that the effect of occasional cognition would otherwise be inexplicable,
so too is the case with the effects of pleasure and so forth.

The inference that "there exists some [entity] which has pleasure and so forth as its effect" and that this is the very nature of the self (*ātman*) does not support any particular position for the proponents of the self (*ātmavādinaḥ*),
because they merely accept that pleasure and so forth possess a cause by means of some unspecified particularity;
yet the self is not of such a kind.
Because [the self] is accepted as having the characteristics of being an eternal agent and enjoyer and so forth,
and since there is no effect-evidence (kāryaliṅga) for the self as it has been thus accepted,
it follows that the self would simply be non-perceptible.

Therefore, why was he—who denies that self by means of non-apprehension characterized as the cessation of perception and inference—refuted and rejected by the proponent of the self? For how could that [non-apprehension], being merely a lack of apprehension, establish the non-existence of the self; and how could it, being a non-probative reason, establish the exclusion of the probandum from the counter-example (vipakṣa) through a reason such as "possessing vital breaths" and so forth?

The Cārvākas maintain that consciousness is indeed the power of the elements (*bhūta*) alone, and that it is the very nature of the elements, just as hardness is the nature of clay; thus, the Lokāyata, even while desiring that consciousness is not actually perceived in clay, says:
[as follows].
From those elements, consciousness arises as cognition, like the power of intoxication; thus,

from that very same lack of evidence— namely, non-perception— he states the exclusion [of the reason] from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) of that which has been presented as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for proving non-omniscience and so forth, such as speech and the like.
The Sāṃkhya, desiring that curd and so forth exist even though they are not perceived within milk and so forth,

says "another [is the enjoyer]"; furthermore, having stated that "the eyes and other organs are for the sake of another because they are composite," he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) by pointing out that compositeness is not observed in things like a rabbit's horn, which are not for the sake of another.
Thus, there is first of all a mutual contradiction in this [argument]. Furthermore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this reason is not established by mere non-perception;

for what necessity is there here that composite things must necessarily exist for the sake of another, such that—on the grounds of their being composites—the Sāṃkhya’s proof of the eyes and so forth being for the sake of another would establish their being for the sake of the Self?
As for what was said— that curd and so forth are not perceived even within milk and so forth— that is not correct,
because there is indeed the perception of curd and so forth within milk and so forth.
What is this? It is called inference (*anumāna*).
And as for inference, it is said that [it arises] from the non-arising from that which lacks capacity;
for if the capacity for curd and so forth did not exist in milk and so forth, then curd and so forth would not arise from that milk which lacks such capacity.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is incapable of producing something cannot arise from it, just as a barley sprout does not arise from a rice seed;

yet curds and the like do arise from milk and the like. Therefore, the capacity for curds and the like exists in milk and the like. This is an application of the method of difference (*vaidharmya-prayoga*) that resembles the effect-reason (*kārya-hetu*), based on the view that curds and the like are indeed the capacity itself, due to the non-difference between cause and effect.

Then, beginning with "athetyādi," the proponent of the established doctrine [asks]: Is that very entity which is later perceived as curd and so forth the same as the power, or is it something else entirely, a distinct entity from the curd and so forth,
such that it would be perceived during the state of milk just as the curd and other products are perceived once their form has been completed?
Because there is no distinction [between them],
if it were otherwise— that is,
if power were a different entity from curd and so forth— then...
In that case, how could another thing exist when there is the existence of something else called "potency"?
The intended meaning is that curd and so forth do not exist at all [in that state].

Because of the capacity to produce curd and so forth, there would be a mere metaphorical designation of "curd" and so on for milk and the like; yet, having first treated non-perception as non-authoritative and then re-establishing it as authoritative, this is a mutual contradiction among these proponents of the Self (Ātman) and other categories—this is the conclusion.
And since there is no negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based on mere non-perception, therefore [the reason] is related to that alone.

A nature that is connected by the mere existence of its cause, when intended as the probandum, would— upon itself being excluded— exclude only that very entity which constitutes its own nature and has been presented as the reason;
the word "or" (vā) refers to the alternatives to be mentioned later,
just as a tree, upon being excluded, excludes the *śiṃśapā*.
Why? Because it is well known that only a particular entity possessing branches and so forth is designated as "śiṃśapā. That tree is the very nature (svabhāva) of the entity called "śiṃśapā";
how then could that entity called "śiṃśapā" exist by abandoning its own nature, which is the tree?
What is the reason?

Because the very nature of the tree itself constitutes its existence as a *śiṃśapā*, the reason—the *śiṃśapā* and so forth—which is identical in essence to that [tree], possesses non-deviation precisely through an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) with the intended probandum, such as "tree," according to the manner described; or, one should supply the words: "or the cause, when it ceases..."
"One should turn away from the effect"—this is the subject under discussion;
why?
"Because of non-deviation," meaning because the effect does not deviate from its cause.
He explains by means of the words "the cause," etc.;
"otherwise" means if,
when the cause ceases, the effect were not to cease.
In that case, what is considered its effect would not indeed be the effect of that cause;
therefore, the cause, upon ceasing, necessarily causes the effect to cease.

Although smoke does not cease even when the cause of fire has ceased in places such as a bedroom, the meaning is that it is intended that there is no production of this [smoke] from anything other than its observed cause.
For this very reason, he says "But the established," and so forth:
"But the established causal relation restricts the nature of the effect to the cause."
By stating that "when this exists, that comes to be; when this does not exist, that does not come to be," one establishes that [the reason] is non-deviant in both ways.

Through either identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from that (*tadutpatti*), there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*); and it is precisely because of this that the cessation of the reason follows upon the cessation of the probandum.

"Otherwise" means: if a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not admitted, how could there be the cessation of one thing upon the cessation of another— namely, the cessation of the probans-property (*sādhanadharma*), which is unconnected, through the cessation of the probandum (*sādhya*), which is likewise unconnected?

For it is not the case that because one is "not horse-possessing"—meaning devoid of horses—one must therefore be a mortal human being; nor [is it the case] that one must possess cattle simply due to the proximity of one thing. How could there be the proximity of another probandum through the mere proximity of a reason that is by nature unconnected to it? There is no such proximity at all.
Since a mortal must necessarily possess cattle, and likewise horses, for this reason,

it is precisely because of an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*)— that is, because the logical reason (*hetu*) is connected to the entity intended as the probandum (*sādhya*)— that the reason brings about its own probandum.
But it is not due to a relation,
because there is no relation residing in two things (dviṣṭhasambandha) since cause and effect do not coexist and pervader and pervaded are identical; therefore,
this is an essential connection (svabhāvapratibandha).
The phrase "characterized by that state" means characterized by the nature of the probandum (*sādhyasvabhāva*) or characterized by its origination from it (*tadutpatti*);

this very essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), known as inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*), is demonstrated through examples of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). This is what is intended.

The very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is the grasper of pervasion (*vyāpti*), because by that very means one grasps the dependence of the probans upon the probandum; thus, the absence [of the probans] when the probandum is absent is already grasped. It is only because that means of valid cognition which grasps their inseparable connection has been forgotten that it is demonstrated by means of the two examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). And since the absence of the probans in the case of the absence of the probandum becomes ascertained through the recollection of the inseparable connection resulting from the manifestation of that means of valid cognition, therefore, in the case of the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*):

In that case, regarding this reason characterized as effect or essential nature, a real substratum (*dharmin*) consisting of a factual entity is necessarily and invariably not accepted; however, in the case of the non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*), it is indeed accepted.
For in that instance, the perception [of the opposite] must be demonstrated.
What is the reason?
He states that "the substratum (āśraya) is not required," and so forth, beginning with "and in its absence.

This means that in the absence of that—namely, in the absence of the pervader (vyāpaka) and the cause (kāraṇa)—the logical mark (liṅga) called the "pervaded effect" (vyāpyakārya) does not exist; thus, even from the statement of negative concomitance (vaidharmya) which is devoid of a substratum, there is the understanding of the exclusion (vyatireka).
For what reason?
From which [reason], and so forth.

In the case of an essential identity reason (*svabhāvahetu*), the existence of the probandum as that [reason]—that is, its being pervaded by the probans—is made known; in the case of an effect reason (*kāryahetu*), the state of being the cause of the probandum—that is, its causality—is made known. This is for the sake of a person who does not know these, meaning one who does not understand the relation of existence (*tadbhāva*) and the relation of causality (*hetubhāva*).
He explains that [with the words] "For in the example," etc.:

the presence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in that [example]— that is, its being of the same nature as the probans (*sādhanasvabhāvatva*)— is made known through its necessary connection with that alone.

When the production of "being produced" (kṛtakatva) is accompanied by the mere means of proof (sādhana), impermanence (anityatva) is already established; the fact that this [impermanence] is of the nature of that [being produced]— that is, its being of the same nature as the means of proof—
is precisely what makes its existence known through such a [logical connection].
But it is not by means of impermanence arising later from another cause,
as some are mistaken in thinking; rather, showing that [the subject] possesses only that [quality], he says:
"Yaḥ" and so forth:
the meaning is that whatever cause produces a produced nature (*kṛtaka-svabhāva*) produces it as being precisely of an impermanent form;
by this means, the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the object of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is made known through the example.
But it is not merely the seeing and being seen that is otherwise; for if no such means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is demonstrated,
then [the conclusion follows] from the existence of a single property— that is, from the existence of the property to be proven (*sādhana-dharma*).

Since there is no rule that it must necessarily be accompanied by another property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), there would be a suspicion of the probans (*sādhana*) deviating from the probandum (*sādhya*).
Even if a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed to be demonstrated by means of an example, what is established thereby? To this he says:
"And by that means of valid cognition, there is a necessary connection with that alone," meaning a necessary connection with the probans alone.
To explain how this is made known, he says:
"Because that which is produced has a cause, it is produced as such; that which is produced is perishable, having the nature of existing for only a moment.
It perishes by virtue of its very momentariness, and not after remaining for another time—this is the meaning."
But how is it that it arises in such a way from its own cause alone? To this he says:
"from another," meaning from a cause of destruction other than its own cause;
for the nature of that produced thing is denied—that is, its nature as impermanent—is denied by what will be stated hereafter.
The connection is that "the state of being a cause is manifested by that means of valid cognition";

that is, either the state of being a cause, or the state of being a reason (*hetubhāva*), or the state of being a cause (*kāraṇatva*) of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) with respect to the proof (*sādhana*) is manifested.
By the statement "because the means of proof exists only when that [subject] exists," the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is demonstrated by way of an example.
To the question, "Of which probandum (*sādhya*), then, is the state of being the reason (*hetubhāva*) being demonstrated? he replies:
"Of another object (*arthāntara*), that is, of something distinct from the means of proof."

Thus, when the state of being that [effect] and the state of being its cause have been established by the means of valid cognition demonstrated through the example, then for the essential nature (*svabhāva*) which is the probandum, there exists the state of being the essential nature of the probans when that [probandum] is present.
When the causal status of the cause is established,
the connection with the subject at hand is that "in the absence of fire, smoke does not arise";
and "that" refers to fire, which possesses the nature of impermanence.

Regarding the phrase "of that": for *kṛtakatva* (the state of being produced) and for smoke, respectively, either the essential nature (*svabhāva*) or the word "or" (*vā*) signifies a reason; the word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of conjunction.

Since this is so, how could this produced thing—whether it be smoke or [the state of being produced]—exist without its own essential nature, which is impermanence, or without its cause, which is fire?

"It would not exist at all"—in such a case, regarding an object whose form has not been explicitly stated, when the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is being explained, the negative concomitance is established even without a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Therefore, as for what was said by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara: [Note: Second Chapter = *Dvitīyamāhnikaṃ*; Chapter = 300 Ślokas. *This note belongs to the base text, which was not keyboarded.* In this manner, when the negative concomitance is being discussed, it is established even in the absence of a substratum within a dissimilar example; therefore, that which was stated by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara—

"The negative concomitance (vyatireka) of the logical mark is not obtained from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa); it would not be understood even by those who have exerted effort because of their lack of understanding"— this [objection] has been refuted.

Furthermore, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of the logical mark (liṅga) with the counter-example (vipakṣa) is not at all obtained; for in the absence [of the probandum], that [mark] would not be understood even by those who have exerted effort due to a lack of cognition. Thus far.

An example must be stated for those who do not know the relationship between the presence of the effect and the presence of the cause, in order to demonstrate that relationship; however, for those who already have the presence of the effect and the presence of the cause established by their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and who ascertain that the reason is merely a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), the reason itself serves the purpose of those who are knowledgeable regarding that relationship between the presence of the effect and the presence of the cause—
namely, for the sake of ascertaining positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Since that very object to be established is already established for oneself, what is the use of stating it? Thus,
at the time when positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) have been ascertained,
even if an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) is presented for the sake of a fool, then even upon that presentation of the illustration, there is a lack of similarity (*vaidharmya*).
The negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is indeed established by the aforementioned method even without a substratum;
therefore, what is the use of relying on a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*)? Thinking thus, the Master [Dignāga] rejects the substratum in works such as the *Nyāyamukha*.
For it is stated in that very same work: "In that case, when the opponent accepts that space (*ākāśa*) and so forth are eternal..."
"In that case, how can there be a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of 'being produced' with respect to the 'eternal'? To this, the Master, rejecting the [notion of a] substratum (*āśraya*), says:
"In that case, there is no doubt at all; because of the absence of that [eternal thing], [the property] does not occur therein."
This is what is meant:
for one who has grasped the necessary connection (pratibandha), the absence of the pervaded (vyāpya) is established there—in space and so forth—due to the absence of the pervader (vyāpaka);
and the absence of impermanence is established because of the non-existence of the permanent. This is the sense.

Since the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is stated by means of two examples, for that reason, when the logical reason (*hetu*) has its relationship [to the probandum] already known, the recollection of the second one arises through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), even though only one of the two— either the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) or the example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*)— is explicitly mentioned.
Connecting this also with the words of the Teacher, he says "yadāha" (as it is said), etc.; and this passage occurs in the *Nyāyamukha*.
