The word "or" (vā) refers back to that same [context], depending on the preceding alternative; for it demonstrates both by means of either a similar instance (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta) or a dissimilar instance (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta),
thereby demonstrating positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka).

In that treatise as well, the Master— considering that the demonstration of the presence of the effect and the presence of the cause is made respectively through examples for the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) and the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*)— states, by means of presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), that the second [member] is established through the statement of either the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*),
respectively; he says this very thing:
For it is thus:

when it is stated that "whatever is produced is necessarily impermanent," it is clearly ascertained by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that this property called impermanence is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of that which is produced, and that it is invariably concomitant with it—that is, it follows upon the mere fact of being produced.
Now, one might object: is it not also the case that the cause necessarily exists in the effect?
And since that [impermanence] is not its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), he says "not a different object" (anarthāntara); [to the question] "how then does it follow only that [the entity]? he says:
The phrase "due to the necessity of its existence" means that whenever there is the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), there is necessarily the state of impermanence (*anityatā*).

Now, one might object: "The nature of impermanence is not ascertained through perception as being invariably concomitant with everything that is produced, because it is not certain that 'this [thing] is momentary. Therefore, how can it be said that this is 'seen by a means of valid cognition' (*pramāṇadṛṣṭa*)?"

Now, [the opponent may argue] that because destruction is independent with respect to produced things, it is necessarily concomitant with their existence, and thus it is observed through inference. This is incorrect,
because even if destruction were causeless, it would only be causeless at the very moment the destruction of a jar or the like is perceived, and not at any other time.
How then is there momentariness?
If a jar exists for only a single moment, would it not follow that its destruction occurs even before its production?
[Objection: Just as production from its own causes occurs by virtue of existing for a single moment, so too might production occur by virtue of existing for multiple moments.
For causal complexes are observed to possess diverse powers;
and if destruction were not to occur somewhere at some time,
then because it would depend upon time and substance, its independence would be lost.

Because it does not depend on a cause of destruction, otherwise there would be no destruction even in the second moment, as it would depend on that time and so forth. Now, existence—characterized by causal efficacy—is pervaded by both succession and simultaneity; and since succession and non-succession are excluded from eternal things, existence, being excluded from them, remains only in momentary things. Thus, the property of being produced, when conjoined with existence, serves as a logical indicator [of momentariness].

That too is incorrect, because if things are momentary, a sequence cannot be apprehended; for that moment of cognition by which the preceding object is apprehended does not [apprehend] the subsequent one, and that by which the subsequent one is apprehended does not [apprehend] the preceding one—how, then, can there be an apprehension of sequence? For that which is prior... [Note 79-1: *Cig-śog*.]

Immediately after the apprehension of one object, if there were an apprehender of another, it would have to be an apprehender of successive moments; or else, it would follow that this [apprehender] is non-momentary.
Furthermore, for that Buddhist for whom time itself does not exist, how could there be an apprehension of succession?
For there is no apprehension of objects belonging to different times.
In the absence of time, succession consists precisely in the form of multiple entities;
thus, even for that which is eternal, its agency of succession is not contradictory.
And just as the eternal possesses a manifold nature due to its agency of succession, so too would this apply to the momentary.
Now, if [the cause were] like a moment, then in the second moment even that which is eternal would cease to exist due to the absence of its effect;
that is incorrect because time itself would be absent.
Or, let it be that there is a perception of succession; even so, how can existence be pervaded by both succession and simultaneity?
For causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is possible through another mode apart from succession and simultaneity.
Nor can the non-existence of another mode be ascertained merely because it is not perceived despite being perceptible.

For in this way, the ascertainment of non-existence would occur only in specific locations and so forth, but not at all times; nor can non-existence be ascertained through the non-perception of the unobservable, because of the resulting doubt. Therefore, since existence does not cease even though succession and simultaneity are impossible for eternal things, how can existence have momentariness as its inherent nature? Thus argue Śaṅkarasvāmin and others.

Or, let it be granted that existence is pervaded by succession and simultaneity because there is no other alternative; nevertheless, the impossibility of succession and non-succession in eternal things is not established by perception and other means, because eternal things are beyond the reach of the senses. And since that [impossibility] is not established, the exclusion of existence from those [eternal things] is not established; and since that is not established, existence is not proven to have momentary nature as its essence.
Furthermore:

Because [the capacity for action] exists, there would be an inference of succession and simultaneity, since [action] is pervaded by those very two; however, there is no inference of momentariness therein, because the agency of succession is impossible [in a single moment].
To this it is replied:
succession and simultaneity are indeed established by direct perception.

For the coexistence of entities is simultaneity, whereas succession is the state of being prior and posterior; and that [succession] belongs to successive things which are non-different from it, while its appearance is a single appearance.

However, that appearance of another immediately after the appearance of one is the appearance of succession, and not the appearance of a single thing alone, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
This is true even in that case: when there is the appearance of one [moment], there is not [yet] the appearance of the other; for if it were present, there would be a simultaneous appearance.
Therefore, when two successive moments are grasped by the preceding and succeeding cognitions, the succession is indeed grasped, because they are non-different from it.

The apprehension of sequence is established solely through the arising of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding order—such as "this follows immediately after that"—triggered by the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by previously experienced objects; for even when sequential things are apprehended, if a conceptual construction of order does not somehow arise, the non-apprehension of sequence is established. For this very reason, it is said that there is no apprehension of sequence even when sequential things are apprehended as one. Furthermore, how could there be an apprehension of sequence even for one who maintains the existence of time?
Since all effects belong to a single time,
the claim that there is a sequence of effects due to a sequence of causal conditions belonging to different times is untenable, because time is one;
for this very reason, there can be no production of an eternal entity.
Now, if time is sequential because it possesses a prior and posterior nature,

then surely its own sequence— if it were dependent on another subsequent time— would lead to an infinite regress. On the other hand, if its sequence exists by its very nature, then likewise there would be a sequence even for many effects that lack such auxiliary factors.
For us, however, time exists as a specific great element (*mahābhūta-viśeṣa*) that is the object of cognitions such as "prior" and so forth, and is well-known in the world;
and because of its differentiation, the cognition of sequence and so forth is indeed logical.
Furthermore, agency is not possible for an eternal entity by any other means.
For if it were to perform its single effect or multiple effects at once through some other mode, it would then be non-existent at other times due to the absence of an effect;
and if it performs the effect again and again, that constitutes nothing but succession, so no other mode is possible.
Furthermore, if it does not perform the effect at once through another mode, nor does it perform it repeatedly, then it would be a non-entity.

Because it is never a non-agent, that very object— such as a jar— which is established by perception as performing purposeful action (arthakriyā) through either successive or simultaneous means, is indeed cognized as non-momentary from the cognition "this is that very same thing.
Furthermore, its capacity toward the production of a single effect exists only at that specific time, neither before nor after, because that effect is absent [at those other times].
And that capacity (*sāmarthya*) is non-different from [the entity itself]; this should be understood likewise even in the production of successive effects.
Furthermore, because there is a difference in entities due to the difference in capacities, the restriction of succession and simultaneity applies only to the momentary.
Therefore, wherever there is existence (*sattva*), there is the cognition of momentariness itself, even when succession and simultaneity are being perceived.
This very restriction regarding succession and simultaneity that applies to momentary things is precisely the impossibility of those two in permanent things.

Therefore, this perceived permanence in jars and the like is contradicted by existence (*sattva*); thus, it is said that the contradiction of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) with respect to both succession and simultaneity is established for the permanent.

And just as existence is pervaded by momentariness in the case of observed objects like jars, so too is it in unobserved cases without distinction; having thus apprehended the pervasion through a universal induction, to whatever extent existence is ascertained in them, to that same extent there is the inference of momentariness.

If, however, there were no certainty regarding existence (*sattva*), then—just as in the case of a rabbit's horn—there might be a suspicion of non-existence regarding those [entities], and consequently, momentariness would not be cognized.
Nor should it be thought that inference is redundant because momentariness is established even in that case by a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*);
for once a person has grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the object to be proven is understood through the mere certainty of existence alone, rendering the arousal of a subverting proof pointless.
This method of grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been explained in detail in the *Nairātmyasiddhi*, and thus should be understood from that very work. However,

for those who seek to infer momentariness from existence (*sattva*) based on the pervasion of existence by momentariness everywhere— due to the absence [of existence] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)— the inference itself would not even arise.

Since momentariness would be established everywhere through the very means of valid cognition that grasps pervasion (*vyāpti*), the subject (*dharmin*) would not be unestablished, because the entire threefold world is perceptible; yet the reason (*hetu*) would also be unestablished. Furthermore, if the absence of counter-examples (*vipakṣābhāva*) were established for the entire subject under consideration by virtue of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*), then, since the probandum (*sādhya*) would also be established, there would be no arising of inference at all.
Since no other subject (*dharmin*) is established, how could there be the operation of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*)? This is trivial.

Therefore, it is established that for this "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) qualified by existence, the property called momentariness is its essential nature (*svabhāva*) and is invariably concomitant with it alone; or, the essential nature of this momentariness is invariably concomitant with producedness alone, as seen through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Alternatively, even for producedness and the like devoid of the qualification of existence, when momentariness is to be proven, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).

For if that which was the very same intrinsic nature (svabhāva) in its first moment were also present in the second moment, then it would be a case of coming into being after having not existed, just as in the first moment;
and consequently, there would be momentariness.
Alternatively, if in the first moment there is only the birth of the produced thing and no persistence, while in the second moment there is only persistence and no birth—
Even so, there would be momentariness, because of the non-difference between the birth and that which is born,
and between the duration and that which endures.
Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be duration in the second moment without birth;
if there is birth, then there is no duration, because that [birth] occurs in the second and subsequent moments.
Since this applies everywhere, there is only origination and no duration; thus, there is indeed momentariness.
And since origination is produced by causes, the state of being produced (kṛtakatva) resides in that [origination] alone, not in the duration;
therefore, because being produced is contradictory to non-momentariness, there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva).

Furthermore, the pervasion of this "producedness" (kṛtakatva) by "momentariness" has been stated in detail in the *Nairātmyasiddhi*; it should be understood from that very source (*Pramāṇavārttika* 1.224).
Therefore, the pervasion of producedness—even though it is not included within [the category of] existence—is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Regarding this, it is said: its nature is observed through valid cognition to be invariably concomitant with that [property], because of the necessity of its existence;
for just as in the case of being produced, there is a necessary presence of impermanence.

Thus, for a person who has cognized that nature—that is, who has cognized that which is produced to have the nature of impermanence—there arises, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the certain conviction that "in the absence of the probandum, impermanence, the produced thing does not exist."
Because, in the absence of impermanence—which is its very own nature—an entity does not exist; for how could that which constitutes its nature, namely "being produced," exist? What is the reason?
Because of the non-difference between the probandum and the probans;
otherwise, if "producedness" were to exist even in the absence of "impermanence," then it would not necessarily follow that "impermanence" exists when "producedness" is present.

The phrase "so it is" (*tatheti*) connects with what is to be said later: just as there is an understanding of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) in an application based on similarity (*sādharmya*), so too does the recollection of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) occur in an application based on dissimilarity.

Regarding the phrase "in the absence of that" (*tadabhāve*): when it is stated that "in the absence of eternity (*nityatva*), being produced (*kṛtakatva*) necessarily does not exist," then from that very application of dissimilarity, one who understands its presence [of the probans] [attains the desired conclusion].
If it is asked how a person who knows that the means of proof has the nature of the probandum can know its existence [in the subject],
he says "tathā hi" (for instance), and so forth.
This property called impermanence is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this producedness (*kṛtakatva*), by virtue of which producedness does not exist in its absence;
otherwise, if impermanence were not the intrinsic nature of the produced, [producedness would not cease when it is absent].
At that time, because it would be illogical for "producedness" not to exist in the absence of that [impermanence],

there arises a recollection of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) through the realization of the essential nature of the reason— that is, through the realization that being produced has impermanence as its very nature.
This is what is meant.

The very existence of the probans in the probandum itself constitutes its non-existence in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa); thus, there is identity between positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka), as well as their mutual pervasion (anyonyavyāpti). Therefore, from the cognition of the positive concomitance in the probans, the cognition of the negative concomitance follows, and from the cognition of the negative concomitance, the cognition of the positive concomitance follows; this is indeed inference.
Consequently, the claim in the *Nyāyamañjarī*—that for Kīrti, who accepts [the force of] implication (sāmarthya), the restriction to two [types of concomitance] is lost—is refuted.

Alternatively, this is not a [separate] means of valid cognition at all; rather, there is no fault because a single sentence, employed either through the method of agreement (*anvaya*) or the method of difference (*vyatireka*), conveys both meanings solely by virtue of convention.

Having thus explained the comprehension of both [meanings] from the employment of either one in the case of the essential nature as a reason (*svabhāvahetu*), he says "likewise," etc., regarding the effect as a reason (*kāryahetu*).

When a universal generalization is made by means of a pronoun— such as "wherever [there is smoke], there fire necessarily exists"— then from this very statement of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the certainty arises that smoke is the effect of fire.
What is the reason why fire necessarily exists where there is smoke?
Otherwise, if fire were not the cause of smoke, then because there would be no necessary connection (*anubandha*) between that other entity, fire, and the smoke,
there would be an absence of the restriction (*niyama*) regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of smoke;
and consequently, the nature of smoke would possess independence.

"Therefore" means by virtue of independence; even in the absence of that—that is, even in the absence of fire—the nature of smoke would not be deficient, and thus its non-existence would not follow. But this is not the case; therefore, smoke must be accepted as an effect. For when smoke is admitted to be an effect, its cause, fire, necessarily exists there.
This is precisely what is being established.
"Existence as another thing" means that when that which is considered the effect exists, there is the imposition of its own nature—that is, the presentation of its essential form.
The "effectness" of the effect is its existence precisely when that [cause] exists, namely, when the cause exists;
and this state of existing only when the cause exists is present in smoke.

Therefore, for a person who has understood through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that smoke is an effect [of fire]— thinking "smoke is an effect"— it follows by implication that "in the absence of fire, there is no smoke. Now, he explains the process of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) through negative concomitance (*vaidharmya*) with the words beginning with "tathā" (likewise).

When it is stated that "where there is no fire, smoke does not exist," for one who has understood from this statement of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that smoke is an effect of fire, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is necessarily understood by implication—that where there is fire, smoke exists.

Otherwise, if it were not stated through the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) that smoke is the effect of fire, then in the absence of fire, one would ask what smoke would not be; [the answer being] that it would indeed exist, and thus there could be no certainty regarding negative concomitance at all.
Therefore, this is established:

when there is a difference in meaning, that which necessarily does not occur in the absence of something else is the effect of that [other]; and thus, from the statement of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is understood.
Here, the opponent states an objection beginning with "But surely" (*nanu ca*), etc.:
the effect of permanent and impermanent objects is the "effect of permanent and impermanent objects"; its existence is the "state of being that" (*tattvam*).

Even in the absence of that [object], it is as follows: auditory cognition is a unique property of sound alone; therefore, it is not known therein whether auditory cognition is the effect of a permanent sound or of an impermanent one. Consequently, auditory cognition is neither the effect of a permanent object nor the effect of an impermanent object; yet, even in the absence of such [an object], auditory cognition does not fail to occur, even in the absence of both permanent and impermanent objects.
The phrase "it is excluded when that is excluded" means that as long as there is an absence of eternal objects, it does not exist, because it is absent in non-eternal things such as jars;
nor does it exist even when non-eternal things are absent, because it is absent in eternal things such as space.
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) says: "It is certainly not the case that it does not exist.
It is not possible to understand that "the property of being audible does not exist in the absence of both the eternal and the non-eternal";
however, if there were the certainty that "it exists by virtue of the absence of those two," then it would necessarily be its effect (kārya).
But there is no reason why it should not exist simply because it does not exist when those two are absent; for from that very audibility, which is itself both eternal and non-eternal, doubt arises.
Otherwise, if audibility were ascertained to be absent in both eternal and non-eternal things, how could there be doubt regarding sound through the consideration of its presence?
Therefore, there is no exclusion of audibility from both the permanent and the impermanent at all;
how then is it said that audibility does not exist in either the permanent or the impermanent because of its being "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa)? To this he says:
"But only," and so forth.
Because there is no certainty regarding the presence of audibility in things that are both eternal and non-eternal,
it is said that audibility does not exist in either the eternal or the non-eternal;
however, if audibility were observed in both the similar instances (sapakṣa) and the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) when proving something such as non-eternality, [it would not be a valid reason].

Bhaṭṭa and Udyotakara maintain that there would be doubt regarding the word "syāt" because it possesses audibility, just as there is regarding [the property of] being knowable; and since this [property] is not observed in either the similar instance (sapakṣa) or the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa), there is consequently no certain cognition.

Now, if it is argued that the entity of sound is sometimes permanent and sometimes impermanent, and that audibility is its property (*dharma*), and therefore doubt is expressed on this basis— that is incorrect; for in that case, it would be the very fact of being a property of the entity that constitutes the cause of doubt, not audibility itself.
To this it is replied:

if indeed it were established that wherever there is audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*), there is the absence of both the permanent (*nitya*) and the impermanent (*anitya*), then there would be a non-apprehension of the permanent and the impermanent.

However, it is not the case that audibility is absent in things like a jar, which are characterized by impermanence and so forth; therefore, its absence in sound [is not established], and thus, because of its audibility, there remains only doubt regarding it.
But surely, audibility is the capacity for auditory cognition, and a permanent entity lacks such capacity because it is contradictory for it to perform a causal function;
so how can there be doubt from this, since there is rather a certainty of impermanence?
He thinks as follows:

if mere capacity (*sāmarthya*) alone were the reason (*hetu*), then that would simply be existence (*sattva*); thus there would be no fault, precisely because it is common to the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). The same should be understood regarding [the reasons] such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth.

Now, regarding the capacity for audible cognition, that which serves as its cause is not established anywhere as being pervaded by impermanence; how, then, could impermanence be established from this? Because it is an *asādhāraṇa* (uncommon) reason, [one might argue] that this very sound is established as being pervaded by impermanence, since impermanence is established therein by that very subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), and thus the property of audibility would be redundant.
In this way, one should understand the non-informativeness of uncommon reasons.

Therefore, it is established that in the case of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), the relationship of cause and effect between the probandum and the probans must be stated by means of two examples; it is not merely a matter of observation and non-observation.
For in this way, through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the cognition of the second [term] would arise from either one of them.

He says, "Otherwise it would not be so," beginning with the words "But when," etc.; [he means that] in that case, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) itself— namely, "wherever there is smoke, there is fire"— would not exist, because of the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

And when positive concomitance (*anvaya*) itself is not established, how can there be the establishment of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) by implication—namely, that "in the absence of fire, smoke does not exist"? Likewise, since mere non-perception is being indicated through dissimilar instances (*vaidharmya*), the absence of the reason in the absence of the probandum is not established; how then, by means of that, could there be a recollection of positive concomitance?
As it has been stated, [the reason] is characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) and origination therefrom (*tadutpatti*).

When one exists—that is, when the effect or the essential nature (*svabhāva*) as a logical mark (*liṅga*) exists—for the sake of establishing the other, namely for the sake of establishing the cause or the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*):

since it is impossible to establish the other when that [mark] is absent, provided there is no such connection (*pratibandha*) as previously described, there is an absence of the cause and the essential nature; that is, an absence of the reason (*hetu*) and an absence of the pervading essential nature (*vyāpaka-svabhāva*).

Therefore, for the reason just mentioned, when there is the negation of some effect or pervaded property— and by the word "and" (ca), when the conventional usage of that negation is to be established— the logical mark (liṅga) serves as the probans (hetu).
What is the reason?

Because those two—the cause and the pervader—when present, turn back their own dependent effect and their own pervaded nature; thus, one who wishes to establish the negation of some object, whether it be an effect or a pervaded entity—and by the word "also" (api), [the negation of] conventional usage as well—[must rely on these].
The cessation of the reason (*hetu*), the cause (*kāraṇa*), and the pervading nature (*vyāpaka-svabhāva*) is to be designated as a "reason" (for non-existence).
Why? Because, as it is said: "if there were no impediment," and so forth.
The meaning is that there is no other obstacle than those two;
"proper" means logical or reasonable, and "perception" refers to the perception of such a thing as it would be if visible—
that is, the non-perception of its own nature (*svabhāva*) is the reason for its negation.

And this is not the cause of the negation itself; rather, it is called the "cause of the negation" because it is the cause of the conventional usage that has negation as its object. Why? Because such non-perception—that is, the non-perception of what is perceptible—is itself the nature of the negation.
"The non-apprehension of the cause" refers to both the non-apprehension of the cause and the non-apprehension of the pervader;
"of both" means of the negation and of the conventional usage of negation.
Thus is this non-apprehension.
Having been described briefly in three ways, it is further described in many ways;
as for how it was previously divided into eightfold in this very same context, he says:
Regarding the phrase "that which is contradictory to each of those" (*tattadviruddha*), etc.:
the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the triad of essential nature (*svabhāva*), cause (*kāraṇa*), and pervader (*vyāpaka*) under discussion;
thus, that which is contradictory to this triad—essential nature and so forth—is itself of exactly three kinds.

The distinctions are those of the contradictory of the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddha*), the contradictory of the cause (*kāraṇaviruddha*), and the contradictory of the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddha*).

"That which has the contradictory of that as its first" (*tadviruddhādi*)— by the word "first" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the contradictory effect (*viruddhakārya*) and the effect of the contradictory cause (*kāraṇaviruddhakārya*).
And that [is] "the non-going and the going of those two which are opposed to it";
the meaning is: the non-going of that and the going of what is opposed to it.
The distinction between those two lies in their application; therefore, due to that difference in application, they are stated in various ways.

In that regard, by way of the non-perception of the thing itself, three types of non-perception are subsumed: non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*), and non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
By way of the perception of what is contrary to them, there are likewise exactly three.

The perception of what is contradictory to the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), the perception of what is contradictory to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*), and the perception of what is contradictory to the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*)—

by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the perception of the contradictory effect (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*) and the perception of the effect of what is contradictory to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*) are included;
thus, there is a summary of the eightfold non-perception (*anupalambha*) previously mentioned.
With the words "Indeed, it is of three kinds," etc., he states the meaning of the verse.
The connection is that there is the non-apprehension of a reason whose existence is apprehensible—that is, one which is capable of being perceived.
The phrase "whose existence is apprehensible" also applies to the pervader and to its own self.
The connection is as follows: that threefold reason for negation is said to be of many types by virtue of its formal application (prayoga).
To the question "In what way is it by virtue of its formal application?", he says:
"By means of formal applications distinguished by the non-comprehension or comprehension of those respective [objects] that are contradictory and so forth."

This very point is analyzed by the passage beginning with "by its non-perception" (*tasyāgatyeti*), which means: by the non-perception of the essential nature, the cause, or the pervader (*svabhāva-kāraṇa-vyāpakānupalabdhi*);

and by the perception of that which is contradictory to it (*tadviruddhagatyeti*), which means: by the perception of that which is contradictory to the essential nature, the cause, or the pervader (*svabhāva-kāraṇa-vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

"By means of the perception of a contradictory effect" (*viruddhakāryagatyā*) refers to the application of various types [of non-perception], such as the perception of an effect contradictory [to the cause] (*kāraṇaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*), as was previously stated in the "Examination of the Varieties of Non-perception" (*anupalabdhicintā*).
Since it is thus a signifier by virtue of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), therefore—

either through the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) which acts as the regulator that establishes the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) between the probandum and the probans, or through the essential nature (*svabhāva*) characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) which acts as the regulator— [the signifier is established].

The meaning of the "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*) of the effect, the essential nature, and the mark is that they do not exist without the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Furthermore, there is no inseparable connection for a unique (*asādhāraṇa*) reason, because it is a cause of doubt.

If, however, there were an inseparable connection, the property to be proven would already be established in that subject (*dharmin*) by the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that determines that connection; how then could such a reason be a prover?
Therefore, as for what was stated by the venerable [author]: "The word *avinābhāva* (inseparable relation) also applies to all objects;
it does not bring about for us the comprehension of a connection suitable for inference."
If, first of all, that inseparable relation is not subsequently distinguished [from other properties],

then it would exist even in the case of the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) [property]; thus, that which is an uncommon property would be rendered its own by that very [relation] and would consequently be non-causal.
The objection that "if it is known merely as 'it does not exist without [the other],' it follows that the cause is [merely] a non-occurrence" is refuted,
for the very rule is indeed inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).
If it is argued that [the reason] does not exist without the probandum, and thus [the pervasion is established], then for what purpose is the restriction (niyama) stated once again?
This is true.
In order to refute the views of others, he indeed maintains a restriction other than inseparable connection (avinābhāva),
as Bhaṭṭa has said:
Thus, when the relations asserted by others have been rejected,
the relation called "restriction" (niyama) is now stated according to our own view;
for there are two possible ways in which relations such as the causal relation (kāryakāraṇabhāva) and others may exist.
Through both restriction and non-restriction,
restriction constitutes a factor for inference; for all these cases of non-restriction are not causes for the arising of inference.

Nothing whatsoever is inferred from mere restriction alone; therefore, it is established here that the relation is exclusively restriction itself. This is intended as the relation between the indicator and the indicated, and it has already been defined previously.

The claim that for one who correctly remembers the rule, there arises through the perception of a single member of the rule a cognition of the other members of the rule— which constitutes an inference regarding those members—
is thereby refuted.
Thus, having rejected the relations asserted by others,
the relation called "restriction" (niyama) is now stated according to our own view;
for there are two possible ways in which relations such as cause-and-effect and the like may exist.
Regarding certainty and uncertainty: certainty may indeed be a constituent part of inference;
however, all these uncertainties are not causes for the arising of inference.
For nothing whatsoever is inferred from certainty alone.

Therefore, in this context, only the restriction (niyama) is determined as the relation; it is intended as that which belongs specifically to the indicator with respect to the indicated, and it has been previously defined. For one who correctly remembers the restriction, [the cognition arises] from the perception of even a single member of the restricted [pair].
The cognition of the restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*) regarding its constituent parts is an inference with respect to those possessing those parts;
for in the absence of a relationship such as that of cause and effect, there would be no restriction at all,
since there is no necessity of coexistence among things that are unconnected.

Since mere paleness and the like are not effects of fire, and since a logical mark (*liṅga*) functions as a means of cognition only in dependence upon place, time, and other factors, there is indeed a restriction; so how can it be said that there are two possible ways [of relation] even when the relationship is one of cause and effect?
Now, it might be argued:

Even for one who accepts relations such as that of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), as long as the restriction (*niyama*) of the probans (*sādhana*) with respect to the probandum (*sādhya*) is not ascertained, it cannot be a factor for the cognition of the probandum. Therefore, even when the relation of cause and effect exists, it is the restriction itself that must be accepted as the relation, because only that is a factor for cognition. To say that "only that [restriction] is a member of inference (*anumāna*), while the others are merely causes for its manifestation" is incorrect.
For restriction (*niyama*) is simply dependence upon that [the cause], and that [dependence] has the nature of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*).

Therefore, the ascertainment of restriction is precisely the ascertainment of identity and causality; it is not, however, an ascertainment of restriction through observation and non-observation, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

[Objection: "But surely, just as there is deviation regarding the determination of the rule [of concomitance] based on observation and non-observation, so too would there be deviation regarding the determination of the causal relation.
[Reply: That is incorrect, because it is accepted that the determination of the causal relation occurs precisely through specific instances of observation and non-observation.
And this very point will be stated right here: as for what is said by Umveka—

that when smoke is seen in fire hundreds of times, the cognition of a restriction arises through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (anyathānupapatti), namely, that "this smoke is invariably present in fire"— [it is not so].
"It is argued that the perception of smoke where there is no fire is a sublater [of the rule],
and since such a case does not exist, smoke is necessarily restricted to fire; but this is incorrect."

For if there were no causal relation (*kāryakāryatva*), then since the non-perception of smoke in the absence of fire would be a mere non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) and thus not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), it would not constitute a sublation [of the possibility of smoke]. Consequently, because smoke might still be suspected to exist even in the absence of fire, how could there be a necessary restriction (*niyama*) of smoke to fire? Therefore, it is established that this restriction arises either from the causal relation or from essential nature (*svabhāva*).

The rule of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva-niyama*) arises from the ascertainment of the relationship between cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and so forth; furthermore, the ascertainment of the rule of inseparable connection does not result from non-observation, nor from observation alone.
It is not the case that the rule of inseparable connection is ascertained merely by the non-observation of the reason (*hetu*) in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*).
Neither from observation, nor from the observation of the coexistence of the probandum and the probans,
nor from a causal relationship, nor from an essential nature that acts as a regulator.
The rule of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva-niyama*) arises neither from observation nor from non-observation;
therefore, the invariable concomitance of one thing with another is due solely to their causal relation (*tadutpatti*).

Otherwise, if there were no production from that [cause], what necessary connection would there be for others—those things intended as the probandum—to have a mark (*liṅga*) that is not essentially identical to themselves?

However, if the mark is not a separate entity, then the property to be proven must be admitted to be invariably concomitant with that [mark] alone; otherwise, if it is maintained that the cause of impermanence is something other than the cause of "being produced"—such as a hammer or similar instrument—then what necessary connection could there be for that [other] property?

Just as in the case of a dye on a cloth— where, once the cloth has been produced, there is no necessary rule regarding the subsequent appearance of a color caused by safflower and the like— so too, if impermanence is desired to be the cause of a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), not only is this fault present, but there is another fault as well; thus he says:

Furthermore, [the passage] beginning with "api ca" means that the property called "permanence" would have to be something entirely different from that which constitutes its own nature, such as being produced (*kṛtaka*). For if it is admitted that the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is caused by something else, two consequences are entailed: its non-occurrence even when the probans (*sādhana*) is accomplished, and its having a different cause.

And this is not possible without a difference in essential nature (*svabhāvabheda*), because it is not logical that when that essential nature of the probans (*sādhana*) has been established, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—if it were unestablished or produced by a different cause—could have that same essential nature; nor is it logical for the essential nature of a previously established mark (*liṅga*) to be produced by a different cause. For indeed, this is the world-renowned distinction between entities: the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), which is the conjunction with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmayoga*).
In this context, completion and non-completion are two contradictory properties;

likewise, this very thing is the cause of differentiation— that is, the difference in causes (*kāraṇabheda*) and the difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrībheda*), among which the difference in causes is to be understood here as the producer of differentiation.
By this, difference itself and the cause of difference have been stated;
however, the appearance of difference is what apprehends difference.
If those two—the superimposition of contradictory properties and difference—are not accepted as the causes of difference, then they cannot be the differentiators.
In that case, since there would be no distinction between any object and any other thing, the entire universe and the whole world would become a single substance.
If it is argued that unity is indeed desired for everything because there is no difference in the three *guṇas*, [the author] says:
"And therefore," due to this oneness, there would be simultaneous origination and destruction.
The meaning is that upon the arising of one thing, there would be the arising of all, and upon its destruction, the destruction of all; furthermore,
if simultaneous arising and so forth were not admitted, everything would be functional as a cause for every effect.
It would not be the case that "all things are one";
rather, if their distinct natures are accepted through differences such as utility and so forth, this would either be a different name for those very distinctions,
or it would be a designation of "one" applied to many.
What is the reason?
Because, having accepted that the objects are mutually distinct, they are designated as such;
that is, they are designated as "one."

Now, it might be argued that impermanence is the connection with existence occurring between prior non-existence and posterior non-existence, and that this [impermanence] is indeed already established at the time of the production of the produced thing; it is merely destroyed later and not manifested at a subsequent time.
This too is incorrect.
Since destruction has not yet arisen, how can there be impermanence existing in the interval?
And even when destruction has arisen, how could this [impermanence] exist in the interval,
or possess the nature of being produced?
"Since the entity itself does not exist," and so forth— thus the opponent [objects]:
even if it is not a different thing and even if it does not depend on a cause of destruction, according to your own view, impermanence [remains].
Because impermanence is not established at the time of the entity's existence—
since that impermanence is not established while the entity exists— it is thought that impermanence occurs after the entity; thus,
it is considered equal [to permanence] in being of a nature other than that [of the entity].

He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "not so" and so forth, by showing that the equality of their not having that nature remains even if those two were produced from causes that are either different or non-different from the object.

Specifically, he argues that just as production would occur even if they were caused by something other than the object, there would likewise be a difference between them even if they were caused by what is not other than the object; thus, the lack of that nature is equal in both cases.
The acquisition of a previously non-existent nature is called "completion" (*niṣpatti*), and impermanence (*anityatā*) consists in the cessation of an entity;
therefore, since completion itself does not exist, how could there be a conjunction of contradictory properties?
[The opponent asks: "If, then, impermanence is not a real entity, how can there be a relationship characterized by identity between the probandum and the probans? To this, he says:

For that very entity which exists at a given moment— its very state of persistence— is its "dharma"; thus, it is the nature itself, characterized by cessation, that is called impermanence, and that alone is the probandum.

Because the identity of the reason and the probandum would imply that the meaning is distinct [from the entity itself] and that impermanence is formless, [it follows that] "by means of that, the impermanence of the entity comes into being. By such statements as these, no form whatsoever is predicated of the entity; rather, the point expressed is that its perceived form does not exist, for if another property were being predicated, it would follow that the cessation of the entity itself is not being taught.
If the entity itself were impermanence, then how could there be this difference in expression, namely that "impermanence is a property (dharma) of the subject (dharmin), the sound"? To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "even though there is a difference in expression," etc.:

even in that difference of expression consisting of the distinction between property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*), which arises from the difference in the expressive words, we shall state the underlying cause later on. By this, [the argument] that was stated by the learned scholars such as Aviddhakarṇa, Uddyotakara, and others, is also refuted.
If the destruction of the cause occurs at the very moment of the production of the effect— just as there is the simultaneous sinking and rising of the two ends of a scale—
and if there were no relationship of cause and effect, since the destruction of the cause is the very arising of the cause,
then by the statement that "destruction is indeed existence," it would follow that the effect is produced together with the cause.
Furthermore, if destruction were indeed the entity itself, then the entity would lack existence even in its first moment; moreover,
destruction is understood by the world as the cessation of the entity, not the entity itself,
and because destruction would exist at all times, the entity would have to exist perpetually.
Now, if the destruction of the cause were distinct from the arising of the cause, then impermanence would not have the nature of being produced;
furthermore, if destruction were a separate entity that arose, there would be no cessation of that moment—so how could there be momentariness? Thus, that [objection] is refuted.
For destruction is held to be twofold: consisting in the cessation of an entity and the entity itself.
Thus, an entity that has arisen performs its function, and at the time of that function, the destruction consisting in the cessation of the cause is indeed well-known in the world;
it is not held to have the nature of an entity.

Nor is it non-different or different from the arising of its cause, because it lacks any intrinsic nature (*nīrūpatva*); rather, one merely performs the negation of difference and non-difference regarding it.
As he will state:
"For this conceptual distinction would exist in the case of an entity, since affirmation conforms to a real thing. (Verse 6)
Thus, the argument that "since destruction is distinct [from the entity], the moment does not cease" is refuted;

for since the cessation in the first moment occurs precisely at the time of the arising of the second moment, an entity that persists for only a single moment is designated by the term "destruction," and this destruction, being of the nature of an entity, is itself of the same nature as its cause.

And [if one were to argue that] it would cease at the time of the effect’s production, then it would exist at a time different from the effect; nor does it exist at all times, because the entity itself is non-existent [at those other times].

Alternatively, by these two terms denoting the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*)—namely, "this is perishable" (*vinaśvara*) and "its destruction is [present]" (*vināśo 'sya*)—one and the same entity, which is excluded from being imperishable, is expressed through the exclusion of one distinction while not excluding others. Thus, it is said that the entity itself is destruction; therefore, everything is well-established.

If, then, the entity itself is impermanence (*anityatā*), then since that [impermanence] is also directly perceived when the entity is directly perceived, why is it not determined as such? To this, he says:
The connection of the words "tām" and so forth is as follows:
even while seeing— that is, even while directly perceiving— the nature of things, which is their state of existing for only a moment and is termed impermanence, one does not ascertain, that is,
one does not determine it.

Why is its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) the property of abiding for only a moment? He says: because it arises from its own very cause as having the property of abiding for only a moment. Furthermore, he asks: what is it that one sees yet does not determine? He says: [it is the following...]

"One of dull intellect" (*mandabuddhi*) means one whose intellect is dull due to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) in the form of permanence and so forth, which have been cultivated throughout beginningless *saṃsāra*. Otherwise, why would there not be certainty for all beings regarding an object perceived [as it is]?
By this, it is stated that although yogis perceive similar appearances, because they lack dullness of intellect, certainty regarding momentariness arises.

If, then, one were to suspect that because there is no determination of impermanence through ignorance, the determination of impermanence would not occur even when an entity has perished, [the author] states the cause of external error as well,
beginning with "by the perception of existence" (*sattopalambhena*): that is, by that perception of existence itself, and not of non-existence, [it is called] "by the perception of existence."

This is what is meant: at the very moment the subsequent moment arises, because the preceding moment has ceased, there is no interval between the preceding and succeeding moments due to their non-existence; thus, because of this immediate succession (*nairantarya*), their difference is not perceived. Furthermore, since at all times—even in the second and subsequent moments—only the existence of that very thing is apprehended, there is the state of being "thus" (*tathābhāva*). This refers to the existence (*sadbhāva*) of what was previously seen. Regarding the doubt concerning that, which takes the form "Could this be that very same thing?", [the author] says it is a "doubt" (*śaṅkā*) because even a deluded person might see something and think, "This is that very same thing. Deceived and misled by such a doubt, one does not reach a definitive determination.

"In that case," he says, "there would be no determination of the causal relationship even between fire and smoke, because their difference would not be perceived due to the lack of an intervening absence.
He continues with the words "due to the arising of a similar [moment]," and so forth;
for the perception of a subsequent similar [object] is observed to be the cause of the delusion of identity even in cases such as mother-of-pearl.
And since this has been analyzed in the *Nairātmyasiddhi*, it should be understood from that very work (*Pramāṇavārttika* 1.225).

Therefore, because another moment arises that is similar to the preceding moment in every respect, one who is deceived by that similarity does not determine the subsequent moment as being different from the preceding moment; rather, [he thinks] "this is that very same thing. For this very reason, there is no cognition of the destruction of the preceding moment, nor a cognition of the arising of the subsequent one.

However, because fire and smoke are absolutely dissimilar, even when they exist in immediate succession, their distinctness is apprehended, and thus the determination of their causal relationship occurs. The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to indicate an impossibility; therefore, the meaning is this: if there were a deviation in the perception of existence, or if there were a deception due to the arising of a similar subsequent [moment], then such deception would indeed always exist—this is the opponent's position.

Alternatively, [the author] asks: "How is it that one does not determine [the object] even while seeing it? He replies: "One who was previously deceived by the apprehension of existence—that is, by the superimposition of a previously perceived state upon that which is currently being cognized through the apprehension of existence—does not determine it."

Anticipating the objection that "in this case, determination would occur only at the perception of the first moment, because there was no prior apprehension of existence," he says: "or [it is] deceived by the production of a similar subsequent [moment]."
The word "or" (vā) has the sense of "and" (ca);
and because one is deceived by the production of a second moment that resembles the first moment, one does not reach a definitive determination.
To this, he says: "In that case, even for yogins, there would be no certainty."
Regarding the phrase "one of dull intellect":
because of the existence of signs that deceive both externally and internally, ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) form a certain conviction;
however, for yogins, even when there is the perception of something similar, a certain conviction does indeed arise due to their sharp intellect.
Therefore, it is established that even while perceiving the nature of momentary existence, one who is deceived by the production of successive similar moments does not discern it.
[Objection: But if an entity were indeed momentary, there would have to be an appearance of the preceding and succeeding moments as distinct from one another.

And since it does not appear [to consciousness], how can it be said that one does not determine it even while seeing it? Alternatively, if it is argued that because momentariness is non-different from blue and so forth, its apprehension occurs upon the apprehension of blue—
this is correct.
However, this is what is being examined here: is this blue non-momentary, or is it momentary in nature, or is it a continuum?
In that regard, if it were non-momentary, then how could there be an appearance of momentariness within the appearance of blue?
Now, if it is argued that this very nature of momentariness is unestablished, how can it be said that there is an appearance of moments within the appearance of blue?
And because moments do not appear, there can be no appearance of blue in the form of a continuum.
Now, if it is argued that when there is the appearance of mere blue, there is also the appearance of momentariness, that is incorrect;
for the apprehension or non-apprehension by perception depends precisely upon appearance or non-appearance.
It is not otherwise;
thus he said:
"Whatever it apprehends, it does so by means of its appearance as that."
Furthermore, it has been stated that there is no appearance of moments;
and if momentariness were not distinct from blue and so forth, then since momentariness would be ascertained at the very time blue is ascertained, inference would be rendered useless.
As for the one who says this:

It is argued that momentariness is simply the state of being the object of a single cognition, because what appears now is the state of being an object of a present cognition, which is excluded from being the object of preceding and succeeding cognitions;

thus, the moment is perceived by direct perception as distinct from preceding and succeeding moments, and since inference merely reflects upon what has already occurred through perception, inference is not redundant.
This is incorrect.
For if that single cognition were non-momentary, then the object would also have to be non-momentary;
yet if it is momentary, how is that known?
If you say it is because the object too is the content of that same single cognition, then the realization of momentariness would result in an infinite regress.
Now, if the manifestation of the moment of cognition is admitted, why is that [manifestation] of the moment of the object not also admitted?
Otherwise, because even a single moment would be the object of multiple cognitions, it would follow that it possesses multiplicity. Bhaṭṭa Vāsudeva, however, says:

The claim that "the non-appearance of preceding and succeeding moments due to their destruction is itself the appearance of non-momentariness; therefore, every perception grasps non-momentariness, and it is merely by means of the inference of momentariness that error is established"—
this too is untenable,
because since the thesis is contradicted by perception, the inference cannot even arise.
Furthermore, if even non-conceptual perception were erroneous, there would be a contradiction with the text stating, "even while seeing [the relation] due to the apprehension of the connection";
therefore, what was said is incorrect.
To the objection that "one does not determine [the object] even while seeing it," it is replied as follows:

Just as there is a sequence of preceding and succeeding among the moments of the object, so too is there such a sequence among the moments of cognition; therefore, by that preceding moment of cognition, only the preceding moment of the object is grasped, not the subsequent one.

If it is argued that even by means of the subsequent [cognition], only the subsequent [object] appears and not the prior one—since these two do not appear together in a single cognition—how could there be a distinct appearance such as "this is other than the prior"? To this it is replied:
the very appearance of a thing's own nature (*svarūpa*) is its appearance as distinguished from others, just like the appearance of Mount Sumeru as distinct [from other mountains].
And since that [nature] exists even for a single moment, why is there no manifestation of discrimination? Furthermore,
from the cognition "what was seen is being seen now," it follows that the nature of what was seen is indeed one thing, while the nature of what is currently being seen is another.

For indeed, one who perceives for the first time sees only the present intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity, and not what was previously seen; thus there is only a distinction between these two.

However, because there is no interval—due to the absence of preceding and succeeding moments between two instances that are entirely similar—a cognition of separation does not arise as it does in the case of a jar and a cloth, nor is there non-difference, since they do not appear as undivided.

For indeed, when one proceeds toward a mother-of-pearl shell thinking, "This is that very silver of ours," there is no non-difference [between them] because of the absence of a manifestation of the distinction between the mother-of-pearl and the silver;

therefore, just as in this indeterminate cognition (nirvikalpaka-jñāna) there is the manifestation of the mother-of-pearl's own nature which is the manifestation of its non-distinction from other things,
so too it would be for a single moment.

If the only objection were to ask why the preceding moment is not remembered distinctly, the answer has already been given: it is not remembered because one is deceived by the production of a subsequent [moment] that is similar [to the first]. But even so, the moment does not appear, since an entity is not perceived as having the duration of the passage of a single atom.
But if there is no manifestation in a single moment, how can there be a manifestation of a non-momentary thing, since it does not manifest at every moment?
Furthermore, since a thing as it arises is perceived by direct perception as being devoid of prior and subsequent forms, how can there be a grasping of its momentariness?

Nor is it perceived as non-momentary, precisely because its connection with prior and subsequent times does not appear in the present perception; for the very non-appearance now of that nature which was connected to the prior time is "destruction," while the appearance of another nature is "origination. Thus, how can it be called "non-momentary" when the destruction and origination of prior and subsequent moments do not appear? Nor is the present [entity] of the nature of multiple moments; for if multiple moments were possible at this time, it would possess a form already grasped and so forth, and thus there would be no novelty.
For it is not by means of a certainty arising from direct perception that one determines "this exists right now";
rather, one determines "it exists now," while it is by means of inference that it is established that "it exists right now."
Therefore, it is established that "even though seeing, one does not determine [the object]," and so forth.

Now, an objection is raised: if there were a determination by perception that "it is eternally similar," then the cognition "this is that very same thing" would be an error; however, since the realization "this is that very same thing" always arises in a firm form, how can it be an error? To this, Bhaṭṭa says:

Ślokavārttika, Chapter on the Eternity of Words (Śabdanityatādhikaraṇa), verses 373–374: Since it has been established that [the word] exists at that time and is moreover identical [to what was perceived before], where the mind becomes firmly settled in the notion that "it is exactly the same," there the recognition [of identity] is understood to be an error.
In this case, the firm cognition "this is that very same thing" arises constantly; because its existence exceeds [the mere presence of the object], its validity is established.
Furthermore, there is limited scope for [discrepancy] therein due to differences in place, time, and so forth.
Present existence has not been apprehended by a previous cognition,
nor is there always a determination of similarity through inference; for such [inference] is sublated by perceptual recognition, since recognition does not arise from inference.

Nor is recognition invalid due to the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), because as long as its invalidity is not established, there is no arising of inference, and as long as there is no arising of inference, there is no invalidity of this [recognition]; thus, there is the fault of mutual dependence. To this, it is replied:
By the word "that" (*sa*), an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) connected with a previous time is made the object;
by the word "this" (*ayam*), one connected with the present time is made the object.

And there is no difference whatsoever between these two, nor is there any non-difference, because a real entity possesses a single intrinsic nature consisting of both its present state and its future form.
Therefore, since it is precisely difference that appears when there is recognition, how could this [recognition] subvert the inference of momentariness?
Or rather, the object's connection with a previous time does not exist now, because that previous time no longer exists.
It has been stated that, in this case, there would only be a connection with the present time for the entity, and not a connection with a prior time, due to contradiction;

therefore, that portion of the cognition which grasps what was non-existent—namely, the connection with a prior time—is erroneous. Otherwise, it would have to grasp the actual state of the object as clearly manifest in its infancy and so forth, yet it does not do so.
Consequently, how could there be sublation by inference from a cognition such as "this is that very same [person]," which is erroneous because it superimposes a previously perceived form?
Wherever there is the operation of the sense-faculties (*akṣa*), perception (*pratyakṣa*) arises as its grasper;

however, since existence at a prior time does not exist now, where could there be an operation [of the senses], given that it is not present? Nor can there be [an operation] through non-difference from that [present existence]. Therefore, how could a cognition that grasps the identity between existence at a prior time and existence at a subsequent time be perception?
And when that which was perceived in the state of childhood and so forth is recognized in the state of old age,
neither in that object nor in the recognition itself does permanence appear;
rather, only the reality that "this is that very same thing" is determined.
Nor is there a difference in reality between the states of childhood and old age;

nor can the postulation of permanence and so forth be inferred from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the apprehension of reality, since such apprehension can arise even from the illusion caused by the production of similar subsequent moments.
It is like hair that has grown back after being shaved;
for in this case, it would follow that there could arise a recognition in the form "this is that" based on a distinct universal of "hair-ness."

Nor can there be a continuous cognition (*anugama*) of something other than what is non-different; for the forms that are inclusive (*anugata*) and exclusive (*vyāvṛtta*) are absolutely distinct due to their mutual lack of connection.
Consequently, the recognition "these are those very same hairs" is caused solely by the production of similar subsequent moments, and for this very reason, it is an illusion.

Likewise, the emergence of inference is indeed appropriate due to the suspicion that this [recognition] might be erroneous in the case of jars and so forth; nor is there a circularity of dependence, because it is not by means of inference that the invalidity of recognition is produced, but rather it is known as such, since it is established as invalid in its very nature from its own causes,
owing to the apprehension that "what was seen is being seen."

For a thing does not possess the state of having been seen previously, because at that time it possessed only the nature of being currently perceived; nor does it possess it now, for the very same reason.
Nor can there be a connection with a prior time for that which is being perceived now, since it did not exist previously;

therefore, recognition—which grasps [an object] by superimposing the quality of "having been seen"—arises as invalid because it is erroneous. Furthermore, the emergence of inference is not caused by the invalidity of this [recognition], but rather by its necessary connection with the probandum; thus, [inference] serves as the sublater of recognition.
This detailed analysis of the refutation of recognition has been set forth in the *Nairātmyasiddhi*; therefore, it should be understood from that very work.
Consequently, this remains established:

even while perceiving that nature which is the property of momentary existence, one does not ascertain it because one is deceived by the production of a subsequent similar [moment] and thus fails to determine the destruction of the preceding moment.
But how is it known that one who is deceived by the arising of a similar [moment] does not determine [the object]? To this he says:
"The final," and so forth.
The "final moment" is a moment that does not link up with another similar moment; for those who perceive it, it is determined to be "destroyed."
It is understood that this [entity] perishes at every single moment even prior [to its end], yet it is simply not ascertained because of the aforementioned causes of deception. [Objection:
But how can there be an ascertainment of perishability even for one who perceives the final moment, since at that time there is still the perception of existence?
For one who perceives only existence does not understand its absence. To this, he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "paścāt" (afterwards), we do not say that certainty arises from the mere perception of the final moment; rather, having perceived the final moment, [the certainty] arises afterwards. At that time, it is no longer perceived, and that [non-perception] is its effect.
Furthermore, when smoke arises from the proximity of fire, wood, and so forth, it is not observed once the horse or other such things are removed;
however, it is indeed not observed when the fire and other such factors are removed.
Thus, through perception and non-perception acting in mutual conjunction, causality is established without doubt only with respect to those very factors intended as causes.
Regarding the phrase "that [effect]," the aforementioned characteristic of an effect exists in smoke; therefore, smoke arises only from fire.

Furthermore, since smoke occurs whenever fire is present, its not being produced by non-fire is stated [as a reason]—whether on the grounds that what exists or does not exist at some time cannot be produced, or because it lacks a cause, or because its cause is invisible. Among these, the first position is not tenable, as was discussed in the third chapter of the *Pramāṇavārttika* in the section beginning with "If it is argued that everything is incapable."
We shall state that smoke does not have the nature of being causeless; he will state right there that it also does not have an invisible cause.
Because [the effect] conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consisting of fire and so forth— [leaf 37 is missing]—
it might then be argued:

The nature of this invisible entity is such that it produces smoke only when fire and other factors are present, and only at the time of burning camphor and the like does it produce that which is endowed with fragrance and so forth, and not otherwise.
If it is asked: "Has the production of smoke ever been observed without fire, such that you could say 'no' [to its existence]? [the answer follows].
How then can it be said that there is no causal function of fire, given that smoke exists when fire exists?
Furthermore, at the time of the production of smoke, fire—though perceived at all times—is present only by a mere coincidence (*kākatālīyanyāya*); thus, this designation is unworldly.
Alternatively, that very nature of the invisible [fire] is such that if it were not assisted by fire, why would it produce smoke only upon the proximity of fire and so forth, and not before or after?
Therefore, smoke is produced by its cause only when fire and other factors are present, and not otherwise; thus, even in that case, smoke would ultimately be produced by fire alone.

Furthermore, just as the dependence of smoke upon place, time, and so forth is recognized because it does not arise without them, so too, since it is observed never to arise without fire, by what means could its dependence upon fire be denied?
And dependence on that [cause] is nothing other than being its effect.

Just as the existence of smoke only when there is the existence of the invisible [fire] is accepted as being produced by it, why is it not likewise accepted that [smoke] is produced by fire because its existence is observed whenever fire exists at all times? Furthermore, only those things in whose presence a thing is seen to arise possess causality, since the prior existence of all [potential causes] is equal.
And thus, since smoke is produced by a causal complex that includes fire, visibility, and so forth, how could there be any deviation from fire?
Another, however, says:
"Even if there is such a cause-and-effect relationship between fire and smoke, they cannot be grasped by a single cognition, because they exist at different times."

Nor can it be by means of that previous non-conceptual [cognition], for by it only the previous object-in-itself was grasped, and not the cause-form of the effect, because the latter is not perceived due to its future existence; nor can it be by the subsequent [non-conceptual cognition], for by that too only the subsequent object-in-itself is grasped, and not the effect-form of the cause, because the former is no longer apprehended due to its having passed away;
nor can it be by means of conceptual cognition, since this same objection applies equally there as well.
"Because no one has ever apprehended that 'this [effect] has arisen from this [cause],' for that very reason it is not apprehended even by memory, due to the absence of prior experience.
To this, it is replied:
First of all, in its unarisen state, the effect does not possess a relationship with the cause simply because it is non-existent; and in its already accomplished state, it is likewise [not related].
Because it is independent,
the cause likewise remains unrelated to the effect during both the states of the effect's production and non-production;
nor is there a relation of causality between these two, because they exist at different times.
This designation of "this is the effect" and "this is the cause" is merely conceptual.
Therefore, the very acquisition of its own nature from the cause is what constitutes being an effect;

likewise, for the cause, its status as a cause consists simply in its prior existence relative to the effect. Since this acquisition of self-nature and prior existence are non-different from the entity itself, they are indeed apprehended by perception. Thus, how could the causal relation not be grasped by perception? It is only when the effect is observed that one conventionally designates, "this is the effect of that," or "this is the cause of that."
Since the relation of cause and effect is not possible between two things that are not cause and effect,
nor can their causality be made non-different from one another through the connection with the relation of cause and effect due to contradiction,
nor can it be different because that would entail the consequence that they remain non-cause and non-effect by their very nature.

Even in the case of cause and effect, what is the point of postulating a cause-and-effect relationship as a separate entity distinct from their own nature (*svarūpa*), since they possess the form of cause and effect by their very nature?

Therefore, the causal relationship between them is simply the state of being prior and subsequent. Consequently, when a preceding object is perceived, that which constitutes the cause—characterized by its immediate succession to the effect—is necessarily perceived as well.
Furthermore, when a subsequent object is apprehended by a subsequent cognition immediately after its cause, it is apprehended as being precisely of the nature of an effect;
for that immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is non-different in essence from that [effect].
For this very reason, there also arises the recollection, "this occurs immediately after that," because the immediate succession has been experienced.
But Aviddhakarṇa says:
"The state of invariable concomitance (avinābhāvitva) is established when, having seen one [instance], a second or subsequent instance is seen;
however, for the proponent of momentariness (kṣaṇikavādin), there is no persistence of the observer."
Furthermore, it is incorrect to claim that there can be no recollection of the invariable concomitance between one object and another because of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),

for the first moment of an object is apprehended by the first moment of its cognition, and because recollection is possible through the causal relationship between moments falling within a single continuum.

And how the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) exists in the case of momentariness has already been stated and will be stated again in *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.33. [Objection: Even so, since moments are not ascertained, how can there be an ascertainment of the causal relation? Nor can it be ascertained by means of a continuum (*santāna*), because that continuum does not exist as something distinct from the members of the continuum (*santānin*). There are only the members of the continuum themselves, existing at prior and subsequent times.
And in that case, since when one moment exists, another does not, there is only the appearance of a single moment; how, then, can there be the appearance of a continuum?
Since that [continuum] is absent, how can there be a causal relationship?
That is incorrect.

Since a real entity consists of a single atom, the appearance of a continuum is merely the appearance of gross-natured, successive [moments] occurring without interval.
