And because there is a determination of oneness through similarity—due to the failure to discern the distinction between moments therein—the causal relationship between the moments existing within a single continuum cannot be ascertained.

However, as for those [moments] existing in distinct continua, because they are of a different nature due to the progression of the continuum, that determination [of identity] does not occur; therefore, the claim that "the determination of the causal relation between the fire-continuum and the smoke-continuum is stated based on the cognition of a smoke-continuum preceded by a fire-continuum" is trivial. Furthermore, Adhyayana says:

"If the causal relation is grasped between two particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), how can there be a relationship of the signifier and the signified between two universals (*sāmānya*), since they are distinct?"
That too is incorrect,
because it is accepted that the universal consists of multiple particular characteristics;
as it has been said:

"Because it establishes merely the thing as excluded from what does not possess its form, and because it does not rest upon particulars, the logical mark (*liṅga*) is said to have the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object. (Pramāṇasamuccaya).
Therefore, the apprehension of the relation of universals is indeed the apprehension of the relation of the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and nothing else.

Now, for the Buddhist who maintains the theory of inference, all the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) existing in the three worlds would have to be apprehended as being pervaded by fire; for if even one were not apprehended, the logical reason (*hetu*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Yet, perception is not capable of doing this, because its object must be proximate.

Nor is it the case that the pervasion of other specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is grasped through inference, because that would entail the fallacy of infinite regress; therefore,
that [objection] is incorrect, since perception apprehends the smoke-particular only when the fire-particular is present.
In these cases, one determines that the nature of smoke—which is excluded from non-smoke—is exclusively the effect of fire, which is itself excluded from non-fire;

and just as it is here, so too in other places and times, one determines that this very nature is produced by fire alone. Otherwise, it would not be perceived through direct perception as being connected with fire;
for if smoke were the effect of both fire and non-fire, its cognition would occur as being connected to both, rather than as being connected to fire alone.
And since it is perceived that this form occurs only from fire even in other instances, by virtue of such certainty, how could there be any deviation of smoke from fire?
Furthermore, this inference belongs only to one who is able to discern that form as distinct from steam and the like, and not to anyone else.

Even for one who maintains that universal concomitance (*sāmānyavyāpti*) is grasped, inference occurs only through the ascertainment of a smoke-universal that is restricted to fire, because there is a suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) when a smoke-universal is observed in things such as a cowherd’s water-pot in the absence of fire.
Furthermore, this ascertainment of a smoke-universal restricted to fire is possible only by first ascertaining individual instances of smoke connected with fire.
And it is not possible for anyone, by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), to grasp a smoke-universal qualified by individual instances of smoke connected with fire in every place and so forth.

Nor is it the case that the universal of smoke (*dhūmasāmānya*), as qualified by a particular instance of smoke connected with fire in the kitchen or elsewhere, has been apprehended [as pervaded], because a particular instance does not persist in other locations.
Furthermore, that universal of smoke which does persist is not invariably concomitant with fire.

Therefore, the objection is equal for the proponent who maintains the apprehension of a universal pervasion: how is it that the universal of smoke, in its specific form, is apprehended as being everywhere pervaded by fire?

Now, as for the claim that there is no subverting evidence against smoke being produced by fire elsewhere, and that its universal is established because of the cognition "this is that very same thing"—and that we too accept that its universal is established because of the arising of the cognition "this is that very same thing," so what is the difference between us? This is trivial.
Demonstrating this very point, he says:
If that smoke were to exist in the absence of fire— that is, in the absence of its cause— it would transcend its causality and become causeless;

or else, if that smoke, which is perceived as being connected with fire, were to exist in the absence of fire— that is, in the absence of its cause— it would not be perceived through direct perception as having the causality of being connected with fire, yet it is so perceived.
Therefore, it is not only because of repeated observation in that manner, but also from the aforementioned direct perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*);
for what reason? Because fire, which is not the cause, does not exist even once, let alone repeatedly.
"Indeed, oil does not arise even once from sands because [they lack] the causal capacity," and so forth; by this he states the meaning of the verse,
and the passage beginning with "indeed" is the justification for that very point.
By this, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is stated; for one who asserts deviation (*vyabhicāra*), smoke would exist even without fire. And by this, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is stated:
"that" means because it exists without fire, it is not caused by that [fire], nor is fire its cause; thus, the sense is that it would be causeless.
If it is argued that smoke is not causeless because fire has other causes— such as a circle of spears on a mountain peak— and smoke has those as its causes, this is not so;
for the same logic applies even when another distinct entity is postulated as the cause.
For instance, even in the absence of that [fire], if it occurs again when other causes are present, then that other cause would not be the cause either. Furthermore,
is that fire and that other cause of the same nature as producing smoke, or are they not?

If it has the nature of not producing smoke, then how could smoke arise from that fire, or from something else such as the head of Śakra? Since those things do not have the nature of producing it—that is, they do not have the nature of producing smoke—smoke would simply not come into being.
Why?
Because that which does not have that nature, being itself of a nature not to produce smoke, would fail to produce it, and thus smoke would lack a cause.
Now, if it is argued that the other [substance] has the nature of producing smoke, then both would possess the status of fire, because fire is defined by the nature of producing smoke;
this will be explained later in the passage beginning with "Certainly not that very same [thing]," where the proponent of deviation (vyabhicāra) speaks.
Alternatively, it is not said that smoke produced from fire arises from something else;

for if that very same [smoke] were to arise from elsewhere, there would be the consequence of causelessness (*ahetutva*), because such a thing—being identical in nature to the property produced by fire—would exist from something other than its cause. Thus says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*).
In that case, is it intended that the cause is similar to the effect, such that it is said: "How can that which arises from something dissimilar be of such a nature?
No, because it does not have a different meaning;

for when fire is seen as the producer of smoke, how is it that smoke, arising from that dissimilar [cause], becomes of such a nature—that is, it comes to possess a nature identical to the properties produced by fire?
This is what is meant:

just as there is a similarity among the various types of smoke—such as that produced from grass, leaves, and so forth—relative to one another, so too there is a similarity among the various types of fire—such as those produced from grass, leaves, and so forth—that generate smoke, relative to one another.
Therefore, when a particular type of smoke is observed to arise from a particular type of fire, it follows that such a type of smoke arises only from such a type of fire.
But that which arises from non-fire is indeed of a different nature, like steam and so forth.

If it is argued: "Surely, by means of a moment of smoke produced by fire, a moment of smoke produced by that [fire] is of the same nature; thus, even from something of a different nature, something of that same nature comes into being."
For a subsequent moment of smoke produced from fire is not exactly like another such moment of smoke produced from fire;
nor is it the case that steam and the like possess that same likeness even when they are determined to be such.

Even in the case of a smoke-moment produced by a smoke-moment, only another smoke-moment produced by a [specific] smoke-moment becomes such [an effect], and not any other; therefore, since such an effect arises only from such a cause, how can there be any deviation? By this...
If things were momentary, how could their modes of existence depend upon anything? For those whose existence occurs from something other than their well-known causes,
the arising of smoke would be possible even from non-fire, just as smoke might arise from that [other cause].
"How could the arising of that [smoke] from the head of Śakra be prevented?"—this is refuted;

for of the first moment of smoke produced by fire, there is another moment of smoke produced by fire that is similar to it; and of the second moment of smoke produced by that [first] moment of smoke, there is another second moment of smoke produced by smoke that is similar to it.
Likewise, this applies to the third and subsequent moments as well; thus, even with respect to the moments, such a thing is non-deviant.
He states this very point:
"For that which arises from such [a cause] must itself be of such [a nature]."

If even from something entirely different—even from what is dissimilar to fire—the effect were to be of such a nature as smoke produced by fire, then there would be an absence of the restriction of causal power (*tacchaktiniyamābhāvāt*).

Since there is no such restriction regarding the power of causes—whether similar or dissimilar—namely, that "a similar cause produces only a similar effect and a dissimilar one produces a distinct effect," it follows that the difference in the cause is not the differentiator of the effect. Consequently, the manifold variety of the universe (*vaiśvarūpya*) would be without a cause.
If it is argued that there is no lack of cause because production occurs from some cause or other, he says:
"Or else everything would arise from everything," and so forth;
for if production occurred even from that which lacks the capacity, then everything would be born from everything.
And it is not so;
therefore, [the argument] beginning with "tasmāt" and ending with "na sa dhūmaḥ" is incorrect.

The word "tat" (that) means: therefore, that fire which possesses the observed form from which smoke is seen arising, [is excluded] from that which is of a different genus, namely non-fire; such is the meaning.
And likewise, if there were no cause, smoke would have to exist eternally or not exist at all;
for what reason? Because an uncaused entity does not depend on anything else for its own production.

If it is argued that because there is no dependence on other causes, even in the absence of dependence on other causes, it may occur occasionally by its own nature, he says: "For [it would follow] from dependence... and so forth.
This is what is meant:
since that which is unestablished is non-existent, how could it possess occasional occurrence by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*)?
On the other hand, that which is established does possess an intrinsic nature; however, it is merely questioned how that very establishment occurs in certain instances.
He explains this very point with the words beginning "sa hi" and so forth:
it would never not exist; that is, it would exist at all times.
What is the reason? Because when that exists—namely, when the existence of the nature of smoke exists [the fire must exist].
Because there would be no deficiency due to the independence from causes,
smoke would not exist at that time either, just as it does not at the observed time.
Distinguishing the latter half because there is no difference in the time when smoke is absent, he says: "For,
by way of dependence..."

In consideration of the appropriate place and time, since there are two periods— the period of existence and the period of non-existence— of an effect, the mention of "time" is intended as an illustration (upalakṣaṇa) because it is conjoined with the suitability and unsuitability for the occurrence of that existence, namely the production of the effect, respectively; the same should be stated for place and substance as well.
If this is not accepted, then since it would be impossible to establish a restriction between two places and times— both equally capable or incapable— which possess or do not possess that effect,
the possession of that [cause] must belong to the time of the effect itself.
Because the restriction that "one thing possesses causal efficiency while the other does not" is untenable.
Both those times— the presence and absence of the effect— would have to possess the effect, because of the similarity of their capacity;
or else, neither would,
because of the equality of their incapacity.
Therefore, it is precisely the time of its existence that possesses the capacity;
or rather, it is by depending upon that [capacity] that absences become occasional.
Let it be so for the desired locus, time, and other factors, provided they possess such capacity.
The causal state does not [arise] by that much alone; therefore,
he says "And that," and so forth,
because if there were no cause in this way, there would be either constant existence or non-existence, yet such is not the case.
Therefore, and so forth:
that which it proceeds by way of avoiding is independent of,
and that wherein it operates is dependent upon.
If it is asked: "Even if it were indeed situated in some place or the like, how could it still be dependent on that? he says:
"For thus," meaning that its existence in such a manner consists in its existing elsewhere by the exclusion of one [place].
If it is argued that while an entity indeed depends on location and so forth,
no assistance is rendered to it by that location and so forth,
he replies with the words "tatkṛtopakāra" (assistance produced by that), etc.
"Because of the impossibility of a restriction [stating] 'tanniya-māyogāt' means: because a restriction such as 'it must not exist in that very place and so forth' is impossible;
'tat' means therefore."
The mention of place and time is an illustration that includes substance as well;

"where" refers to the place and so forth where it was seen once by means of the aforementioned perception, and "again not seen" means when those very same [factors] are present but one of them is deficient.

"Otherwise" means: if its nature were not produced by that [cause], then how could "that"—namely smoke—which is restricted to a specific causal complex such as fire—come to be elsewhere than from fire? It could not come to be at all.
Alternatively, it would not be smoke;

for smoke is indeed a specific nature produced by that [fire], namely, produced by fire. Likewise, the cause—fire—is also a nature capable of producing such an effect, which is the nature of being fit to produce smoke.
Even in the state devoid of smoke, the causal capacity indeed exists;
therefore, the definition is not under-extended (*avyāpin*).
Thus, when the mutual dependence of fire and smoke as having a restricted nature is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*), [the definition holds].
If it is maintained that this smoke exists even from something other than fire, then that nature which produces smoke does not belong to that non-fire;

for when smoke arises from what is not fire, at that time a nature that produces smoke has arisen precisely from what is not fire, and how could that which is the nature of what is not fire be the nature of fire?
Furthermore, because fire would lack the nature of producing smoke, it would not produce smoke even once;
likewise, smoke itself would lack the nature of being smoke.
To this, he says "na ca" (nor... and so forth.
If smoke were to arise from something other than fire, it would not be smoke;
for what reason? Because it would arise from a non-fire that lacks the inherent nature of producing smoke.
And if it were admitted that fire possesses the nature of producing smoke— that is, even non-fire has the nature of generating smoke—

then by the reasoning that "this very thing is fire because its form is the producer of smoke," the non-deviation of smoke would be easily grasped; for this purpose, he states the two verses beginning with "the nature of fire" (*agnisvabhāva*).
The phrase "having the nature of fire" means: if it has the nature of producing smoke;
then that Śakra’s head would indeed be fire, because it possesses the nature of producing smoke.
Alternatively, if that Śakra’s head does not have the nature of fire...
Regarding that, he asks why it would not occur upon the head of Śakra, and answers with the verse beginning "dhūma" (smoke), etc.
For indeed, from what [reason] is it so?
Because the analysis of the compound is: "that which has smoke as its causal nature" (*dhūma-hetu-svabhāva*); how is that? Because it possesses a specific capacity (*tac-chakti-bheda-vān*).

If it is admitted that smoke arises— that is, its production occurs— from something other than its cause (namely, from what is not fire by nature) by means of that power which produces smoke and acts as the instrument, then that smoke would be without a cause, as was stated previously. This is because it would be distinct and dissimilar from other things such as fireflies, which are not causes of smoke.
"How so? and so forth—the opponent asks:
"Now, if one does not admit that a single thing such as smoke arises from something of a different class, how [could it arise] from distinct things that are mutually heterogeneous?"
He explains how the production of a single effect occurs from multiple cooperating causes with the words "just as," and so forth.
By the word "etcetera," [factors] such as light and mental attention are included.

This being the case, consciousness arises from that which has the nature of the eye and also from that which does not have the nature of the eye, such as form and mental attention; yet this is not without a cause.
In the same way, smoke should arise both from fire and from that which is not fire, namely the head of Śakra.
The opponent thinks that [the effect] will not be causeless;
[the author] replies with the words "Certainly not anything," etc.,
[stating that] among the eye and so forth, each one individually, possessing that nature— the nature of being a producer— without depending on the others, is certainly not a producer.
For if it were so, then because each individual cause would be deviant, [the effect] would be without a cause;
however, it is the totality (sāmagrī) that is the producer,
having the nature of a producer.

By the mere fact that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the producer, its nature as such is already established, because that which does not possess that nature is not a producer; why then is it stated separately that "it has that nature"?
True, but it is stated for the sake of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*):
that its nature as such exists only in the state of the causal complex.

The collective meaning is that the cause is all other causes combined in a single effect— neither prior, nor posterior, nor separate— due to their presence being determined by the capacity of their own respective causes.
Some, however, read the word "vā" (or).

Regarding the statement "the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the producer, or it has that as its intrinsic nature (*tatsvabhāva*)," the word "or" (*vā*) here serves no purpose; thus, this is simply a corrupt reading.

For if, having stated "the causal complex," visual consciousness were to arise even from another causal complex, then because it would be produced from something distinct, it would follow that it is causeless (*ahetukatva*).
That very causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is inferred from the effect; it is not [inferred] from each individual cause separately, for there would otherwise be deviation (*vyabhicāra*). This is the sense.
It might be argued: "The first moment of smoke is produced by the causal complex of fire and so forth, but that [moment] cannot serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*), because it is not ascertained."

And as for the connection with smoke that is apprehended, since that is merely the cause of previous smoke, how can there be an inference from it of the causal complex consisting of fire and so forth? To this he says:
"And that very [complex], etc.," because the continuity of the effect is established by its own nature.
The basis is the primary cause,
because without the causal complex (sāmagrī), the continuum of smoke itself would not exist;
therefore, having unified the continuum of smoke as the effect of fire, one infers the causal continuum of the burning [fuel] and so forth.
For it is not possible for one of limited vision to engage in conventional discourse through the analysis of individual moments; thus,
it must be that fire itself is inferred as a whole.
Furthermore, the objection that "there is no purpose for those seeking causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) by means of that [conceptual object]" has already been answered by the very act of raising it.
At that time, the meaning is as follows:

that same causal complex (*sāmagrī*), proceeding in a continuous stream, is the cause for the persistence of the nature of the effect and for the occurrence of the continuity of effects; for, in dependence upon each preceding moment of fire and so forth, each subsequent moment of smoke arises.
For there is no such rule that only one single moment of smoke is produced by fire and no other;

rather, as long as the fuel has not been entirely reduced to ashes, the production of moments of smoke is not contradictory. Therefore, it is not contradictory for one who seeks a purpose to infer a continuum of fire capable of causal efficiency—having ascertained elsewhere a continuum of smoke exactly as it was produced by a fire proceeding in a continuous series through the generation of successive moments of combustion, as previously established by direct perception.

Furthermore, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of smoke whose continuum of fire has been interrupted is one thing entirely, while that of smoke situated in a dwelling or similar place where the continuum of fire has been interrupted is another; and since people clearly perceive the difference between these two, how could there be any deviation (*vyabhicāra*)?
Alternatively, it may be explained in another way.
Now, one might object: "Is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) not distinct from its constituent members?

And since it is a single unity, only a single effect should be produced. Otherwise, because each member possesses its own capacity, there would either be a multiplicity of effects or the production of a single effect only successively. But this is not the case; therefore, how can it be said that the complex produces a single effect? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And that very [collection]," and so forth;
and "that very causal complex" (sāmagrī) means that it is precisely the complete [factors] that are denoted by the word *sāmagrī*.
What is the reason?
By its abiding in its own nature— that is, by the presence of its own form— it becomes the substratum for the effect;
for it is thus considered that if the production of the effect were due to the causal complex alone, then the individual members of that complex would lack causal agency.
And thus, there would be contradiction with empirical experience; even if all [causes] were causal agents, there would necessarily be a multiplicity of effects,
or else they would produce a single effect only in succession.
Nor does their uniformity arise from the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*),
for that would entail the non-existence of the causal complex itself;
therefore, those [causes], having arisen as restricted to the production of a single effect solely by virtue of their own causes when they are complete, are designated by the term "causal complex."
Furthermore, there is no obstacle to many things performing a single effect,
nor do we hold the view that the cause itself becomes the effect— by which the multiplicity of causes for a single effect would be contradicted.
Just as the priority (prāgbhāva) of a single thing is observed to be its causality when it has a single effect, so too is it for multiple things.
Or, just as those very [causes], when complete, produce a single totality characterized by conjunction,
why should they not likewise produce a single effect?
This argument is trivial.

And because that [cause] is a producer of a totality (*sāmagrī*), for that very reason there is no non-sequential production by the auxiliary factors; rather, the meaning is that there is sequential production.
With the words "as for what... and so forth, he raises the objection regarding production from a heterogeneous cause and then refutes it.
The meaning is that this very point—which was stated as "the production of such [an effect] does not arise from something of a different kind"—is demonstrated here.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), one includes such cases as an arrow from a cow's horn or a scorpion from cow dung;
"there too" means even in the case of the production of an effect from a heterogeneous cause.

"Even when designated thus" means that even though a lotus-root (*śālūka*) or the like produced from a dissimilar cause is designated as a "lotus-root," there is indeed a difference in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) compared to a lotus-root produced from its own seed—that is, one originating from a lotus-root characterized as its own seed.
What is the reason? Because of the difference in the nature of the causes (*hetusvabhāvabhedāt*).
Because of the difference in the intrinsic nature of the two sets of causes characterized as the causal complex,
that plantain tree which arises from a seed and from a bulb is such;
and it is mutually distinct due to the difference in its causality.
And this difference is not something to be proven; thus he says "clearly" (*sphuṭam*) and so forth,
[explaining that] one analyzes [the object] in terms of the difference of the entity (*bhāva*).
The aspect that has been well-discriminated from causes of error— that is, ascertained through its distinction from similar aspects—
is "positive concomitance" (anvaya), which means it exists only when that [object] exists; and "negative concomitance" (vyatireka) is its non-existence only when that [object] is absent.

Positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) constitute "positive-negative concomitance" (*anvayavyatireka*). Therefore, when the nature of an effect is observed to follow a particular cause that is to be followed, that following nature is its cause. The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that which has this [following nature] as its cause.

However, when it is stated with reference to the cause, then the nature of that which is to be followed—such as fire—is its cause; that is, it is the cause of that which is considered the effect, such as smoke.

And since, in this way, there is a restriction on the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of cause and effect through mutual dependence, it follows that there can be no production from a cause that is distinct— that is, of a different class (*vijātīya*). Therefore,
[the certainty of the relationship is established] by means of both seeing and not seeing even once, as previously described.

Since the causal relationship is established through perception and non-perception, it arises from that establishment of the causal relationship; thus, the comprehension of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the comprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) do not occur otherwise. Therefore, apart from the ascertainment of the causal relationship, there is no comprehension of positive and negative concomitance through mere observation and non-observation alone.
What is the reason for this?
Since the comprehension of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is dependent upon seeing and not seeing [the reason] in its entirety, it is bound solely to such observation;

for in this way, observation establishes positive concomitance if the reason were seen in every instance of the similar class (*sapakṣa*), and likewise, non-observation would establish negative concomitance.

If it were the case that the non-observation of the reason in all instances where the probandum is absent— just as the fact that smoke is once established as an effect in a single instance entails its being so everywhere—
then the claim that certainty regarding positive and negative concomitance would arise from observation in some similar instances and non-observation in others would also be false.
Since permanence is observed in some incorporeal things such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, this is stated on the basis of what is established for the opponent,
whereas it is not the case in other instances such as pleasure (*sukha*) and the like.

"Otherwise"—that is, if [the reason] were impermanent—then the observation of the reason, *amūrtatva* (formlessness), in one instance would not establish its presence everywhere; therefore, such observation is fallacious with respect to positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Likewise, since formlessness is observed in some cases, such as pleasure (*sukha*), even though permanence is absent there—and is not observed in other cases, such as a jar, despite the absence of permanence—thus, the non-observation of the reason in a single part of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is not a proof for the determination of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Therefore, the determination of positive and negative concomitance, as well as the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, arises only from the determination of the causal relationship between the reason and the consequence; thus says the opponent.

"Now," [it may be asked], "since the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) has been established for the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), how is it established for the essential-reason (*svabhāvahetu*)? But was not the inseparable connection already established for the essential-reason previously, by the statement beginning with, "Indeed, existence itself is the reason when it follows upon mere existence"? True.

He thinks as follows: "If an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is described as existing only in that [subject] with respect to its nature as it truly is (*yathābhūta-svabhāve*), then it would follow that it is merely a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*).

Thus, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*), considering that the fault of being a part of the proposition's meaning is avoided by the subsequent proof of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), reiterates the previously stated inseparable connection as depending solely upon that [subject].
"Non-separation also exists in the case of essential nature," and so forth; that is,
non-separation also exists in the case of the essential nature as a reason—
in what kind of probandum?
The phrase "for that which conforms to the mere existence [of the probans]" (*bhāvamātrānurodhini*) is the explanation of the very first [part of the definition],
namely that "the inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*) belongs to the existence of the probans, such as producedness (*kṛtakatva*).

Because, in the absence of that [the probans], there would be an absence of the probandum-property (sādhyadharma) which follows upon mere existence; for what reason? [This note belongs to the base text, which was not keyboarded. If it were dependent on a cause, then when that [cause] is absent, the effect would necessarily be absent. Therefore, since the probandum is established by the mere presence of the probans, the latter cannot be absent when the former is present. Thus, the probans is not non-existent when the probandum exists. Consequently, the probans is not inconclusive (anaikāntika). Furthermore, because the probandum is established by the mere presence of the probans, the probans is not contradictory (viruddha). This is because it does not exist in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa). Therefore, the probans is neither inconclusive nor contradictory. It is only when the probandum is established through the exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*) that the probans is considered valid. Otherwise, it would be inconclusive. For example, consider the following: "Sound is eternal, because it is intangible. In this case, although the probandum—eternality—is established by the mere presence of the probans—intangibility—within the similar class (*sapakṣa*), such as space (*ākāśa*), the probans is nevertheless inconclusive with respect to the dissimilar class, such as atoms (*paramāṇu*) and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). This is because the probandum is not established by the mere presence of the probans within those [dissimilar instances]. Therefore, the probans is inconclusive. Furthermore, if the probandum were established by the mere presence of the probans, then even in cases where the probandum is not established, the probans would still be valid. For instance, consider the following: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced. In this case, although the probandum—eternality—is not established by the mere presence of the probans—being produced—within the similar class, such as a pot (*ghaṭa*), the probans is nevertheless valid. This is because the probandum is established by the mere presence of the probans within the dissimilar class, such as space. Therefore, the probans is valid. Thus, it is only when the probandum is established through the exclusion of others that the probans is considered valid. Otherwise, it would be inconclusive. Therefore, the probandum is established by the mere presence of the probans. Consequently, the probans is not inconclusive. Furthermore, because the probandum is established by the mere presence of the probans, the probans is not contradictory. This is because it does not exist in the dissimilar class. Therefore, the probans is neither inconclusive nor contradictory. It is only when the probandum is established through the exclusion of others that the probans is considered valid. Otherwise, it would be inconclusive. For example, consider the following: "Sound is eternal, because it is intangible. In this case, although the probandum—eternality—is established by the mere presence of the probans—intangibility—within the similar class, such as space, the probans is nevertheless inconclusive with respect to the dissimilar class, such as atoms and mental factors. This is because the probandum is not established by the mere presence of the probans within those [dissimilar instances]. Therefore, the probans is inconclusive. Furthermore, if the probandum were established by the mere presence of the probans, then even in cases where the probandum is not established, the probans would still be valid. For instance, consider the following: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced. In this case, although the probandum—eternality—is not established by the mere presence of the probans—being produced—within the similar class, such as a pot, the probans is nevertheless valid. This is because the probandum is established by the mere presence of the probans within the dissimilar class, such as space. Therefore, the probans is valid. Because there is no difference between the probandum and the probans, [the author] explains their non-difference with the words "that which... and so forth: that very entity, such as the impermanent, which conforms to the mere state of being produced (*kṛtakabhāvamātra*), is called its "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*). That same entity, by virtue of not depending on any other cause, is in reality—that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth—the entity itself, namely "producedness. And how could that entity exist while abandoning its own self, which is its intrinsic nature, namely impermanence?

"In that case, [the reason] would be only a part of that very thing"— this is the opponent's indication of the position; the thesis (*pratijñā*) is the collection of the property and the property-possessor (*dharmadharmin*), and its "one part" would be the reason (*hetu*), consisting of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).

For instance, as long as one says "sound is impermanent because it is impermanent," so long does one say "it is impermanent because it is produced"; thus, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). This is the meaning of *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.33.
"This is not a fault," says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*), because [in the verse beginning with] "all things" (*sarve bhāvāḥ*) and so forth,
the first verse provides the seed for the conceptualization of phenomena (*dharmakalpanā*).

The collective meaning is as follows: by the second [verse], the conceptualization of phenomena (*dharmakalpanā*) is stated; by the third, the avoidance of the fallacy that the thesis (*pratijñā*) is a part of its own subject is explained.
[This is shown by] the suffix *ghinuṇ* [in the word *vyāvṛtti*], signifying that all entities possess a differentiation from both their own-being (*svabhāva*) and other-being (*parabhāva*).
All entities, by their own nature— that is, by their own form and not by another’s form— are excluded from both the similar and the dissimilar,
because they are established in their respective natures,
that is, because they abide in their own nature.
Is it not the case that a cow is distinct from a horse and so forth by way of its genus (*jāti*);
that a horned cow is distinct from another individual cow by way of its substance (*dravya*);
and that a white cow is distinct from another horned individual cow by way of its quality (*guṇa*)?

Thus, it is said in this regard: the differentiation of all entities, ranging from the highest down to the atom, is produced by qualifiers such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, and not by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
First of all, no differentiation is produced by genus and the like for entities that are already non-different.

In that case, [the cause] is incapable of producing either difference or non-difference, because it is ineffective toward them; nor is there a distinction among those already distinct, because such distinctions would be redundant;

nor is the conventional usage of "difference" established by these [causes], since the conventional usage of difference is established simply through their appearance as distinct in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by virtue of their own essential nature.

Furthermore, the difference between universals (*jāti*) and so forth, on the one hand, and their possessors (*tadvat*), on the other, cannot be established through anything else [than those very entities themselves], for that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If difference exists by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), why is it not simply accepted as belonging to the entities themselves? What is the point of postulating universals and the like?

Even he who thinks that a single thing must consist of all things when there is no exclusion of others— otherwise, there would be no distinction at all— if there were not the mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) of entities.
This too has been refuted by him,
because it is impossible for non-existence (abhāva) to effect a distinction between existing things (bhāva);
nor is mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) possible among things that are non-different and produced from the same cause.
If they are distinct, how can they be established?
If they are established as distinct, how can there be mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)?
It has been stated that if it is argued that "all entities are distinct," this is an inference whose locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*), because all entities are not objects of perception.
For this very reason, this is not being considered as falling within the scope of perception;
however, another says:
although entities are distinct by their own nature, they nonetheless possess properties such as genus (jāti) and so forth, because these are indeed perceived.
Nevertheless, non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-vijñāna*) perceives only the mere existence (*sattāmātra*) among the constituents of a cow, not its distinction from others;

for the apprehension of difference is indeed the apprehension of a specific quality (*viśeṣa*), and a specific quality is not grasped without conceptualization. Thus, it is the object of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), not of the non-conceptual;
as it has been said:
Particularities (viśeṣas), however, are perceived by conceptual cognitions;
some of these reside in each individual substance, while others are established in many.
That [cognition] which has arisen conceptualizes them through its nature of both exclusion and inclusion.
Furthermore, as for the one who says that what arises with respect to a cow or a horse is not distinct from perception itself,
and therefore there is no appearance of a distinction between types of perception in non-conceptual [cognition], [that is incorrect].

Even by means of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), difference is not apprehended; for the apprehension of the difference between entities is caused by the apprehension of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), and this mutual non-existence is itself a form of difference. Furthermore, non-existence is not graspable by perception (*pratyakṣa*), since perception does not determine that "a horse exists in a cow"; therefore, perception is the grasper of mere existence (*sattāmātra*) alone.
As it has been stated by Maṇḍana:
"The wise say that perception is a prescriptive [means of knowledge] and not a negating one;
therefore, the scripture concerning oneness is not contradicted by that perception."
Both of these [positions] are untenable, because pure existence does not appear,
whereas cows, horses, and so forth appear precisely in their own specific forms.
Thus it has been said:
"That [argument] is joined with truth, because a distinct form is perceived in each individual substance;
for it is not understood that a difference does not exist simply because it is impossible to describe."
As for the one who says that there is no difference at all between entities—
since the nature of a cow is exactly the same whether a horse is produced or not, and nothing further has arisen— how can there be a difference on this basis?
Or, let there be a distinction; yet it is not graspable by perception in the form "this is distinct from that," because such an operation does not exist in perception, as he said:
The argument that "this [cognition] is not capable of performing so many functions" is also refuted;
for cows, horses, and the like, their very arising in their own respective forms constitutes difference.

And since those [objects] appear as if directly perceived in their own respective forms, the claim that such an appearance constitutes an "appearance of difference" in the world is quite trivial; therefore, [the argument holds] because of the reason stated: "due to the establishment of their own respective natures among those things situated before one."

One who apprehends difference through perception apprehends it by means of a universal synthesis; therefore, the result of the means of knowledge that grasps the pervasion (vyāpti) is that "all entities partake of exclusion. Furthermore, since it will be demonstrated that universals (jāti) and so forth do not exist as separate entities, it follows that there is no ultimately real relationship between property and property-bearer (dharma-dharmin).
Now, it might be argued: "Are not things called 'of the same class' (sajātīya) because of their connection with a universal (sāmānya)?
And if no universal exists, how can one speak of exclusion from what is of the same class? This is not so.

There is no state of having a common form for entities that have already arisen as similar due to their connection with a universal (*sāmānya*), because they are produced in that way from their own causes alone. Therefore, as Uddyotakara says: "Cowness does not exist in the cow such that, prior to its connection with cowness, it would already be a cow; thus, cowness would be useless."

Rather, at the very moment an entity exists, it is already connected with "cowness"; for prior to its connection with cowness, the entity does not exist, and that which does not exist cannot be designated as either "cow" or "non-cow."

That has already been refuted, because at the very moment an object exists, it is already established as having the nature of a cow; what, then, would be the use of its connection with "cowness" (*gotva*)?
Nor can there be a common form for dissimilar things through their connection with a universal (*sāmānya*).
Since a universal (*sāmānya*) does not exist for them at all, it is accepted that a universal is the state of being common (*samāna*) among things;
and if it is accepted that entities possess a common form by virtue of a universal, then as long as there is no connection with a universal, those entities are not common.
And as long as they are not similar, there can be no connection with a universal; thus, there would be the fault of mutual dependence.
Therefore, they are produced as similar from their own causes alone; for that reason...

If it is held that no universal other than this is accepted— since the difference from a brindled cow is equal for both a black-spotted cow and a horse— then where could "exclusion" (apoha) possibly be postulated? Thus [the opponent's position] is refuted.

Furthermore, it is said that [universals do not exist] because the conceptualization of "non-cow" occurs only with respect to universals themselves, and because those things which are dissimilar are conceptualized as having the nature of the object to be excluded (apohya).

Because they appear as "the same" in non-conceptual cognition through their very manifestation, there is the appearance of a universal; otherwise, just as with a Bāhuleya horse, there would be a perception of difference even between a Śāvaleyas and a Bāhuleya due to their being distinct in every respect.
Yet, the cognition "they are the same" does occur; therefore, this [cognition] itself is the universal.
Thus it has been said:
"The apprehension of the dual-natured object occurs through non-conceptual cognition," or else, [it is said] that the universal is not apprehended in conceptual cognition.
Even that which has been apprehended by non-conceptual [cognition] is indeed grasped by conceptual [cognition], because it appears as something distinct;
for it is thus:

Those very individuals such as the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*) that are apprehended by the cognition "this is a cow" appear in non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition as well; the only difference is that the former apprehends them without any conceptualization whatsoever, while the latter apprehends something else through conceptualization. Thus, there is a difference in their intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*), but not a difference in their appearance (*pratibhāsa*).
Therefore, the universal (*sāmānya*) appears even in non-conceptual cognition.
That too has been refuted,
because certain things appear as identical due to their own causes,
and the nature of a universal is dependent upon individuals; furthermore, non-conceptual cognition does not apprehend the dependence of an object.
Since it apprehends the object through its own independence, how can it be said to apprehend a universal? Furthermore,
because a recurring form does not appear simultaneously in many [individuals] in the same way that it appears in each one individually,

for this very reason, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)— apprehending a recurring aspect among things that are entirely distinct— is erroneous, as it is sublated by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*).

Alternatively, [the conceptual cognition] that grasps a universal already grasped by non-conceptual [perception] would not be a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), because it grasps what has already been grasped.

If, on the other hand, it is argued that it grasps what was not previously grasped because it grasps [the object] as qualified by conceptualization, then in that case, memory and so forth would also not have the status of grasping what was not previously grasped, since their objects are those being remembered (and thus already grasped).

Furthermore, if it is argued that conceptualization grasps what was not previously grasped because it grasps the thing as qualified by universals (*jāti*) and so forth—even so, if the state of being qualified by universals and so forth is a real property (*pāramārthika-dharma*) of the thing, then it must have been grasped even by non-conceptual perception; how then could it be said to grasp what was not previously grasped?
Now, if that [universal] is conceptualized, how can its apprehender be valid, since its object is superimposed?
Therefore, it is established that universals and the like do not exist at all.
How, then, is it said that "entities partake of exclusion" (vyāvṛtti)?
There is no fault here, for this designation is made by means of an imagined property;
therefore,
the exclusion of the non-cow (*agovyāvṛtti*) is what is conceptualized as the universal (*sāmānya*) to be expressed by words.
"In the *Apohavāda* section of the *Ślokavārttika*, it is clearly stated by them that the very entity of 'cowness' (*gotva*) is expressed by the word 'non-cow' (*agopoha*)."
It will be stated that what is being negated is the ultimate cow-nature (*gotva*), and not the imagined one. [Objection:

If the relationship between property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*) does not exist ultimately, how then is there a distinction between cognitions such as "sound is produced" and "sound is eternal," given that their object is the single nature of sound?
Now, if these [cognitions] are devoid of objects, how can there be apprehension and activity regarding external things based merely on the seeds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)? Or,

if activity arises from the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an external object, even so, since the determination of "producedness" is itself non-different from "impermanence," how can there be a distinction between cognitions?

Since there is no real distinction between the produced and the impermanent, there is no actual difference in cognition because there is no difference in the latent impressions (vāsanā) produced by the experience of those [objects]; to this he says "because," and so forth:

because all things are excluded from everything else, therefore, based on whichever [exclusion]—such as being permanent or unproduced—the objects such as sound and so forth are excluded, those [cognitions] are dependent upon that.

The distinctions between properties, such as impermanence, producedness, and so forth, are conceptualized—that is, they are superimposed by conceptual constructions—based upon the exclusion of what is excluded [from the particular].

What are they like? They are "those which penetrate its specific features"; that is, they penetrate those specific features of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) characterized by the form of the exclusion of non-produced things and so forth.
The meaning is that they have the nature of immersing themselves in that [object] and the nature of appearing as non-different from it.
This is what is being said:

by means of this gateway—namely, "it is not something produced"—the very latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of "produced" is awakened; since this is its very nature, the conceptual construction arising therefrom, while being "produced," is non-different from its own form, and thus it apprehends the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the word as precisely excluded from the "produced," but not as "impermanent."

Likewise, by this door as well—that [the object] is not eternal—it is precisely the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of impermanence that has been awakened which possesses the capacity [to produce cognition]. Consequently, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising therefrom apprehends the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the word as being non-different from its own form and as being excluded from the eternal; it does not, however, apprehend it as "produced" (*kṛtaka*). Therefore, a distinction arises in the cognition. And because the object appearing in the conceptual construction is sublated, it is not external; thus, the conceptual construction is merely an appearance of the external due to the force of the latent impression. For this reason, the object appearing in the conceptual construction in the very form of an external thing is called its "own form" (*svākāra*).
But there is no superimposition of the external upon its own form due to similarity,
as it was said in the *Nāmanimitta-prakaraṇa*:
If it is argued that the cognition occurs with respect to the object due to similarity and error, this would not be the case at all times; furthermore,
there would be no spatial error [in the cognition], because the cognition arises from the object itself.

"Of such a [cognition] characterized by the appearance of an external object"— by this [phrase], it is addressed that which is said: "The grasping of the form of the [cognition] itself as being identical to that [external object], though the form is absolutely dissimilar to the external, is intended to mean a similarity produced by the exclusion of others."

Just as a cloth, although entirely dissimilar to a jar, when determined as being qualified by the absence of trees, is determined to be similar to a jar in the sense that it is "not a tree"— since the exclusion of trees is common to both the jar and the cloth— so too, although the object of conceptual construction (vikalpa) is extremely dissimilar to the left side, it is determined on the left side because of the apprehension of similarity produced by the exclusion of others.
That is refuted, because the conceptual cognition appearing as an external object arises from its own causes alone;
nor is similarity produced among dissimilar things by means of the exclusion of others.
In that case, since it is incapable of producing either difference, non-difference, or similarity, there is no exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*) that could constitute similarity;
for even among similar things, how could similarity be produced by the exclusion of others? Similarity exists by its very own nature.

Nor does it occur that first there is the appearance of its own form, and subsequently there appears the superimposition of an external object— which is intent upon grasping a similarity produced by the exclusion of other things—
for indeed, when the nature of a mirage has not first appeared, the superimposition of water caused by the grasping of similarity is impossible;
and prior to the superimposition of an external object, there is no superimposition of the object upon its own form.

Since conceptual construction itself is non-existent— or if it does exist, it is of the single nature of pure awareness— it cannot resemble an external object. Consequently, in the absence of any similarity produced by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), how could it be perceived as having an external form?

However, the operation of inference does not have as its prerequisite the apprehension of the exclusion of others, because the logical mark (*liṅga*) is established through its connection with that [positive entity]. And when it is perceived that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) penetrate the specific nature of that [object], then their operation occurs precisely in a positive form; since the essential nature of the thing is determined as being enjoined, the exclusion of others is understood by implication. Therefore, for us as well, the meaning of a word is indeed a positive injunction (*vidhi*).
Furthermore, there is a connection through affirmation and negation with that which is superimposed as being external.

Now, it may be argued that conceptual construction appears as grasping a determinate form; therefore, by conceptualizing an object as devoid of any other form, one conceptualizes that determinate object.
Therefore, that determination of a specific form which has the exclusion of others as its object— how can it be said that the word-meaning is exclusively a positive injunction?
That is incorrect,
because there is no cognition [in the form] "I am conceptualizing the exclusion of others."
Furthermore, that which is not conceptualized does not appear as an object of conceptualization;
for if one conceives of a specific object while conceptualizing only the exclusion of other forms, there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*),
because the other form would also have to be apprehended through the exclusion of others by virtue of its own specific nature.
If, by way of a positive form, one conceptualizes another form, then that determination of a restricted form would not be preceded by the ascertainment of the exclusion of others;
nor, as in the case of "I see an object possessing a universal," is there any appearance of a qualifier-qualified relationship between the universal and its possessor.

Furthermore, the Naiyāyikas and others have postulated the perception of an individual qualified by a universal (sāmānya) in accordance with specific cognition; likewise, others [the Buddhists] maintain that although there is no such apprehension as "I am conceptualizing an exclusion" (nivṛtti), nevertheless, because the superimposition of something external and similar [to the object] would otherwise be inexplicable, the form of the external object is superimposed upon the form of the conceptual construction (vikalpākāra) which refers to the exclusion of others.
This is logical, since a conceptual construction arises through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā) alone, having determined an external form even in the absence of similarity.
As it has been said:
The nature of the determination (*adhyavasita*) of that object arises from the innate disposition (*prakṛti*) produced by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of its experience;

likewise, such is the nature of the latent impressions of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that it appears in this manner. Furthermore, even if a cognition that superimposes an external form has as its cause a similarity (*sārūpya*) produced by another cognition, it does not have the exclusion of other things (*anyanivṛtti*) as its object.
For the cognition of water in a mirage does not have similarity as its object, because its object is the superimposed water;
nor is the fixed nature of entities produced by the exclusion of others,
since that [exclusion], being a non-entity, lacks causal efficacy.
Furthermore, since it arises from its own causes alone,
there is no determination of a fixed form [in the object] that has the exclusion of others as its domain, because this [determination] has a fixed form as its domain.
For this very reason, it is not apprehended by perception itself as being preceded by the exclusion of others.
Furthermore, it will be stated that it is not logical for the exclusion of what is other than that to be a distinct entity;
nor is it logical for it to be inexpressible in terms of being either identical to or different from that,
for in that case, it would simply be a non-entity, like the horn of a hare.
Furthermore, it could not be accessible through perception because it is formless,
nor could it be accessible through inference because the inferential mark (*liṅga*) is unestablished due to the absence of a [necessary] relationship.
Nor can that [exclusion] be postulated on the grounds that its fixed nature would otherwise be inexplicable;

for there is no absence of other things in the case of those whose nature is not fixed, and as for those whose nature is fixed, how could their fixed nature result from the exclusion of others? This is because things with a fixed nature arise from their own causes alone.
Therefore, the exclusion of others is understood only after the determination of a specific form;

for instance, when "pot" is said, it is understood by implication that "it is not a non-pot. Thus, this [exclusion] is merely constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) and does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Consequently, it is established that through word and logical mark (*liṅga*), a real entity is presented in a positive form, while the negation of others follows by implication.
And he will say accordingly: "From those very words directed toward that [object], the exclusion of others is understood," and so forth (1.128).
Therefore, as for what was stated by Kumārila:
However, a word that performs the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) has not been described in your position;
for here, what is understood from words such as "cow," "gavaya," "elephant," or "tree" is not mere negation, but rather a positive manifestation.
Verbal cognition proceeds by way of determining a positive form;

therefore, only in those words that are joined with the negative particle (*nañ*) does the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*) become a subordinate factor, whereas in other cases it is understood as the word's own nature itself.
In the *Ślokavārttika*,
this is established: [the existence of the object] is proven because even a word-meaning in the form of a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is accepted.
How, then, is there a distinction between the Buddhist doctrine and that of others, or how can it be said that the object of both word and inferential mark is *apoha*?

Is there not indeed a great difference, since conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is accepted by others as having ultimate reality as its object, whereas it is accepted by Buddhists as having a mentally constructed (*kalpita*) object?
The conceptualized form is called "exclusion" (apoha) because it is based on exclusion;
or else, it is so called because by means of it [the object] is excluded.
Alternatively, the mere negation of others, which is implied by the sense [of the word], is called "exclusion" (apoha) because it is the act of excluding.
However, it is called "exclusion" (*apoha*) because the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is excluded therein.
Therefore, in dependence upon various things that are mutually differentiated, properties whose distinctions are imagined are made objects of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
Consequently, to demonstrate that conceptual constructions have distinct objects and that words which share those same objects are not synonyms, he says:
Therefore, and so forth:

since the various properties (dharmabheda) are thus conceptualized, that specific particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇaviśeṣa) which is established as having the nature of impermanence— relative to that which is to be excluded and to permanence— is [the object] by means of which property or by means of which word [it is expressed].
Just as by the word "impermanent," sound itself is called a "dharma" because it denotes a property;
it cannot be expressed by anything other than that.
By means of a word such as "produced" (kṛtaka), which is other than the word "impermanent" (anitya),
there is a distinct determination [of the object] through the apprehension of an additional entity that is to be excluded.
For that reason, conceptual constructions do not have a single object,
nor are words synonyms;
therefore, as for what is said:

The claim that there can be no relationship of the signifier and the signified between two things that are identical, nor a relationship of the signifier and the signified between two things whose forms are conceptual constructs,
is refuted;
for it is precisely the particular (svalakṣaṇa) as excluded from the unproduced (*akṛtaka*) that falls within the scope of the logical reason that makes something known.

Because that which is known as "produced" (kṛtaka) is a means of cognition (*gamaka*), and because it consists of a real entity (*vastu*) excluded from the eternal (*nitya*), [the author] states the meaning of the verse—refuting the non-dualist position (*advaitavāda*) with the words "for all... and so forth—by saying:
"those whose stability is in their own nature, in themselves, are thus [described]."
For all entities indeed abide in their own nature; they do not mix themselves with another nor make themselves one with it.
What is the reason?
If it is thought that when those two are being mixed, there arises the consequence of the other becoming non-other, resulting in its attaining the nature of the self; [this is the objection].
Furthermore, with respect to all things, cognition arises as having the nature of both exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and inclusion (*anugama*);
and that [cognition] is not possible without a dual nature.

Therefore, particulars have a universal nature and universals have a particular nature; thus, an entity possesses both forms. In this case as well, there is either the non-difference of one form from many distinct things, or the non-difference of a distinct thing from one.

In that regard, he says "of those" (*teṣām*) in order to refute the first position: it cannot be said that the form (*rūpa*), which is non-different—that is, of a single nature and not distinct—which belongs to those entities (*bhāvānām*) is [itself] those entities.
Why? Because at that time, there is an expectation for the word "its" (*tasya*).
Because those [individuals] lack that undivided form, there is indeed non-difference;

furthermore, regarding the claim that there is non-difference from something distinct from the one, he says: for in that case too, it would be that very same thing, because of the existence of the undivided.
If form were to have the nature of non-existence, then that very form would be non-different for them, not different;
why is this? Because that very non-different form exists.
Now, it might be argued that their difference is indeed admitted; to this he replies:
"Therefore, because there is no other entity distinct from that non-different self which could possess a different nature or manifold forms."
Now, it might be argued that the very difference which belongs to the particular is itself the non-difference of the universal,
as it has been said:
But regarding one who asserts a distinction within the universal, [the opponent] says that even in this case, having shown it specifically, it must be accepted;
for there is a contradiction in the distinction of that very [universal],
since it is impossible for that single entity to possess multiplicity.

Now, it might be argued that the distinction of the universal occurs through its particularities and not by way of its own nature; in that case, because the inclusive (anugata) and exclusive (vyāvṛtta) forms would not be mutually connected, there would necessarily be a complete difference between them.
To this, he says:
And that [universal], being of a single form, is established within itself—within its own nature—as something entirely unmixed in its manifested form;
and since it is not perceived as mixed when it is actually unmixed, it is indeed false.
Now, one might argue that this falsity does not apply because the universal is in some way non-different from the individual.
Regarding this, he says: "This is not established because superimposition and the like are impossible for the cognitions of horses and so forth;
for indeed, there is no difference between the universal (*jāti*) and the rest from the individual (*vyakti*)."
That is incorrect;

for identity and difference are contradictory, such that by the very same form through which something is divided, it cannot have non-difference. Furthermore, difference and non-difference do not appear simultaneously in a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Moreover, if difference is apprehended by one [cognition] and non-difference is apprehended by another, how could the cognition apprehending that [non-difference] not be erroneous?
Otherwise, because that [universal] is of a single nature,
its status as a universal would not exist due to its non-mixture with others, since it would be a distinct entity, like a jar; however,
Uddyotakara says:
The inclusive cognition regarding cows and other such things is produced by a cause distinct from the individual bodies and so forth,
because it is a specific [cognition], like the cognition of "blue" and the like;
and that cause is called a "universal" (sāmānya) because it produces identical manifestations.
See Nyāyavārttika 2.2.65.

Regarding this as well, he says [the following], demonstrating that neither is a state of similarity produced for things already similar by means of some other object, because they are already established as such, nor is it produced for things dissimilar:
"Another entity" means that existence (*sattā*), cowness (*gotva*), and so forth, are not the universal (*sāmānya*) of those particular individuals, because they do not possess that nature;
for a universal is held to be the state of being common (*samāna*) among particulars, yet those particulars are of dissimilar form.

Alternatively, because it does not possess the nature of those [individuals] and is a distinct entity from the individuals— just like [their] unity— if you claim that this [universal], though being a distinct entity, is inherent in many [individuals] and is therefore their *sāmānya*,
then the same consequence would apply to duality and other effect-substances (*kāryadravya*), for duality too is inherent in multiple substances.
By the inclusion of the term "etcetera," plurality and so forth are also intended; likewise, conjunction— which inheres in multiple substances—

and the effect-substance known as a composite (avayavin), which inheres in its constituent causal substances— would consequently entail the status of being universals (sāmānya) in the case of duality and the rest.
Regarding the claim that "only that [entity] in which, when another entity exists, the differences become identical is a universal (sāmānya), not everything," he says:

"For it is not the case that other things—those that are dissimilar and distinct—are made identical by another related entity characterized by oneness; for such an entity is useless for producing a state of identity or non-identity between distinct things."
Furthermore, since they appear as having different locations and so forth, how could they be identical?
At most, the particulars (bheda) would merely possess that [quality], meaning they would possess a single property;
for instance, the elements, the planets, and the constellations have long threads tied around their necks for the purpose of worship.
"Just as by means of a single thread around their necks, living beings possess it yet do not become one, so too are the individuals [related to the universal].

If it is argued: "Indeed, since the thread possesses form (*mūrtatva*), its possession by those [beings] is logically perceived; however, this is not the case for the universal (*sāmānya*) in individuals, because the universal is formless (*amūrtatva*)."
This is not so, because it is not accepted that [the universal] is inherent in them, and because they exist as distinct entities;

and for this very reason— that even when there is a single relation, the individuals are not identical— they cannot be the objects of a non-different cognition, nor can they be the objects of a non-erroneous cognition of a single form.
Just as the primary elements (bhūtas), being by nature devoid of qualities, are not the objects of cognitions that possess the forms of multiple qualities, so it is in this case as well.

Thus, even when there is a connection with many [individuals], it is established that another entity is not their *sāmānya* (universal), because that would entail the consequence of [universals such as] duality and so forth;
yet they are perceived as "similar. Therefore, it is indeed the very nature of those two distinct things themselves [that constitutes the universal].
The cognition that unifies these two as "this is one form" appears as having a universal as its object by means of its own internal aspect;

it does not appear as "these two are related to a single universal," namely, as being related to one and the same universal, such that a universal established by valid cognition as a separate entity would exist.
"Like the elements" (*bhūtavat*) is the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
The meaning is that cognition does not apprehend the elements as being connected by a single quality in the same way [as one might think];

or rather, it means that the cognition whose object is the universal does not appear in such a way as if the two distinct things were connected by a single [universal], just as the elements are connected by a single [quality]. Now, it might be argued:

For a universal is a qualifier of individuals, and a qualifier produces a cognition colored by itself with respect to the qualified object; therefore, it does not appear as a separate entity from the individuals. Now, even if it is a qualifier, it cannot be identical with the qualified object—just as a staff is not identical with the staff-bearer—so how can there be an appearance of non-difference?
Because they are also one in their aspect of non-difference, there can be no relationship of qualifier and qualified;
therefore, the cognition of the identity of the universal with the individual is nothing but an error.
If it is argued that this is not an error because such a cognition occurs at all times, [we reply:]...
Thus it is said:
"For that which is perceived as having one form, yet is perceived otherwise at another time, is false; but that which is always understood through that very same [form] is not so."
That is incorrect;
for it would follow that the universal is non-different from the individual,
and because one must admit a difference in cognition, such as "this is a cow" and "this is cowness."
Furthermore, the cognition of a relation between a universal and its possessor—such as that between lac and crystal—is not non-erroneous;
for the cognition of a crystal, which lacks the color of lac, as having the color of lac is indeed erroneous.
Thus, [the claim of] identity between the universal and its possessor [is untenable].
If it is argued that "grasping" (*graha*) is an error (*bhrānti*),
and that cognition perceives only the universal (*sāmānya*),
yet because the inherence (*samavāya*) of that [universal] within the perceiving cognition is subtle, this grasping of individuals as non-different from the universal is an error; [we reply:]...
How can it be said that "it perceives that"?

From what source is the certainty that this cognition perceives an ultimate universal? Because it always has as its object the non-difference from the individual, it has no seed; thus it is seedless, and consequently it is an error, since such [a perception] is impossible.
For an error arising without a cause is not possible,
just like the error of [perceiving] water and so forth;
and since this error is a cognition that conflates even things that are not actually conjoined, it must therefore have a cause.
Regarding the claim that "that which is the cause [of the cognition] is the universal," he says:

those very particulars (bhedāḥ) have a single effect, namely the cognition of that universal; they are thus "those having a single effect" (tadekakāryāḥ), and this is the seed of error—this will be demonstrated later.
Furthermore, it is not logical that there should be an illusion of a single form among individuals through the superimposition of a universal upon what is perceived;

for similarity is the cause of such illusion, yet the universal is absolutely distinct from the individuals, since the universal lacks the form of color and configuration, whereas the individuals possess the form of color and configuration.
Now, it might be argued:

"The superimposition [of identity] upon distinct individuals is not caused by similarity; rather, even among things that are absolutely distinct, there is an error consisting in the determination of oneness—'this is that very same thing'—which does not occur without a single form. To this we reply: if this were so, then simply by virtue of being related to a single [object], they would become objects of an erroneous cognition of a single form even without a cause for such error.

At that time, in those elements (*bhūta*) which possess number, conjunction, the substance as effect, and—by the word "etcetera"—disjunction and so forth, and which are endowed with a single quality, there would arise an illusion of a uniform form; yet such an illusion does not occur. Therefore, even in the case of individual entities (*vyakti*), the illusion is not caused by oneness.

The word "tad" means "therefore": just as the universal (*sāmānya*) is intended to be distinct from the individuals (*vyakti*), so too it is not a universal because it does not enter into the cognition of a universal and does not appear [in it];

or, even if a universal were to exist, that universal would abide within its own self—that is, its own intrinsic nature—and thus there would be no mixing with other things in the form of individuals; furthermore, because it does not reside in individuals, it does not possess the nature of a property (*dharma*). This is the meaning.

"Therefore"—that is, because of the establishment of their own intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), these entities such as jars and so forth are distinct and separate from what is considered similar (by virtue of being perceived as having an identical form) and from what is other (i.e., heterogeneous), because they possess a single nature by way of their own essence; this is to say that they are established through their own intrinsic natures. This explains the meaning of the second verse.
Since those entities are differentiated from this or that [other], their differentiation is "that-differentiation";

therefore, they are distinct by nature. For the purpose of communicating these distinct natures, words—by which a convention has been established—are employed as instruments; through such words, the various properties, such as being produced and so forth, are cognized. Even though there is a difference [among them], there is no plurality of natures within a single specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
How, then, is there a multiplicity of properties? He says:
"by taking up distinctions from this and that.
