That is to say, by taking up—that is, relying upon—the distinctions from whatever [objects] they are excluded; those words which have been established as conventions for the purpose of manifesting each of those distinct natures, they are restricted to being denoters of this distinct nature.
Therefore, a single word does not denote all [particulars] which possess distinct natures; thus, although those words do not individually denote all differences,
because they enjoin one particular difference, they enjoin the nature of each distinct [particular],
and consequently they are restricted to that very *svalakṣaṇa* (particular) whose nature is distinct from others and which is determined by the word.
And that [conceptual cognition] has as its object precisely that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), meaning it has that as its domain;

for is it not the case that the object appearing in verbal cognition—which is determined as being external—is something entirely different from the common [universal], while the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is something else? To the question of how these [cognitions] can have that [particular characteristic] as their object, he says:

Thus, since an object is apprehended by words as excluded from even a single thing—whether it be from that which is not its cause or that which is not its effect—there exists a differentiation of that particular (svalakṣaṇa) which is excluded from many [non-causes and non-effects]; for this reason, those [words] are said to have that [particular] as their object, though they do not have it as their object exclusively.
Alternatively, they are established in the particular of that property which is the locus of exclusion; that is, they culminate in the attainment of it.
Why is this?
It has already been explained that even for him there is a distinction from one [of these]; concluding this,
he says "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Since there is exclusion from both similar and dissimilar things, therefore, for a single entity, there are as many exclusions from other forms as there are other forms; these, in relation to those other forms—
that is, with respect to other forms— are conceptualized as distinct properties.
It is so called because heterogeneous things are excluded by these;
for what reason?

Because it is distinct from that [heterogeneous thing] which has as its cause and effect something impossible in that subject (dharmin) who serves as the limit (avadhi) of the exclusion, namely, that intended subject in which such an effect and cause are impossible.

Therefore, because they are excluded from that which does not have those effects and that which does not have those causes, there are as many verbal designations (*śruti*) as there are exclusions; these are established for the sake of conventional usage by means of the exclusion of what does not have those effects and causes.
That which has that intended effect and cause is "that-effect-and-cause" (*tatkāryakāraṇa*);

for example, sound has auditory consciousness as its effect and effort as its cause. That which does not possess such [effect and cause] is "not-that-effect-and-cause" (*atatkāryakāraṇa*). By the exclusion of that, there is the analysis: "those whose purpose is practical activity (*vyavahāra*), characterized by engagement and withdrawal, is the object (*artha*)—that is, the fruit.
Thus he states the object.
That for which effort (*prayatna*) is the cause is called "produced immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantarīyaka*).

Therefore, the term "sound produced immediately after effort" is used for the purpose of excluding lightning and the like, which do not have that as their cause—that is, which do not have effort as their cause.
That whose effect is auditory cognition (*śrotrajñāna*) is "auditory" (*śrāvaṇa*); by this term, "auditory sound" is meant for the purpose of excluding that which does not have that as its effect.
Since all conventional transactions (vyavahāra) are based on causal efficiency (arthakriyā),
and since causal efficiency is characterized by the relationship of cause and effect, the exclusion of that which is not its cause or effect must also be applied to words such as "pot" (ghaṭa).
He explains the third verse beginning with the word "therefore" (tasmāt).

Because distinct exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) and verbal expressions (*śruti*) are each restricted to their own respective distinctions, therefore— even though there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a single substratum (*dharmin*)—
the phrase "by name" (*nāmnā*), which is a gloss for "by the substratum," means "by the word.

The meaning of the phrase "whatever particularity" (*yo viśeṣaḥ*) is that a property (*dharma*) characterized by being produced (*kṛtaka*) and so forth is conceptually constructed (*kalpita*) and thus perceived.

It cannot be made known by anything other than that intended word "produced" (*kṛtaka*) and so forth; it cannot be conveyed by another word such as "impermanent" (*anitya*). Therefore, the reason is not a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*), because the words "impermanent" and "produced" have different meanings.
[The opponent asks: "How so? and so forth.

Although both word (*śabda*) and inferential mark (*liṅga*) are mentioned here—and although the inferential mark is the subject under discussion—the inclusion of "word" is for the purpose of demonstrating that, like the inferential mark, it lacks a real object; by this, the authority of the Veda is refuted.

Now, it was stated that an object is presented by word and inferential mark in the form of a positive injunction (*vidhi*); how then can this doubt be raised that "exclusion (*vyavaccheda*)" is what is presented? How is this understood?
This is not so.
"Exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*) is defined as that by which something is excluded; it refers precisely to a mental form (*ākāra*) superimposed as an external reality.
Therefore, how is it understood that it is this very [form] that is conveyed by words and logical marks through affirmation (*vidhi*), and not the actual nature of the thing?
Alternatively, "exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*) refers to that in which something is excluded;
it is said to be the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). That very thing is the object [of direct perception]. (Note 120-1: *thaḥi-dañ-kyis*.)

It is established and determined by means of words and logical marks (*śabda-liṅga*) through a positive formulation (*vidhi-rūpeṇa*); however, it is not the case that the actual nature of the thing, characterized by an ultimate relationship between property and substratum (*dharma-dharmin-bhāva*), is being established. How is this known?
The response begins with "by another means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntarasya*) and so forth.

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: if the relationship between property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*) were ultimately real and entirely non-different, then, because an object would be fully determined by a single means of knowledge or a single word upon its apprehension, there would be no further operation of another means of knowledge or another word, since they would lack authority by virtue of grasping what has already been grasped. Yet, other words and so forth do indeed operate; therefore, the relationship between property and property-bearer is merely conceptualized (*kalpita*).

Although the imagined relationship between property and property-bearer (dharma-dharmin) has already been established by the very refutation of the previous [notion of] universals, there is no fault in establishing it again by this other method;
demonstrating this very point,
he says "For instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of one":

since the reality of the object's own nature—which is devoid of any distinction between property and substrate—is partless, and since it exists as a perceptible entity by its very own form, what other unperceived part could there be? What other nature, distinct from the nature already perceived through direct perception, could there be that would need to be examined by means of instruments of knowledge known as inference?
The plural number is used because of the diversity of individual instances.
Since every [object] is indeed perceived because an entity is partless, it should not be subject to investigation by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
thus, the explanation begins with "one," and so forth:
for the nature of an object is one and partless; that must first be admitted as being perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), wherein inference (*anumāna*) operates.
What is the reason?
Because proof is impossible when the subject (*dharmin*) has not been previously established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
since the logical mark (*liṅga*) would be unestablished due to its lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), the subject must therefore be already well-known.
This is what is meant:
there would not even be the operation of the *liṅga* (the logical mark), let alone the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that ascertains the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*).

For example, when "impermanence" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), sound is established by perception; because its own nature is established by the very means of perception, there is the establishment of all its aspects.

Why? Because there is no such thing as an unestablished nature other than the nature of sound—that is, a nature other than the nature of sound which is unestablished; or, if such an unestablished nature were to exist, it would not have that [sound] as its nature, because it would not have the nature of sound, given the contradiction between being established and being unestablished within a single nature.
He says that very thing with the words "na hi" and so forth;
yoga is the persistence of a dharma not yet obtained.
One for whom the persistence of the attained Dharma is security—
that single yoga which is both security and [the means to it]— is "one whose Dharma is equal," so to speak.

That which does not share the same acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) with a certain intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has a different acquisition and preservation; since it has a different acquisition and preservation, it is not logical for that to be its intrinsic nature,
because the conventional usage of difference is based solely upon that [distinction], and this constitutes the determination of plurality.
"Otherwise" means that if this cause of differentiation is not accepted, then it follows that the conventional usage of non-difference would be impossible;
this was stated in the context of the passage beginning with "for this is the cause of difference and non-difference.
Therefore, in the case of a perceptible subject such as sound (*śabda*), etc.:
Because of the complete determination of its intrinsic nature—

that is, because the intrinsic nature of the subject (*dharmin*) is understood in its entirety— there is no scope for the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely inference, regarding that subject; it would be devoid of an object.
If it is argued that the same fault applies to you as well, he says "no" and so forth:

by means of a cause consisting of the appearance of a similar subsequent moment and so on— which serves as the basis for error— one might join or superimpose another quality upon it through conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*).
Alternatively, stability and so forth— just as the word "iva" (like) implies similarity—
might be superimposed upon it, just as the form of silver is superimposed upon mother-of-pearl.
How so?
Because one perceives the similarity between the form of mother-of-pearl and the form of silver, such as their commonality of being white and so forth.

The form of the mother-of-pearl itself, whose specific qualities have not been determined, is said to possess a similarity of form because it is the basis for a similar cognition; however, there is no such thing as "similarity" that exists commonly to both [the object and the superimposed thing].
What is meant is this:
if another quality were not joined [to the object] by means of the cause of error, then my objection would hold; but rather, [the quality] is superimposed.

Therefore, some maintain that another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates for the purpose of excluding superimposition (*samāropa*); thus, when an object has been experienced and ascertained, another means of valid cognition would not operate because it would be grasping what has already been grasped (*gṛhītagrāhitva*). However, when an object has been experienced but not ascertained due to superimposition, another means of valid cognition—inference (*anumāna*)—operates for the purpose of excluding that superimposition.
That is incorrect,
because the connection of the logical mark (*liṅga*) with the exclusion [of the opposite] is not established;
nor would the cognition of the probandum remain doubtful as long as the exclusion of the opposing position has not first been effected by the reason, since the reason is connected with the probandum.
And where there is no probandum (*sādhya*), there can be no counter-position (*tadvipakṣa*) to it, because of their mutual contradiction.

Therefore, the logical mark (*liṅga*), while ascertaining its own pervader (*svavyāpaka*) in a positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa*), by implication (*arthāt*) negates the superimposition (*samāropa*) of anything else.
But even so, how is that negation [established]? For even when the inference of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) has proceeded, there is still the superimposition of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇika*).

It is true that when the non-momentary nature of an object has been negated through inference alone, it is demonstrated that this cognition— though produced by that [object]— does not possess a non-momentary form, but rather its appearance as such is superimposed due to the arising of a subsequent similar moment.
Therefore, inference proceeds toward the ascertainment of precisely that [object], such as its momentariness, which was previously experienced but not yet ascertained.

Even in a case where there is no superimposition of error, and where experience—due to the absence of practice and so forth—is incapable of producing certainty, there still occurs the operation of another means of valid cognition for the sake of certainty; for by the ascertainment of one aspect, the thing is ascertained in its entirety.

Moreover, that object does not appear [to consciousness] whose nature is not ascertained in any respect whatsoever. Therefore, even in that case, when one means of valid cognition operates, the non-operation of another would indeed necessarily follow.
The explanation beginning with "yadi" (*if*, etc. is as follows:
the analysis of the compound is "that whose nature is every perceived reality.

Likewise, [it refers to] a cause of error characterized by the production of a subsequent moment similar [to the preceding], which obstructs certainty—that is, which hinders the certainty corresponding to what was perceived.
The stability of other qualities and so forth would neither be joined nor superimposed.
Just as when mother-of-pearl is perceived even in its specific form, the form of silver might be superimposed due to its similarity to silver, so too [in that case],
the operation of another means of valid cognition would be rendered unnecessary;
such is the opinion held.

It is not that there is a superimposition of silver upon the mother-of-pearl due to the perception of a specific form; rather, because one perceives a universal form of silver, there is such a determination.
To this, he says "no," for indeed two forms cannot coexist in the mother-of-pearl.
What is the reason for one form being identical to silver and another being distinct, and for there being such a restriction?
For otherwise, there would always be the undesirable consequence of cognition appearing as a variegated manifestation in the form of both the universal and the particular.
Or, regarding "non-apprehension through discernment":
this means that when there is no apprehension through the discernment or distinction that "this is the universal" and "this is the particular," the conceptual construction of duality is impossible;
for instance, the conceptualization that "there are two forms on the mother-of-pearl shell" would be untenable.
Because there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in postulating duality without a difference in appearance—

since one might as well postulate duality in other things intended to be unitary— and because there would be the consequence that the subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), such as "this is not silver," would never arise.
Therefore, since two forms are impossible in a single mother-of-pearl shell,
a person seeing the form of the shell sees only its specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*), not a universal (*sāmānya*).

Because [repeated] practice and other factors that produce determinate cognitions would otherwise be fruitless, one who fails to determine it thinks, "I am seeing this specific form of the shell as if it were the universal form of silver."
"Therefore" means that from the observer's conceit of grasping a universal form of silver, there arises the superimposition of silver upon the mother-of-pearl;

or rather, he thinks, "I perceive that which is the commonality— the identical form— of both the mother-of-pearl and silver," and from that perception of form, this observer's superimposition of silver occurs.
For indeed, the very same form of silver that was apprehended by me is the form of this [object] as well; therefore, there arises the cognition: "This is that very silver."

Just as there is the superimposition of silver upon mother-of-pearl, so too, with respect to a perceived substratum such as sound, because of the production of a subsequent similar moment through the arising of successive similar moments, a person whose distinction between the preceding and succeeding moments is unperceived superimposes that state—that is, superimposes existence—due to the cause of delusion. (Note 123-1: That which has become a locus of certainty. (Note 123-2: Because it is not definitively established.)

Because there is a delusion regarding stability, therefore, however many "other-natures" (parabhāva)—such as permanence and so forth—there may be for this [object] which has a momentary, selfless nature and so on, exactly that many superimpositions (samāropa) arise according to their respective causes; that is, they arise from whatever cause corresponds to them. Since these [superimpositions] are excluded by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), those [cognitions] arising as the exclusion of such superimposition are, by implication, the exclusion of that superimposition. Thus, when they arise, they are the means of valid cognition designated as inference (*anumāna*).
The plural number is used because of the distinction between individual instances; thus,
those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which have exclusion as their result and the negation of superimposition as their result, would be fruitful and purposeful.
There is no activity directed toward the communication or illumination of an unperceived part of an object,
because that part of the object is already perceived when the partless substratum (dharmin) is being seen;
what is the reason for this?

Since it is impossible to perceive a partless entity through only one of its parts, for this very reason, when an object is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), every quality and the entire nature of that object is indeed seen. Nevertheless, because of the presence of delusion (*bhrānti*), one does not ascertain [it as such]; therefore, for the sake of such ascertainment, the means of proof (*sādhana*)—namely inference (*anumāna*)—proceeds precisely in a positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa*). This has been stated quite clearly; thus, there is no need for another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) regarding what has already been seen by direct perception, for the purpose of grasping what was previously unseen.

Rather, by the statement "activity proceeds from a certainty based on what has been seen," the meaning of the injunction (vidhyartha) is clearly expressed; however, the exclusion of other [means] follows by implication,
as in the case of the phrase "the apprehension of the real object" and so forth.
The particle *ca* (and) serves to indicate a conjunction with respect to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The underlying intention is as follows:

if the apprehension of a real entity (*vastu*) is admitted to occur through inference (*anumāna*), then by the ascertainment of even a single property—such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*)—of a subject (*dharmin*) such as sound, there would follow the ascertainment of all properties of that subject, because the subject is partless (*niraṃśatvāt*). Consequently, other inferences, such as those for permanence (*nityatva*) and so forth, would be rendered futile. This is the intended meaning.

If one accepts that what is established by inference is *apoha*— defined as "that by which an externalized superimposed form is excluded"— then this aforementioned fault does not apply. Alternatively,

if *apoha* is defined as "that in which [the superimposed form] is excluded," and this refers to the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is accepted as being grasped by inference because it is non-different from its own form, then this fault likewise does not follow.
The explanation beginning with "not only" is connected as follows: "in some case where the locus (dharmin) has been perceived through direct perception";
the meaning is "in some [particular] locus perceived through direct perception."
Since not every substratum (dharmin) is perceptible, there is apprehension in some cases; by the principle just mentioned, there is an absence of other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

At that time, even inference is held to convey an entity such as sound through affirmation (vidhi), because it functions through the determination of the real object (vastu-adhyavasāya) and thus effects the exclusion of superimpositions (samāropa-vyavaccheda).
Thus, when there is the apprehension of the nature of a thing by way of a positive affirmation (*vidhi-rūpeṇa*),

and upon the ascertainment of one property (*ekadharmaniscaye*), there follows the ascertainment of all properties because they are not distinct from it— that is, because they are not distinct from the ascertained property— even though this non-distinction exists, there is no operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntarāvṛtti*), meaning no further application of inference (*anumānāntarāpravṛtti*).
If it is argued that there is no certainty regarding all phenomena, he says "no," and so forth; "in that" refers to the phenomenon ascertained by the first inference.
Being one whose nature as a dharma is determined by the thought "that is its self," it is certainly not logical for it to be undetermined;
explaining that this fault does not apply in the case of *apoha*, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "But when," etc.:

when, moreover, by means of inference—which effects a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the real object—one implicitly effects the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropavyavaccheda*), and not directly, because this [inference] is a means of cognition (*jñāpaka*), then the following [objection] is refuted: that the very exclusion of superimposition would not result in activity toward another object in practical discourse (*vyavahāra*), because it is not ascertained by inference.

In that case, since the exclusion of one superimposition of "unproducedness" by means of a single inference based on "producedness" does not constitute the exclusion of another superimposition of "permanence," another inference—such as that of impermanence—is set forth for that purpose, namely, for the sake of excluding other superimpositions.

Therefore, the external object is not grasped by conceptual cognitions in its own intrinsic form; rather, the external object is grasped only as unified with the cognition's own internal aspect (svākāra).
And since that which is unreal is excluded by this [cognition], it is called *apoha*; and while this is established, another person, not understanding the intended meaning,
says "But surely," and so forth.

The misconception (*viparyāsa*) that superimposes a form contrary to the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) proceeds; from that misconception, there arises the ascertainment of an unperceived object through a logical mark (*liṅga*). However, this is not an absolute rule, because inference is possible even for one who is free from misconception.
Thus he says:
The phrase beginning with "yathā" (for example) means that, due to "akasmāt"— that is, from smoke appearing unexpectedly and suddenly in a certain place— there is the cognition of fire.
For, when fire is apprehended there [in that place] without cause, the superimposition of non-fire is not possible;
therefore, it is not the case that exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is performed everywhere by implication through inference—
so says the Teacher.
For in this context, regarding the operation of inference as a means of apprehending the actual nature of a thing, the following answer has been stated:

if the locus (*dharmin*) is apprehended by perception, then because its properties (*dharmas*) are non-different from that locus, all [properties] would be apprehended, rendering inference useless. Alternatively, if a difference between the property and the locus is admitted, then there can be no relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) with the locus, precisely because their difference is admitted.

Furthermore, impermanence and the like do not arise from the nature of the subject (*dharmin*), nor does the subject arise from impermanence and the like; consequently, there would be no cognition of an unrelated property in that subject. This has also been stated in the passage: "Because inference is impossible therein for that which is neither cause nor effect."

Therefore, even in that case, when fire is cognized from the sudden perception of smoke, for the person who perceives that [smoke] and perceives the location, there is indeed a lack of certainty regarding its nature— that is, a lack of certainty regarding the nature of possessing fire;
and that [lack of certainty] is rendered indeterminate precisely because of error, due to the apprehension of the location as being identical to one devoid of fire.
He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "sa ca" (and that),
or rather: how can there be no determination of its intrinsic nature?
However, certainty would indeed arise from non-erroneousness,
yet uncertainty also occurs;
therefore, the cognition of the subject (*dharmin*) does not grasp the actual nature of the thing, but has exclusion (*apoha*) as its object.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "And that," etc.:

"And that" refers to the person; "by means of its exclusion" means by means of the exclusion of fire; thus, even though that place contains fire, he determines it as being devoid of fire by means of his intellect.
By what kind [of mind]?
By that which is liberated from the cultivation of the existence of fire,
and devoid of the conceptualization of the existence of fire.

How is it that one who is not mistaken is indeed mistaken? Because of grasping at that which is not that [object] as being that [object]. For instance, as long as one does not perceive smoke in that location, one determines that location to be similar even to another location devoid of fire.

Even if, in some cases where there is a connection with experience, a certainty arises here, one must still entertain doubt regarding that [object]; and since doubt rests upon two sides, it necessarily touches upon the opposite of that position as well. Therefore, even when doubt is eliminated, how can there be an exclusion of the other?
Indeed, one who understands the inferable object solely through the logical mark (liṅga) remains possessed of both error and doubt concerning that inferable object.

Because a person who is free from the superimposition of that [non-fire] aspect and free from doubt regarding the superimposition of the non-fire aspect would not, in the apprehension of that— that is, the apprehension of fire— follow a logical mark (liṅga) nor rely upon a property of the subject (pakṣadharma).

Thus, one should not pay heed to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that logical mark (*liṅga*) to the extent that one follows it; rather, because one does pay heed to it, the cognizer—possessing superimpositions (*samāropa*) and doubts regarding its form—removes those superimpositions by the power of the logical mark, and in some cases removes doubt. Therefore, in all instances, the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropavyavaccheda*) is effected through the cognition of its own pervader (*svavyāpaka*).
Therefore, by the manner already stated, [inference] has exclusion (*apoha*) as its object— that is, the exclusion of others— as its object; but not directly, otherwise,
if the apprehension of inference were intended to occur without superimposition (*samāropa*).

When the subject (*dharmin*) has been established by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what further nature could there be for that unestablished subject—other than its already established intrinsic nature—for the sake of which the logical mark (*liṅga*) would operate? Surely, there might be a need [for it] when doubt or error arises; as it has been said:
Furthermore, these conceptual constructions do not arise and perish entirely without being cognized;

nor can it be imagined that there is a doubt regarding the superimposition of their forms by following a logical mark (*liṅga*) in order to apprehend them, because even in the position where certainty does not [initially] arise,
it is possible to follow a logical mark for the sake of ascertaining the probandum (*sādhya*).

Otherwise, by the statement "when the locus (*dharmin*) is established, what remains unestablished beyond this?", the cognition whose object is the locus would itself have a conceptualized object; thus, the superimposition upon the locus is not established. How, then, could the exclusion of superimposition result from that inference?
True;
however, this is the intended meaning:

as long as there is no ascertainment of the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), there is no arising of inference, because the reason (*hetu*) remains unestablished (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, when there is a certain cognition of smoke as being connected to a specific location that possesses fire, this very [cognition] is a misconception (*viparyāsa*), because it is a determination in a manner other than [the actual state].

For the misconception here does not consist merely in the form "fire is not present here"; rather, even the cognition "this is a location other than one possessing fire" is a misconception. Therefore, in this inference as well, there is indeed a negation of superimposition (*samāropa*) in the form: "This location possesses fire; it is not a mere location. Let it be so; nevertheless, the inferential mark (*liṅga*), functioning within its own object for the sake of excluding that [superimposition], performs the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

Furthermore, as for this conceptual cognition that arises subsequent to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since it occurs in the absence of superimposition (*samāropa*), how could it effect the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)?

Moreover, according to your own view, it must necessarily be admitted that its object is the exclusion of others, because a universal (*sāmānya*) has a universal as its object and is characterized by the exclusion of others.
Therefore, he says:
"In some cases," and so forth:

even when some [object] such as a form is seen through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the cognition that arises subsequent to it has a universal as its object— that is, it has a universal as its referent— and for this very reason, it is conceptual (*vikalpaka*).

That object in which no other part—the form of the counter-correlative—is superimposed is "thus" (asamāropita); [the cognition] operating upon that [object] has as its domain the exclusion (*apoha*) of only that [other part].
Therefore, the meaning is this:

conceptual cognition, while grasping the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) devoid of superimposition through the differentiation of its own form, is erroneous; thus, it merely determines the external object as being devoid of such superimposition, but it does not grasp the actual nature of the external thing itself.

Therefore, conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka-jñāna*)— which has as its object the exclusion (*apoha*) of another superimposition precisely when there is a restricted determination of that [particular] alone—
or rather, conceptual cognition which operates when that other part is not superimposed, has as its object the exclusion of that very [part] alone; that is to say,
it has as its object the delimitation of that specific "other part" which is not superimposed.

This is what is meant: even where superimposition has occurred, the negation of that superimposition is not established by means of words or logical marks (*liṅga*), because of the absence of a [necessary] relationship. For this very reason, it is not produced; and since destruction is causeless, [negation does not arise], but rather [the cessation occurs] simply through the natural exhaustion of the preceding superimposition.
When there is a determination of impermanence and so forth through word and logical mark, and no further superimposition arises, the negation of superimposition is thereby accomplished.
Likewise, even when something is seen by perception, who can prevent the exclusion of the superimposition of another conceptual construction?
Therefore, it is not the case that a different kind of exclusion of superimposition was stated previously and now a different kind is being stated; thus, there is no inconsistency in the statements.
Therefore, this [objection] is refuted:
that for one who hears the word "cow," there would first have to arise the cognition "this is not a cow," such that the vocal sound "cow" would then proceed for the purpose of excluding the non-cow.
Ślokavārttika, Apohavāda, verse 92:
When the operation of words and logical marks is conceived as consisting in the exclusion of others by producing certainty regarding their own objects.
Thus it is established that activity occurs solely by way of affirmation;
therefore,
if this word "cow" is capable of excluding others, [it functions as such].

If it is argued that another word must be sought for the cognition of "cow" regarding the individual cow (*janaka-gavi*), this is refuted by the fact that the word "cow" (*gaur iti*) is itself capable of excluding other things.
Janaka [says]: "Another term must be sought for the cognition of 'cow' with respect to a cow";
likewise, it is said:
"Even though words and logical marks do not function toward that which is devoid of apoha..."
"Nevertheless, it is logical that cognition belongs to the cognizer as it relies upon an object," so says the *Ślokavārttika*, in the *Apohavāda* section,
verse 92.

This is precisely what we accept: that the function of an object signified by a word or a logical mark (liṅga) consists in the negation of other things, not in the function of the word or the logical mark themselves.
Therefore, as Kumārila says:

Because negation is formless and lacks differentiation, there can be no relationship between a mark and that which is marked; nor can it be expressed by words, nor can there be a relationship of the signified and the signifier, because both types of exclusion (*apoha*) are non-entities,
just as in the world, according to your own view, there is no such relationship between a sky-flower and a hare's horn.
If the meaning of a word is conceived as being merely negative in form, then emptiness (*śūnyatā*) would be something denotable by the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*) in another manner;
it would be expressed by words for distinct universals (*sāmānya*) based upon words for particulars (*viśeṣa*). (36)
If the denotable object of apoha were [the exclusion itself], then all [terms] would be synonyms.
(Ślokavārttika,
Apohavāda 42)
Likewise, if the differentiation of exclusion (apoha) were due to the differentiation of the objects to be excluded, then that [differentiation] would be merely figurative;
and since there is no differentiation of an exclusion— which is devoid of intrinsic nature— on account of the differentiation of its substrata,
how could it be differentiated by exclusions that exist externally?
Regarding this, the *Ślokavārttika*, in the *Apohavāda* section,
states: "But surely, through the distinction of the excluded objects (*apoha*), the distinction of the exclusion itself will be established."

Its distinction is not intrinsic; even that which arises from another is merely figurative. (47) Furthermore, since even the substrates with which it is associated do not differentiate it in reality, the claim that it would be differentiated by external objects of exclusion (*apoha*) is an excessive conceptualization. (52)
This is refuted; for mere exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is not an object of words and the like.
He explains the verse beginning with "that which" (*yad*), and by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), he includes sound and so forth.
The certain knowledge that "this has no mark" or "this consists of such-and-such a form and so forth" arises only when there is no superimposition;
for when a form or other quality is perceived through direct perception, there can be no superimposition of a contrary aspect at that time.
How, then, does it have exclusion as its object?
Thus much explains the first half of the verse; he speaks now to explain the second half.

The connection with the subject at hand is as follows: because that certain cognition (*niścayajñāna*) is absent regarding the object of superimposition (*samāropa*), it has the exclusion of that [superimposition] as its object;
this is precisely what he says.
In a particular distinction where there is no superimposition upon a person, there can be no unstable certainty regarding that object of superimposition—such as [certainty that it is] "selfless.
What is the reason?
It is because of the relationship of sublation between the mind of certainty and the mind of superimposition.
Because there exists a relationship of sublation between certain knowledge and the superimposing cognition that is its opposite,

[the author], establishing that very relationship of sublation, says "for not," etc.: even if an entity is perceived as distinct from everything— both homogeneous and heterogeneous— it is not recognized in every aspect exactly as it was seen.
The connection is with the words "it is not ascertained";
for what reason?
Because in some cases of difference, such as momentariness and so forth, an intervention is possible.

It pertains to the cause of error (*bhrāntinimittagata*). For example, even when one perceives a mother-of-pearl shell that is distinct from all other things, there is no certain determination [of its nature] because the cause of error—the similarity to silver—is possible in the case of the mother-of-pearl.

However, in a form where no cause of error exists, for that perceiver, there arises a certain determination following the experience, which is of the nature of memory (*smārta*). Thus, although there is no difference in the perception of all forms, this [determination] is "recollection" (*smārta*), meaning it has the nature of memory.
[Objection: But since it does not arise with the mental imprint "that," how can it have the nature of memory? [Reply:
True;
it is called "having the nature of memory" because it takes as its object that which was the object of non-conceptual [perception], having unified it with its own [present] form.

Since a determination occurs regarding an object that is free from superimposition even though there is no difference in its being perceptual, it is understood that there exists a relationship of sublated and sublator between superimposition and determination. From this causal relationship of sublated and sublator, it is understood that the activity of this determination—characterized by the absence of superimposition—occurs when there is a distinction from superimposition. [The opponent objects: "Granted that its activity occurs when there is a distinction from superimposition, nevertheless, it does not have 'exclusion of others' (anyāpoha) as its object, because its activity proceeds in a positive form (vidhirūpeṇa). To this, he says:

The exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is precisely the discrimination (*viveka*) [of the object] from that [superimposition], and the exclusion of others is precisely the discrimination from superimposition (*samāropa*). Therefore, because it functions with respect to that which is devoid of superimposition, that [ascertainment] also [has that as its object]. Thus, not only is the determinate cognition (*niścayajñāna*) "sound is impermanent" a domain of the exclusion of that alone (*tanmātrāpoha*) according to the previously stated reasoning, but even that determinate cognition which follows upon perception has as its domain the exclusion of that alone; it does not determine the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the real entity.
Why is this?
For instance, even when there is a determination of a certain aspect such as "form-ness" (rūpatva), it is observed that another aspect such as "momentariness" is not apprehended.

If, however, the determination of the nature of a thing were made by a conceptual ascertainment (niścaya) following upon direct perception, then—since a thing is partless—that ascertainment would be impossible; and because it is impossible for there to be no determination of other aspects once its [own] nature has been determined. Furthermore, the activity of either a conceptual ascertainment or a word proceeds solely through the determination of the object, and not by way of grasping the actual nature of the thing itself.

Therefore, as many superimpositions of parts or superimpositions of other forms as have occurred or not occurred with respect to a single [object], so many are the determinations (*niścaya*) and so many are the words that operate toward their respective objects for the sake of excluding those [superimpositions]—that is, for the purpose of removing the superimpositions.

For that reason, those determinations and words have distinct domains and distinct objects, because they have as their object an external thing that is non-different from their own respective forms as determined by their own respective causes; it is for this reason that this is so.
That which exists as an object superimposed by the intellect does not follow from another object or another cognition,
nor does it produce the intended effect; therefore, even that [conceptual image] cannot be said to be the denotatum in reality,
provided that the word-meaning is a mental manifestation (pratibhā) whose object is an external thing.
If the external world is determined to have a single nature, how can there be diverse appearances?
Or, if these [appearances] are without objects because they exist as mere mental impressions (*vāsanā*), how could there be cognition and activity regarding external things?
"If it is held that activity always occurs through a resolve toward something external within one's own domain,
then it follows that the referent of a word is unreal, because one acts based on such an error," so says the *Ślokavārttika*.
This is rejected because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is intended to have a constructed object;
otherwise, it would follow that the true nature of the thing is grasped by means of cognition (*buddhi*) and verbal expression (*śabda*).

When [the object] is pervaded by a single word and made the object of all its aspects, then, being pervaded by a single cognition— whether it be of the nature of ascertainment— one aspect or one object is "another object" (anyaviṣaya),
meaning that which is both another (anya) and an aspect (ākāra) or an object (viṣaya).
Because no other aspect of that object exists as a cognizable object,
or because it is not the object of any other word, cognition, or means of knowledge that could denote that object,
words that function subsequently toward an already perceived object would be synonyms.

Just as in the case of words such as "tree" and "pedestal," there would be no occurrence of a cognition that follows distinct objects—such as "the taste is sweet, oily, heavy, cold," and so forth; thus, the consequence [of your view] is that they must have a single object.
Stating this in order to refute the ultimately real distinction between property and substratum (dharma-dharmin), he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "yasyāpi" (of whom also, etc.):

even for that Vaiśeṣika for whom various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—that is, qualifiers such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth—are distinct from one another due to their mutual dependence on a single object, such as a jar; for that object which possesses these various adjuncts, the cognition that grasps it through affirmation (*vidhi*) is of a determinative nature. And since that cognition is distinct for each individual adjunct, one who demonstrates the difference in objects for cognitions has, by implication, already demonstrated the same for words.
He explains this with the words beginning "yopi" and so forth:

limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the like are mutually distinct from one another and distinct from their substratum—that is, distinct from the possessor of the adjuncts (*upādhimat*). These [distinctions] are based upon those [adjuncts], meaning they are based upon distinct adjuncts. The mention of "verbal cognition" (*śruti*) is merely illustrative; the same applies to mental cognitions (*buddhi*) as well.
They exist as the substrata for the conditions of persistence,
and they function as denoters precisely within those very objects of cognition.

He provides the answer: "Therefore" (*tat*) means for this reason, there is no undesirable consequence (*aprasaṅga*) characterized by synonymy among other words and cognitions such as "this" (*ayam*).

Regarding the phrase "of that too" and so forth: when the possessor of attributes (upādhimat), which is non-different from those powers that are the cause or factor for the assistance provided by various kinds of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), is apprehended— that is, ascertained— in its entirety by a single determinate cognition (niścayajñāna).

What would be the distinction, what the specific difference, between the substratum and the collection of limiting adjuncts? If [the former] were uncertain, the latter would all likewise be uncertain.

But surely, even though a relation exists between fire and smoke, it is observed that when fire is not ascertained, smoke is not ascertained; in the same way, when the locus (dharmin) is not ascertained, its properties (dharmas) will not be ascertained.
But would this very non-perception not be impossible,
given that the nature of fire is grasped in its entirety by a determinate cognition,
since it is determined precisely as the cause of smoke and so forth?
Since smoke and the like are also ascertained, it follows that their essential nature is not grasped through ascertainment; for in that case,
even by non-conceptual [perception], there would be no grasping of them in their entirety, because smoke does not appear [therein] and thus its being an effect [of fire] is not grasped.
This is not so;
for the causality of fire with respect to the production of smoke is stated to be its mere prior existence (*pūrvabhāva*),
and since that [prior existence] appears in perception, how could there not be a cognition of fire as the cause of that [smoke]?
Therefore, this is the meaning:
in reality, there is no mutual dependence between fire and smoke,
because there is no relationship between them in their states of being already established or not yet established.
Smoke exists only when fire exists; thus, these two are called cause and effect.

However, because a property (*dharma*) and its locus (*dharmin*) are mutually dependent, if the locus were ascertained in its entirety, there would necessarily be a direct ascertainment of all its properties, rather than their implication through the force of the object (*arthād ākṣepa*).

But when a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurs that determines an external object—rather than apprehending it directly—it is logical that other properties are implied by the force of the object, since the determined object can be distinguished from others.

Furthermore, if there is mutual dependence, as long as there is no determination of the property (dharma), there can be no determination of the substratum (dharmin); and as long as there is no determination of the substratum, there can be no determination of the property. Thus, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (anyonyāśrayatva).

Now, is it not the case that the relationship between the qualifier (upādhi) and the qualified (upādhimat) is said to be precisely the relationship between the locus and the located (āśrayāśrayibhāva)?
And that [causal relation] exists only between two things occurring at the same time;
yet there can be no relationship of benefactor and beneficiary (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*) between those two because they exist at different times— so how can this be asserted?
It is true that when something qualified by one attribute is apprehended, everything [related to it] is apprehended;
however, others maintain that the relationship between the produced and the producer is one thing, while the relationship between the beneficiary and the benefactor is another.

For instance, although the substance of the jujube fruit is produced by its own causes, it is assisted by the bowl; therefore, this relationship of the assisted and the assister is accepted between two things that exist at the same time. With this intention, it was said:

"Alternatively, a property being ascertained, because it necessarily depends upon a substratum, implies the cognition of that substratum, and since [the cognition] belongs to all properties that depend [upon it], there is the ascertainment of everything."
Therefore, because it functions as a means of cognition distinct from verbal testimony, the relationship between property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*) is merely conceptual.

Furthermore, on this view, there is no redundancy in employing other means of cognition when postulating the difference or non-difference of properties; for since they are not real entities, difference and non-difference do not exist in an ultimate sense.

Moreover, since other properties must themselves be postulated by means of other means of cognition, how could there be a postulation of the difference or non-difference of properties in their absence? Thus, [the objection] is trivial.

With the words "Even though" (*yadyapi*) and so forth, he explains the meaning of the verse: although distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are admitted as the respective causes for the cognition of other words and other cognitions when apprehending an object possessing those adjuncts,
that object— the possessor of the adjuncts— is nonetheless grasped and made into an object by the words and cognitions.

In that [entity] possessing those [qualities], there is no internal differentiation within its own nature—that is, within its own essence—regarding those powers which serve as the basis for the assistance provided by various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Consequently, if it is apprehended even through the medium of a single adjunct, it is apprehended in its entirety. This being so, what limitation could there be regarding its specific adjuncts? Rather, all of them would necessarily be determined.
Why is this?

If it is argued that because the possessor of attributes (upādhimat) is apprehended through the mediation of a single attribute by virtue of its being the benefactor of all attributes, it is only the essential nature (svarūpa) of that possessor which is apprehended, and not its status as a benefactor of the attributes,
he replies with the words "for not," and so forth.
For there is no connection [here] with the phrase "the fact of being an auxiliary to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is something other than that which is not grasped";

rather, because for that which possesses the limiting adjunct (*upādhimat*), when it is grasped in its own form, the state of being an auxiliary does not differ from its own nature (*svarūpa*). Since this is so, for this reason, "of this" refers to that which possesses the limiting adjunct.

Since the very apprehension [of an object] by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*) or essential form (*svarūpa*) is itself an apprehension by way of its being a benefactor (*upakārakatva*), let it be that there is an apprehension of the possessor of attributes (*upādhimat*), whose nature consists in benefiting all attributes through the medium of a single attribute;
however, how can there be an apprehension of the attributes themselves, which are distinct from that [possessor]? To this, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "of those two," etc.:

there is a mutual connection between the collection of attributes (*upādhi*) and the substratum possessing those attributes (*upādhimat*) within the self (*ātman*), by virtue of their own nature; that is to say, because the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary (*upakāryopakāraka*) constitutes the very essence of their connection.
Consequently, when one perceives the single entity that possesses the nature of the benefactor, both are apprehended due to that connection.
He explains that [the cognition] "of the substrate and the substratum" refers to that which has become the self, and so forth.

For when the substratum of attributes (*upādhimat*) is apprehended, its status as a benefactor—which is its very essence—is apprehended; and when that is apprehended, the status of the attributes as being benefited—which is their very essence—is also apprehended, because the apprehension of the state of being a benefactor is inseparable from the apprehension of that [substratum].

Therefore, since both the attribute and the substratum of the attribute are apprehended in a single cognition, when that substratum of attributes is apprehended as qualified by even a single attribute, there is the apprehension of all attributes, because their apprehension is inseparable from the apprehension of that [substratum]. This is due to the fact that the apprehension of the attributes is inseparable from the apprehension of the [substratum].
If it is argued that "otherwise"—that is, if the adjuncts (*upādhi*) are not apprehended—then [the substrate] would likewise not be apprehended;
even as "the possessor of adjuncts" (*upādhimat*), it would not be apprehended as being "beneficial to the adjuncts.

If it is further argued that at that time, the benefit of the possessor of adjuncts is apprehended only with respect to that very adjunct which is the cause for the application of the term "cognition," and not with respect to the benefit of other adjuncts—the author replies:
Regarding the phrase "for [the nature] is not indeed other," and so forth:

the idea might be that the nature which assists another—that is, the nature of an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*) which assists something else—is not apprehended; however, in reality, everything is indeed apprehended because an entity is partless.

Since that which possesses an adjunct (*upādhi*) is apprehended simply as "the benefactor" without regard for its specific relation, and not as "the benefactor of this [particular thing]," the adjuncts themselves are not apprehended; therefore, he says "nor also," etc.

"Apprehended in such a way" means apprehended as "the benefactor"; thus, when [the substratum] is apprehended as the benefactor, there is no apprehension of the adjunct, which is the effect of that benefit.
What is the reason?
Because there would follow the consequence that even the benefactor of that benefactor would not be apprehended;
this is what he states.
Because it is a correlate, there can be no apprehension of that which is the benefactor (upakāraka) even as "benefactor" without the apprehension of a second correlate;
thus he provides an illustration of such a case, saying "like the relation of owner and owned."
For there is no apprehension of ownership without the apprehension of the owner;

therefore, even when a single cognition or word functions by way of a single attribute (*upādhi*), there follows the apprehension of all attributes and the substrate of those attributes in its entirety.
Consequently, this same undesirable consequence applies even in the theory that attributes are distinct entities, that is, even in the view that attributes are things separate from the substrate.
"The various cognitions of words would result in being synonyms"—

with the words "But even so" (*athāpi*) and so forth, the opponent raises this further objection: those powers by which the possessor of power (*śaktimān*) assists its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), those powers are distinct from the possessor of power.
Therefore, because of this distinction,
this undesirable consequence does not apply;
for when there is a perception of the non-difference of the power that assists a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), there is a perception of all powers.
And because of that apprehension, this undesirable consequence—that all limiting adjuncts [would be perceived]—does not arise;
he states the answer in the verse beginning with "dharmopakāra... and so forth.

Dharmas are limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); if those powers (*śakti*) which constitute their assistance are admitted to be distinct from that possessor of power (*śaktimat*), then what do those powers become for that possessor of power?
They become nothing at all; the meaning is that they are not related to it.
This is because, if there is no assistance [rendered by them], then [they are unrelated].
If it is maintained that for the sake of establishing a relationship with those powers, an assistance [provided by them] is required,
then further, distinct powers that assist those powers must be admitted.
Furthermore, for the sake of establishing the relationship between those powers by means of which one provides assistance, another assistance would have to be postulated;
in that case, yet another power would have to be postulated, and thus there would be an infinite regress.
He explains that [with the words] "yadi" and so forth;
"pratyupādhi" means with respect to each respective limiting adjunct (upādhi).
The capacities that constitute its auxiliaries belong to that [entity] which possesses limiting adjuncts; they are not identical with it,
nor are they its essential nature, but rather distinct from it.
Nor do they experience or appropriate any benefit from that which possesses the limiting adjunct; rather,
what are they said to be in relation to it?
Why is it said that "the powers belong to the possessor of the limiting adjunct" (*upādhimataḥ*)?
Because there is no [inherent] connection.

For the sake of establishing a connection, if one were to admit that these powers—which assist the limiting adjunct—receive assistance from the possessor of the adjunct, then by which powers would this possessor of the adjunct assist those very powers that assist the limiting adjunct?
If those [powers] are held to be identical with its own self, then this possessor of adjuncts (*upādhimān*), being one and partless due to its powers being identical with its own self,
establishes the apprehension of [the object] in its entirety by benefiting the powers that assist the adjuncts, as shown by the passage beginning with "tathā hi" (for thus).
When one limiting adjunct (upādhi) is apprehended, the apprehension of a distinct power that assists that adjunct— which itself is assisted by other adjuncts—
is what is meant by "the apprehension of that"; thus, it refers to the apprehension of the power that assists the adjunct.

That which assists [the substrate]—that is, which assists the powers that assist the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—is of what nature? It is an entity (*bhāva*) that has appropriated all the powers that assist the limiting adjuncts, wherein all the powers assisting those powers that assist the limiting adjuncts are inherent to its own self; such an entity, once grasped, causes all the powers that assist the limiting adjuncts to be grasped, and these grasped powers, in turn, cause the limiting adjuncts that assist them to be grasped. Thus, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) remains: what difference would there be between this and the previously mentioned case where [the entity] is not ascertained?
Now, if it is thought that this fault must not occur, and those capacities which assist the capacity are themselves held to be distinct from the entity possessing the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*),

then further capacities assisting those [first] capacities must also be postulated as distinct; and since capacities assisting those would likewise require others, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of both the limiting adjuncts and their capacities.

Furthermore, because there is no finality and thus an undesirable infinite regress regarding the capacities of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) themselves— which must depend on ever-further successive capacities— the connection [of the effect] occurs through this unfolding;
for the limiting adjuncts are connected to distinct capacities, those [capacities] likewise to other distinct ones, and so on,
with each subsequent capacity connected to preceding distinct capacities, resulting in an infinite regress.
But it does not [exist] in that which possesses the adjuncts;
therefore, that single possessor of adjuncts is assisted by those adjuncts. (Note 136-1: Because it is indicated by means of being known.)
With which powers (*śakti*) has it never been grasped even at any time?

It is that whose nature consists of the assistance of those [powers], meaning it is of the nature of the powers that assist the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), namely, the powers of those powers that provide assistance to the adjuncts.

The meaning is that since capacities are distinct from [the substrate], they cannot be apprehended as possessing those capacities— namely, the capacity for the assistance provided by limiting adjuncts— and therefore, even as "possessors of limiting adjuncts," they cannot be apprehended; thus, the postulation of limiting adjuncts is entirely redundant.

Thus far, when the application of the word and the cognition occurs with respect to that which possesses the limiting adjunct (upādhi), the aforementioned fault has been stated; now, when they occur with respect to the limiting adjuncts themselves, another fault must be stated,
and he introduces the position regarding the limiting adjuncts (upādhipakṣa) in order to state that.

If, however, words and cognitions were to adhere to— meaning they would resort to as signifiers— merely those adventitious attributes (upādhi), which are distinct qualifiers, that are devoid of any eternal substratum, then [the following would occur].

Because that which possesses the limiting adjunct (upādhimat) is not co-present with verbal cognitions— that is, it is not made an object by them— therefore, through the cognition of that [substratum], and thus through the cognition of the possessor of the adjunct,
there is the cognition of every adjunct even by means of a single verbal cognition.
Regarding this as well, he states the fault with the words "tadāpi" (even then) and so forth,
referring to that [entity] possessing limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Since it has been established that there is no implication [of the probandum],
he asks: "How is it redundant in that case?"— referring to the locus possessing the limiting condition (*upādhi*).

Regarding the phrase "purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*) and so forth: placing purposeful action at the forefront, one engages in activity; thus, that conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) which has purposeful action as its basis (*āśraya*) or objective support (*ālambana*) is so described.
This includes every single conventional practice concerning what is beneficial or harmful, undertaken by those who act with deliberation.

And since there is no third possibility, that [universal] exists through two modes— affirmation and negation; this third case is the *itthambhūtalakṣaṇā* (the instrumental used to denote a characteristic) according to Pāṇini,
and the adjuncts therein, such as "cowness" and so forth, are incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Furthermore, since the distinction between individuals—which is capable [of causal efficiency]—is expressed by the word itself, what is the use of fruitless verbal usages?

And because the distinction between individuals, which is thus capable of purposeful action, is not expressed by words, then the intended adjuncts such as "cowness" (*gotva*) would not be adjuncts; they would not be qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Because, when a word or a cognition functions with respect to something possessing an adjunct (upādhimat) by way of that adjunct,

there is an absence of the subordinate member— the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa)— relative to some principal entity (pradhāna) which is the substantive (viśeṣya); and it is in relation to that, namely in relation to the principal, [that this occurs].
Thus they are called "limiting adjuncts" (upādhi);
this is the established definition of a logical limiting adjunct.
But when it is the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) themselves that are expressed by the word, then,

because that possessor of the adjunct is neither implied nor conveyed by the word, those adjuncts do not constitute members of any primary entity; the meaning is, therefore, that they are not adjuncts at all.

If it is argued that even if only the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is denoted, there is no fault— namely, the fault of the uselessness of word-usage— because the possessor of the adjunct is indicated (*lakṣita*) by those adjuncts which are themselves indicated by words, through their definition or delimitation (*pariccheda*), then that same consequence of having to grasp all adjuncts applies equally [to your position].
He states that very point in the passage beginning with "sa tāvat" and so forth;
the word "saḥ" (he) refers to the possessor of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

Because of the necessary connection (*nāntarīyakatā*), the possessor of attributes (*upādhimat*) is perceived without deviation even by a single attribute; since it is partless (*niraṅśatva*), it would be perceived in its entirety, and thus the consequence (*prasaṅga*) of grasping all attributes would remain as it was. [Objection:
This consequence applies only where there is a direct denotation (*codanā*) of the possessor of attributes by means of a word.
But it is not the case that [the word applies] there by virtue of the object; therefore he says:
"For what distinction is there here?"—[namely,] that words would directly denote this [object] as possessing such an adjunct (upādhi).
Whether the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) are indicated by their own forms or indicated by words, they would indicate the possessor of those adjuncts; what difference is there? None at all.
For in that case, that possessor of adjuncts is determined at the time of indication precisely through the power of its adjuncts.

If it is argued that [the universal] "benefits all" means it benefits all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then, as before, there follows the undesirable consequence of having to apprehend all those adjuncts; therefore, what was said regarding "indication by indication" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*) is of no avail, because it is afflicted by the previously mentioned defects.
Since there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) if the powers that benefit the adjuncts were distinct from them, those powers are not distinct.

Therefore, when it is accepted that the substratum (*upādhimat*)—which is assisted by a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—is the object of apprehension, then the distinct capacities (*śaktibheda*) that assist other limiting adjuncts cannot be other than [identical with] that nature which assists the single limiting adjunct. (Note 138-1: These are well-practiced.
Note 138-2: The section known as "The Knowable.")
When that [substratum] possessing limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is seen, those [adjuncts] which were previously unseen become non-different from it;
for this reason, they are apprehended along with it.
When that which possesses attributes (upādhimat) is apprehended, there is the apprehension of its entire nature as it is assisted by all those attributes.
This is also what Bhaṭṭa maintains:

that attributes are indeed distinct from one another; therefore, when a single attribute is determined in a substratum (dharmin), there is the determination of all attributes because of their difference [from one another].
Thus it is said:
"That which persists through things characterized by appearance and disappearance is the substrate (dharmin),
or else it is that in which cognition occurs prior to the apprehension of the attributes."
152. Regarding a subject (*dharmin*) possessing infinite properties (*anantadharma*), the word would be merely a means for determining one property, but not for determining all;
thus, that [position] is also refuted precisely because it entails the faults inherent in both sides. 178.
That which persists through things characterized by appearance and disappearance is the substrate (dharmin);

or else, it is that in which cognition occurs prior to the apprehension of the attributes (dharmas). When a substrate possesses infinite attributes, there is the determination of only one attribute [at a time].
"Word would be merely a means [of cognition] and not a definitive determination of everything"—
this is from the *Ślokavārttika*, in the section on perception (*pratyakṣapariccheda*).
With the words beginning "If," etc., he anticipates the opponent's intention.

Even when an object has been grasped in its entirety by a single definitive cognition (*niścayajñāna*), another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) might still be required for the sake of eliminating error;
he explains this very point with the words "it might be so" (*syād etat*) and so forth.

When there is the apprehension of an object that is partless and without divisions, what other part could there be that is not apprehended at that time of apprehending the partless object? Everything is indeed apprehended; however, although it is apprehended, it is not ascertained due to error, and thus another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) proceeds.

With the words "If it is thus," and so forth, the proponent of the established doctrine [siddhāntavādī] demonstrates that whatever subsequent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is desired for the purpose of removing error is established as having exclusion (*vyavaccheda*)— that is, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)— as its object, by the same reasoning previously stated, just like that aforementioned subsequent means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, another cognition of ascertainment that arises at a later time than the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) also has exclusion as its object;
for what reason?
Because it operates upon an object free from superimposition (asamāropa).
He explains the verse beginning with "tattarhi" [then, therefore] as follows:

since it has the result of excluding the superimposition (*samāropa*) of another form, it is established that its object is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*); likewise, by way of negating a superimposition that is about to arise, every other preceding determinate cognition (*niścayajñāna*) also has the exclusion of others as its object.
What is the reason?
Because it functions with respect to an object that is a superimposition of what does not exist;
he says this very thing:

Furthermore, because of this reason— that there is no superimposition upon the form through which [the object] is apprehended— it is established that the initial certainty, occurring in the absence of superimposition, has exclusion (*anyāpoha*) as its object.

Even when an object has been grasped through certainty, one who desires another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of removing error would have to admit that the object of certainty is not actually certain;
otherwise, error would be impossible.
And that is untenable, as he says:
Furthermore, etc.:
how could that form which is not determined by determinations (niścaya) be the object of those determinations?
What is the reason?
For this very reason, the apprehension of an object by determinations (*niścaya*) consists precisely in the determination of that object;

if that which is intended as the object of determination were itself undetermined— just like other forms— and if that which is not intended as the object of determination were instead grasped by those determinations, [then the determination would fail].
"How so? and so forth.

The opponent [objects]: Even for the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others), who desires a further means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the purpose of excluding superimpositions regarding what has been grasped by perception, if an aspect that is not being ascertained is nevertheless accepted as being grasped by perception, or if grasping occurs solely by virtue of ascertainment, then the same logical consequence applies: how can a form that is not being ascertained be said to be grasped even by perception? Thus, the difficulty is equal.
He refutes this with the words "no," and so forth;
the intention is that [perception] is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
The word "that" refers to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
As for that which is said to "grasp" the aspect of blue and so forth, that grasping does not occur through ascertainment; rather,
what then?

By means of manifestation, there is the manifestation in every respect of a partless entity; thus, "in every respect" [is said]. (This note belongs to the base text, which was not keyboarded.

Direct perception is not that which determines [an object].

"Grasping is that [appearance]"— therefore, the grasping or non-grasping of perception occurs not by virtue of certainty or uncertainty respectively, but rather by virtue of appearance or non-appearance.
Consequently, even when there is no certainty, it is not contradictory to establish that something is grasped by perception based on mere appearance.
It is not the case that, as with perception, determinate cognitions grasp an aspect merely by its appearing— even if it is not determined— and fail to grasp it merely by its not appearing;
for if one asks why this is so,
he says "moreover" (*kiñcit*) and so forth.

Just as, upon seeing a person, even one who determines his humanity may act with uncertainty and engage in different types of worldly behavior regarding another, such as a thief; for indeed, through the determination of humanity, behavior consistent with that— such as placing trust— is observed,
whereas through the non-determination of thievery, behavior consistent with that— such as fear— is not observed.
And therefore, since there is a specific engagement corresponding to a certainty, that [certainty] is apprehended by means of that certainty;

and since there is a specific non-engagement corresponding to a lack of certainty, that is not apprehended— it is for this very reason that [the passage beginning with] "therefore" and so forth was stated.
Regarding this form [of cognition],
if its apprehension were not established by way of certainty as being "otherwise," then even in the case of a single form...
The opponent asks: "Even regarding a form intended to be ascertained, there would be no apprehension of it by means of the ascertainment that 'it is this';
what then is the reason [for this]?"
"Distinct from everything" means being excluded from both similar and dissimilar classes.
"In that very way" means that, according to experience, there arises no conceptual determination (*niścaya*) regarding all these differences that is merely mnemonic (*smārta*).

This is because, for the sake of excluding other forms within one difference, the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others) must admit the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) toward other differences.
"Due to the deficiency of auxiliary conditions," says the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī);
for it is not mere experience alone that is the cause of certainty, but rather repetition and other such factors are also auxiliary conditions;
therefore, certainty occurs only with respect to that form where these [auxiliaries] exist, and not elsewhere.

[Objection: But surely, since it is seen at all times even in the form of momentariness, there must indeed be habituation (*abhyāsa*), and thus certainty would arise. [Response: What is intended here by "habituation" is not merely the object that has been experienced and ascertained; for a momentary thing cannot be ascertained through experience because of the possibility of causes of error (*bhrānti-nimitta*). Therefore, how can there be habituation with respect to it? Consequently, this remains established: habituation occurs only with respect to that form where certainty arises.
He states that very point with the words "therefore" (tataśca) and so forth:
[it refers] to a particular (viśeṣa), characterized by blue and so on, which is excluded from everything else.

Even when that which is devoid of parts, undivided, and apprehended by perception in its entirety is present, that particularity for the determination of which there exists a causal condition (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) is what is cognized—that is, determined.
He explains this with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*) and so forth:
"in all particulars, such as momentariness and the like, [it is known] at least by means of mere experience."
Since the production of certainty depends upon other causes for experiential cognition (*anubhavajñāna*),
he says "experiential cognition indeed," and so forth.

The phrase "according to the habituation to conceptual construction" (*yathāvikalpābhyāsam*) means that it produces [certainty] by means of whatever habituation to conceptual construction one has, acting as its auxiliary cause.
He provides an illustration with the words "for example" (*yathā*) and so forth:

although there is no difference in the sight of the form of a dead woman, the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of a corpse, a beloved, and food arise respectively for the mendicant, the lover, and the dog, according to their respective habitual practice of such conceptualization.
And it is not merely the practice of conceptual construction that acts as the auxiliary cause;
rather, there is another as well— thus he says "therein," etc.
Even there, although there is no difference in the perception of form,
there is a sharpness and keenness of cognition;
