as in the case of yogins, through the sharpness of their cognition, there is a determination of momentariness and so forth by mere perception.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of [the factors such as] purposefulness (*arthitva*) and capability (*sāmarthya*) is intended; these and others are the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) for the arising of the ascertainment of difference from experience— that is, from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)— which serves as the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).
If, then, the aforementioned causes do not exist for many certainties, how can there be a sequential occurrence of those certainties? To this he says, "And of those very [causes]," and so forth;
"of those" refers to the causes of certainty, [and their sequence arises] from the differences in the degrees of proximity.
That very certainty which has the most proximate cause for certainty arises first;
by the word "first" (ādi), he provides an illustration starting with "the sequence of certainties according to the distinctions of degrees of intensity," and so forth.
When the teacher is like a father, then, although there is no difference between being the progenitor and the instructor for a single person,
upon seeing the father approaching, one determines, "My father is coming," and not, "The teacher is coming."

Because the cause for determining paternity is more proximate [than other reasons], one might object: "Even though there is practice in the conceptualization of momentariness and selflessness, for those who do not perceive reality, the certainty of momentariness and so forth does not arise from perception. To this, he says:
"That too," and so on.
When there is no cause for error, [ascertainment] occurs, but not from the mere presence of a causal condition for ascertainment;
because, in this way, when there is no cause for error and the totality of auxiliary conditions is present, ascertainment arises from perception, and not from that [perception] alone.
Therefore, it is not the case that [the object] was not experienced, and so forth.
And thus, it is established that exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*) is what is conveyed by words and logical marks (*liṅga*).

Now, if this exclusion is non-different from the object itself, then once it has been made the object of a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or word, other [means] would be redundant, because the object would have been ascertained in its entirety.

Now, even if [the object] is distinct, since it is dependent upon that [single property], when a single object characterized by the exclusion of one [particular] is ascertained by a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then—by the aforementioned reasoning—all exclusions would be ascertained, and thus other means of valid cognition and so forth would not function;
therefore, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) is equal [for both sides].
That is not correct.
Since there is no mutual exclusion among entities— whether they be non-different or different—
but rather they have arisen as distinct solely from their own causes, as has been stated and will be stated;
[the author] says the following regarding how designations such as "exclusion of others" and the corresponding cognition nevertheless proceed:

Regarding the phrase "there too" and so forth: there too, when the word-meaning is an exclusion of others (anyāpoha), there is both the exclusion from another, as well as [the cognition] "this is excluded from another."
Those words which express properties (*dharma*) and property-bearers (*dharmin*), as well as the determinations (*niścaya*) which have both as their objects, follow convention (*saṃketa*).

Through conformity with convention, the distinction between the objects of property and property-bearer is conceptually constructed; however, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), there is no exclusion at all—this is the meaning.
He explains this [as follows]:

Regarding that, by the passage beginning with "there, the exclusion of others" (tatrānyāpoha), he will state that there is no such thing as an exclusion from a horse that is a separate property (dharma) distinct [from the cow], nor is there a subject (dharmin) excluded from the horse that is itself qualified by that exclusion; rather, the exclusion itself is the excluded.

If the exclusion from horse (aśvavyāvṛtti), which constitutes non-horseness, were distinct from the cow-substance, then that exclusion from horse would also have to be excluded by the cow-substance because of their difference.
Consequently, since the cow is being excluded from that non-horseness (the exclusion from horse), it would follow that the cow possesses that very nature [of non-horseness],
which entails the absurdity that it is a horse, just like a horse.

For in this way, the cow is excluded from the exclusion of the horse— which is characterized by non-horseness— if the cow were to possess horseness; and since that would entail the cow becoming a horse,
the cow's exclusion from the horse would be non-existent.
Because a cow and a horse are [allegedly] one and the same,
it has been stated by the Jains and the followers of Jaimini that "everything would become a single entity consisting of all things, due to the transgression of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha)."
Regarding them, this was stated in the Ślokavārttika:
"If the exclusion of others were a distinct entity, then cows, horses, and so forth would be identical."

Nor is the cow non-different from the exclusion of the horse, because it would follow that one could not have the cognition "this is a cow" upon the exclusion of the horse; furthermore, it would follow that a horse would arise when a cow perishes, since the exclusion of the horse would have already ceased to exist.
Therefore, exclusion does not exist at all.
Therefore, as it was stated by Bhaṭṭa Uddyotakara:
"Is this exclusion of the non-cow (agopoha) a distinct entity from the cow?
If it is distinct, is it dependent [upon the cow] or independent?"

If [the universal] is dependent, then because it is dependent upon that [substance], it is a quality (*guṇa*); in that case, the word "cow" would denote the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), and not the cow-substance itself.
Consequently, there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "the cow stands.
Alternatively, if it were non-dependent, in what sense would there be the meaning of the genitive case?
If the "exclusion of the non-cow" (gorapoha) is non-different [from the cow], then it would simply be the cow itself; thus, there is nothing undesirable [in this].
Furthermore, if this exclusion were one and yet related to many individual objects, then that very thing would be "cowness" (gotva).
That has been refuted,

because there is no such thing as the exclusion of another; rather, an entity produced from its own causes in its own form is simply excluded from others, and that exclusion from others is merely conceptualized,
since in ultimate reality there is no exclusion.
Therefore, that which is the exclusion is itself the excluded;
for both [the exclusion and the excluded] refer to one and the same thing.

Furthermore, it is precisely this thing, as excluded from others, that constitutes the probans (*liṅga*), the probandum (*liṅgin*), the relation, and the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

For conceptual construction (vikalpa), superimposing its own form as non-different from that which is excluded from others, causes a person to engage with it; because it performs this function so effectively, it is precisely that [exclusion of others] which is the external object of the word. This is also stated by Kumārila:
Perhaps the exclusion (*apoha*) would apply to only one entity or to all entities;

if it were from only one, then just as the substance "cow" is designated by the word "cow" through the exclusion of the horse, so too would it apply to a lion and the like, because the exclusion of the horse— which is the cause for the application of the word "cow"— is present in those cases as well.
Thus it is said: "Therefore, because they consist of the exclusion of non-horses (*aśvāpoha*), all those [animals] such as lions and so forth,
while bearing that cause— the exclusion of non-cows (*agopoha*)— would be called 'cow'."
Ślokavārttika, 57:
Now, [if it is argued that] the exclusion (apoha) of the cow-substance is from everything...

In that case as well, if the things to be excluded (*apohya*) are horses and so forth individually, then because the things to be excluded are infinite, the exclusion (*apoha*) itself could not be established;
furthermore, because the things to be excluded are distinct, a plurality of exclusions would follow, and consequently,
even with respect to a single individual (*piṇḍa*), there would arise the cognition of multiple universals (*jāti*) due to the multiplicity of those universals.
Therefore, as in the case of different species such as horses and so forth,
a single universal denoted by the word "cow" is not established.
(Ibid., 60)

Nor can all of them be excluded in their collective form, for a collection must either consist of parts or be a single entity; however, it is impossible for the things to be excluded to possess the nature of being parts or the like, nor does a collection exist as something distinct from them. If it were not distinct, then the problem of infinite regress remains exactly as it was before.
Nor can they be excluded in the form of a universal, because a universal is not a real entity;
and if it were to be excluded, it would follow that it is a real entity—
therefore, that [position] is incorrect, for:
Since all entities arise each with its own specific form, their exclusion from everything else is already established by their respective causes.
If it is then asked how this [exclusion] is known,
does a cow— possessing the nature of past, future, present, near, and so forth— appear in direct perception?
If you say "no," how is it that the exclusion of everything else (*sarvāpoha*) is not established by perception there?

For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not exclude other things by grasping them with its two hands; rather, its very illumination of an object of a specific form constitutes the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
Therefore, the apprehension of the exclusion (*apoha*) of everything occurs precisely through the manifestation of an object with a determinate form in perception.

And that [perception], while determining its own object, determines everything that is not thus as being "other. Consequently, a simultaneous negation of all other things is made in a general and undifferentiated manner, because a universal (*sāmānya*) consists of an undetermined specific form.
As it has been said:
"Because it establishes merely the thing as excluded from what does not have that form,
and because it is not established through a distinction of gender, [inference] is declared to have the universal as its object" (Pramāṇasamuccaya).
Therefore, it is indeed accepted that whatever is excluded possesses substantial reality;

yet there is no evidence whatsoever for the claim that being excluded entails substantial reality, since even non-existence (abhāva) is excluded, and it has already been stated that this [non-existence] lacks substantial reality.

Consequently, by means of the exclusion of "non-cow" (*agopoha*), which is characterized by the simultaneous exclusion of everything else, the nature of "cowness" (*gotva*) resides even in a single individual body.

The claim that distinct universals such as non-horseness, non-lionhood, and non-buffalooness are conceptually constructed by the successive exclusion of individual horses and so forth, and that words function to denote these [entities] through that medium, is trivial. For if there is no distinction in the referent— the object excluded from exclusions—
how can there be a distinction between the word and the cognition, such as "excluded from exclusion"?
For instance, the word "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*) is one thing, while the word "the excluded" (*vyāvṛtta*) is quite another;
likewise, there is also a distinction in cognition,
such that when "exclusion" is mentioned, only a mere property (*dharma*) is perceived.
To this, he says "sound," etc., [referring to] the subject (dharmin) as being excluded.
The cognition arising from a word that denotes both a property (*dharma*) and its substratum (*dharmin*) is "verbal cognition" (*śabdapratipatti*).

[The compound] "word and verbal cognition" (*śabdaśca śabdapratipattiśca*) is a *virūpaikaśeṣa* (an elliptical remainder consisting of dissimilar terms); thus, the meaning is that there is a distinction between the word and the cognition [it produces], and yet there is non-distinction regarding that cognition which arises from the word. The establishment of the relationship between the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*) is the convention (*saṃketa*); [the phrase refers to] the distinction of that [convention].

Furthermore, the distinction between conventions will be demonstrated immediately thereafter by the passage beginning with "the exclusion of other differences" (*bhedāntarapratikṣepa*); the ellipsis to be supplied is that "in reality, there is no difference in the denotata of the words *dharma* (property) and *dharmin* (substratum)."
To the objection beginning with "But surely," etc.,
[the author] replies with "Of the two," etc., as if asking: "If there is no difference in what is to be expressed, why is a distinction in convention not logical?"

And this genitive case is used in the sense of the agent, according to the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*; for while both [agent and object] would apply, the restriction *karmaṇi* is optionally set aside by the alternative *śeṣe vibhāṣā*.
The meaning is that a single referent is expressed by both the words *dharma* (property) and *dharmī* (possessor of property).
If one [thing] were to be denoted by two [words], then the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) would be redundant.

Likewise, if there is no difference between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), then the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*)—as in "the cowness of a cow" (*gorgotvam*)—which expresses a distinction (*vyatirekinī*), would be impossible; for that case-ending expressing distinction functions by relying upon a real difference (*vastubheda*), since it is based on a difference [between entities].
Just as in the case of "Devadatta’s water-pot," so too [is it] when, in the absence of a convention and in the absence of an ablative case ending,
[the objection] is raised against Pāṇini.
First, in order to dispel the fault regarding the absence of case endings, he says "of the two," and so forth.

Even when two words denoting a property (*dharma*) and its locus (*dharmī*) express a single referent, the case-ending is "separate"— that is, the word *vyatirekiṇī* (meaning "expressive of distinction") is placed after *vibhaktiḥ*, like the word *ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive) [which follows *vibhaktiḥ*]. The word *śabdaḥ* is displaced in the sequence [and should be understood as following *vibhaktiḥ*].

It follows as if the object were divided, or it reveals [this division] through a slight trace (*leśa*) caused by differences in convention (*saṃketa*) regarding the denotable (*vācya*); for this reason, [it appears so], but not because of an ultimate difference in the thing-in-itself (*vastu*),
as he explains.
By the passage beginning with "Not indeed of words," [it is shown that] [cognition] depends on the nature of the object; that is, it depends on the external particular (bāhya-svalakṣaṇa).
What is the reason?

Because there would otherwise follow the undesirable consequence that words could not function even with respect to non-existent things if they were subject to human desire, "those" words have their functions restricted by desire; thus, in whatever manner they convey a distinction— as in the case of "the king's man"— they appear as if distinct [from the object].

Just as when [the self] is not distinct [from the seer], one says "the self itself is the seer of the self," so too these [words] are employed by assuming a distinction even though the object is non-different; they reveal that object as if it were distinct without obstruction.
For this reason, although the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is in reality non-different, [the words function] in that manner.
He states "cow" as denoting the substratum (*dharmin*) and "cowness" as denoting the property (*dharma*);
although these two express a single entity, [the distinction is made] for the purpose of conveying a specific object, namely, the cow as excluded from non-cows.

When the convention is established such that, for the purpose of manifesting "cowness" (gotva)— which has the exclusion of non-cows as its cause— the word "cowness" denotes merely the exclusion of non-cows,
then, despite this distinction, there is no separate referent; thus, the genitive case does not occur in the expression "this [entity] has cowness" (*asya gotvam*).
The analysis of the compound is "that which has an object distinct [from the subject].
It appears as if presenting the property (*dharma*) as a separate entity from the substratum (*dharmin*), even though it is not a separate entity— that is,
even though the property is non-distinct.
What is the reason?

Because of the habitual observation of the usage [of the genitive] when there is a difference in entities; for instance, in cases such as "Devadatta’s water-pot" (*devadattasya kamaṇḍaluḥ*), due to the habitual observation of the usage of the genitive case.
This is what is meant:

let it be that [the object] is distinct from the thing itself, or let it not; in any case, the use of the ablative case-ending (*vyatireka-vibhakti*) follows merely the speaker's intention. It is simply through the habit of observing usage that the word presents its meaning as if it were distinct.
Thus, it is by the mere employment of the case-ending.
Even though there is no difference in meaning in all such cases—
for instance, in expressions like "cow" (*gauh*) and "cowness" (*gotvam*), there is no ultimate difference between the property (*dharma*) and the possessor of the property (*dharmin*)—

nevertheless, elsewhere as well, even when there is no difference in meaning, there is no restriction on a word that functions by denoting a distinction (*vyatireka*) because it is employed according to human intention.
And having observed that words function by the power of human intention even when such an external denotable object does not exist,
he says "just as," and so forth:
a single entity is expressed by the singular number in a certain context.
In the expression "yathā tvam" (as you),
although there is no distinction in that [object] and no distinction in its oneness, that very same object is expressed by the plural "yūyam" (you).
Therefore, since the plural is observed even when referring to a single entity, it is understood that the application of words does not correspond exactly to the objective reality.
If it is argued that, based on the extended rule (*atideśavākya*) "the plural is used for the second person and for a teacher according to some," the plural may be used even for a single entity,
this must be considered: does the extended rule effect a plurality for that which is actually one, or does it merely prescribe the use of the plural where it was not otherwise obtained?
The first position is not tenable, because things cannot be established by mere verbal assertion alone;
as for the second position, it is already established that the application of words occurs through mere intention.
Thus, the fault regarding the absence of case-endings has been refuted.
Pāṇini 1.2.58 introduces the very objection regarding the fault of the absence of convention (*saṃketābhāvadoṣa*) in order to refute it,
beginning with the words "prayojanābhāvāt tu" and so forth.
There is no purpose [for stating the distinction] because the single entity is denoted by both the words "subject" (dharmin) and "property" (dharma);
yet that purpose certainly exists, for in relation to "cowness" (gotva), there are other distinctions such as "substanceness" (dravyatva) and "earthiness" (pārthivatva).
Their "rejection" is non-acceptance;

these two, rejection and non-rejection, belong respectively to those two words denoting the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin). Of what kind is the distinction in convention (*saṃketabheda*) between them?
It is that which conforms to the desire of the cognizer—that is, it follows the wish of the listener. What is its "footing" (*pada*)? Its purpose (*prayojana*).

This is what is meant: when a cognizer, being no longer desirous of the form excluded from others, seeks to know a cow-individual as excluded specifically from a horse, then— as long as one does not superimpose upon it an exclusion from the horse that is a distinct entity and express it accordingly by means of a worldly, property-denoting word preceded by convention— one is unable to communicate the intended object to another.
Therefore, with respect to that [non-horse], it is said "this is its non-horseness.

For in this way, because the substratum (dharmin) is not primary, there is no implication of a form excluded from others; and since the exclusion is only from a single thing, namely the horse, it is not stated in such a way as "it is a non-horse," for by that [expression] "non-horse," there would be an implication of a form excluded from other things as well.
Furthermore, one who speaks of something that has not been sought after by another, nor even sought after at all, would surely be considered insane.

Moreover, when someone seeks to know a cow-individual as excluded from horses—its form being defined by such exclusion—even then, as long as the speaker does not superimpose the individual as qualified by its exclusion from horses and express it through a worldly term denoting the substratum (dharmin) in accordance with the convention, the object sought after by the other cannot be communicated. Therefore, for that person, it is said: "This is not a horse."

For in this way, by virtue of the primacy of the subject (*dharmin*), there is an implication of a form excluded from others, and the cow-individual is thereby described as excluded from horses; yet it is not stated in that manner as "it possesses non-horseness," because that would entail the consequence of not implying a form excluded from others that the other person desires to know. And how could one who speaks of a matter not desired to be known not be considered insane?

Furthermore, all verbal usage is preceded by convention (*saṃketa*), and convention itself is necessarily preceded by objects constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*). Therefore, it is logical that even through conceptual thoughts, the cognition of the relationship between property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*) occurs by this very same door.
Consequently, as for what was said—that words denoting properties and property-bearers function with respect to objects either excluding or not excluding other distinctions—let that be so.
As for the question of how there can be a cognition of the subject (dharmin) and its properties (dharma), that objection is refuted;
clarifying this very point through the commentary, he says:
"When this," and so forth.
"Practice" (pratipatti) refers to the hearer.

Therefore, "from that"—meaning from something other than a horse, such as a buffalo—and so forth; "exclusion from that" means the nature excluded from buffaloes and the like. Its "existence independent [of others]" means its existence independent of [other] entities, specifically in the case of a particular body, such as a cow.
One desires to know merely the exclusion of the horse, [asking] whether there exists a form of this [object] that is excluded from the horse;

it is for the purpose of making known such a thing. Thus, in accordance with what the cognizer wishes to know, and for the purpose of making known that very distinction from the horse, by means of a word for which the convention has been established in that manner—namely, a convention established regarding the mere exclusion of the horse while setting aside other distinctions—the state of being a non-horse (*anaśvatva*) is awakened to and revealed by the word as "this mass possesses the state of being a non-horse."

The exclusion [of the object] from horses and the like is primary; with respect to that, there are further exclusions [of it] from buffaloes and the like. The cognizer, having no further desire for those [further exclusions], perceives that [object], namely the individual entity (*piṇḍa*).
In other words, one who wishes to know the substance "cow" as qualified by the exclusion of "horse" does so without having rejected other exclusions such as "buffalo" and the like; thus,
it refers to that [cognition] in which other exclusions have not been abandoned.
In that very context, when there is the exclusion of non-horses, speakers employ a word denoting the subject (dharmin), saying "this is not a horse";
he explains how they employ it as follows:

Others read it as: "tathā prakāśanāya" means for the sake of manifesting the exclusion of the horse (*aśvavyavaccheda*) without rejecting other exclusions; that is, for the sake of manifesting the exclusion of the horse itself without rejecting other exclusions. Thus they recite.
Even then, this is the meaning:

why would they employ or express— by means of the word denoting the subject (*dharmin*) "this is non-horse"— the exclusion of the horse (*aśvavyāvṛtti*), which consists in the exclusion of the horse, while other internal distinctions remain uncontradicted?
"For the sake of manifesting that [object] while not excluding other differences" means:
by means of that very word expressing a property (*dharma*) which excludes other differences,
for that very reason, in the previous case, other differences were excluded by that word expressing a property.
Having taken the meaning of the other word (*anyapadārtha*) in a general sense, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) must be applied;
this is then connected with the phrase "subsequently, according to the function of the word.
Otherwise, it would result in the refutation [of the opponent's view] on the grounds that it is a different kind of distinction (*bhedāntaratvāt*).
In this way, the derivation [of meaning] should be understood for other words of a similar kind as well.
The co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of two words with different bases of application is their occurrence with respect to a single substratum;
it is the relationship between the qualified and the qualifier (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇabhāva*), which is the relationship between that which is to be excluded and that which excludes.
An example is "gotvam asya śuklam," where the word for quality (*guṇaśabda*) takes the neuter gender because it possesses the gender of its denoted object;
others, however, read it as "śuklaḥ."
And they explain it thus:

for a word denoting a quality (guṇaśabda), when employed while excluding other distinctions and referring to the quality alone, takes a masculine gender; however, for words such as "white" (śukla) that refer to the quality alone, [masculinity] applies, whereas for those that refer to the substratum possessing the quality, the gender follows that of the thing designated (abhidheyavat).

And thus, since these two [terms] function solely as properties (dharma-mātra), there is neither co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) nor the relation of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva).
To the question "Why is there no co-referentiality?", he says:
"tanmātra... and so forth.
This explains that [properties] such as co-referentiality with an object exist only in the reflection appearing in the intellect,

and not in the external particular (svalakṣaṇa), because the latter is inexpressible; it is only through conceptual determination (adhyavasāya) that these are said to belong to the external object as well.

If a single cognition produced by two words were to arise with respect to a single substratum (*dharmin*) appearing as endowed with two properties, then there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). But in this case, because the difference [between the two] has been excluded by their respective exclusions (*tanmātraviśeṣa*), the cognition—being colored by the qualification of "cowness" alone—is the cognition of that which serves as its substratum; thus, there is a relation of qualifier and qualified. This is because the single substratum endowed with both "cowness" and "whiteness" does not appear to the cognition as a non-different entity serving as the basis for coreferentiality; that is to say, the cognition does not apprehend a single substratum as being joined with both cowness and whiteness.

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "of that which has it as its substrate": that very *gotva* (cowness) is the substrate of that cognition; because the individual cow (*gopiṇḍa*) does not appear as identical with the mere *gotva*—which is its specific [qualifier] that excludes other properties—it is so that when one employs the expression "this has *gotva*," a cognition arises that apprehends the property in its abstracted form. This note belongs to the base text, which was not keyboarded:

Similarity (*sāmānyatva*).

 A cognition arises.
Therefore, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);

and because the cognition has no further expectation regarding other differences due to the very exclusion of other properties, there is no relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).
However, in the second case—the position that words denote the substratum (*dharmin*)—there is both grammatical coreferentiality and the relation of qualifier and qualified, as in "the white cow."

He states the reason for the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words "tathā" and so forth; that is, by means of the cause which is the conventional designation (*saṃketa*) of the word denoting the property-bearer (*dharmin*) upon an object whose other differences have not been excluded, in accordance with that convention.
"Joining" (*yojana*) is the synthesis within a single substratum (*dharmī*).

"Exclusion-properties" (*vyavacchedadharmāḥ*) are properties whose cause is exclusion; they are "synthesized" (*saṃhṛta*), and being both these [properties] and "all-exclusion-properties" (*sakalavyavacchedadharma*), it is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
By means of those properties acting as instruments, [one perceives] that which possesses differentiation.
Because a single substratum (*dharmin*) possessing multiple distinct properties appears to the intellect through the presentation and indication of words— as if it were one—
the intellect appears to present that single substratum as if it possessed multiple properties; however,
the substratum presented as such by the appearance of the intellect is not actually one in reality.
Since the distinction between property and substratum (dharma-dharmin) constructed by conceptualization is unreal,
some read "of the one alone" (*ekasyaiva*);
in that case as well, it should be understood that this is logical only by virtue of the determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) of the cognizer.
Consequently, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established;

and because the word denoting the substratum (*dharmin*) functions without excluding other distinctions, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) arises for the cognition produced by it, since that cognition depends upon other distinctions that have not been excluded—such as "the cow is white" or "blue.
And the word "and" (*ca*), as before, refers back to the preceding reason.

This alone is the pervader of all linguistic usage, and not anything else such as a universal (*sāmānya*), quality (*guṇa*), and so forth, imagined by others, because those [concepts] are sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus he says, "This very difference," and so on:
this very difference between two words denoting a substance and its state consists in the characteristic of excluding or not excluding other properties (*dharmāntara*).
"Everywhere" means in both the general and that which possesses the general, as well as in the quality and that which possesses the quality.
In every instance, whether it be an action or that which possesses the action, a word denoting the substratum (dharmin) expresses a substance (dravya),
while a word denoting the attribute (dharma) expresses a state or activity (bhāva).
Since this is so, for that reason there is no distinction whatsoever between those two— the word for substance and the word for existence— in their referent from the perspective of ultimate reality;
he explains this with the words "Therefore," and so forth.
There is no difference whatsoever in terms of being the instrument by which it becomes the object of a definitive cognition (*niścaya-pratyaya*).

For instance, just as when "cowness" (*gotva*) is stated, there is a definitive cognition regarding the exclusion of the non-cow (*ago-vyavaccheda*) within that very [referent], so too when "cow" (*go*) is stated— although this is a denotation of that which is excluded from non-cows while not rejecting other distinctions— nevertheless, the definitive cognition pertains only to the exclusion of the non-cow, whereas for the other distinctions, there is merely a non-rejection.

And that very same thing is the referent of the word (*śabdārtha*) where a verbal ascertainment (*śābdo niścayaḥ*) occurs; thus, there is no difference in the expressed object (*vācya*) between two words denoting an entity (*bhāva*) or a substance (*dravya*). Only the mere exclusion or non-exclusion of other distinctions (*bhedāntara*) differs.
He states this very point in the verse beginning with "One [word] denotes that very [thing]," and so forth.
The word "dharma" is "one" (eka) because it is that word by which other differences are rejected—that is, excluded as non-cow (*ago-vyavacchinna*).

The word "dharmin" is "other" (anya) because, without rejecting [the particular], it causes one to understand that very same individual (*piṇḍa*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); thus, there is no difference regarding the determination of the substance itself, but they differ merely in terms of rejection and non-rejection.
Thus, there is no difference whatsoever between the act of going and the statement "Devadatta goes"; this same principle should be applied elsewhere as well.

Furthermore, he says "desiring to make [the meaning] known," etc., because even the fourfold application of words—based on the distinctions of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and relation (*sambandha*)—is subsumed by this very distinction of properties inherent in the entity.
Desiring to make known that meaning characterized by the exclusion or non-exclusion of other distinctions,
[the speaker] employs either a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)— that is, a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix— or even a primary derivative (*kṛt*).

If one were to express [an object] by means of a word such as "white" (śukla)— whether it ends in a suffix termed *kṛt*, or is some other word distinct from *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes, whether it be a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) or an underived (*avyutpanna*) term—
then there exists no further distinction [of the object] beyond the specific characteristic of either excluding or not excluding other differences.
He explains that [with the words] "to such an extent" and so forth;
"to such an extent" refers to that which is characterized by the exclusion of other differences.
Or rather, the connection is that [the agent] should show [the action] even when it has been performed;
this is when the root *pac* (to cook) occurs with reference to an action such as placing [the pot] on the fire, which resides in the agent.

And in that very case, when the suffix *ghañ* is applied, the word *pācakatva* denotes the relation between the action and its agent, namely inherence (*samavāya*). Thus, the word *pāka* has the same meaning as the word *pācakatva*; both of these convey an object excluded from non-cooks (*apācaka*), with no other distinction between them. However, when the meaning of the root *pac* is the action of cooking (*viklitti*) residing solely in the object (*karman*), how could the word *pācakatva* denote a relation?

Because the meanings of "the state of being a cooker" (*pācakatva*) and "cooking" (*pāka*) are distinct, or because it must be indicated by another [element]— such as a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*)— other than a primary derivative (*kṛt*) or secondary derivative (*taddhita*), in order to convey such a [distinction].
These notes belong to the base text, which was not keyboarded: [Note 151-1] Regarding "Śes-pa-byod-pa-la" (To one who knows). [Note 151-2] Regarding "Bcod-pa-ñid-ces" (It is called cutting).
[Note 151-3] Regarding "Raṅ-gis-byas-paḥi-gśuṅ-legs-gzan-gyi" (Of the well-spoken treatises composed by oneself).

The connection is as follows: one should demonstrate [the meaning] by means of a convention established by oneself for the purpose of making known other distinctions, just as in the cases "Devadatta sleeps" or "the whiteness of the cloth.
Here too, the very same meaning that belongs to the word "one who sleeps" (śāyaka) is [present], with other distinctions excluded.
It is the same for the expression "it lies" (*śayyata*).

Just as in the case of "the white cloth," that very object which is excluded from what is non-white and has other differences rejected, is the same [object] when expressed as "the whiteness of the cloth"—this being merely a difference in phrasing. Thus, by the mere expression of an exclusion residing in a single substratum (*ekadharmi*), whether its other differences are rejected or not rejected, that very entity is, in ultimate reality, nothing other than a distinct object, though it is divided into the forms of property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*).
The connection is that "it does not arise again.
What is the reason?

Because the terms *dharma* and *dharmin* have been established as conventions to indicate a single entity that possesses internal distinctions—whether rejected or un-rejected—of exactly such a nature.
Alternatively, by the mere expression "in that way"— that is,

by the mere expression of a property (*dharma*) that is a distinct entity— the nature of that property is, in ultimate reality, indeed a distinct entity; for the term "property" has been conventionally established to indicate that very thing which is of such a nature, independent of other distinctions, and excluded from others.
"Now, as for the objection beginning with 'nanu ca' and so forth:
it is said that a relation is expressed; thus, the relation between the action of cooking and the agent who cooks is characterized by inherence (*samavāya*).
For instance, it is observed that when a nominal suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) follows a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, it expresses a relation, as [the author] has stated:"

According to the principle that "in compounds, primary derivatives (kṛt), and secondary derivatives (taddhita), there is the expression of a relation," the word *pācaka*, being a derivative ending in a *kṛt* suffix,
does not denote the action of cooking (*pāka*) itself— which is of the nature of an activity— but rather denotes the state of being a cooker (*pācakatva*).
This is what is meant:
the action is indeed distinct from the agent, and the relation between the two is likewise distinct.
Therefore, even though the verb *pacati* expresses an action residing in the agent, the meaning of the word *pāka* (cooking) is not identical to that of the word *pācaka* (cook).
He refutes [the objection] with the words "not indeed by cooking" (*na vai pākena*) and so forth:

by means of "cooking"—which resides in the agent and is not a real entity (*vastubhūta*)—an agent called "the cooker" (*pācaka*), distinct from the act of cooking, is designated by the word "cooker. Such an agent, as described by the Vaiśeṣikas and others, would be an independent agent distinct from the action, where the relationship between the action and its factors (*kāraka*) would be a real entity. However, such is not the case here.
Since that independent agent, distinct from the action, is what will be refuted, [the opponent’s position fails].
For if the action or the agent is not distinct [from the substance], how could there be a relation such that it is expressed by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*)? This is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, as for the phrase "of this," the referent of the word *pācaka* (cook) is a mere entity (*vastumātra*)—delimited from non-cooks and not excluding other distinctions—and that very thing is the cook. (Note 152: As it has been asserted.)

One must supply the phrase "the denotation of a word is also denoted as 'being a cooker' (*pācakatva*)," because that very [denotation], from which other distinctions have been rejected, is what is being expressed.
But the relation is not denoted, because it lacks existence;
for that very thing which is the referent of the word "cook" is also the referent of the word "cooking," as indicated by the particle "also" (api).

Another explanation is that by the word "not by cooking" (*na vai pākena*), in the view of those who advocate for the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), the "cook" is designated as something entirely distinct and separate from the act of cooking,
just as it is described by the opponent.
Since that which would be the substratum of the relationship between action and its factors is unestablished,
rather, the exclusion of the non-cooker is expressed by the rejection of other distinctions.
He states that very point with the words "that which again," and so forth;
the word "that which" refers to the denotable object characterized by the exclusion of non-cookers, wherein other differences have been rejected.
This has been demonstrated immediately following the word "pāka"; that very thing denoted by the word "pāka" is also denoted by the word "pācakatva," and not a relation,
because that [relation] is unestablished.
Since these false conceptual constructions are non-abiding and arise from the power of unreal entities,
how then is it understood that there is no action distinct [from them], nor any inherence (*samavāya*) in them? To this,
he says "just as," and so forth.
Or "its inherence" refers to the inherence of the action and its factors;

and because there is no difference between exclusion and that which possesses exclusion, for that reason, that which possesses a universal is denoted by words as having the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object.

Thus, whatever fault exists in the position that [the word denotes] that which possesses [the universal], that same fault would apply to the theory of exclusion (*anyāpoha*); therefore, the description of the position that [the word denotes] that which possesses [the universal] has been rejected.
For if a separate existence between the universal (*jāti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*) were admitted, the fault raised against the "possessor" position (*tadvatpakṣa*) would follow;

this is because words denote an object qualified by that [universal], namely, an object qualified by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). The phrase "raised against the possessor position" means that which was stated regarding the *tadvatpakṣa*.

For instance, it is argued that if a word, having denoted a universal, were to apply to its possessor, it would lack independence. Consequently, since the word would be controlled by the universal—which serves as the cause for the word’s application—it could not imply the mutual differences residing in the individuals; thus, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with those individuals.

Furthermore, there would be the fault that the application of words to that which possesses [the universal] would be merely figurative (*upacarita*), and so forth. Thus, having stated the [objection regarding] exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), the entire consequence— that sound (*dhvani*) existing as independent in that which possesses [the universal]— is refuted and rejected by this very [argument], because there is no difference between the exclusion and that which possesses the exclusion.
For in that case— namely, the position that [the word] possesses that [property]— having taken up another entity (arthāntara), that is, having taken up a real (*vastubhūta*) universal (*sāmānya*),
there is a lack of independence because it does not directly denote the possessor of the universal in another object that possesses that [universal].
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the faults of non-co-referentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇya*) and metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) is intended.

However, in the theory of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), because there is identity between the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and that which possesses the exclusion (*vyāvṛttimat*), a word does not function with respect to one object by taking up a different object; therefore, he says "nor... and so forth, [stating] that there is no fault such as lack of independence (*asvātantrya*).
"The exclusion of one thing from another is not different from that which is excluded;

for it has just been stated that between two words—one expressing the property (*dharma*) and the other the property-bearer (*dharmin*)—there is the expression of only a single distinction of exclusion.
To this, the opponent asks: "How so? and so forth.
The word "now" [indicates] that because the exclusion and its possessor are identical, a single excluded particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) lacks continuity and is not associated with other objects.

How could the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), which constitutes the very nature of that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), be a universal (*sāmānya*)— being non-concomitant like the particular itself? Moreover, it is never observed as a universal.

With the words "In that cognition," etc., the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) states that because it appears in that same single form within a conceptual cognition of a universal, it is called a "universal" (*sāmānya*)— where "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*) means that which excludes [other things] by means of this single form.
This is what he says:

exclusion is not a single entity inherent in the excluded particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) that constitutes a universal; rather, it is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising at a time subsequent to the experience of the excluded particular characteristics, which—by its very nature—arises as if displaying a single form among things that perform a single function.
By the power of that conceptual construction, a universal (sāmānya) is postulated even among things that lack a universal; and by this, the object of words and so forth is directly shown.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
The intention [of the phrase] "not at all anything" and so forth is that there is no entity that exists as a real thing (*vastu*).
If so, how then do linguistic conventions such as universals (*sāmānya*) and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) function? To this he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "sound" (*śabda*):

that conceptual cognition which has sound as its basis— acting as its cooperative cause— arises through the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), joining together even properties that are not actually conjoined, thereby making them appear as if they were of a single form.
Based on the appearance of a single form in that cognition, the universal (*sāmānya*) is established;
and based on the appearance of a single substratum (*dharmin*) endowed with two properties, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established.
Furthermore, this conventional usage of "universal" and so forth is established as pervading even non-existent things.
To explain how it is devoid of real objects, he says "of objects," and so forth:
because there is no actual conjunction of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the conventional usage of universals (*sāmānya*) is devoid of real objects.

And because there is no differentiation within a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the conventional usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is without a real object. Now, one might ask: since all this conventional usage proceeds by way of diverse forms, how can it have the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object? To this, he says:
[the phrase] "the objects of all that conventional usage, such as universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, are its common substratum" is the connection [to be made].
That effect and that cause are concordant; the state of those things which possess a cause corresponding [to their effect],
by means of that state acting as the instrument.

Objects that are distinguished from other causes and effects serve as the basis for all conventional usage, such as "universal" and so forth; for this reason, it is said that the object [of conceptual cognition] is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

However, the exclusion of others does not appear therein, because only the external object appears in its own form as a positive entity (*vidhi-rūpa*). Furthermore, since a person impelled by a determinative cognition (*niścaya*) is led toward a specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)—which is excluded from the undesirable—by avoiding what is undesirable, for this reason too it is said to have the exclusion of others as its object; it is not dependent on appearance, because the positive entity itself appears.
Therefore, as stated by Bhaṭṭa Uddyotakara: "What is the referent of the word 'cow'—is it a positive entity (bhāva) or a non-entity (abhāva)?
If it is a positive entity, is it a cow or a non-cow?"
If there is no cow, then there is no dispute; if, however, "non-cow" is the meaning of the word "cow," that is an extraordinary feat of verbal skill;
and if it is non-existence, that is incorrect.
For indeed, upon hearing the word "cow," there is no comprehension of non-existence;

and the meaning of a word is understood through comprehension, yet no one understands non-existence from the word "cow. Likewise, regarding this exclusion (*apoha*) expressed as "a cow is not [non-cow]," does it have the cow as its object or the non-cow as its object?
If it has the cow as its object, how can there be the non-existence of a cow in the cow itself?
Now, if it does not have the cow as its object, how can there be a cognition of something else through an exclusion (*apoha*) that has a different object?
For when the *khadira* tree is being cut, the cutting of the *palāśa* tree does not occur.
Now, regarding the negation "a non-cow is not a cow" applied to a cow: by what means has the state of being a non-cow ever been attributed to a cow, such that it could be negated?
Cf. [Nyāyabhāṣya 2.2.61].
Ślokavārttika. Apoha. Nyāyavārttika 2.2.71: refuted.
Because the word "cow" has the actual cow as its object, whereas [the word "non-cow"] has only a conceptualized object, there is a dispute;
or rather, just as the negation of a cow occurs even in the absence of superimposition, as was stated previously, this [objection] is trivial.
Therefore, it remains established that the meaning of a word is indeed a positive injunction (*vidhi*).
Demonstrating this very point,
he says "therein" and so forth;
that which is independent of its own nature [as an external reality] with respect to the subject (dharmin) appearing to conceptual cognition is described as such.

By virtue of appearing to the intellect as "one" and "excluded from many," a single substratum (dharmin) excluded from many is established through the appearance of that single substratum excluded from many within the intellect;
it is by virtue of this [appearance] that a single substratum is determined to be excluded from many.

The sense is that although [an entity] is excluded from many [others], it is precisely that real substratum (*dharmin*) which is made the object of words by speakers, because they utter words in order to produce conceptual reflections (*vikalpa-pratibhāsa*) of that very kind; thus, the exclusions [from others] are imagined there as distinct properties (*dharmabheda*).
The point is that since the conceptual appearance excluded from others (*anyavyāvṛtta*) is made an object by words, its status as a positive object (*vidhiviṣayatva*) is established.
He states this because it is not only made an object by words, but also by conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "the experience of each respective particular characteristic" (*tadanubhava*) refers to the experience of that specific *svalakṣaṇa*; the "impression" (*vāsanā*) is the capacity deposited by that experience; its "awakening" (*prabodha*) is the state conducive to the production of an effect; and those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) whose "birth" (*janma*) proceeds from that [awakening] are what "objectify" [the thing].
By what kind [of conceptual constructions]? By those "whose objects are determined to have that nature" (*adhyavasitatadbhāvārtha*).

That external state which is determined (*adhyavasita*) within the appearance of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa-pratibhāsa*) is precisely that "state of being determined. Those conceptual constructions for which such an object is the domain are "those [constructions] having as their object that which has a determined state.
This means, in effect, that they proceed by unifying the perceived (*dṛśya*) and the conceptualized (*vikalpita*).
There is an alternative reading, *adhyavasitatadbhāvārtha*, which is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that object which has a determined state."
The connection [of the words] is as follows: "even a single [entity], excluded from many [others], has its existence determined as that [object].
Therefore, the conventional usage of "universal" and so forth arises by virtue of the appearance in cognition.
And in that very context, within the appearance of cognition characterized by the exclusion or non-exclusion of other differences— expressed as "this is"—
the term *vyavahāra* (conventional usage) is used in the sense of an object (*karmasādhana*); thus, conventional usage consists precisely of the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*).
This is what is meant:

it is being elaborated that those two— the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*)— which are established within the appearance of cognition, are inexpressible in terms of either identity or difference from one another.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the fault previously stated regarding the positions of identity or difference between the ultimate nature of phenomena (*dharmatattva*) and their substrates (*dharmin*)—namely, the futility of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, characterized by independence and the like—is not present here; this is what is meant.
Furthermore, he states another fault regarding the positions of identity and difference with the words beginning "for not" (*na hi*).
A property is not something other than the property-possessor;
for what reason?
Because it is not designated as a separate entity.
Since that which is excluded [from others] is denoted by both the word for the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and the word for the property (*dharma*) from one and the same [source],
it is not the case that the property-bearer is identical to the property;
why is this so?
For it would follow that words denoting properties, just like those denoting substrata or those denoting qualifiers, would also entail the implication of other exclusions.
Likewise, because it conveys the intended object through its activity (*ceṣṭā*),
the word "dharma" does not convey a particularity whose distinctness has been excluded; therefore,
no distinction is made in its conventional designation (*saṃketa*).

The word "dharma" conveys an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) that precludes other distinctions; thus, there is no establishment of a separate convention for this. This aforementioned inexpressibility of the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) in terms of identity or difference refers to the object appearing in cognition as the referent of a word; however, in the case of a real entity (*vastu*), namely the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), [such inexpressibility does not apply].
"Because it does not exist [as a real entity], it is inexpressible in terms of identity or difference; however, the object of words and so forth is established according to how it appears.
To this, the opponent replies with "But surely... and so on, pointing out that such usage is observed in actual linguistic practice.
In the expression "cowness belongs to the cow" (*gorgotvam*), the genitive case is used;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of other case-endings such as: "cowness is established in the cow," or "the word 'cow' applies to the cow by means of cowness as its cause."
Furthermore, because properties such as "cowness," "substance-ness," and so forth are many,
the observed linguistic differentiation among those many properties— such as the expression "cowness, substance-ness, and earth-ness"— would not be possible.

Since it has been stated here by the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*)— in the context of the non-difference between the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and its properties (*dharma*), and the absence of ultimate difference—
that "the operation of words does not depend at all upon the intrinsic nature of their objects," and so forth.
Furthermore, in order to establish [the point] by means of an additional argument, he says "api ca" and so forth:
for those proponents whose words are governed by reality— that is, dependent upon the actual state of things.
"Words are not dependent on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).

This means that those words whose primary or principal basis is the speaker's intention itself would be "dependent on the speaker's intention. [If this were the case], the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would not occur, nor would there be differences in number (*vacanabheda*), and so forth. Thus, the objection regarding the genitive, differences in number, and so on—where "and so on" (*ādi*) includes these—is addressed by the phrase "the genitive, differences in number, and so on."
The objection regarding the absence of *taddhita* suffixes— such as "the state of being a cow (*gotva*) is the cow (*go*)"—
is directed against those who maintain that [entities] are real things (*vastuvādins*).
These words, such as the genitive and others, are logical insofar as they are intended— that is, desired— to be employed in certain cases even when there is no difference in the entity,
because of their necessary connection with the entity.
Because it is dependent upon the actual object,
like smoke and so forth; for smoke, being tied to fire, is capable of making fire known, but cannot, by contrast, be employed to make water known.
In that case, if words were tied to real entities, this objection would apply: "If there is no exclusion (*vyatireka*), how can there be the genitive case and so forth?
To show that this very [objection] does not exist, he says: "But when," and so on.

Whatever speech, in whatever manner and by whatever means, is employed by speakers as a signifier— whether for the purpose of establishing difference or non-difference— being independent of external objects,
that speech is a signifier according to its respective application.
He explains this with the words "For not," and so forth:

when there is a distinction of entities (*vastubheda*)—that is, a difference [between things]—the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhīvibhakti*) occurs; and when there is plurality, the plural suffixes such as *jas* and others occur. This established rule (*vyavasthāna*) of grammatical operations (*vaiyākaraṇānām*) does not function by itself, independent of the intention of a person, but merely through the presence of the entities themselves.
That is to say, it functions solely by the power of convention;
this very point he expresses with the words "But those [cognitions], therein," and so forth.

However, those such as the grammarians, considering that the sixth case-ending and the plural number are employed according to convention to express distinction (*vyatireka*) and plurality (*bāhulya*) respectively, derive from them— namely, from the sixth case-ending and so forth— the corresponding cognition; thus, for others as well, there arises the cognition of distinction and the like.
This is because such linguistic usage is observed;
however, there is no restriction regarding the use of the genitive and other cases based on the actual force of the entities themselves, even when there is an abundance of distinctions—
and the same applies elsewhere as well.

Even though there is no difference between the property (*dharma*) and the property-possessor (*dharmin*), and since the entity is a single unity, how is it that [grammatical forms] such as the genitive case and the plural number are employed by speakers in respect to properties like "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*)? It is because they rely upon a distinction between property and property-possessor characterized by the exclusion or non-exclusion of other differences; and because they rely upon a plurality indicated by different exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) among properties such as "being produced. Thus, these forms become causes for cognition exactly as is appropriate, according to their respective order.

In this regard, since it is established that words are bound solely by intention (*icchāmātra*), and because they function according to human will, proceeding under the influence of that will, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear from words— which do not reveal the actual object. Therefore, for those whose conceptualization arises according to habituation— that is, according to the habituation to a particular convention— the awakening of conceptualization, the arising of conceptual thought, occurs through its causes.
The meaning is: [it refers to] the causes of the conceptual construction (vikalpa) in the mental continuum of the listener that corresponds to the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*).

Such is the case for these words regarding the objects to be expressed; this reflection on their application—such as the use of the genitive case and so forth by the Naiyāyikas and others—is "by virtue of that," meaning by virtue of the word, that there is a determination of the real entity (*vastu*).
The assertion that a distinct entity exists—
on the grounds that the genitive case is used in "the cowness of a cow," and therefore the universal must be distinct—
is merely a display of stupidity and a demonstration of ignorance regarding the established rules for word-meanings.
"Thus," and so forth, says the opponent:

"The conventions established in this manner regarding properties (*dharma*), substrata (*dharmin*), and so on— meaning that the terms 'property' and 'substratum' are established by either excluding or not excluding other distinctions—
and by the word 'and so on,' terms such as 'substance-ness,' 'earthen-ness,' and the like, which are expressed in the plural, are established through the distinction of exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*)."

Furthermore, it is not the case that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) arises simply because of a real distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), nor that the plural number is used because the properties such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) are distinct in an ultimate sense; for how could there be such a response as "it is so," and so forth?
Likewise, because conventional usage would be impossible;
that is, if there were a real distinction between the property and the substratum which are the objects of conventional usage,
and if there were an ultimate difference between properties themselves, then conventional usage regarding universals and so forth would be untenable.
He explains this very introductory statement with the words "na hi" and so forth.

Since there is no other possible mode for a real entity (*vastu*), one must admit that between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), which are the objects of conventional usage, there must be either mutual identity (*tattva*) or difference (*anyatva*). These two alternatives—namely, "in case of difference" and "in case of identity"—are presented for the purpose of exposing faults in both positions. Otherwise, if the opponent had already adopted the position of difference based on the distinction of separate entities (*vyatireka-vastu-bheda*), the presentation of the position of identity would not be appropriate to the context.

Regarding the phrase "connected with that": if it is accepted that words function according to reality, then the relationship between the universal and its possessor, or among words themselves, is rendered possible;
we shall explain this very point later.

"Established by the nature of things" (*vastukṛta*) means that because things possess both unity and plurality, there is a distinction in the application of words, such as the difference in the application of singular and plural numbers. For instance, the word *dārāḥ* ("wife") is accepted as being eternally plural and masculine; when this word *dārāḥ* refers to a single woman, it is because a distinction [of number] is established therein.
Since the term "Ṣaṇṇagarī" denotes many cities with a single word, establishing them as non-different, what external basis could there be for this? None at all.

This is because, in cases such as "a row of palaces," the establishment of both difference and non-difference depends on the nature of the word itself, indicated by the use of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*).

If it is argued that "the nature of space is spaceness" (*khasya svabhāvaḥ khatvam*), what is the basis for the genitive case of separation (*vyatireka-ṣaṣṭhī*) in the phrase "the nature of space"? Furthermore, if it is said that the word *khatvam* is a derivative formation (*taddhita-vṛtti*) from the sentence "the nature of space," then what is expressed by the term *tattvam*? This is not so; for the abstract suffix (*bhāva-pratyaya*) does not occur in the sense of "nature" (*svabhāva*), but rather in the sense of "being" (*bhāva*).

Furthermore, there is no purpose served by demonstrating the formation of a secondary derivative (taddhita-vṛtti), since the distinction [between the two] is already shown by either one alone. Regarding this, some explain that both [the derivative and the sentence] were stated for the sake of demonstrating their pervasion, on the grounds that all linguistic usage is encompassed by both the derivative and the sentence.
Others, however, explain it otherwise.
He explains with the words "yadā... [and so forth] the following: if [the term] "the nature of space" (*khasya svabhāva*) expresses a distinction, what is its basis?
Likewise, if the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) in the expression "spaciousness" (*khatvam*) denotes a distinction, what is its basis?
When— at which time—
others read the word *yat* [as the cause], meaning "from which" (*yasmāt*),
by that very [cause] such plural forms as *dārāḥ* and so forth come to be.
The point is that because there is oneness, only the singular number would follow.
Even for a single woman or for grains of sand (*sikatā*), there are many powers (*śakti*); therefore, the difference in powers is the cause of the plural number.
Thus, "everywhere"—that is, even in cases where the singular is intended, such as *vṛkṣaḥ* ("tree") and so forth.

Since there is no object that possesses a single power and everything possesses multiple powers, if this were the case, the effort to establish the rule "the singular number is used for a single thing" would be futile.

If it is argued that even though there is a difference in capacities (*śakti*), because there is no difference in the entity (*vastu*) and no difference in the substratum of the capacity, the singular number is used— as in "tree" or "cloth"— in cases where the referent is otherwise a single entity;
Here too, in the case of "wife" (*dāra*) and so forth, the singular number is used because there is no difference in the entity—namely, that it refers to a single woman.
Since this is so, the differentiation in the application of words does not depend on the incapacity of the entity itself;

therefore, this rule for the application of words, being established without a basis in reality and without reliance on external entities, demonstrates the independence of human will in the employment of language.
Regarding Pāṇini 1.4.22:

if it is argued that there exists a single collective entity (*samāhāra*) consisting of six cities, whether of the nature of an action or of a quality, and therefore the singular number should be used, [the author] says:

For cities themselves are not anything [substantial], since a substance that is a part of a city is not admitted; how then could there be a collection (*samāhāra*) of those cities, whether consisting of action or quality, on account of which it might be stated thus? Since action and quality are dependent upon a substance, he asks: "What, then, is the substance? and replies with the words beginning "palace" (*prāsāda*).

Since it is not admitted that a city is a substance produced by the collection of heterogeneous elements such as palaces and so forth, how could the collection of those— namely, the collection of palaces and the like— be a substance called a city? For, to the extent that a city is accepted, it is held to be the collection of palaces, archways, persons, and so on.
Because all those things, such as palaces and the like, are not in conjunction,
it is maintained that substances initiate other substances only when they are accompanied by conjunction;
there is no conjunction among separate entities such as a palace, a person, or a wall.
By means of which there would be a substance called a "city" produced by palaces and so forth.
It might be thought:

although there is no conjunction of the palaces and so forth in their entirety, nevertheless, for those palaces, persons, and so forth that do possess mutual conjunction, the city will indeed exist as consisting of that conjunction. Even so—[these notes belong to the base text, which was not keyboarded]—it is designated [as such].
<note n="160-2">It is impaired.</note> <note n="160-3">In what manner.</note> <note n="160-4">Like a general resemblance.</note>
It is *pa-la*.
The substantiality of the city is unestablished because conjunction belongs to the category of qualities; therefore,
he says "not conjunction," and so forth.

The city is not of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because heterogeneous substances such as wood and bricks do not originate a new composite substance (*kāryadravya*); thus, even a palace is not substantial in nature, but is held to be of the nature of conjunction. Furthermore, since conjunction is a quality (*guṇa*) and qualities are themselves devoid of further qualities, how could there be a conjunction belonging to the palace, by virtue of which the city could consist of that conjunction?

He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "of the palace" (prāsādasya) and so forth; and because it is not conjoined with another [entity] by way of a different object, there is no conjunction [that constitutes] a city.

By the word "ca" (and), that which was just mentioned— that there is no conjunction because palaces and so forth are separate and not in contact— is conjoined [with the previous point] such that "the city is not a conjunction.
Thus, by the absence of conjunction in both ways for palaces and so forth, the nature of the city as a conjunction is refuted.
If it is argued that the city will consist of the same number as that of the palaces and so forth, he says:
"Precisely for that reason, there is an absence of number.
Because the palace consists of conjunctions, for that very reason there is an absence of number in the palace, since qualities (guṇas) are themselves devoid of qualities.
For number also has the nature of a quality;
that [number] and conjunction constitute "that-conjunction," meaning a conjunction whose essence is the palace.

If it is argued that "city" is that existence (*sattā*) which is qualified by its conjunction with men, [we ask]: since this *sattā* is unitary and eternal, and thus devoid of any internal distinctions, how can there be a qualifier? For palaces, men, and so forth do not qualify *sattā*.
Because no excellence can be added to it, existence is without qualification;
the intention is that if "city-ness" were inherent in that [existence], then city-ness would have to apply everywhere.
"And because existence (sattā) is one":
this means that among substances, qualities, and actions, there is only one all-pervading existence,
even when there is a plurality of cities— meaning, even when there is a plurality of collections of palaces and so forth which serve as the basis for the arrangement of those cities.

Otherwise, if the city were essentially nothing but existence (*sattā*), how could there be a plurality of cities? [The opponent suggests: "If it is argued that the 'city' is the mutual concomitance between the two—the palace, the person, and so forth—and existence itself—then, this being the case, the cognition of a 'city' would not occur everywhere."

The opponent considers that because palaces and the like are absent everywhere [in a single location] and because there is a plurality of palaces and so forth, the use of the plural number is established; to this,
he states the following reply:
Regarding the passage beginning with "anupakārya" (that which cannot be assisted) and so forth:
what kind of assistance can there be between existence (*sattā*) and a palace (*prāsāda*), which stand in a relationship of neither being assisted nor assisting?

For the meaning of "cooperation" (*sahakāra*) is twofold: characterized by the production of a distinct moment (*viśiṣṭakṣaṇa*) within a continuum (*santāna*) through the conferring of mutual excellence (*atiśaya*).

The performance of a single effect by those things that have arisen as capable due to their own prior causes—these notes belong to the base text, which was not keyboarded:

Without obstruction (*abandhya*).

To those who are neither the object of benefit nor the benefactor.
Regarding the [proposition] "of the benefactor and the non-beneficiary":
first, it cannot be the former definition, because existence (*sattā*) is incapable of having any excellence added to it;

nor can it be the second, because just as existence alone is incapable of producing the cognition of a city, so too would it be [incapable] even when accompanied by palaces and the like; or else, if it were capable, it would produce [that cognition] even when alone.
And if a city were the mutual conjunction of its two parts,
then even a single city would consist of multiple entities, because it consists of palaces and other such structures; for there is a multiplicity of men, connections, and existences.
The word "city" (*nagara*) would be in the singular number; by the term "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), a conjunction consisting of palaces is expressed.

Thus, for those things that are "in such a state"—that is, for the existences of the conjunctions of persons joined together with one another—there is a certain object, namely, the cognition "this is a city."
If it is argued that when a word is to be produced,
there exists a single, undivided power,
and that this undivided power is the cause for the singular number;
What is the reason? Because power is not distinct from the essential nature of the thing.
Since [the capacity] is not distinct from the entities such as the person (*puruṣa*) which possess a real form, it would likewise be manifold; how then could there be a singular number based upon it?

Alternatively, if one were to admit that the capacity is distinct from the essential nature of the entity, then for that capacity—which is not assisted by the person, the conjunction, or existence—there could be no dependence upon the person and the other factors.
And thus, the sense is that there would be no relationship such as "the power of the person" (*puruṣa*) and so forth.

Now, if it is maintained that even for a power that is distinct [from the person], a benefit (*upakāra*) produced by the person and so forth is required in order to establish its dependence upon the person and so forth, then,
when such a benefit to the power produced by the person and so forth is being postulated—
If there is a power by which persons and the like first assist that primary power,
then for that power which assists the primary power, there would be an infinite regress if it were distinct from the [original] power; or, if it were not distinct,
then even if the first power is intended to be designated by the singular number, the consequence of non-distinction would apply to the power as well.

And since there would be no distinction [between the universal and its instances], there would be multiplicity just as in the case of a real entity; thus, the contingency of using the plural number for many things remains exactly as it was. This argument is trivial.

Furthermore, if one postulates a "power" (śakti), the genitive case in the expression "the nature of space" (*khasya svabhāvaḥ*) could not exist, as it relies upon a distinction [between the possessor and the possessed].
Moreover, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is also referred to by the word "genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhī*) figuratively, because it is the cause of the genitive case.

Therefore, this is another point: the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) based on a distinction (*vyatireka*), as in the term *khatvam* (the state of being space), would not be possible. For, according to the etymological derivation "the nature of space (*kha*) is *khatvam*," the production of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) implies a basis in distinction, as per Pāṇini 1.4.21.
Alternatively, the connection and the division of the text should be made according to what is appropriate.

"A skull" (*khaṭvā*)—these [notes] rely on the distinction (*vyatireka*). [These notes belong to the base text, which was not keyboarded:

Third Fascicle.

= The Third Daily Lesson (*tṛtīyam āhnikam*)

Without realization (*avijñāna*).

That very corpse (*sa eva mṛtaśarīraḥ*).
The ellipsis to be supplied is that "the formation of a *taddhita* derivative would not occur.
[In the expression] "the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of space (*khasya*)," the genitive case would not be possible;
for there is no intrinsic nature or entity other than the referent denoted by the word "space" (*kha*).

If it is argued that there exists a universal called "earth-ness" (*khatva*) which serves as the basis for either the ablative case in the sense of separation (*vyatireka-ṣaṣṭhī*) or for a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*),
[the author] replies with the words "Not there," and so forth.
