Because space is of a single nature, there is no generality of "spaciousness" (khatvasāmānya) in it;
even though existence (sattva) and substantiality (dravyatva) exist in space, nevertheless, they are not the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of space.

Nor can "existence" (*sattva*) or "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) be the basis for the abstract suffix in the expression "the nature of space" (*khatva*), because these two are common to jars and other things; furthermore,
they are not the causes of the word or the cognition [of space].
The cause is held to be the cognition whose nature consists in being the basis for a corresponding designation, nor are qualities such as omnipresence (vibhutva) [the cause];
by the word "etc. (ādi), oneness, priority, and so forth are included.

Thus it is said: "the nature of space. Since a quality such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*), which is a distinct entity from substance, cannot logically constitute its nature, it cannot logically constitute the nature of space;
for it is not tenable that one distinct entity should be the nature of another distinct entity.
If all-pervasiveness and the other qualities have space as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),

then, since those qualities such as all-pervasiveness would have space as their intrinsic nature, it follows that they must be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). For instance, whatever constitutes their quality-nature (*guṇasvabhāva*) would result in space alone being produced, and since no other nature exists, they would be without intrinsic nature.
The point is that if those [qualities] lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), then space would have no distinct intrinsic nature of its own.
If it is argued that even properties such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*) must have an intrinsic nature that is a different entity [from space], he says:
"Of that too," and so forth.
The analysis of the compound *tasya* [as] *vibhutvādeḥ svabhāvaḥ asya* is "that which has pervasiveness and so forth as its intrinsic nature.

Regarding the [objection of] over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): that other entity (*arthāntara*) which is intended to be the intrinsic nature of pervasiveness and so forth must itself also have another entity as its intrinsic nature;
otherwise, because it would not be distinct from pervasiveness, it would likewise lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), just like that [pervasiveness].

Thus, because there is no finality in searching for successive intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), and because even a single established intrinsic nature is non-existent, the first nature—that of space—is not apprehended; therefore, the intended meaning is that this very [non-apprehension] constitutes the absence of difference (*vyatirekābhāva*).
In this way, the group of the six categories (*padārtha*)—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—is [refuted].
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), terms such as *prāsādamālā* ("row of palaces") and others are to be included (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.4.6).
[Objection: How can there be a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when there is no distinction (*vyatireka*)?
For among those six categories, a universal (*sāmānya*) as denoted by the word "group" is not possible,
because universals are admitted only in the case of substances, qualities, and actions.
Likewise, neither number nor conjunction is possible [in this case], because since those two belong to the category of qualities (*guṇa*), they exist only in a substance (*dravya*).
To the question "How so? and so forth, the opponent replies:

"If one does not admit that 'now' has a nature distinct from the object itself, then since it is certain that the referent denoted by the word *sva* and the referent denoted by the word *bhāva* do not exist [as separate entities], how can there be a designation as a distinction, namely 'the nature' (*svabhāva*)?"
The meaning is that, since there is no basis for differentiation in the mere word "space," it would be more logical to refer to it as non-differentiated;
he refutes this with the words "of space," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of *kha*": it refers to the object denoted by the word *kha*, namely another object such as earth (*pṛthivī*) and so forth. That which is its common form—excluding other unmentioned particulars through non-consideration—is the basis for the application of the word *kha*. This is a form not shared with other substances; thus, in this inquiry, [it is] that which is not conjoined with other objects...
...it is said "the intrinsic nature of space" or "spaciousness" in such a way that it may be understood: "this is the intrinsic nature of space, and not of anything else."
By this rejection of other distinctions, since a single excluded form is not being denoted, something else indeed has been stated as the cause for the expression of exclusion;
by that, designations such as "the non-existence of a jar" are established.
Others, however, say:

When the word *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) is used to designate the intrinsic nature of space (*kha*), it designates it merely by the exclusion of other intrinsic natures, but not by the non-exclusion of another [specific] intrinsic nature.
The word *kha*, however, designates that very same [nature] without excluding other forms.

Therefore, due to this slight distinction characterized by the exclusion and non-exclusion of other intrinsic natures, it is designated as distinct, such that "this is the intrinsic nature of space" or "the state of being space (*khatva*). This, however, is not very consistent, because there is no cognition of the exclusion of any other distinct difference.

The opponent says, "By stating that the form which is the basis for the application of the word 'self' (*sva*) is spoken of as such without reflecting on its nature as being common to other objects, you have effectively stated that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself is the denotable object.
To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) replies: "But not all [objects], etc., nor [is it] not [the case], etc."

The connection is as follows: that very form which is excluded from everything and consists of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not what is presented by words in a cognition arising from words.
Why? Because of that specific characteristic, just as in the case of sensory cognition.

If it is argued that since there is an appearance in verbal cognition, it would follow that [the object] is either beyond the senses or, conversely, that it is perceptible; what then is accomplished by the word? To this, he says:
"Only," and so forth.

"This one" refers to the speaker, who— deceived by the determination of identity between the perceived object and the conceptual construction, and with the intention "I shall cause [the listener] to understand such a unique object"— by means of the word acting as an instrument, deposits into the conceptual construction of the listener that form which is superimposed as being external to its reflection.

He asks: Is it the case that even for the teacher Diṅnāga, this [consciousness] was intended as being unassociated with that [object], having its own nature [as such], and not grasping the form of the object? To this he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "yadāha" and so forth:

when a word such as "heaven" (*svarga*), whose referent is unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*), is uttered, there arises for the listener merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of an object; this conceptual construction has the nature of an external object as its determined content, but it does not grasp the actual external form itself.
By this, [Dharmakīrti] demonstrates that even this Master [Dignāga] intended the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) to be the meaning of a word.

It is not the case that when a conceptual reflection is produced by a word in the listener, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is respectively understood or communicated by the speaker and the listener;
for if the particular characteristic were communicated by a word, then even upon hearing words such as "heaven" (*svarga*), [the particular characteristic would be perceived].
Just as for those who have experienced it—
like those who directly perceive heaven and so forth— there would be no difference in appearance;
even for the listener, there would be a comprehension of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the form of heaven and so forth.

And since the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not apprehended through a word, this listener—though not actually apprehending it from the word—is nonetheless satisfied, thinking, "I have apprehended the particular characteristic itself," because he determines that reflection of conceptual construction to be the very nature of the entity, that is, the undifferentiated nature of the thing, and thus determines it to be the particular characteristic.
Why?
Precisely because it is of such a nature.

Even though the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not directly apprehended, the comprehension of the word-meaning occurs precisely because it has the nature of a determined (*adhyavasita*) specific characteristic;

and since the word-meaning is cognized through the determination of the specific characteristic, it is said in this way that "the word expresses its own form," according to the statement: "The unique form, which is the basis for the application of its own word, is expressed by not referring to a form common to other objects."
Furthermore, it is not because consciousness arises as a mere manifestation of its own intrinsic nature;
therefore, this remains established: that the meaning of a word is prescriptive (vidhi) because its object is unreal, and thus it differs from the position of others.
As for the question "How so? and so forth, the opponent [objects].
The analysis of the compound is: "those things whose form is exclusively excluded [from others].

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) states that because there is no connection between those entities and anything else—namely, a universal (sāmānya) distinct from the entities themselves—it has been explained [that universals do not exist].
To the question "In what manner is it said [they are excluded]?", he says:
it is the non-association (*asaṃsarga*) of things that are unmixed and mutually distinct with a single thing of a different class;
for example, the non-association of individual cows with the single nature of a non-cow—it is this very non-association [that constitutes exclusion].
The commonality (*sāmānya*) of the various individual cows—which are excluded from that non-cow nature distinct from them—is "cowness" (*gotva*).
In this same way, other universals (*sāmānya*) are also to be understood.
This is what is meant: [the universal is the commonality of individuals excluded from what is other than themselves].

The term *samānām* is a genitive used in the sense of the agent; thus, the meaning is that "the state of being common (*sāmānyam*)" refers to entities that, though excluded from those of a different class, arise with a common form—this is the definition of a universal (*sāmānya*).

Furthermore, it is precisely this universal that possesses the nature of a logical mark (*liṅga*), the nature of that which is marked (*liṅgin*), and their relationship, because it is a real entity (*vastu*) and because it performs a causal function (*arthakriyā*).

Consequently, it is the object of purposeful activity and the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), according to how it is determined (*adhyavasāya*), but not the form of the cognition itself.

Because it is the opposite of that, having thus refuted the indirect criticism regarding the position of superimposition (*samāropa*), [the author] sets aside the indirect criticism regarding the position of exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) precisely by not accepting such an exclusion. Having established that entities which are themselves excluded from others, when determined as a unity, constitute the universal (*sāmānya*), he says "Moreover... and so forth, in order to remove the criticism stated by others even with respect to the universal that is the form of cognition (*buddhyākāra*).
Depending on entities that are distinct, or depending on the particular (svalakṣaṇa) which is excluded [from others], a cognition arises that manifests as a single object;
by means of its own nature, its own form, as a single form, it [conceives] the form of another.
It is called *saṃvṛti* because it conceals— that is, it covers over— the characteristic that is mutually excluded [from others].
By what kind of convention?
It is that by which the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is concealed, so it is called "convention" (*saṃvṛti*).

Having their various meanings concealed and their various meanings veiled, even though they are self-differentiated, they appear as if non-differentiated by some form— such as the form of "cowness" (gotva)— which is imagined through the exclusion of heterogeneous things; and thus, like that [form],
the mental image residing in the cognition appears as if mixed with it, yet it does not follow after other objects or cognitions.
"And that [cognition] which does not produce the intended object is also not to be called [a cognition of that object] in reality," and so forth; this is refuted [by the following]:

"The form of the cognition residing in the intellect does not follow after another object or another cognition, and since it does not produce the intended object, it too is not to be called [a cognition of that object] in reality."
Therefore, by the power of the intention of the intellect and by the power of superimposing a single form, the universal is proclaimed as being common;
that is to say, it is the form superimposed by the intellect alone that is called the universal.
Just as it was conceptualized and superimposed by her, so too that universal is non-existent from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Now, if it is admitted that the appearance is non-different [from the particular], how can it be said that the universal is non-existent?
It is not [the case that it cannot be so said].
Because that which is intended to be distinct from individuals appears as non-distinct,

and because if it were identical in its entirety, it would— like the individuals themselves— not possess a commonality (anvaya), the cognition of a recurring [universal] would be nothing but an error;
furthermore, if there were both difference and non-difference, it would appear in both forms simultaneously.
Furthermore, it is not the case that at the very same moment there is the appearance of "cow" in a particular cognition, there is simultaneously the appearance of "cowness belongs to this" therein.
Now, it might be argued:
whatever is present where another is absent must be distinct from it, just as the non-blue is distinct from the blue.

And since the universal *gotva* (cowness) does not follow after the brindled cow (*śāvaleyānuvṛtti*), it must therefore be distinct from it in other individuals. Consequently, the perception that grasps the *gotva* as non-different from the brindled cow would have to be erroneous, because it grasps as non-different that which is actually distinct and has been apprehended by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, for a single entity, there cannot be difference in one form and non-difference in that very same form, due to contradiction.
Nor is there a distinction among things by way of their specific forms and non-distinction by way of their general form;
for if this were so, the specific forms would possess a single location and so forth, which they do not.
Furthermore, there would be no distinction in appearance between the universal and the particular, because they would be non-different in every respect;

or, if there were a difference, since their forms would be respectively inclusive and exclusive, they could not be conjoined with one another, leading to the consequence that they are absolutely distinct.
And if that [universal] were non-different from each individual instance, how could there be a single universal?

Nor is it logical to claim that there exists a single universal because of the recognition "this is that very same one" upon seeing a second or subsequent individual—even though [the universal] was not grasped at the time of seeing the first individual—since the component of memory, "that," cannot arise in the absence of a previously experienced object, namely a universal.

Consequently, just as it was not grasped in the first individual, so too it would not be grasped in each instance of the second and subsequent individuals; how then could the cognition "this is that very same one" arise?

Nor is it reasonable to postulate the apprehension of a universal in the first individual on the grounds that memory would otherwise be inexplicable, because there is no appearance of a recurring form through either indeterminate or any other type of cognition;
nor is its apprehension there as a property (dharma) reasonable, because a universal possesses a single recurring nature;
nor can it be said that it is apprehended by the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) as being related to preceding and succeeding individuals.

Because it would follow that perception arises in the form "this is precisely that," and because the previous manifestation is no longer present—given that perception is held to be characterized by the ascertainment of a presently present object—it is therefore logical to postulate that very [exclusion] as its cause, and nothing else. This is because when one particular instance excluded from non-cows is experienced, and another instance excluded from non-cows is being experienced, there arises through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) a mistaken cognition of a single form, "this is that very same thing. Thus, that [exclusion] alone is rightly conceived as its cause.
And because cognition is erroneous, this universal form is established [as belonging] to cognition and not to the external;
however, according to how it appears, it is the universality of external objects themselves that is called "cognition," and so forth— thus he explains the meaning of the verse.
This is connected with the phrase "cognition is conceptual.
"Different from those" means distinct from them; those things which possess this distinction from what is other than them are "those excluded from others" (*tad-anyavyatirekiṇaḥ*).
The meaning of "exclusion of the dissimilar" (vijātīyavyāvṛtti) is as follows: [the conceptual cognition],

conforming to— that is, imitating— the nature of its own latent predispositions, which is the essence of the predispositions for conceptualization, possesses the capacity to produce a non-differentiated cognition with respect to things that are actually different.
For in this way, its own cause is imitated by it,
if a single form arises even among these distinct entities.
This refers to the objects (padārtha).

Having superimposed [this] upon the objects of experience— that is, having projected it— she displays those very entities as if they were non-different, creating them by making them appear to have a single form.
"It shows [things] as if they were of a single form"—this is what is meant.

Now, if it is maintained that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises through the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of an object, how can a conceptual construction with a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*) arise, given that the universal has not been experienced?
To this, he says: "And that," and so forth.
Those entities for which there is one common goal and one common means—
for example, for things such as jars, the goal is the single act of holding water and so forth,
and the means is the single lump of clay and so forth.

Those entities which have a single object to be accomplished and a single means of accomplishment— because they possess that state by means of that [means] acting as an instrument— they are distinguished from other entities that have different objects and means to be accomplished; for those who discern this, that is their *prakṛti*, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), characterized by the production of a conceptualization of a single form despite being distinct by nature.
The cause of such conceptual construction is its latent impression (*vāsanā*),
and it is the very nature of that impression that this cognition appears in such a way, superimposing its own form onto another object.
That is to say, it appears as apprehending a universal that is non-different from the individual;
therefore, as for what is said by one who would claim, "This cognition [of identity] is merely mnemonic (smārta) because of its non-difference [from memory]."
"Surely, even in the case of the son of a barren woman, there exists the possibility of being remembered"—
this [objection] from the *Ślokavārttika*, *Anumānapariccheda* 160,
is thus refuted.

Because distinct experienced [moments] possess the capacity to produce a cognition of a non-different form regarding their own objects by acting as a single causal agent, they are like an experienced object with a clear form possessing the capacity to produce a memory of its own object that is not clear.

That which arises from the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the conceptualization of phonemes—arising, respectively, directly and indirectly from the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of those [distinct moments] for the sake of those who discern—is such [an arising];
and this very cognition [of identity], namely "this is that," is called a conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).

By means of this cognition— through its own form appearing as the form of another object— the term *saṃvṛti* is formed using the suffix *ktin* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*). Thus, those entities have their distinctions concealed— that is, their multiplicity is hidden— by that cognition which conceals them.
"In some form" means they appear in the conceptual cognition as superimposed by conceptual thought;
"of these," and so forth.

The connection is as follows: by those persons who conform to the appearance in cognition—that is, the form of a conceptualizing cognition—a single form presented by that cognition is called a "universal" (sāmānya).
Of what things is this universal said to be?

The grammatical connection is "of these very things revolving in the intellect, [there is] this [universal] belonging to those things revolving in the intellect. Having experienced the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), these forms of jars—which are indistinct within conceptual cognitions such as "this jar is white" or "another is black"—are the entities revolving in the intellect; it is of these alone that the universal is the correlate.

It is not the case that particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are qualifiers, because they do not appear in a general cognition and because they lack a connection [to it]. Rather, it is only those things existing within the cognition—which appear as if external—that serve as qualifiers. This means that they appear as if external. He states the reason for this appearance of externality:

Some say that because of the grasping of a specific form, there is a determination of an external object due to the imitation of a clear configuration belonging to the conceptualization of an external object;
however, this is incorrect.
For it has already been explained that the superimposition of externality is not caused by similarity;
therefore, the specific form is the form of the jar and so forth, and its "grasping" is the experience [of it]. From that [experience], there is a manifestation as if external.
This is what is meant.

A conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), arising through the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of a jar or other objects, determines its own form as non-different from the external jar and so forth; it does not, however, grasp [the object].
Therefore, regarding an object designated by a word, doubt sometimes arises because of this non-grasping.
In that case, the conceptual construction, by virtue of its own causes alone, determines its own form as non-different from the external object.
But it is not due to similarity, because a similar object does not exist and is not perceived.
Now, even among those forms existing within the intellect, what other form indeed appears as distinct from their own nature that could be a universal?
This is true.
Regarding this, some say that because they are not distinct from a single cognition, they possess oneness;
others, however, say that each of them has the nature of a universal in relation to its own individual manifestation.
Both of these views are incorrect, because there is no appearance of a single [universal].

Because others accept a universal (*sāmānya*) on the grounds that those [cognitions] are determined as having a single form, it is stated thus according to their intention; however, for the Master, what is intended is the appearance as "similar" and not as one. And so he will say:
"Alternatively..."
Let it be that the appearances within cognitions are distinct, yet they are apprehended as "the same" because of the grasping of that [commonality].

If it is argued that the universal (*sāmānya*) is merely the form displayed by conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) residing within the intellect, and since that [form] is positive in nature (*vidhirūpatvāt*), how can it now be said that the universal is the "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*)?

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) maintains that it is precisely this [object] which, appearing as it is determined by conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), is called "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*),
because it is derived through the perception of an object distinguished from others.
If the universal is the form of conceptual construction, how is there the cognition of external objects as having a common nature?
As it has been said:
"Or rather, these [cognitions] are without an object, existing merely as a result of mental impressions (*vāsanā*)."
To explain how practice and engagement with external objects could otherwise occur,
he says "tameva" and so forth.
When that conceptual cognition grasps what appears as "that"—namely, the manifestation of conceptual thought—it appears as if it were grasping a real entity.
Why? Because of the natural delusion of conceptualizations; by their very nature, due to the delusion of grasping an object as non-different from their own internal forms, they appear thus.
[The author] asks: "How then is it said that [conceptual cognition] has exclusion (*apoha*) as its object? and he replies:

For that conceptual cognition, arising with respect to particular characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) which are distinguished from others by virtue of determinative judgment (adhyavasāya), is understood to have distinction as its object through its effect;
it does not do so by making the nature of distinction itself its object.
But another, not understanding this intention, says:
The phrase beginning with "nanu" means that external [objects] are [derived from] universals (*sāmānya*), while particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are internal;
for in this way, both the external and the internal are included.
It is said: "How does conceptual cognition arise with respect to those individual particulars (svalakṣaṇas), which are distinct from one another and do not exist within them? To this it is replied:
He refutes this with the words "the commentators" and so forth;
for they, in establishing the object exactly as it exists, distinguish it thus:
"the appearance in conceptual cognition is one thing, while the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is another."
Practical agents do not analyze in this way;

rather, those practical agents, believing that what appears in conceptual cognition—which is their own objective support—is itself the external particular (svalakṣaṇa) capable of causal efficiency, [act accordingly].
This very point is clarified as follows:

The object of perception is the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), while the object of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the appearance of a universal (*sāmānyapratibhāsa*). Having unified these two, one proceeds toward an object that performs a causal function by means of a firm conviction (*adhimukti*) that "this very particular is being made an object of conceptual cognition and is being denoted by a word. Because of this intention of the speakers, it is said—by virtue of the speakers' intention alone—that "conceptual cognition arises with respect to distinct entities," since one acts after unifying the perceived and the conceptualized.

By stating this, it is implied that there is no superimposition of the external upon one's own internal form; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of acting toward one's own internal form alone.
Nor is there a superimposition of one's own form upon an external object, as in the case of the superimposition of water upon a mirage;
for if that were so, it would follow that one would act solely out of a desire for the result being superimposed.

If there were no difference between the perceived object (*dṛśya*) and the conceptualized object (*vikalpya*), would it not be like the case of one seeking water who, in the delusion of water, [perceives] the merging of the perceived and the conceptualized? Furthermore,
if there were no distinction between the perceived and the conceptualized, there would be no engagement with external objects.
If the non-difference of the conceptualized from the perceived were the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it would follow that the word-meaning is the specific characteristic;
yet there is no unification of the perceived and the conceptualized, because perception does not have the conceptualized as its object,
nor does conceptualization have the perceived as its object.
And since the object is not perceived in the past and so forth, how can those two be unified?
To this it is replied:

when there is an experience of an object, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises—produced by the awakening of its latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—bearing that object’s form; this conceptualization determines its own form to be non-different from the external object, but it does not actually make them non-different.

Because of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the object of conceptual construction as having the nature of the perceptible, it is said that there is a unification of the perceptible and the conceptualized.

That which is worthy of being seen, or that which can be seen, is called "the perceptible" (*dṛśya*); thus, even the object of conceptual perception is considered perceptible. By this, the perceptibility of even a future object indicated by scripture is established, as is the case with non-existence (*abhāva*).

For this very reason, a cognition of non-existence, though its own form is the nature of non-existence, cognizes by superimposing it upon the absence of a real entity; thus it is said to have non-existence as its object, but it does not actually grasp non-existence.
Because all conceptual constructions (vikalpa) lack an objective referent,

it is stated that conceptual cognition does not arise with respect to the particularities (svalakṣaṇa) and their distinctions merely by virtue of the force of that [object's] intentionality, but rather by virtue of its being produced by that [intentionality].
Likewise, it is said that speakers convey through words objects as distinct from those not performing that function by means of their being so characterized;
yet, if one asks why commentators do not likewise realize the identity between the perceived and the conceptualized, he replies:
"Because of the difference in appearance and so forth. For the appearance of the perceived object is vivid, whereas that of the conceptualized is not.
Because that which is bound up with conceptual construction cannot possess clarity;
because, by the force of the word "etcetera," even when the visible object has ceased, the conceptual construction does not cease;
and because it either performs or does not perform purposeful action.
The "investigators of reality" (*tattvacintakāḥ*) are those who follow logic (*nyāyānusāriṇaḥ*) and are commentators (*vyākhyātāraḥ*).

Regarding the genitive case here as one of residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), the phrase "investigators of reality" means they are investigators *of reality* and not of what is non-reality; for, since there is a requirement merely to exclude other related entities, the specific relationship of action and agent (*kriyākārakabhāva*) is not intended to be expressed.

Alternatively, having formed a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) of the word *cintayati*— which ends in the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134— with the word *tattva*, the suffix *kan* is added as a pleonastic (*svārthika*) affix; therefore, the prohibition of genitive compounds by the rule beginning with "by [words ending in] *tṛc* or *aka*" (Pāṇini 2.2.15) should not be suspected here,
for it does not perceive non-difference.
Regarding the phrase "of the visible and the conceptualization," this refers to Pāṇini 2.2.15 in its current context.
The opponent [the *codaka*] begins with "If," etc., conforming to the intention of the listener: "If the establishment of a universal (*sāmānya*) occurs only with respect to external things,
then let the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) not be a universal either."
What is the reason?
For users of language do not have the understanding that "it is not thus" or that "exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is expressed by the word."
And the Venerable [Dharmakīrti], demonstrating this same equality, said:
"Indeed, it is not merely... and so forth; thus, there is no such apprehension, because [the object] is of the nature of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha).
Even though you maintain that the universal (*sāmānya*) exists through such forms as being distinct from individuals and so forth, there is nevertheless no cognition [of it] in that way.

For those such as the Vaiśeṣikas, it is distinct from its substratum (*āśraya*), whereas for the Sāṃkhyas and others, it is non-distinct; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of [theories such as] its complete presence in each individual is intended.
In that regard, first of all, the difference of the universal does not appear at all.

In this case, since the cognition "this is a universal" does not arise, there would be the manifestation of the individuals alone even though they are non-different [from the universal], and not of the universal; furthermore,
if it were both different and non-different, the defects belonging to both positions would ensue,
nor is it logical for it to be fully present in each individual.
For if it were restricted to a single individual, it would be related to only one thing and not to many;
yet this is not the case for a universal (*sāmānya*), because it is related to many, according to the definition that "the state of being common to many is a universal.

Furthermore, if its relation to many is established because it is recognized (*pratyabhijñāna*) in other individuals, then—even as in the case of the qualities of the elements—it would be a single entity related to many, rather than being fully present in each individual.
Because it is not perceived as having multiple relations within each individual instance;
or, if it were so perceived, there would be an appearance of multiple instances therein.
Furthermore, because it does not appear in the intervals between instances, it is said to be fully present in each individual one.
Therefore, does its connection with many [individuals] become established in a single instance by this much?
Furthermore, it has been stated that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is not tenable in respect to a universal (*sāmānya*).
Consequently, it is established that neither its subsistence in each individual (*pratyeka-parisamāpti*), nor its eternity, unity, and pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*) appear [to consciousness].
If there is an equal absence of apprehension in practical discourse for both a real universal and for exclusion (*apoha*),
then what is the basis for this [latter]? To this, he says "merely," and so forth.

The exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is the state of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) being devoid of what is dissimilar; it is said to be the cause for a cognition that possesses a non-differentiated form.
Why?

Because that *anyāpoha*, characterized by the absence of the dissimilar, exists everywhere even among distinct entities, and because such an *anyāpoha* is not contradictory to being the cause of a universal cognition (*sāmānyabuddhi*).

For instance, just as one perceives a single tree as excluded from non-trees, so too does one perceive another; therefore, a cognition of a single form arises in that regard, and there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka-pramāṇa) here.
He states the third cause:
"And because of the observation of conventional usage," and so forth; that is,
because it is observed to be based on the exclusion of others (anyāpoha).

And this will be demonstrated by the passage beginning with "and this [word] is called 'sound' because it functions by excluding other things," showing how this conceptual cognition appears as having a single form. (Note 172-1: Oneness and Pervasiveness.)
Thus, the meaning of the sentence is that such an external universal does not exist;
therefore, the intention is that a real entity (*vastubhūta*) as a universal cannot be the basis for conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*).
And he states the reason for the non-existence of the universal:
Regarding the phrase "because," and so forth:
individual instances (*vyakti*), which are particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),
do not follow after [one another] nor do they become mixed.
By this, the acceptance of a non-distinct universal is refuted;
then, for the purpose of refuting a distinct [universal], he says:
"that which follows as something else."

If that which is desired as a persisting universal, distinct from its particulars, does not appear in perceptual cognition—surely this same fault of non-continuity and so forth applies equally to the positions of identity and difference regarding the universal even when it appears in conceptual cognition; how, then, can a universal be accepted?
For at least a common form certainly does appear.
As long as it is not understood that [the object] is devoid of both difference and non-difference, so long is it merely an ornament (alaṅkāra), because it is established as being unreal;
for this very reason, it is said to exist according to its appearance,
as they enter into or become mixed with one another.
If there were mutual interpenetration [between particulars], then due to the attainment of a single form, there would be an absence of difference;
for that reason, it would follow that the universal itself does not exist.
Therefore, the universal is the property (*dharma*) which serves as the basis for the cognition of a single form among distinct things that are similar.
The meaning is that [the universal] would exist because there is no difference from those [individuals].
Furthermore, the phrase "other than the individuals" (*anyad vyaktibhyaḥ*) is explained by the word "distinct" (*vyatirikta*);
likewise, it means "in that form" (*tena rūpeṇa*) within the cognition of the universal.

By this, the non-perception of an essential nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) has been stated for the purpose of establishing the conventional designation of the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*) that meets the conditions of perceptibility;
nor should a universal that does not meet the conditions of perceptibility be admitted,
because how could a universal that does not appear manifest itself through its own nature as a universal?
One should cause another— meaning that which possesses a universal—
to be grasped or designated by means of its own form.
The connection with the preceding context is "how else?
It is intended that the occurrence of non-differentiated naming and cognition among individuals is due to the power of the universal;
therefore, the collective meaning is that the universal must indeed be accepted as meeting the conditions for perception.
Thus, first of all, since that which has attained the characteristic of being apprehended is not perceived, a single entity cannot be related to many;
even if it were granted that a single entity could be related to many, its nature as a universal (sāmānya) would still be untenable— this is what he states with the words "na ca" and so forth.

By the phrase "by them," it is meant by those distinct individuals; by the phrase "is said," it is stated that even in the case of conjunctions and produced substances such as duality and so forth, the consequence of having a universal nature would follow, because this undesirable contingency has already been addressed.

Therefore, a universal is not simply something that is one and related to many; rather, a single universal is that which is the cause of a non-differentiated designation and cognition, whereas duality and the like are not all [universals].
If it is argued that this is because the aforementioned verbal cognition lacks a cause,

then how could there be the occurrence of a single-mode cognition— that is, the functioning of a cognition with a uniform form— regarding a difference between individuals elsewhere, when that uniformity has not been brought about by a universal from another [universal]?

"Because of its connection with that," says the opponent. The Teacher [Dignāga] states: "Number is the occurrence of a cognition elsewhere than those individuals, even from a universal other than them, due to its connection with those individuals."

This locative case ending (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of a state (*bhāva-lakṣaṇā*); when number exists and when the composite substance (*avayavin*), which is an effect, exists—and by the word "etc. (*ādi-śabda*), when conjunction and so forth exist—the suffix *sat* applies to them as well, and thus they too attain the status of a universal (*sāmānya*). This is the collective meaning.

If it is argued that because number and the other categories are non-common in nature (*asāmānyātmaka*), the occurrence of a single uniform cognition with respect to a substance cannot be due to their power, [we reply]:
But is not that very self-nature of the universal (*sāmānyātman*) under investigation?
What, then, is this "self-nature of the universal"?
Since the universal characteristic itself is not perceived apart from [particulars] such as number,
this is not manifest; that is precisely what he says.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In that case," etc.:

when it was asked, "What is this nature of the universal (*sāmānyātman*)?", you stated that it is the occurrence of a non-different cognition among individuals when there is a relation between one [entity] and many; and from that—that is, from the cause of the occurrence of the cognition—the definition of a universal is: a single entity related to many.
In this regard, we state the general definition:
there exist multiple relata belonging to those things such as effect-substances (kāryadravya) and so forth— the word "and so forth" (ādi) including duality and the rest.
From those [atoms] as well, there would arise a cognition of a single form regarding the substances that serve as their substrata; for what reason? Because the causal conditions are present.
For it is accepted that the production of a single cognition regarding universals (*sāmānya*) arises precisely from the cause of multiple relations;

and since the state of being related to many [individuals] exists even in the case of substances (*dravya*) and so forth— which serve as the cause for a single cognition— therefore, because the single cognition occurs [in both cases], number and the other categories possess the nature of a universal.

"Otherwise" means that even if they possess the aforementioned general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), if the nature of being a universal (*sāmānyātmatā*) is not admitted in the case of number and so forth,
then let it not be admitted in other cases either that are considered to be universals.
What is the reason?
Because there is no distinction;
and thus, when even substances and so forth attain the nature of universals, there would be a confusion of the forms of substances, qualities, and so on.

The connection is as follows: "the appearance of a single form to the conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) is the universal (*sāmānya*)," and that [universal] is of the nature of cognition (*jñāna*). These notes belong to the base text, which was not keyboarded.

Investigation (*dbyod-pa*).

It is the appearance of a single aspect to the conceptualizing cognition;
the connection is that it is the universal, and because it is of the nature of knowledge.
Just as in the case of cognition, that which is said to be a real universal will indeed be a real entity, for it will be the form of the intellect.
And since that cognition arises with respect to the objects of words as having the form of a real entity (*vastu*),

therefore the denotable object should be conceived as being the real entity itself, not a non-exclusion (*anapoha*) by the cognition; this [view] he refutes with the words "that is not," and so forth.

That universal which is asserted to be of the nature of cognition is not distinct from that cognition, just like the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of cognition itself; how then could it become a different external object?
The meaning is that it cannot be a universal for those [external objects].
He explains that with the words "of cognition," etc.;
because that which has the nature of cognition does not exist in those objects.
It is true that there is no inherence of that which has the nature of cognition within individual objects; rather, it is because of the determination of its existence within that mental reflection,
and because of the determination of it as an external entity.
If it is argued that there is thus a uniform linguistic usage due to error, this is precisely what the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) accepts;
for individual instances (vyakti), though having a single effect by their very nature, are excluded from those things that do not have that effect.

The author of the treatise intends that the cause (*nimitta*) for such a conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), and thus that cognition has its basis in the exclusion of others; however,
the opponent does not accept such a cause,
and for this very reason, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) interrogates him regarding the cause itself.
Regarding the passage beginning with "there," etc.:

since those individual instances (*vyakti*) are non-entities, and since you do not accept that these instances—which by their very nature are excluded from what is heterogeneous—possess a single causal function, what could be the basis for the arising of cognition?
There is none at all.
For indeed, the opponent does not accept that distinct entities excluded from heterogeneous things are the cause of a single cognition;
nor is there a real, ontological universal (*sāmānya*).

Consequently, if a cognition of a universal were to arise without a basis—that is, without a cause—it would occur everywhere. Thus, the single-form cognition "cow" would also occur with respect to trees.
He states another meaning of the passage beginning with "not distinct from knowledge" with the words "Alternatively," and so forth.

Previously, the term "another meaning" (*arthāntara*) was used; [the following] notes belong to the base text, which was not keyboarded:

Because it is logical.
[Note 175-2]: Of the knower. Now, after the external [object] has been explained, another cognition is being described;
for this very reason, he says:
But how [is it] for another cognition?
For what kind of cognition?
For one that occurs at a different time.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*) that arises from one individual cow, and [the conceptual cognition] that subsequently arises from another individual cow;
for a universal (*sāmānya*) would have to exist either by pervading multiple cognitions or by pervading external individuals.
But since both [subject and object] are non-existent for the appearance of cognition,
he says "therefore" (tataśca), and so forth.
"Another individual" refers to the external object;
"therefore" is the conclusion,
which he explains with the words beginning "for not," and so forth.
"By someone" means by way of a general form;
thus, the meaning is that there is a grasping of these [objects] as "similar.

Now, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) asks: must not the basis for this conceptual construction (vikalpa) be stated, since if it were to arise without a basis, it would follow [absurdly] in all cases? To this, he says:
The application of designations and conventions, such as "mutual exclusion" and so forth,
has as its object that which is mutual exclusion.

Taking "artha" (object) to mean that which has the result of being made known, such a mutual differentiation (*itaretarabheda*)— characterized by the mutual exclusion (*anyonyavyāvṛtti*) of entities— is the seed of this false conceptualization (*mithyāvikalpa*). The "designation" (*saṃjñā*) is the act of establishing a convention (*saṃketakriyā*) for the purpose of which that mutual differentiation has the result of being made known.
He explains with the words beginning "of which" (*yasya*):

for the sake of communicating that mutual difference (*itarētara-bheda*), a convention (*saṃketa*) is established; [this is done] by knowing through differentiation the entities to be accomplished as distinct from those not to be accomplished—that is, from those not to be produced by it—and thinking, "Having excluded those, one shall engage in those [entities] that are its effects by avoiding those that are not its effects. It is for this purpose that the convention is established.
Thus, this aforementioned mutual differentiation is the seed— that is, the cause— of that false conceptual construction which appears as a single nature and possesses a single form;
"grasping that very [differentiation]" means grasping the differentiated, and this is stated by virtue of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*).
Furthermore, there is no grasping of a real entity by conceptualization;

rather, conceptualization appears in this way as a single form through its own uniform nature, because it arises from the nature of the latent impressions of conceptualization (*vikalpavāsanā*). This conceptualization, characterized by the general form "this is a conceptualization," manifests as such due to the very essence of the habitual tendencies of conceptualization.
But how is it that distinct particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) have a single, non-distinct effect consisting of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a single form,
by virtue of which they are said to have "a single effect"?

Because they are distinct from others that do not produce that effect, the non-difference of individuals is asserted; this is refuted by the statement beginning with "prakṛti," based on the declaration that "the connection with one [universal] is the commonality of those things excluded from it."

*Prakṛti* is *svabhāva*. "Recognition of a single form" (*ekākāra-pratyabhijñāna*) and "single reflective awareness" (*ekapratyavamarśa*) form a copulative compound (*dvandva*), as do "experiential cognition" (*anubhavajñāna*) and "cognition of an object" (*arthajñāna*).
Thus, it is a [double] copulative compound consisting of "single reflective awareness" and "cognition of an object."
Because the rule regarding prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) is subject to exceptions,
the word *arthajñāna* has not been placed first despite having fewer syllables;
rather, the analysis of the compound is "that which has these as its beginning" (*te ādī yasya*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), effects such as fire or a house are included;
"one object" (*ekārtha*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning that which consists precisely of a single unifying cognition (*ekapratyavamarśa*) and so forth.
Regarding its accomplishment (*sādhane*), i.e., its establishment, certain [causes] are restricted (*niyatāḥ*) even though there is difference (*bhede*), i.e., plurality (*nānātve*).

By their own nature (*svabhāva*) or by their very essence (*prakṛti*), like the sense faculties and so forth—or even if there is absolute difference [between them]—some things have arisen from their own causes as similar, while others have arisen as dissimilar; this has already been stated. Among those, the ones that have arisen as similar produce a cognition of a single form through that very nature, even without a universal (*sāmānya*), just like the sense faculties and so forth.

In this context, the phrase "restricted to the accomplishment of a single synthetic cognition" (*ekapratyavamarśajñānasādhane niyatāḥ*) is presented as the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), whereas the phrase "the accomplishment of a single object such as the cognition of an object" (*arthajñānādyekārthasādhana*) is presented as the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) because it is established for both parties.
For this very reason, it is analyzed first.
The phrase beginning with "just as the sense-faculties" (yathendriya) means that the sense-faculty, light, and mental attention produce a single visual consciousness; this is the connection.
He provides an illustration of what is established by the power of the thing itself (*vastubala-siddha*).
Regarding "the self" and so forth: based on the tenets of other schools, the mind (*manas*) is eternal, atomic, and swift; thus, the mind is atomic in nature.
The "contact with these" refers to the contacts between the self, the sense organs, the mind, and the objects.
Based on the statement, "The self (ātman) is conjoined with the mind (manas), the mind with the sense organ (indriya),
and the sense organ with the object (artha)," there is a dvandva compound consisting of the self, the senses, the mind, and the objects, as well as their respective contacts;
thus, [the term is] *ātmendriyamanorthāḥ*.
The opponent’s own admission is that [the sense organs] produce consciousness by means of their respective contact as an auxiliary condition;

yet, even in the absence of such [a universal], this is determined by their existence. That is, it is determined by their having a single effect, for the opponent does not accept a "universal" called "the state of being a producer of visual consciousness" belonging to the eye and the other [senses].
Nyāya-bhāṣya 1:1:4. Now he explains the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*):
"such as the *śiṃśapā*," meaning the *śiṃśapā*, *khadira*, *nyagrodha*, and so forth, even though they lack mutual concomitance (*parasparānanvaya*).

Even in the absence of a universal such as "treeness," the *śiṃśapā* and other [trees] produce a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of a single form, namely "tree," or else they produce, through that recognition or otherwise, purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*) achievable by wood— such as burning or building houses; this is the point under discussion, namely, "according to the respective conditions" (*yathāpratyayam*).
When they obtain the auxiliary condition of fire, they produce burning;
when there is a convergence of conditions favorable to a house, they produce a house—
the word "etcetera" (ādi) including effects such as chariots and so forth.

But even though there is no difference in their being distinct entities, water and other such things are not by nature capable of performing the causal function accomplished by wood, because they do not have that as their effect;
regarding this point, he provides an example:
"like visual cognition in relation to the ear and so forth."
Just as the ear, sound, and so forth are not capable of producing the cognition of form—
the word "and so forth" [implying] that they would likewise be incapable of producing the cognition of taste and so on—
it might be argued as follows:
Since the fact that many [individuals] perform a single action each cannot be established without a commonality, he says "fever" and so forth;
"together" means accompanied by other individuals.

"Each individually" means that they are observed to have a single form in a single effect, such as the alleviation of fever, just like medicinal herbs; the word "or" is used in reference to the previous example, whereas others, such as curd and *trapusa* fruit and so forth, do not [function in this way].
He explains with the words "Just as," and so forth:
"In that case, when the pacification of fever and other ailments is to be performed, do they not depend upon a general property called 'medicinalness'?
What is the reason?"
Even though there is difference, because they have that as their nature—
that is, because their essential nature consists in the activity of pacifying fever and so forth—
if the individual instances were devoid of efficacy, [the universal would not exist].
There might be a dependence on a general property,

yet even when that [general property] is not distinguished— and even when the difference is not distinguished— there are cases such as yogurt-cucumber and the like; for instance, yogurt that has only slightly begun to coagulate is called "yogurt-cucumber."
Others explain the compound *dadhi ca trapusaśca* as a *dvandva*; they argue that among those individual instances such as *guḍūcī*, which perform a single function in that manner,
there exists some "something" (*kiñcit*) which is both distinct and non-distinct [from them].
As it has been said:
"In the case of an action that is being produced (*nirvartyamāna*), the genus (*jāti*) is also the instrument (*sādhana*);
for that [genus] is the motivator of the action for the sake of the manifestation of its own substrate."

The meaning is that because of that very generality (*sāmānya*), there is a single effect characterized by the pacification of fever and so forth; therefore, the example is unestablished (*asiddha*). To this, the Proponent of the Established Doctrine (*Siddhāntavādī*) replies: "That is incorrect, because the generality is without distinction."
Because it is unitary and eternal, the universal is undifferentiated and thus does not perform that specific effect; rather, it performs the general effect of pacification.

Otherwise, since there would be no distinction in the universal, it would follow that even when those individual instances such as *guḍūcī* differ according to their field of growth and so forth, that effect of pacifying fever and the like would also lack distinction—whether occurring slowly or quickly, and so on.
For those [medicines] produced in an excellent field, there would be rapid pacification [of disease], whereas for those of the opposite [quality], there would be slow pacification;
furthermore, by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of "even slower" and "even faster" is intended.

Moreover, due to the application of *gūḍūcī* and other substances—which differ according to the preparation of the field and so forth—there would be no gradation of qualities, such as health and the like, in the body.
Because the universal is one; if, however, a distinction of the universal is desired through the differentiation of fields and so forth,
then, when a distinction is admitted for the universal, there would be a difference in its intrinsic nature, since difference is characterized by distinction.
Consequently, there would be a loss of its own nature; for the universal's single nature would be lost,
and because of the cause of permanence— since the universal does not benefit from the individuals— it follows that the universal does not perform any causal function.

For if the universal were to produce [the effect], then, because it is eternal and thus incapable of having any excellence imparted by auxiliary causes, it would not depend on others; consequently, being independent of auxiliaries, that universal would produce its own effect all at once.

Alternatively, if it does not produce it, then it does not possess the nature of producing it, because there is no difference between its non-producing state and its state at the time of the effect; therefore, it would not produce it even at the time when the effect ought to arise—this is the meaning.
However, he says that for individual instances (*vyakti*), which are impermanent, there is no such fault in their being causal agents, beginning with the words "But the individuals... and so forth;
"refinement" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the sprinkling of water and the like.

Those whose arising is distinguished, and likewise that which possesses distinction—this note belongs to the base text, which was not keyboarded

Thinking, "It will be translated.

That from which there is no further emergence.

It is not tenable to claim that the specific effect— characterized by the alleviation of fever and so forth— is produced by a subordinate universal (*avāntara-sāmānya*) such as "swift efficacy" which resides in those individual instances; for if that were the case,
it would follow that the effect would arise in a person even without the use of the medicinal herbs.
"In that manner" means like a specific individual;
"some" refers to those of the same class; "recognition as one," etc.—the word "etc. includes such things as fetching water from a single source.
The phrase "to those who do not perform that" means they are said to be non-different from difference because they do not perform such things as recognition,
and not because of a connection with a single universal.
Having established non-difference by way of the effect, he states it by way of the cause with the words "or by one," and so forth;
just as the various types of jars are said to be non-different from those not produced by effort because they are distinguished from things not produced by effort.
"Even though there is a difference in effort for every individual jar, nevertheless, because it is the cause of a single act of recognition, that [effort] also possesses oneness;
this will be established later.
To this, the opponent asks: "But how so? and so forth.

That universal (*sāmānya*) which has differentiation (*bheda*), exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and cause (*nimitta*) as its nature, is that by means of which the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)—which is excluded from those things that do not produce its effects and those things that do not serve as its causes—is to be cognized as "common" (*samāna*). Otherwise, it would be something entirely different. That which is other than the particular, appearing in the form of conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), is incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*); it is by means of that universal characterized by differentiation that [the particular] is to be cognized as "common."

[Objection: But was it not already stated that a universal is spoken of because we grasp a specific form of those very entities existing within the intellect—which, by conforming to the appearance in the intellect, seem to flash forth as if external? [Response: It is true that the persistence of doubt remains;
however, this point is raised in order to demonstrate an additional fault.
In order to demonstrate the fault, he says, "What follows from this?
(kiṃcātaḥ); the other [the opponent] expresses the intention of the question with the words beginning "If... (yadi).

If the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is that which is to be cognized, how can it be the object of conceptual construction? For it is by the power of the intention of a conceptualizing cognition that a universal characterized by difference is established; this is because of the statement: "By the power of its [the cognition's] intention, the universal is proclaimed as being existent."
If the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) were to be cognized as identical with such a universal (*sāmānya*), then it would be the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);

but this is not tenable. Alternatively, if it is held that what is cognized as identical is a form existing within the intellect (*buddhi*) that is entirely different [from the particular], [then that too is untenable].
Regarding this as well, he states the fault:
"Or how could causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) come from something else?
For causal efficiency does not arise from a form that is merely a mental appearance (*buddhipratibhāsi*)."
Therefore, since they are said to be non-different from those things that do not produce that effect, the establishment of a universal by way of its effect is not tenable.

Furthermore, because the form existing within the conceptual cognition is the universal, and because universals such as impermanence are not perceived in the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), the particular would lack that nature—that is, it would not possess the nature of impermanence and so forth.
Moreover, since impermanence and the like are not perceived in the particular, these properties such as impermanence would consequently be non-entities.
He refutes this with the words "no," and so forth;
he adopts the position that the conventional usage of terms such as "universal" (sāmānya) applies only to a form appearing in the intellect,
and thus he says:
"An object appearing in cognition," and so forth;
this is the summary statement (*grahaṇakavākya*),
and the following is its explanation.
This is connected with the phrase "this conceptual cognition.

Although it does not have that [particular] as its object—meaning that although its object is the nature of the real thing—it nevertheless appears as if it has that as its object, as if its object were the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); its own nature is such that it determines that state and superimposes an external existence upon it.
And since it has determined that [object] as being of that nature, it is therefore considered to have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone as its object.
If one asks, "How is it that its very nature consists in having determined that nature? he says:
"Because its essence arises from the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of that [particular characteristic]."

The experience of that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) deposits a latent predisposition (*vāsanā*); from that arises the production of that universal (*sāmānya*). This is its nature or essence (*prakṛti*, *svabhāva*), by which it comes to possess the form of the determined object—this is the meaning.

Those entities such as jars, which have identical effects and are the causes of a cognition with a single form, appear as if they were grasping a non-differentiated object, because [the universal] is produced from them through a continuous succession.
However, there is no such thing as a universal entity, whether distinct or non-distinct [from its particulars], which could be apprehended.

In reality, it is the exclusion from others—the difference (bheda) consisting of a distinct nature (svabhāva) from those dissimilar things that are other than those intended to be of the same class—that constitutes its "identical form" (samānākāra). This is the analysis of the compound: that which has as its identical form the very exclusion from others.
Because it arises from that [exclusion] and because it excludes [the dissimilar], the exclusion from others is called its "identical form."
Regarding that knowledge just mentioned, [the phrase] "as if one" means as if it were common to all individual instances, or as if it were performing its function (*arthakriyākārin*).
If one asks, "But why does it appear in such a way? he says:
"Of those engaged in worldly transaction," and so forth;

likewise, "having determined"—that is, having determined the very portion of conceptual construction (*vikalpāṃśa*) as being external, as being a unity, and as being capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). (Note 181-1: *Ñes-pa*.
Note 181-2: *Ḥdogs-te*.)
Because of the activity of those engaged in worldly affairs (*vyavahārin*),
others read "by those engaged in worldly affairs" (*vyavahāribhiḥ*).
Since this is connected with the preceding term "determination" (*adhyavasāya*), the instrumental case alone is employed.
However, it is not [the case that the genitive is used] because of the prohibition of the genitive by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā* (Pāṇini 2.3.69);

otherwise, if there were no external determination (*bāhyādhyavasāya*) regarding the aspect of conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*), then even when such a conceptual differentiation has arisen, there would be no purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) directed toward the object.
Even that conceptual reflection appears as if it were capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritā*) by virtue of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the person engaged in conventional practice;
therefore, if it is asked why the conceptual reflection itself is not the reality— appearing as if distinct from those things that do and do not perform such functions— the author replies:
And so forth: that reflection of conceptual construction is neither reality nor a real entity;
for what reason?
Because the deviation [of a reason] from the investigation by way of its capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*) is not a constituent part [of that investigation],
we shall demonstrate this immediately hereafter (Pāṇini 2.3.69).

In that regard, those objective forms which, having proceeded by way of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), appear in conceptual cognition— those objects appearing in conceptual cognition are grasped as being "identical" through that universal characterized by difference,
namely, as being "excluded from something," that is, through exclusion from what is of a different class (*vijātīyavyāvṛtti*). For it is thus:

Even though the various trees appearing in conceptual construction appear as if excluded from non-trees because they possess an externally determined form, so too does "the other" [i.e., the universal];
thus, it is grasped as being similar to the particular (svalakṣaṇa). This is how the connection is made by modifying the gender and number of the words.
What is the reason?
Because in that conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) where there is a manifestation of a universal (*sāmānya*), the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not manifest.
Thus far, the conventional usage of "universal" with respect to the object manifested in cognition has been explained.
Now he states the conventional usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words "those very [objects]," and so forth;
those very objects that appear in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Being as if excluded from something—just as varieties of lotus are excluded from what is not a lotus—they appear again as possessing exclusion from other things, such as the non-blue;
and thus, because a single substratum (*dharmin*) accompanied by these two exclusions appears, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Furthermore, this aforementioned conventional usage of "universal" and "coreferentiality" regarding objects appearing in cognition is established as having a false object.

For what reason? Because even for those conceptual forms which are themselves non-existent, there exists a nature of phenomena (dharmasvarūpa) that follows a single form and follows two exclusions (vyāvṛtti).
The conventional usage of "universal" (sāmānya) arises from its being presented by a conceptualizing cognition as appearing in a single form;
and the conventional usage of "grammatical coreferentiality" (sāmānādhikaraṇya) arises from a single entity appearing in multiple forms.

If every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has only a false object, why are conceptual constructions such as "impermanence" and "selflessness"—which arise by way of [reasons] like "being produced"—considered valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whereas eternal conceptual constructions are not? To this, he says:
"And all this," and so forth; the connection is that "all this is a cognitive distortion" (*viplava*).
This delusion, which consists of the form of universals and so forth— namely, the notion "this is [such-and-such]"—
is produced by the latent impression (vāsanā) deposited by the perception of nothing but particularities (svalakṣaṇas).
Because, through a continuous succession, all conceptual constructions (vikalpa) are dependent upon the perception of a real entity (vastu);

for even conceptual constructions such as "permanent" and so forth arise solely from the perception of a real entity, being dependent upon the perception of a continuous production of similar successive moments. Thus, while it is equal for all conceptual constructions to be dependent upon the perception of a real entity, [there remains a distinction].

Although conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "impermanence" and so forth—which arise in dependence upon that [particular]—do not manifest that [particular] itself, and although they do not manifest the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), they are non-erroneous with respect to the real object (*vastu*).

This is because the form of impermanence and so forth, which is superimposed [upon it], exists in the real object; it is merely that it does not manifest in the form of the unique particular. Thus, the conceptual construction is called an "error" (*vibhrama*), just as the error regarding a jewel in the luster of a jewel is non-erroneous even when the actual nature of the jewel is not grasped, because the luster of the jewel is connected to the jewel.

Furthermore, since the illusion of a jewel arises by means of its light, conceptual constructions such as "eternal" and so forth do not function in this same way; for even though they are dependent upon the perception of a real object, they superimpose an aspect that does not actually exist in that object.
Thus he says:
"Of others," and so forth;
the connection is with the phrase "correspondence regarding the object for other conceptual constructions such as permanence," even though they arise from that same differentiation.
The meaning is that even when there is production, because there is no difference in the object;

that is, having abandoned the pursuit and ascertainment of the specific feature observed—characterized by momentariness and so forth—one grasps some generality, whether distinct or non-distinct from the particular. Through this grasping of a generality, there is a superimposition of stability and other such qualities onto that particular, just as in the case of the cognition of a jewel which has arisen due to the similarity of brilliance and so on in the light of a lamp; thus, that cognition of a jewel does not correspond to the actual jewel-object.
Since [the cognition] is not connected even indirectly to the jewel when it has been determined [as such],
and since conceptual constructions (vikalpa) have only false objects, there is no capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyākāritva) in those objects that are the domains of conceptual construction;
therefore, what was stated— namely, "how could there be causal efficiency from anything else?"— is established as proven.

If it is asked: "How then is the universal, characterized by the exclusion of what does not produce that [effect], established with respect to objects that are the referents of conceptual construction?"—[we reply:
No, because those things which appear as if they were external manifest, by virtue of performing a single purposeful action, as if they were distinct from those that do not perform that action.

Regarding what was stated— that because impermanence and so forth are not perceived in the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it lacks that nature— he says "nor also," etc., for the purpose of refuting that.

Since there is no such thing as "impermanence" apart from a shifting entity, by which [entity] the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—being unrelated to it—could be disconnected from impermanence;

rather, the shifting entity itself is impermanent, because the particular characteristic itself has the nature of impermanence. In this same way, "selflessness" (*anātman*) and so forth should also be understood.
When the particular (svalakṣaṇa) is being grasped by that perception, impermanence is indeed already grasped; it is merely not ascertained because of the presence of causes for error.

Therefore, the function of inference consists solely in the ascertainment of that [impermanence]. Thus, it is established that the cognition of impermanence regarding the particular occurs precisely through that ascertainment.

If the particular itself is impermanent, how is there a cognition of the object as "this is impermanent" or "this has impermanence" in the form of a subject (dharmin) and a property (dharma)? To this, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "moment" (*kṣaṇa*), etc.:

because the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—which is of such a nature, namely, having a mobile form—is apprehended as existing for only a single moment due to its non-presence beyond that moment, those who perceive the final moment at a later time conclude: "This is impermanent," and so forth.

When there is the intention not to exclude other distinctions, [the cognition is] "this is impermanent"; when there is the intention to exclude other distinctions, [the cognition is] "its impermanence. In this way, the perception of the relationship between property-bearer (dharmin) and property (dharma) occurs because it is constructed by conceptualization (*vikalpa*). To the question, "How can there be a relationship of property-bearer and property regarding external reality? he says:
"Its being a property," and so forth.

The meaning is that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), while entering into that very nature of phenomena—the nature of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇadharmatā*)—determine those specific characteristics.

Following words for which conventions have been established based on differences in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), there are phenomena of various forms as well as phenomena of a single form; these, along with their exclusions, constitute a copulative compound (*dvandva*).
[These refer to] various properties (*nānādharmān*), such as impermanence, being produced, and so forth.
They demonstrate that a single property, such as impermanence, belongs to many things like pots and so forth, and that the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of those pots and so forth is their impermanence—

the word "entities" (*vastuni*) is to be supplied here. Furthermore, a reality consisting of various properties and so forth, established through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is not the ultimate truth, because conceptual construction apprehends what is not a real entity.
For this very reason, he says,
"showing [the object].
If it is argued that, because they grasp what is not a real entity, they would consequently be without a basis, he replies:
