Nor do those [conceptions] refer to "this" or "not this," because they are based on the perception— the direct experience— of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which consists of the differentiation of conceptual objects and has forms such as impermanence and so forth;

for it is by seeing the particular characteristic in its ultimate form of impermanence and so forth that conceptions, arising through the power of that perception, proceed by determining the perceived aspect.

Since conceptual constructions proceed by verbalizing exactly what has been perceived— such as the aspect of impermanence— and do not follow after something else like the conceptualization of permanence and so forth, that which was stated [by the opponent],
namely that "their nature is non-substantial" (avastu-dharmatā), is thereby refuted; thus he says:
"No," [it is said];
for those properties such as impermanence and so forth do not have non-existence as their nature.
What is the reason?

Because that which has such an intrinsic nature appears, manifests, and is determined as having properties such as impermanence; that is to say, if impermanence and so forth appear as the very properties of the real object, then what is the delusion produced by conceptual construction? To this he says:
"Of an object," and so forth:
the apprehension of a single object in manifold forms, and the apprehension of many as one.
The meaning is that the apprehension of the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*) as distinct from one another is an error, that is, a delusion.
To the question, "What, then, is the reason that the apprehension of them as identical and so forth is an error? he says:
"Of that [apprehension], whether as one or many," and so on.
Of the various particulars such as jars and so forth that perform a single function— meaning those performing a single function such as the fetching of water—
and likewise, regarding the desire to know the nature of things, which is the desire to know their status as performers of a single function.
This is for the purpose of making known its state as such and making known its performance of a single function,
because it has been established in that manner;
that is, it has been fixed in a single form, such as "pot," for the sake of simplifying linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*).
Likewise, even for a single entity that performs multiple functions—

such as a jar, which performs the functions of producing visual consciousness, holding water, and occasionally providing knowledge regarding its existence— in order to reveal its actual state when there is a desire to know that state, and to demonstrate its possession of multiple functions, it exists in such a manner [as it has been fashioned].
Because [things] are established in such forms as "visible," "earthen," "impermanent," and so forth,
the same should be stated for other cases as appropriate;
it is not due to a difference in the underlying entity (*vastu*) that multiple properties are established within a single object (*padārtha*).
What is the reason? Because it is impossible for that very same single entity to possess multiplicity;
therefore, the apprehension of multiplicity in what is one is declared to be an error.
Likewise, he states that even the establishment of unity for what is manifold occurs only by way of exclusion from non-causes, and not due to an actual identity of things, saying:
"because it is impossible for the manifold to be one.
Thus, the apprehension of the manifold as one is an error.
Thus, even the apprehension of a distinction between the property and the property-bearer is indeed erroneous;
for what reason? Because a separate universal has already been refuted.

By stating "particulars do not follow into another" and so forth, [the author] asserts that properties are indeed distinct from the substratum; consequently, the referent of a word will correspond to the actual state of things.
To this, he says "of those," and so on.

Because there is a difference in the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) or essence (*svabhāva*) of those properties such as impermanence and so forth, if one accepts the referents of words according to their actual state, then grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be impossible in cases such as "the blue lotus" or "sound is impermanent.

This is because qualities such as "blue" and universals such as "lotus" possess mutually distinct essences; therefore, words expressing them cannot function with respect to a single substratum, and thus coreferentiality is untenable.
Therefore, the point is that the determination of word-meanings does not correspond to the actual state of things.
With the words "of that limiting adjunct" (*tadupādheḥ*) and so forth, he anticipates the opponent's intention:
there is no fault because a single substance, which has those qualities such as blue as its limiting adjuncts, is denoted by both a quality and a genus.
The fault of the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) does not exist;
he states the answer beginning with "not assisting" (*anupakāriṇī*), and so forth.
A substance does not provide any assistance to the properties—such as blue color and so forth—which are intended to be its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);
for no assistance whatsoever is rendered by the substance to the quality of blueness or to the universal of lotus-ness.
Consequently, since dependence is impossible for those [qualities] like blue that cannot reside in a substance which provides them no assistance, [the relation between them is untenable].

Dharmas such as blue and so forth are without limiting adjuncts (anupādhi) because they lack dependence on anything else; otherwise, it could not even be said that "this is the limiting adjunct of that."

If it is maintained that the dependence of properties (*dharma*) has substance (*dravya*) as its object, then even in that case of dependence, one must admit that they are produced by the substance; otherwise, their dependence upon substance would be impossible. Furthermore, the producer must be accepted as momentary (*kṣaṇika*), because a non-momentary thing is incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Consequently, because of the non-coexistence of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) regarded as effects and the substance regarded as the cause, [the two cannot exist simultaneously].

The simultaneous non-denotation of the two— the qualifier and the qualified— which are of the nature of real entities, occurs because the specific quality intended as the cause has at that time ceased;
this applies even to "one," which is the qualified entity possessing its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
If it is argued that the word-meaning is not an actual entity because it involves an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and a demonstration [of what is implied],
since the word denotes only a particularity superimposed by the intellect;
this might be the opinion.

If it is argued that while that which has perished may be the object of a word as appearing in cognition, but for a qualifying attribute (*upādhi*) that is still existent, the word denoting it must have the real thing (*vastu*) itself as its object— the author replies with the verse beginning "buddhipratibhāsa... and so forth.
That designation whose object is a mental appearance is "thus";
when that state exists, let every designation—even those intended to have specific qualifiers—as its object likewise be only an object of a conceptual mental appearance.
What is the reason?
Likewise, because a single entity possessing distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and various qualifiers appears in the intellect when it is apprehended,
one must admit that there is a conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*) that mentally supplies [the adjuncts] once the entity possessing those adjuncts has perished;
and at that time, in the absence of the entity possessing the adjuncts, the adjunct itself is also absent, since it lacks independence.
If a single entity possessing distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) does not appear [as such], how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)?

However, when it is accepted that both the qualifier and the qualified appear in conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), then a single cognition arises which apprehends one substratum (*dharmin*) as grasped by two imagined properties (*kalpitadharma*); thus, coreferentiality is not contradictory.
With the words "the beneficiary" (*upakārya*), etc., he anticipates the opponent's intention.

Regarding the objection stated [by the opponent] beginning with "there is no fault, since this is merely the superimposition of the intellect upon one thing," [the author] replies: Since an attribute (*upādhi*) that exists simultaneously with its substratum and possesses an established form lacks dependence (*pāratantrya*), it would not be an attribute; yet, if it were previously dependent, that very state of dependence constitutes its being an attribute. To this, he says:
"No," and so forth;
for that which is unestablished—equivalent to the horn of a hare—possesses neither dependence nor the status of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in any way.

Since there is no dependence for what is non-existent, whether it be existent or non-existent, one must therefore regard the dependence of limiting adjuncts as something superimposed by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Having done so, [one engages] in the conventional usage of dependence.

"In every way" means in every manner; just as the intellect is followed in the conventional usage of dependence (*pāratantrya*), why is that same superimposing intellect not followed in the conventional usage of the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*)?
For it is logical to follow that [intellect], since it is impossible to engage in conventional usage without relying on the appearance of an object as presented by the intellect.

Regarding the point previously stated—that when an object is apprehended by a single word or a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), all the properties that constitute the very nature of that object are necessarily implied by the force of the object itself, rendering other words and so forth redundant—this would hold true for the position of the Realist (*vastuvādin*) who asserts that "the nature of a single object is perceived," and so on; yet this would be so only in accordance with the appearance in the cognition [of that object].
Why is this?
Because the appearance in cognition lacks any real objective basis (*nirvastukatva*), there is no possibility of faults that arise from the causal efficacy of real entities (*vastusāmarthya*).
By using the plural number, he expresses this:

not only is the fault of the other [terms] being redundant (*vaiyarthyadoṣa*) avoided, but likewise, there is an absence of a separate universal (*sāmānya*), and because it is impossible for limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) to possess dependence on another.

The absence of the relation between qualifier and qualified, the absence of coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) due to the fact that a single entity possessing distinct limiting adjuncts (upādhi) does not appear as such in cognition, and so forth— all those [objections] that were stated are likewise impossible here; this is precisely what he expresses with the words "that is non-different" and so on.
For in this way, the form appearing to that cognition appears as non-different;
therefore, having modified the statement to "therefore the universal [is established] so that it does not contradict experience," it connects with what is to be said next:

when "blue" is stated, although the single aspect of blueness is made an object by way of the exclusion of the non-blue (*anīla-vyāvṛtti*), the conceptual cognition effects the exclusion of doubt regarding that very aspect of blue, and not regarding any other aspect.

Therefore, that form appearing in cognition—which has an uncertain aspect and so forth—is such because the aspect of the lotus, which is excluded from non-lotuses, has not been ascertained; since the word "lotus" is applied with expectation toward another aspect in which no ascertainment has arisen, it appears as something to be grasped by the cognition that has arisen—this is the connection.
By this, the cause for the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) has been stated.
Regarding grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*),
he says "distinct," and so forth;
that is, even when there is a synthesis— that is, a presentation— of distinct word-meanings characterized as "blue lotus" and so on.

Since a form appearing as a mental reflection (*buddhipratibhāsa*), which is embraced by two properties (*dharmadvaya*) yet undivided due to their sharing a single substratum (*ekadharmitā*), appears in conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), the categories such as universals (*sāmānya*) are not contradicted according to how they are perceived.

Therefore, as for what Bhaṭṭa says— having grasped apoha as merely the exclusion of others— that there can be no relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between those two properties because the exclusion of non-lotuses is absent when there is the exclusion of non-blue things, and the exclusion of non-blue things is absent when there is the exclusion of non-lotuses, and because that [relationship] is absent, there is likewise no relationship of qualifier and qualified between the two words that denote them.

Nor can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two things expressed by the words, because they are distinct; nor can coreferentiality be mediated by the fact that both exclusions (*apoha*) reside in a certain object, because an exclusion, being a non-entity, lacks the property of being something that can be contained within a locus.
Furthermore, it is not accepted that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of the word, nor is any other locus admitted.

Nor is it refuted [by us] that there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between two words even when their respective exclusions (*apoha*) and particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) exist, because a single objective domain is not perceived; for it is accepted that the object of words and the like is one's own internal form (*svākāra*), which is distinct from the external [object]. Therefore, in words such as "blue lotus," the denotation of the word's meaning is indeed accepted. Thus, everything is well-established.

Furthermore, the connection [of the sentence] is to be understood by changing the grammatical number [of the subject] as follows: "the distinction between property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmin*) of this mental appearance (*buddhipratibhāsa*) is not contradicted according to how it is perceived."
He says "from many" and so forth:

since the appearance in cognition from a manifold object is unreal, how could there be a distinction between many objects? It is merely said thus by virtue of the person's conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).

Regarding that appearance in cognition, when there is a desire to know the affirmation or negation of its distinction from a single object—such as, "Is sound impermanent? Does it not possess the quality of being visible?"—the very same entity that constitutes the appearance in cognition is what is demonstrated; this is the connection.
He explains by what manner [this occurs]:

The connection [of the words] "rejected," etc., is as follows: or rather, even the distinction between property and property-bearer (dharma-dharmin) is not contradictory for this entity; if one asks why, he says:

When there is the possibility of a distinction from an external object based on its difference from many things, then, regarding the inquiry into the affirmation or negation of that [external object] which is distinct from one [of those many], such as "Is sound impermanent? Is it visible? It is not," that very same external entity is demonstrated; this is the connection.
To the question "By what is it demonstrated?", he says "pratikṣipta" (rejected), etc.
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: having prompted by means of the word "dharma" (property), one establishes it as if it were a distinct property (*dharmāntara*).
For instance, when a prompting is made by the word "dharma" such that "impermanence is not visible," impermanence and so forth are established as if they were a distinct property.
He asks: what is the reason for this?
Likewise, because it appears to the intellect, [it is] a phenomenon (*dharma*). [Note 188-1: In the mind.
Note 188-2: Without making distinctions.]
Because, when there is an injunction by means of a word, a cognition arises that apprehends a property (*dharma*) as something distinct [from the substratum],

it is "without distinction"— that is, without excluding all particular differences— that another external nature, whose own internal differences are not excluded, is established as the subject (*dharmin*) and demonstrated by the word. This is what is meant.

Having prompted with the word "dharma" (property) and presented as if it were a distinct property, and then having prompted again with the word "dharmin" (subject) and established another nature as the subject, that very same external object is demonstrated: "impermanence of sound," or "sound is impermanent and not visible.
It is not [the case that] "sound is impermanent and not visible."

By the phrase "through a portion of the existence of the entity," it is meant that because of the distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), whether other distinctions are excluded or not, the conceptual cognition appears as if possessing distinction— as if having a distinct form—
but there is no actual distinction in the real object.
Cognition is not differentiated by a difference in the object;
for what reason?
Because of the aforementioned fault, since it is impossible for properties to be dependent upon a substratum (dharmin) that provides no assistance.

Likewise, there is a distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*), which is impermanence, and the probans (*sādhana*), which is being produced (*kṛtakatva*); therefore, he says "tathābhūta" and so forth.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: for those various properties (*dharma*) that are thus constituted and whose internal differences have been excluded, a distinction of verbal expression and a distinction between the probandum and the probans are made by means of the indication of their multiplicity. What is the purpose of this? He says: [it is done] by means of those distinctions of appearance consisting of properties—which have as their basis the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of that real entity (*vastu*) excluded from this and that—meaning, by means of those distinctions of appearance whose essence is the conceptual cognition’s reflection (*vikalpabuddhipratibimba*).
Why is it done? He says: [it is done] for the sake of... [the following].
Regarding the passage beginning with "tatsvabhāva" (of that nature),

he states a summary verse for the sake of easily grasping the very subject at hand; this is because those [cognitions], through a mediated process, are connected to the object for the purpose of realizing or attaining that very excluded (*vyāvṛtta*) real nature (*vastusvabhāva*).
Regarding the phrase "having that as its intrinsic nature" (*tatsvabhāva*) and so forth:
it refers to the cognition (*dhī*) which is known to arise subsequent to the experience of that intrinsic nature of the object;
the word "also" (*api*) is placed out of its logical order.
Even though it is devoid of an object, it appears as if for that very purpose and as if directed toward a real entity;
by virtue of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), it is established upon the exclusion (*bheda*) of those things that do not produce that effect.

Because it arises through the power of that experience and because it corresponds to the object from which [the cognition] has excluded [other things], it is said to be "established" in that [object]. When such a cognition has arisen, the objective form within it— which, due to the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized, appears as if external, as if common across similar individuals, as if one, and as if excluded from other dissimilar things— [is the universal].
But that [object] is indeed excluded [from reality], because the form of the cognition is unreal;
that form of the cognition is devoid of reality (nistattva) and lacks intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva).
For what reason?

Because that which is not a factor of investigation (*parīkṣānaṅga*) is incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and since only that which is capable of causal efficiency is a factor of investigation, it follows that by virtue of not being a factor of investigation, it is incapable with respect to causal efficiency;

and because the form appearing to the intellect (*buddhipratibhāsi-rūpa*) is devoid of reality (*nistattva*), he says that the conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) directed toward it proceeds only with a false object (*mithyārtha*).
"Objects," and so forth;

"qualified by cognition" means they have ascended onto the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*), and being thus qualified by cognition, they possess the nature of exclusion because they consist of an exclusion from what is heterogeneous—
just as the objects that are lotuses possess the nature of exclusion from what is non-lotus.

Thus, by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), they appear as if non-different through their nature as lotuses, but not in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), because the nature of cognition (*buddhi-rūpa*) is unreal.
By this, the cause for the conventional usage of a universal (*sāmānya-vyavahāra*) has been stated; furthermore, it is those very same [individuals] that are excluded from others.
Those very objects, distinguished by cognition and possessing the nature of being excluded from others, further appear as excluded even from other similar things—
just as those same particular instances of blue are [excluded] from the non-blue; and this is because a single object, embraced by two exclusions, appears.
The seed of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) has been stated;
he states that very thing in the passage beginning with "teṣām" and so forth.
The grammatical connection is as follows: "the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of those objects appearing in the intellect is extended.
In the phrase "of those" (*teṣām*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) with reference to the conventional usage.
Of what nature is that which has false objects?
He states "by means of which instruments" with the words beginning "sāmānya" (commonality) etc.;
"samānādhāratva" (the state of having a common locus) means that which has a common locus (*samānādhāra*).
Because the designation has the state of being (bhāva) as its primary focus,

the conventional usage of universals is extended through cognitions and designations that have universals as their objects and share the same referential domain; by other [cognitions and designations], the conventional usage of co-referentiality is extended.

Although in this context linguistic usage consists solely of verbal cognition (*śabda-jñāna*), nevertheless, by attributing to both cognition and the word an active operation (*savyāpāratā*), they are regarded as instruments (*karaṇa*).

Thus, it is intended that the very activity characterized by the manifestation of the object belongs to those two alone, and is designated as "linguistic usage"; hence there is no fault, just as in the case of whether cognition is considered the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or the result (*phala*).

And all that linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), characterized by cognition and verbal expression, has as its basis the mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)—that is, the mutual exclusion (*parasparavyavaccheda*)—of the particular natures (*svalakṣaṇa*) of things, because it arises through the medium of the experience of excluded objects. Thus, by virtue of having mutual non-existence as its basis, that convention is said to have "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as its object; however, this is not because its object is the exclusion of others itself.
Since this linguistic convention has as its object a ritual injunction (*vidhi*), it is not the basis for the acquisition of a real entity (*vastu*) nor for the attainment of a real entity;
nor does every convention serve this purpose, but only that convention which possesses an indirect connection with such a real entity.
He states an example with the words "as in the aforementioned inference" (*yathoktānumitau yathā*);
"the aforementioned inference" refers to the alternative types of inference mentioned previously.

This is because, apart from conceptual constructions such as "stable" and so forth, there is no connection to a real entity even indirectly, since the real entity itself lacks a stable or similar nature; for both inferential conceptualization and other types of conceptualization are equally erroneous insofar as they determine an object through their own internal mental images.
"Just as with the light of a lamp and a gem":

just as the cognition of a gem regarding the light of a gem is erroneous, so too, although the light of a lamp is equally erroneous, the radiance of the gem is grasped as being the gem itself; thus, when the gem is the object to be attained, it is consistent with reality.
But the meaning is that the conceptualization of [objects] as stable and so forth is not, like the light of a lamp, a reliable [correspondence].

If the linguistic convention of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth applies only to objects residing within cognition, then, because such conventions would be absent regarding external objects, there would be no engagement with them; therefore, he says:
Regarding "tatra" and so forth: the word *tatra* is used either to introduce a statement (*vākyopanyāse*) or for the purpose of specification (*nirddhāraṇe*).
In that regard, among individuals, those individuals that share a single effect are distinguished;

for even though there are many, they have a single effect—just as various types of jars have the same effects such as carrying water—and thus they perform that specific effect while excluding what is not their effect. That exclusion of others is the basis (*āśraya*) for those cognitions and designations by which even a manifold object is led to be treated as a unity.
The meaning is that it attains a common conventional usage; thus, in dependence upon a subsequent generality, even a single thing performs multiple functions.
Just as a jar performs functions such as being the object of visual consciousness and the fetching of water, so too, in the illumination of its existence,
it manifests the performance of manifold functions.

By means of the reason consisting in the distinction from those things that do not produce that effect, various properties— such as "the jar is visible," "it is earthen," and so forth— are established; thus, the linguistic usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) is demonstrated as pertaining exclusively to external objects.

If the conventional usage of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth regarding external objects were ultimately real, then [the following consequence] would follow; thus he says: "It is stated according to how it is perceived.

In accordance with conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), the referent of a word (*śabdārtha*)—the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—is stated according to how it is perceived, even though it does not exist ultimately.
And since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) has been described according to how it is perceived—

because this coreferentiality of the word-meaning is not possible with respect to a real entity (*vastu*), and because the linguistic convention of property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmin*) pertains to an object appearing in cognition— he says [the following] in order to summarize what was under discussion.
"Regarding 'dharma' and so forth:

there is a distinction between the determination that 'this is the property (dharma)' and 'this is the substratum (dharmin),' and the non-distinction [between them] is of such a nature as 'this is the property characterized by being produced (kṛtakatva),' or 'this is what is produced.'"
And this [is so] because it is superimposed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);
the analysis of the compound is: that by which the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha*) has not been examined, and the meaning of the thing (*vastvartha*) has not been taken into account.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: just as in the world even that which has ascended to the intellect is perceived through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of its having that nature, so too is that division of properties (*dharma*) and so forth; thus, the arrangement of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is postulated by the learned in accordance with worldly perception.
For what purpose?
For the sake of entering into the ultimate truth and for the sake of fathoming the intrinsic nature of things such as impermanence, he asks:
what, then, is the reason that conventional designations such as "oneness" and so forth are impossible with respect to a real entity? He says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "they are conjoined," ultimate realities do not conjoin by themselves;
therefore, there is no conventional usage of a universal (sāmānya) with respect to a real entity.
Things are not differentiated by properties such as "being produced" and so forth, because it is impossible for a single entity to possess multiplicity [simultaneously].

Therefore, when many forms are determined in multiple objects, or a single form is determined in a single object, that is an error—an illusion—of conceptual cognition. For this reason, ultimate objects are neither conflated nor differentiated.
For that reason, this generality of many things,

as well as this distinction between properties (*dharma*) and property-bearers (*dharmin*), and even this distinction— the conventional usage of diversity— is [a construction] regarding mental objects (*buddhy-artha*), not regarding external particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

If it is asked, "Since the appearance in cognition is unreal, how then can there be a distinction of properties such as 'being produced' (kṛtakatva) and so forth within that particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa)? he says:
"And of that very [appearance]," and so on.

Why is it that the distinction between properties (*dharmabheda*) is conceptually constructed for that very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) through the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), rather than the relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*) occurring merely by perceiving the real entity (*vastu*) itself? To this, he says: "The probandum," and so forth.

Because the perception of the real thing is lost in this conceptual construction that "this is the probandum" and "this is the means of proof," or else, why is it that by means of inference—as if it were perception—the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself, as qualified by the universal, is not apprehended? To this he says:
"the probandum," and so forth.
Since the perception of the real entity (*vastu*) is lost when there is a conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*) of the probandum and the probans,

how could there be a grasping of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as qualified by the universal? To dispel the doubt that masters such as Ācārya Dignāga have asserted that the particular, conjoined with the universal, is what is apprehended, he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "difference" (*bheda*), the meaning is that even in this statement—"difference is perceived as conjoined with the universal"—it should not be understood that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself is being indicated; rather, it should be understood that it is external differences themselves that are determined (*adhyavasīyante*) as conjoined with that universal characterized by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), but they are not actually apprehended (*gṛhyante*). Thus it must be understood in that case as well.

Others, however, read the masculine form "bhedaḥ," stating that "the particular (bheda) conjoined with the universal (sāmānya) is the object of apprehension"; in this reading as well, the meaning is: "the particular conjoined with the universal is the object of apprehension."
The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not to be understood;
if one asks what the reason is for it being understood in that very [context],
he says "common" (*samāna*), and so forth.
A single form in many things is a common form;
a manifold nature in one thing is a differentiated form;
by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of the forms of the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin) is intended.
That particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) cannot be apprehended in any way whatsoever.
Why?

Because within that single particular characteristic, it is impossible for many distinct properties—such as being produced, impermanence, and so forth—to exist; specifically, it is impossible for those various distinctions, which are the actual forms of things, to coexist within that single particular characteristic.
For it is not logical that a single entity should possess multiple forms, because a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is partless; summing this up, he says "that form," and so forth.

Therefore, that particular (svalakṣaṇa) is differentiated from everything else and is unique; thus, there is no verbal expression (śruti)—that is, no word—that conveys that particular by means of its unique form, nor is there any conceptual construction (kalpanā) [that does so].
This is what is under discussion.
The meaning is that there is no grasper of a particular (svalakṣaṇa) by way of its unique intrinsic nature;
for what reason?
Because both words and conceptual construction function only through universals (sāmānya).

By stating that there is no scripture (*śruti*) that establishes that [particular], it has been asserted that words are not applied to the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); therefore, he raises an objection with the words "But what... and so forth.
Those made objects by convention are the conventional (*saṃketinaḥ*).
They say that words are a convention for the sake of practical usage;
at the time of such usage, however, that specific particular (svalakṣaṇa) does not exist upon which the convention was established.

Because even a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is momentary, there is no persistence of that very same form at another time; or, if it were not momentary, there would be no convention because of the absence of cognition, and thus there is no persistence of its being an object [of cognition] at another time—let alone among particular characteristics differentiated by place and time. For this reason, the ellipsis is supplied: "a convention is not made with respect to that particular characteristic. He explains this with the words beginning with "for not" (*na hi*).
The phrase "api nāma" means "how indeed might it be?
The connection is as follows: "of a word whose relation was established at the time of convention," [referring to] "previously";
and "later" refers to the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahārakāla*) with respect to a single, identical particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
He states "of that," and so forth, to explain why it is not logical [to claim] "for what reason?"
"Of that" refers to what was perceived at the time of the convention; because it does not fail and persists through various differences of place and time during the states of practical usage,
for a difference observed in one location cannot possibly exist elsewhere.
According to the Śeṣika (Vaiśeṣika) view, it is distinct; according to the Sāṃkhya view, it is non-distinct.
Because it pervades individual instances of the same class, the universal is all-pervasive;
therefore, there is no fault regarding the absence of [the universal] at the time of linguistic usage.
At the time of linguistic usage, there is no fault of the referent of a word being non-existent,
because the universal (sāmānya) is the referent of the word; since that [universal] exists at both the time of the convention and the time of usage due to its unity,
the particle *api* is used in the sense of "how indeed" (*kathaṃ nāma*).

With the intention that "at the time of practical activity (*vyavahāra*), having understood from an uttered word objects capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-kṣama*), how indeed might a person proceed toward their accomplishment— that is, toward the accomplishment of causal efficiency?"— expressive words are associated with objects. He explains this with the words "Certainly not," etc.,
[stating] that an intention (*tātparya*) or a passion (*vyasana*) is never independent of a result.

Whether it be this world establishing conventions, or one not yet making conventions, or one employing words for conventionalized objects— all such linguistic activity, as well as any other attention, apprehension, undertaking, or worldly transaction, is for the sake of a result and is never without fruit.
For what reason? Because that which has a fruitless undertaking is to be disregarded and not accepted by those who act with foresight;
"tad" means for that reason.

This practitioner, when directing someone toward a certain intended object or establishing a convention, ought to aim for the result itself; that is to say, he must necessarily take account of the purpose.
And "that" refers to the result, characterized by the attainment of the desired and the abandonment of the undesired, as is appropriate in each case. This is the connection.

Since the human goal (puruṣārtha) is intended to consist precisely in the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired, this person—having understood the means and the non-means for those two desired results—would, with the intention "I shall act toward the means of the desired and desist from the means of the undesired, or I shall cause others to do so," employ words; and the listener too would attend to the injunction. It is indeed reasonable that there should be an employment of words in the sense of "I shall cause another to engage in worldly transaction," because the employment of words is subordinate to the other.
But as for the cause of engagement and withdrawal being self-evident, what is the utility of the word?
True;
however, this presentation was made on the grounds that one who, through the habit of employing words, understands [the matter] by oneself, might sometimes understand it in this way.
"Otherwise, it would be subject to neglect"—because, in the absence of a result, the application of a word would be something to be neglected.
Since this principle is thus established, a universal (*jāti*) is incapable of purposeful action; therefore, it is not the object of words.
He explains this with the words "for not," and so forth.
The universal (jāti) is not capable of performing functions such as carrying or milking;
therefore, for one who desires carrying, milking, and so forth, an injunction regarding the universal is fruitless, and thus the employment of a word for that purpose [is useless].
Furthermore, as for the causal efficiency (arthakriyā) characterized by one's own cognition which is attributed to the universal—
A person does not engage in activity for the sake of that [individual], because it is established solely through the use of the word.
If it is argued that the use of the word will be for the purpose of conveying the universal (*jāti*) alone,
he says "not so," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of such a kind," since it has been stated that the employment of words for a fruitless purpose is to be disregarded— referring here to the context of carrying, milking, and so forth— then, if the universal (*jāti*) were the denoted meaning, there would be a cognition of the sentence-meaning from the sentence "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*).

Since the universal "cowness" lacks connection with the action, there can be no cognition of the sentence-meaning through indirect indication (lakṣitalakṣaṇā) either; for such a cognition does not occur, as it would involve a highly protracted process: first, the cognition of universals from the words, then the cognition of particulars from those universals, and finally the cognition of their syntactic connection from those particulars. Thus, the cognition of the sentence-meaning would be of a delayed nature.
Now, even if the exclusion (*apoha*) is what is expressed, how can there be a cognition of an external object, given that exclusion is devoid of form?
Nor is it logical to apply words to a portion of cognition, because such a portion does not perform any purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
This is true.
It will be demonstrated that the application of a word to that [object] is appropriate precisely because it appears as having causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*) alone;
however, even so, since that portion of cognition is a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), how can it be denotable by words?
To this, it is replied:

First of all, its own part, which is non-different from the external object, indeed appears in conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*). Its appearance does not occur because it is grasped by the conceptual cognition—since that would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of determining [the object] in its entirety, and such is not admitted [by you]. Nor is its "grasping" merely the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of it as having the nature of an external object; for it is not grasped by way of its own form as it actually exists. And if it is not grasped, how can there be an appearance of it?
However, if it possesses the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of cognition, then its manifestation is logical because its own part (*svāṃśa*) has the nature of consciousness (*samvit*).

Therefore, if the nature of the part of ignorance and of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not admitted to be the specific characteristic of cognition, then there would be no manifestation at all. Furthermore, how could there be a determination of its own part by means of a conceptual construction that is of the nature of non-cognition? For this [determination] is a property of cognition.

Consequently, precisely because it possesses the specific characteristic of cognition, the part manifests within the conceptual construction; that [part], being non-different from the external object, is established as the object of the conceptual construction.

Because that very form of consciousness is determined by conceptual construction as non-different from the external object, for this very reason conceptual construction is said to have the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, and not the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), since neither the [external] object nor its own part [the cognition] is grasped in its own nature.
Therefore, even the particularity of the cognition itself—which is its own part—is of the nature of a universal because it is superimposed as having an external essence; and so he will state later.
If it is argued that [the universal] is the object by virtue of having the nature of cognition, then it follows that the universal is [the object];
and since this is accepted, it is similar in its having the nature of the object to be excluded (*apohya*). (Pramāṇavārttika 3.9) And it is indeed logical that this [universal] is denotable by words.

Regarding the phrase "indirect indication" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*) and so forth, the opponent [says]: It is true that the universal (*sāmānya*) does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*), but rather only the individual (*vyakti*). However, because it is impossible to directly express the individual, a word is applied to the universal; thus, the word indicates the universal.
And through the connection with that universal indicated by the word, the individual is also indicated.
This is unconvincing;

for when the word "cow" is uttered, it is not the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) that is perceived, but rather the individual cow itself that is determined— though indeed it is not called by that name, it is nevertheless so described.
Regarding the passage beginning with "not impelled by words" and so forth:
even if there were indeed a relationship between the universal and its possessor, how could [the word] apply to a specific individual that is not impelled by words?
It could not at all.

The meaning is this: although a relationship exists between the staff and the bearer of the staff, no prudent person, when told "cut the staff," cuts the bearer of the staff, because he was not enjoined by the word [to do so]. Likewise, when the universal (jāti) is enjoined, activity toward the individual (vyakti) is not logical.

If it is argued that since activities such as carrying or milking are impossible in the universal, activity will instead occur toward the individual—even though the individual was not directly enjoined by the word—the author replies:
"Nor indeed," and so forth:
if a speaker were to urge an effect that occurs only in one case toward a subject in which it is impossible, he would be a babble of incoherence for the person being addressed;
however, from such an urging of what is incapable, there can be no engagement with what is capable, just as in the case of urging the milking of a bull.
For when someone says, "He milks the bull," the listener does not proceed to milk a cow—distinct from the bull—simply because milking is impossible in the case of the bull but possible elsewhere;
rather, he thinks only this: "This speaker is uttering an incoherent rambling."
It might be thought:
"Just as there is no activity toward a female cow when a bull is being urged because of the absence of a connection, let there be no activity toward a female cow;
however, when the genus (jāti) is enjoined, there will be activity toward its individual instances (tadvyakti) because of the connection. To this, he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "na ca" (nor), the phrase "of another object" refers to the universal (*sāmānya*) and the relation (*sambandha*); the phrase "of another object" [refers] to the individual (*vyakti*).
Indeed, this very point has already been stated in the passage beginning with "even though the relation exists when that which is not denoted by the word [is present]."
The restatement is indeed for the purpose of providing further injunctions; it thus restates that very same point as the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
"Indeterminate," and so forth: that staff whose relation [to its possessor] is indeterminate is described as such;
for indeed, even in the absence of the person holding the staff, the existence of that [staff] is found. Therefore...
Regarding the phrase "in that case," the meaning is that if one says "not in the possessor of the staff" (daṇḍin), then no activity occurs when the staff itself is enjoined;
whereas the point is that when the universal (jāti) is enjoined, there is a cognition of the individual (vyakti) due to their necessary connection.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tad" and so forth, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) states that the lack of a fixed connection [to a specific object] is equal even in the case of a universal (*jāti*);
if it is asked how this is so, he replies:
Regarding the passage beginning with "of individuals" (*vyaktīnām*),

one might argue that just as words such as "brother" (*bhrātṛ*) and so forth, while denoting their own primary referent, imply a second [referent], so too do genus-words (*jātiśabda*); therefore, he says:
Regarding the phrase "but words such as 'brother' and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes words such as "son.
This is because, since they are denotable by relational terms, their establishment depends precisely upon another related entity; such is the meaning.

They might "exclude" (*ākṣipeyuḥ*) another, namely a second [relative] such as a brother; and this "exclusion" consists in the generation of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) having the form of a relation with that second [person], but not in the actual presentation [of the object itself], since a conceptual construction arises even when the related object has perished.
"It is not so," he says, beginning with "apeta" etc., stating the dissimilarity (vaidharmya): if [the words] were denoters of related entities, then this fault would arise.

There would also be the undesirable consequence that even for those classes (*jāti*), such as the Pāṇḍavas and others, whose individual instances (*vyakti*) have departed and perished, there would be a constant persistence [of the class] through its connection with those departed instances, due to words denoting those classes. For their persistence by way of connection with departed instances would only occur if the departed instances themselves were to persist;
or else, because it would follow that those instances which have departed from their related classes would persist eternally through those very words.

If it is argued that the opponent’s statement "always," etc., intends the persistence of the individual because the capacity for its relation [to the universal] is perceived at both the time of its appearance and its disappearance,
this is what he says:

Just as words such as "brother" and so forth, while denoting their own primary referent, imply a related person without further qualification, so too do genus-words; this is the answer given by the phrase "at all times."

If it is asked, "What is the reason that the word 'cow' does not apply to a specific individual capable of bearing a load, carrying a calf, and so forth, at all times— both during the time when that individual is present and when it has passed away?"— the author replies with the words beginning with "sahita" (accompanied).

This is the locative dual; for there is no implication of a particular [entity] capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)— whether in its state accompanied by or unaccompanied by the universal (*jāti*)—
therefore, this is what is meant:

If it is argued that there is no such fault— namely, that because the past and future individual (vyakti) is implied by the genus-term (*jāti-śabda*) as being of the nature of the word’s referent (*śabdārtha*), so too the present individual appears in both ways (as both word and referent) without distinction, and thus the cognition of the individual does not fail to occur through the injunction of the genus related to that individual—

let it be so; however, since that individual is also implied by the injunction of the genus precisely as its qualifier— that is, as the qualifier of the genus— the genus alone cannot be the denotable object.
However, the alternative position—that the possessor of that [universal] would be the denotable object—would be adopted;
and we shall point out the fault in that immediately thereafter.
This was stated while provisionally accepting the relationship between the universal (jāti) and its possessor (tadvat).
But he says "nor indeed" and so forth, because there is no connection at all;
what is the reason?

Because there is no mutual assistance between them— since they stand in neither the relation of producer nor produced— and because there is thus an absence of connection, it follows that even the indication of the individual through the mention of the universal is stated to be purposeless, as there is an absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Even for one who maintains that the universal is non-different from the individual, there would have to be an appearance of the individual in verbal cognition just as in perception;
however, its definition [of universals] is untenable even with respect to the aspect of difference.
With the words "In this way," etc., he anticipates another position.
"Tadvān" means possessing that [universal];
"alam" means capable;
"tatra" means in that which possesses it.
And he, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī), provides the explanation of this very point with the words "And that word," and so forth; [the meaning is:
"In that case"—that is, regarding the individual (vyakti)—what is the use of another, imagined universal (sāmānya) acting as an intervention or an interposer?
The opponent says, "And because of infinity," and the reply is, "This infinity is equal";
he explains this very point as follows:
With the words "This might be so," etc., [the author explains that] even in the case of that which possesses [a universal]— that is, even in the case of that which possesses a genus (*jāti*)—

since it must be stated that only individuals (*vyakti*) qualified by a genus and so forth are the things to be expressed, for this reason, the connection of the word must necessarily be established "therein," i.e., with respect to the individuals.
Why?
Because a word whose relationship [to its referent] has not been established does not denote; therefore, the genitive case is used for the agent.
The meaning is that it is because the word for which a connection has been established is not denoted by that [other word];
or, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Furthermore, because a meaning that has not had a connection established with a word cannot be denoted by it,
that connection cannot be made with the possessor of that [meaning], due to its infinity.
Therefore, this position is also untenable.

If it is argued that because the word’s relation is established with the universal— which is related to those [individuals] and thus related to the individuals— the relation is in fact already established for the individual through its connection to the universal and the [other] individuals.
The answer to this has already been stated:

even though a relation exists for a universal, there is no cognition of another individual based on a convention established for one genus; nor is there a relation between the genus and its possessor, as it was said that even when a relation exists, there is no comprehension of the "staff-bearer" from the word "staff."

Furthermore, since it has already been explained that there is no relationship whatsoever between a universal (*jāti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*), the author of the *Vārttika*— having thus far stated his own position regarding the object of words and logical marks as being positive (*vidhi*) in nature by means of the passage beginning with "all entities" (*sarvabhāvā*) and so forth— now asks, beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*), in order to demonstrate the intention with which the Master Dignāga asserted that the universal is characterized by difference (*bheda*).
The opponent asks as follows:

"Just as the word 'cow' is conventionally assigned when the nature of a cow is not [directly] perceived from the word 'cow', so too, there is a commonality (*sāmānya*) among all those things that perform a specific causal function—namely, those that perform the intended purposeful action—as distinguished from those that do not perform such a function. Since all those things performing that function are distinct from non-performers, why is the convention not established for that very sameness of difference (*bheda-sāmya*), which is characterized by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)? Why is it not established? Thus he questions the other.

He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "yām arthakriyām" and so forth: with reference to, or intending, the performance— that is, the accomplishment— of an object characterized by burning, cooking, and the like, this person employs, or applies, words toward objects that produce the intended causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).

Because those things that perform a specific function (*tatkārin*)—which produce the intended causal effect—are distinct from other things that do not perform that function (*atatkārin*), those performing the function are undifferentiated insofar as they are excluded from everything of a different class.
Therefore, since there is no difference among these objects in that regard [of being excluded from others], why is a word not applied to that which is characterized by exclusion from others?
The intention of the question is that, by virtue of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*), there could be a cognition even of that which is qualified by such exclusion.

In the same way, regarding the position that [the universal] possesses the genus (*jātimatpakṣa*), the fault stated by the Master Dignāga in the passage beginning with "because that which possesses it is not independent" (*tadvato nāsvatantratvāt*) applies; since that fault is equal [to the one previously mentioned], that very fault is introduced. Thus, he accepts [the opponent's objection] by saying, "Let this fault be," on the grounds that the word is not employed to denote the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) as a distinct entity.
This has been explained by accepting that this fault does not exist; however,
what was said thus means that while one universal (jāti) is sufficient, another universal is not tenable.

He explains with the words "it might be" (*syāt*) and so forth: even when a thing is admitted as the referent of a word (*śabdārtha*) by virtue of being excluded from others that do not perform that function,
[the term] "possessing that" (*tadvat*) refers to that which possesses the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
There is no distinction between this position, which possesses exclusion, and that [other] position;
he states this very point in the passage beginning with "For who," and so forth.
You have stated that "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*) is what is expressed, while the opponent has stated "universal" (*jāti*), and so forth;
in this regard, what difference is there between the two, other than a difference in terminology? There is none at all.
The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) says: "Let it be granted that there is another universal (*jāti*) which is a real entity (*vastubhūtā*);
however, since the fault is equal [in both cases], why is exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) accepted as the basis, rather than a universal that is a real entity?"

Regarding the passage beginning with "jātim api hi" and ending with "tadabhāve": since there is an absence of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), there is also an absence of this [universal], that is, of a universal that is a real entity (*vastubhūtā jātiḥ*).
This is because, when there is no differentiation among entities, a universal—which by nature inheres in multiple objects—cannot exist.
And it has been stated that no non-difference of genus is produced;

therefore, a difference must necessarily be admitted. And is that difference [of one] from that which does not produce that effect? [If so,] there is a difference of those others from that which does not produce that effect, while there is a non-difference of those others which do produce that effect. Let there be a cognition of non-difference qualified by that [difference], within those things qualified by non-difference.

It is called "practice" (*pratipatti*) because it is the objective support for practice; however, the word "practice" is not used here in the sense of the action itself (*bhāvasādhana*), nor in the instrumental sense (*karaṇasādhana*) as in the view that "entities are practiced by means of this [word] as an instrument through this exclusion."
Regarding the phrase "in every respect" (*sarvathā*):

if the object to be expressed is either distinguished by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) or distinguished by a universal (*jāti*), then the faults such as infinity (*ānantya*) and so forth, which were raised against the position [that the individual is the referent], would apply equally because it is impossible to avoid them. If it is asked, "Why then is the universal alone not accepted? he replies:

Regarding the passage beginning with "arthāntara" and so forth: if it is argued that a distinct entity (*arthāntara*)— a real universal (*jāti*)— is the purpose of a universal, namely the production of a non-different cognition (*abhinnapratyaya*) with respect to diverse things, [the author] says:

Regarding the phrase "of that object": since the universal (*jāti*) is what is to be proven, and by another [means]—namely, by non-difference characterized as the exclusion of what does not have that effect—that object is indeed proven by the universal as well, why then is there an acceptance of exclusion while abandoning the universal? To this, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "that," [the phrase] "of that admission" refers to the admission of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
For it has been stated that if that were not admitted, the very postulation of a universal (*jāti*) would not even exist.
Now, since exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) must necessarily be indicated by the word, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*), and so forth:
the speaker utters the sound (*dhvani*) with the intention that the listener should act by avoiding what is other than the intended object.
The particle *eva* has the sense of "only" (*evārthe*), and its position is displaced; it is to be understood immediately after the phrase "by the exclusion of others than that.

Thus, by means of the sound (*dhvani*), when there is no exclusion of that intended meaning from those unintended things, the meaning is expressed as being "unexcluded" (*avyavacchedena*). This is the sense.
He explains this very point with the words "how might the hearer proceed? and so forth:

"With the intention, 'How indeed might the hearer proceed toward objects intended by the speaker—objects that perform the desired causal function—by avoiding what is undesired and by excluding what is not intended,' he employs [the word]."

If the exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*) were not expressed by the word, then activity would be permitted both toward that which is intended to be conveyed and toward that which is not intended; and if that were the case, there would follow the absurdity of the uselessness of employing the name of that intended object. For instance, when "Bring it" is said, a mere thing is implied; therein, the word "fire" is employed to exclude what is not intended, as in "Bring the fire."

But if, even when that [word] is employed, the non-bringing of fire is not excluded, then there would be no purpose in uttering the word "fire," because by the word "bring" alone, the non-bringing is already rejected; thus, both bringing and non-bringing would be permitted. Consequently, since there would be permission for both engagement and withdrawal, the mention of its name would result in futility—this connects with what was stated previously. In this way, if there were disregard for the injunction regarding one intended object such as fire, and one performance characterized by bringing and so forth, there would be no verbal expression of words at all.
This should be connected with what is to be stated later— namely, "if there is no expression of the exclusion of others" or "if there is permission for engagement and withdrawal"— because,
according to the method already described, there would be a disregard for the single injunction regarding both engagement and withdrawal.
The remainder is to be explained as before: [the objection is] that there would be no impulsion toward an activity characterized either by engagement or by cessation;
thus, the linguistic usage of words would be destroyed, and since this is not the case, it must necessarily be so, and so forth.
And that [exclusion] is the exclusion of others;
"in those other than it" means in those things possessing a single effect that are distinct from those not having that effect,
because it is undifferentiated for all of them due to their being excluded from what does not have that effect.
Thus, since the exclusion of multiple referents is also a property of the universal (*jāti*),
[the term] "that" refers to the exclusion; it is qualified as "restricted," meaning that for whom there is an acceptance of such [an exclusion],
because if that were not accepted, it would follow that the universal itself does not exist.
That which has a fixed denotation is so described;
otherwise, the employment of words would be fruitless in the absence of such a denotation.

The "meaning of the universal" (jātyartha)—characterized by the continuity of cognition and verbal expression across individuals—is established as that by which [the universal] is proven. This is done by taking the word *prasādhana* in the sense of "that by which something is proven."

The meaning is this: having abandoned such exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), the postulation of a separate entity as a universal (*sāmānya*) is merely a stubborn adherence to what is useless; it is merely an attachment to a non-entity, and there is no other reason for it whatsoever.
Why?

Because, according to the way it is postulated, this universal is incompatible with characteristics such as permanence and omnipresence. This is the intention of the Master Dignāga in stating [the term] "exclusion of others" (*anyavyāvṛtti*).
"No," and so forth—the opponent [objects]:
"It is certainly not the case that exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is not produced by the word; rather, it is indeed produced.
For what purpose, then, was the universal (*jāti*) mentioned? To this, he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "pravṛtti" (activity) and so forth: the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) states that for those who seek purposeful action (arthakriyā), the object of such activity is the universal (jāti); therefore, when we speak of the universal, we are actually speaking of exclusion (vyavaccheda). Thus it is said, "the universal is [defined as] exclusion," and so on.
If there is an exclusion that is the denotation of this word, or if there is an exclusion belonging to this possessor of a universal that is the denotation of the word— then,
having considered that the purpose of words is precisely this much: the engagement with the desired object through the exclusion of others.

Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tatra*): when it is necessary to induce activity toward a desired object by means of exclusion, or regarding that very object of activity, what need have you for another [universal] in general?
This is the objection raised by the opponent, beginning with "nanu" and so forth.
The Master says: "It has been stated";
thus, "for instance" (*tathā hi*) is the demonstration of the lack of logical validity, and that is the *jāti* (futile rejoinder).

Because it lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), the universal (*jāti*) is not fit for purposeful activity; nor is the universal cognized from the word "cow," as this has already been explained. In that regard, [it was stated] with the words "the universal is unfit for causal efficiency" (*anarthakriyāyogyā jātiriti*) and so forth.

If it is argued that a person’s activity toward a substance capable of causal efficiency will occur by means of the universal (*jāti*), the author replies with the words "by means of that" (*taddvāreṇa*) and so forth,
[anticipating the objection] beginning with "even if a connection exists, how could one act when it has not been indicated by words? (*aśabdacodite saty api saṃbandhe kathaṃ pravartteta*).
If it is argued that "only one who possesses that [quality] is enjoined by way of the genus," he says "likewise the injunction" and so forth;
the connection is with the word "separation" (vyavadhāna) being stated, through a change in gender (*liṅga-pariṇāma*).
It has been stated there that the intervention is general;
why then is it not applied directly?
[The answer is given] by the passage beginning with "What is the intervention there by another? and so forth.
It might be thought:

neither the universal alone nor the individual alone is the basis for the application of words; for the universal alone lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and the individual alone cannot be the object of verbal expression.

Therefore, since the universal and its possessor together constitute the object of application, and it is precisely these two taken as a whole that are the meaning of the word, he says "of the universal and its possessor," etc.,
regarding the status of being the object of application; that is, when it is accepted that they are the objects of application— which is activity based upon words.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Why are exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and that which possesses it (*tadvat*) not accepted as objects of purposeful activity?
The underlying intention is that exclusion and its possessor are established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that because exclusion—which is of the nature of a word—is a mental construction, it lacks reality, and therefore, since it is not a means for causal efficiency such as carrying or milking, it cannot be an object of purposeful activity; [the response follows].

If it is argued that this lack of being a means of accomplishment (*asādhanatva*) applies equally to the universal (*jāti*), since the universal is also incapable of performing functions such as carrying or milking— just like its possessor— and therefore the fault characterized by the absence of activity does not arise for either the universal or its possessor because they both accomplish purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) replies:
"It is equal," and so forth.
The word "tat" refers to the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsādhanatva*).

Thus, having first explained that the Teacher Dignāga asserted the status of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) as the referent of a word— even though it is non-existent— by means of the logic of the "obstructer," he now states that the positive entity itself is the referent of a word,
beginning with the words "and [the cognition] which grasps the thing," and so forth.
If it is asked, "How can that which has a non-existent thing as its object incite a person seeking purposeful action (arthakriyā)? he replies with the words "That [is] an error," and so forth;
"that" refers to the verbal cognition (śābdapratyaya).
It is precisely delusion that impels a person toward action; as to how this is so, he says:

even though there is no external object as an agent, because one's own mental appearance possesses the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it is treated as an agent since it is the object of such a determinative conceptualization (*adhyavasāya*).

If one asks, "How then is there correspondence with the real object (*vastu*) in the case of inference and so forth?", he says: "In correspondence with the real object," and so on; this occurs when there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with that which is to be proven (*sādhya*).
But how is there a necessary connection?

Because of the arising of the thing— that is, the arising of the object to be proven which serves as the cause— otherwise, in the absence of such a connection, there can be no correspondence between the cognition of words and so forth [and the actual state of affairs].
If it is argued that there is no error because [the cognition] arises from a real entity— that is,
if one considers that verbal and other cognitions which accord with a real entity arise from that very entity, thinking this constitutes the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader—
this is not so.

The point is this: even though the object has actually arisen, because there is no appearance of that [object], and because there is no appearance of the object's true nature (*vasturūpa*), there is error due to the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that [object], which is to say, the conceptual determination of the object.
Consequently, since there is no contradiction between the arising of the object's nature and error, the reason (*hetu*) possesses a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitā*).
For instance, the illusion of a jewel in the luster of a jewel certainly accords with the actual jewel.
Establishing the very same point of deviation, he says "vitatha" and so forth;
this is what he means:

If there were a contradiction between error and correspondence, then the non-deviation of error from its object— namely, its correspondence with a non-existent thing— would be established; however, that is not the case,
because the definition of error is a false appearance, not non-correspondence.
"By way of being inseparable from that" means by way of being inseparable from the real entity (*vastu*), which is to say, because it arises from that;
this correspondence does not depend upon appearance— that is,
it does not depend upon the appearance inherent in the real entity.
Since even that which does not appear as such is consistent precisely because it is tied to the real object (*vastu*),
it is therefore established that verbal cognition, although its appearance may be false, is consistent when there is a connection with the real object.
Now, if, on the other hand, verbal cognition is held to correspond exactly to the real object...

At that time, when the mind is directed toward an external object according to its actual state and its true nature— that is, when there is a superimposed cognition, meaning a cognition of an object as it has arisen otherwise through the power of words—

given that such an engagement is admitted, the universal must be accepted as the apprehended object of that verbal cognition, because there is no prompting by a word regarding the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, because that universal (*sāmānya*) which is the object of apprehension is incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), there is no purposeful activity directed toward it—that is, toward that universal which is the object of conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*).

If, on the other hand, activity were to occur elsewhere—meaning in the particular (*vyakti*) other than the universal—even though it is not directly denoted by the word, this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);

for instance, upon hearing the word "cow," activity might occur even toward a particular horse. If it is argued that this is not so because there is no relationship between the universal of "cowness" (*gotvasāmānya*) and the particular horse, [we reply] no; for even if a relationship exists, activity is impossible toward that which is not denoted by the word, as has been stated previously.

Now, if it is held that not only the universal (*jāti*) is denoted by the word, but rather the possessor of that universal (*tadvān*), then, since the apprehension of that [possessor] must be admitted, the faults such as the uselessness of the universal (*sāmānyavaiyarthyādi*) already mentioned would apply; for one might ask: "Why should the word be applied directly to the individuals themselves, rather than to the universal? Thus, the uselessness of the universal has been stated.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), defects such as infinity (ānantya) and others are included. It is the universal (jāti) alone that is denoted by the word;
however, because that universal is inherent in individuals (vyakti), it cannot be apprehended in isolation. Therefore, it is apprehended as being unified with the form of the individual.
He raises that very doubt with the words "jāti" and so forth:

"If it is argued that a cognition in which appearances are blended by means of both its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)— appearing as a 'blended manifestation' (*śliṣṭābhāsa*)— induces activity toward an individual (*vyakti*) that performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*)."
In that case, neither the universal nor its possessor is apprehended in their own form; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
What is the reason?
Since even for a single universal or its possessor, that which is the stability of its own nature— the unmixed form— is not grasped by a deluded cognition that presents it as something fused,

and since one must therefore admit the activity of such a deluded cognition, the view of the proponents of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is nothing other than the very position of the opponent.

"Thus," and so forth—the opponent [objects]. The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) replies: "This fault does not apply to that universal which is understood through multiple individuals (*anvayin*)."

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the author] refers to the sequence ending with the fetching of water. Even though there is a difference [between individual instances] and they are mutually distinct, one observes that they perform similar purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*)—such as cognition and so forth—by virtue of being properties of the real entity (*vastudharma*). Having observed this, a person may indeed associate objects with those sounds—which consist of internal verbalization (*antarjalpa*)—and whose scope is that excluded nature (*viśleṣa*) which is a distinct essence differentiated from other things that do not produce that effect, thinking, "This is that very same thing. The word "even" (*api*) is placed out of its logical order; it means that this occurs even when [the object] is seen at another time.

The collective meaning is as follows: even when there is the perception of something different and distinct from an object previously seen, one might—due to being deceived by its performing a similar purposeful action (arthakriyā)—superimpose identity upon it and thus form a recognition (pratyabhijñāna). To the question, "How then can things that are distinct perform an identical purposeful action? he says:
"This has already been stated," and so forth.

Because this was stated previously in the passage beginning with: "In the accomplishment of a single object, such as a single reflective awareness, a cognition of an object, and so forth" (verse 1.75).
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: for a person who perceives that "it is one" among similar things and "different" among other distinct things,

these entities— while being excluded from others that do not possess that [quality]— by the very nature of things (*vastudharmatayā*), that is, by the very essence of the thing (*vastusvabhāvenaiva*),
produce a false cognition (*mithyāpratyaya*) in the form "this is that very same thing."
To specify what it is like, he says "that" and so forth:

that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from those things which do not produce that effect—namely, the exclusion of objects that perform a single causal function—is the object of the verbal expression (*dhvani*); with that [exclusion] it is "conjoined," meaning "associated," which is to say, "accompanied by a linguistic designation."
If they produce [cognition] by virtue of being the nature of things (*vastudharmatā*), why do they not do so at all times? To this he says:
"By their own experience," and so forth.

That which is the self-experience of those entities (*bhāva*) produced previously—the latent impression (*vāsanā*) characterized as a capacity (*śakti*) for the arising of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)—is what [produces it].
