Its awakening is its orientation toward the production of an effect; and the awakening of that [latent impression] occurs only through the experience of objects belonging to that same class.
Since awakening characterized in this way does not occur at all times, recognition is not possible at every moment.
Thus, "the distinction between the mixed" means that the difference between the two individuals perceived earlier and later is "mixed," that is, unified by it.

"Otherwise" means: if one does not accept that there is an erroneous recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) even regarding distinct things— based on the superimposition of unity through similarity consisting in having a single effect—

but rather [accepts it] because of their connection with a single universal (*sāmānya*), then there would be no cognition possessing a single form, which would result from the connection of distinctions (*bheda*) that possess such a connection.
The meaning is that there would be no cognition of a single form regarding many [objects];
for even when men are joined with a single staff, they are not apprehended as being one.
He states this very point:
The phrase "as in the case of those possessing staffs" (yathā daṇḍiṣu) clarifies precisely that [point] expressed by "for it is not so" (na hi);
"therein" (tatra) refers to among those possessing staffs.

"In another" means as follows: when one who possesses a staff is different from another who possesses a staff, that staff-substance which was seen in the first person possessing a staff would [be perceived] here in the second person possessing a staff; however, it would not be by way of that [substance] that [the cognition] "this very same person is the one possessing a staff" arises.
Alternatively, just as when many [objects] are joined with a single staff, although each one is indeed a staff, there does not arise the cognition "this is that very same staff"; likewise,
because individual instances are joined with a single universal, there would not arise the cognition "this is that very same [instance]," but rather the cognition "that is here."
If it is argued, "Let it be so," he replies with "Not so" and so forth;
the conclusion is made with "That" and so forth.

"One" is common [to many]; even for a person who perceives this in various individuals, a cognition that possesses a single form—like the connection of differences (bheda) with a connection (saṃsarga)—is not logical.
However, for the proponent of *anyāpoha* (the exclusion of others), this is not a fault; thus he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "vibhrama" (error) and so forth, the meaning is "by the power of delusion.

If it is argued that it is not logical for there to be an error— on the grounds that there exists a single, real entity as a universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by a uniform nature (*ekarūpatā*) which serves as the cause (*nimitta*) for recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), and yet such a thing is absent— then [the response follows].

"Those very [entities]" refers to excluded (vyāvṛtta) entities that function as the causes for a single object, such as cognition; "experience alone is the door" means it is the cause. Because they are by nature—that is, by their own essence—the cause of an error-result, which is to say, the cause of a delusive result, they are the instrumental condition (nimitta).
[Objection: But if a delusion of water and so forth were to arise in relation to a mirage and the like even without similarity, would there not be the fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga)?

If similarity is accepted [as the basis for the cognition of identity], why is a universal (sāmānya) not also accepted? To this he says, "In the case of mirages, etc.," where the first word "etc. includes such things as ropes.
By the second [reason],

it is shown that even though they are distinct, those two— the water and the mirage— are the causes (janaka) and basis (nimitta) for the experience that serves as the ground for the conceptual identification (*parāmarśapratyaya*) "those very same things," which takes the form "this is that very water" regarding the appearance of a non-differentiated form.
This means that there is no similarity whatsoever between dissimilar things.
Even among similar things, it is only the identical intrinsic nature that serves as the cause of error,
and not similarity itself; for instance, the cognition consisting in the experience of water deposits a latent impression (*vāsanā*) that reflects the form of water.
And that latent impression (*vāsanā*) is awakened not only by the experience of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of water, but likewise by the experience of the object known as a mirage,
because it is by its very nature (*prakṛtyā*) of such a character.
Therefore, just as from the experience of water there arises a conceptual cognition (*parāmarśapratyaya*) characterized by the form of water, so too does it arise from the experience of a mirage;
and thus, these two entities termed "water" and "mirage" become the causes for the delusion of water by means of the experience of those respective objects.

Nor does this lead to an over-extension of the principle, because although the nature of a mirage and water are equally non-aquatic, it has already been stated in the discussion on universals (*sāmānya*) that the essence of a mirage arises from its own causes as something possessing similarity, rather than becoming similar by virtue of being conjoined with a universal similarity. Having thus refuted the view of Uddyotakara and others, he speaks in order to refute the Mīmāṃsaka position:
"Not indeed," and so forth.

For instance, in the cognition of water (*jala-jñāna*), two things appear: the generality of water (*jala-sāmānya*) and its connection with a place and so forth. Therefore, when there is a sublating cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) stating "it is not [there]," it is the connection with the place and so forth that is sublated, not the generality of water. Consequently, the cognition of water has the generality as its very object; thus it is said.

In that case, regarding the mirages, there is no distinct universal such as "water-universal" (jala-sāmānya) that exists separately; for if the water-universal were admitted to exist in the form of water, then the cognition apprehending it would be a cognition grasping an existent object by virtue of grasping a real entity (vastubhūta-sāmānya).
Now, it might be argued:
The cognition of water is indeed based upon the generality of water (jala-sāmānya) as it exists in other locations and so forth; it is not an error.
As it has been stated in the *Ślokavārttika*: "In all cases, the external object is the objective support (*ālambana*), though its nature is altered by place and time."
Nirālambana 108:

If it is asked, "How then is there the erroneous cognition of water in a mirage? [the answer is: "It is because the universal of water (jala-sāmānya), which exists in another location and so forth, is superimposed (samāropa) upon that [mirage].
To this very point, he says:
"It did not exist," and so forth:
[the opponent argues that] there is no error because of the superimposition of the form of water upon mirages where it does not exist;
"no," and so forth: [the proponent replies] this is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
That cognition of water does not grasp the generality [of water], nor does it grasp the generality of water situated in another location;
why is this? He says:
"And that which... and so forth.
This cognition of water superimposes upon those mirages a certain aspect—that is, the unreal aspect of water;
as to why that which is being superimposed is nonetheless an object, he says:
"of that which has not been made an object," and so forth.
This means that at the time of the arising of a conceptual construction, since a universal has not been made an object, there can be no superimposition of it, just as there is none of any other form.

For no other form, such as fire and so forth, is superimposed there, because at that time it is not an object of cognition. And that form which is superimposed as non-different from the external is precisely what appears as the object; yet that superimposed form of water does not exist in those mirages, because it is sublated. Therefore, the cognition of water possesses no universal (sāmānya), in the sense that "this [cognition] has a universal as its object."
Likewise, the opponent argues that even in the case of real water, the cognition of water—which superimposes the form of water upon what is not water—is non-universal (*asāmānya*);
and so forth. [The opponent continues:
There is indeed another universal of water (*jala-sāmānya*), and when that is apprehended, there occurs the superimposition of it—that is, the superimposition of water—and not otherwise.

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) states: "If the superimposition of 'water' upon real water were to occur even in the absence of the universal of water (jala-sāmānya), then there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga);
for the superimposition of 'water' would then occur even with respect to fire and other such things.
Thus he concludes with the word "satī" (upon the real).
If there is a grasping of beings that possess water— such as those whose nature it is to perform a single function like drinking or immersion— is the attribution of "water" not desired?
If it is argued that distinct things cannot possess the power to perform a single function without a commonality (sāmānya), he replies with the words "And necessarily," and so forth.
And this has been established [in the following way]: "The means of accomplishing a single purpose consists in the single reflective awareness, the cognition of the object, and so forth. (PV 3.72)
In this context, others, however, interpret the passage beginning with "for there is no other generality whatsoever" by taking the word *sāmānya* (generality) to mean "similarity" (*sādṛśya*).
That interpretation of theirs is not very consistent, because [the word] lacks the expressive power to convey such a meaning as "that which is perceived in that way," and so forth.
For similarity is not perceived as having the nature of water;
therefore, because they arise from the power of a single cause, it is logical that the individuals themselves— and not the universal— possess the aforementioned powers.
"From others" means from those things that have such effects;
"of such a kind" means having a single form; "according to the nature of the thing" refers to the positive concomitance (*anvayībhāva*) in not deviating from the actual state of the object.
Since the particular characteristic exists as devoid of universality,
why does the conceptual cognition not perceive it by transcending that [particularity]? Why, then, does it superimpose an unreal universality upon it?

The meaning of the phrase "according to the nature of things" (*yathābhāvam*) is as follows: "unmixed" (*asaṃsṛṣṭa*) means that a thing (*bhāva*) possesses distinctions—that is, mutual differences—which have not attained a state of uniformity. Such a thing is described as being "unmixed."
This incapacity of conceptual constructions to grasp things as they truly exist arises from what cause? From the power of ignorance.
Knowledge is the grasping of reality;
because it is the opposite of that, conceptual construction itself is ignorance.
"Manifestation" (prabhava) is expressed by the word "origin" (prabhava).

The meaning is: "by the power of conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*). For it is the very nature of conceptual construction not to grasp an object as it actually exists, because it is by its very essence erroneous. If it is argued that—since there is no real universal (*sāmānya*) existing as a thing—it is illogical for conceptual construction to have "destruction" as its delusion, he replies with the words "And not," and so forth.
Here, the internal distortion is said to be the very nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);

the meaning is that it is the nature of conceptual construction itself by which it becomes an error, even without depending on a resemblance to external objects. An error having the form of hair and so forth is a "hair-delusion" (*keśavibhrama*).

Just as that [consciousness] becomes erroneous by relying on an internal distortion (*viplava*)—the grasping of unreal forms—while being independent of external objects, so too is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) [erroneous] because it grasps the form of an unreal universal (*sāmānya*); this is the intended meaning here.
The seed of error is the internal distortion, because [conceptual construction] arises from that. (Note 209-1: "To be entangled in what has fallen.")
This meaning is not intended here;
this will be made clear later.

However, in the passage "because it arises from ignorance" (*avidyāprabhava*), by the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*), that which is the seed for the manifestation of duality within the continuum where the obscurations have not been abandoned is what is meant.

Consequently, "arising" means origination; likewise, "distortion" (*viplava*) occurs at that very moment. Such is the seed-nature of all cognitions, namely, their arising from ignorance (*avidyā*); therefore, he says:
"Because of arising from ignorance, there is distortion," and so forth.
Since distortion—that is, error—results from the arising or production from ignorance, it would follow that even visual consciousness and the other [sensory cognitions] would be distorted.
With the words "no," and so forth, he states his own intention:
"of that" means of ignorance; conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the cognition that superimposes a general form, because that is its defining characteristic; thus he says.
"Indeed, it is conceptual construction itself," and so forth; "it" refers to ignorance,
and "by its own nature" means by its very essence.
With the words "not so," and so forth, he dispels the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*):

because those [cognitions] are non-conceptual by virtue of having the form of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), they are not, like conceptual cognitions, erroneous by their very nature; rather, for some, error arises through a disorder of the sense faculties and so forth.
Having explained [the process] according to the system of external objects, he now states it according to the system of internal cognition,
beginning with "And not," etc.; this is what he says.

Granted that the meaning of the term "ignorance" (avidyā) may be conceived in whatever manner it has been proposed through the form of the objection, nevertheless, there is no fault of over-extension (atiprasaṅga), because such a consequence is accepted [by us].
Nor does this defect of being erroneous apply even to those cognitions of the eye and so forth, since they too are distorted;
he says precisely that:
Regarding the phrase "of non-dual [cognitions]," and so forth:
the self-cognition (*ātmasamvedana*) of the visual and other consciousnesses is indeed non-dual, because it is understood that no duality exists therein;
for [the object] appears as distinct [from the cognition] at the same time as the cognition itself.
Blue and other such objects, which are considered to be the apprehended,
are not ultimately real because they cannot withstand analysis as being either one or many;
and consequently, that which is the subject-nature of consciousness— the state of being the apprehender with respect to them— is also unreal.

But it is not so, because that cognition is perceptible and because self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is not distinct from the form of the apprehending subject which is erroneous; thus, self-awareness would also be erroneous. If this is argued, we say no: if it were non-existent in its own nature, there would be no manifestation at all, like a rabbit’s horn.
Furthermore, even error must possess reality in its own nature, otherwise its status as an error would be impossible.

Since cognition has the single form of the consciousness of its own nature, and that consciousness is indeed of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), how could consciousness not be real? Alternatively, the appearance of duality is an illusion, and an illusion must have reality as its substratum,
just like the illusion of two moons and so forth.
And reality is non-dual, being the opposite of duality, and it is precisely the nature of self-cognition;
it is not the mere absence of duality, because that [absence] would be non-existent. How then could that [absence] not be [the object of] cognition? Thus, regarding the aforementioned objection...

And as for those [cognitions] which appear in the form of the apprehended and the apprehender, we shall state in the third chapter that these too are erroneous because they manifest in such a manner. (Note 210-1: It is the root text.)

For this very reason, although self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is established as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) for those who possess the appearance of duality, it is not determined to be the vision of reality (*tattvadarśitva*). If one asks, "How is the distinction between valid and invalid cognition (*pramāṇāpramāṇavibhāga*) [established]? he says:
"Of all," and so forth.
Error is the state of being mistaken;
that which appears as such is a fallacy of valid cognition.
The distinction between their respective states is as follows:
the basis is the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is the seed of delusion; its transformation is the removal of obscurations, where the prefix *ā-* denotes a limit.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: the establishment of validity [occurs] because, through the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), there is a correspondence with what is desired, which is always capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Purposeful action is characterized by the cognition appearing as burning, cooking, and so forth;
and that [cognition] is "capable" of it, and is "desired" because it is sought after by the person.
The analysis of the compound is "from its correspondence" (*tasya saṃvādanāt*).

The restriction is that it is "from correspondence as if with the intended object," and not "only from correspondence," because even from a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), correspondence may sometimes be impossible due to a deficiency in the cognizer's faculties.
Thus, "correspondence with the intended [object] capable of purposeful action" (*arthakriyā-yogya-abhimata-saṃvādana*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Likewise, it should also be understood that [it is] because of not being in conformity with what is intended (*abhimata*). For in this way, the cause for the determination of what constitutes a pseudo-means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*) would have been stated.
In the Vijñānavāda, since external objects do not exist, how can there be a correspondence with what is intended as being capable of causal efficiency?

This is not a fault, because the term "capable" (yogya) is used to designate even a cognition appearing as water that is capable of producing a cognition appearing as burning, cooking, and so forth—just like a cognition appearing as fire.

Thus, the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated for visual and other sensory cognitions, as well as for those produced by signs such as smoke which appear as fire and the like.
However, regarding the cognition of "non-self" and so forth produced by such marks as "being created," I have stated that it is false;
for the cognition of non-self and so forth is false because it functions through the superimposition of a general form.
Nevertheless, because it is conducive to tranquility (*praśama*), it possesses validity (*prāmāṇya*). Tranquility is the abandonment of passion and the like.

For those who grasp an object through its general aspect as being selfless (*anātman*) and so forth, and cultivate that [insight], there is the abandonment of passion and the like upon the completion of that cultivation, by means of the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of selflessness and so forth.
But in what case is even something false seen to be conducive to tranquility? To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "the perception of a mother" and so forth:
although the perception of a mother toward one who is not a mother is false,
it is a cause for the non-arising of passion.
And this example is given by way of such similarity;
however, the perception of [the object] as one's mother and so forth is not the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including the inclusion of the perception of [the object] as one's sister and so on.
This suffix *vati* is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhy-artha*).

Even when an external object is perceived, because a real universal (*vastubhūta-sāmānya*) does not exist, if every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is erroneous, then just as the conceptual construction of water arising from the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a mirage—which is devoid of the universal "water"—is erroneous, so too is the conceptual construction of water arising from [what is taken to be] real water, even though that water is empty of the nature of water; for it is erroneous because it functions by apprehending something as what it is not (*atasmims tadgraha*).
Why is it that for one there is correspondence with the object, while for another there is not?
To this he says "marīcika" (mirage), etc.

And for the other [he says] "sattyajale jalajñānasya": because the universal of "water-ness" (*jalatva-sāmānya*) is absent in the case of the cognition of water in real water, the mirage and the water are distinct entities; therefore, even though there is no difference in their production from that [cause], such is the connection [of the argument].

And even when there is no distinction [between them], there is delusion (*vibhrama*); for just as in a substance such as a mirage that is devoid of water, there is a delusion consisting of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of water due to the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the generality (*sāmānya*) of water, so too in the case of real water—because that [conceptualization] also consists of grasping something as what it is not—the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of drinking and so forth is not achieved.
In this regard, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of water is capable [of such efficiency], whereas the mirages are incapable;
therefore, because they arise from those [mirages] as their cause, the conceptual construction of water occurs with respect to both real water and mirages.
In their respective order, these are correspondence and its opposite; "the other" refers to non-correspondence.

Because [the object] is unsuitable—such as the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a mirage—it should be understood that the form of water is not suitable for that which does not have the nature of water.
The refutation begins with the words "vikalpa" and so forth;
it explains that very point: [cognition] is bound to the object, meaning its arising occurs by conforming to the form of the object.
Regarding the passage beginning with "na hi" and ending with "yathārtham": it is an *avyayībhāva* compound meaning "not exceeding the actual state of things" (*padārthānativṛttau*).
Furthermore, the particle *eva* is to be construed out of its original position (*bhinnakrama*).
The meaning is that a cognizer does not arise at all in conformity with its object.
If it is asked, "In that case, how was it stated that the cognition of water arises from mirages? he says:
"When [the conditions] exist," and so forth.

In the case of mirages, a visual consciousness and so forth arises erroneously; when that [consciousness] exists, there occurs the illusion of water which superimposes the form of what was previously experienced. Thus, because it arises through a succession [of causes], it is said to "arise from the mirage" (*marīcy-udbhava*).
The term *yathāsvabhāvam* is an avyayībhāva compound as explained previously.
It has been stated that jars and the like, being incapable of producing the illusion of water, are "non-water."

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: because it does not produce [its effect] according to its own nature (yathāsvabhāva) by means of an object called a mirage— which, for a discerning person, is capable of producing the error of water— it is said to be "arising from that" (tadudbhava).
The meaning of the phrase "according to its own nature" (*yathāsvabhāvam*) is precisely "conforming to its own nature" (*svabhāvānukāra*), and so forth;
for it conforms to its own nature, thus it is called "conforming to its own nature."
By means of presenting a reflection that corresponds to its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)— that is, by superimposing it upon cognition—
he says "But that [cognition]," and so forth, to explain by what that [reflection] is directly produced.
The water-delusion arises from water; the specific distinction between it and a mirage is its defining characteristic, which is determined through differentiation.

Due to a lack of proficiency regarding that [distinction], and by virtue of the awakening of one's own latent predisposition—the seed of the water-delusion—[the delusion] is produced through its corresponding activation.
By what kind [of cause]? By that which depends on conditions (*pratyayāpekṣiṇā*). "Condition" refers to the perception of a mirage and the recollection of its similarity to water;
from these [two], it is the conclusion. The analysis of the compound is as follows:

a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is itself an error (*vibhrama*); that conceptual error whose birth arises from a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone—an entity distinct from things of a different class—is thus described. This is the grammatical analysis (*vigraha*).

It does not arise from the perception of a universal that is distinct [from the individual], because that would entail the consequence of the cognition "it is here" even when [the individual] is not present; nor does it arise from the perception of a universal that is non-distinct [from the individual].

The connection with the subject at hand is "recognition" (*pratyabhijñāna*). Regarding the phrase "because there is no continuity as in the case of individuals," this means that since it lacks continuity in the same manner as individuals— that is, when consisting of individuals— the universal form itself does not exist.
"Of another" refers to the proponent of the universal;
"that" refers to the form of the universal; "from the isolated" means independently of the individual instance.
The commentary beginning with "na hi" explains why it is not so; he asks: "Why is it not so? and says: [the following].

Regarding the passage beginning with "nityam" and ending with "tanmātravijñāne," he explains it by means of the section beginning with "yadi. This refers to the apprehension of a mere generality (*sāmānyamātra*).
"By this" refers to the cognition having a general form;
"by this" refers to the cognition having a general object; and "that" refers to the non-apprehension of the particular.
If the related object— that which is endowed with a universal (*sāmānya*), namely the possessor of that universal (*tadvat*)—
and its possession of the universal (*tadvattā*),

as well as the universal itself and its substratum, were all apprehended by that cognition, then the ascertainment of the possession of the universal could not occur preceded by the apprehension of both [the universal and the substratum].
He explains with the words beginning "yadā" why, due to the apprehension of the universal (*sāmānya*), there is linguistic usage and activity directed toward the individual (*vyakti*):
"na tāv iti," [meaning] "not those two," namely the universal and that which possesses it.
If it is thus [asserted] that "this is the universal of this particular,

and that is [the particular]," then, since the relationship between the universal and its possessor has not been apprehended, there can be no apprehension of that [relationship], and consequently no apprehension of the universal.

"In that which possesses it" means in that which possesses a universal, "like another object"; for at the time of perceiving a horse, there is no cognition of the horse through the cognition of the cow-substance when it is not apprehended in its [the horse's] own form.
"Assisted by a single entity" means assisted by a universal.
This is the explanation of the phrase "it might be so" (*syādetat*):
"of that" means of the cognition;
"there is one auxiliary cause" means that the universal (*sāmānya*) serves as an auxiliary cause.
Then, [the cognition] is accompanied by that [particular], which is to say it is accompanied by the universal;
and thus, because both the universal and its possessor (tadvat) are apprehended, the apprehension of the possessor is established through the apprehension of the universal—this is the meaning.
Thus says the Teacher (Ācārya).
A single entity, as a universal, removes—that is, eliminates—the plurality of these individuals.
But why is the elimination of their plurality desired? To this he says:
"And because of plurality," and so forth.
And the word "hyarthaḥ" (the meaning of 'hi') [is explained] by the phrase "in those individuals," beginning with "why," etc.
Because of that single commonality,
the diversity among the particulars is said to be the cause of their not being the basis for a single cognition;
it is because of this diversity that the individuals do not produce a single cognition.

Even if there were a single connection with the universal, since the particulars are diverse, they would not lose their distinctness; thus, as before, there would be no cognition of them in a single form, and the individual forms, though manifold, would not be grasped as one under the name of a "universal."
He explains with the words beginning "no," etc.:
if it were contradictory to the non-production of difference, then even though the universal exists, a single cognition would not be produced by those [particulars] from the differences.
By "those" is meant the particulars (*vyakti*).
Furthermore, he says "individually" to show that it is not [the case] without all [of them] together.

For instance, when a *śāvaleyā* (a brindled cow) is absent, the cognition of "cow" does not arise with respect to a *bāhuleyā* (a black cow); likewise, in the absence of that [individual], it does not arise with respect to others either. Thus, even though every single individual is absent, those individuals lack the capacity to produce—by means of that single universal—a cognition consisting of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
For this reason, there is no apprehension by the intellect through the cognition of a universal of those individuals; he states that very point with the words beginning "How," and so forth.
In that case, regarding the cognition of a universal form,
the phrase "because of its existence" means because of the existence of the cognition of the universal;
by this, the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is stated.

The formal argument (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: that which occurs even in the absence of something else cannot have that thing as its cause; for example, a barley sprout that arises even in the absence of a rice seed.

And yet, the cognition of "cow" occurs in each instance—such as in a *bāhuleya* cow—even in the absence of a *śāvaleyā* cow. This is a contradiction of the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddha*), because being caused by that [specific individual] is necessarily pervaded by the absence of it [in other instances].
He states that the universal (sāmānya) possesses power there [in the cognition],
beginning with the words "asati" and so forth;
for if the universal were non-existent, the cognition of the universal would not occur.
By this, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) has been stated;
and by the phrase "otherwise," since the cognition of a universal occurs when a universal exists, the positive concomitance (anvaya) has been stated.

The opponent says: "If it is maintained that only individuals accompanied by the universal possess the capacity for the cognition of the universal, then—by the reasoning already stated—the capacity belongs to the universal alone and not to the individuals;
thus, this fault does not apply."
"Even in the absence of one [of the objects]" means even when each individual object of the [five] sense-fields is absent;

for instance, just as visual consciousness arises having the collection of blue and so forth as its object, and even when each individual blue and so forth is removed, visual cognition still occurs with respect to the remaining collection of colors— and it is not by this much that the blue and so forth lack causal efficacy in the collection, but rather they certainly possess it.

Just as in the case of a cognition of a collection of individual blue things and so forth, so too here, even when each individual is excluded from among the particulars, there still occurs a cognition of the universal;
therefore, it follows that it cannot be concluded that the particulars are individually incapable [of producing it] at all times. This is the connection [of the argument].
Furthermore, regarding the argument beginning with "that which exists even in the absence of X," the Master [Dharmakīrti] states that it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and thus "unequal" (*viṣama*).
This means that the example of blue and so forth, which is being introduced (*upanyāsa*), lacks similarity with the subject under discussion (*prakrānta*).
"It is not so for the individual in any way whatsoever" means that there is no capacity in either individual instances taken separately or in their totality;
he explains this as follows:
Regarding the phrase "of blue and so forth," and so on:
since capacity is observed even in each individual [element],
just as blue and the others are distinct by virtue of their own respective forms, so too are the visual consciousnesses.

Due to the distinction in their own forms, the visual consciousness produced by a collection accompanied by blue is not the same as that produced by one lacking it; and that which is produced by the latter is indeed different from the former. Therefore, because the consciousness colored by the form of the collection follows the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) with respect to each individual blue and so forth, the capacity of each of them is established. Thus, even in the case of a collection, the presence of causal power is not contradictory.
"So be it"; this means that, like blue and so forth, [the object] never exists either individually or in combination.

If the cognition of "cow" produced by a universal conjoined with a *śāvaleyā* cow were one thing, and that produced by a universal conjoined with a *bāhuleyā* cow were another, then the capacity of individual particulars to produce a cognition through their own substratum would be inferred;
however, there is only one single recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) across all individuals, because it possesses a single uniform form everywhere.
Even though individual instances do not exist [as causes], since this [cognition] arises from the universal alone,
the individuals are indeed incapable in that regard;
for this reason, they would not be apprehended by that cognition of the universal.
"Among those individuals, 'relative to one or another' means relative to some particular individual;
'that' refers to the universal alone, independent of individuals;
this he explains with the words beginning with 'atha'."

Although there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of the weaver (*kuvinda*), who is a cloth-maker, for even in the absence of each of many shuttles (*vema*), he produces a cloth with just one of them— nevertheless, it cannot be asserted that the production of the cloth occurs from that weaver alone when he is devoid of the shuttles.
Because a weaver does not produce a cloth without a shuttle— since a solitary [weaver] lacks the capacity to produce cloth—
likewise, a universal alone is not the cause of that [cognition];
such is the view of the Master Ācārya.

By asserting that the universal (*sāmānya*) is capable [of producing cognition] in dependence on any one of those individuals, you admit that the universal is assisted by the individuals, because dependence is impossible for that which provides no assistance.
If this is so, how is it that those individuals, while assisting that single universal, do not also produce a single cognition?
The word "and" (*ca*) is used here in the sense of "but" (*eva*).
"How could they not assist that very single cognition whose nature is recognition? That is to say, they would indeed assist it.
He explains this with the words "distinct" (*bhinna*) and so forth: "the performance of a single function by distinct [entities], that is, by those possessing different characteristics."

Since there is no universal (*sāmānya*) that would contradict the performance of a single purposeful action such as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), this entire undertaking is for the sake of establishing the universal. The sense is this: the individual entities (*vyakti*) have committed no offense by not performing that cognition known as recognition; rather, it is [the universal] which performs it, and nothing else does so. Therefore, it is precisely that [the universal] which performs it.
And so, what is the use here of this "internal goiter"?
An internal goiter is a lump of flesh situated between the forehead and the head; it is called such because it is like that—that is to say, it is useless.
This is the meaning.
It might be thought that distinct things possess a single power of assistance toward a universal, and therefore they assist the universal directly rather than the cognition; to this,
he says "just as," and so forth.
Thus, let that very cognition which is produced by the universal [of "oneness"] be what it is;
what is the use of the fruitless assistance of the universal?
This is how it is considered.
In cognition, individual instances do not operate by way of imparting their own forms to it,
because the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) does not appear in the cognition of the universal;
rather, they function merely through their predominance (ādhipatya).
And just as that [objection] applies to the universal, it applies equally to its cognition; furthermore,
if the individuals assist the universal, then that universal essence would become an effect of those individuals,
because assistance consists precisely in production.
Clarifying that very point, he says "for not," and so forth;
"excess" (*atiśaya*) means a distinction (*viśeṣa*), and because that is absent, its own nature (*ātman*)— its intrinsic being (*svabhāva*)— is "without excess."

Because of the absence of an auxiliary [factor] for the universal (*sāmānya*), as before; even when an auxiliary is present, there is no one who maintains it— this is the connection [of the sentence].
Because this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),
for in that case everything would be a benefactor to everything;
therefore, one must accept that an excellence (*atiśaya*) is produced in the beneficiary by the benefactor alone.
And since that excellence is of the very nature of the beneficiary, its production is itself the assistance;
[the opponent] says "a different entity," etc., [meaning] that the excellence produced by the individuals is indeed a different entity from the universal, and not something else.
What benefit is produced for that universal (*sāmānya*) by that other entity (*arthāntara*) which constitutes the assistance?
And what [benefit] is there for that other entity, the assistance itself, by virtue of which it would have a connection with that universal through that assistance?
Since the individual instances (*vyakti*) would also be providers of assistance by virtue of producing that assistance which is related to the universal, [the universal would be dependent on them].

Since the universal (*sāmānya*) is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the assistance (*upakāra*), the relationship between those two is characterized by the relation of substratum and that which is supported (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*); therefore, he says "of that," and so forth, [meaning] when that assistance has that [universal] as its substratum.
This is because it has that generality as its basis;
or, since that generality has it as its basis, it is considered the basis for that assistance.

It assists, thus it is an "assistant" (*upakārī*); due to the absence of that [assistance], a universal is "non-assistant" (*anupakārī*). Assistance is that which is produced by a universal; one who possesses such assistance is an "assistant," and by the negation of that, one is "non-assistant," meaning "that which cannot be assisted."
And these two points are conveyed by way of a double entendre;
therefore, the meaning is as follows:
what kind of relationship of support and supported (āśrayāśrayibhāva) could there be, respectively, between a universal that provides no assistance and an assistance that receives no assistance?
Or else there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);

for if the relationship of support and supported (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) were to exist even for that which provides no assistance, it would follow [absurdly] in all cases; or, if assistance is admitted, it must be one produced by the universal (*sāmānya*).

If it is argued that the restriction of that assistance pertains to the universal itself, and therefore no other particular is an assistant to that universal because it produces that assistance [only indirectly], [we reply:
"dependent on that" means dependent on the particular; that is, the substratum—namely, the universal—is the basis for the assistance in relation to that [assistance].

If that assistance is conceived as being rendered through its application, then since the universal is eternal and thus incapable of being assisted, what indeed is this so-called "dependence upon the individual"?
It is none at all.
To the question, "What then is it that depends [on something else]?
he says: "tadutpatti... and so forth.

That which has its arising (*utpatti*) from that which is to be depended upon (*apekṣaṇīya*) is "that which has the nature of arising from that" (*tadutpattidharmabhāva*). This refers to a phenomenon (*dharma*), that is, an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because it is dependent upon its own nature—that is, because it is constrained by it—it indeed requires an auxiliary cause;
the word "nāma" (indeed) indicates what is well-known.
If it is argued that even a universal (*sāmānya*), though characterized by non-arising, requires [an auxiliary], he says:

"Anādheya," etc.: that which has an *ātmaniśaya* (intrinsic excellence) that is not to be added (*anādheya*)—that is, not produced (*anutpādya*)—by those auxiliary factors is "of such a nature. This [term] is a further *bahuvrīhi* compound; such being the case, it refers to the category of the universal (*sāmānyapadārtha*). The note marked "218-1" contains illegible text.
And to say that it "depends on others" is contradictory; for this is established by the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*),
since dependence is pervaded by the presence of an excellence to be produced (*atiśaya*).
This is contrary to that [position]: the state of being incapable of receiving any further excellence (*anādheyātiśayatva*).
Whatever connection (*pratibandha*) there may be between some entity and some substratum, all such [connection] arises only in the context of being produced or being an effect.
If it is argued that the substratum performs a benefit for the dependent entity that is not identical with its own self (*anātmabhūta*), he replies:
Regarding the passage beginning with "parabhāva" (other-nature) and so forth:
because there is no assistance rendered to it, that is, because no assistance is rendered to that which is to be assisted; for when one thing is assisted, another is not thereby said to be assisted.
If that [universal] is its substratum, then what is this relationship of substrate and superstratum for something that provides no assistance? All of this must be explained;

nor is there the fault of tautology, because previously it was stated by way of the relationship between the assisted and the assister regarding the universal and its possessor, whereas now it is stated by taking up the actual, objective relationship pertaining to all objects.
Therefore, because it produces a different effect, that which is considered the substratum is of no assistance;
if it is argued that even such a thing is helpful, he says: "Of that which is of no assistance," and so forth.
Since this is so, therefore, in the production of a cognition— specifically, in the production of a recurrent (anvayi) cognition—
it is evident that this universal necessarily possesses the status of being the effect of that [manifestation], that is, the status of being the effect of the manifestation.

If, out of fear of the aforementioned defects, one were to admit that the universal alone— without depending on individuals— possesses the capacity to produce a cognition of concomitance (*anvayivijñāna*), then because the capacity of individuals would never be established in producing such a cognition of concomitance at any time, the individuals would be ungraspable; for that which is not a cause cannot logically be an object of cognition.
"Because it appears in cognition"—
for that which is incapable, such as a rabbit's horn, does not appear in a cognition that conforms [to its form]; rather,
it is the individuals that appear.

Therefore, even if they possess a universal, they are not capable [of producing it]; thus, for those individuals whose contribution to the cognition of the universal is unestablished, how could there be an appearance of them in the cognition of the universal?
There is none at all.
If it is asked how the very assistance [of the universal] is unestablished, he says "sa eva" (that very [thing]), and so forth.
"Saḥ" refers to the assistance; for if a universal is admitted, it is that very [universal] which possesses the capacity there, not the individuals.
As it was said by them: "Even without those [causes], with respect to a cognition produced individually," and so forth. (1.105)
He says "because," etc., [in response to the question]: "Let there be no assistance from the individuals; why then does their appearance not occur in the cognition of the universal?
[The reason is] "because of the over-extension" (atiprasaṅga).
If that which provides no assistance were an object, then everything would be an object of every consciousness.
If it is argued, "Let there be no [actual] object, but why should there be no appearance? he says:
The phrases "not of that which is not an object," etc.,
and "of that which does not assist," etc.,
have "of that which does not assist" (*anupakārasya*) as an alternative reading.
In that regard, it should be explained that "non-beneficial" (anupakāra) refers to that object from which no benefit for the effect of consciousness is derived;
since it is not an object [of cognition], this includes the past, the future, and so forth—
the word "and so forth" (ādi) including such imagined entities as *pradhāna* and *Īśvara*, according to their respective scriptural sources.
The phrase "of non-existent things" indicates that this is not a general reason;
by the words "let them be," etc., he states that [the argument] would result in proving what is already established;
and the phrase "having those as their objects" means having past objects as their objects.
To the objection, "If there is no object, how will it be included among them?"— and because the appearance thus conforms to such meanings as these, he says,
"Even though there is no object," and so forth;
"not assisting that" means not assisting that object which was experienced and has now passed away.
Because it imitates only an object that has already passed away through an indistinct form, there is no such thing as a "past direction" whose form it could imitate;
furthermore, that manifestation is essentially identical with the consciousness itself, since an indistinct form does not exist externally.
He states the reason for its imitation of that form:

Regarding the passage beginning with "tadrūpānubhava" (experience of that form): the meaning is that whatever kind of experience of a present object has arisen, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by it gives rise to a cognition that arises in the form of the experienced object. This is logical in the case of the past, because the object was experienced during its present state; but how [is this possible] in the case of the future and so forth?

For there is no direct experience (*anubhava*) of that [primordial matter]; rather, it is the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) associated with verbal expression (*abhilāpa*), arising from such words as "there will be an object of such a nature," which—because it is self-cognized—is itself the experience of that form. Thus, there is no fault, since the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is produced by that [experience].

In this same way, regarding conceptual constructions of *pradhāna* and so forth, the production of the latent impression of the experience of conceptual constructions bearing the forms of word and object should be explained according to the scriptures.
Thus, since it follows that past objects and so forth would not be objects [of cognition], the statement that "an object is that which provides assistance" is indeed absolute;
likewise, because individuals whose assistance is unestablished are not objects, they do not appear in the cognition of a universal.
Consequently, as for what was stated:
It was stated that individual entities are incapable [of being the cause] of cognition because they do not appear [in it];
now, even while granting their appearance, he states that the reason is inconclusive.
Regarding the passage beginning with "existence and non-existence" (*bhāvābhāva*):

when there is the existence of an object, there is the existence of consciousness, and when there is its non-existence, there is the non-existence of consciousness; this conformity to the existence and non-existence [of the object] is the reason from which the causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*) of the object with respect to consciousness is understood.
But it is not because of its appearance;
for, according to the actual state of things, even though the universal does not appear, its causal efficacy is admitted in conceptual cognition.
He says this very thing:
"Even though it does not appear," and so forth: for a universal does not appear as distinct from the individual;
even that conceptual cognition in which a universal appears has only the form of color, shape, and so on.
For even there, no other general form (sāmānyākāra) distinct from the forms of color and so forth is perceived;
nor is the universal (sāmānya) of the nature of color, shape, and so on.
Therefore, the universal does not appear as a real entity (vastusthityā).
Nevertheless, according to your view, because that [object] exists as something non-manifesting,

it is "cultivated" (bhāvyate)— that is, produced— within consciousness; thus, "existence" (bhāva) is said to mean causal capacity (sāmarthya), in the sense that "by this, the effect is brought about."
Showing that even though they appear, they lack causal efficacy, he says "of those that appear" and so forth:
they are called *viplavas* because they "deviate"— that is, they depart from being real entities— such as [the appearance of] hairs and the like.
The analysis of the compound is "errors" (*viplavāḥ*).

For these indeed appear in visual perceptions such as those of one suffering from ophthalmia; nevertheless, because they are non-existent, the incapacity of the etymological derivation of the word "existence" (*bhāva*)—as explained previously—is expressed by the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*).
The meaning is that they lack the capacity for the production of consciousness.

Even if such capacity were present, since their appearance is observed—that is, because they do appear—it is stated that the argument "capacity implies [the production of] an appearance" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
How could those [atoms], while assisting a single [cognition], not produce a single cognition? (1.107)
Regarding what was stated there, he anticipates the opponent’s response with the words beginning "abhinnapratibhāsā," meaning "having an undivided appearance" or "having a single form."

When those specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) are distinct, their form is "that form" (tadākāra). That cognition in which this [form] is superimposed or placed is "such" [a cognition]. And such a cognition is one that appears as non-distinct; for it would not be so if it were produced from things that possess entirely different characteristics.
And since there arises a cognition appearing as non-different, it does not arise from things that possess distinct characteristics alone, but rather from a universal entity (*sāmānyapadārtha*);
this [objection] is refuted by the words "no" and so forth.

This explains that if particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or their own forms (*svākāra*) are held to be the producers of cognitions possessing universal forms (*sāmānyākāra*), then this is logical; for how could there be a cognition with a non-differentiated appearance regarding things that are distinct?
And that [particular] does not exist, because there is no appearance of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) in cognitions that manifest a universal (*sāmānya*).
For, if one were to admit the appearance of the particular in cognitions grasping a universal, three alternatives would arise:
(1) that the particulars appear in cognitions of the eye and so forth by the very same form that they appear in cognitions of the universal; or...

Alternatively, that very form which appears in the cognition of the universal must be admitted as the two-fold nature of the particularities themselves; for by means of one [nature] it appears in the cognitions of the eye and so forth, while by the other it appears in conceptual cognitions.

1. Regarding the first position: just as in the case of cognitions of the eye and so forth, there would be an absence of universal-cognitions (*sāmānyabuddhi*) in the absence of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); yet this is not so, because those universal-cognitions exist even in the absence of that particular characteristic. 2. He states the non-existence of the second position:
Regarding the phrase "by another aspect" (*ākārāntareṇa*) and so forth:

because the particular aspect (*asādhāraṇa*), which is distinct from the general aspect (*sāmānyākāra*), appears in its own cognition—that is, in the cognition of the eye and other senses—the form of particulars is not merely the general aspect. He speaks thus in order to refute the third position.
"Because of the impossibility of [one thing] possessing manifold forms" means that it is illogical for one thing to be manifold due to the contradiction between oneness and manifoldness,
and because of the resulting over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); thus, if one were to imagine manifoldness in what is one, oneness would not exist anywhere at all.
Furthermore, since the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) does not appear in the cognition of a universal,
this cognition of a universal form cannot be one that apprehends distinct objects.
Having the form of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its basis, it appears as if its form were non-different from reality; yet,
although it arises from distinct objects,
it is produced by nature as inherently erroneous, relying upon the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience that grasps the specific characteristic.

And if it is argued that the individuals [of the lineage] are said to be the cause of that [conceptual cognition] through a traditional succession, then [the opponent asks]: "If the cognition of a universal does not have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its manifestation, how does it cause people to engage with the particular characteristic? To this, [the author] replies:
"Even though it does not manifest that [particular characteristic]," and so forth.

Even though it manifests the specific characteristic (*asvalakṣaṇa*), because of the delusion of determining an object within its own manifestation—which is not an actual object—it causes the world to engage in conventional practice; that is to say, it causes [people] to act by conflating the perceived and the conceptualized.
[The opponent objects: "If the cognition of a universal has the form of a universal, then that very thing must be the ultimate universal. To this, he says:
"But that [universal], in that [cognition]," and so forth.
That appearing universal form does not exist in external objects,
because it is not perceived as distinct from them,
nor— as non-distinct— because, like the individual particulars themselves, it lacks persistence [in other instances].
To the question, "How then is there the appearance of a non-different form among individuals? he says:
"Other than difference, [there is] the non-different. Difference is *anyāpoha* (the exclusion of others); that very thing is non-different with respect to each individual.
For instance, just as one individual cow is excluded from non-cows, so too is another;

in this manner, it is the very particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves—excluded from what is heterogeneous and undifferentiated—that are called "difference" (*bheda*). Furthermore, this word *bheda* is a particle (*nipāta*) that resembles a form ending in a case-suffix.
The word *anya* has the same meaning as [the term] "other," but it is not here a derivative of the suffix *-tva*; for the locative sense (*saptamy-artha*) is not intended.

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: there is no other appearing form in objects that is non-different from the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) by way of the aforementioned mode; rather, the particular itself, which is non-different from the exclusion of dissimilar things (*vijātīya-vyāvṛtti*), exists everywhere as something non-different, because of the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of non-difference.
And as for the determination of non-difference, that very difference is its indirect cause.
[Objection: But surely a non-different form appears in cognition; how then can it be said not to exist in the objects? To this he says:
"And that is formless."
And the word "also" (*ca*) is used here for the sake of emphasis;

for that form which appears in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), because—as was just stated—it is impossible to establish it as either identical to or different from reality in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). Since the cognition grasps precisely that form, its very arising in that form constitutes its "grasping. Thus, it is said that because it grasps a form that lacks any real substance (*arūpa*), it "goes astray," meaning it becomes erroneous (*bhrānta*). This was explained previously.
Since it has already been stated that this incapacity of conceptual constructions arises from ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth,
[the author], having now set aside the refutation of that fault, says "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so on, in order to demonstrate that the same fault applies equally [to the opponent's position].
"It is not equal," says the opponent;
"in that case," [the opponent argues], "since the cognition of a similar form arises from that very same universal (*sāmānya*) with respect to distinct individuals, the objection is not equal.
To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) replies with "But surely" (*nanu*), and so forth.
In that regard, among the individuals, the appearance— the form— of that existing universal is not perceived;
or rather, "therein" means in conceptual and non-conceptual cognition,
it might be as follows.
He says "for that [is]... and so forth, because there is an appearance of that [object] within conceptual cognition.
For that conceptual cognition is perceived—that is, it is experienced—as possessing color and shape.

If it is argued that the universal (*sāmānya*) is simply the form of color and so forth, he says "and not," etc. "Such" refers to the form of color and configuration; because color and configuration are qualities (*guṇa*), and because a universal is distinct from a quality.
Nor [is it] from that— namely, from color, shape, and so forth.
Having thus refuted the universal as something distinct, [the author], desiring to refute it as something non-distinct, says "ākṛti" and so forth.

Similarity, which is essentially identical with the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), is the configuration (*ākṛti*); that itself is the universal (*sāmānya*). One who holds the doctrine of that [universal] is a Sāṃkhya; he whose habit it is to speak thus is so designated. Because that universal is non-different from the specific characteristic, it does not subsist in other objects—that is, in the second and subsequent individuals—just like the specific characteristic itself.

For this reason, that universal (*sāmānya*) has likewise arisen as nothing but the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); therefore, because of the cause of its difference [from particulars], a non-different appearance of that which exists is not tenable with respect to individuals—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Thus, having accepted the non-different appearance as stated by Uddyotakara and others, it was said that since a universal—whether distinct or non-distinct—is untenable, this single-form appearance among individuals is merely an illusion. Now, he states that there is no single appearance among individuals:
Alternatively, as for what was stated beginning with "let it be so," namely that "a cognition with an undivided appearance does not [arise] toward distinct things"— let that be so.
The meaning is that this is indeed accepted,
because the manifestation of cognitions— namely, universal cognitions— is distinct;
for what reason?

By the words "samānāḥ" (identical), [the author] explains through the phrase "naiva... and so forth that there is the apprehension of those individuals; he explains that within those—namely, the cognitions of the universal—there is a single appearance, which is non-different.
What is the reason?
Because those individuals are apprehended as being "similar.
Now, one might ask: given that they are apprehended as similar, why is it not logical for there to be a single appearance (*ekapratibhāsa*)? To this, he says:
"Not indeed," and so forth;

rather, it would be "that very same thing," meaning that which was previously seen is this very thing being seen now, but not "this is similar to the previous one," because the conventional usage of "similarity" is based on a distinction between two things,
as indicated by the phrase "of the two," and so on.
If only the universal were grasped by those cognitions, then this fault would arise;
however, both the universal and the particular are grasped by the cognition of the universal. Therefore, because both are grasped, there is no fault.
Since the particulars, being endowed with that very same universal, are apprehended as "similar," the Teacher [Dignāga] says "even so" (*tathāpi*);
for even if the apprehension of both [the universal and the particular] is assumed, it would follow that "this is that."

If it is argued that "generality" (*sāmānya*) is that which was previously seen in one individual (*vyakti*) and is now seen here in another individual— and thus it is called "similar" (*samāna*) because the generality is absolutely distinct from the individuals, such that the generality of cowness (*gotva*) and so forth is a different entity entirely which constitutes the similarity of those individuals by virtue of which they are "similar"—
then [we ask]: how, and in what manner, can there be a similarity between this [generality] and that other thing, namely the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is distinct from the generality?
The intention is that it is not by anything [external]; for, if a universal were to be postulated as the commonality of individuals due to its imitation of their manifested forms,
that would not be possible, because the universal is absolutely distinct from the individuals.

Nor are there others equal to this by which it might possess that equality; for equality does not arise from the imitation of the form of individuals or the like, but rather from its connection with them—
that is, from its connection with individuals.
If it is argued that the universal belongs to the individuals because it is their universal, this is not so;
for what reason?
Because it is unconnected—that is to say, independent of the individuals and not assisted by them.

If it is accepted that the universal (sāmānya) possesses similarity due to its connection with the relation characterized as inherence (samavāya), there follows an over-extension (atiprasaṅga): even number, conjunction, and effect-substances would possess the nature of a universal.
Consequently, through connection with those, there would arise a uniform cognition (samānapratibhāsa) regarding the objects numbered and so forth. How so? [The opponent asks: "And so on."
By the inclusion of the term "identical," a difference in manifestation among individuals is established;
however, this is contradictory because if these individuals are identical, how could they be apprehended by distinct cognitions? This is stated as an absolute restriction.
The meaning is that [the objects] would also result in being grasped by a non-differentiated cognition.

For instance, where there is some generality and some particularity, it is logical to have the apprehension "they are similar"; otherwise, as in the case of a jar and a cloth, there would be a manifestation of non-difference rather than the thought "they are similar.
He explains this as follows:
Regarding the passage beginning with "nanu" and so forth:
by the phrase "in these individuals," he expresses the specific form [of the object];
the words "the non-different appearance is established" are to be supplied as an ellipsis.
By this, the nature of the universal (sāmānya) has been stated;
thus, because both common and uncommon forms are apprehended, individuals are apprehended as being "similar"—this is the collective meaning.
Now, does a single or manifold appearance exist among those things that are similar, such that it can be said in this way?
If it is argued that the cognition "it would be here" arises because particulars possess a universal nature (sāmānyātmakatva) and thus appear as "similar," then we ask:
in the absence of a recurring appearance (anugata-pratibhāsa), how can it be established that a universal exists?
Nor is it reasonable to postulate a universal based on the impossibility of otherwise accounting for their similar form;
for some things arise from their own causes as necessarily similar, while others arise as dissimilar, and it has already been stated that their similarity of form cannot be derived from a universal.

Therefore, as it has been stated by Bhaṭṭa: "No one at all is able to cognize cows and the like without distinction, [if they were] in the form of an exclusion (apoha) whose similarity is unestablished."
Now, even if there were no similarity of form, if one were to conceive of exclusion (apoha),
why is this "exclusion of non-cow" not conceived for both the cow and the horse?
For the difference from a *śābaleya* [cow] is the same for both the *bāhuleya* [cow] and the horse.
Furthermore, no universal other [than exclusion] is accepted; and where could the operation of apoha take place?
Moreover, it is impossible to define even the horses and other things to be excluded (apohya) without the presence of a single common property; thus, that apoha is not established.
In the *Ślokavārttika*, it is stated:

"Even without a universal (*sāmānya*), since cows and other such things arise from their own causes as similar entities, even if one does not accept that 'similarity' (*sārūpya*) is a distinct entity, they are nonetheless admitted to be similar."

And since all those things such as horses and so forth, which possess such forms, are negated without distinction by way of their not having the form of a cow, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. However, the Teacher (Ācārya), demonstrating that although things indeed arise from their own causes as identical, nevertheless the cognition of them as identical does not occur through the power of a universal (sāmānya),
says "no," and so forth.
"In the perception of that" means in a cognition that apprehends the individual or in a cognition of the universal;
"of the distinct and non-distinct" refers to the particular and the universal.
"Similarity as having a single effect" means that similarity or equality consists precisely in having a single effect; by that alone are the individuals perceived as identical,
and not by means of an ultimate universal (*pāramārthika-sāmānya*).

Thus, similarity consists in having a single effect; therefore, those things which have that [single effect] are the objects of exclusion (*apoha*), while those which do not have a single effect are what are excluded—this is established. Furthermore, as to how even things that are absolutely distinct can produce a single effect, this was explained previously. He asks: "Why are they not perceived as identical by virtue of their commonality? To this he replies:
"Indeed not," and so forth;

in the cognition of an object— that is, in the cognition of experience— there are two distinct aspects due to the conceptualization of two objects, through the conceptualization of them as either identical or non-identical.
"To the state of being an object of conceptual construction" means to the state of being an object of the conceptual construction that superimposes unity;
"in that manner" means by means of this conceptual cognition through its homogeneous form.
Regarding the passage beginning with "nanu" and so forth,
the opponent [states] that the cognition of those individuals is its effect, and that this [cognition] differs; this much of the verse is recited in reference to the phrase "in each object."

The commentary beginning with "tadvat" (in that manner) regarding "evambhāvam prati" (with respect to such a state) refers to cognition that manifests that [universal] as well as cognition that manifests the individual.
Similarly, due to the difference between individual instances (vyakti),
how is it that individual instances do not have a single effect?

It might be argued that individuals do not have a single effect through the cognition of direct experience (*anubhavajñāna*), but rather with respect to that conceptual construction (*vikalpaka*) which superimposes a single form; to this,
he says "tad dhi" and so forth.

For that [cognition] which is the knowledge of experience is the effect of those individual instances (*vyakti*), not conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*), because the latter exists even in the absence of the individual instances.
And as for that very conceptual cognition arising with the thought "they are similar," what is the similarity among the individuals?
It is the removal of cold and so forth, as in the case of cloth and other such things; this is what is included by the phrase "and so forth."
The term *pratidravyam* is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*); the sixth case ending is replaced by *am*.

The meaning is that it does not differ because of the difference of substance—that is, because of the difference of each individual substance, which is the cause of difference; such is the view of the Teacher (Ācārya).

Because it is the cause of a single reflective awareness—that is, of a cognition of a single form regarding its own object—the cognition, whether non-conceptual or conceptual, appears as non-different by virtue of being the cause of a single cognition. Thus, through being the cause of a cognition that is determined to have a single form, the non-difference of the individuals appears.
This is what is meant.
Although the cognitions apprehending the nature of each individual object are distinct, nevertheless, through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), their unity is determined.
And by this similarity of having a single effect, the unity of the individuals is [established];
however, the unity of the experiential cognitions is not figuratively attributed merely on the basis of being the cause of a single reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).

Nor is the unity of individuals metaphorically attributed to them on the grounds that they are the cause of a cognition of such an experience, because there is an absence of an erroneous cognition [regarding their multiplicity] and because there would be an absence of a secondary metaphor upon a metaphor; furthermore,
the meaning of the verse would not have been explained in accordance with the meaning of the commentary.
Now, if the determination of identity among individual instances is due to their similarity in having a single effect, how then is there a determination of identity among cognitions,
given that they lack a single common effect?
Now, if it is argued that even individual instances (*vyakti*) will produce the determination of oneness by their very nature, what is the use of similarity through a single effect?
This objection is not valid, for this was stated precisely with the intention of the teacher Dignāga.
Therefore, unity is accepted based on the determination of unity,
but not from an ultimate standpoint; thus he says,
"It has been explained," and so forth.
Because it has been stated in [Pramāṇavārttika 1.42], "All entities participate in exclusion by virtue of their own nature," the word "therein" refers to those particulars that are not conjoined.
A cognition with a single form is indeed an error because it apprehends that [object] in what is not that;
if it should be argued that error is impossible without a universal, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "tān tu" and so forth:
objects that dispel error produce, in succession, particularities (*svalakṣaṇa*) that are excluded [from others], but they do not do so directly by their own nature;
this is due to their inherent disposition (*prakṛti*).
The word "ca" (and) serves to draw back [the term] "niveditam" (it has been explained).
This also refers to what was stated in that very context—that [it was] explained in sequence—and its explanation is: "being the causes of conceptual construction."
Because it is the cause of conceptualization, experiential cognition (*anubhavajñāna*) is itself a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
The meaning is that they become the causes of the experiential cognition which is the cause of conceptualization;
individual entities (*vyakti*) produce that experiential cognition, and that [cognition] is an error consisting of a single form—this is the sequence of the argument.
With the verse beginning "But that of these," etc., he states the meaning of the *kārikā*:
Is the difference of all entities—the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)—of the nature of their distinction from what does not produce that [effect]? That is said to be their non-difference.
Why?
Because of the production of a single result corresponding to the self— such as cognition and so forth from the object, or the fetching of water and so forth from the sense organ—
or alternatively, [because of the production of a single result] from any [cause].
[Objection: But surely this undifferentiated form belongs to cognition alone; how can it belong to the individuals? [Reply: To this he says:
"But that form of these external things is indeed undifferentiated, because they are perceived as such. [Question: Why is there such a perception?
Because it is produced by some single factor such as cognition and so forth, that form is called "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) and not a universal (sāmānya);
what is the reason for this?
The exclusion of the nature of that which does not perform that function;
for this is what is meant:

by the cognition "cow, cow" occurring with respect to each individual, the very nature excluded from the nature of that which does not perform that function—that is, the nature as distinguished from the nature of that which does not perform that function—is made the object.
However, the universal is not a separate entity [from the particular]; therefore, it is called a "particularity" (bheda).
This is the explanation of the latter half of the verse.
Now, one might ask: "How can there be oneness of cognition and so forth?
To this he says, "That too," and so on; this is the explanation of the first half-verse.
The connection is that even that effect, such as cognition and so forth, appears as non-different;
"by nature" means by its own essence,
[referring to those] which "assail non-difference," that is, which determine non-difference.
With the words "tathābhūta" (being such) and so forth, he states that even individuals are causes of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) through a mediated succession.

The connection is as follows: because there exists a determination of non-difference (*abhedāvasāya*) regarding that [conceptual construction]—namely, cognition and so forth—the individuals also produce a single cognition sequentially, since they are the causes, by way of being the basis, for the knowledge of experience and for practical purposes such as fetching water.
To specify what kind [of cognition it is], he says:
Regarding the phrase "having a mixed form" (*saṃsṛṣṭākāra*) and so forth:
that by which a single, mixed form is superimposed upon individuals is "thus [mixed]. The analysis of the compound is as follows:
"nature-difference" (*svabhāvabheda*) is a form excluded from others; that very thing is its "ultimate, non-figurative" (*paramārthānupacarita*) nature. This is the grammatical analysis (*vigraha*).
Since conceptual construction (vikalpa) is derived through a succession [of causes] by way of the exclusion of specific individualities (svalakṣaṇa),
has this point not indeed been stated immediately prior in the passage beginning with "But those distinct entities..."? True.
However, since they become the causes of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in a gradual sequence, the meaning of the very first [verse] has been clarified by this.
[One might argue: "There will be a universal (*sāmānya*) that exists as a real entity (*vastubhūta*) consisting of the distinction between single effects.
To this, he says: "And that," and so forth.

And that state of having a single effect is simply the nature of exclusion—that is, the differentiation from those things which do not have that effect; it is not a real universal. Why? Because no other persisting, concomitant entity is observed apart from the individual particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), and because of the refutation previously stated.
He explains with the words "na hi" and so forth:
