if the universal were visible— that is, met the conditions for perception— and existed as distinct from the individuals through differentiation, then, because it would be eternal and thus incapable of having any new qualities added to it, how could it, being unattached to any particular individual, be the cause of cognition?
The intended meaning is that it is not at all accepted that such [an object], which is manifested by its substratum, serves as a cause for cognition;
this should be connected with the phrase "this too has been stated."
Since this too has been stated previously— that because such a universal does not exist— therefore, the convention [also does not exist], and so forth.
The word "that" (tat) is connected with "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha);

the cognition (vit) is the knowledge of this exclusion— which is superimposed by conceptual thought as non-different from its own form— and the acquisition is that which is preceded by such [cognition].
The term *tadvit* is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "that which has that very thing as its object and result";
the suffix *ṭhan* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) to indicate that this [convention] belongs to Maya.
The collective meaning is: "for the sake of the comprehension of external objects as determined by conceptual construction.

Since every undertaking is for the sake of a result, the root *vid* (to find/obtain) in the sense of "attainment" is also implicitly included; otherwise, the formulation of the convention would be purposeless.
Now, one might object that it should be a *bahuvrīhi* compound—namely, *tad-vid-artha* ("that which has the attainment of that as its purpose")—because this is more concise.
Because the possessive sense (*matvartha*) is already expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the case endings for that sense do not arise; this results in brevity (*lāghava*).
Thus it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "A *bahuvrīhi* occurs in place of a *karmadhāraya," and so forth—*Vyākaraṇa-mahābhāṣya*.
This is not a fault;
for it has also been stated there that in some cases the *karmadhāraya* compound itself serves the purpose of expressing "all means" (*sarvasādhana*) and so forth.
Furthermore, because it belongs to an open class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), the word *dvandva* should be understood there as including all such meanings as "all means" and the rest.
112. Ibid.,
the commentary beginning with "yoyam" (this which...).

The mutual distinction (*anyonya-viveka*)—the nature of things as excluded from others—is for the sake of their cognition and for the sake of determining them; thus, even a convention (*saṃketa*) being applied to one's own mental reflection (*svapratibhāsa*), which has the form of an external object superimposed upon it, would be appropriate because it is logically consistent.
To the question "For what purpose is it applied?", he says:
"That which does not produce that," and so forth.

The meaning is that, for the sake of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) by means of the exclusion (*viveka*) and avoidance of those things which do not perform the intended causal function, there should be no engagement with those things that do not perform such a function.
Strengthening this very point by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "yadi" (*if*):

the purpose of that exclusion of others (*anyaparihāra*) is for the sake of cognition. If the convention (*saṃketa*) does not produce that [cognition], then at the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), it would not touch upon the exclusion of others.

Alternatively, if the convention is not for the sake of cognizing that [exclusion], then the convention is for the sake of cognizing an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that is excluded from what is of a different class (*vijātīya*).

Then, because that nature which is excluded from others is not touched by the word—not only at the time of convention but even at the time of practical usage—and is not made an object [of cognition] by it, one would not proceed by way of excluding others.
This is what is meant:
when an object excluded from others is made an object [of cognition] in a positive form, then the exclusion of others would be understood.
He says this very thing with the words "for not," etc.;
"separation" (*viveka*) means a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
[The phrase] "from those which perform that [function]" refers to those which do not perform that function.

For if a convention were established for the sake of cognizing that distinct intrinsic nature (svabhāva), then in practical usage (*vyavahāra*) as well, it would be indicated by the word in that very way; and thus, one would proceed by excluding other things. Therefore, it is logical that even the convention should have that [distinct nature] as its object.
But surely, since the cognition produced by a word grasps its own internal form by superimposing it as something external, it is false;
and if that is so, how can the word that produces it correspond to reality, and how can it have "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) as its object?
To this, he says: "And that... and so forth.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: that conventional term (*śruti*) which exists for the purpose of understanding the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) also generates a cognition (*dhiyam janayantī*).
Of what specific nature?
Not performing an action,
within its own form which is not external.

The third compound is *tatkāri-tulya-rūpeṇa arthakriyākāri-bāhya-eka-rūpeṇa avabhāsa-adhyavasāyaḥ*; the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is added afterwards to that [compound] which possesses this [quality]. What is meant is this: it is the determination (*adhyavasāya*) which, though its own form is not external, determines it as if it were external—so to speak.
By this, it has been explained that the purpose of the Veda is [to prompt] activity.
If it is asked, "In the absence of a real entity (vastu) such as a universal (sāmānya), how could there be the production of that [activity]?", he says "vastu" and so forth.

The distinctness of things—that is, their mutual difference—is the seed or cause of that [conceptual cognition] through a traditional succession; thus it is so described. And because it apprehends the inclusive form and the excluded forms as unified, the verbal testimony, even though it produces what is not real, is not non-concordant with the object.
Why is this?
This is what is meant: because it serves as a factor for the exclusion of that which does not perform that function,
and because it serves as the cause for the non-exclusion of what is of a different class.

If the word (śruti) were to produce a cognition that determines an object as excluded from others, then it would cause a person to act toward that very particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) excluded from others, and thus it would be non-contradictory. Furthermore, at the time of the convention, the basis for this word is a nature that is indeed mutually distinct; for it was established there [as such].
Thus, because it is indirectly based on the distinction between real entities, [the word] functions with respect to the object.
It is not considered non-conformative, because even at the time of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), it brings about the attainment of a real entity that is indeed excluded from others.

Now, one might ask: since there is a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the entity by way of a positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa*), how can the word have "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as its object? To this, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "tataḥ" (therefore) and so forth:

since verbal testimony (*śruti*) has as its basis the distinction between entities by virtue of being a factor for the exclusion of what does not perform that function, for that reason [the words] have other-exclusion (*anyāpoha*) as their object.
He states these two very points [in the following].
"By virtue of being based on its agent" means that, within that exclusion (*apoha*), there is the state of being an agent and the state of being dependent;

and this dependence occurs by way of denoting its own object, since it functions as a factor for the exclusion of what does not perform that function. Thus, through the word, there is the state of being an agent within that exclusion.
Because it functions at the time of linguistic usage and at the time of convention by way of relying on the distinction between objects, the word (*śruti*) has its basis in that exclusion (*apoha*).
He states the meaning of the verse with the words "one," etc.:
[it is] that which arises by superimposing—that is, by attributing—to objects a single form (*ākāra*) that appears as its own [mental] reflection.
And that [cognition], being a mere self-reflection, does not perform an action because it is a false appearance;
yet, determining that very [reflection] as if it were performing an action,
it is explained by the phrase "by this, no action is performed," and so forth.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: it is that cognition which consists merely in the distinctness of objects and merely in the exclusion of others.
To the question, "Even though the Veda produces a false cognition, why is it called a false cognition? he says:
In a uniform determination— that is, a determination of a single form—
it serves as a factor for the exclusion of others,
because it functions as a factor for the exclusion of anything other than the intended object by way of being the basis for such differentiation.

In the ultimate sense and in reality, it is said to be non-erroneous with respect to those things that are distinct from it and distinct from what does not produce its effect; for indeed, verbal expressions such as "impermanent" or "produced," having been established by convention based on the exclusion of a real entity as it truly is— namely, its exclusion from what is permanent and so forth— become causes for the attainment of such an entity in practical usage by functioning as the means of excluding others.
Therefore, because it is derived from the principle of seeing things as they truly are, there is even concordance with scripture (*śruti*).

Alternatively, since that scripture was conventionally established for the exclusion [of what is not real] regarding the state of things as they are, its existence among entities is ultimate; it is by this slight degree that there is non-contradiction. However, words do not have a necessary connection to a real object in the way smoke and such have; for they are dependent solely upon intention.
Demonstrating precisely this non-contradiction, he says:
For instance, in the phrase beginning with "tathā hi," from what source could that exclusion— the differentiation— be real or true among those entities?

Since exclusion (vyavaccheda) must necessarily be admitted even when a universal (sāmānya) is accepted in every respect—otherwise, if there were no excluded nature, it would follow that the universal itself does not exist—it was stated [in the previous section] that "even though a universal was mentioned there, it is real. To this, he says:
"Not one," and so forth.

The single category of generality (*sāmānyapadārtha*) is distinct from the individual (*vyakti*) according to Vaiśeṣikas and others, whereas it is non-distinct according to the Sāṃkhyas; however, it does not exist among them—this is the connection [of the argument].
Why?
Because it is impossible and untenable, as both a generality that is entirely distinct and one that is non-distinct are contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
The subverting proof has been stated previously and will be stated again: if, however,

the universal were expressed by a word even as it appears [in cognition], then, upon the inclusion— that is, the objectification— by the word of that universal which does not exist in the real entity (vastu),

or if one were to admit the imposition of that universal— which is subverted by valid cognition— upon the external real entity, the real entity would be utterly cast aside, being extremely remote [from the word].
From what?
From word and knowledge—that is to say, from the word and from the knowledge expressed by it;
or else, it would be cast far away and abandoned by word and knowledge.
Why? Because that [object], which is intended as its object— namely, sound and so forth— and which is intended as that [object] of the universal, is by its very nature a real entity (*vastu*).

Because it does not touch upon— that is, it does not apprehend— any other real property (*vastudharma*), real nature (*vastusvabhāva*), or particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) distinct from the universal, and because it determines [the object] as non-different from its own form despite not apprehending the particular characteristic,
for that very reason that verbal cognition is said to have "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as its object.

[Objection: Since there is a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the external object itself in a positive form (*vidhirūpa*), how can it be said that [the word] has "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) as its object?
To this, he says "others," etc.

The meaning is: because the word is applied—that is, because the convention (*saṃketa*) is established—among individual instances of the same class, by taking up without distinction the specific exclusion (*vyāvṛttibheda*), which is the nature excluded from those of a different class, and by relying on the mere form that is excluded from those of a different class among objects that are excluded from those of a different class.
By this, it is explained that the word (*śruti*) is based on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), because it functions by means of the avoidance of what is other;
thus, the status of the word as the agent (*kartṛbhāva*) with respect to the exclusion of others is stated.

With the words "not a tree" (*avṛkṣa*) and so forth, he anticipates the objection of the opponent, the proponent of the theory of exclusion (*anyāpoha-vādin*): it is claimed that the object "tree" is not apprehended by way of a positive form (*vidhi-rūpa*), nor is the object "non-tree" apprehended;
rather, they are distinguished through mutual exclusion (*anyonya-vyavaccheda*).
In that case,
if the apprehension of the object "tree" occurs through the exclusion of non-trees (*avṛkṣa*), and if it is admitted that the apprehension of the referent of the word "tree" is thus established,
then the apprehension of both "tree" and "non-tree" would be mutually dependent.

For instance, when the meaning of "tree" is apprehended through the exclusion of the meaning of "non-tree," it is admitted that the apprehension of the tree is preceded by the apprehension of the non-tree, because it is impossible to exclude what has not been apprehended;

and since the apprehension of the non-tree also occurs through the exclusion of the meaning of "tree," in that case as well, the apprehension of the non-tree results in being preceded by the apprehension of the tree.

Some maintain that because it is impossible to establish the meaning of "non-tree" without grasping the tree— since it must be defined by its exclusion from that— it follows that between a tree and a non-tree, if there is no apprehension of either one, there is no apprehension of both; and since there is no apprehension of either, they argue that the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) regarding a word for an object excluded from others, as previously described, is impossible.
And thus says Uddyotakara:

"As long as one does not perceive 'cow,' it is not logical to have a cognition of 'non-cow'; and as long as one does not perceive 'cow,' one does not have a cognition of 'non-cow'—thus, there is an absence of cognition for both."
Bhaṭṭa has also stated this very same point:

"If a non-cow were to be excluded as something already established, it would consist of the negation of 'cow'; therefore, that which is being negated must be declared to be the cow itself, and nothing else."
If it were of the nature of the exclusion of non-cows, there would be a circular dependency:
if the cow is already established as the object to be excluded, the application of exclusion is redundant;
but if the cow is not established, there is no non-cow, and in its absence, how could there be a cow?
Therefore, they maintain that a real universal (*sāmānya*) must be accepted as an entity,
and that the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) regarding it functions solely in a positive form.
He explains with the words beginning "yadi" (if):
"of that" refers to the tree characterized by the exclusion of non-trees;
thus, he states that for the time being, there is neither the apprehension of the tree nor of the non-tree.

Regarding the passage beginning with "unrecognized" (*avijñāta*) and so forth: for a person by whom a tree is unrecognized, there is the form of its exclusion—that is, the form of the exclusion of the tree—because that [exclusion] has not ascended into the mind. This means that if both the tree and the non-tree were to ascend into the mind, then there could be a convention (*saṃketa*) regarding the tree by way of the exclusion of the non-tree.

And since the tree has not yet ascended [to its state], how can there be a convention regarding the object "non-tree" for them? With these words, he states that this same fault applies equally to the opponent as well; thus, the sense is that whatever resolution the opponent offers, that very same one shall be mine as well.
He explains [the verse] beginning with "ya ekam" [as follows]:

When a convention (*saṃketa*) is being established through the exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*), there are certain proponents who, while accepting a single entity as a universal (*sāmānya*), raise the objection of the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Even in that case, when a convention is established regarding a real entity characterized as "treeness" (vṛkṣatva), which is common to them, two alternatives arise: is what is not a tree excluded or not? If it is excluded, then those [non-trees] must be admitted to be known.
Because there is no exclusion of things unknown, and that [exclusion] is not tenable with respect to those [unknown] objects; thus he says:
"How so? and so forth;
"How can [the cognition] be known without the apprehension of the object, the tree?"—this much is the portion of the verse.
The word "prior" (prāk), however, is taken according to the *Miśraka* commentary;
its meaning is: how could those that are not trees be known prior to the apprehension of the meaning of "tree," without first apprehending the meaning of "tree"?
However, those who read the word *prāk* (before) in the verse should not read the word *artha* (meaning).
For at the time of the determination of "non-tree," there is no apprehension of the meaning of "tree," because the apprehension of "tree" is preceded by the apprehension of "non-tree.
Nor is it logical to have an apprehension of the meaning of "tree" without the determination of "tree," since that too is preceded by the apprehension of "tree."
He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "na hi" and so forth; "tadā" means at the time of the convention, [referring to] the cognizer.
To the question, "Why does it not know that for which a convention is established?",
he says "tad" and so forth.

Since he has approached [the teacher] out of a desire for that [knowledge], specifically for the sake of knowing the tree and the non-tree, and because he is present there due to his seeking the convention,
how could it be that he does not know the tree and the non-tree after the convention has been established?
Or rather, "because he has approached out of a desire for that" means that he has proceeded because of his desire for the convention.
Therefore, at the time of the convention, there is no cognition of tree and non-tree for the learner;
and how could he, being ignorant of tree and non-tree, comprehend the exclusion of the non-tree? He would not comprehend it at all during the convention.

And when there is no cognition of the exclusion of non-trees, that which is other than those trees is not excluded; therefore, "that in which there is the placement of the convention for the object 'tree'—which is other than that [non-tree] which has not been excluded"—is the compound.
The compound is formed by splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*) as *saptamī* (locative), and the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is applied because it exists in that word.
Alternatively, there is another way [to explain the suffix]: the suffix *ṇini* is used because it is his nature (*śīla*) to indicate that which is not excluded from the others;

that is to say, [it is used] after a word that has been conventionally established (*saṃketita*) with respect to an object that is not differentiated from non-trees, whose form is thus completely blurred.
"Other than the tree" (*vṛkṣādanya*) means "other than that" (*tadanya*). "Residing in that" (*tasmin niveśaḥ*) refers to the application of a convention (*saṃketa*).

The compound *aparihṛta-tadanyaniveśa* is a *karmadhāraya*, meaning "that [application] which has not been abandoned and which resides in other than that. This belongs to the word "tree," as explained previously.
The collective meaning is this: because the referent "tree" is not excluded from non-trees, it follows that a word being conventionally designated for that [referent] would also apply to non-trees,
just as it does to the various individual trees.

Therefore, from such a word as "tree," at the time of linguistic usage, there would be no directed activity by people engaged in worldly practice toward a specific object possessing branches and so forth— namely, an activity that excludes non-trees—
but rather, there would be activity toward both trees and non-trees without distinction.
Like what?
Like the distinction between trees;
for from the word "tree" alone, when devoid of context and the like, there occurs no application toward a specific tree such as the *khadira*, to the exclusion of other trees.
He explains [the phrase] "not because" (*na hi*) and so forth by stating that at the time of convention (*saṃketakāle*), there is no exclusion (*avyavacchedāt*) of those [objects].

By the term "convention" (*saṃketa*), the time of convention is expressed; "by the exclusion of others" (*parārthavyavacchedena*) means by the non-exclusion of the referent "tree" from what is other than a tree, such as a non-tree.
In the second explanation, however,
it should be explained as "without the exclusion [of other referents] through the convention of the word 'tree' with respect to another tree that is not a tree";
[the phrase] "from that which has been introduced" means from that which has been conventionalized.
The explanation of "like a tree" by way of excluding that [non-tree] and excluding non-trees is "like the particulars such as the *śiṃśapā*.

Here, [the compound] *śiṃśapādayo bhedāḥ* is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), meaning "the particulars themselves are the *śiṃśapā*s and so forth. The suffix *-vati* is used in the sense of the locative case.
In the sūtra, however, it is *vṛkṣabhedāḥ*, which is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

For since particular instances such as the *śiṃśapā* are indeed particulars of the "tree," the application [of the term] is entirely appropriate. Furthermore, just as the word "tree" does not function toward these [particulars] by means of mutual exclusion (*parasparavyavaccheda*), so it has been explained in the analysis of the Sūtra itself starting with the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth.
Some, however, read two negations: "without prescribing [one thing] and without excluding another."
Having stated that in a convention one expresses the object and does not exclude anything else,
this appears to be incorrect; for it is impossible for a word to function apart from affirmation and negation,
since by asserting the presentation of one thing, affirmation is necessarily accepted.
Furthermore, if [the word] "without performing" (*avidhāya*) were not used, the two words [in the verse] would be contradictory;
therefore, the negative particle (*nañ*) must be understood as belonging to the word "without performing" itself.
Thus, the reading should be: "without performing—that is, having prohibited—anything else."
The meaning is that, having excluded other things, one does not establish another object of convention by means of that prior exclusion;

rather, without performing a positive injunction preceded by a negation, one performs only a mere affirmation. For this very reason, even in the commentary [the verse] stating "having shown one," it refutes the notion that an affirmation is made through the exclusion of something, asserting instead that the establishment [of one thing] is necessarily preceded by the negation of others.
However, the mere injunction is indeed accepted;
by the word "one," he explains that because the convention is made with respect to the universal, it is thereby made with respect to all individual instances.
By saying "this is a tree," he demonstrates the nature of the convention; that object with respect to which the convention was made is understood even in practical usage.
For that reason, this faultless position just mentioned belongs to the proponent of the universal as a real entity (*vastu-sāmānyavādin*):
namely, that the convention is applied either to the universal itself— which is perceived exactly as the object was seen—
or to its correlate, that is, the substratum (*āśraya*) which is related to that universal.

In that case as well, even when a convention is established by means of a mere affirmation (*vidhi*), two alternatives arise: one who establishes the convention "this is a tree" might formulate it either as "this is also a *taru* (tree)" or "this alone is a *taru*. In the first case, since the status of being a *taru* is not excluded for anything else, there would be no necessary engagement in practical usage; thus, that same logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) remains.

If, on the other hand, [it is argued that] "this very thing is a tree," then the exclusion of the non-tree (*ataru-vyavaccheda*) itself has been accepted. Consequently, since at the time of the convention the one who understands [the term] would not have known trees and non-trees, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) remains.
Thus he says:
He explains with the words "one," etc., that the undesirable consequence does not cease:
"This is a tree, and this very thing is a tree."
"Gati" means "manner"; thus,
the opponent [argues] that there is no fault in either of these two manners, and so forth.
Because that which is contrary to it—that is, distinct from it—is easily known through the observation of its mode of appearance (*dṛṣṭopalaṅkṣaṇa*).
He explains this very statement of apprehension, beginning with "For one [thing] alone," etc.:

"For when a person perceives some single universal such as 'treeness' (*vṛkṣatva*) and experiences a cognition regarding another object—which lacks that universal and is distinct—that is differentiated from the form of the former and possesses a form distinct from the form previously observed; for that person, based on that experience, there arises a determination of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-niścaya*), a determination of distinction, in the form: 'this is other than what was previously observed.'"
By this, the nature of the determination of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-niścaya*) has been stated.
Its function is "discrimination" (*tadvivecana*), which establishes the distinctness of an object by discriminating between what was previously seen and what was not seen.

Since the differentiation from that [other] is already established by the phrase "different from that" (*tato 'nyat*) alone, the further inclusion of the term "differentiation" (*vivecana*) is for the sake of clarity.

This being the sequence, the cognizer who possesses the ascertainment of dissimilarity according to experience differentiates an object possessing branches and so forth— which possesses a specific universal— from other forms.
Having placed that [tree] before him and pointed it out as "this very tree," he is instructed and made to grasp the convention;
then, wherever he does not perceive that universal essence corresponding to the convention, he himself understands that very thing to be a non-tree, even without the operation of words.

Thus, when a convention is established by taking as its basis that universal-nature which has been determined through its own discernment from other forms, it becomes established for all individual instances of the same class,

because the universal is present everywhere and because the determination "this is exactly that" has been made; for once the convention is established, that which is contrary to what was observed is easily understood.
If it is argued that there is no such fault as previously stated because the determination "there is no tree elsewhere than here" arises,
and that this applies equally to the proponent of *anyāpoha*, [the author] replies with the words beginning "This is not... and so forth.
Because the unique form perceived at the time of establishing a convention does not persist— that is, does not follow along— in any other individual instance,
and because there is no perception elsewhere of that very distinction which was grasped as "this is a tree" at the time of convention,

for that reason, the perception that arises as having a distinct appearance regarding the particular (svalakṣaṇa) seen later, which was previously seen at the time of convention, [is not a cognition of the same object].
If the cognition [of "tree"] were produced based on individual trees, then even with respect to another tree—a different individual tree—the cognition "this is a tree" would not occur.
For instance, whatever specific tree was perceived at the time of the convention is distinct from pots and other such things; likewise, any other specific tree is also distinct from them.

Just as the cognition "this is a tree" does not arise with respect to pots and the like, so too it would not arise with respect to that other specific tree; rather, the cognition would only be "this is a non-tree. This is the meaning.

The Master [Candrakīrti] says, "In that case," meaning that even there—in the case of a conceptual form (*vikalpākāra*)—when a convention is made regarding a generality (*sāmānya*), this is the same; thus he provides a rebuttal to the charge of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
This is what is meant:
it has already been established previously that all entities are distinct from their own causes.
Therefore, trees and non-trees appear as distinct entities even in non-conceptual cognition;

and while the conceptualization of "tree" is said to occur among trees by way of a positive affirmation (*vidhi-rūpeṇa*), likewise, the conceptualization of "non-tree" arises among non-trees through the negation of "tree. Thus, how could there be any mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*)?

[Objection: Even if the conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) of a tree is apprehended in a positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa*), nevertheless, because it arises by way of the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of non-trees and so forth, it depends upon the apprehension of non-trees and the like; consequently, that very same fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya-doṣa*) remains. [Response: This is not so, because the exclusion of non-trees and so forth is simply the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the tree and so forth. It is precisely through the experience of that [nature] that the conceptual cognition of a tree arises, and it does not depend upon the apprehension of non-trees and the like. Therefore, how could there be mutual dependence?
In that regard, within the conceptualization of a tree, a non-differentiated form of "tree" appears through each particular instance such as the *śiṃśapā* and so forth;

and since that [form] is established prior to linguistic convention by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*)—because it is of the nature of cognition—it is precisely therein that the word is conventionally assigned. Therefore, as for what was stated by Bhaṭṭa:

Prior to linguistic convention, exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is not apprehended by the sense faculties; nor does linguistic convention apply elsewhere. Having seen what, then, could that convention be applied? Furthermore, because it is devoid of positive concomitance (anvaya), no inference (anumāna) exists here either.
"Even the experience of its relation [to the word] is not possible for it by that means," thus the *Ślokavārttika* refutes [the objection].
He asks why the refutation of mutual dependence is equal [to the other], and says "because," etc.:

because there is a single form of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) among individuals of the same class, which is a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*); that cognition which has such a designation (*ākhyā*) is described as "thus."
By this it has been stated that recognition, despite the individual objects being distinct, superimposes unity upon them;
and thus, the seed for the claim that a convention established in one instance becomes established everywhere among individuals superimposed with unity by conceptual cognition has been explained.

By the phrase "for in one [instance]," he states that the nature of that reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is restricted to a specific form, as it is devoid of any reference to heterogeneous objects.

The meaning is that it is established in that single determinative cognition (*ekapratyavamarśajñāna*) which occurs with respect to all homogeneous things through the exclusion of the forms of heterogeneous objects.
By this also, the seed for the distinction between homogeneous and heterogeneous entities has been stated;
therefore, he says:

By the word "tat" (that), one type of consideration (*parāmarśa*) is grasped; by the word "atat" (not-that), its opposite is grasped. That and not-that are "tad-atau"; the causes of those two are "tad-atad-hetavaḥ."
He distinguishes them— that is,

he separates those which are the causes for the conceptual apprehension of forms such as "one branch" and so forth from those that are the opposite of this; this has already been explained by himself even prior to the conventional designation (*saṃketa*).
In this context— specifically in the passage beginning with "The means of accomplishing a single object consists in a single reflective awareness, a cognition of an object, and so forth" (PV 1.75)—
both a universal that is distinct [from its particulars] and one that is non-distinct are refuted, as well as being subject to future refutation.
Entities differ by their very nature and are distinct by their own essence;
for instance, while some perform functions such as cognition and so forth—where the word "and so forth" includes activities like fetching water—others do not.

Since those [entities] possess by their very nature the capacity to produce that [effect] or not to produce it, this cognizer, by himself and without the operation of words, distinguishes and makes a division between them, and thus perceives which are the causes of that [effect] and which are not;
therefore, how can there be the fault of mutual dependence?
For that cognizer who himself realizes those things which are causes and those which are not causes— of him,
the phrase beginning with "revolving in his cognition" and so forth refers to the object; it depends on the verbal action "he would realize," [meaning] that cognition which,
having distinguished the causes from the non-causes, establishes them.

It should be understood that because those [external objects], which appear as revolving around and mounted upon that cognition, manifest— as if appearing— as causes for the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpikā dhīḥ*), they are likewise [the cause] through their connection with the word to be discussed; however, those things appearing in conceptualization are not the actual causes, because they do not exist externally.
This is stated solely because of the practitioner's own determination;
the connection here is with the phrase "appearing as if devoid of the nature of a cause," and the use of the word "as if" (iva) is as explained previously.

The connection here is as follows: those things which are not the causes of a cognition that apprehends [them] through a single form appear, by way of their own nature, as if deficient; yet, due to the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized, they appear as if having a single form together with the external object—this being so even after the time of the initial convention.
Thinking that one should apprehend those entities as distinct from those that do not produce such effects,

the word— being an expression— is applied and conventionally established for that distinction, namely the nature excluded from heterogeneous classes, which has been superimposed by conceptual thought as non-different from its own form. This is the aforementioned distinction.
From that scripture, the cognition apprehending—that is, realizing—in conventional practice, perceives through delusion a single entity;

the meaning is that the cognition, apprehending within homogeneous individuals that nature which is excluded from heterogeneous ones as non-different from its own form, beholds it as if it were a single entity.

Consequently, since there is the realization "tree" with respect to all things that are the causes for a single conceptual determination, what was stated—that if [the universal] were realized through perception, it would not occur in another individual—is refuted.
Furthermore, as for what was said by Bhaṭṭa—
that horses and the like are not denotable by the word "cow"— how is it that you did not observe the word "cow" applied to them at the time of the convention? If [you claim] it was not seen there...
"In that case, everything other than that single lump and so forth would have to be the object of exclusion; thus, there can be no denotation of a universal," so says the *Ślokavārttika*.
That too has been refuted;

for when the word "cow" is conventionally assigned to a single individual, the object [of that convention] is followed through into other individuals, because there arises the cognition, "This is that very same cow.
Nevertheless...

With the words "of these" (*teṣām*) and so forth, he states the meaning of the verse: the connection is that [the cognition arises] because of the continuity (*anvaya*) of those objects which distinguish themselves from heterogeneous things and which, by their very nature (*prakṛtyā*), are the causes of such conceptual constructions (*vikalpaka*).
It is by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāvena*), and not, on the other hand, due to a connection with a single universal (*sāmānya*).
If that is so, why do they all not produce a conceptual determination (*parāmarśa*)? He says:
"By virtue of the condition" (*pratyayavaśāt*).
The cognition of experience (*anubhavajñāna*) is the condition; it is through that medium that they generate conceptualization.

Because the causes of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—which consists of a single unifying reflection (*ekapratyavamarśa*)—of such a nature are present through their positive concomitance (*anvaya*), just as one particular tree by its very nature is the cause of such a conceptual construction, so too are the second and subsequent ones; it is in this manner that there is positive concomitance. However, there is no single entity in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*).
Therefore, due to this reason of positive concomitance, they are "fit for a single unifying determination" by virtue of having a single effect; this is the completion of the sentence.
If it is argued that the term "taddraṣṭuḥ" (of the seer of that) refers to the seer who performs a single function across various individuals,
and thus the words should have been "tasmād draṣṭuḥ" (from that seer)—
because of the prohibition of a genitive compound by the rule *kartari ca*— we say no.
Because the remaining genitive case is intended [here],
and because the word *draṣṭṛ* ends in the suffix *tṛn*,
the genitive is prohibited in that context by the rule "not after [a stem] ending in *tṛn*" (*tṛn na*).
The compound *sādhanakṛta* is a *kṛdanta*-compound consisting of the word *tat* in the accusative case;
however, others maintain that based on the rule "its prompter" (*tatprayojaka*) and others, this prohibitive sūtra is understood to be non-universal (*anitya*).
In other similar grammatical indications of this kind, such resolutions should likewise be stated.
By virtue of being the cause of that cognition— that is, by virtue of being the cause of that conceptual cognition—

and by virtue of its exclusion from others; and by virtue of its exclusion from those things which are other than the causes of the recognition of a single form, namely those things which are not causes of such conceptual cognitions.
For even those things that are not as they appear do not become causes for conceptualization once they have ascended into it, because they do not exist externally;

for this very reason, even though they are conceptualizations of a non-causal form, they are non-existent because their existence is merely that of a mental construct (*avastusattva*) as thus determined.

It has been explained that [the author] has stated that cognitions— which are superimposed by way of being the cause of the knowledge of that [object] and by way of the exclusion of others— are devoid of the nature of a cause, insofar as they do not possess the form of a cause.
By the phrase "those whose internal and external distinctions are undivided," he explains "those which are of a single form.
The analysis of the compound is: "those in whom the distinction between the external and the internal is undivided";
the meaning is that they are apprehended through the unification of the perceived object and its conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
The cognizer for whom a convention is established follows that cognition;
whatever his cognition was at the time of the convention, [that is what he relies upon].

Those entities which are devoid of the form of non-causes, which produce a single effect, and which possess a single nature— in those very things upon which this word "tree" has been conventionally applied—
they are "trees"; thus, following that [exclusion], one forms such a conceptual image.
Recalling that [memory],
while abiding in the conceptualizing consciousness,
one [perceives] those aforementioned entities— which are the causes of that consciousness— as distinct from their opposites.

Thinking, "How indeed could one understand [the meaning] even at the time of linguistic usage from hearing the word 'tree' [if it were not based on such exclusion]," the author of the convention applies it with this intention: "When the nature [of the object], which is excluded from what is not its cause, has been made an object by conceptual thought, the maker of the convention applies [the term].
(123) But surely, there is no persistence of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is excluded [from others], at the time of linguistic usage?
Nor is there a positive concomitance (anvaya) of the universal form appearing in conceptual cognition within another conceptual cognition, because that form is non-different from its own cognition.

Furthermore, there can be no cognition by a listener of a [universal] belonging to a speaker, nor by a speaker of one belonging to a listener, because as a property of another's mind, it is beyond the senses.
And since a convention cannot be established between the communicator and the person to be communicated unless [the object] is cognized by both equally, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "one's own and another," etc.:

having shown that entities which are the objects of convention appear as one— due to the cause of error characterized by performing a single function among the conceptual alternatives of both oneself, the speaker, and another, the person to be informed— it is this that is meant.

Just as one person with cataracts, having seen two moons, when instructing another person with cataracts, instructs them based on exactly what he himself has seen and not on what the other has seen— since that is not perceptible to him— and yet it occurs to him, "This very thing has been communicated by me to the other," and the other person also, perceiving the form of two moons arising within his own mental continuum, thinks, "That very thing which was communicated to me by the instructor has been understood by me."

In the same way, although there is a difference between the mental forms (*buddhyākāra*) of the speaker and the listener—each of which is determined as having an external form—the convention is established because they determine them as one. Furthermore, at the time of linguistic usage, it is precisely that [form] which is cognized through the determination of oneness. Thus, the cognition, superimposing its own form—which is non-different from the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) excluded from others—as being identical with that [external object], apprehends it; this is the meaning of the word "of that" (*tasyāḥ*) [referring to the cognition].
It appears as if it grasps a single object;
therefore, as Bhaṭṭa says: "The activity of words and logical marks does not occur apart from positive concomitance (*anvaya*)."
Without those two [exclusion and concomitance], there can be no cognition of exclusion; nor can there be concomitance in that which is unique (asādhāraṇa).
Furthermore, since exclusion itself is unestablished, where could non-deviation be asserted?
And if that [non-deviation] is absent, those two [means of knowledge] would lack the status of valid cognition.
The *Ślokavārttika* [responds]:

Since this has been refuted— namely, that even though one understands the relationship through word and inferential mark (*liṅga*) with respect to a single particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) excluded from others, one nevertheless understands the relationship with other things of the same nature due to the determination of identity— how then can there be faults such as the lack of positive concomitance (*anvaya*)?
However, if one relies upon a real universal (*sāmānya*) as an ontological entity, the distinction between "tree" and "non-tree" is not tenable;
thus he says, "But not again," and so forth.
A single entity, a universal (*sāmānya*), is visible and meets the conditions for perception; it exists within those particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Just as jars and other objects are distinct from various types of trees, so too are *dhava* trees and others distinct from one another.

Even when these distinct things are perceived, there must be some universal whose presence or absence allows one to distinguish between what is a tree and what is not a tree—such that where this universal is seen, it is a tree, and where it is not seen, it is not a tree.
He asks, "Why does it not exist? and replies with the words beginning "of that," etc.:
because a universal that is distinct [from its instances] is not perceived as separate from the appearance of branches and so forth.
For two appearances are not perceived in trees and the like: one having the form of branches and so forth, and another having the form of non-branches and so forth;
nor can it be said that it is the very form of the branches and so forth that appears as the universal, because that [form] is precisely the form of the branches and so forth.
"The staff-bearer is like a staff" is an example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta);
for just as the staff is perceived as distinct from the staff-bearer,
it is not so with the universal (sāmānya).
Furthermore, because a universal—which is distinct from another object possessing branches and the like—is not apprehended separately, it cannot be perceived within individual instances;

and how could there be the perception of another by means of its own nature if it has not itself been apprehended? For one who maintains that the universal is not a separate entity, since the form (*ākṛti*) seen in one instance is non-different from the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it would likewise be impossible to perceive it in another instance.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of that which possesses it and that which does not": at the time of convention, there is the form of a single tree perceived;

that which possesses this is the "possessor of it" (*tadvān*), namely, a particular tree seen later at the time of linguistic usage that lacks the previously perceived tree-form. That which does not possess it is the "non-possessor of it" (*atadvān*). Since it is established by logic that these two respectively constitute "tree-ness" and "non-tree-ness," the individual [tree] would be the very same one seen at the time of convention, and not the one being seen at the time of linguistic usage.

Since the form perceived at the time of linguistic convention is not seen elsewhere, it has been argued that the theory of exclusion (anyāpoha) as the meaning of words lacks universal applicability; wishing to refute this, [the author] first presents a mere outline of the opponent's position,
beginning with the words "Let it be so," and so forth.
Why is there no exclusion of other objects (*arthāntara-vyavaccheda*) in that case? He says:
"For [there is] no non-cognizable," and so forth; from which [it follows], i.e., from that which is non-cognizable.

If it is asked why the "unknowable" (ajñeya) does not exist, he says "therefore," and so forth: by one who maintains the theory of exclusion of others (anyavyavacchedavādin), the knowable must be apprehended as distinct from the unknowable; otherwise, how could there be an exclusion of the knowable from the unknowable?
Furthermore, it is only when the knowable is made an object by way of its distinction from the unknowable that the latter—regarded as unknowable—attains the status of being knowable;
for it is impossible to demonstrate an exclusion from that which has not been made an object.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of terms such as "the whole" (*sarva*) and "collection" (*samudāya*).
As stated by Bhaṭṭa Uddyotakara:

"The claim that the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is incorrect, because it is not universally applicable. Where a dual classification exists, there one thing is cognized through the negation of the other; for example, in the word 'cow,' the cow is cognized through the negation of the non-cow."
Furthermore, this [usage] does not apply to every instance;
for there is nothing whatsoever that is "not-all" which could be excluded by the word "all. If you think that "one" and so forth constitute the "not-all" and are excluded by the word "all"—
In that case, because it would entail the fault of denying its own object, a word functioning by excluding "one" and so forth would be meaningless; for,
since the parts are negated and no whole distinct from the parts is admitted, there would be nothing left for it to signify.

Thus, all words denoting a collection (*samudāya*), functioning by way of negating a portion [of that collection], would result in being meaningless because a collection distinct from its constituents is not admitted. Furthermore, since words such as "two" (*dvi*) and so forth have conjunction (*samuccaya*) as their object, when one or more [of the members] are negated, those being negated would no longer constitute a conjunction;
therefore, words such as "two" and so forth would be meaningless.

"This is not a fault," says the Teacher (Ācārya), because a certain word is employed by a speaker for the sake of directing a person who possesses expectancy toward some specific object, having first turned that expectant cognition away from whatever else it might be directed toward; by the phrase "for the sake of directing [it] toward a specific object," the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is stated.
By the phrase "having turned [the word] away from something," the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is indicated.
As for the reason why a word is turned away from something and established in something else, he says:
"of its object," and so forth.
Because the meaning of a word is determined;
otherwise, if no object were excluded by that word, the employment of the word would be useless.

Therefore, in words such as "knowable" (*jñeya*)—where the word "etc. (*ādi*) implies [words] such as "all" (*sarva*) and "universe" (*viśva*)—[the same principle applies]. (Note 243-1: *cung zad kyang*.)
In these [cases], P.V. reads *vyavacchedyo*.
In what kind of things?
In those brought forward for practical usage—
that is, in those presented for the sake of verbal usage characterized by injunctions and prohibitions.
"In those things situated within worldly usage"— that is to say,
among those factors of conventional discourse— there exists some object of exclusion in whatever manner;
this is what is meant.

"Whatever is the ultimate purport of a word, that is the meaning of the word. Since even an affirmative sentence has the function of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), exclusion is also called the meaning of a word; thus, there is no inconsistency.
He explains this with the words "for every word," etc., asking:
why does every person—whether a worldly person or an investigator—not transgress [this rule]? He says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "tasya" (of that), the meaning is as follows: because that word has the fruit of engagement and withdrawal; that is to say, because it aims at engaging [someone] in something after having withdrawn them from something else. Otherwise, the employment of words would be fruitless.
Regarding this, he says "yadi" and so forth:

if this speaker did not turn someone to be instructed away from something undesired for some reason, nor cause them to engage with something desired, then— because of the non-authorization of the object as it actually is— prior to the employment of the word, the object would not have been authorized by the word in the form in which it exists for the cognizer, being [otherwise] entirely obscure in nature.
The meaning is that because permission has been granted for whatever kind of thing it may be,
in all worldly transactions one should not utter any speech; what is the reason?
Since linguistic usage is inseparable from determination,
he says "just as," etc., in order to prove this very point.

For in this case, when it is said, "Bring water," the hearer necessarily has an expectation regarding the specific instrument; and to provide a restriction in that regard, it is said, "with a jar. Thus, this word "jar" becomes fruitful by first denoting its own primary meaning and then implying the exclusion of other instruments. Otherwise, even if the word "jar" is employed, if one were to bring water somehow or other—whether with hollowed palms (*añjali*) or by some other instrument—the intended purpose would not be fulfilled, regardless of whether the bringing of water was meant to be in small quantity or large quantity. This is the meaning.
If even the word "water" does not function to direct one toward a specific action by excluding other actions, then its employment would also be purposeless;
thus he says "tathā" and so forth:
there would be only the bare statement "bring."

Of what nature is it? It is that in which the instrument (karaṇa) and the action (karman)—namely, the pot designated as the object and the impulsion designated as the verbal command—are not explicitly projected; that is to say, when there is merely the statement "bring this," a person becomes oriented toward the activity of "bringing" in such a manner. Thus it is described. Furthermore, when there is the activity [of bringing], the person becomes intent upon it.
If, by the word "bring" (*ānaya*), one were not to exclude [the act of bringing] from other activities, then even the word "bring" would not need to be uttered;
this is precisely what he expresses in the passage beginning with "In this way, the bringing... and so forth.
"Or some other performance"—
what else could it be besides bringing [the fire]?

If the performance of actions such as eating, as well as non-performance— that is, the non-doing and non-bringing— were intended [by the injunction], then one would not even say the verb "bring," nor specify "bringing" as distinct from something else;
however, the reading found in some manuscripts, "nayanam anyadvā," is not correct.

Since the word "bringing forth" (*ānayana*) has been introduced [as the subject], there is therefore an object of exclusion for words such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*) when they are brought into common usage; just as there is for those, so too for words such as "knowable" (*jñeya*) when they are brought into common usage, there is an object of exclusion such as "unknowable" (*ajñeya*).
When there is no suspicion of non-difference, the suspicion regarding unknowability and so forth is "suspicion of another" (*anyāśaṅkā*).
The meaning is that there is no suspicion of non-existence when the suspicion of unknowability and so forth is absent;

for instance, when there is the suspicion that "sound is unknowable in its form as impermanent and so on," this [reasoning] is employed [to show] that "it is knowable in the form of being impermanent and so on."

In that context, it is precisely that unknowability which was suspected by way of aspects such as impermanence that is here excluded. Likewise, in the statement "all objects are knowable by the cognition of the Omniscient One," that very unknowability suspected in relation to the cognition of the Omniscient One is what is to be excluded.
Thus, someone has said:
Because things that are indefinable (nirupākhya) do not exist, there is no operation of cognition toward them; therefore, they are "unknowable.
Here too, this very state of being unknowable is superimposed [upon them] and is what is to be excluded.
This is because even non-existence is made an object [of cognition] in the sense that "it is not the case that everything is non-existent."
The same should be understood regarding the use of the word "knowable" (*jñeya*) elsewhere,
as well as in the case of the word "object of cognition" (*prameya*),
and likewise in the statement "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary," where some imagine that momentariness applies only to certain things like lamps and not to everything.
By means of that exclusion, the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is established;

for when there is the doubt as to whether "someone has come" or "everyone has come," it is precisely that arrival of a particular person which was suspected— such as "the whole village has come"— that is to be excluded.

Likewise, when it is said that "the five groups of consciousness have a collective object" (*samudāyālambana*) or "they have a partial object" (*ekadeśālambana*), the state of having a partial object is thereby negated.

In this same manner, regarding other terms such as "two" and so forth when employed in conventional discourse, the specific exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) should be stated according to the context and as appropriate.
This is the general meaning here.
It is not said that exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is expressed by a word by positing a non-existent counter-correlate—which is grasped by a distinct cognition—within two groups;
rather, even when [the object] is such as it is, the form that is superimposed upon it as being otherwise by the hearer is also precisely what is to be excluded by the word.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
In that regard, the phrase "for there," and so forth,
means that whatever constitutes a point of doubt— the object of doubt— for the dull-witted person being instructed,
that very thing is what is to be excluded by words such as "the knowable" (*jñeya*).
If it is argued that no one at all suspects [the existence of such a person], he says:
"Or, not suspecting," and so forth;
that is, if he does not suspect anything at all.

The intention is that one who possesses certainty regarding things as they truly are does not require any instruction from another speaker at all. The removal of doubt is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the listener; when that [refinement] is absent in a statement, how could a speaker who produces such a statement—and thus fails to provide the refinement for the listener—not be insane?
Therefore, a speaker employs a word while intending to produce a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) in a listener who possesses an expectancy;
for what reason?
Because words have been established by convention solely for the purpose of that impression—that is, solely for the purpose of the listener’s mental impression.
Granted that for words such as "knowable" (*jñeya*) and so forth—which are employed in discourse for the sake of practical usage—there is an exclusion (*vyavacchedya*) as previously described;
however, how is it with those words such as "knowable" which are not employed in discourse but exist in isolation?
For in those cases, there is no occasion for doubt on the part of the cognizer. To this, he says:
The meaning is that there is no expressive word not included within such sentences as "those things not brought into linguistic usage," and so forth;

for a speaker desiring a result first employs [a sentence] such as "Devadatta, bring the cow," with the intention: "I shall communicate this object, connected with a specific action, to him by means of this word."
Therefore, it is only word-meanings already endowed with action that are denoted,

and not a subsequent syntactic connection of word-meanings that have already been denoted; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-occurrence of case-endings such as the accusative in examples like *gām*.
Therefore, there is usage only of those [words] situated within a sentence;
this is precisely what he states in the passage beginning with "of that which is contained in a sentence," and so forth.
The intention is that it alone serves to convey the meaning.
As for those [words] which are recited in groups such as *sarvaviśva* and so forth by means of the *vaiyākaraṇas*, or which are refined through the analysis of base and suffix;

Likewise, according to the etymologists (*niruktakāra*), those [individual words] are to be regarded as mere means for the comprehension of the sentences themselves— standing in the same relation as a "line-drawn gavaya" (*rekhāgavaya*) [is to the actual animal]— but they possess no worldly meaning whatsoever;
therefore, it is only the words situated within the sentence that possess semantic significance.
And while remaining in that very state, reflection on the meaning is performed;
thus he says, "But where," and so forth.

Regarding the word *eta* (these), which refers to those words situated within sentences that function as the subject of inquiry when the investigation into their application proceeds— it is said that the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), based on the etymology "that by which another is excluded.
However, as for those words not situated in such application, such as *jñeya* (knowable) and so forth, he says that because no referent is possible for them, there is no investigation at all.
Regarding the phrase "anirdiṣṭaprayogam" and so forth:
"nirdiṣṭa" means "taken up" (upātta); thus, "nirdiṣṭaprayoga" is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is a practice that has been specified.

Subsequently, this is combined with the negative particle *nañ* in the sense of non-existence (*abhāva*) to form an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule "an indeclinable [is compounded] with a case-inflected word," etc. (*avyayaṃ vibhakti...*).
And thus, by the rule "the third case [suffix] is used for the seventh [case] in the sense of the seventh [case] optionally," there is the substitution of *am* (elision).
This means that in the absence of an expressed application, the question is: "What is the meaning of the word *jñeya* alone, as introduced by the sentence?
Others hold that this is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
For the act of questioning (*praśnakriyā*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*),
and it is a rule that adverbs (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) function as objects (*karman*).

Now, if this were a *karmadhāraya* compound, since it would function solely within its own constituent members (*svapadārthavṛtti*), one must explain how the act of questioning could be qualified by it.
Pāṇini:
Now, if it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that in which the word 'jñeya' (to be known) has its application unspecified"—then the word (*śabda*) is qualified, not the action (*kriyā*).

However, when the analysis is as follows—"that in which the question (*praśna*) has its application unspecified"—then it is the action that is qualified. Even in that case, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "question," the locative case alone is appropriate: "in the question whose application is unspecified" (*anirdiṣṭaprayoge praśne*).

If it is asked what the reason is for the fact that the meaning of the word "knowable" (*jñeya*) alone is not [the object], he says: "Therefore," because from that word "knowable" there is no apprehension of a real entity (*vastu*) anywhere at all.
Since the word "knowable" (*jñeya*) is never used in isolation within linguistic practice— which consists of injunctions and prohibitions— how could there be any comprehension of its meaning?
Even when the word "knowable" is employed alone after a discussion has begun with words such as "Is [the self] knowable in the form of impermanence and so forth, or is it unknowable?",
any comprehension of the meaning that arises occurs only through the sentence itself, depending upon the preceding and following words in context.
Since a word accompanied by other words constitutes a sentence, there is no comprehension of a word-meaning from a word independent of other words;
just as there is nothing expressible by isolated words such as "knowable" (*jñeya*) and so forth, so too it is with isolated words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*).
But surely, when one says, "Shall I bring water with a jar or with my cupped hands?

and employs the word "with a jar," even for a listener who was unaware of the context, a cognition in the form of a jar certainly arises from hearing the isolated word "with a jar" alone; so how can it be said that there is no cognition from an isolated word? To this he replies:
Regarding the passage beginning with "yāpi" and so forth:
that cognition in which the object sought to be known is incomplete is "one whose object is incomplete.
To the question, "In what way is its object incomplete? he says:

"According to the observed usage" means that in as many instances as the application of the word "jar" was observed by him in the context of being engaged in injunctions for actions such as bringing or taking away, in accordance with those [instances], there arises in the preceding sentences a cognition characterized by expectancy— such as "is this meaning intended? or "what indeed is this?"— and because of this state of expectancy, it is merely a delusive error (*viplava-bhrānti*) whose form appears incomplete in its meaning.

This explains that there is no comprehension of meaning from the mere hearing of isolated words; rather, when one hears an isolated word, the impression of comprehending its meaning arises because the intellect is presented with it through its similarity to a meaningful word previously encountered in sentences. Just as the comprehension of meaning from hearing an isolated word such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*)—based on following previously observed usage—is to be known as a cognitive error, so too is it in the case of words such as "knowable" (*jñeya*).
According to observation and according to the perception of usage—

following the instances where the word "knowable" (*jñeya*) is seen being employed in various sentences— there certainly occurs a confusion in the comprehension of the meaning upon hearing the word "knowable" alone.
By this, he states in every respect the equivalence between words such as "jar" and words such as "knowable.
Furthermore, regarding what was said:

"A word such as 'all,' which functions by excluding 'one' and so forth, would be meaningless because it negates the parts [of the whole], and since a whole distinct from its parts is not admitted [by you]."
That is incorrect,
because the objects of cognitions such as "one" and so forth are distinct from the objects of cognitions such as "collection" and so forth that appear [in perception];
and those particular states which are the objects of cognitions such as "collection" are themselves called the "possessors of parts" (*aṅgin*), since any other possessor of parts has been negated.

And in whatever manner those [atoms] are asserted by the opponent to be the initiators of properties such as a collection (*samudāya*), in that very same manner we assert them to be the objective supports (*ālambana*) for the cognition of a collection, precisely because there is no contradiction.
Therefore, the negation of "one" and so forth regarding all terms such as "collection," "duality," and so on, is indeed logically consistent;
thus, [the passage beginning with] "therefore" and so on.

Since every sentence is restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇa*), and only those words situated within a sentence possess meaning, therefore the employment of all words [is necessary]; this is the conclusion. "Because of its fruitfulness" means because of the fruitfulness of that employment of words.
Thus, when the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is the denotable meaning of all words according to the aforementioned method,
as stated by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara:
"Is this *anyāpoha* held to be denotable, or is it non-denotable?"
Whether the denotable [object] is expressed in a positive form or through the negation of another,
if its denotation consists of a positive essence, then the extremist view must be abandoned;
for it has been described that in all cases, the meaning of a word is the negation of other things.

If exclusion (*apoha*) is expressed by means of the exclusion of non-exclusions (*anapohavyudāsena*), then if you maintain this position in each case, there will be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) for you;
moreover, if you maintain that this "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) is simply inexpressible (*avācya*).
Therefore, your statement that "a word effects the exclusion of others" would be contradicted;

for only in those words where there is a connection with the negative particle (*nañ*) would there be a portion consisting of the exclusion of others, whereas in other cases, one's own nature itself is understood.
That is incorrect, because it is accepted that the meaning of the word is affirmation (vidhi), and that the negation of other things follows from that [affirmation] as a matter of course;
for if affirmation alone were the meaning of the word, then the negation of other things would follow from it.
How, then, is the statement by the teacher Diṅnāga—that words denote entities as qualified precisely by the exclusion of other things—not contradicted? To this, he says:
"And the application," and so forth.
By this, he demonstrates that even at the time of establishing a convention, a word functions by way of a positive form (vidhi-rūpeṇa), let alone in actual usage.
The meaning of "tree" is that which is distinguished from, or excluded from, non-trees such as jars; the sense is that it does so by abandoning what is not a tree.

The application of the convention for the word "tree" should be understood as its placement; by the phrase "having excluded that," it is stated that the word "tree" is not applied to what is not a tree.
To the question, "Where, then, is that placement? he says:
Regarding the distinction among trees that are being distinguished: the distinction from non-tree is the nature distinct from non-tree.
For just as one particular tree is distinct from that [non-tree], so too are all varieties of trees [distinct from it].
*Ślokavārttika*:

Therefore, that difference among them is superimposed by conceptual cognition as a unity upon all [individuals]; thus, it appears in an identical form. When that difference—which is in its own nature distinct—appears in an identical form, the application of the word occurs.
And in the phrase "this very [is it]," the word "and" (ca) has the sense of restriction;
that is, this very form appearing in conceptual construction is non-different from the external object.
Alternatively, that very difference—characterized by a nature distinct from non-trees—is what was taught by the Master Diṅnāga.
To the question "How is it stated?", he says:
"A certain portion of that entity is understood through the exclusion of others";
we shall clarify the meaning of this in the commentary on the *Arthaviniścaya*.
One might ask: "Why is that portion of the real entity, as qualified by the exclusion of others, not apprehended in its ultimate sense? To this he replies:

"Its nature (*rūpa*)—that is, its intrinsic being (*svabhāva*)—is nothing at all. This is because a distinction (*bheda*) consisting of exclusion (*nivṛtti*) is non-existent, and because that which appears in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is a delusion of the intellect (*buddhi-vibhrama*).
If difference has no form whatsoever, how then can it be said that a word expresses only entities as qualified by the exclusion of others? To this he says:
"In the cognition of that," and so forth.

When there is the cognition of that aforementioned nature of difference—which is excluded from what belongs to other classes—precisely through its being apprehended in a positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa*) from words, the exclusion of others is understood.
For instance, when "tree" is uttered, the exclusion of non-trees is understood by implication;
and by this much alone, the state of being qualified by the exclusion of others has been stated.
But from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified;
thus he says "no," and so forth.

In that context— whether regarding the meaning of a word as the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), or regarding the treatises of the Teacher (*ācāryagrantha*)— it is not understood that some "other" object, which is excluded from what is other,
is qualified by some characteristic consisting in the exclusion of others.
Therefore, as for what was said by Bhaṭṭa: "A unique particular (*asādhāraṇa-vastu*) is not understood as possessing exclusion (*apoha*);
or else, how could a relationship be postulated between a real entity (*vastu*) and a non-entity (*avastu*)?"
By its mere existence as its own nature, it could not be a qualifier;
rather, that by which the qualificand is colored through its own cognition is the qualifier.
Furthermore, from words such as "horse" and so forth, there arises no cognition of apoha.
In this context, it is accepted that the cognition of the qualified object does not arise when its qualifiers are unknown;
nor can a qualifier of one nature produce a cognition of a different nature.
Furthermore, how could something be called a "qualifier" if it pertains to a cognition of a different nature?
And in that whose nature is to be understood through non-existence, there is no substantiality in the qualified object;
for a thing qualified by an exclusion (apoha) cannot be the denotable referent,
as stated in the *Ślokavārttika*.
Thus [the objection] is refuted;
but surely, how can a single word have two functions characterized by both injunction and prohibition?
To this he says:
Nor does a word perform both functions; it does not effect the pair consisting of the expression of its own meaning and the exclusion of others.
What is the reason?
Regarding the phrase "anyonyābhāva" (mutual non-existence),
the word *iti* indicates the reason (*hetu*):

because the absence of the distinction from non-trees is the meaning of "tree," and the absence of that [tree] is the meaning of "non-tree," by virtue of being mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*).

Therefore, from the word "tree," through the very comprehension of the object "tree," there also occurs—by implication—the comprehension of the exclusion of non-trees; thus, the word does not have two direct operations.
Consequently, if this word "cow" is capable of excluding others...
One must seek another word for the cognition of "cow" in the case of Janaka;
for words do not have cognitions as their fruit, nor can there be two fruits for a single [word].
How could the cognition of a negation and the cognition of an injunction be the fruit of one and the same [word] in your view?
Thus [the objection] is refuted:
if this word "cow" is capable of excluding others, then another sound must be sought as the producer of the cognition of a cow regarding the animal.
Words do not have cognition as their fruit, nor can there be two fruits for a single [word].
How could the cognition of both negation and injunction be the fruit of one [word] for you?
If the difference expressed by words were to persist everywhere, then that itself would become the ultimate universal; therefore, he says:
The meaning is this: that distinction which follows as the object of the word "this" is formless and devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Regarding that which is formless, the seeing by the speaker and the listener—which consists in unifying the perceived object and the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and [viewing it] as possessing a form—is a confusion of the intellect, a delusion (*bhrānti*).
He explains this with the words beginning "being established" (*niveśyamāna*).

The connection is as follows: because an object such as a tree is differentiated, [the word] excludes that [object], and having abandoned it, it is applied; to the question "where? he says: [it is applied to the universal].

Regarding the phrase "of those being divided," and so forth: this has been explained in the commentary on the verse (*kārikā*). The analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is: "that word by which the exclusion of others (*tadanyavyāvṛtti*) is implied through the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktārtha*)."
And this very distinction, which appears as having a uniform form, has been indicated by the teacher Diṅnāga;
how so? He says:
"By means of the exclusion of other objects, some part of that entity is apprehended."

Likewise, by the phrase "words denote entities as qualified by the exclusion of other objects," and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of such statements as "the auditory cognition, performing the exclusion of other word-meanings, denotes [its object]";
the passage beginning with "for that... is the justification for this very point.
For that word "tree," while expressing its own nature as distinct from non-trees, functions precisely by implying the exclusion of other objects—namely, those objects that are not trees.
What is the reason?
It is because the distinction residing in one [object], and so forth.

For just as specific types of trees, such as the *khadira* and others, are by their very nature distinct from non-trees, so too are non-trees distinct from trees— since distinction resides in both relata.
