In that regard, because the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is inseparable from the expression of that distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) which appears in a single form and pertains to the tree-meaning (the object) associated with the word "tree," it is therefore inseparable from the exclusion of what is other than the tree-meaning, namely, the non-tree.
For in this way, the object "tree" would be expressed as having a form excluded from "non-trees," provided that the exclusion of the object "non-tree" is understood therein.
That very thing—the difference appearing to conceptual cognition when [an object] is distinguished from another—is the distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
By means of its exclusion—that is, by the exclusion of other objects—understood through implication according to the principle already stated, [the tree is established].
The phrase "and the portion of the real object has been reached by the cognition" (*gato ca buddho bhāgo vastunaḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

The intended meaning is that because [the cognition] is brought about through the door of perceiving the excluded real object (*vyāvṛttavastu*), and because it is determined (*adhyavasāya*) as having the nature of the real object, it is said that "the portion of the real object has been reached.
This is what is meant.

A word conveys in verbal cognition a mental image (*ākāra*)—which is the manifestation of conceptual thought (*vikalpabuddhi*), superimposed as a unity upon those [cognitions] that produce the reflective awareness of that [object], while being excluded from those that do not produce such awareness—an image in which the distinction between the external and the internal is undifferentiated. This is because it is precisely this [image] that manifests in verbal cognition. And by conveying this, the word implies the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) by the force of the meaning (*arthāt*). It was with this intention that the Master said: "By the exclusion of others, some part of that real entity (*vastu*) is understood."

Furthermore, no portion of an external object is apprehended by means of the exclusion of others—which constitutes the meaning of a word and functions as a qualifier—because such an exclusion of others simply does not exist.
Thus, it has been established that "no portion of that object is understood through the exclusion of others.
Now, in order to establish the point that "words express entities as qualified precisely by the exclusion of other word-meanings," he says:
Regarding the phrase "due to its movement" (*tadgateḥ*) and so forth:

because the movement of that [universal] consists in the movement toward the exclusion of others, and because it serves as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), there exists the state of being a limiting adjunct of difference; thus, that very [universal], when qualified by that difference, is said to have "gone."
Or rather,

it is because the understanding or apprehension of that aforementioned distinction of objects, derived from the word, is accompanied by a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), and thus that [restriction] serves as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

That [cognition] is so described because its apprehension of that [object] has as its limiting condition (upādhi) the exclusion of everything other than it, since that exclusion is implied by the object itself;
for being invariably concomitant with the exclusion of others is precisely what constitutes being a limiting condition.
This is what is meant.

The exclusion of other objects (*arthāntaravyāvṛtti*) is understood from the object itself because it is inseparable from it; therefore, that very differentiation (*bheda*), being understood from the word as qualified by the exclusion of others, is said by the Master (*Ācārya*) to be "comprehended. [Objection: But surely, the exclusion of other objects constitutes the ground for the application of the word, by which external objects such as cows and so forth are denoted by words like "cow" as being thus qualified; [this cannot be so] because [such exclusion] is not perceived.
The phrase "like a staff-bearer" (*daṇḍivat*) is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*); for just as one is called a "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) by way of the staff,
it is not so that one is [called] "possessing exclusion" (*vyāvṛttimat*) by way of exclusion.
Why is it that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is not a distinct entity? He says:
"For of the two," and so forth; because the distinction between the two—tree and non-tree—which are mutually differentiated, belongs to both.
The meaning is: because it resides in both trees and non-trees, and because its intrinsic nature is distinct from both trees and non-trees.
Therefore, even when the difference residing in the tree is expressed, it is the difference residing in the tree in relation to the non-tree.
Even when its distinct nature is denoted by a word, there occurs an inseparable implication of the other;

for, in relation to what is non-tree, there is an implication of the distinction residing in the tree—characterized as the exclusion of the non-tree—and in relation to the tree, there is likewise an implication of the distinction residing in the non-tree—characterized as the exclusion of the tree.
The word "iti" is used here in the sense of a reason.
For this reason, because that [exclusion] is its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), it is said that "that which is qualified by it has gone"—this is the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) to be supplied.
As for the phrase "not of those two," there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified between the difference residing in a single entity and the exclusion of others.

If it is asked: "What, then, is this difference residing in a single entity, and what is the exclusion of others, such that through the word there arises a cognition of the difference residing in a single entity, which is invariably concomitant with the exclusion of others?"
It is said:

first of all, that which is denoted by the word "tree" is the form possessing branches and so forth, appearing as a reflection in conceptual cognition; appearing as if it were of a non-different nature across all trees and as if distinct from those things that do not possess that nature, it is "the exclusion residing in the one," meaning its own distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In the same way, the exclusion residing in the one should be understood for that which is denoted by words such as "jar" and so forth.

And while establishing this differentiation of classes, the word indirectly conveys the exclusion of dissimilar things, characterized as a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*). This is that "exclusion of others" (*tadanya-vyāvṛtti*).

Now, one might ask: "If a portion of the real entity (*vastu-bhāga*) qualified by the exclusion of others is not being cognized, for what purpose was it stated [above] that 'it is qualified by the exclusion of others' and so forth? To this, he says:
"In the denotation of a single exclusion," and so on.

And this very distinction, which is distributed as it is and resides in a single [entity], is what is expressed by the word; the cognition of that [distinction] itself is the apprehension of positive concomitance (anvaya).
However, the apprehension of the exclusion of others (anyavyāvṛtti) through the force of the meaning is the apprehension of negative concomitance (vyatireka).
Thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), a word comes to possess meaning;

therefore, by the instruction of positive and negative concomitance, the instruction of positive concomitance is seen to be direct, while that of negative concomitance is [seen] through implication. By means of that instruction, the teacher Diṅnāga, demonstrating that words serve as components of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), stated: "The portion of reality is understood through its exclusion (*tadvyāvṛtti*)."
Likewise, he says "or distinguished by that," whereby the word "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*) expresses negative concomitance (*vyatireka*),
and the word "part of the real entity" (*vastubhāga*) expresses positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

By this, the following is also explained: the meaning is that a word expresses its own referent while performing the exclusion of other words (*śabdāntarāpoha*). In that context, that very distinction residing in a single [referent] which appears in conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) has been explained; that alone is the "own referent" (*svārtha*). Therein, the "exclusion of other referents" (*arthāntarāpoha*), characterized as a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), consists in the exclusion of other referents; "performing" that means causing it to be understood by implication. Furthermore, if the application of words such as "tree" were preceded solely by the exclusion of others, then the explanation beginning with "by the instruction of positive and negative concomitance" (*anvayavyatirekacodanayā*) would be redundant.
Therefore, positive affirmation alone is the meaning of a word;
for this very reason— that when one particular is denoted, the exclusion of others follows by implication— it is said, "for this very reason," and so forth,
because the object's own nature consists of its particulars.
That object which is the referent of the word "tree"— the form possessing branches and so forth that appears in conceptual cognition— is of a differentiated nature;
it has a distinct intrinsic character because it is excluded from non-differentiated forms, being itself [so constituted].

Therefore, because the word expresses its own meaning (svārtha) in the form of a distinction, the exclusion of others is understood by implication alone. For in this way, the understanding of the word "tree" occurs precisely as a distinction from non-trees, provided that the exclusion of non-trees follows from the meaning. Consequently, the function of the word is solely the expression of its own meaning; the exclusion of others occurs through the meaning itself. Thus, there are not two functions for the word.
Now, one might object: "A prescriptive sentence conveys only a positive connection (*anvaya*), not the prescription or prohibition of anything else;
likewise, a prohibitive sentence is understood as conveying only a mere negation, not the prescription or prohibition of anything else. To this, he says:
"For [there is] no connection," and so forth.

Positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is the prescription of a specific object, as in "cut down the tree"; therein, the exclusion of what is not a tree by implication is negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Where that [negative concomitance] does not exist, it is indeed non-negative concomitance (*avyatireka*); such a positive concomitance does not exist for me.
However, all of that is merely a negation;
therefore, it is said by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara:
"He by whom the word-meaning is not accepted as being of a positive form..."
"Nor could there be a negative concomitance (vyatireka) for that [inference], since this [concomitance] is preceded by that [positive concomitance]," as stated in the *Ślokavārttika*;
[this objection] is refuted because it is accepted [by us].
The connection is as follows: "either there is no positive concomitance (*ananvaya*), or there is a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) devoid of positive concomitance.
In this context, *vyatireka* is the negation of the specific instance;
therein, the understanding of the remainder by implication is *anvaya*.

This very point is established by the passage beginning with "of a single positive concomitance" (*ekānvayasya*). If there is no thing to be excluded—that is, if there is no object to be set aside—then an injunction is fruitless. For example, if one says, "Cut down the tree," and by implication there is no exclusion of what is not a tree, then the employment of the word "tree" would be useless. In that case, there would be no exclusion [of non-trees] therein. Thus, the use of the word "tree" would be devoid of purpose.

Alternatively, when there is a desire to know on the part of the hearer—such as "Which tree shall I cut? Or another?"—the prohibition of others is indeed understood when it is said, "Cut the tree"; otherwise, the statement would be fruitless due to the absence of anything to be avoided. Likewise, even when a hearer devoid of such inquiry is urged by the words "Cut the tree," he proceeds toward the tree alone and not elsewhere;
for the speaker employs the word with the intention that "He shall proceed toward this very tree and not elsewhere."

And since the apprehension of a sound follows the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) devoid of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), nor likewise [is there one] for the exclusion of one thing; that is to say, for the negation of a single negation.
In some cases, when an object is made the subject of a negation, because its existence is absent, any formulation [of a rule] would be fruitless.
For instance, if in the prohibition of drinking liquor— which is the specific object— the act of drinking were not to exist elsewhere than in liquor,
then the specific prohibition of drinking within that entire prohibited domain would be redundant.

In this context, since the sentence "one should not drink *surā*" fulfills its purpose by prohibiting the mere act of drinking *surā*, even though the drinking of water and so forth is not explicitly enjoined by the words, nevertheless, the possibility of drinking anything other than *surā* is not thereby precluded; thus, the understanding of the connection [of the prohibition] arises through implication (*arthāt*). Otherwise, the mention of *surā* would be meaningless.

Alternatively, when the question is asked, "Is *surā* to be drunk like water and such, or not?", and it is replied, "*Surā* is not to be drunk," the understanding arises that it is specifically *surā* [that is prohibited]; therefore, what is being negated here is not the drinking of water and such, which is the subject under discussion.
Therefore, since the meaning of a word consists everywhere exclusively of the form of either affirmation or negation,
what then is the difference between sentences of affirmation, negation, and exclusion?
There is a great difference.
For an injunctive sentence, having primarily expressed an injunction, implies the prohibition of other things;
and a prohibitive sentence, having primarily expressed a prohibition, implies the injunction of other things.
However, a sentence that establishes an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) primarily expresses the injunction of something else preceded by a prohibition. Thus, there is indeed a distinction.

Now, one might object: "If the exclusion of others is understood through implication, then why not accept that this alone is the ultimate reality of things, by which they are apprehended as qualified?
Why, then, is it explained that 'it is qualified by that' because it has reached that state through having that as its limiting adjunct? To this, he says:
"And this [exclusion], etc."
That difference characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-lakṣaṇa*) which was intended as a qualifier by the teacher Diṅnāga is formless and devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*);
since it possesses neither a distinct nor a non-distinct form, one might ask: "How then is there the cognition that things are different from those of a dissimilar class? To this he says:
The perception or cognition of that difference as possessing form— that is, as being connected with an entity— is merely a distortion, a delusion; thus,
this same explanation should be understood to apply even to the verse regarding that which is independent of such an external object.
Now, if there is perception by virtue of possessing form, how can this be a cognitive error?
To this he says, "by that very [form]," and so forth.

That perception of difference which occurs by virtue of possessing form—that is, by virtue of being related to an entity—is precisely *not* ultimate; it is not a real thing because of its non-existence.
The distinction expressed by "this" is of a negative (prasajya) nature; for if it were otherwise— were it not intended in this way—
the exclusion belonging to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a real entity would not itself be a real entity.
What is the reason?
It is because of the determination that "this is different from that.
This is what is meant:
For if that [exclusion] were a real entity, it would have to be either non-different or different from the trees;
if it were non-different, there could be no cognition of the distinction expressed as "the tree's difference from this non-tree."
Furthermore, because the exclusion from non-trees (*avṛkṣavyāvṛtti*) is not distinct from the single *palāśa* tree itself,
the exclusion from non-trees would not belong to the *dhava* and other trees; for that exclusion, which is of the same nature as the *palāśa*, does not extend (*ananugama*) to them.

Now, if that [palāśa] were distinct from "non-palāśa," then there would have to be a distinction of the palāśa from the exclusion of non-trees; and for the palāśa, which is itself being excluded from the exclusion of non-trees, there would follow the state of being a non-tree, just like a non-tree.
Consequently, the cognition "this tree is distinct from this non-tree" would not occur, yet it is indeed accepted.
Therefore, that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is not a real entity (*vastu*), because of the determination (*īraṇā*)— that is, the verbal expression (*uccāraṇa*)— "this is different from that.
And this [mention of expression] is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication), intended to include cognition (*pratīti*) as well.
He explains by means of the passage beginning with "rūpaṃ hi," for since *rūpa* is said to be the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
If the nature of a thing were its differentiation— namely, its exclusion from others— and if that [exclusion] were its form,
then it would be the case that its nature would consist in the form of being excluded from non-trees.
"Of that nature" means being of the same essence as that excluded particular characteristic (*palāśa-svalakṣaṇa*);
"or not of that nature" means being other than that, because a real entity cannot transcend being either identical to or different from [another].

With the words "tādrūpye" and so forth, he states the fault in the first position: If that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), which serves as the universal (*sāmānya*) by which all distinct trees are seen to be excluded from non-trees, were identical with the *palāśa*—that is, if its identity with the *palāśa* is accepted as being non-different from the *palāśa*—then, on the grounds that this very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *palāśa* itself is the exclusion, it follows that only the *palāśa* would be distinct from non-trees, and not others such as the *dhava* tree;
consequently, [the *dhava*] would not be differentiated from what is not a tree.
He asks, "What is the reason?
and says, "For not," and so forth;
for the exclusion from what is not a tree is the very nature of the *palāśa* tree itself.
The presentation of the second position begins with the statement that its form cannot belong to another, such as a horse, nor can it be that very [form] itself;
that is to say, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *palāśa* tree itself cannot be the form of that difference.
If this form and its intrinsic nature were held to be distinct,
then the form consisting of exclusion from *palāśa* would be something entirely other;
or else, the form of the distinction itself would be something other than the [object's] form.

Furthermore, because it would be something other [than that exclusion], the entity consisting of the *palāśa* tree would, for that reason, be excluded from that which has the form of the exclusion of non-trees. Therefore, for that reason...
There would be no distinction of that *palāśa* tree from the heat, the sun, or the tree itself;
for indeed, whatever object has a distinction from something, it must exclude that very thing from which the distinction arises.
That very thing becomes that; for, through the exclusion of non-trees— that is,
by ceasing from that which has the nature of the cessation of non-trees— the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *palāśa* tree would become like a non-tree, as if it were a non-tree.
Or, let there be no identity between the tree and the non-tree; nevertheless, the statement "this is its difference" would not be possible.
Furthermore, if this difference from the non-tree were distinct from the *palāśa* tree itself, then it could not be said that "this difference from the non-tree belongs to this *palāśa*.
The phrase "for indeed... (*na hi*) and so forth provides the justification for this very point.

One distinct entity is related to another as its correlate; when such a state of being a correlate is admitted, the relationship must be accepted as either a relation of properties (*dharmarūpa*) or a causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
Since a relationship between two distinct things is impossible without a cause-and-effect relation,
in that case, the exclusion (vyāvṛtti) is the cause and that which possesses the exclusion is the effect;
thus, the "difference" produced by that [cause] is indeed another entity, generated by that particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) which possesses the exclusion.

If a name were given to another category [of difference] simply because it is not distinct from the category called "difference" as conceived in terms of being an effect, then all effects of causes elsewhere would also be differences or exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*).
And this is not the case;
therefore, let there be no designation of "difference" even for other things that are intended to be differences.
Now, if it is not said that "the effect is difference," but rather that "difference is the effect," even then he says:
"And if difference is admitted to be a distinct entity..."
Furthermore, this difference (bheda), even though it possesses exclusion (vyāvṛtti), must itself have a further difference;
otherwise, the difference would not be a distinct entity (arthāntara) at all.

Consequently, regarding the difference of the *palāśa* tree from "non-tree," if one considers that difference to be different from the *palāśa*, then that difference [of the difference] becomes a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the difference, and thus that [adjunct] is the difference from the *palāśa*.

That distinction for which a specific limiting condition (*upādhi*) exists is a "distinction conditioned by that" (*tad-upādhi*); the state of being such is its "nature" (*tattva*). Therefore, this distinction of the *palāśa* tree from non-trees would not be a distinction belonging to the *palāśa*, just like [the distinction of] another substance.

For just as another substance, such as a jar and so forth, is not a distinction of the *palāśa*—because the distinction it has in relation to non-jars is merely a limiting condition—it is the same in this case.
The intention is that [difference] is independent.
Now, one might object: "Even if difference is indeed a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of difference, why does the *palāśa* tree not possess difference? To this, he says:
"For not... and so forth.
Because of the specific indication "this is from that," this exclusion of non-trees is [expressed] as "from that," namely,
from non-trees.
The word "of this" (asya) must be supplied;

for by specifying a particular distinction—namely, "this is the distinction of this *palāśa* tree from that other tree"—the distinction (*bheda*) is established as a property (*dharma*) belonging to the *palāśa* through its dependence on another. And such a designation through dependence is only possible if there is no [absolute] non-difference, because it involves the exclusion of other distinctions.
But it is not so if difference were a separate entity;

for if difference were a separate entity, then—since it would be a limiting adjunct (upādhi) of difference—the jar would not possess difference, just as the *palāśa* tree does not [possess the difference of the jar].
Consequently, there could be no specific designation such as "this is different from that."

Thus, in this way, regarding the position of difference (*vyatireka-pakṣa*), even the difference of a *palāśa* tree from what is not a tree must itself possess form; consequently, that too must exist as distinct from its own substratum.

And so, since all differences would have a distinct nature and would thus function as limiting conditions (*upādhi*) for further difference, they themselves would not be differences of form; therefore, no difference whatsoever would exist.
He says this very thing:
Regarding the passage beginning with "tataśca" and so forth:

"in the absence of a limiting adjunct" (*upādhyabhāva*) means that when there is an absence of a limiting adjunct characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), which is a property (*dharma*), then because everything would be a substratum (*dharmin*) by virtue of being a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāvāntara*), difference itself would be non-existent, since that [difference] consists in the form of a substratum.
This is also the view of one who thinks thus.

If exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) were possessed of form (*rūpavatī*), then the fault inherent in the positions of identity or difference would apply; however, since it is formless (*nīrūpā*) and yet entities are apprehended as qualified by it, that [objection] is untenable,
for the exclusion of others is understood from words precisely through the apprehension of those [entities].
Because it contradicts the text: "In that [state], no one whatsoever is understood as superior or other" (Prajñāpradīpa 1.128).
Furthermore, because existence is incompatible with that which is formless— just like the horn of a hare—
and precisely because it is formless, perception cannot be its apprehender, nor can inference,
due to the absence of a [necessary] relationship.
The exclusion of others is understood from words precisely as directed toward those [objects];

therein, no particular [object] is understood by anyone as distinct. Nor can there be a postulation of that [exclusion] on the grounds that a fixed form would otherwise be inexplicable, because there is simply no relation [between the word and such an exclusion].
Furthermore, because things arise from their own causes with determined forms— as was stated in the intervening passage, "All entities participate in exclusion by virtue of their intrinsic nature"—
nor can that [exclusion] be a qualifier if it has not been apprehended.
For indeed, when the staff is not perceived, the cognition "one who possesses a staff" does not occur;
nor is that [cognition] dependent on anything, because it lacks a form (nīrūpatvāt);
and a qualifier cannot be unrelated [to its substratum].

Nor does the word "tree" apply to trees and so forth preceded by the apprehension of the exclusion of others, because it has been stated that there is no such cognition; furthermore, since exclusion is formless and thus not perceived, the conventional designation cannot function.
How, then, could it be an object of a word? Therefore, through the medium of direct experience, the certainty arises: "This is a tree, not a non-tree."

Therefore, the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*) is conceptually constructed by means of the conceptualization of negation; and a word, when applied to a tree or the like according to convention, implies the exclusion of others through its meaning—that is to say, it implies the conceptualization of the exclusion of others. This is the sense.
If it is argued that "a specific portion of reality is understood by means of the exclusion of others," yet these exclusions— which function as universals— are not accepted as external entities;

Nor, this being the case, can the universal as imagined by others be [the referent], for it would follow that an external object itself must be the denotable thing, and there is a fault in that; thus he asks: "How then?"
This is an illustration regarding the indication by means of a word of an undifferentiated, partless entity; it applies equally to its presentation by means of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
For that very same undifferentiated entity, which is distinct from one thing, is likewise distinct from another as well.
To explain: by that very nature through which a word is distinct from the "unproduced" (*akṛtaka*), it is also [distinct] from the "corporeal" (*mūrta*) and the "impermanent" (*anitya*).
Because that [object] is partless,
and because when a single distinct difference from the non-artificial is indicated by the word "artificial"— that is, when its distinct intrinsic nature is communicated—
this is effected through such a mark (*liṅga*) by means of the inclusion of all differences; thus, there is the comprehension of an intrinsic nature that is distinct from everything.
In that case, regarding an entity that lacks parts, how could other means of knowledge, such as verbal testimony, not be redundant?
If the injunction were conveyed by a single word, other words would be redundant;
if it were established by a single inferential mark, other means of knowledge would be redundant.
He refutes [this objection] with the words beginning "Because... (yasmāt).

This very point of contention has already been refuted previously by the passage beginning, "Therefore, whatever specific property is perceived by which [means]... (tasmād yo yena dharmeṇa viśeṣaḥ saṃpratīyate). However, it is presented again for the purpose of providing further elaboration.
The superimposition of another form upon objects is "conjunction with the object" (*arthaśleṣa*); and that is manifold according to the difference in cognition.
In this regard, those [forms] are to be expressed as distinct from the external within the subject (*dharmin*) appearing to the intellect.

Since it is precisely the mental form (buddhyākāra) superimposed as external that is denotable by a word— and not the external object nor the mental form alone, because these are particular characteristics (svalakṣaṇa)—

in that case, with respect to the substratum (dharmin), a single sound operates through the removal of the connection between a single object by means of cognizing its own referent in a positive form (vidhirūpa).
And the *liṅga* (logical mark) functions in the exclusion [of other meanings] through the conjunction of a single referent;
in that case, the efficacy of other means of knowledge (*śabda-pramāṇa*) lies in the exclusion of superimposition by way of denoting its own object— this is the sense.
Furthermore, there exists no external object as a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) distinct from cognition,
nor any external object as a universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) distinct from the particular characteristic, which—
by being denoted— could lead to an understanding of the entire nature of a thing.
Because of the capacity of the thing and by the power of the thing itself,

since a word effects an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) by means of its own denotation, for that reason, while effecting each respective exclusion, how can the word have diverse results and yet have a single substratum?

The meaning is that, having determined [the object] as capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-yogya*), one superimposes its own appearance— which, although not performing causal efficiency, is of the nature of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)— as being something that performs causal efficiency.
"In that very [place]" means in the manifestation of cognition (*buddhi-pratibhāsa*) which has been superimposed as external.
In what state does it appear as if its form were mixed with various causes of delusion?

When [an object] appears as if its form were conjoined with aspects such as permanence due to causes of error—such as the arising of a subsequent similar [moment]—those words like "impermanent" are applied according to convention for the purpose of excluding whichever superimposition [is intended], since the convention was made regarding one's own appearance. Why? [Because it excludes that specific superimposition.]
Explaining that they function precisely in accordance with convention to exclude each respective counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*),
he says "na ca" and so forth.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "hy" (for/indeed);
for since the operation [of a word] occurs according to convention, one word does not effect an exclusion that is to be accomplished by another word.
What is the reason?

The meaning is as follows: because of the specific restriction of convention (*saṃketa-pratiniyama*), a mental form (*buddhyākāra*) is applied to a word for the purpose of excluding each [of the other objects] within an undifferentiated external reality; thus, even at the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra-kāla*), by means of denoting its own object, it causes that very exclusion to be understood.
The mention of "sound" (śabda) is merely illustrative; it should be understood that the same applies to the "inferential mark" (liṅga) as well.

Now, one might object: since the referent of a word possesses the form of the external object as determined by conceptualization, and because the word thereby apprehends its object in its entirety—characterized by other [words]—how is it that other words are not rendered redundant? To this, he says "na ca" and so forth;
the word "ca" here functions as a restrictive particle.

No object whatsoever— neither a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) distinct from a portion of cognition, nor a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) separate from the particular, nor that characterized by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)— is projected, grasped, or expressed by means of a word or a logical mark (*liṅga*).

For if it were, then through the expression of such an object, there would necessarily be a complete comprehension of the thing-in-itself by the force of the object itself, since the object is partless.

Because it has been stated [in the passage beginning] "Since, therefore, there is a distinction from the properties... even if there is a distinction of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi), there is the apprehension of the self which is non-different from the capacities that are the factors for the assistance of the various adjuncts," that there is no apprehension whatsoever [of the self].
To the question, "Why is a thing implied by words that are themselves distinct [from it]?
he says, "Of words," and so forth;
this is what is meant:
The meaning is that because words determine as external that which is actually not external—the form of cognition—therefore they appear as if they were apprehenders of discrete, external objects.
Furthermore, the "distortion" (*vipralava*) of cognition consists in the grasping of the form of cognition as having an external nature;
and since words have that [form] as their object, they too are subject to such distortion.
If it is asked, "Why is there not comprehension of the entire object even when there is a failure of the intellect, due to the power of the thing to be expressed?", he says:
"And in that case," and so forth.

In that case, regarding the distortion of cognition (*buddhi-viplava*), although the form of cognition is a real entity because it is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of knowledge— since no real entity exists where there is no real object—
it is nonetheless a non-entity, for it is superimposed by words or conceptual constructions as being non-different from an external object.

Therefore, neither sound nor conceptual construction has the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, because not even a single external thing or a form of cognition is apprehended exactly as it is.

If all words have only the distortions of the intellect (*buddhiviplava*) as their objects, how can words such as "produced" (*kṛtaka*) or "impermanent" (*anitya*) be non-deviant with respect to a real entity that exists in such a manner?
To this, he says: "In such a manner," and so forth.
The connection is as follows: "this conventional usage" [occurs] "by way of the experience of an object" that is distinct from the uncreated, eternal, and so forth;
what kind [of usage is it]?
Regarding the phrase "nānaika" and so forth:
"nānaika" means both "various" (nānā) and "one" (eka); that [term] and "dharma" form a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Then, there is a three-membered *dvandva* compound consisting of the words "difference," "non-difference," and "words.
Only differences and non-differences of various properties appear in the cognition; these very appearances are the "distortion" (*viplava*) because they are erroneous.
"Following that" means having proceeded with that form [of appearance].

For this reason, when that conventional usage is connected to its [real] basis—that is, when there is an indirect connection to production in that such-like particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—there is non-deviation from it;
that is, non-deviation from the real entity (*vastu*).
For just as verbal forms such as "produced" are erroneous, so too do entities exist in reality in the form of being "produced" and so forth; thus, non-deviation should be understood in this manner.

He says this very point in the passage beginning with "tato 'pi" (even from that): from that verbal convention, which is characterized as inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) and has as its object a distortion of the intellect (*buddhiviplava*), and which is therefore false— that is, erroneous.

"At the end of its occurrence," that is, upon the completion of its occurrence, it refers to an object that is precisely of such a nature—namely, having the form of being produced and so forth—and not one having the form of being unproduced and so forth.

By this, the essential nature of non-deviation is stated, because there is correspondence with cognition; that is, because a cognition grasping the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) arises, or because there is correspondence between the word and the cognition.

He states that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established only when the meaning of a word is this very exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), and not in reference to a real entity (*vastu*),
beginning with the words "not, however, distinct," and so forth;
for the distinct forms— such as universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), and the like— are the grounds for the application of words.
Because the cognitions and words grasping that [object] have a single entity as their object, the word has a single substratum; this is the connection.
For if a cognition with distinct forms were to proceed having a single entity as its object, then the word, following that [cognition], would likewise be so.

And thus, it would follow that a word with multiple meanings could have a single substratum, which would constitute grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); yet that is not the case, because it involves a contradiction.
To explain: for the words "blue" and "lotus," the referent would have to be either a single entity or multiple entities.
In the first case, since a partless entity would be denoted in its entirety by a single word alone, [the other word would be redundant].
There would be no application of a second term, or if it were applied, there would be synonymy; thus, there is no plurality of results.
In the second position, there is no single substratum because, like the words "pot" and "cloth," there is a plurality of objects.
Now, it might be thought that the word "blue" denotes a substance qualified by the quality of blueness,
while the word "lotus" also denotes that very same substance as qualified by the genus "lotus."

Therefore, [the claim that] "because the two qualifiers are distinct, the word has multiple objects, whereas because the qualified object is non-distinct, it has a single substratum"— that too is incorrect;
for when a substance qualified by the quality blue is denoted by the word 'blue', it is denoted in its entirety, since it is partless.

Furthermore, if another essence of the substance, qualified by the genus "lotus," were not already denoted [by the substance-word] such that it could be denoted by the word "lotus," then there would likewise be synonymy. Alternatively, if the substance as the qualificandum were distinct due to the difference in qualifiers, then even in that case, they would not share a single substratum.
However, for the proponent of Apoha, this fault does not apply; thus he says:
Regarding the phrase "as described" and so forth: that referent of a word (*śabdārtha*) which has as its basis the appearance (*pratibhāsa*) in cognition is described in that way.
Demonstrating how there is no fault, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "vicchedam" and so forth:

a single word "blue," while indicating one exclusion—namely, the blue nature as excluded from non-blue—functions without rejecting another, such as the lotus nature as excluded from non-lotuses; the meaning is that it does not exclude it.
That [nature], namely the intrinsic nature excluded from non-lotuses,
being pervaded, occupied, and implied by that word "blue," appears as a single unity in the mind when the word "lotus" is employed;
for there is the appearance in conceptual cognition of a single substratum endowed with the two properties of being blue and being a lotus, which are brought about by the two respective exclusions.
And when this is so, there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by virtue of conforming to the cognition;
what is meant is this:
due to the employment of the word "blue," the substratum appearing in cognition appears as having the very form of blue.

In that case, by implication, the non-blue is excluded, but the nature [of the object] as excluded from non-lotuses is not excluded; for even when the word "lotus" is employed, it is perceived as having the form of a lotus, and thus excludes the non-lotus, but does not exclude the nature already excluded from the non-blue. However, when both words are employed, a conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) arises in which a single substratum appears as endowed with the two properties of being blue and being a lotus. Consequently, the word has multiple results while having a single basis; thus, there may be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in accordance with the cognition. Therefore, as for what was stated by Uddyotakara:

Furthermore, for one who holds that the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), it must be explained how the exclusions of "non-blue" and "non-lotus" can be coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*). On the other hand, for one according to whom the meaning of a word is that which is being positively enjoined (*vidhīyamāna*), a substance qualified by a genus and a quality is denoted by the two words "blue lotus," and the genus and the quality reside in the substance; it is not, however, the case that the exclusions of "non-blue" and "non-lotus" [reside there].

Therefore, the claim that there is no referent for grammatical coreferentiality (samānādhikaraṇa) is refuted, because it is accepted that the meaning of the word being prescribed [is indeed such a referent]. 133

Furthermore,
if it is admitted that a word effects the exclusion of superimpositions by means of denoting its own object, [what follows?]

Alternatively, in the act of exclusion— that is, in the taking as its object of an excluded nature— there would be at least some slight contact (*saṃsparśa*), characterized by attainment, with the property of the thing, the nature of the thing, which is differentiated from what is of a different class. What is the reason?

"Real" (*satya*) means that which exists; for it is the determined, delimited nature (*svabhāva*) with respect to that object. Thus, when words denoting a single entity are accepted, there is no contact with the property of a real thing, because a universal as a real entity does not exist. If one asks, "How so?"— The answer is as follows: A word such as "existent" (*sat*), being applied to many things, cannot denote a single entity. "In the Buddha," and so forth;
that is to say, because there is non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension, there is non-existence.

Since such a fault exists when the object of a word is a real entity (*vastu*), for that reason the teacher Diṅnāga stated that words and cognitions have as their object the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), which is the appearance within conceptual cognition.
What kind of cognitions [are meant]? The meaning is that they have universals as their object and are conceptual.
This qualification applies to cognitions alone and not to words, because the latter deviate from having universals as their objects.
What is the reason?
Because these words and conceptual constructions can occur with respect to a real entity (*vastu*),
he explains by means of the passage beginning with "If indeed" (*yadi hi*):
if the real entity itself were made the object— that is, if it were apprehended— it would not, however, be determined (*adhyavasīyeta*) as having a positive form.
"This very [consequence]," as just mentioned, is the undesirable result that all objects would be cognized in every respect by virtue of the objective power (*vastusāmarthya*) of things;

by the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the absence of the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), the non-operation of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), and so forth.
The author is the Master Diṅnāga.

These two—the cognition and the word—are said to have the form of conceptual construction (vikalpākāra), because by means of them something else is excluded; they thus have that [exclusion] as their object.
If, in this way, a single entity were made the object of cognitions possessing distinct forms, [it would follow that it possesses those various forms].

If it were denoted by the word in exactly that same way, then there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because two words with distinct referents would be functioning with respect to a single substance; however, this is not possible.
For instance, would that universal denoted by the word be non-different from the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), or would it be different?
In that case, according to the first position,
since the nature of the object is one, from what source could there arise a cognition that is diverse in form, consisting of the aspects of universal and particular?

Furthermore, since the universal is not distinct from its own particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it follows that the particular consisting of a *śāvaleyā* cow, from which it is excluded, must be the same as the particular consisting of a *bāhuleyā* cow; and yet, the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) consisting of a *śāvaleyā* cow would be concomitant with the *bāhuleyā*. Thus, for a single entity, both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) would pertain to a single substratum.
And that is incorrect; thus he says, "positive and negative concomitance," and so forth.
That which has a single object—that is, a single domain or scope—is what is described by those two terms.
He explains [the verse] with the words "that one" (*tadekam*) and so forth: precisely because it is one, it is partless, since a single thing lacks parts;
"form" (*ākāra*) refers to that which is fashioned, namely the appearance in the intellect (*buddhipratibhāsa*).

If its differentiation— that is, the differentiation of the substrate consisting in the multiplicity of things— were apprehended by cognitions possessing distinct forms, then it would be differentiated.
If it is argued that because the entity does not exist in that way—
since an entity consists of both the universal and the particular— even a single entity can be grasped by cognitions of different forms, [the author] says:
"And also by that nature," and so forth.

Because it shares the same acquisition and preservation (*ekayogakṣema*) as the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), that is, because it possesses the same acquisition and preservation as the particular characteristic, it is non-different from it in that very way; therefore,
this [phenomenon] such as grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would not occur— this is the connection [of the argument].
What is the reason?

Because two words that have mutually exclusive meanings— meaning, because they possess distinct grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) by way of excluding one another's referents— it is impossible for them to function with respect to a single object or as being based upon a single substance.
He explains the portion of the verse beginning with "anvaya" (concomitance) by means of the passage beginning with "na ca" (nor).

When the single essence of a thing (*vastvātmā*)—the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal (*sāmānya*)—is one and the same, then, because the particular of a brindled cow (*śāvaleyasvalakṣaṇa*) consists of the universal of cowness (*gotvasāmānyātmakatva*), there is a presence (*vṛtti*) of that [universal] in the spotted cow (*bāhuleya*); yet, because it also consists of the particular, there is an absence (*avṛtti*) in that very same [spotted cow] at that time. Thus, [the two] are applied simultaneously.
And that [position] is untenable because it involves contradiction and is sublated by valid means of cognition.

If it is argued that because it is non-different from its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the universal (*sāmānya*) does not exist elsewhere, and therefore there is neither occurrence nor non-occurrence of a single thing in multiple locations, [the author] says "nor... and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "of the universal" (*sāmānyasya*),
the intention is that there is neither occurrence nor non-occurrence for a single entity;
[the author] says "no," because according to the systems of Sāṃkhya and others, there is no difference between the universal and the particular.
The passage beginning with "that" (*tad*) is a justification of this very point:
for that entity, being of a single form and a single nature, must be either a universal (*sāmānya*) or a particular (*viśeṣa*).
Because the particular is not distinct from the universal, it would be the universal alone;
or because the universal is not distinct from the particular, it would be the particular alone; but a single entity cannot possess two forms.
For, since this distinction as "universal" and "particular" does not exist when there is no difference in form,
or else— if such a distinction were to exist— there would be no non-difference between the universal and the particular; as was stated previously, therefore, this is the very nature of the entity.
"Indivisible" means partless;
if it were merely a universal (*sāmānya*), then it would follow along with or enter into another individual (*vyakti*); or else, if it were of the nature of a particular (*viśeṣa*) alone...
In that case, one would not seek [the other],
because two contradictory properties cannot coexist in a single thing; this is precisely what he states.
"Furthermore," and so forth;
[the author] states that even Vaiśeṣika and others assert that the universal, which is denoted by words, is indeed distinct from the substance.

If a difference between the individual and the universals were admitted, then linguistic usages based on non-difference— such as usages involving grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth— would become groundless.
The term *yathāsvam* is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) formed with the distributive particle *vīpsā*.
For instance, words such as "blue lotus" express their respective universals (*sāmānya*)— the blue and the lotus— which are mutually distinct;
even when the word "blue" is held to denote the quality of blueness, there is still the expression of distinct objects,
for that cognition has a single substratum (*dharmin*) as its object.
The meaning is that since this cognition (*buddhi*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound— meaning "that which has a single object"— and thus undergoes the *pumvadbhāva* (masculine gender substitution),
how could its substrata (*āśrayāḥ*) be its cause?
Consequently, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

If words such as "blue lotus" were to produce a cognition whose object is a single substratum (dharmin) conjoined with two qualifiers, then there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) through the presentation of a single referent; however, that is not the case.

This is because the universal (*sāmānya*), which is distinct from the individual (*vyakti*), is what is denoted by [the word], and those [words] do not imply (*anākṣepaka*) the particulars contained within it. "Implication" (*ākṣepa*) consists in the occurrence [of the word] without abandoning those particulars; but it is not so here.
Why?
Because it is free from expectancy;
for when the word "tree" denotes tree-ness itself, [it is complete].

In that case, because it is devoid of qualification, the word would be complete with just that much; how then could it imply *dhava* trees and the like? And since they are not implied, how could *dhava* and the others be the particulars of the meaning of the word "tree"? Furthermore, since they are not its particulars, how could there be the relationship of qualifier and qualified in the expression "the tree is a *śiṃśapā*"? To this, he says:
If it is argued that the aforementioned fault does not apply because the substance is denoted as qualified by its general property (*sāmānya*), we say no,
for this has already been answered.

Even when a substance qualified by its qualifiers is denoted, because the entire [meaning] is understood from a single word through the inherent power of the thing (*vastu-sāmarthya*), another word does not apply to that same object; and if it were to apply, they would not be synonyms.

Thus, for those who maintain that the referent of a word is a real entity (*vastu-śabdārthavādin*), the possibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth is in no way possible;
furthermore, it has already been stated that even a universal (*sāmānya*) is not possible for them.
For instance, when the universal is not distinct from the particular, then—just like the particular—it does not follow after other individuals and thus is not a universal;
even if it were distinct, how could it be the universal of another? This would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and so forth, as previously stated.
However, for the proponent of exclusion (*vyāvṛttivādin*), this is not a fault; thus he says:
"Everywhere," and so forth;
"these faults" refers to the absence of general co-referentiality (*sāmānya-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the like;
"for just as," and so forth.
A single cow-individual, such as Śāvaleyā, is distinct from that nature of non-cow; likewise, another individual, such as Bāhuleyā and so forth, is also distinct.

Therefore, the nature excluded from heterogeneous things is identical everywhere. Thus, because the nature—which is distinct from heterogeneous things—is superimposed by conceptual cognition (vikalpabuddhi) everywhere without distinction upon its own form, there is no fault regarding the lack of a universal (asāmānya).
Furthermore, the objection that "there is no remainder" [and thus] the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) and so forth has already been stated previously.

Having thus established that a single [universal] is denoted by a word—[a universal] which, while indicating exclusion [from others], exists without rejecting its own nature as excluded from heterogeneous instances, and which is everywhere superimposed by the intellect as non-different from its own form—[the author] now states that even in the absence of a non-different form, a single word is applied to entities that produce a single effect: "By means of such [arguments] as 'indicating a distinction, it exists without rejecting the one' (1.133), etc., having first demonstrated that the nature excluded from heterogeneous things is everywhere designated by a single word through its superimposition by the intellect as non-different from its own form, he now says: even without a non-different form, a single word is employed for entities that have a single effect."
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "api ca" serves either to raise an objection regarding that effect in order to challenge the notion of a single effect,
or to raise an objection regarding those things which have a single effect.

Regarding particulars that have a single effect— even though they are devoid of a single [inherent] existence— a single uniform term has been established and conventionally assigned by elders who are conversant with worldly usage.

The meaning is this: the single term is applied to things that have a single effect, based on their exclusion from those things that do not have that effect—that is, based on their exclusion from what is of a different class.
(138) Now, one might object: "If the application of words does not occur in a universal (*sāmānya*), then it must occur in the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), since nothing else exists."
Furthermore, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not denotable by words; for this reason:

first, the communicator, intending to establish a convention based on a single effect, takes as his object entities existing in the three times and establishes the convention with respect to those very entities for the purpose of communication at the time of linguistic usage.
Therefore, although entities that revolve within the intellect are of a universal nature, nevertheless, when many of them manifest as if external, a single word is applied to them;

it is not the case that, while a universal of a distinct form exists in all those individuals, a separate auditory expression (śruti) was not designated for each individual. To this, he says "gaurava" and so forth.
Because of the [unwieldy] prolixity, the impossibility, and the futility of expressing distinctions— that is, of a distinct verbal expression denoting difference—
or rather, because of the expression of difference, i.e., the statement of distinction; and we shall clarify this in the commentary (*vṛtti*).
The uniform application of a single term is not made for a universal that exists as a real entity;
what is the reason? Because the intrinsic nature—that is, the specific form—of all things is established without confusion.
By stating "the form which belongs to the brindled [cow]," and so forth, he asserts that it possesses an established intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
therefore, the universal is not non-different [from the individual].
Even if it were different, since it would remain fixed within its own intrinsic nature, how could it be the common form of the individuals?

For it has been stated that things are not identical by virtue of being different; rather, the causes of the cognition of forms such as the dewlap and so forth are those which do not produce other effects, and their exclusion from those [other effects] is the excluded intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of both—
namely, of the *śāvaleya* and the *bāhuleya*.

Therefore, since the exclusion of what is not its effect is not contradictory even for distinct things, that very [exclusion] must be accepted as the non-difference of objects and the cause of the non-difference of words, because the non-difference of words is not tenable without the non-difference of the object. To the question, "How then is there a single designation for many things if it proceeds from the non-difference of the object alone? he says:
Therefore, and so forth:

that "single-ness of effect" (ekakāryatā) which was intended as the object of the objection—"there is one word for many"—is also to be understood as a difference [from others] precisely because of their not having that effect;
that is, the nature of many things is to be seen as distinct precisely from that which does not have their effect.
But there is no such thing as a universal called "being an effect of that" [i.e., being an effect of fire].
And showing that even without a universal, the application of a single word to distinct things is not contradictory, he says: "In the case of the eye, etc. and so forth.
The analysis of the compound is: "that of which the single fruit is visual consciousness (rūpavijñāna), [beginning] with the eye (cakṣurādi).

Regarding the word "in some cases" (kvacit): it means at whatever time those [causes] capable of producing consciousness are intended to be presented; or alternatively, the connection is that one may employ a conventional expression at a certain time.
To the question "For what purpose would one do so?", he says:
without distinction— that is, generally—
because it is possible to reveal to others the collection of causes for that effect, which is the single effect of visual consciousness.
But when the uncommon causal function of the eye and so forth is being enjoined, then a single term is not conventionally applied to them;
this means that [the term is used] for the sake of perceiving the entire collection of causes simultaneously, at one and the same time.
"Even in the absence," and so forth;

the meaning is that even though there is no separate universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by having a single effect—namely, the commonality of form (*rūpasāmānya*)—among those [faculties] such as the eye, [one might argue] that "existence itself (*sattā*) is their universal. If this is claimed, it is not so, because since existence is without distinction, it would follow that visual consciousness would arise at all times and in all places.
"Without an undifferentiated object" means without a real entity that is a universal;
"among many," such as the brindled cow and so forth;
"of these" refers to the particulars, such as the brindled cow and the like.
If there were a universal (sāmānya) belonging to those particulars, then, because the word would be applied to that universal, it would be applied to every particular;
yet, without a single universal, the application of a single word to many things is not logical.
Consequently, when that word is being conventionally established, it would be established as referring to only one particular.

And likewise, since a single function that has been established in one particular instance does not produce a corresponding cognition in another distinct instance of a different nature, a second individual cow would not be perceived from that word as "cow," because of the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*) there which serves as the basis for such proximity.

If it is argued that even in the absence of conformity to an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), a cognition directed toward a brindled cow (*śābaleya*) will produce a corresponding notion regarding a non-proximate black cow (*bāhuleya*),
the author replies with the words "And in the case of what is not proximate," etc.,
because this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
From the word "cow," there would also be a cognition of a horse;

thus far, it has been stated that without a single universal, there can be no application of a single word to many things. Now, [the author] speaks of the futility [of such a universal], even while granting its existence.
Regarding the phrase "and among them," and so forth:
for instance, a single word is applied to many [objects] either to convey a single meaning that functions in multiple ways,
or else to indicate those very same distinct entities without confusion.
Regarding that, he states the non-existence of the first [alternative] with the words "because there is no restriction to a single object" (*ekārthaniyogābhāvāt*).
If there were a restriction of the word to a single object, then there would be the communication of a single object.
He states the absence of a second [property] with the words "distinct," and so forth;
the ellipsis to be supplied is: "for the cognitions of distinct entities such as the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*), which possess distinct natures and are unmixed."
"Separately" means when the application— that is, the conventional designation— of a single word has been made for each individual distinction.
Later, at the time of practical usage (*vyavahāra*),

for the sake of non-confused comprehension according to how things were enjoined— since there would be a failure to discern the distinction between those things enjoined— the application of words to them would not be fruitful.
In this way, indeed, the application of words to individual particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*) one by one becomes fruitful.

The intention [of the opponent] is this: "If one were to hold that the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are cognized from that word without confusion, and since the application of a single word is indeed made toward many [particulars], there must therefore exist a real entity (*vastubhūta*) called a universal (*sāmānya*).
To this, the Teacher [Dharmakīrti] replies with the words "tasyāpi" and so forth.
One alternative is that a single entity exists as a universal, and for this very reason, a word should be applied by people even without a specific purpose;
he states the second [alternative].
Regarding the phrase "that [it] knows," and so forth:
"that" refers to the universal; "by the power of the object itself" means without depending on the operation of a person.
It causes one auditory organ to vibrate and brings it forth;
indeed, that dual [process] does not exist at all without a purpose and human effort, since there would otherwise be no application.
He says "What then is that? and so forth, [explaining] that it is for some purpose; [this applies] to these words in conventional usage.
By the phrase "having understood the object as that which establishes [the goal] or its opposite, one should practice," he states the absence of the first alternative;
by the phrase "they are being pointed out," he states the absence of the second.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "they are pointed out and designated by those desiring to engage in conventional usage.
In this regard, according to this principle, many causes would be employed—that is, they would operate—toward a single effect;
that [is what is meant by] "many."
From which collection of causes does that [effect] arise?

Regarding this very effect, those who wish to engage in linguistic convention must necessarily rely on the fact that its multiple causes—characterized by their exclusion from what is not that effect—possess a single functional unity; thus, it is proper to designate them by a single word.
He states the fault in designating them by multiple words:
The phrase beginning with "tasya" (of that) and so forth means "by distinct [words]";
this has been stated while accepting the application of words to specific individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
He says "and not," etc., [meaning] that this very thing is not possible for this entity.
"An uncommon form" means that which is not common to others; "uncommon" (*ananyasādhāraṇa*) refers to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Nor does this apply to the application of multiple words.
And this is a sequential elaboration of [the reasons] "due to respect, incapacity, and futility.
If one asks, "Why is there futility? he says: "Only," and so forth.

By this speaker, for the sake of this particular task, those things which serve as causes are to be enjoined; this much is the purpose. As for whether those causal factors are enjoined by a single word or by many, the speaker has freedom here in the act of enjoining.
Since it is so, therefore this single word, proceeding on the basis of the speaker’s intention toward many objects to be expressed, does not deserve criticism.
If it is argued that "it is impossible for a single word to be applied to many [objects]," he says:
"And this is not... and so forth.
This is one *śruti* (scriptural statement);
the analysis of the compound is "that whose application is impossible.
Why does he say it is not "impossible to apply"?
Because it is dependent on desire: that which is dependent on desire is impossible to set in motion;
for if [it were so] even in one instance, and so forth.
For in that case, regarding the universal (sāmānya) imagined by others, the application of a single word does not occur through the actual state of things,
but rather by the power of the speaker’s intention;
for it would not be so if the speaker’s intention were absent.
The intention is this: how could this single word function with respect to even a single [object], and yet it does not?
Thus, the very desire to make it function with respect to even one [object] is the cause.
He says, "Or in the case of desire," and so forth, meaning that even when there are many [causes], there is no contradiction regarding the causal power of the entity (*vastu*).
Even if one were to postulate a single [Vedic text] as the cause for the desire to set [the tradition] in motion here,
there would be no purpose for this one Vedic text, and so forth.
For the application of a single word to many things is not fruitful without a single underlying entity;
he asks what was said previously regarding this.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of the divided," etc.:

when there are various divisions such as the *śāvaleyā* (the brindled cow) and so forth, the cognition arising from the single word "cow" occurs by way of differentiation from those things that do not serve its purpose;

that is, it occurs by way of differentiation from horses and the like, for whom the effects and purposes—such as the tasks of carrying loads or milking—that are to be accomplished by those specific cows do not exist.
But why is it that a unity existing as a real entity (*vastubhūta*) is not being questioned? To this he says:
"Nor, however, is there a single term for diverse things because of the unity of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor because of the unity of a universal (*sāmānya*) existing as a real entity;
for it is illogical [to maintain] that such a thing exists either as distinct from or non-distinct from the universal."
Let it be granted that the universal is distinct; nevertheless, even that [universal] is established within that very nature as something unmixed. He says this very thing:
Regarding the phrase "according to their own [nature]" and so forth:

since things whose intrinsic natures are established by their respective characteristics do not possess a mutual commingling of forms, how could a single word—based on a universal and having a single cause—apply to distinct entities?
The intended meaning is that it could not.
For things do not become identical by virtue of being different from one another;
this was already stated previously in the passage: "All entities, by their own intrinsic nature, are established in their respective intrinsic natures. (1)
In this context, he states "that which has that as its purpose," etc., [meaning] that for the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others), this is not a fault.

Since the exclusion from those things that do not serve that purpose is not contradictory even for distinct entities, let that very difference from non-purposeful things be the non-difference of those things that serve that purpose; because this exclusion exists everywhere, let it be the cause of the non-difference of words. Furthermore, since a real, ontological universal (*sāmānya*) is in no way tenable, [let the aforementioned be the case].

Regarding the statement that "those types of cows have those purposes, namely the purposes of carrying loads and milking," it means they are stated as being distinct from horses and the like, which do not have those purposes.
Furthermore, their status as having that [single] effect is nothing other than their difference from others;
that is to say, their non-difference consists precisely in their nature being excluded from others.
By this, the portion of the verse beginning with "tatkāryatāpi" (and their having that effect) has been explained.
With the words "Just as," etc., he explains [the verse] beginning with "In the case of the eye and so forth, [it has] the single fruit of visual consciousness," and so on;
the phrase "in the contact of the self, the sense-faculties, the mind, and the object" is stated according to what is established by the opponent.
The analysis of the compound is: "those for whom the cognition of form (*rūpavijñāna*) is a single effect.

Those for whom that cognition of form is the effect are "those having that as their effect" (*tatkāryāṇi*). The "commonality" (*sāmānya*) of those [causes] is their capacity to produce a single effect without distinction; the "instruction" (*codanā*) regarding this is its manifestation.
When its occurrence is established, by what occasion does the possibility of an inquiry arise? He says:
"From what [does] form-consciousness [arise]?"—the meaning is that this occurs when a question is posed regarding the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) without further qualification.

The connection [of the passage] is as follows: for the sake of brevity in conventional usage (*vyavahāra-lāghava*), and for the purpose of conveying many things by means of a single word, one should establish a linguistic convention (*śruti*) such that the collection of causes for the cognition of form—beginning with the eye—is called "lake" (*saraḥ*) or "arrow" (*śaraḥ*).
With the words "api nāma" and so forth, he explains precisely this brevity of conventional usage;
[the phrase] "of those causes" refers to the causes of visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna-hetu*).
And it is not the case here— in the eye and so forth—
that there exists a commonality (*sāmānya*) among the eyes and other [faculties] such that, by means of an inclusive form, they would produce a single visual consciousness.
If it is argued that "existence" (sattā) exists,
then, because it is without distinction everywhere, visual and other consciousnesses would arise everywhere; moreover,
there can be no differentiation of existence due to the difference of its correlates, since, being eternal, it cannot admit any added excellence.

Since the eye and the other [faculties] have that [single effect] as their sole purpose— namely, the single effect of visual consciousness— they are distinct from those things that do not have that purpose, i.e., from those that do not produce visual consciousness. Thus, their very distinction from those things that do not produce that effect constitutes their non-difference, because all of them equally possess the exclusion (vyāvṛtti) from those things that do not produce that effect.
Just as there is no difference among the eyes and so forth because they are all equally excluded from what does not produce that effect,

and just as a single term is applied to the eye, visible form, and so on— even in the absence of a single universal— to indicate their single causal function, so too are all things of this same class, and so forth.
Words that denote a collection (*samūha*), a continuum (*santāna*), or a specific state (*avasthāviśeṣa*) are "words for collections, continua, and specific states.
With reference to a word denoting a collection among these, he says: "those which are collective," and so forth.

Since all those [qualities] such as color, taste, and smell are indistinguishable in their causality toward a single effect— such as the fetching of water— within that effect, there is no difference among those colors and so forth.
For, considering that all [things] have a single effect, it is on account of that state of having a single effect (*ekakāryatva*) that the absence of distinction is stated;
it is not because there is no distinction in their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
When it is merely necessary to demonstrate the capacity to produce a single effect, the formulation of a distinction is pointless.

Considering that an injunction by means of a word distinct from [specific] forms and so forth would be fruitless, this worldly user of language employs a single word, "jar," for the purpose of enjoining all [objects] simultaneously toward a certain task; he does so with respect to specific forms and so forth that are identical in their function, such as holding water.
Now, one might ask: since forms and so forth are indeed distinct, how can they be perceived as non-different from the single word "jar"? To this, he says:
The phrase "even those," and so forth,
means that although there is no difference in their distinction from form— which is of the same class— and from taste and so forth— which are other—
[the former] serves as a factor for the application of that [term].

Because they are the instrumental factors for specific tasks such as fetching water and so forth, they are distinguished from others—that is, from things like cloth which are incapable of performing those functions; thus, their very distinction is their non-distinction.
From that non-distinction, and because of that non-distinction, all [qualities] such as color and so forth are understood without distinction—by way of the universal alone—from a single word, "jar."

If it is argued: "If the jar is merely the visible form and other qualities themselves, and not a substance distinct from them, then how can there be a distinction expressed as 'the form and other qualities of the jar'? To this, he says:
"In that regard," and so forth.

Regarding the distinction expressed as "the color and so forth of a jar," its meaning is that the color and so forth have the jar as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and not the cloth or other things;
he explains this very point with the words beginning with "water" (*udaka*).
The specific characteristic of fetching water is that it cannot be accomplished by anything other than a jar;
by the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of any other effect to be accomplished by a jar.
The compound is formed through a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) based on the rule: "the locative case [is used] when [the word denotes] capability for that effect."
This is the meaning here:
words such as "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth denote forms and the like in a general sense, as being endowed with the capacity for any effect that is to be accomplished by form;

however, the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*), by virtue of its connection with the capacity for a specific effect, denotes forms and the like as distinct from the natures of cloth and so forth, which are also composed of form and the like.

Therefore, through the operation of the two terms "of the jar" and "color and so forth," because a cognition arises in the form of a universal and a particular, the relationship of universal and particular and the distinction [between them] are employed; this very point is stated by the words beginning with "the universal.

The accomplishment of the effect of the universal—that which is to be established as consisting merely of color and so forth—is achieved by means of that well-known nature (svabhāva) within that [subject].
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used either to denote a characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*) or as a cause (*hetu*).
