Thus, by means of words such as "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth, which function as instruments (*karaṇa*), [beings] being well-known [in their respective capacities] perform a specific effect; for example, the fetching of water, which is to be accomplished by a jar (*ghaṭasādhya*).

Its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is that by which it is accomplished; thus, that which has such a designation or name is "of such a nature," and by that [means], those [objects]— namely form and so forth— are distinguished and are spoken of in this way.

Furthermore, in this case, regarding the conventional usage "this is a jar" with respect to the collection of form and so forth, there is no substance distinct from form and so forth that possesses the aforementioned characteristics—that is, a whole (*avayavin*) of such a kind as something distinct from form and so forth.
For the whole is held by others to meet the conditions for perception, based on the statement: "A substance is that which is visible and tangible."
The meaning of the statement is that [the whole] is not perceived apart from form and so forth, since it is accepted as having attained the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*).
Furthermore, it will be demonstrated in the second chapter how atoms alone are the objects of direct perception even without a composite whole (*avayavin*).
If [it is argued]: "If the jar is merely form and so forth in combination, then how is there the singular number 'jar' when there are many [atoms]?"—to this he says:
Regarding the phrase "the singular number" and so forth:
just as among many things a single word serves to indicate a single capacity,
so too the singular number indicates that capacity which those [factors], such as form and the rest, possess toward a single effect, namely the fetching of water.
The meaning is that the singular number is used by superimposing unity upon them on the basis of their performing a single function;
however, there is no single power existing in them,
nor is the singular number independent of external reality or dependent solely upon convention.

And this has been established by the passage beginning with "for those for whom words are dependent on real entities" (1.66); now, he speaks with reference to those words that denote a continuum (*saṃtāna*).
"Thus," and so forth:
cause and effect are "hetuphale";

their distinction consists in being related as material cause and its product (*upādānopādeyabhāvena*), [and] in belonging to a single continuum (*ekasantāna*) rather than having different substrata (*anāśrayatva*).
The root *bhū* is transitive when it signifies "attainment" (*prāpti*);
thus, [the compound] is a *dvitīyā-tatpuruṣa* based on the rule *sādhanaṃ kṛtā*.
Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi*: those for whom the "become" (*bhūta*)—meaning produced or accomplished—is the cause or the fruit.
Because the word *bhūta* belongs to the *ākṛtigaṇa* class beginning with *āhitāgni*, it is placed at the end of the compound;
thus, they accomplish a single thing,
just as sprouts, stalks, leaves, and so forth, result in a single fruit.

And just as those very sprouts and so forth are produced by a single seed acting as their material cause, they too do not consist of a single moment; this is for the purpose of simultaneous perception.

Because of this similarity— either by virtue of having a single effect or a single cause— the terms "rice" and so forth, which denote a continuum (*santāna*), are established as conventions at the time of the convention and subsequently employed at the time of linguistic usage for the sake of brevity.

This is because, when there is a desire to know the continuity [of the process], it would be futile to employ multiple words such as "seed," "sprout," and so on, due to the lack of distinction [between them].

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), words such as "human" and so forth are included, because by them too there is the designation of a continuum differentiated by stages such as infancy, childhood, and so on.
[Objection: But are not words such as "rice" (*vrīhi*) also indeed collective terms, since they denote a collection of [qualities] such as color and so forth?
This is true;
however, it is stated thus because it expresses a continuity of results arising from specific causes and effects.

Likewise, a collective term (*samudāya-śabda*) becomes a generic term (*jāti-śabda*) with respect to multiple collections, and the same applies to a term denoting a particular state (*avasthā-śabda*).
There is no fault here, for it is simply said that "a certain word" is used with the intention of expressing a specific meaning.

Just as the color and other qualities of a jar are referred to by the singular term "jar" based on a particular basis, so too should it be understood that the color and other qualities of rice are not referred to by the singular term "rice"; for this very reason, he says:
"It should be stated as before" refers to the discussion concerning the terms for the states;
thus he says, "Those who... and so forth.
Even those atoms of blue and so forth— whether as distinct [entities] such as blue, yellow, and so on, being independent of one another, or as a totality, being mutually associated—
are for the purpose of being perceived simultaneously by visual consciousness, or for the purpose of obstructing the arising of another in their own location,
or for the purpose of determining many [objects] from a single word.

In that context, those factors which are employed in visual consciousness and which denote specific states, and which obstruct the arising of another [consciousness] in their own location, are called "visible" (*sanidarśana*).

If it is asked, "Since those things such as blue and yellow are entirely distinct and possess resistance (*sapratigha*), how can they be expressed by a single term such as 'visible' (*sanidarśana*)?"— to this he replies:
"By way of the commonality of difference from others than those."

If it is argued that, because they are distinct from other things that are non-demonstrable and non-resistant, their very difference constitutes a universal (*sāmānya*) since all of them are excluded from those [others], and for that reason even words such as "demonstrable" and so forth are merely collective terms (*samudāya-śabda*) denoting an aggregation of atoms;
Since even a single atom is designated by terms such as "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*),
having explained the application of these terms by way of their effects, he now speaks by way of their causes.
Just as color and other qualities have a single effect, so too, when there is an injunction regarding that effect—
meaning, when there is an injunction regarding that capacity of color and the rest which has a single effect such as holding water—
the meaning is that it is designated by words such as "pot" through its distinction from other things, such as [other] pots.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of rice (*brīhi*) and so forth is effected; it is the subject under discussion that those for whom a convention has been established are made known.

Likewise, even with respect to the cause, there is a manifold meaning; the connection is to be understood through a shift in the phrasing as: "a single word makes known that for which a convention has been established. This should be seen as being solely for the sake of practical usage (*vyavahāra*) by way of brevity (*lāghava*).

Just as all the offspring of a brindled cow (*śabalā*) are designated by the term "brindled" (*śābaleya*) because they share a single cause, and the offspring of a black cow (*bahulā*) are designated by the term "black" (*bāhuleya*),
and whatever sound is produced by human effort as its cause is called "effort-sequent" (*prayatnānantarīyaka*) because it is generated by that same common cause—
wherein "effort" (*prayatna*) is the volition "I shall do" (*kariṣyāmi*).
The suffix *cha* is applied according to the rule "that which exists there" (*tatra bhavaḥ*), because [the word] belongs to the class of *graha* and others (*ākṛtigaṇa*).
The mention of "place" (*deśa*) is not remembered in that context; therefore, the suffix *kan* is added as a pleonastic (*svārthika*) suffix.
And this was stated with reference to a specific cause; however, based on the mere fact of being a cause in general, he says:
"or it is produced."

Since everything else— whether its birth depends on causes or whether it follows immediately upon an effort— is designated as "produced" (*kṛtaka*), having thus stated it by way of affirmation, he now speaks by way of negation:

Regarding the phrase "tathā" and so forth: by negating that which is the effect of that visual [object], such as blue and so on—namely, visual consciousness—it is stated in a general sense by the word "non-visual" that sound is not capable of being perceived by visual consciousness; thus it is called "non-visual."

Even the term "impermanent," when established by the exclusion of the permanent, does so precisely through the negation of its effects; for others regard the permanent as a real entity (*vastu*), and since such an entity neither constitutes a probandum nor a probans, it cannot enter the path of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, one must accept that which functions as a probandum and a probans.
By the negation of its being an effect, [the self] is non-eternal;

furthermore, the word "self" (ātman) is sometimes employed to indicate something independent with respect to a certain effect, and thus the word "non-self" (anātman) would function by excluding that which does not have such an effect.
Having expressed this through the negation of the effect, he now speaks by means of the negation of the cause.

The connection of the passage beginning with "that" (*tad*) is as follows: by the negation of that which is the cause of this [world]—which [others] hold to have an owner and to be non-empty—it is proclaimed for the sake of conventional usage that this entity consisting of sound and so forth is ownerless and empty.
For it is held by others that whatever is presided over by an independent self (*ātman*) and so forth is "possessing an owner."

In this way, even that which is non-empty is [designated as such] precisely because it is presided over by a presider; and "presiding" is the appropriation of that which is to be presided over, for otherwise presiding would be impossible.

Therefore, words such as "having an owner" function by way of a cause. For others, there is no presider with a fixed nature among entities that perish moment by moment and are dependent solely upon a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), such that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would proceed in dependence upon him.
Therefore, by negating the reasons as they were stated, [beings] are established as being without owners and empty;
and so it is with other things as well— such as suffering, non-emptiness, being without a protector, and being without a refuge.
"According to what is appropriate" means by the negation of certain effects and the negation of certain causes.

This is because [the characteristics] such as suffering and emptiness are established through the negation of effects such as pleasure and non-emptiness, since these are established as having the effect of being non-adverse;
and because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are adverse due to their nature of transformation (*vipariṇāmadharmitva*).

Because there is no independent protector and so forth due to the negation of such functions as "being without a protector" or "having no refuge," it is thus explained that the fourfold application of words occurs by way of both affirmation and negation regarding cause and effect.
If it is asked: "But since there is no such thing as 'non-empty,' 'non-eternal,' and so forth to be excluded, how can words such as 'empty' express the exclusion of others?
[The author] replies with the verse beginning "Empty," etc.:

"As has been stated. According to whatever conceptual construction one adopts based on a particular philosophical tenet (*siddhānta*), one intends to—i.e., constructs—the form of "empty," "eternal," and so forth; having conceptually differentiated that form and projected it onto the mind, the designation "empty" and so forth is made by means of excluding that [form], namely, by excluding the forms of "non-empty" and so forth imagined by others.
He asks "Why? and replies with the words beginning "of the intellect" (*buddhi*): the exertion of the intellect is the volition (*saṃkalpa*) [in the form] "I shall superimpose this object."
Likewise,
"all" refers to that word which possesses such a confusion; because of its state as such, he says this by means of the inclusion of the term "all."
Even in the case of that which has become a real entity...
this is what is meant: the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a real entity is not enjoined or removed by words in its own form.
The entire conventional practice of affirmation and negation is manifested solely by the conceptualizing intellect;

therefore, in words such as "impermanent," there is no counter-entity such as "permanent" to be excluded. Thus, the objection that [the term] lacks a counter-entity (*apratipakṣadoṣa*) is raised—that is, it is pointed out—and by the word "etcetera," the objection that there is no negation (*apratiṣedhadoṣa*) in the negation "there is no self," and so forth, is likewise raised.
The utterances and arguments of the evil-minded, such as Uddyotakara and others, are incoherent—that is to say, they are irrelevant;
for one whose intellect follows the path of logic would not propound what is incoherent.
Therefore, those objections raised by them are to be disregarded and are not worthy of serious consideration; this is the meaning.
Regarding the passage beginning with "atha," etc.:
the word "api" (even/also) is displaced [in the sentence].
Even because of the occurrence of a single entity, namely the universal (*sāmānya*), there is a multiplicity of individual instances (*vyaktibheda*).
"Single accent" (ekaśruti) means a single accent;
if that [single accent] belongs to this "many" (aneka), it is "possessing a single accent" (ekaśrutimān), meaning it would be denotable by a single word. This is the sense.
He considers that there is no distinction whatsoever in the sense that [the word] is one because it has a single function, or because it is associated with a single universal among many;
for this very reason, he explains [the passage] beginning with "not only," and so forth.

The very distinction of those things that produce a certain effect from others that do not produce that effect is precisely what constitutes the non-distinction among all those things that do produce that effect; therefore, they are denoted by a single word.
Alternatively, even by means of a single occurrence—that is, through the operation of a single universal—how could there be any contradiction in multiple objects being denoted by a single word?

Just as there is no contradiction in the application of a single word to many things on the basis of their having a single effect, so too is it the case with a universal that exists as a real entity (*vastubhūta*).
Therefore, the intention is that even the conceptualization of a real universal is indeed logical;
thus the Master says, "It is stated," meaning that the form intended for that real universal is perceived.

Since "perceptibility" (*upalabhyatva*) is intended as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for that which is desired [as the object], the compound is formed according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā* (Pāṇini 2.1.32).

The meaning of the sentence is that the universal (*sāmānya*) does not exist, because it is not perceived apart from the individual (*vyakti*), despite having reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). Alternatively, if its non-perceptibility were admitted, then designations, recognition, and so forth—which depend upon the observation of that [universal]—would not occur.
The connection is with the word "stated" (*uktam*).

[This refers to] the designation by a single word for many things, the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) which is a cognition of an identical form, and—by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*)—the inclusion of such points as: "there would be no application of a term toward an individual based on a universal," and so forth.
For indeed, that which is not itself perceived cannot induce a designation or recognition based on perception in another instance.
By this word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "they would not exist," etc., other previously mentioned defects are also included;
for if things were identical with something else, those not possessing that [essential nature] could not truly be said to possess it.
Likewise, since the universal (jāti) is not employed in functions such as carrying loads or milking, and so forth,
by this he states that there exists a subverting means of valid cognition (bādhaka-pramāṇa) against the conceptualization of universals.
Therefore, designations and the like cannot be based on that [individuality];
however, since there is no contradiction when they share a single effect, it is logical that designations, recognition, and so forth are produced by that very [single effect].
Thus, he states another refutation as well.
Moreover,
for one who maintains that the universal is a real entity, it must be admitted that its occurrence is not restricted to a single locus;
for it is not logical that something which does not occur in a locus should serve as the cause for its designation and so forth.
And that activity of the universal in its own substratum would either be its being supported (ādheyatā),
since it abides by virtue of that [substratum], or it would be manifestation (vyakti), which is perception through the power of the substratum. This [latter] would be the activity.
Both of these are not tenable in that universal;
he explains this with the words "that which is this," and so forth.

Having raised the question— "What is this mode of existence (*vṛtti*) of that universal (*sāmānya*), which is a real entity consisting of 'oneness' existing in multiple substrata, that causes a single word to apply?"— he himself states two alternatives,
beginning with "being contained" (*ādheyatā*) and so forth.
Alternatively, the word *kiṃ* is used in the sense of negation; the meaning is: "What kind of subsistence (*vṛtti*) is this? None at all.
For instance, the subsistence of a thing would have to be either its state of being contained within its own substratum, or...

Just as jujube fruits exist within a vessel as their support, so too would the manifestation (vyakti) have its occurrence in the locus of that universal (sāmānya), because the universal is made manifest by those loci;
in that case, if occurrence is intended to mean being contained (ādheyatā).
In that case, individuals must be accepted as the substrata for that [universal].

Furthermore, since the universal is admitted to be eternal, it cannot be something to be produced or infused prior to the arising of the individual; therefore, because an eternal entity cannot be assisted by its supports, the individuals—regarded as supports—are not actually its substrata.
He explains this with the words beginning "For that which is eternal... and so forth.

Now, if permanence is not accepted, then even in the case of impermanence—because of the arising of one after another, that is, the arising of this and that [distinct entity]—there would be a manifold universal due to its multiplicity. Just as there is difference among particulars because of their manifoldness, so too [if the universal were manifold], it would be impossible to have a single cognition regarding that universal; for the reason that a single cognition is impossible, the phrase "a permanent universal is accepted" is connected [to the argument]. Furthermore, the intention is that what could a permanent universal do such that a substratum (āśraya) or support (ādhāra) would exist for it? It could not. This is the intended meaning.
It is not a substratum because it provides assistance; rather, it is because that universal inheres (*samavāya*) in that locus.
If so, how then does "cowness" (*gotva*) operate in cows?
Regarding the relationship of substratum and superstratum:
what, then, is this relationship of substratum and superstratum? It is inherence (*samavāya*); it is in that [relation] that "cowness" (*gotva*) resides as the possessor of occurrence.
"Subsistence (vṛtti) is inherence (samavāya), because it is the cause of the cognition 'here'";
anticipating that inherence is impossible in the absence of a relationship of benefactor and beneficiary, [the author] says "What is this? and so forth.
*Nyāyavārttika*:
"Not separate," etc.— the opponent [states that] those established as being in non-distinct locations are "inseparably established" (*apṛthaksiddha*).
Regarding their relationship as substratum and superstratum, which is inherence (*samavāya*),
the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) says:
"This very nature of being a substratum for that which provides no assistance, we do not consider possible."
Why?
Because it would lead to an over-extension;
for if one were to accept that something which provides no assistance can be a support (āśraya).
If it is argued that, in that case, everything would be the substratum of everything, [we reply] that this is not so, because it is perceived that nothing inheres in everything.

Now, it might be objected: "In the absence of a relationship of assistance (upakāra), since [the universal] 'cowness' (gotva) inheres in all [individual cows], there would be no cognition of it from a single [individual]; this is precisely the objection raised.
To this we reply: This relation characterized as inherence (samavāya) is indeed distinct from the relationship of assisted and assister (upakārya-upakāraka-bhāva) and the like;
and since that [inherence] does not exist everywhere, how can there be such an over-extension (atiprasaṅga)?
It is said:
it is true that conjunction occurs only for that which is already inherent in something.
Furthermore, inherence in that [substratum] consists in dependence upon it,
and dependence of one thing upon another consists simply in its arising from that;
thus, in this case, the basis for the cognition is simply arising in a successive sequence, not inherence— thereby the argument from presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is exhausted.
In the case of a state of being "higher and higher" (uparyupari-bhāva)...

it would not be so; nor is there an inherence (*samavāya*) of things that are not already inherent, by which their state of being inherent might be established, because that would entail the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that everything would be inherent in everything.
Concluding [the argument], he says "therefore" and so forth:

"Inherence belongs to two things that are not established separately, such as the substance that is originated and the substance that originates it; conjunction belongs to things that are established separately."
Just as there is inherence of fire and smoke in a single object, which is "inherence in a single object" (ekārthasamavāya);
or, for example, the case of color and taste in a single substance;
by the word "etcetera," the relation of "inherence in what is conjoined" (saṃyuktasamaveta) is included.

The compound *vastubhūtāḥ sambandhāḥ* (relations that have become real entities) or *sambandhā vastūnām* (relations of entities) is either a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) or a genitive determinative compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
The inclusion of the term "real entity" (*vastu*) is for the purpose of excluding those [relations] constructed by conceptualization (*kalpanā*).
They do not differ from the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), nor do they exist in any other way.
Establishing this very point, he says "mutually," and so forth:
because there is no obstruction— meaning no dependence— among things that mutually assist one another, or among those that do not assist anything other than what is intended as their substratum.

The connection with the subject at hand is as follows: because there is no obstruction and because there is no [intrinsic] relation, all relations between things do not differ from the relation of cause and effect.

Now, one might object: "If there is assistance [rendered] by a substratum, there is certainly no mutual relationship of assisted and assister between the two things residing therein; so for what purpose was the phrase 'or from another' introduced?
This is true.

However, even if there is no direct mutual assistance, one might still postulate a connection through a mediated sequence by virtue of their dependence on a single cause; this is the point of the introduction.
If it is argued that a relationship of mutual assistance between things inhering in the same object is not at all accepted, he says "even though" and so forth.

Therefore, since there would be the consequence of the aforementioned fault due to the absence of assistance from a single substratum, and because of the fear of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), the fault has been stated. And since there must necessarily be assistance for the two things inhering in a single object by means of their own substratum, the proponent explains—by way of that self-assistance which is the assistance rendered to himself—that he is connecting the other [second] inhering thing as well, declaring: "These two inhering things are connected here.
This is what is meant.

Just as for another [type of relation], there is a connection between two things inherent in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyin*)—even though they are not mutually connected—due to their inherence in a single object, so too for us, there is a connection between those two by virtue of having a single effect. Therefore, even in that case of inherence in a single object, the connection with the substratum is produced solely by the causal relationship; it is precisely through that causal relationship that the connection is superimposed.
This is because the status of being a support (*ādhāra*) and so forth occurs only by way of assistance (*upakāra*).

Therefore, this substrate such as a brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*), which does not assist the universal within its own self, being called the "substrate" (*ādhāra*) of the independent universal, is merely a decoration of the Cārvākas; for it is a "decoration" (*maṇḍana*) in the sense that it is something by which one is adorned.
Why is there a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word *yācitaka* (borrowed)? Because, just as for a poor man who lacks in himself the ornaments borrowed from another,
so too does the universal possess the status of being a substratum for the universal that resides in its locus.
Alternatively, it may be analyzed as an instrumental compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*) expressing an action (*bhāva-sādhana*),

just as the act of adorning occurs by means of a borrowed ornament; likewise, the designation "substratum" (*ādhāra*) for that which is the locus of the universal is due to its being requested from another to serve as a support, and not because of its actual state of being, since there is no real benefit derived from it.
1—The opponent asks: "How so?
For a bowl is not the producer of jujube fruits, since those fruits are produced solely from their own causes.

Furthermore, regarding what was stated—that in all cases relations between entities do not differ from the relation of cause and effect—that is considered inconclusive (*anekāntika*). For instance, when a jujube fruit (*badara*) or similar object, which has the nature of moving to another location, is produced in that very place where its preceding material cause—the jujube fruit itself—is located; specifically, it is produced in the same spot connected to the bowl (*kuṇḍa*), because it does not go elsewhere.
This is the power (*śakti*) of the bowl and other things regarded as supports (*ādhāra*) with respect to the jujube fruits and other things regarded as supported (*ādheya*).
He explains [the passage] beginning with "by nature" (*prakṛtyā*) and so forth:

that which is "unequal in location" (*asamānadeśa*) by its very nature (*prakṛtyā*), that is, by its own essence (*svabhāvenaiva*), is described as such; it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound because it functions as a signifier even while depending on the word "nature."
And it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is of such a nature and is an effect.
Furthermore, the "effect" refers precisely to the jujube fruit (*badara*) and so forth as comprised within successive moments;

the production of that [effect] is the very property (*dharma*), that is, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), of the heavy substance—the jujube fruit and so forth—as comprised within the preceding moment.
The state of producing an effect in the same location is caused by the support;
the meaning is that the capacity to produce something in a location identical to its own is produced by the support.
Therefore, the bowl is the auxiliary cause for the preceding moment—which serves as the material cause—of the subsequent effect, the jujube fruit.
In that very place, at the very location of the moment of the material cause (*upādāna-kṣaṇa*), the bowl is called the "support" (*ādhāra*) because it produces the effect, namely the jujube fruit;

by this, it is stated that the relationship of support and supported exists between the moments of the bowl and the jujube fruit, both of which depend upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīna*).
Otherwise, if the aforementioned assistance were not rendered by the bowl to the jujubes, there would be no such designation as "the jujubes are here in the bowl."
Since a designation for that which has a fixed substratum is impossible without a cause,

this designation is produced by the assistance rendered by that [substratum]; thus, in the case of "the jujube fruits are in this bowl," this designation is produced not by the assistance rendered by the substratum, but rather by the conjunction between the bowl and the jujube fruits.

Furthermore, the intention of the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) who asks "How then... and so forth is as follows: if momentariness is accepted by you, conjunction and the like are postulated;
however, if the non-momentariness of entities were admitted, there would be no arising of conjunction and the like at all—this is the meaning.

The intention [of the opponent] is that there is no basis for the designation "the conjunction of those two"—namely, the pot and the jujube fruit—because they lack the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary (*upakāryopakārakatva*).
To this, the opponent replies with the words "by those two," etc.;
since the conjunction is produced by those two—the pot and the jujube fruit—it is asserted to belong to them.

Reflecting that the opponent has stated that conjunction is produced by two [substances] alone and that inherence exists in both [relata], the proponent of the established doctrine says "sa" (that), and so forth.
Why does that conjunction not reside or arise in one and the same bowl or jujube fruit?

For the questioner, this is the underlying intention: if those two entities called "bowl" and "jujube fruit" [are distinct], [then why do they not act as the substratum for] the production of the conjunction or the attainment of the state of being its support?

If it is argued that since each [of the two] possesses a capacity by its own nature, why then do they depend upon one another, and that therefore these two distinct entities are capable only when joined together, the author replies with the words beginning "tad" (that).
The point is this: that which is individually incapable, such as the potsherd and the jujube fruit, remains just as incapable even when joined together, because it is non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*).
However, momentary things, though individually incapable, become capable when combined after having acquired specific qualities produced by auxiliary causes; thus there is no contradiction.
Consequently, [non-momentary things] cannot provide assistance toward conjunction.

The opponent [argues]: "An object called a 'jujube in a bowl' does not exist through conjunction, because it possesses that as its property," and so forth, beginning with the words "of that which is conjoined."
Because of the assistance provided by the pit and the jujube fruit to each other— namely, whatever nature the jujube fruit possesses due to the assistance of that pit,
or whatever pit exists due to the assistance of that jujube fruit.

The Teacher asks: "What is this capacity that belongs not to the two [substances] alone, but which, by virtue of producing a specific quality, brings about the conjunction of the bowl and the jujube fruit, or leads to their assuming the state of container and contained?"
What is this "assistance" (upakāra) between things such as jujube fruits and bowls, which stand in the relation of produced and producer?
There is none at all.
If it is asked how it is that there is no relation of produced and producer, he says:

The meaning of the passage beginning with "svarūpa" (intrinsic nature) is as follows: since the intrinsic nature of the jujube fruit (*badara*) is established by other causes alone, it is not an effect; therefore, the jujube fruits possess neither the state of being produced (*janyatva*) nor does the bowl (*kuṇḍa*) possess the state of being a producer (*janakatva*).
For the opponent does not desire that the intrinsic nature of the jujube fruits and so forth arise from the bowl or similar objects.
Since they are produced from their own causes alone,
it is not the case that the form of the jujube fruit is produced by the bowl, but rather a different form [is produced]; therefore,
he says "pararūpa" and so forth.
In that case, [the action] would reside in the substrate;
for if it were otherwise, one thing could not assist another through its own activity.
"In both ways" means by way of its own nature and the nature of another.
Because, according to the method just described, that which does not provide assistance— such as a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and so forth— is ineffective;
and this has been stated almost entirely, the word "mostly" (*prāyas*) signifying a great majority.
It is mostly said to be almost expressed; because *rājadanta* and others form an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), the word *prāya* is placed at the end [of the compound].
And this meaning and its function have been attained by them, which is the production that serves as an aid.
The word *prāya* has been explained in detail starting from verse 108; others say that it means "similar," such that "almost spoken" (*uktaprāya*) means similar to what has been stated.

The meaning is that this assistance rendered by the receptacle, such as a bowl, to the contained object is equal to the assistance to the nature of the universal provided by its substrate as previously described.
The conclusion is expressed by the words "all indeed," etc.;
the connection is that all relations between entities are established on the basis of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
If it is argued that there would be no distinction among them, he says "of the producer alone," and so forth;
or rather, they are established through distinction— that is, differentiation— by virtue of the relationship between cause and effect.
To explain how there is a distinction, he says "of the producer alone," and so forth; the meaning is: by the force of that specific assistance which the effect receives from its cause.

For instance, in the case of jujube fruits (*badara*) and the like, which possess the property of moving downward, there exists a relationship of support and supported (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) through a functional utility (*upayoga*) characterized by their arising in the location of their own material cause (*svopādāna*).

Furthermore, in the case of lamps and jars and so forth, there is a relationship characterized as that of the manifestor and the manifested (*vyañjaka-vyaṅgya-lakṣaṇa*), consisting in the production of a nature capable of generating cognition, brought about by the lamp. Thus, in other relationships as well, the appropriate explanation should be stated accordingly.

Now, [one might object] that all relationships between entities are included within the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), but this is not so; for the relationship characterized as conjunction (*saṃyoga-lakṣaṇa*) does not fall within the causal relationship, since this [conjunction] exists only between things that arise simultaneously.

Now, if conjunction is not possible in the case of non-momentary entities, it might then occur in the case of momentary ones; however, no difference in their own nature (*svarūpa*) is perceived between the states of being conjoined and being unconjoined in the case of a bowl and a jujube fruit.
Therefore, conjunction certainly exists even in non-momentary things, because it is so perceived.
As Dharmakīrti has said:

"If conjunction were not something distinct from its constituents, then the field, seed, water, and so forth—being indistinguishable [from one another in that regard]—would always produce their effects, such as sprouts; but this is not the case. Therefore, because the effect is not produced at all times, the field and other factors depend upon other causes for the production of the sprout."

Just as the causal complex consisting of a lump of clay and so forth is dependent upon a potter and other factors for the production of a jar, that which is independent of the field and other such factors is established as conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Furthermore,
since this conjunction is perceived as a qualifier of two substances, it is established by direct perception as being a distinct entity from them.
For instance, when someone is told by another to "bring [the conjoined things]" regarding two substances that are joined, he brings only those two substances whose conjunction he perceives,

and not merely any substance; furthermore, for a person standing at a great distance, this cognition— which apprehends a forest as being without intervals even though it has intervals— arises as a false cognition, and a false cognition never arises without the experience of a primary object.

For indeed, one who has not previously experienced the sight of a cow does not have the delusion that "this is a cow" when seeing a gavaya; therefore, a primary relation (saṃyoga) must necessarily be accepted.
Likewise, by the negative statement "Caitra is not wearing earrings," it is not the earring itself that is negated, since it exists elsewhere, such as in another location;
rather, it is Caitra’s conjunction with the earring that is negated.
Likewise, even by this affirmative sentence "Caitra is wearing earrings," neither Caitra nor the earrings are being enjoined, because both are already established;
therefore, by the method of elimination (pāriśeṣya), it is the conjunction that is enjoined.
Thus, conjunction certainly exists.
Nyāyavārttika: To this it is replied:
Just as it is accepted that fields and other factors initiate conjunction by attaining a specific state, why is it not likewise accepted that they initiate the effect even without conjunction?
Otherwise, it would follow that conjunction would always be the initiator of another conjunction.
Nor does a third conjunction appear when a substance conjoined [with another] is apprehended in its own nature by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*).
Nor, in conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), does a further conjunction appear as a qualifier for the conjoined substance, apart from the word "conjunction" itself.
Nor can the postulation of conjunction be based on the impossibility of accounting for the cognition of "conjoined" otherwise;
for it is only two entities existing in a state of having arisen without an interval that serve as the cause for the cognition of "conjoined.

And as long as those two are intended to be the objects of the cognition of "conjoined" by virtue of being the producers of conjunction in that state, why not accept them as the objects of that cognition precisely by virtue of being the causes of the cognition of "conjoined," even in the absence of conjunction?
Nor is it the case that, through some traditional succession,

a cognition appearing as continuous within an interval [of non-existence] is preceded by the experience of a primary object, because it is not metaphorical, being the object of a non-erroneous cognition; likewise,
in cases such as "Caitra is wearing earrings," neither the earring related to Caitra is negated nor is it affirmed.
There is no such thing as conjunction;

therefore, the cognition that two things "are conjoined" applies only to those two things that depend upon the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*), just as in the case of a bowl and a jujube fruit. Consequently, conjunction itself is included within the very relation of cause and effect.

The cognition that "these two are conjoined" or "this belongs to the conjunction" occurs solely by means of the exclusion of other distinctions; it does not, however, arise from the force of a real, ontological conjunction.
And since there is no real relationship apart from the relation of cause and effect, [it follows that] "this is that," and so forth.

If it is argued that the relationship is such that the very capacity for production in the jujube fruits (*badara*) and so forth constitutes the substratum (*ādhāra*) for the pits (*kuṇḍa*) and so forth— that is, the substratum of the universal must be the substratum by means of the capacity for production itself— the author replies with "no" and so forth;
"it" refers to the capacity for production.
Regarding this general point, he explains it with the words "for not," etc.:

production in the very location of its own material cause is the specific kind of production; that which has such production as its defining characteristic is the state of being a substratum (ādhārabhāva). Thus it is.

He explains [the passage] beginning with "athā" and so forth: because it is unproduced—since the universal is unproduced due to its permanence—it persists even in the absence of that [particular] and thus in the absence of a substratum; therefore, the persistence of the universal does not depend upon the power of a substratum.
"Of that" refers to the universal (*sāmānya*). "Even in its absence" means even in the absence of the individual (*vyakti*), because the universal persists in a location devoid of individuals.
For if the universal did not exist in a location devoid of individuals, then when a new individual arises there, it could not have a connection with the universal;
for it cannot come from elsewhere, since it is inactive (*niṣkriyatvāt*).
And an individual situated in a different location cannot be the locus of that universal, because it occupies a different location;
for since the universal is unitary, there is no such thing as its occupying different locations.
If this is argued, then it follows that all individuals possessing a single genus would occupy a single location.
Furthermore, not all [atoms] would possess birth;
and if it is asked how a single [atom] can exist in different locations, let this be another fault of his.
With the words "having the nature of falling," etc., he states the reason for the accumulation [of atoms].
The word *hi* has the sense of *ca* (and);

the word *api* is for the purpose of indicating acceptance (*abhyupagama*). Even if this mode [of argument] were accepted, it would be impossible to establish it with respect to a universal (*sāmānya*).
This presentation is for the purpose [of showing] that the universal has the property of not falling; however, it is not possible for that which is not a producer to be a sustainer.
For this very reason, he says:
Regarding the phrase "here too" and so forth:

here too, if one were to accept a "stabilizer" (sthāpaka) on the grounds that it prevents falling, then if some proponent of logic did not inquire further into the nature of this prevention of falling, only then could the stabilizer be considered non-productive (ajanaka).
The intention here is "in accordance with one's own tenets.
In this regard, the following objection may also be raised by the proponent:
Is that prevention of falling which is produced by the stabilizer identical to the object being stabilized, or is it a different entity from it, or is it merely the absence of falling?
It is not identical with the object itself, because it is admitted that its own nature is produced from something else; nor is it a different entity, as he says:

"If a difference in entity were admitted, then the support would have utility only insofar as there is a connection to that very [different] entity; but what kind of obstruction or hindrance could there be for a falling jujube fruit or the like toward that which has become a different entity? None at all."
The point is that, consequently, even the jujube fruit and such would fall from within the vessel and so forth.
If it is argued that the non-falling of the jujube fruit is brought about by the prevention of falling through a different purpose (arthāntara) provided by the support, he says:
"Even if there is no falling due to the prevention," and so on.
When it is admitted that the falling of the jujube fruit and other such objects occurs due to a factor called "obstruction" (pratibandha), an equivalent objection applies:
Is this falling, which is produced by the entity called obstruction, identical in nature to the jujube fruit or is it a different entity?
If it is a different entity, then the utility of this very obstruction would reside in that [different entity] alone, and so forth.
Everything stated immediately above applies equally here;

furthermore, if the non-falling of jujube fruits and the like is produced by that very factor called "non-falling," then the same objection applies there as well— thus he says, "and there would be an infinite regress."
With the words "Therefore," etc., the third position is introduced:
how could that absence of falling be produced by anything?
It is not produced by anything at all.
The point is that non-existence (abhāva) cannot be an effect;
if it is asked how there can then be the designation "he produces non-existence," he says "non-existence," and so forth.
Regarding the designation "it makes [something] non-existent," no effect called "non-existence" is intended;
why? He says:
"of that," and so forth.
The intention is that because this non-existence (abhāva) is an effect, it must necessarily be an existence (bhāva).

Now, if it is argued: "Just as a cloth does not have the nature of a jar despite being an effect like a jar, so too non-existence will not have the nature of non-existence despite being an effect like an existence."
For even a jar and the like possess the nature of a positive entity (bhāva) precisely because they have the property of coming into being;
and since that [property] exists even in non-existence (abhāva), how could it not be a positive entity? If you argue that it is not a positive entity because it appears as a negative entity (abhāva)—
It has been stated that there is no [distinction] in non-existence because there is no appearance [of it as such];

for while the mutual distinction between absences is perceived— as in "the absence of a jar" and "the absence of a cloth"— the difference between the cloth and so forth is not due to the absences appearing as a single unity.
Since this is so, therefore, the instruction that negates the activity of an entity— that it "produces non-existence"—
is for this very reason clarified by the statement that it means "it does not produce an entity," and so forth.
The meaning is that whatever is the referent of this statement, that much alone constitutes the non-existence of the other;
and thus,
since the prevention of falling is merely an absence and not an effect, [it cannot be produced].
"This" refers to the bowl and so forth;
for that reason, "this" refers to the jujube fruit and so forth,
which is held fast by some support such as a bowl.
The meaning is that, being unimpeded by falling, it would never remain stationary but would always fall;
the conclusion follows with the words "therefore," and so forth.

By the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that even by the designation "the substratum" (*ādhāra*), the production of an effect—comprised in a subsequent moment—occupying the same location as its material cause (*upādāna*) comprised in the preceding moment, is what is being described.

Therefore, this mode [of support] is also impossible in the case of a universal; in order to demonstrate this very impossibility, he says, having provisionally accepted it: "Even though it does not produce [the object], it is a 'supporter' (*sthāpaka*) because it prevents its falling."

Regarding the passage beginning with "Let it be so," etc.: let there indeed be a prevention of falling—that is, a prevention of its [the arrow's] descent—on the part of the obstructors such as the hand and so forth; this is because they possess the nature of non-production [of the fall], due to their performing that prevention of falling.
Regarding a substance that possesses motion—that is, one that is active—the substratum would be a "supporter" by establishing a "station" for a universal which, being incorporeal, is inactive.
For there is no falling of a universal such that its prevention could constitute station;
rather, the station of that universal is said to be simply the non-deviation from its own essential nature.
Furthermore, that non-deviation from its own nature does not depend upon a substratum because the universal is eternal; yet, even if it were admitted,
it would be illogical to claim that the persistence of the universal depends upon a substratum.

When the distinction between difference and non-difference— that is, the investigation into whether it is other or not other— is being carried out regarding that state (*sthiti*) by way of its generality (*sāmānya*), he explains [the point] with the words "let it be so," and so forth.
"Caused by the basis" means that this stability depends upon the basis;
that very basis brings about a stability distinct from itself, not a general [stability].
That stability is tied to the universal; therefore, because it is connected through a connection, the universal is indeed assisted. To this he says, "And that," etc.;
"that" refers to the stability which is a distinct entity.

For there is no cause whatsoever that obstructs that [non-existence] in respect to the universal; what, then, would be accomplished by the substratum of the universal? This is the ellipsis to be supplied.
If it is argued, "An obstruction to non-existence in respect to the universal is indeed admitted," he replies with the words "And if there were an obstruction," etc.
Or, if an obstruction is admitted,
then if there is a "causing to endure," it is the endurance of that endurance which was produced by the substratum that is generally brought about.
Consequently, since the stability produced by the substratum is dependent upon the universal,
the same logical consequence applies there as well regarding the production of stability for that stability:
does that stability which is produced by the universal for the stability dependent on the substratum constitute the very essence of the stability caused by the substratum, or is it distinct from it?
If it is of the nature of the self, then since that [stability] has already been effected by the substratum alone, how could it be effected by the universal?

And if it were distinct, then that same [question] regarding stability would apply: what would be accomplished by the universal for the first stability produced by the substratum? Or, if a second stability is produced by the universal—
If that [subsistence] is dependent upon the subsistence produced by the substratum,
then it must be stated what the cause of that dependence is;

for if there were another third subsistence produced by the subsistence produced by the substratum— which itself was produced by the general property— the same consequence would follow, resulting in an infinite regress.

Therefore, because there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), the assistance provided by the universal (*sāmānya*) toward the subsistence (*sthiti*) produced by the substratum (*āśraya*) cannot be determined; thus, there is no cognition that "this subsistence produced by the substratum belongs to this universal. Furthermore, if production (*janana*) is what constitutes the connection (*pratibandha*), as is the subject under discussion, then another subsistence is not produced by the universal for the subsistence already produced by the substratum;
rather, it is that very first subsistence which is produced.

In that case, let the universal alone, being capable, effect its own persistence; what is the use of depending on a substratum such as a brindled cow (*śābaleya*) for the sake of bringing about that persistence?
For dependence upon that which provides no assistance is not logical;
thus, "dependence" indeed implies a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with it.

The sense is this: regarding this matter, that which is called "dependence" (apekṣā)—namely, the dependence [of a universal] upon something else—is a connection (*pratibandha*) with that object of dependence, which is its being dependent upon it. And since that connection is impossible for that which is eternal and incapable of having any excellence added to it, the universal alone would produce its own persistence; therefore, there is no other substratum (*āśraya*) that serves as a cause of persistence.
Consequently, the claim that the substratum is the support (*ādhāra*) of the universal because it effects its persistence is untenable.
Regarding what was stated as "the discernment of difference and non-difference," the position of difference has first been set aside; now,
relying on the second position,
he says "non-difference," and so forth.
Or, if it is accepted that there is no difference [between the universal and its persistence] due to their identity, then that very nature of the universal is the form of its persistence;
and since that nature of the universal exists eternally, the persistence of this universal is not produced by any substratum. For this reason, etc.
The conclusion is stated with the words "tad" and so forth.
"Tad" means "therefore"; "asya" refers to the universal (*sāmānya*).
Thus, regarding the two positions previously mentioned—that subsistence (*vṛtti*) is either inherence (*ādheyatā*) or manifestation (*vyakti*)—the refutation of the first has been established.
2— Relying on the second position, he says "atha punar" and so forth;
"avyaktasya" means of that which is unmanifested.

Since cognition is not the cause of manifestation, that which is the illumination of its manifestation by means of that substratum would itself constitute the existence of the universal in that substratum.
The Master says "no," because the production of cognition within oneself— that is, regarding one's own object—
is the general fitness for that purpose which conforms to others.
That which is known as a manifested object (*vyaṅgya*) is dependent upon other causes;
and that which is the cause of its capacity to produce a cognition of itself— such as a lamp— is indeed a producer (*kāraka*) of that manifested object,
because it brings about the production of an object such as a jar, which was previously incapable [of producing a cognition] but subsequently becomes capable of producing a cognition.

If, however, even prior to the proximity of a lamp or other such factors, the jar and so forth were already capable of producing a cognition of its own form, then since this capacity of the jar and so forth existed beforehand, there could be no dependence upon that [lamp]; for the universal, being eternal and unchangeable, would have no need for such dependence.
Therefore, the meaning is: why should the aforementioned definition of "manifested-ness" not apply to the universal itself, rather than to its substratum?
"Another" means that which produces an entity distinct from its own continuum is called a manifestor (*vyañjaka*).

Of what nature is it? It is capable of producing a cognition of its own object and is dependent upon a homogeneous material cause (*upādāna*); that is to say, it is dependent upon the preceding moment included within its own continuum.

Just as a lamp, by producing a subsequent moment of a jar that is capable of generating consciousness while depending on the preceding moment of the jar situated in darkness, is called an illuminator—
if it is objected that "if the jar were the effect of the lamp, then upon the accumulation of the lamp, there would also have to be an accumulation of the jar," we say: no.

The difference in the effect arises from the difference in its material cause (*upādāna*), not from the difference in its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*); and since the lamp and such are merely auxiliary causes for the manifestation of the jar, how could there be the consequence that the jar itself possesses magnitude and so forth?
Or, even if manifestation were being produced, this same consequence would apply equally; thus, this [objection] is trivial.

Nor does a moment similar to the manifested moment arise from a lump of clay, but rather from a lamp and so forth; how then could there be the production of such [an effect] from something of a different nature? And as for the term "independent," it is like the impact [of a drumstick], which, depending on a homogeneous material cause, produces a sound capable of generating a cognition of its own object.
For there is no sound prior to the impact by which a sound could be dependent upon a homogeneous cause;
for others maintain that sound is also manifested (*vyaṅgya*). This having been said, [the opponent asks]:
"If, then, the producer itself is the manifester, what then is the distinction between the causes that are producers and those that are manifesters? To this, he says:
The phrase "in another [world]" (*paratra*) and so forth means in something other than the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), which is intended to be the producer (*kāraka*);
the capacity to generate cognition is not implied for that which is produced (*janya*).
For it is not the case that an effect is produced by a causal factor, such as a seed, only when it is capable of generating a cognition of its own object;

rather, being a causal factor consists merely in the act of production, whereas being a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is defined by the specific quality of producing an effect capable of generating a cognition of its own object.
If it is argued that although the manifested object acquires the capacity to produce cognition from the manifestor, it is nevertheless not produced [by it],
the author replies with the words "yadi hi" and so forth;
"yataḥ" means "from the manifestor."
If it is the manifested,
then that capacity belongs to the manifestor; this capacity of the manifested exists prior even to the proximity of the manifestor, because it is inherent in the very nature of the manifested.
If it is argued that, just as the manifested object exists prior [to its manifestation], so too does the capacity— which is of the very nature of that object—
depend upon it; therefore, the capacity, being distinct from the manifested object, is produced by the manifestor, [the author] replies:
Regarding "paretyādi" and so forth:
"in this" refers to fitness;
that very thing is fitness itself.
The word "tataḥ" (from that) refers to the manifestor; thus, there follows the same undesirable consequence as in the case of duration.
What was stated previously—that if duration were something other [than the entity], then the substratum would produce that very duration, and so forth—would apply here as well.
The word "that" (*tam*) refers to the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*);

nor is it something other than the suggested meaning. Since nothing is added to the suggested meaning by its production, it is not required [as a cause]. By this, its status as a benefactor (*upakāritva*) is stated;
therefore, to negate that on the grounds of its being ineffective (*akiṃcitkaratva*) is a contradiction.
Regarding the statement that "the producer alone is the manifester," he points out its fallibility with the words "of that [fire]," etc.:
for smoke is not the producer of fire, yet because it is its effect, it is its manifester.
By the word "etcetera," [the author] includes the crane and so forth; he refutes [the objection] with the statement, "The crane [indicates] the presence of water," and so on,
but fire does not produce a cognition of its own specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) within itself by depending upon smoke as a logical mark (liṅga).
Why?
Because fire, which is intended as the object of inference (*anumeya*) in such a state, is not its direct producer;
otherwise, there would be no distinction from perception, since [the cognition] would have the specific form (*svalakṣaṇa-ākāra*) of the fire itself.
By the words "only" (*kevalam*) and so forth, he demonstrates that the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) alone is its direct producer;
the material cause is the cognition of the logical mark (*liṅga*), and not the power of the object— that is, the power of the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire.
What is the reason?
He explains how it is that the cognition of fire occurs even when that fire is absent— that is, even after the fire has previously ceased to exist.
"By way of succession," and so forth.
"Following the mark" refers to the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that recollects the mark;

for instance, when a certain person has seen smoke in a particular place, and the smoke has vanished while the fire remains, once a conceptual construction recollecting the smoke arises there by some means, he subsequently recollects the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), thinking, "Smoke was here before, therefore fire was also here. In this manner, through a succession of steps, the knowledge of fire indeed arises from smoke produced by fire.
With the words "nor indeed," etc., he applies what was stated previously to this very point:
inferential cognition, which appears in a generic form,
does not have a proximate object as its domain.
For [conceptual cognition] occurs even when an object has perished and when one has not yet arisen;

and even when an object is present, it has already been explained previously that its production does not depend on the power of the object—starting with the passage "for conceptual constructions do not proceed exactly according to the existence [of their objects]" and so forth.

Furthermore, because they do not determine existence and non-existence, it will be demonstrated in the third chapter that their capacity does not arise from the manifestation [of the object], and so on.
By "direct utility" is meant the capacity to produce a cognition that conforms to its own nature;
"therein" refers to the production of a cognition of itself as its object;
and "the other" refers to such things as a lamp.
The word "thence" (tataḥ) implies [a cause] such as a lamp;
what is meant is this: not every manifestor is called a producer.
However, since only that which receives assistance from another entity capable of producing a cognition with its own form is not subject to deviation [from that form],

it follows that even a universal depends upon a substratum for the production of a cognition with its own form; therefore, by that [universal], the self must be accepted as being perceptible through its substratum.
Furthermore, this acquisition of a self cannot arise from anything whatsoever for the universal (*sāmānya*),
because that universal is accepted as being eternal. Thus, it is the universal.
The opponent’s connection [to the text] beginning with "naiva" is as follows: "We say that it is the manifestation of the inherence in its own substratum.
If it is asked how inherence in its own substratum can be a manifestation, he says:
"In its own substratum," and so forth;
"that" refers to the universal (sāmānya),
and "elsewhere" refers to its own substratum.
The Master [Dharmakīrti] has stated this,
for he has already argued that we do not admit the possibility of something being a substratum (*āśraya*) if it provides no assistance, and so forth.

For by asserting that "it is the cause of cognition when it inheres in its own substratum— whether that be the self or something else"— the proponent intends the category of the universal (*sāmānya*) to be a cause of cognition dependent upon its own substratum and its inherence (*samavāya*).
And consequently, by means of that inherence in its own substratum, the universal would become the producer of the effect;
for what reason? Because the nature of its cause—the cause of cognition—exists prior to [the effect] through its inherence in its own substratum.

If it is argued that this [reason] is unestablished because, once there is inherence in its own substratum, the nature of the cause of cognition subsequently exists due to that inherence in its own substratum, and thus the universal has the nature of producing cognition eternally, he says "eternally" and so forth.

The phrase "the existence of its own nature" means that if [the universal] has the nature of producing cognition, then even prior to its inherence in its own substratum, and even in a place devoid of individuals,
there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the arising of a cognition having the form of the universal from the universal alone (148–49).
The opponent [responds]: "No.

The individual (vyakti) is the substratum (āśraya) of the universal (sāmānya); its "cultivation" (saṃskāra) is the conferring of capacity (yogyatādhāna). For that reason, the individual is not a manifestor (vyañjikā) of the universal, such that the universal would be produced by it.

Rather, it is [the cognition] of that which grasps it—namely, that which grasps the universal—from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) [that arises], as was the subject under discussion in the phrase "even though...
and so forth. The Master [Dignāga] has provided "like collyrium" and so on as a dissimilar example (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*).
Just as the refinement of the sense faculty is logical in the case of collyrium and the like, it is not so in the case of manifestation (vyakti).

Why? Because [the verse] uses the locative dual "in the times of its presence and absence" (bhāvābhāvakālayoḥ) with respect to manifestation—which is intended to be the manifester of cognition or understanding—and [the author] explains this by means of the words "it is refined" (saṃskṛtam) and so forth.

The sense faculty, when refined by ointments and other such means, attains a certain excellence inherent to itself; that is to say, it acquires a specific quality for the sake of cognition, as a cause for cognition, in order to produce a distinguished knowledge.
If one asks why the locative case is used here by the rule "the connection with an action [occurs] from a cause" (*nimittāt karma-saṃyoga*),
he says "clearly," and so forth.
The connection is made by changing the case-ending of "pratipatteḥ" (from realization);
for indeed, a sense-organ impaired by cataracts and the like produces an indistinct cognition,
whereas that very same organ, when refined by collyrium and other remedies, perceives with clarity.
If it is argued that the conditioned sense-faculty attains a specific excellence for the sake of cognition,

yet there is no difference in cognition resulting from [the application of] collyrium and the like, then— since those things which do not produce such [excellence] and those collyriums and so forth which do not produce a difference in cognition would not be its conditioners, they would consequently not be conditioners of the sense-faculty.
Just as there is a refinement of the sense organ through the application of collyrium and the like, it is not so from the manifest form; for what reason?
Because [the cognition] occurs during both the time when that [manifest form] is present and when it is absent, and so forth.

For instance, at a time when the manifesting cow-individual (*govyakti*) is absent, a visual consciousness arises with respect to a tree or other objects; if that same [consciousness] were to arise with respect to a tree or other objects even in the absence of that cow-individual, then it would follow that the refinement of the sense-organ (*indriyasaṃskāra*) caused by the cow-individual is perceived later—provided there were a refinement of the object (*viṣayasaṃskāra*).

However, even when there is a refinement of the object, there is no difference in the cognition regarding another object; therefore, that [refinement of the organ] is also not tenable. To this, he says:
"Regarding the object," and so forth:
if there is a certain refinement (*saṃskāra*) of an object such as odor, even though there is no difference in the sense faculty,
then indeed there would be no distinction in the perception of the sense faculty with respect to another object.

Nevertheless, the refinement of the sense organ would not be beneficial; rather, it would be the cognition that grasps the refined object which, by receiving that refinement, would be the beneficiary—this is the connection [of the sentence].
What is meant is this:
For objects are restricted; they are the means for producing only that cognition which possesses their own form, and not for one endowed with a different form.
Therefore, because the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of an object is restricted, it does not contradict [the fact] that it produces a specific apprehension only of its own object.

However, the sense faculty is an equal means for all the various objects it grasps; therefore, its refinement would result in being a differentiator of the apprehension regarding every object grasped by it.

It is not that the individuality of the object (*vyakti*) imparts a refinement (*saṃskāra*) to the sense organ for the sake of producing a cognition with a clear form regarding every visible object perceivable by that organ;

rather, if it is argued that the individuality is beneficial because it bestows the power of vision upon the sense organ toward the universal (*sāmānya*), which was previously invisible prior to the emergence of the individual,
then from the very perception of that which transcends the senses, the refinement of the sense organ is clearly understood.

That which was previously incapable due to the absence of a manifest individual (*vyakti*), but later becomes capable through its presence—that distinction of individuals, which reveals the object called "universal" (*sāmānya*) that is beyond the senses—how could it not be a differentiator of cognition everywhere? The meaning is that it is indeed a differentiator.
This is what is being said:

even in the case of visible objects, an embellishment of the sense organ (*indriya-saṃskāra*) produced by ointment and the like—which, by imparting the power to perceive a clear form where [previously] there was only an indistinct one—is observed to be a differentiator of cognition regarding every object graspable by that sense organ.
What then? The implication is that if [the sense organ] were to manifest an object beyond the senses, it would likewise manifest other supersensuous things, such as atoms and so forth.

If it is argued that the specific individual (vyakti) effects a refinement of the sense organ for the very purpose of perceiving the universal (sāmānya), and therefore there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga), [the author] says "one," and so on.

If it is admitted that the refinement of the sense organ (*indriya-saṃskāra*) is restricted to the perception of a single universal, then there would be no refinement of the sense organ capable of revealing other universals— such as *sattā* (existence), *dravyatva* (substantiality), and so forth— which are inherent in that very same particular instance, such as a brindled cow (*śābaleya*); yet, such a capacity is indeed required.

If it is argued that the refinement of the sense organ is for the purpose of perceiving all universals (sāmānya) inherent in the individual [object] and not just one alone, he says "and by the individual," etc.;
"in the perception of those" refers to the perception of those universals inherent in the individual.
If it is argued that, regarding those things manifested by that manifestation,

even when there is a determination of "substance-ness" (dravyatva) and "object-ness" (arthatva) upon seeing a mere substance from a distance, there is no determination of "cowness" (gotva) and so forth; and that for the perception of that which is not determined, no distinct latent impression (saṃskāra) has been produced— then [the author] says:
The connection is that "or there would be no single determination.

The word *eka* (one) has the sense of "other"; thus, there would be no determination even of another thing—such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*)—which is intended to be determined, because it is other than that which is undetermined. This [explanation] does not belong to the base text, which was not keyboarded.
(Note 291-1: Fifth Chapter = *Pañcamamāhnika*) There would be no determination.
What is the reason?
Because that individual, being composed of non-differentiation, lacks any distinction among those universals inherent within its own self;
for that individual is not proximate to some [universals] and not to others.

Therefore, it has been explained that the refinement of the sense organ by means of an individual instance (*vyakti*) is not possible—either because there is a determination of the universal for all [instances] or because there is none for any at all;
now, however, even while granting this, it is said:
"by the individual instance," and so forth.

Since, in both cases, the universal possesses the nature of producing cognition from the individual (vyakti), it does not deviate from that nature of producing cognition; for it is not logical for that which is capable to depend upon auxiliary causes (sahakārin). Thus, it is said that the sense organ is "cultivated" (saṃskṛta) as an auxiliary for that universal, and [the argument follows] from the state of being such.
Since a universal (*sāmānya*) is eternal and cannot have any excellence added to it, what could this "assistance" (*sahakāra*) mean? It means nothing at all.
By the words "for [it] is impermanent," etc., he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Because it obtains from the auxiliary a self that is distinguished [from its previous state],
why [is it said] "that" [referring] to the auxiliary?

For that very self which is the producer of these momentary things did not exist prior to the presence of the auxiliary causes; rather, it comes into being from those auxiliary causes at the very time when they are present. Thus it is held.

Regarding the phrase "of these": surely, even for momentary things, how can there be a dependence on auxiliary causes for the attainment of a specific nature, given that those which exist simultaneously cannot be mutual benefactors or beneficiaries?
And as for the moment that arises, it cannot require auxiliary causes at the times of its existence or non-existence;
thus, it is incorrectly stated that "one requires [auxiliaries] because they are beneficial. This is not a fault, for this is said with reference to existence (*sattā*).
Therefore he says: "Their very state of being produced is mutual dependence," meaning without reaching another, that is, a cooperative cause (sahakārin).
That nature is a capable nature;

for that universal (*sāmānya*), when isolated and devoid of auxiliary causes, that which was previously not of the nature to produce cognition can never again become so— this is the connection [of the sentence].
The intention is that [the universal] is eternal;
furthermore,

since the opponent has accepted the refinement of the sense faculty on the grounds that when there is a refinement of the sense faculty by means of the individual instance (*vyakti*), the universal produced thereby would be [perceived], [it follows that] from the individual instance...
Nevertheless, he says "the individual" and so forth, [meaning] that the consequence of being produced by an individual would follow;
this is its auxiliary cause.
If it is accepted that the universal is the cause of cognition by acting as a cooperative factor for the sense faculty which has been refined by the individual instance, then—
since the sense faculty is the effect of the individual instance— it would follow that the universal is said to be the indirect effect of the individual instance.

Granted that the individual instance (*vyakti*) may indeed be the manifestor (*vyañjikā*) of the universal (*sāmānya*), it is nonetheless not logical for it to possess the universal (*jāti*), because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Thus he says "Moreover" (*api ca*), etc.:
if it is maintained that the particular individual instance, which is the manifestor of universals—that is, of generalities—possesses a universal.

In that case, a lamp or similar object, which is the manifester of "cowness" (gotva) and so forth, because of its nature as a manifester, would thereby become possessed of that cowness and so forth; the meaning is that it would become a substratum of cowness, just like a brindled cow (śābaleya) or similar individual.
He explains by means of the words "For he who... and so forth:
[the objection being raised is] that even lamps and the like possess the quality of being causes of cognition with respect to universals such as "cowness" (gotva) which are manifested;
if one asks how this is so, he says:
"Light," and so forth;
therefore, light possesses causality with respect to cognition,
"therefore" meaning because of its being a cause of knowledge.
"Such as lamps, etc."—
by the word "etc.," the refinement of the sense faculties and so forth are included,
because these too are causes of cognition.
If it is argued that the manifestation of the universal occurs only as something distinct from the individual (*vyakti*), whereas this is not the case with a lamp or similar objects,
[the author] replies with the words "for indeed" (*na hi*) and so forth:
for there is no manifestation of the universal from the individual other than its being the cause of cognition.
For if the manifestation of a universal were produced by the individual and not by something such as a lamp,
then there would be a distinction; however,
that is not the case, because it is impossible to produce an excellence in its intrinsic nature.
The meaning is that because the universal is eternal, its inherence [is likewise eternal]; and thus, the nature of "cowness" (gotva) inheres in the individual cow, but not in things such as lamps.
Regarding the phrase "of that," since it has been stated, "What is this inherence (samavāya) between the universal and that which is neither produced nor productive?",

let us grant that there is indeed inherence; nevertheless, for this universal, there arises in conjunction with the individual (vyakti) merely an inherence, and no other specific quality characterized by the production of cognition exists.
