"‘As before’ means as prior to the inherence in the individual; even after the inherence in the individual, although there is no difference whatsoever in the universal, [the opponent] might argue that it nevertheless produces a cognition of its own object solely by the power of inherence. To this, he says:
"If the universal is accepted as the cause of cognition," and so forth.
When it is accepted that a universal inheres in that which is its own substratum and in which it is inherent,
[it would follow that] it inheres in that which is the substratum of its own substratum and in which [the former] is inherent.
Otherwise, other properties such as color and so forth, which are likewise inherent in atoms, would also necessarily become visible;
for since inherence is a single entity, it is indistinguishable everywhere.
Just as inherence alone reveals the universal even though it is beyond the senses, why should it not likewise reveal the color and other qualities residing in the atoms?

Since this fault exists in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), therefore the very fact of being a cause of cognition constitutes the manifestation of the universal by the individual; and since such a mode of manifestation is identical even in the case of a lamp and so forth, that same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) follows, namely that [the lamp] would be the possessor of "cowness" and the like.

Therefore, there is no inherence (*ādheyatā*) of the universal in its own substratum, nor is the manifestation of the individual by its own substratum the mode of the universal's existence in that substratum.
Consequently, because it does not exist [therein], the universal cannot be the cause of a single-form cognition regarding the diversity of individuals;
for it is not logical that something which does not exist in a particular locus should be the cause of a cognition of that locus by means of its own presence.

Therefore, for this very reason— namely, because a single universal does not reside in multiple locations— if those disputants hold that the genus (jāti) is either different from or non-different from the individual (vyakti);
But when individuals that have never existed before appear now, or are seen later on, the word [exists];
the particle "pareṇa" (after) following "śabdāt" (from the word) is for the purpose of emphasis;
therefore he says:
"Existence indeed," and so forth;
that is to say, for those things which exist as real entities, their "birth" occurs through their own capacity by means of their own apprehension.
The phrase "in another [instance]" refers to producing a cognition regarding a different individual;

what kind of cognition does it produce? It produces one that conforms to its own nature and follows a single form. Insofar as it produces such a cognition, it requires a relation, because without a relation, the production of a cognition with its own specific form would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, the relation of that [universal] with another individual— of a universal that exists and is present— is not possible, whether one maintains the position that it is identical to them or the position that it is different from them.
Why?
Because it is impossible for a distinction between individuals—which is either a separate entity or not a separate entity—to be observed in one place while appearing elsewhere in another individual;
he establishes this very point with the words "For that... and so forth.
For that cognition, which grasps a real entity— that is, which grasps a real universal— is unitary;
having arisen with respect to one individual instance, it would "leap over" or go toward another individual instance,
meaning that it would grasp that other instance as well in the form of the universal.

If some real entity (*vastubhūta*) in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*) were observed in one particular individual (*vyaktibheda*) and [were to exist] elsewhere— in that other particular individual where it would have to be perceived—
then that observation of it elsewhere would not be possible for a universal that is a real entity; such is the connection [of the argument].
What is the reason?
Because if non-difference from the substratum were admitted, there would be no persistence;
for that which is not distinct from one thing and constitutes its very nature cannot persist as something else.

Even if the universal were distinct from its substratum, it would not depend upon the individual because the status of being a substratum has been refuted by the immediately preceding negation of the relationship between container and contained; thus,
if the universal were separate, it could not produce a cognition of its own form in another individual due to the absence of a connection.
In that case, since it is the same even with respect to the first individual, why is it said "in previously unperceived individuals"? One should simply say "in individuals.
Furthermore, one must also state that it is because what is seen in one place cannot possibly be seen elsewhere;
for even in a single location, seeing [the universal] is impossible without a relation [to the individual].
This is true;
there is no fault in saying that this was stated while provisionally accepting that position— so thinks even he who holds such a view.
In the positions of identity or difference, the perception of something other than the universal is not possible; however, for us, the universal is indeed both different and non-different.
For instance, a universal without particularity cannot exist, just like a rabbit's horn.
When a variegated object appears simultaneously— such that its identity with some aspect and its difference from others appear at once—
then all distinctions such as "otherness" and "non-otherness" completely dissolve.
In order to refute that [objection], he says "For the nature... and so forth (*svabhāvo hi* etc. at Ślokavārttika, Ākṛti 10.
The connection [of the sentence] is that [an entity] does not transcend being either identical to or different from its own nature (*svabhāva*).

Now, one might object: "Even when there is no difference in space, time, or intrinsic nature, a distinction between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) is nevertheless accepted on the basis of their having the forms of 'concomitance' (*anugata*) and 'exclusion' (*vyāvṛtti*).

To this he replies: because a concomitant form—that is, an intrinsic nature that is not that [particular], namely an intrinsic nature consisting of exclusion—does not transcend being different [from the particular].
The meaning is that the universal, which has a recurring form distinct from the excluded particular forms, would necessarily be something else [than those particulars].
To the question, "How is it that being other than that form is simply being different? he says:
The phrase "this very [thing]" and so forth means that which is not that, i.e., that which does not have that form;
the meaning is that this alone is the definition of otherness.
The suffix -vat is used here in the sense of the genitive case, as in the case of other forms;
for indeed, because suffering is different from pleasure, it is considered to be suffering by virtue of having a nature that is not pleasure.

By this much, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been stated by means of "otherness" (*anyattva*), which is characterized by not having that nature; and since this characteristic of otherness is without distinction, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) has also been stated with respect to the intended universal (*sāmānya*).
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

that which, while being a real entity (*vastutva*), does not possess a certain nature, is necessarily other than that [nature]; for example, just as suffering is other than pleasure because it does not possess its nature. Since the conventional designation of "otherness" is what is to be proven through this lack of identity, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Thus, first of all, it has been demonstrated that if the universal lacks the nature [of the particular], it must be something other [than it].
Now, he says "And that," etc., to show that if being other is not accepted, then it follows that it must be identical.
If it were non-different from the individual, then that universal would be of the very nature of the individual;
for if it were not so— that is, if it were not of the nature of the individual— it would follow that it is different [from the individual],
just like any other distinct entity, as was stated immediately prior.
"Let it be that the universal is non-different [from the individual]; nevertheless, it would still follow after another individual.
To this, he says "na caika... and so forth.

This means that for that which has the nature of a single individual, there can be no "entry into" or "following after" (anugama) another individual—that is to say, no assumption of the nature of another individual.
Why? Because it would follow that the [universal] being cognized would be nothing other than an individual.

If the universal, consisting of a *śābaleya* (a brindled cow), were the very essence of a *bāhuleya* (a black cow), then the *bāhuleya* would be produced as nothing but a *śābaleya*, since there is no distinction from the universal whose essence is the *śābaleya*, just like a *śābaleya* itself. Therefore, how could it be a different individual? Consequently, [the cognition] follows along—that is, it is concomitant—with respect to a universal that is non-different from the individual.
Nor is it the case that from a separate universal there arises a cognition that conforms [to particulars]; this is the point under discussion.
Why?
Because that separate universal, having no locus in any particular, does not function [there].

Since activity is impossible without a relation, and because the relation between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), as well as the relation of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*), has been refuted by such statements as "manifestation is the state of being contained; therefore, it is not tenable in that case," one might ask: "In that case, what other relation will there be between the universal (*sāmānya*) and its possessor (*tadvat*)? To this, he says:

In the phrase "of another as well" (*anyasyāpi*) and so forth, the ablative case in *vyaṅgyavyañjakabhāvādeḥ* ("from the relation of the manifested and the manifestor," etc. is used; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the relation between locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) is intended.
Because there exists no other relation whatsoever— apart from these two relations previously refuted— between a universal and its manifestation, for what reason?
Because the universal, being eternal, cannot be assisted by any particular manifestation and thus lacks any necessary connection (*apratibandha*).
For it has been stated that there is no connection whatsoever for that which lacks a causal bond;
by this, the portion of the verse beginning with "even if there were otherness, because of the lack of a substratum" (152–53) has been explained.

If it is argued that even a universal, despite lacking a connection to individuals, produces a cognition that conforms to its own form [within them], he replies with the words "Because of the lack of connection" (*asambandhāt*) and so forth;
the analysis of the compound is: "that which has no connection to this."

The meaning is that there would be cognition of everything everywhere; "that" (tad) refers to "therefore this" (tasmād ayam), [stating] by means of the cause, which is the perception of a single universal, according to the Sāṃkhya.

Regarding that universal which is intended as a real entity (*vastu*) because it subsists in one particular instance of a brindled cow, when one seeks its subsistence in another distinct instance, its identity with or difference from that instance cannot be established, since there is no other possible mode of being for a real entity;
thus, the aforementioned fault applies. Therefore, the claim that a recurring cognition arises from a real universal is untenable.

Since this is so, therefore, regarding objects that are mutually distinct, this cognition—which possesses a single form and a single aspect—is nothing but an error, because it functions by superimposing non-difference upon things that are different.
To the question, "From where then does it arise? he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "vikalpa" (conceptual construction) and so forth:

it has already been stated that conceptual constructions arise from the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) which, by their very nature, produce such constructions through the experience of objects as excluded from those of a different class; he says this because they have emerged from that [source].
Regarding the phrase "distinction of entities" (*bhāvabheda*) and so forth:
the distinction of entities—that is, of their effects—from those things that do not have those effects;

and the latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of such [entities], as well as its nature (*prakṛti*)—that is, its intrinsic character (*svabhāva*)—are established as its substratum, as was determined previously. In this context, two factors are presented: the distinction of entities as the cause through a mediated succession (*pāramparyeṇa*), and the latent impression as the cause directly (*sākṣāt*).

If indeed the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) alone is the denotation of a word, how then are there words such as "the effect of Pradhāna," "the effect of Īśvara," and so forth? By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of terms such as "the world is the effect of Pradhāna," "the world is the effect of Īśvara," and "the transformation of the Word-Brahman" (*śabdabrahmapariṇāma*) is intended.
Regarding internal and external entities,
those whose distinctions (*bheda*) do not consist of that [Prakṛti]— that is, whose distinctions do not have the nature of being effects of the Pradhāna and so forth— are described as such.
Even if their distinction were to arise from being an effect of the non-pradhāna, then it would follow that their distinction has the nature of being an effect of the Pradhāna and so forth.
And that very non-difference belongs to all [things];
therefore, by means of that non-difference which is without a cause, they exist everywhere.

Yet, according to the view of the proponent of the exclusion of others (anyāpohavādin), that [non-difference] does not exist, because entities consist of effects such as the "unmanifest" (apradhāna) and so forth.
And therefore, the intention is: how is it that they do not function non-differently toward things that have become thus?
Consequently, the implication is that the determination of apoha is non-pervasive.
He refutes this with the words beginning "they too," etc.;
the connection is that those very terms for the effects of *pradhāna* and so forth also operate upon an object appearing in conceptual cognition.
To the question "How so? he says:

Regarding the phrase beginning with "saṃketa" (convention): it refers to that convention which, by the power of desire, is applied to an object that is not actually as it appears, [asserting] that the world is the primary effect.

Because the stream of consciousness has been refined by the successive transformation of moments through that latent capacity (*vāsanā-śakti*) deposited therein, it perceives all external and internal objects. Even though these objects exist as experiences in perception, it does so without regard for their actual differentiation—that is, without regard for the differentiation existing in the thing itself as a non-primary effect.

This means that even if there is a perception of objects that are merely non-primary effects according to the nature of things, it nevertheless occurs without regard for the true nature of the object.
Thus, due to such conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), one determines even those entities that are non-primary effects to be primary effects in accordance with linguistic convention (*saṃketa*).

The meaning is this: consciousness (*caitanya*) is imagined by the Sāṃkhya as the effect of a primary matter (*pradhāna*) that is not so [ultimately] real; since there is no absence of the effects of primary matter through the exclusion of that [consciousness], the conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*) that appears in relation to its object is itself "exclusion of other" (*anyāpoha*) by way of excluding what is of a different class. He asks, "Of what nature are those words? and says:
"From grasping," and so forth:

the strengthening of the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*), which is the cause of conceptual construction, is the power of grasping; from that comes the "origination," meaning the arising, of that conceptual construction. From that [power] they have arisen.
This is what is meant.

If it is argued that even though there is no such differentiation in reality, nevertheless, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)—which is merely superimposed by conceptual construction—is the factor for the application of words, and therefore this fault of non-pervasiveness does not apply;

and if one asks why a real universal (*sāmānya*) existing as a substantial entity is not accepted in those things when words like "pradhāna" and "effect" function without distinction, he replies with the words "For not... and so forth.

The meaning is that since the universal (sāmānya) is absent due to the absence of individuals, there can be no universal in those things which— though superimposed as being the effects of the primary cause— are not actually such effects. However,
he states that for the proponent of *anyāpoha* (the exclusion of others), there is no such fault.
The phrase "tathā" and so forth means by way of the conceptualization of being an effect of the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and other such causes.

The "distinction" (*bheda*)— that is, the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*)— of that which is other than those [effects], namely that which is not an effect of the *pradhāna* and so forth, would occur for cognizers through the force of their conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding those entities superimposed as being effects of the *pradhāna* and so forth.

If it is asked: "Why is it that, by the very force of the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that [cognition], there is no universal (*sāmānya*) as the cause for the recurring cognition (*anuvṛttipratyaya*) among individuals such as the *śābaleya* cow and others?"—this is not so;

because even by that proponent of universals who postulates a universal, the exclusion (*bheda*) from heterogeneous things (*vijātīya*) among those *śābaleya* individuals and the like must necessarily be accepted as being inseparable (*nāntarīyaka*), otherwise the existence of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth would be unestablished.
That very difference is sufficient—that is, capable—regarding the effects of a universal, which are characterized by the application of a single term and so forth;
thus, the postulation of a universal is purposeless.
This is what is meant.

Just as even in the case of entities that are effects of the Pradhāna, the words "Pradhāna-effect" and so forth, as well as the cognitions thereof, occur in a uniform manner even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*), why is it not accepted that in the case of cows and the like, the words "cow" and so forth, and the cognitions thereof, likewise occur in a uniform manner? Why resort to a postulated ultimate universal?
For even by others [the Naiyāyikas], the occurrence of a single denotation and cognition among many universals is observed even in the absence of a [higher-order] universal.
As it has been stated by Bhaṭṭa and Uddyotakara:

"Therefore, the word for a universal (sāmānya-śabda) is based on that occurrence of a single [entity] in diverse [individuals], or else on the production of a single cognition regarding existence (sattā) and so forth."
Therefore, the meaning is as follows:

just as the word "universal" and the cognition thereof apply to "existence," "substance-ness," and so forth—each of which possesses multiple things through inherence—even in the absence of a [single] universal, and just as that which is "possession of inherence in multiple things" is not itself a universal such that it would exist identically in existence and in substance-ness; [so too applies the case at hand].

Because of the statement that "universals are devoid of further universals," and because the application of those two— namely, word and cognition— is not figurative since they are grasped by an unerring intellect,

therefore, just as their application to [the universal] existence (*sattā*) and so forth occurs without another universal, so too does it occur in the case of the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and others without a universal.

The meaning is this: just as a brindled cow (śābaleya) is excluded from non-cows, so too a black cow (bāhuleya) is excluded from non-cows, and so too a fragmentary cow (khaṇḍa) is excluded from non-cows; why then is the occurrence of a single designation and cognition not accepted?

It might be argued that in all cases the cognition of a universal is indeed held to be without an object, yet without a real universal, there would be no non-discrepancy (avisamvāda) in some instances; to this he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "yadi" (if): the word "yadi" serves to indicate an admission;
that is, if it is admitted that this [cognition] is devoid of an object in all cases.

The notion of a universal is not meaningful if it refers to entities that exist— namely, those excluded from non-cows— or if it refers to entities that do not exist in reality— namely, those such as Primordial Matter (pradhāna), the Lord (īśvara), and so forth, which do not exist as effects.

Since that which has been superimposed by her [the conceptual cognition]— possessing an undifferentiated form— is non-existent among external objects, and because this constitutes the apprehension of the unreal,
it is nothing but a cognitive distortion (*bhrānti*). Therefore,
there is no concern whatsoever regarding the determination of an object for this universal-cognition (*sāmānyabuddhi*), as it is itself devoid of an object.

If all cognition of a universal is erroneous, how then is there correspondence with reality through inference? To this he says, "In some cases," and so forth: because in some particular object there is non-discrepancy [with reality] arising from that cognition, due to its being connected as cause and effect, as previously described.
And this has been explained previously,
where there is a connection with a real entity, as in the case of the aforementioned inference, by the words "as in" and so forth (1.83).

Because an inferential conceptualization does not involve a real entity— that is, because it does not apply to a real entity that exists as such, possessing an undifferentiated form graspable by inference,
there is no discrepancy with the real entity, unlike perception; this is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
What is the reason for saying "even when it is not so"? It is because [the cognition] occurs even when the object has passed away, by means of a causal chain following the logical mark (*liṅga*);
or alternatively, because the cognition of an undifferentiated form occurs even with respect to an object that is "not so," that is, one devoid of a universal (*sāmānya*).
Thus we shall inform you,
and it has already been informed.

If it is argued that because it conforms to existence and non-existence, its capacity [to function as a cognition] lies within [the realm of positive entities], and that the cognition of a universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*)— by superimposing non-difference upon distinct entities through the non-distinction of its own form— apprehends them as having a positive nature (*vidhirūpatayā*), then how can it be said that its object is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)? To this, he says "difference," etc.

The phrase "by the power of the perception of distinct objects" (bhinnapadārthadarśanabalena) is an ellipsis for "because this general cognition arises through the capacity of the experience of specific particulars (svalakṣaṇa) as excluded from those of a different class.

The inclusion of the term "abundantly" (bahula-) is for the purpose of demonstrating that conceptual cognition (vikalpabuddhi) functions even in the absence of a real entity, such as in the case of a rabbit's horn and the like.

The meaning is that when those distinct particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are [perceived], because of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an entity through the non-differentiation of its own form (*svākāra*), and because of the determination of its own nature by unifying the perceived object (*dṛśya*) and the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
cognition arises by the power of seeing distinct things, and once arisen, it apprehends those very same distinct things as if they were non-different from its own form.
Therefore, "having difference as its object" means having a distinct entity as its object.

It is indeed logical that conceptual constructions such as "impermanence" and so forth—which arise by way of the perception of a real entity—have difference as their object, because they are produced through the power of perceiving a real entity;
however, this is not the case where no such distinct entity exists.

If it is asked, "In the case of conceptual constructions such as 'eternal' and so forth, and conceptual constructions such as 'the horn of a hare' and so forth, how can those [constructions] have difference as their object?", he says:
Likewise, regarding the phrase "in the case of existence" and so forth:

just as cognitions of impermanence and the like—which arise through the force of experiencing the apprehension of the intrinsic nature of distinct entities—function by determining their own internal reflections (*svapratibhāsa*) as being distinct entities, and thus have difference as their object;

in the same way, when there is the conceptualization of existence itself—that is, when there is the conceptual determination of one's own reflection as being distinct external entities—even though there is no other [external] object, because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "permanent," "primal matter" (*pradhāna*), "effect," and so forth, or "hare's horn" and the like, possess the quality of having difference as their object with respect to those non-existent things such as permanent primal matter, effects, and hare's horns.
It exists only as a distinction among individuals residing within its own substratum,
and not in a place devoid of individuals;
this has been stated by Bhaṭṭa:
Furthermore, since the universal (sāmānya) is perceived only in individual objects (piṇḍa) and not in the space between them—
nor do some [philosophers] accept that which is called a "universal" as being like space (ākāśa)—
its subsistence in each individual (pratyeka-samavetatva), being observed, will not be negated. (Ākṛti 25)
And this being so, there will be no multiplicity [of the universal] for a single cognition.

(Vana0 30) And just as a single individual, though perceived again and again at different times, remains non-different, so too the universal, although residing in different substrates, remains the same. (Vana0 33)
Udyotakara also says in the *Ślokavārttika*:

"By what means is the omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) of the universal (*jāti*) accepted, such that the nature of 'cowness' (*gotva*) would exist even in a lump of clay or a clay cow? Rather, it is called 'omnipresent' because its occurrence (*vṛtti*) exists everywhere within its own domain."
What, then, is the specific object of "cowness," wherein cowness exists? And where does cowness reside?
Where does the cognition of recurrence, caused by "cowness," occur? And where does "cowness" produce that cognition of recurrence, which is its proof?
Furthermore, what is the purpose of establishing the cow, given that the genus "cowness" (gotva) is eternal?
For there is no manifestation of cowness apart from the object possessing the hump and other such features.

When a Buddhist proclaims that "cowness" is not an entity distinct from individual cows because it is not perceived in the intervals between them, he should be questioned regarding what this "interval between individuals" is:
is it space, or rather non-existence, or perhaps another substance?

If space were [the cause], then "cowness" would not exist therein, for space is never perceived as a cow; by this, non-existence and [the theory that] substance is something distinct [from its qualities] are also explained,
as well as the fact that specific cognitions do not arise without a cause (*ākasmikatva*).
This cognition, which partakes in the exclusion of the individual substance (*piṇḍa*), arises from another cause when it is produced;

for indeed, it is observed that cognitions partaking in the exclusion of the substance arise from another cause, as in the case of the cognition of "blue" with respect to skins, clothes, and woolen blankets. And that other cause is the universal (*sāmānya*);
therefore, the universal is omnipresent throughout all individuals.
Because it exists even in a place devoid of individuals,
there is no perception of the universal therein due to the absence of an individual that could manifest it;

and only that specific individual in which the universal is perceived is capable of manifesting the universal, as is understood through the principle of the impossibility of perceiving the universal otherwise, and not any other.
The Nyāyavārttika. Regarding this, Bhaṭṭa says:
Alternatively, even though [the universal] is omnipresent, its manifestation occurs in accordance with its capacity;
since capacity is to be inferred from its effect, manifestation is caused by perception. Therefore, that alone in which the manifestation is perceived is indeed the locus of the capacity.
And for that very reason, this [universal] is not perceived in all individuals;
for even though they are distinct, some possess the capacity while others are incapable,
and there can never be any objection regarding the inherent power of things.
"Fire burns, but space does not; who here is to be questioned about this?
— *Ślokavārttika*, *Ākṛti*.

Regarding those two positions, the intention [of the author] is as follows: if [the universal] resides only in its own substrate, then how could there be the occurrence of a universal residing in a substance that is in a different location from a jar or other object produced later—in a place devoid of "jar-ness" (ghaṭatva) and the like—at the time of the production of a new jar or similar object? It is not possible at all. This is the meaning.
If there were such a possibility— that the universal belonging to that previous substance would pass over to the substance subsequently produced— then it would be so;
however, that is not the case, as he says in the passage beginning with "yasmāt" (because).

Regarding the term "that" (tad), it refers to the universal (sāmānya). As for the phrase "from the previous substance" (pūrvadravyāt): from that in which it was previously inherent, the "about-to-be-arisen substance" (utpitsu dravyam)—the substance desiring to arise, such as a prior jar—does not move, because, being formless, the universal is devoid of action.

If it is argued that even though it does not move from the previous substance, there will nevertheless be a connection with a different location, just as a reflection appears in a mirror, [the author] says:
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "Indeed, it is not logical" and so forth;

for a real entity called a "universal" (sāmānya), which subsists in another substance—that is, a substance located in a different place from the substance about to arise—does not move from its previous substratum and does not pervade the interval between those two; that is, it does not pervade the interval between the two things produced before and after. Therefore, its conjunction with a substance located in a different place from its own substratum is indeed not logical.
For how could one who asserts that there is no conjunction of a reflection with a mirror located in a different place from the original object (bimba) not be insane?
Through the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), an erroneous cognition arises there— appearing as a reflection upon a mirror—
as it has been described in the case of objects with opposing transformations, such as the surface of a diamond-mirror and the like.

Since there is no possibility for entities whose nature is like that of mountains and so forth to arise, even those who maintain that another entity arises therein have no connection with the original object; thus, this [position] is trivial.
Prior to the substance that is about to arise, the universal does not exist there in the location where it is to arise,
because its presence in a location devoid of an individual is not admitted;
yet after that, once the individual has arisen, that universal exists.
Since an individual devoid of a universal is not admitted,
[the universal] does not arise together with the individual in that location because it is eternal;
nor is the arising of the universal identical to the arising of the individual, because they are distinct.
Alternatively, if there were no distinction [between the universal and the particular], then the relationship of universal and particular would not exist;
furthermore, this is a presentation by way of a conclusion of that which was previously stated: "This has not come from any prior specific individual, nor does it go away."

In as many ways as the existence of a universal in another individual is possible, those very ways are not admitted while the universal is nevertheless asserted to exist there; this is a contradiction.
And because it is difficult for the wise to endure, it is a burden.
For this very reason, he said:
"Who is this? and so forth; for how could a wise person tolerate what is improper?
But a fool, due to ignorance, being incapable of investigating what is proper and improper, might even tolerate it.
As for what was said elsewhere, "due to dullness," [the opponent objects]:
"Surely, even when a universal arises in a substance that is about to arise, its state of inherence must be understood from perception alone;

and that perception of inherence in the individual exists even when the universal has not yet arisen—so what is the use of its arising? Furthermore, the nature of the universal is held to be inherent in the individual."

Therefore, although it is inherent in that previous substance, it appears as if it does not move from there while being inherent in the substance about to arise; thus, how could it be said that "it does not go" and so forth? This objection is stated for the sake of refutation. [The author replies: "It is true, because this is accepted.
For this refutation would apply to one who does not accept the appearance of the universal (*sāmānya*); however, since it does appear, [the objection fails].

But for one who considers the appearance of a universal (*sāmānya-pratibhāsa*) to be false (*alīka*), how can it be refuted? For the Master has demonstrated through such passages as "the substance that is about to arise does not go there, nor was it there, nor has it arisen," that even in the absence of a universal, a cognition appearing as a universal arises;
and truth does not follow merely from appearing.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the double moon and such phenomena would possess reality;
furthermore, invalidation by perception is not the sole form of invalidation,
since invalidation by inference is also a form of invalidation.
If it were possessed of parts, then by one part it would occupy its previous location, while by another part it would pervade the substance about to arise in a different location;
or else, if it were partless, it would have to abandon its previous location—
neither of these two possibilities exists, as he says:
And with the words "na ca" and so forth,

he clarifies the portion of the sūtra beginning with "pūrvam ādhāram" by means of the Miśraka commentary, stating that [the effect] occupies a location different from the location where it was about to arise.
Regarding the phrase "of the two," he explains that it refers to two substances produced earlier and later, stating that "it would be twofold" through the words beginning with "distinct."
First, he states the initial position: [the object exists] by way of having various parts as its nature, through the abandonment of its previous substratum.
The phrase beginning with "not manifold," and so forth,
is stated according to what is established by the opponent;
however, it has already been said that a single entity consisting of multiple parts is not admitted.
Because of its connection with two distinct parts called "aspects" (aṃśa) which are mutually different—
that is, because of its connection with those two parts located in different places—
light, being composed of parts, connects with the jar by means of one of its own parts.
Just as with other things such as jars and so forth, the same applies to ropes, bamboo, staffs, and the like through their own respective relations;
this is the support for the statement beginning with "not indeed" (na hi).
Now, if it is held that a universal exists in many things because it possesses parts, even so, how could a single entity exist in many?
For it would be the parts of the universal that exist [in those things].
And as for those parts of the universal that exist in each individual substance at that time,
are they of the nature of the universal or not?
If they are of the nature of the universal, it follows that the one [universal] exists in many places simultaneously.
Furthermore, it is not logical to say that a single universal exists in multiple locations;
if they do not have the nature of a universal,
how can it be said that a universal exists in many places?
Furthermore, if the universal were to exist in one part [of an individual] by means of another part, there would be an infinite regress;
moreover, it is not logical for a single entity to exist in multiple locations without possessing parts.

Alternatively, if it were partless and existed in its entirety within each individual object, then—like the individual objects themselves—it would be unique to each and could not therefore be a universal.
What is the reason? Because that partless universal has a single nature in its relation with one substance, and there is no second nature distinct from it;
and because that universal, being of a single nature, consists in the form of a relation residing in those respective locations.
Because it possesses the nature of being connected to that substance which is the jar located in the space immediately preceding the spot where the jar intends to arise,
there can be no simultaneous conjunction with a different location.
Otherwise—that is, if it were of the nature of a relation with the substance and location where it is about to arise—it would be impossible for that [universal] to have such a relation;
for it could not possibly be related to that previous substance.
Therefore, since the universal has a nature restricted to a single individual, at that very same time it cannot have a relation with a substance located in a different place.

Alternatively, regarding the relation [of the universal], since the universal has a single nature restricted to the previous individual, its abiding in that previous individual and its non-abiding at that very same time through its relation to an individual in a different location would be contradictory; thus he says, "Of one substratum," and so forth.
In this context, "abiding" means in the previous individual.

At that very time, in that very moment, because you have admitted [the existence of the universal] in another individual, and because it is impossible for one thing to persist elsewhere without abandoning the previous individual, therefore, in that previous individual—
It is incorrect to say that this universal has no locus by virtue of its very nature as being restricted to a previous individual;
for what is the reason?
Regarding the passage beginning with "tatsthitā" and so forth:
because it is contradictory for a single universal to exist simultaneously in two natures—namely, that of being present and that of being absent—within that very same individual.

[Objection: But surely, just as its occurrence in another [individual] is possible through the abandonment of one [part], so too its occurrence in many [individuals] is accepted as being twofold, since it is observed to occur through various successive parts.

Likewise, since it is observed that when a universal exists in one place by a certain form, it exists in another place by that very same form at that same time, why is this third mode of subsistence not accepted?
As Bhaṭṭa has said:
"For there is no restrictive rule that subsistence can only be of two kinds."
"For although it is threefold, it may be twofold because it has been seen, just as [in the case of] the *Ślokavārttika*";
thus also says Uddyotakara.
Cowness is neither a whole nor a collection; therefore, the terms "entirety" and "part" do not apply to it.
Since these two terms do not apply there, the question—whether cowness exists in its entirety or by way of a part—is not logical.
How, then, does cowness exist in cows?
Regarding the relationship between substratum and superstratum: what, then, is this relationship of substratum and superstratum? It is inherence (*samavāya*).
In that case, "cowness" is the possessor of the mode of existence (*vṛtti*),

while the mode of existence is inherence (*samavāya*), because it is the cause of the cognition "here. Therefore, since inherence alone is the mode of existence in all instances— both in the previous substance and in the substance about to arise— how can it be said that this is improper on the grounds of the contradiction between a stationary and a non-stationary nature existing in one and the same place?
The *Nyāyavārttika* states this very point in the passage beginning with "sarvatra" and so forth.

In all cases—whether in a previously manifested entity or in a substance about to be produced—it exists even at the moment when the production of that future substance occurs; even then, it does not abandon the substance.

Therefore, there is no contradiction between the states of being stationary and non-stationary within a single locus, because the state of being stationary (as a distinct entity) does not exist [therein].
That is incorrect;
for being inherent in one [individual] is not the same as being inherent in another individual, because it would follow that the other would appear there [in the first].
Therefore, there is indeed a mutual difference between being inherent in one and being inherent in another.

Furthermore, if that [capacity] were non-different [from the universal], then because it would be inherent in a single [individual], there would be a lack of pervasion (ananugama); consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence that the universal itself would lack pervasion elsewhere.

Alternatively, the power of the universal to produce cognition through its connection with one individual, time, and so forth, does not exist by virtue of its connection with another individual and so forth.
Therefore, in one individual, there is the power of the universal to produce cognition, while in another, there is a power that obstructs the production of cognition;
and since these powers are non-different from the possessor of the powers,
this is because a real entity is defined by its powers.
Therefore, the pervasion is established that whatever is a single entity must exist exclusively in one place.
If it is argued that the universal is a single entity, how then could it exist elsewhere as well? [The answer is: because it appears as such [in other locations].
For a manifestation does not subvert that which is non-manifesting, nor does it subvert that which is a non-entity, since even that [non-entity] manifests;
however, the manifestation of a real entity (*vastu*) is what subverts this [non-manifestation], and it has already been stated that no pervasive real entity exists.
For this very reason, there is no sublation of the thesis by perception, because the cognition of the universal is merely a semblance of perception.

If it is objected that there would be a circularity—namely, that as long as this [perception] lacks validity, the inference does not proceed, and as long as the inference does not proceed, this is not a semblance of perception—[we reply: no.
Inference does not function merely on the basis of a doubt regarding the reality of that which appears;
nor does inference function by means of a cause for its own invalidity, but rather by means of a logical mark (liṅga) that is invariably concomitant with its own probandum.
Therefore, there is no sublation of the cognition of the universal; consequently, in ultimate reality, a single entity cannot reside in multiple locations at one time.
For if it were so resident, there would be a contradiction between its state of being established and not established therein.
However, the Teacher, even while conceding this fault, says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "tatsvabhāva" (having that as its nature):
that cognition which has the perception of a universal nature as its basis occurs in relation to every substance, even those of different classes, because [the universal] exists in all forms;
and such being the case, one would [erroneously] perceive even a cow as a horse, and so forth.
He asks, "What is the reason? and provides the analysis: "The self (ātman) of which [is] that which resides in the horse, by virtue of its being a substance (dravyatva)."
Because it conveys the meaning, a *bahuvrīhi* compound may be formed even with words in different grammatical cases;
for instance, "standing on a horse" (*aśve sthitaḥ*) or "that by which the proof is accomplished" (*sādhanaṃ kṛtam*) are compounds,
after which a two-word *bahuvrīhi* is formed with the word *ātman*.

Because of the determination [of the object] through the apprehension of its own nature and through the apprehension of the substance-nature residing in the horse, as well as the determination "the cow is a substance" [Pāṇini 2.2],
this might be so.
The cognition "it is a substance" does not arise from the apprehension of substanceness as inherent in a horse;
rather, it arises from the apprehension of substanceness alone. To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "And of that," etc.:
since there is no other form— characterized by non-inherence in the horse— that exists apart from the single, unperceived, and uncomprehended substantiality (dravyatva) inhering in the horse,
one who perceives the cow as "substance" qualified precisely by that substantiality which inheres in the horse would consequently perceive it as "a horse."

However, for one who holds that the universal "substance-ness" (dravyatvasāmānya) is indeed distinct from the horse, and that [the cow] is qualified by that [universal], such a person, when perceiving a cow, would necessarily perceive it as a horse;
therefore, this is the conclusion.
A partless universal is not simultaneously imposed upon a jar or other objects which possess multiple locations—that is, many locations.
It does not become something that is to be superposed;
by this much, the statement "and not like something possessing parts" is explained.
He explains the phrase "it abandons its former substratum" with the words beginning with "former," and so on.

The phrase "sa ceti" (and that) implies that the abandonment of its previous substratum by the universal is not accepted [by the opponent]. Regarding the phrase "anyatra," it mocks [the opponent's position] as being highly illogical: it suggests that while the universal remains in its previous individual without moving from its own former location, it simultaneously subsists in another substance whose birth occurs in a place other than that former locus of its substratum. 156
If it is argued that the universal, though not moving from the location of its previous manifestation, pervades a substance in another location, [the author] says "where," etc.;
in whatever location this entity, which exists at a later time, resides—

The universal is not connected with that location, because it is admitted to be omnipresent within its own individual instances; furthermore, the claim that it pervades an entity existing at a later time in a location where the universal does not currently reside is a transgression of logical principle. Thus, [the author] mocks this in another way, saying, "This is truly a great marvel! For one who follows the rules of logic cannot possibly conclude that what does not exist in a certain location can pervade that location. (157)
Desiring also to refute the conceptualization of omnipresence, he says "yasya" and so forth;

for that proponent of an omnipresent universal as well, if the universal is omnipresent, then by means of its manifestation— that is, its becoming evident— in a single instance such as a *śābaleya* cow, which serves as the instrument...

That universal (jāti) is indeed manifest—that is, clearly revealed—everywhere, even in a place devoid of individuals and amidst a diversity of individuals belonging to different classes; because it is non-different, being one, it would be perceived everywhere, even in a place devoid of individuals.
This is what is meant.

The sense is this: although there is an absence of a manifesting individual instance (*svavyakti*) both in a region devoid of individuals and in an individual of a different class, nevertheless, because the universal (*jāti*) exists therein in a form manifested by its own individual instance, it would be perceived; otherwise, it would follow that it possesses a plurality of natures. Thus, it is intended that it must be of a single nature. Furthermore, it has already been refuted that there can ever be a manifestation of an eternal universal, since it cannot have any excellence added to it. It is stated [in the verse]: "The occurrence [of a universal] consists in being supported and manifested; this is not tenable in that case. 1.
In this context,

for that very reason, if that universal (*jāti*) is by its own nature eternally independent of any external embellishment, incapable of receiving any excellence (*anādheyātiśaya*), and capable of producing its own cognition;
In that case, it would be perceived eternally, both before and after its manifestation; or,
if it were not capable [of being perceived], then it might never be perceived—
what is the reason?
The meaning is that because it remains at all times of a single nature— whether in its state of having a nature capable of producing cognition or in its opposite—
it is incapable [of producing cognition] when the individual instance (*vyakti*) is absent, but becomes capable when that instance is present.
Therefore, since there is neither constant perception nor non-perception of a genus (*jāti*),
he says "in its own nature" and so forth;
the meaning is that, by virtue of being eternal, it cannot have any excellence added to it.
If the universal (jāti) does not exist [apart from the individual], then why is it said that "it is manifested by the individual alone" in a single instance, and so forth? To this, he says:
"Even granting [that it exists]," and so on.

Although the universal (jāti) is all-pervasive, it is manifested in a single locus; because there is no difference [in the universal] and because the universal is one, it is indeed manifested— that is, revealed— everywhere, even in a place devoid of manifestation and in a different class of entities where the individual manifestations differ.

By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even in those devoid of individuals," it is implied that [the universal] exists even in dissimilar cases and in the distinction between different individuals; furthermore, that universal does not depend upon an individual as its manifestor,
nor would an individual be required to manifest it.
The meaning is that the individual manifestation lacks the capacity to manifest the universal (*jāti*).

For if it were to depend upon a manifesting individual, then in the absence of the cognition of the manifester, there would be no cognition of the manifested; for indeed, when a lamp or the like is not perceived, the perception of a jar or the like does not occur.
Likewise here too, if the individual is not perceived, there can be no perception of the genus;
however, why is the reversal of the roles of the manifested and the manifestor between the universal and its possessor accepted?
For indeed, according to the rule that "cognition does not occur with respect to a qualified object when the qualifier has not been grasped."
The apprehension of the universal (*sāmānya*) is desired even prior [to the apprehension of the individual]; however, it is through that [universal] that the individual is [apprehended].

Therefore, there is a reversal: it is maintained that the cognition of the universal—which is intended to be the manifested (*vyaṅgya*)—occurs even without the apprehension of the manifesting individual (*vyañjikā*).
He explains this with the words beginning "yo hi," etc.

Its own substratum (*svāśraya*) is that wherein the universal (*sāmānya*) inheres and the sense organ (*indriya*) which apprehends the universal; the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of these two is required for the cognition of that universal, and thus it is so described.
Regions devoid of a substratum are those occupied by individuals of a different genus (*vijātīya-vyakty-adhyāsita*), and those devoid of individuals are those where no individual exists at all.
In those [cases], it is not perceived because of the absence of the aforementioned conjunction,
even for one who speaks in this manner.

In some cases, when an individual is perceived, the contact between the sense organ and its substratum certainly exists as a factor that assists the universal, which is present everywhere. Therefore, due to that contact between the sense organ and the substratum, one who perceives that [individual] may perceive the universal—which pervades all locations—exactly as it exists within a particular individual.
If it is argued that "the nature of the universal is visible only where the manifesting individual is, and not elsewhere," he replies:
"Not indeed," and so forth;
"in that" refers to the universal (jāti); "when it is perceived in some individual" (vyakti); "belonging to it" (tadīyām) means related to the universal.

Because it would contradict what is seen and what is not seen in the case of a single [object], the meaning conveyed by the word has thus far been explained by accepting that manifestation (*vyakti*) is the manifestor (*vyañjikā*).
Now, he says the following in order to explain [the passage] beginning with "that [manifestation] does not depend on a particular instance" (*na sā vyaktyapekṣiṇī*).
Regarding the phrase "because it is manifested by an individual" and so forth, its falsity has already been established by what was just stated;

for there is no such thing as the seen and the unseen for a single entity. Therefore, this is merely a restatement of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), presented while closing one's eyes like an elephant, solely for the purpose of pointing out further defects.
"Of that which has become so" means of that which is logical;
"therein" refers to the genus and the possessor of the genus,
because the relationship of the manifested and the manifestor is absent therein as something logical.
"What is the reason? and so forth;
for [the word] "hi" means "because."

In a place devoid of its own nature— that is, in a place lacking a lamp or similar source of light— an object such as a jar, which is manifested by that [light], does not exist; thus, according to the reasoning already stated, manifestation cannot be the manifester of a universal.
What is the reason?
Because of the opposite [case]:
for the opponent maintains that the universal is apprehended first, even without having apprehended the individual.

Since it is accepted that the individual (vyakti) is apprehended precisely through the apprehension of the universal (sāmānya), and since the individual is thus apprehended even when the manifestor (vyañjaka) is not perceived,
the individual transcends the properties of the manifestor;
this very point he states:
"How indeed," and so forth;
the connection is that "she"—meaning the individual instance—would be the manifester of the universal.
"By way of its apprehension" means by way of the apprehension of the universal.

It is contradictory to say that this individual manifestation would be visible; for if it were admitted that the manifestation is seen by the force of seeing the universal (*sāmānya*), such is the case.
That manifestation (*vyakti*) would follow as being itself suggested (*vyaṅgyā*), and the word "and the universal" (*sāmānyaṃ ca*) is to be supplied;
the compound [in the phrase] "like a jar by means of a lamp" (*pradīpena ghaṭavat*) is formed by splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*) of *tṛtīyā*.

Or rather, it is a *sup-sup* compound (noun + noun), meaning that just as a jar is manifested by a lamp, so too is the individual (*vyakti*) manifested by the universal (*sāmānya*). This is the sense of "attainment" (*prāpti*); for without the cognition of that [universal], the individual is invisible in form, lacking the cognition of the universal.
Others, however,
say that in the phrase "it follows that the same [would be] suggested," the word "ca" (and) includes the term "the manifester of the universal";
therefore, the suffix -vat should be understood as arising from a copulative compound (*dvandva*), meaning "similar to both the lamp and the jar."
Because the rule regarding the obligatory prior placement [of a word] is subject to exceptions, the word *ghaṭa* (pot) does not necessarily appear first; rather,
the universal (*sāmānya*) is the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), like a lamp,
and the individual (*vyakti*) is the manifested (*vyaṅgya*), like a pot.
Regarding the phrase "it follows as the meaning of the sentence," by this [statement], what effect does the proponent of the universal perceive as being impossible without a universal?
In this way, according to the method described,
it involves great exertion and, being impossible to accomplish, is a cause of much suffering.

158–59 "Paraspara" and so forth: because they are distinct (*para*) due to their difference (*bhedāt*), that is, on account of being heterogeneous (*vilakṣaṇatvāt*), [they are] non-concomitant (*vyatirekiṣu*), meaning lacking positive concomitance (*ananvayiṣu*).

The mention of "cognition" (*pratyaya*) refers by way of illustration to a single uniform cognition that persists through a series; the connection is that the theory of universals (*sāmānyavāda*) is resorted to because such a cognition would be impossible without a universal belonging to the word.
The Teacher asks, "How so?
To those who do not accept that words such as "cook" (*pācaka*) are based on action, he says this:
without a single object called a "universal" (*sāmānya*), how could one and the same word be expressive with respect to various cooks?
By the mention of the "designator" (*vācaka*), the "corresponding cognition" (*pratyayānvayin*) is indeed already grasped, because without it, the word does not function.
For this very reason, Uddyotakara stated in his *Vṛtti* that there is a persistence of the cognition of the word:

"In the case of 'cow' and so forth, the persistent cognition arises from a cause distinct from the individual body (*piṇḍa*) and so on, because particular cognitions are not accidental, just like the cognitions of blue and so forth."
Having established the proof for the existence of the universal by stating that "the cause [of the cognition] is that universal," he himself raised the following objection:
"Now, you might think: just as words such as 'cook' (pācaka) are applied recurrently, yet there is no such universal as 'cook-ness' (pācakatva)—if it did exist..."
It would follow that [the universal] is manifested at the very time the entity arises; likewise, there would be no recurring cognition (anuvṛttipratyaya) regarding cows and so forth.
This is because you have failed to understand the meaning of the reason [adduced].
Because the cause "since specific cognitions are not without a cause" means that a cognition distinct from the cognition of the individual object arises from another cause,
and not that every inclusive cognition arises solely from a universal;
and this being so, that which is the primary instrument of the act of cooking is designated by the word "cook."

And since that predominance (*prādhānya*) exists even in other cooks, there is no fault; thus, by saying this, Uddyotakara has indicated that he accepts the application of words such as "cook" even without a universal (*sāmānya*) such as "cook-ness. With this intention, the Ācārya also said, "How so? and so forth. Furthermore, it is not logical for the application of words like "cook" to be based on the predominance of the act of cooking;
for if that were the cause, there would be a recurring term "the predominant one, the predominant one," and not the word "cook."
For this very reason, he said "not indeed," and so forth;
"in them" refers to the cooks and others.
"Other" means distinct from the substance;

thus, there must be a single [entity] undifferentiated among all the powers, by which those [agents] such as cooks, though being different, would be perceived as non-different—that is, cognized—by that knowledge, and likewise designated.
This is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa).

If it is argued that there exists a specific action— characterized by placing [the vessel] on the fire for cooks, or consisting of recitation for students, and so forth for others as appropriate— that serves as the basis for a single common notion and the like;

The mention of "cognition" (*pratyaya*) in the phrase "that [is]... is merely an illustration; likewise, the word "also" (*api*) implies "or by another," namely by the cause of the action, such as effort (*prayatna*), and so forth.
With the words "broken" and so forth, he supports this very point;
there, the word "that" (tad) should be connected either with the presentation of the external object or with "its action" (tatkarma).
Because there is a distinction in the ripening of karma,
it is true that those individuals are "thus" [similar] by virtue of a certain transgression, serving as the cause for a non-differentiated cognition.
There is no fault whatsoever; however, because those individuals possess a single form—
just as a substance has a single form due to its partlessness—

if this very [single form] is the basis for the cognition of non-difference, and not some other distinct property (*dharmāntara*) separate from it, then there would be no cognition of distinction such as "the cook's cook-ness" (*pācakatva*).
For it is not logical that there should be a distinction from itself;

"that form" (*tadākāra*) refers to the unmanifested form of that [substance]. A "different form" (*anyākāra*) is a form distinct from that, namely a form of non-difference. That which possesses such a specific quality is "possessing a specific quality other than that form" (*atadākāraviśeṣavatī*);
the meaning is that its form is other than the form of the substance.
This is what is meant:

the cognition "substance" has the form "substance" arising solely from substances; however, the cognition of a "cook" or the cognition of a "negation" [e.g., "non-existence"] arises through a different form altogether. If these were caused by the substance alone, they would be indistinguishable from the mere cognition of the substance itself.

Now, for what purpose are both [terms] stated—namely, "possessing this specific form" (*atad-ākāra-viśeṣavatī*)? It should have been said simply as "having that form" (*atad-ākāra*) or simply as "possessing [that] specific form" (*viśeṣavatī*).

If it were stated as "having a non-different form" (*abhedākāra*), one might designate even the cognition of negation as "having that form" (*atad-ākāra*), on the grounds that there is an absence of substance; yet the opponent does not accept that such [cognition] is based upon another real entity.
Since specific cognitions are necessarily based on other distinct properties (dharmāntara),
when the apprehension of a specific quality alone is produced,
the cognition of Caitra becomes qualified in relation to Maitra.
But it is not devoid of that form, because by the designation "Caitra" and so forth, it is precisely a substance that is being communicated.
However, due to the inclusion of both [aspects], this meaning follows: this cognition has a non-substantial form, yet it possesses particularity because it touches upon a real entity.
Therefore, the Master has stated that in those cases there can be no other cause for the distinction apart from the substance itself;

the connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "just as there is a distinction such as 'the cow-ness of a cow' or 'the cook-ness of a cook,' and just as the specific cognitions have been mentioned immediately above, so it has been explained."
To the question "How was this stated?", he says:
"According to their respective [objects]," and so forth;
the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntaraviveka*) is the delimitation of other objects (*arthāntaravyavaccheda*).
"According to their respective [conventions]" means that for whichever word there is a specific exclusion according to its conventional usage, it is from that [exclusion]—this is the meaning.
For instance, the word "cook" (*pācaka*), while expressing the exclusion of non-cooks, does not exclude other distinct differences and thus denotes the substratum (*dharmin*);
however, the word "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*) expresses that very same excluded entity while excluding other distinct differences, and thus denotes the property (*dharma*).

Therefore, by means of the conceptualization of a distinction between property and property-bearer, the ablative case of separation (*vyatireka-vibhakti*) is indeed employed in the expression "the cook-ness of the cook.

Similarly, since the word "substance" (*dravya*) is conventionally established (*saṃketita*) with respect to a nature that excludes non-substances, a cognition arises following that [convention] which conforms to the exclusion of non-substances. From the word "cook," however, a cognition arises that conforms precisely to the exclusion of non-cooks; thus, according to the exclusion [intended], a cognition characterized by a specific feature is not contradictory even in a single locus, provided it follows the convention.
And this has been established in the discussion beginning with "the rejection or non-rejection of other distinctions," etc.;
the conclusion is drawn with the words "therefore," and so forth.

The connection is as follows: just as there is a distinction among individual entities (*vyakti*), so too because of the distinction among actions (*karman*), action is not the cause of this cognition of non-difference, such as "cook" (*pācaka*).

Regarding those actions of the cooks which are designated as "cooking," the universal of cook-ness (*pācakatva-jāti*) that inheres in those actions is not the cause of the cognition of non-difference among cooks; this is what is being denied by the words "not... because of non-difference" and so forth, as the point under discussion is that the universal is not the cause.
What is the reason? Because it relies upon karma;
that is, because it is inherent in karma.
Action is an entity distinct from substance; as it is related to that [substance],
it is a distinct entity— this is illustrated by the example of "cowness" in relation to a cow (the substance).

For the universal of cowness (*gotva*), which is related to [individual cows] such as Śābaleya, is not the cause of the cognition of "cow" in respect to various horses such as Karka; nor is the genus of action inherent in the actions called "cooking" within the acts of a cook.
Nor are those actions,
which are designated as "maturation," distinguished by the cognition of a "cook," for the mention of "sound" is merely an illustration.
The substance that is the substratum of that action called "cooking" is denoted by the word "cook" (pācaka),
yet the universal of action (karmajāti) does not inhere in that substance.

Thus far, it has been explained how the word "cook" and its corresponding cognition, which have the substance as their object, function as causes of cognition by relying on the connection of the universal of action with another entity [the substance].
159–60 Now he speaks by way of another method, beginning with "tasya" and so forth.

A "different scriptural statement" (*śrutyantara*) refers to a scriptural statement other than the one concerning the cook; the mention of "scriptural statement" (*śruti*) is merely illustrative, as it indicates that [the knowledge] arises from another means of cognition; thus, he speaks of "another scriptural statement" itself.

Regarding the passage beginning with "pāka" and so forth, the word "tataḥ" (from that) refers to the class of action (*karmajāti*), because it is the cause of both the designation and the suffix whose object is the action; such is the intended meaning of the phrase "from the class of action" (*karmajāteḥ*).
This may be the opinion [of the author].

The genus of action (*karmajāti*) does not produce the cognition of a "cook" (*pācaka*); rather, it is the action itself [that produces it] by virtue of its dependence upon that genus of action. Therefore, he says "of that," and so forth;
"of that" refers to the non-differentiating cognition of "cook" and the like.
The analysis of the compound is "that of which action is the cause" (*karmanimitta*).

It has been stated that [the word] is not a cause [of the cognition of identity] due to its difference from the individual (*vyakti*), as in the case of "action belongs to this" (*asya karma*) and so forth.
Now, it was argued that even though action is distinct [from the universal], it is the cause of a non-different cognition by virtue of its dependence upon the universal (*jāti*).
This which was stated is incorrect;
for even in the case of a connection with a genus, the action remains equally distinct.
Furthermore, he states the reason for this accumulation by means of the words beginning with "kiñca" (moreover).
If it is admitted that this cognition of non-difference, such as "cook" and so forth, is caused by action,
then once the action has ceased, the person would not be called a "cook";
yet he is so called on the basis of mere capacity alone.

If it is argued that this designation is not caused by an action that has become a real entity, and thus there is no fault because even past karma exists, [the author] replies with "he indeed cooks" and so forth:
if past karma were existent, it would be perceived just like the present; and yet, karma is held to have attained the conditions for perception.
It might be thought:

"The universal of action (karmajāti) inheres in the action, and the action also inheres in the substance; therefore, by virtue of a connection through a connected thing (sambaddhasambandha), the universal of action is the cause of the cognition 'cook' which has the substance as its object. To this, he says:
"Precisely for that reason," and so forth.

"From that very [fact]" means precisely because the action has perished, the universal has no direct connection with the action, nor is there an indirect connection through the medium of the action; for this reason—namely, its lack of connection—the universal is not the cause of the designation and cognition of "cook" and so forth.
If it is argued that even something unconnected can be a cause, he says:
"No," and so forth;
"inappropriate" means incoherent.
The mention of "sound" (*śabda*) is an illustration; the meaning is that the universal (*sāmānya*), being incoherent [with its substratum], is not the cause of cognition or sound.
Why?
Because it would lead to an over-extension;
even "cowness" would then be a cause for the cognition of a horse.
He explains [the verse] with the words "When it has perished," etc.: that universal is the universal of action, but it does not inhere in the action, because that [action] is non-existent.

Precisely because action is absent, it does not inhere even indirectly in the agent, the cook; therefore, this universal has no connection with the substance, whether through direct relation or through a connected connection.
Otherwise, if it were the cause of cognition and so forth, it would follow that even what is unconnected could be such a cause.

Regarding what was stated, beginning with "And because of the non-existence of the abiding of action," he anticipates another position with the words "that which is past," meaning that which has perished.
Whatever future action there will be for those two— namely, sound and cognition—
that action, being past or future, is non-existent.
The connection is that [the object] is the cause of both cognition and its designation;
as for the question "What is the reason for those two? and so forth—
He explains those two— knowledge and its designation— with the words "asati" and so forth:
that by which a thing is "upākhyāyate," meaning it is manifested or made known, is "upākhyā," namely, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*).

The meaning is this: since it has departed from being non-existent, it is so described; and since that which is non-existent is devoid of the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), how could such a thing serve as the basis (*nimitta*) for words and cognitions?
Now, if it is claimed that even a non-existent thing can function as a cause, then it would necessarily be a real entity (vastu) and not non-existent;
for what reason? To this he says: "the effect," and so forth.
The word *lakṣaṇa* signifies intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
"that" means therefore [the past],
which has its form already passed away.

The proponent of the universal (sāmānyavādin) does not accept that a future entity— which has not yet attained its form, is distinct from the action itself, and is something other than the individual instance (vyakti) and so forth— serves as the basis for cognition and verbal designation;
for he holds that the individual instance is the substance which is the substratum of the action.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) and its maturation (*tatparipāka*) is intended; thus, since those two— namely, the linguistic cognition and that [convention/maturation] which are concomitant— are not the causes for cognitions of words such as "cook" (*pācaka*), the existence of a universal (*jāti*) is not established.
Because of the word "and" (ca), there would be either the eternal existence or the eternal non-existence of both the word and the cognition;
why, then, is the [existence of] a universal (jāti) not established? To this he says:
"Of that," and so forth.
Since that universal (jāti) is intended as the cause for both cognition and verbal designation of what is undifferentiated,

and since those two operate without a [real] cause in the case of objects such as "cook" and the like, just so would they operate in the case of "cow" and the like; on what basis, then, could a universal be postulated?
With the words "power" (*śakti*) and so forth, he anticipates another position:
that the power of the substance which is the locus of the action is what apprehends the word; this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).
He refutes [the opponent's view] with the words "even the capacity of the cognition of a 'cook' and so forth is not the cause," and so on:
"The capacity of a cook and so forth is not the cause for the word 'cook' and so forth."
What is the reason?

Because power is not distinct from the substance, it does not persist [throughout the series] in the same way that the substance does; and because it is not admitted that a non-persistent entity can serve as the cause for a persistent cognition or verbal designation.
Alternatively, if such a cause were admitted, it would follow that the postulation of a universal (*jāti*) would be rendered groundless.
If it is argued that power (*śakti*) is indeed distinct [from the substance], he says "not so" (*na hi*), and so forth.

For if power were not other than the substance, then because that single power would be employed for causal functions such as cooking and the like, it would follow as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the substance— the substratum of the power— would be useless.

The sense is that even if the substance is utilized for that capacity which effects the cooking and so forth, the substance would nonetheless be utilized for the cooking and so forth through a mediated succession (pāramparyeṇa). Why is this so? [Thus asks] the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī).
There is no purpose served by a potency that is a distinct entity; for instance, if one were to admit that the substance is employed by a first potency which brings about cooking and so forth,

and if that [first] potency itself were admitted to be distinct [from the substance], then, in order for the substance to be employed in that potency which brings about cooking, one would have to admit another potency distinct from the substance, leading to an infinite regress (atiprasaṅga).

The meaning is that even for that power (*śakti*) which is to be employed, another distinct power would have to be postulated, and for that one as well yet another, resulting in an infinite regress. Therefore, it must be stated that without a separate power, the substance itself is what is employed in the first power that brings about cooking and so forth.
And thus, when the employment of the substance in the power is intended—
Since that substance is employed only for causal efficiency (arthakriyā) characterized by cooking and so forth, why is it not accepted as such?
What is the use of postulating an "efficacy" (śakti) between the substance and its causal efficiency, which is itself purposeless?
Therefore, by the expression "the efficacy for causal efficiency such as cooking," it is the substance itself that is being denoted.
What kind of effect is that? It is the effect such as cooking and so forth;

and since that substance does not persist through other individual instances (vyakti), the word "cook, cook" and the corresponding cognition would not be recurring (anvayin) with respect to that substance.
The mention of "the apprehension of sound" is, however, an illustration.

If it is argued that in substances such as a cook (pācaka) there exists a universal such as "cook-ness" (pācakatva), and that this [universal], being the invariable concomitant, is the basis for the word and cognition [applied to them], he says:
Regarding the phrase "the universal," and so forth:
