if a universal such as "cook-ness" (pācakatva) is accepted, then it would exist as inherent in the substance at the very moment of the substance's production—that is, even prior to the state of possessing the capacity to perform the act of cooking and so on. This is the meaning.
And thus, even a child born on that very day would become an object of the cognition and designation "cook" and so forth; this is the intended meaning.
Otherwise, if [the status of being a cook] were to exist prior [to the action], it would not exist later either, because there is no difference in that substance.

The capacity for cooking and so forth certainly exists at all times within the substance, but because it was previously unmanifested, it does not serve as the cause for words and cognitions; therefore, he says:
"manifested."
The meaning is that it would have been manifested even earlier,
just like existence and so forth;
for example, like existence (*sattā*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and the rest.

He explains with the words "athāpi" and so forth that [the capacity] exists as long as the substance endures, and that the substance must already be situated in a suitable location for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) to occur.
Since the inherence of that [universal]— namely, the inherence of the universal— in its real object which is the locus of the genus is non-occasional, meaning it exists at all times,
he says "for as many as... and so forth, in order to confirm this very point.
Those universals which, based on the genus of an object, possess the property of inherence and are capable of connection—
[they characterize] the arising of this object.
The connection is made by changing the case-ending [of the word *samavayanti*] to mean "they co-inhere in this, which is the substratum of the universal";
that is to say, it is connected with the substance at the very same time as its own production.
Thus is the consensus;
that is our established doctrine,
as Uddyotakara has said.
Prior to the connection with "cowness," this entity is neither a cow nor a non-cow;
what is the reason?

Because those two qualifying cognitions cannot exist in the absence [of a substrate], and qualifying cognitions do not arise without a relation to a qualified object, nor does an entity exist prior to its connection with cowness.
Furthermore, that which does not exist cannot be designated as either "cow" or "non-cow";
rather, at the very moment an object arises, it is simultaneously connected with the nature of "cowness.
Thus, there is no connection with existence for that which already exists, nor for that which does not exist.
And at the very moment that an entity exists, it is connected with existence; thus says the *Nyāyavārttika*.
Now, if one were to overstep this established doctrine (*siddhānta*) and imagine that the universal comes into being later.
In that case, if there were a deviation from that— namely, a deviation from the established doctrine (siddhānta)—
then because there would be no distinction even subsequently in that substance which is the substratum of that universal, there could be no inherence (*samavāya*) with that universal; that is,
there could be no inherence by means of that universal.
Just as redness, though having the single nature of being a fruit, does not exist previously but exists later,
so too is the case with the generality of "cook-ness" and so forth in a person; therefore, he says:

"Connected with that," and so forth; "due to the deficiency in the nature of what is connected with that" means due to the deficiency in the nature of that which is connected with the universal such as "cook-ness."
The word "that" refers to the universal inherence;
"of him" refers to the person.
For indeed, if one remains in an unimpaired essential nature, there could be no connection with that [inherence].

Furthermore, it is difficult to follow and hard to understand that a substance which exists at that very moment with a nature devoid of generality (*sāmānya*) and inherence (*samavāya*) should later possess generality and inherence;
for even in the case of a fruit such as a mango, if it possesses a single, identical nature both before and after [the ripening], the same objection applies.

At that time, the substance is already connected with the universal; however, it is the universal—requiring the assistance of an action—that manifests it. Since that [assistance] did not exist previously, there is no manifestation of the universal beforehand; therefore, he says:

Regarding the phrase "by action and assistance," etc.: when it is accepted that [the individual] is a manifestor of the universal with respect to the assistance produced by an action— such as cooking— characterized by that [action].
Because that substance is non-momentary and unchanging, it has no dependence upon auxiliary causes;
however, if it were to undergo modification, then the substance would necessarily become momentary due to that excellence (*atiśaya*),
and since it would perish immediately after arising due to its momentariness, how could there be any action?

He explains [the passage] beginning with "by means of assistance to the action" (*karmopakāretyādi*), stating that it is by means of this [assistance] that the action would be the manifester (*vyañjaka*) of the universal (*jāti*), which depends upon that assistance;
the operation (*vyāpāra*) characterized by placing [the pot] on the stove and so forth is the action (*karman*).

Regarding the excellence of assistance produced by that [action], what dependence could there be on it for one whose nature is stable— since, not deviating from its prior nature and not assuming another nature due to the absence of any excellence, there is no production of distinction in an action that imparts no difference?

Furthermore, if an excellence produced by an action is admitted in a substance, then because that action which imparts the excellence is momentary, another excellence must arise in that very substance which is the recipient of the benefit, as its own inherent nature;

for if the excellence produced by the action were not part of the substance's inherent nature, then the substance would not be benefited at all, since something else (an external entity) would have been produced.

Therefore, since a new excellence arises at every moment as an inherent property corresponding to each momentary action, that substance— such as Devadatta and so forth— must also be momentary. Consequently, because of this momentariness,
the action characterized by cooking is performed by a person who perishes in the very place of its own arising, that is, who perishes in the very location where he was produced.
That which is dependent [on action] would manifest the generality of a substance such as "cook" only by being dependent on that action.

Now, if it is asked: "Is it not the case that the momentariness of a substance is established through the first and subsequent moments of action, and how could there be momentariness in the absence of action?"—the answer is: no.
The meaning is that because there is no other action capable of manifesting a universal among those moments produced in connection with an action,
it is therefore established that a genus existing as a real entity does not exist.
"How then? and so forth asks the opponent.
"Just as... and so forth begins the response from the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin):
Just as there is no universal such as "cook-ness" in the case of cooks and the like—this having been established—nevertheless, the inclusive (anvayin) cognition and word apply to them.
Likewise, in another instance as well, the opponent [objects] that without a commonality (sāmānya) there would be no recurrence;
[he says] "tadvat" and so forth, meaning:
how can there be the application of recurring cognition and words among those [individuals], such as cooks and the like, in the absence of a commonality?

Since the term "subsequent cognition" (*tato'nvaya-jñāna*) is applied [to them], it was considered that even in the case of "cooks" (*pācaka*) and the like, there exists a universal such as "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*). Immediately following that, however, it was reflected upon that such a universal as "cook-ness" is not possible in those cases;
for if there is no recurring form (*anvayi-rūpa*), then would those verbal cognitions now be without a cause?

"No," and so forth— the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) states that there certainly exists a cause for those two which is postulated by the opponent; he now sets forth the refutation of that very [cause].
"But what then," and so forth:
a real, external entity as a universal (*sāmānya*) is not the cause for those two; rather, what is their cause? To this he says:

"According to their respective [nature]" and so forth: from whichever awakening of one's own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) occurs, from that there arises a corresponding conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); and from that arising of conceptual construction, words arise in accordance with the conceptual construction.

Furthermore, it has already been largely established that the existence of a real entity is not the basis for conceptual construction and verbal designation, nor is it the basis for the existence of a recurring (anvayi) category;
and this must necessarily be accepted.

For instance, due to the force of their respective latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) for synthesis, by relying on their own philosophical tenets and in accordance with their cognitive predispositions, they superimpose mutually contradictory forms through the imposition of opposing natures—such as "the world is the effect of *pradhāna*," "the effect of *Īśvara*," "uncaused," or "mere conventionality. Thus, despite the appearance of various distinct objects, there is a continuity of both cognition and its designation across these diverse views. Furthermore, even when viewing mutually distinct objects, there is no [contradiction] regarding those things that are conceptually constructed with mutually contradictory forms, such as being the effects of *pradhāna* and so forth.
He asks why that basis— the basis for word and cognition— does not exist,
and replies with the words "of two mutually contradictory [things]," and so forth.
"Without restriction," and so forth—
the opponent [argues that] all cognition and verbal expression would be concomitant with everything everywhere; demonstrating this very point, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "na hyanimittam" (for it is not without a cause),

one considers that the objection is indeed without foundation, since their lack of a cause has already been refuted by the argument beginning with "nanu yathāsvaṃ vāsanāprabodhād vikalpotpatter" (but surely, conceptual constructions arise from the awakening of their respective latent predispositions).

An internal cause alone is accepted for those two; and since that cause lacks any proximity or distance [from anything], it would follow that it is the cause of all conceptual constructions everywhere.
For in the phrase "it occurs without a cause," it should be understood as being "causeless" due to the absence of an external cause.
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) states "not in the case of a non-sign" (nānimitta),
meaning that [the two] do not exist when the sign is not distinguished.
For this very reason, he says:
"because it has specific latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as its cause.
A latent impression that has arrived by way of seeing things as they truly are (*yathābhūtadarśana*) produces a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that determines the existence of that very object.
"Not everywhere" is the collective meaning [of the statement].
"Of such a nature" refers to the form that possesses positive concomitance (*anvayi-rūpa*).
And even in the absence of that external, concomitant cause, it must indeed occur through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); it cannot fail to occur.
He establishes that very point with the words "asleep" and so forth:
in the case of objects perceived by a sleeping person and a person with cataracts— namely cows and the like, and hairs, flies and the like respectively—
and in the case of non-existent things such as a rabbit's horn.

The latent predisposition for inherence (*samavāyavāsanā*) is that by which, through the power of the latent predisposition for linguistic convention (*saṃketavāsanā*), there arises a conceptualization (*vikalpa*)— specifically, an inclusive conceptualization— that superimposes particular forms onto entities such as the "Primal Cause" (*pradhāna*) or "Effects" (*kārya*) according to one's own philosophical tenets.

For there is no external, recurring form (*anvayi-rūpa*) in these aforementioned [objects], because they are just like those perceived in dreams or by those with ophthalmia; and their non-existence was established in the third chapter.

It will be established that for those things superimposed by tenets which are mutually contradictory, non-existence has already been demonstrated by the passage beginning with "simultaneously in one place," and so forth.

Furthermore, those conceptual constructions arise even in the case of things perceived in dreams and the like that lack any real, underlying common nature; nevertheless, objects do not appear in all forms everywhere, but rather only in their specific, determined ways.
And he states the reason for the restriction with the words "by means of distinction alone," etc.; "of those perceived in that very way" means of those perceived through distinction.
Because conceptualization occurs precisely through differentiation,
there is first of all the perception of objects as differentiated when they are mounted upon erroneous cognition during the state of sleep or cataracts;
this is likewise true for those things superimposed by philosophical tenets at the time of hearing their respective tenets.
Even in cases such as "the horn of a hare" and so forth,

at the time of learning the linguistic usage of "the horn of a hare" or "the son of a barren woman," [the cognition arises] because the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of linguistic usage are beginningless;
and it has been stated in this regard, etc.
In the passage "the means of establishing a single object, such as the cognition of an object through a single reflective awareness" (1.75),
[it refers to] the means of establishing a single object, such as the cognition of an object through a single reflective awareness.
Moreover, just as *dhava*, *khadira*, and other such trees are mutually distinct, so too are cows and others.

Since the distinction is equal in both cases, when asked why "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*) resides only in *dhava* and the like and not in cows and the like, the opponent must say this: it is simply the inherent power (*bhāvaśakti*) of the *dhava* and others by which they alone are proximate to treeness, while cows and others are not. In that case, since the objects to be differentiated are equal, by what proximity—characterized as an inherent power—does the universal (*jāti*) reside in some portion of objects intended as its own substratum?
Let that very power of being (*bhāva-śakti*), which pervades and exists as it spreads forth, be the basis for the application of inclusive words and cognitions.
What is the use of postulating such a universal,
when it is asserted that the arising of cognitions does not occur without an object?

They maintain that the universal is distinct from the particular; therefore, it is certain that those [cognitions] would be false if they were produced without it, for they cannot arise without an object.
However, in this case, it does not follow that the existence of the universal is untenable without the other [the particular].
That is rejected;

for the opponent is compelled to admit that just as the occurrence of a universal among certain things is not desired without a universal, so too the cognition of a universal should be admitted to exist without a universal.
For the opponent might argue that those [particulars] would be false if they were produced by that [universal], since it is precisely through that [universal] that they arise.

However, our intended meaning here is this: just as for the opponent there is a certain proximity (*pratyāsatti*) among certain objects—without a universal—by which the universal’s occurrence [is explained], let that very [proximity] be the cause for the erroneous cognition of concomitance and for the word; what is the use of a universal? Thus, there is no fault.
Therefore, this remains established.

"Because it is precisely through the determination of unity regarding exclusion that there is a continuity among entities, and not through anything else"— regarding this [verse 164–65], the Sāṃkhya says:
"Non-cessation," and so forth;
"concomitance with existence" refers to the uniformity of entities,
while "the other" refers to that which is a real entity.
That which is the effect of one seed would not belong to another, such as the earth and so forth;
why?
Because of the absolute difference between those two, the seed and the earth.
He explains [the passage] beginning with "If these... with the words "of these," meaning of entities; just as from a single seed, there is one effect called a sprout.
He establishes that very point with the words "For he who... and so forth: for that which is the seed's own nature of producing a sprout does not belong to anything else, such as the earth;
and that which is superimposed by the intellect and characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is not a producer.
Why? Because exclusion (*vyatireka*), which is characterized by the differentiation from others, lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).
Therefore, only the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the seed is the producer; and that which is the form of the producer is itself the real entity (*vastu*).
And that which produces it— the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that produces the sprout—
is "other"; thus, another [element] such as earth and so forth would produce the sprout within earth and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "sa hi" and so forth:
the word *hi* has the sense of the particle *eva* (only/indeed);
"of that" refers to the seed.
If that earth and so forth were other than the seed, then by virtue of producing the sprout through its nature as a seed, it would be non-different from that seed;
thus, there is a continuity of an existing intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānvaya*).

Therefore, the Siddhāntavādī states with the verse beginning "If... (Śloka, Ākṛti 37, 38) that it is incorrect to say: "Some things, despite having different intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), produce a single effect by their very nature (*prakṛti*), like the sense organs and so forth."
"Even in one [cause] there is the self": that self by which the collection of causes is held to possess the capacity to produce is present even in a single cause among those causes.
[Objection: "In that case, since the effect would be produced by that one [final cause] alone, the auxiliary causes would be rendered useless.
[Response: But is it not the case that even for the proponent of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), there is the uselessness of other causes because all [causes] are productive in the final state? [Reply:
This is not so.
Only when those [factors] are assembled do they possess such capacity, because being momentary, their presence depends upon causes and conditions;
however, for the other proponent of eternalism, since that nature exists at all times, there would be the futility of other causal factors.
Therefore it has been said, "He exists even in one [instance]," meaning that he exists even in a state where other causes are deficient;

this is explained by the words beginning with "if. If a manifold entity, because of its single nature, were the producer—the generator—of a single effect, then that non-different productive nature of those things regarded as causes would exist even when only a single cause is present.
And therefore, since the cause is never deficient in any state whatsoever, even a single [cause] situated anywhere would be a producer.
Strengthening this very point, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "yasmāt" and so forth:

even when a single [cause] such as a seed is present, the non-different generality consisting of the production of its effect does not depart; rather, it is the particulars—the distinct individual instances—which are subject to departure.

For there is no distinction in that seed—which possesses the nature of producing an effect when differentiated—between itself and other factors such as earth; why? Because if there were a distinction, its non-difference [from them] would be lost.
For that very nature which is considered the producer is undifferentiated; since it exists even in the seed alone,
there is no loss or destruction of that undifferentiated form— which is considered the producer— even when one [particular thing] persists,
because the three qualities (triguṇya) exist everywhere, at all times, and in their entirety.
Since those specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) that are distinct states lack a rule of coexistence, their departure might occur;
this has been stated while granting the premise [of such a rule],
for otherwise, how could there be a departure even of specific qualities that are distinct from other states of a permanent entity?
And why are these specific [conditions] not accepted as the producers? To this he says, "of the auxiliary causes," and so forth;
therefore, even when a single factor such as a seed is present, the producer remains in its own state.
Since they are non-abiding, even if there were a single persistence— meaning that even if any one of the factors such as the seed were to persist— the production of the effect would occur;
yet the production of the effect does not occur.

Therefore, even though the general condition remains present, because the effect is absent when any one of the auxiliary factors is missing, the production of that effect arises from those specific features.
Is that effect, such as a sprout and so forth, not produced from a commonality?
What has come to be?
"Of many," and so forth; the meaning is that which is common to multiple auxiliary causes, i.e., produced by multiple auxiliary causes.
"Even when there is the removal of a single particular [cause]" means even when there is the removal of any one of the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*);
by this he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*),
and by the words "again," etc., he states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Therefore, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of the effect pertains only to specific instances (viśeṣa), and not to the universal (sāmānya); thus he says: "But surely, when [the cause] is unimpaired... and so forth.
Even when there is no deficiency and the form is undifferentiated, the effect does not arise while [the cause] remains in that same specific state;
he analyzes this very point with the words "for the effect... and so forth.
Arising from something is a particular property (dharma).
That which possesses [a certain nature] has that as its inherent property (*tadbhāvadharmi*);

if it occurs at some time in a certain place, it is due to the deficiency of its producer. Furthermore, there is no deficiency in the presence of even one among the auxiliary causes for that non-different form which is considered to be the producer.
When that universal form is complete, the effect arises; this indicates that the universal lacks the nature of being a producer [of that specific effect].

(167–68) Now, one might object: "It is not the universal itself that is held to be the producer—by which this fault would arise—but rather it was stated that it is the producer by virtue of its manifold nature. To this, he replies:
Regarding the passage beginning with "yatsākalya," etc.:

since the presence or absence of an effect depends upon the completeness or incompleteness of certain specific factors (viśeṣas), it is from those very specific factors that the production of the effect arises.
When that specific factor exists— which is fit to serve as a cause— your effect arises from it; otherwise,
if it were to arise from something other than that specific factor, namely from a general factor, there would be the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) that everything would be the cause of everything.
Since this is so, therefore only the particulars (viśeṣas) are producers,
not the universal (sāmānya), because the latter is not a producer; thus, those very particulars alone are the real entity (vastu).
The meaning is "ultimately existent.
For what reason?
Because an entity that is ultimate is, by definition, ultimately existent.
"That alone is capable of causal efficiency" (sa evārthakriyākṣamaḥ);
he explains this with the words "for this very [reason]," etc.,
[stating that] "the capacity for causal efficiency is the defining characteristic of a real entity."
The connection is as follows: "Incapacity, however, is the definition of a non-entity; we shall explain it [later].
That which is capable of causal efficiency is here what exists in the ultimate sense (paramārthasat).
By such statements as "3," it is shown that an object characterized by its specific nature (*viśeṣātmaka*), which is capable of performing all causal functions, does not persist [as a commonality],
because a specific feature (*viśeṣa*) does not follow after other individual instances (*vyakti*).
Since that which possesses a universal nature does not follow [from a cause], an effect possessing a universal nature cannot arise from it;
this concludes the argument with the words "therefore," and so forth.
"Because of the fitness for non-purposeful action" means because of the unfitness for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
"Precisely from that" means precisely from the particular (*viśeṣa*), since it is from that that the accomplishment of that [action]—namely, the accomplishment of purposeful action—occurs.
Thus, the incapacity of that which is imagined by others to produce [an effect] has been established.

168–69. Now, in order to refute what has been stated by the opponent— that "the effect of one [cause] would not belong to another because of their absolute difference"— he restates that very objection with the words beginning, "In that case, due to the non-continuity of intrinsic nature" (svabhāvānanvayāt).

Although this has already been resolved previously by such statements as, "In the pacification of fever and so forth, [the cause may act] either together or individually" (1.76), it is presented again here for the purpose of providing further elaboration.

Since the form that is the producer of a single thing, such as a seed, does not exist in another thing, such as the earth, the latter would be a non-producer auxiliary. Furthermore, if it were admitted that something possessing a nature distinct from the nature of the producer could nonetheless be a producer, then—given that the distinction [from the producer] would be no different—one might as well claim that everything, including barley seeds and the like, would be a producer of a rice sprout.
He refutes this with the words beginning "this is not so."

Although the earth and other factors, as well as barley seeds and the like, are absolutely distinct from that nature which belongs to a single rice seed as its producer, some— such as the earth and so forth— are the cause of the rice sprout, while others— such as barley seeds and the like— are not;
the word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of completing the verse,
or it carries the sense of "eva" (only/exclusive).
What is the reason?

This is the nature of things: that from whatever self-nature one [entity] is a producer, all [other entities] that differ from that self-nature must likewise be producers, because there is no distinction in their difference; or else, none at all would be a producer.

This objection might hold if a distinction characterized by a restriction regarding the production of those effects and non-those effects were impossible for these [causes] which are distinct from a single producing self; however, such a distinction is indeed possible.

Regarding the word "therefore": because a distinction is possible, even though there is no difference in their being distinct entities, due to some specific excellence of nature characterized by the determination of a particular effect, a certain thing such as earth is the producer of a rice-sprout and not another, such as a barley-seed.
Why is this? Because that excellence of nature belonging to the auxiliary cause, such as the earth, which produces the rice-sprout, does not belong to the other, such as the barley-seed.
If it is asked what causes this very distinction, he says "for not," and so forth:
fire burns and is hot, whereas water does not burn and is not hot; this does not admit of questioning, because it is established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception.
Only this much would be appropriate to ask:
"For what reason does this have the aforementioned nature?
For there must necessarily be a cause for a difference in intrinsic nature.

Since, if it were causeless and independent, there would be the over-extension [of the fault] of lacking restriction by place and so forth— resulting in the consequence that it would exist everywhere, at all times, and in its entirety—
it is therefore said that its intrinsic nature arises from its own cause, which is regarded as the cause.

For that [effect] as well, its nature of producing that [result] from its own cause consists in its nature of producing from a causal essence that is of such a kind; and that [nature] arises from another of its own causes. Thus, the succession of causes is beginningless.
For there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the differentiation of causes for distinct entities.
He states this very point:
Regarding the passage beginning with "bhinnā" (divided) and ending with "svabhāvāt" (from its own nature), [the author] states that this is because such is the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*),
and that there exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against their being one.

Regarding the passage beginning with "But if there were no difference," etc., the meaning is that because they are mutually non-different, upon the destruction of one, there would be the simultaneous destruction of all; and upon the arising of one, there would be the arising of all.
He explains this by means of the words "Because of non-difference," and so forth.

Since the entire mass of all things is non-different by its very nature, there would be no production of division and so forth; thus, through such a division, there would be no production of one thing and non-production of another, nor the persistence of one and the cessation of another.
"Like one's own self" means that just as for a single particular state there is no arising and so forth through differentiation, so it is here;
by the word "and so forth," [the text] includes such things as the apprehension of one thing and the non-apprehension of another.
In the Sūtra, however, the mention of destruction and arising is for the purpose of illustration;
for it is through that very illustration—namely, differentiation, arising, and so forth—that non-difference is ascertained.
Otherwise, by what means would difference and non-difference be characterized?

"Even of that which has a single form" means even of that which has a similar form; "separation" (*vyatireka*) is division, the state of having distinct origination and so forth, which is the definition of difference (*bheda*);
"non-separation" (*avyatireka*) is non-division, the absence of the state of having distinct origination and so forth.
Regarding the definition of non-difference [between them],
he says "of two opposites," etc., to explain why there is difference despite the presence of qualities such as the arising of division.

Because there is a contradiction between mutually exclusive properties, such as arising and non-arising, within a single essence simultaneously, objects are not merely non-different; rather, they also possess difference.
As it has been said:
For every entity is differentiated by way of its objective form,
and it is in relation to their own intrinsic natures that they are mutually distinct;
for that reason:
If it is argued that this is not so because there would be no consequence of simultaneous arising and so forth,
he says "no," etc., which is the explanation of that very point.
We certainly do not assert that there is non-distinction or identity in every respect,
such that there would be simultaneous destruction and arising, and so forth.

However, regarding this distinction between the external and the internal, there exists a certain self characterized by specific states such as a jar and so forth, which is distinct [from the substrate] and not otherwise; for the nature consisting of the three *guṇas*—namely, the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, the nature of being an object, the nature of substance, and the nature of existence—is pervasive everywhere.

Therefore, the meaning is this: although there is non-difference between the state and that which possesses the state, there is indeed mutual difference among the states themselves, due to the aforementioned distinctions characterized by states and so forth.
169–70. If that is the case, then it must be admitted that because the universal is eternal, it persists everywhere, whereas the particulars are subject to destruction.

Furthermore, when one particular (*viśeṣa*) perishes while that which remains is the universal (*sāmānya*), the latter cannot be the locus of the former, because of the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*); thus, there would necessarily be a distinction between the universal and the particular. Otherwise, if it were admitted that both presence and absence reside in a single substrate, then even two contradictory properties would have to be accepted as existing within a single self.
What other property could be a differentiator? None at all.
Nor are two contradictory properties admitted to exist in one [locus], because they are distinct due to the difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

For indeed, particulars (*viśeṣas*) are distinguished in every respect through their separate production and so forth; the universal (*sāmānya*), however, is not distinguished in any respect because it lacks separate production and the like. Therefore, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "sarvākāra" and so forth:
because one accepts, respectively, two objects— differentiation and non-differentiation— in all their aspects,
the claim that "it is merely a name" means that the designation "differentiation and generality are distinct" would be a mere verbal expression and not a reality.
But the real entity (vastu), consisting of both particularity and generality, is intended to be mutually distinct;
this was stated previously in the passage beginning with, "or by accepting a difference in meaning through the use of different names."
Therefore, these entities— whether particulars or universals— are indeed mutually distinct; that is to say,
they do not share a common fate (*ekayogakṣema*), meaning they are characterized by contradictory properties.
For this reason, there would be no cognition of the distinction between the universal and the particular;
the meaning is that there would be no cognition connecting the universal and the particular to one another.
And due to the absence of such a cognition, even linguistic designation is necessarily rejected.
Because that [cognition] is based upon the intellect,
there would always be a mutual dependence between the universal and the particular by means of it.
For the particulars indeed exist within that universal; thus, the [objection] beginning with "ākṛti" (verse 9) has been refuted. Therefore...
Why is this universal, which is a distinct entity from its particulars and independent of them, [not perceived]?
Because that universal is not produced by those particulars,

the second meaning is this: this entity, which consists of particulars, is a different thing from the universal, because it is not dependent upon that universal— that is, because it is not produced by it.
Because that which is eternal lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*),
it cannot be designated as "this is the universal of this particular," nor can the particular be designated as "belonging to this universal."
This same undesirable consequence applies even if the universal is defined as the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*):
namely, that when one [particular] perishes, its essence remains. For instance, when a *dhava* or a *khadira* tree perishes, the exclusion of "non-tree" certainly persists in other trees.
He refutes this with the words "No" and so forth.

The meaning here is as follows: exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is of two kinds. One is the external [exclusion] consisting in the differentiation from what is dissimilar (*vijātīyavyāvṛtti*), which is superimposed (*adhyasta*) by means of its own form (*svākāra*) and is made an object (*viṣaya*) by conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) and by the word (*śabda*).

It is precisely this that is the object of purposeful activity (*pravṛttiviṣayatva*), because it possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*); for mere appearance in cognition lacks causal efficiency.
Furthermore, that which is understood from a word as merely the exclusion of others—
that which is this mere exclusion of others— lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*); therefore, this objection does not apply.
And because that which is intended by the noble one is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it is non-existent; this is the meaning.
Thus he says:
"Because cessation is devoid of intrinsic nature," there is no conceptualization of abiding or non-abiding.
When a particular is destroyed, does the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) remain or does it cease?
This conceptualization of its persistence or non-persistence is logical.

Regarding that— namely, exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)— it might be argued that since it is associated with the intrinsic nature [of the object] yet does not adhere to the real thing (*vastu*), there will then be a conceptualization of the loss of its own established form within that universal (*sāmānya*) superimposed by conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*). To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "and [it is] a distortion" (upaplava) and so forth:
that general form which appears as non-different from multiple objects is a distortion—a delusion—of the cognition of the universal; therefore, it too does not exist externally at all.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: since even by this reason of being a distortion (*viplava*), the cognition of a universal (*sāmānyadhī*) is "not subject to refutation" (*adūṣaṇā*),
meaning that the aforementioned refutation does not apply to it.
This conceptual consciousness, being of a single form, is without an object because it is false knowledge; if one asks how that is so, he says "that which," and so forth.
Because that universal, which is the object of conceptual cognition and the object of that [cognition] appearing as a single form across many [particulars], neither exists nor does not exist;
why is this?
Since the object of that false cognition does not exist,
he speaks in order to remove the charge of parity of fault and to resolve the objection raised by another method.
As for the phrase "that which, moreover," and so forth:
for that which produces it—that is, the producer of that rice sprout—is the very nature (svabhāva) of that rice seed;
and that form of the rice seed which is the producer of the rice sprout...
To the objection— "How can earth and the other elements be producers if they are different from that which is the producer, namely form?"—
it is replied in response to that introduction or to that very challenge.

We do not say that earth and other factors lack the nature of producing a sprout— that is, the nature of being a producer of it— distinct from that of a rice seed; rather, we say that whatever nature is the producer of one rice seed does not belong to another factor such as earth,
because entities do not share a commonality with one another.
"Any other [element] as well," such as earth and so forth; "not by way of another's form," meaning not by way of the form of a rice seed.
What is the reason?
Because it is not that [reality] and does not have that as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and because there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) here; thus he says:

Those [elements], such as earth and so forth, are distinct from one another according to their respective specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), yet they are by their very nature (*svabhāvena*) producers of a single effect. What contradiction is there in this? None whatsoever, because there is an absence of any subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*).

However, it is not contradictory for earth and the other elements—though lacking the form of a rice seed which is considered the producer of a rice sprout—to have a rice sprout as their effect; therefore, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "of a single form," etc.:
that which is deficient in the form belonging to the producer of a single rice seed—such as the earth and other factors—would not possess the nature of a rice seed and so forth;
it would not be something that does not produce that effect, but rather it would indeed produce that very effect.
The analysis of the compound is "that rice-sprout is its effect" (kārya).
If, however, the seed alone were the producer of the sprout, there would be a contradiction; but that is not the case, as he says:
The phrase "by that very [seed]" and so forth means that by the rice seed itself, its effect— namely that which is called the sprout— is produced;
furthermore, with the words "and also," he recalls what was stated previously.
Since there is an absence of the effect when even one [of the particulars] is missing, it was stated previously— on the basis of valid cognition— that the particulars are the producers,
by way of that nature, namely, by way of that generative form.
That form which is the producer of one seed does not exist in another, such as the earth and so forth; nor is it present to that same extent.
Thus, even though the earth and other factors are non-different [from the seed], they are not producers merely by virtue of the deficiency of the rice-seed's own form, and so on.
The meaning is that even within those distinctions there is non-distinction;
he explains this with the words "it might be so" (*syādetat*) and so forth:
"that very undifferentiated form is a single power; [the object is perceived] through connection with that."

The Master [Dharmakīrti] says "by that," and [the commentator] explains with the words "even though they exist" and so forth, that those particulars are non-producers by virtue of that non-distinct form.
In that general form, those particulars are non-productive;
for what reason? Because that general form, being eternal, does not undergo disappearance.
And this was previously stated [in verses] 167–172–173 with the words: "Furthermore, that undifferentiated form does not depart; for indeed, the particulars are subject to departure. etc.

Having established their difference through the imposition of contradictory properties by means of the verse beginning "Destruction and origination would occur simultaneously" (1.170), he says "Furthermore," etc., in order to establish it also through the difference in appearance.
What is the specific characteristic of the difference in appearance?
It is "not shared by others," meaning it is distinct for each individual instance.
By the word "also" (api), the distinction of origination and so forth is also included as a differentiator;
this is merely being added to what was stated previously, as even the proponent of the Vedānta says:
For the apprehension of difference is caused by the apprehension of non-existence, and non-existence is not graspable by perception;
therefore, by perception only pure existence (*sattāmātra*) is grasped, not difference.
As it has been said:
Since that which arises in relation to a cow or a horse is not distinguished from direct perception,
he says "the principle" (*nyāya*), and so forth.
For that proponent of non-difference (abheda-vādin),
the "distinction in the appearance of cognition" refers to a distinction in the form of cognition,
namely the superimposition of contradictory properties, such as their separate arising, destruction, and so forth.
Or, if that difference in appearance and so forth were admitted while the non-difference of entities is maintained, there would be no difference anywhere;
yet difference is perceived by the world.
Thus, since there is non-difference, this distinction—the distinction of appearance and so forth—is [the only one that exists].
Just as there is no distinction such as appearance and so forth within a single self that is of the nature of pleasure, likewise,
this external and internal distinction is merely a particularity, being entirely distinct from one another.
Of what nature is it?
It is "possessing a distinct appearance and so forth" (*bhinna-pratibhāsa-ādi*); the analysis of the compound is: that of which the appearance and so forth are distinct.
If it is argued that there is also non-difference because even a dual-natured entity is grasped by non-conceptual cognition,
he says "and not here," etc.;
"here" refers to among these differences.

The word "another" (*aparam*) refers to the second [type of cognition], which, by its power— that is, by the power of an undivided appearance— is precisely a distinction (*viśeṣa*), that is, a difference (*bheda*).
But there is no non-difference;
that alone is the particular (viśeṣa), which is the real entity.
As for those other general properties (sāmānyadharma) such as "being an entity" (vastutva) and so forth, they are merely conceptualized exclusions (vyāvṛtti) of that very [particular].
In the passage beginning with "tatkāryam" (that is its effect),
the neuter gender is used due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as "kārya" (effect).
Otherwise, since the particular (*viśeṣa*) was the subject under discussion, it would have been "that" (*saḥ*).
That very form of the particular is called both the effect and the cause; that same thing is called the "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "having as their fruit its abandonment or attainment": those activities whose fruit is respectively the abandonment or the attainment of that very particular—whether it be something to be rejected or something to be adopted—are described in that way.
And that which performs causal efficiency is precisely that particularity itself;
thus, the distinction of a particularity from another of a different class is a mere exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*),
and not some real entity called a "universal" (*sāmānya*).
174–75 For if it were to exist, it would indeed be perceived as something distinct from difference, provided that it meets the conditions for perception.
Since [it is not so perceived], therefore...
For if that universal were an object— that is, if it were a real entity— it would not be logical for its form to be unperceived while it exists as something visible;
why is this so?

Because that [cognition] is produced by a secondary characteristic (upalakṣaṇa)— that is, because the cognition of difference regarding particulars is produced by a secondary characteristic of generality—
[the generality] itself, when not apprehended, cannot be the cause of knowledge in another.

Having thus refuted the appearance-based (*prātibhāsika*) generality according to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas and others, he speaks in order to refute the previously mentioned inferential generality according to the Sāṃkhya view:

Moreover, as in the case of the Sāṃkhya, where despite the lack of distinction between differences, not everything is the cause of everything, so too for the Buddhist, despite the lack of distinction between differences, not everything is the cause of everything.
To which objection, then, does this resolution apply?
He says: "As for what was stated," and so forth, [meaning] "because of its nature as that which produces it."
If it is admitted that earth and the other elements— which are distinct from the nature of producing a rice sprout—
are the producers of this sprout, then because their distinction [from non-producers] is no different, everything would be a producer.
Regarding this objection, the answer has already been stated; however, this second [response] is now being expressed. He asks: "What, then, is the repetition? and says:
If, as stated in the verse beginning with "yadi," there were no distinction characterized by the capacity or incapacity to produce specific effects [verses 175–76],...
Thinking that this objection might arise, he states the meaning of the verse with the words "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth:
"In the same way, it will also be the case regarding the particular."
The connection is that "not everything is the producer of everything" by virtue of the nature of things— that is, through the causal power (*vastu-śakti*) of entities—
provided that non-difference among entities is accepted.
For that [entity] which is accepted as being non-different in all respects, action and non-action in one and the same place are contradictory;
this he explains with the words beginning "in mere difference," etc. (176–77).
The cause (*hetu*) is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*),

while the conditions (*pratyaya*) are the cooperative causes (*sahakārin*). Those whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has been determined— rendered capable of producing a specific effect— by their own causes and conditions, being their own causes and conditions, are described as such.
Since that state is not other than that [entity], those things intended to be non-agents would not be agents;
what is the reason?
Because it does not have that as its intrinsic nature—
that is, because it does not have the intrinsic nature of producing an effect other than that—
of that [effect], namely, of the single triad of qualities (*traiguṇya*).
"In that very same [way]" means in relation to one and the same effect; "in that way" means by that very same undifferentiated manner.
Thus, when a rice seed produces a rice sprout, at that very same time, a barley seed does not produce a rice sprout.
If the self of a rice seed were the very same as that of a barley seed, then it would follow that a single entity could both act and not act in the same respect;
yet there is indeed a distinction in the triadic qualities (*traiguṇya*) through their respective arrangements as a rice seed and so forth.
Therefore, if the difference [between causes] were the cause of some action, then if that difference were the cause of non-action, the auxiliary factors would not produce [the effect],
because they too are mutually distinct.
He explains with the words "not so," etc.;
the meaning is that cognitions of all aspects do not belong to that single object alone.
The meaning is that a synonym is based upon difference;
he explains this with the words beginning "Now" (*atha*).

Because all the various manifestations (bhedas) are employed everywhere in every effect through alternation and succession, this [first view] is stated when the perspective is that the agency of effects belongs only to those manifestations presided over by the power of the Pradhāna (primordial matter), through successive transformations. However,
when the perspective is that the power of the Pradhāna itself, in its successive forms, is employed in purposeful action through transformation, then this [second view] is stated.

The connection is as follows: because of the utility of *śakti*—which is characterized by the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), which resides therein, which initially resides in the entity intended as a non-agent, and which subsequently transforms into another form, namely the form intended as an agent—there is no such thing as a non-agent at all.
That *paryāya* (modification) which has diversity (*bheda*) or manifoldness as its basis is described in that way.
The meaning is: how could the transformation of a single, undifferentiated rice seed into the form of a barley seed and so forth not be illogical?
By this, the statement "how could that [transformation] belong to that very entity? is explained.
Regarding what was stated as "or by power," he says in response:
"or by transformation."

How can the transformation or the attainment of another state be postulated for a power that is non-distinct— that is, indivisible? If it is held that the attainment of other states is indeed identical with the nature of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), then how can any distinction whatsoever be admitted in relation to it?

"Thus, having first refuted the position of transformation (*pariṇāma*) by showing that it entails the loss of the unity of the *pradhāna*, [the author] now speaks in order to refute the views held by the Sāṃkhya, Mīmāṃsaka, Naiyāyika, and others, who accept a universal (*sāmānya*)— whether it be non-different, both different and non-different, or different— that exists either as "vertical" (*ūrdhvavṛtti*), because it persists through all successive states, or as "horizontal" (*tiryagvṛtti*), because it persists across all individual instances."
Furthermore, etc.:

by this [it is shown that] even he who considers himself a Digambara thinks that there is no single universal (sāmānya) admitted among things such as jars and cloths, because they are absolutely distinct.

However, this very substance is subject to transformation through successive states designated as "conditions" (*avasthā*); and because it persists through all these conditions, it is called the "universal" (*sāmānya*).

For instance, when a gold pot is broken and a crown is fashioned, that same gold substance, while perishing in the form of the pot and arising in the form of the crown, remains constant in its nature as gold; thus, it is called the universal because it undergoes transformation through successive states.

Precisely because it undergoes transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), there is no difference between the state and that which possesses the state; otherwise, if the state were distinct from the substratum possessing the state, transformation would be impossible.
Furthermore, when the substance of gold is destroyed in its form as a jar, one who desires a cloth experiences grief;
yet when it arises in the form of a crown, one who desires that [crown] experiences joy.
Furthermore, since there is an absence of destruction and arising due to its nature as gold, one who seeks gold maintains neutrality; therefore,
that which is characterized by simultaneous arising, passing away, and persistence is the definition of a real entity (vastu), as he has said:
One who desires a jar, a crown, or gold undergoes grief, joy, or indifference based on their causes during the states of destruction, arising, and persistence;
for there is no grief without destruction, and no happiness without arising.
Without stability there can be no neutrality; therefore, an entity consists of three aspects.

One who observes a vow of milk does not eat curd, nor does one who observes a vow of curd drink milk, nor does one who observes a vow against cow-products consume both; therefore, an entity consists of three aspects.

It does not arise nor does it perish in its nature as a universal (*sāmānya*), because of the evident persistence (*anvaya*); yet, it arises and perishes through its particularity (*viśeṣa*). That [position] which holds that arising and so forth exist simultaneously in one and the same thing must also be understood here as having been refuted.
If one accepts that the entity possesses both the universal and the particular,

then there would be absolute non-difference and difference: because the universal, characterized by the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) and so forth, is not distinct from the particulars such as jars and cloths, the universal would also consist of the nature of the particular, and thus there would be absolute difference.
Because the universal does not exist, and because particulars do not emerge from the universal, there is identity;
this means that there is absolute non-difference. Because particulars do not exist, there is no single entity consisting of both difference and the universal—this is the sense.
Now, if it is maintained that there is some kind of difference between the universal and the particular,
he says in this regard:
"mutually," and so forth.
If there were some kind of mutual difference between the universal and the particular, whose natures are respectively similar and dissimilar, then their difference would be absolute,
like that of a jar and a cloth; yet no universal is perceived as a distinct entity.
Therefore, no single entity exists that consists of both the universal and the particular.
Even for the Digambara, if such an entity were admitted, there would have to be absolute difference and non-difference;
for when the universal "gold-ness" is non-different from the distinct states such as a jar and so forth, then there would be absolute and total difference between the jar, the crown, and the like.

Because the universal of "gold-ness" (*suvarṇatva-sāmānya*) does not exist [as a separate entity], if it is argued that there is non-difference between the states such as a jar or a necklace due to the universal of gold-ness, then there would be absolute non-difference; that is, by virtue of being exclusively one, there would be nothing but the form of gold itself.

Alternatively, even if there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) between the state and that which possesses the state, if a difference is maintained on the basis of a difference in characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-bheda*), [then...]
For instance, the nature of the universal "gold-ness" (suvarṇatva-sāmānya) is perceived as persisting through all states,
whereas the natures of the states such as the [golden] jar and so forth are perceived as distinct;
therefore, since there is a difference in the defining characteristics (lakṣaṇabheda) between the state and that which possesses the state, there is indeed a distinction— [to this, he replies:]

Regarding the passage beginning with "mutually" (*anyonyam*) and ending with "of the similar and dissimilar natures": if there were a difference between the state (*avasthā*) and that which possesses the state (*avasthātadvatoḥ*), then there would be a mutual difference between those two— an absolute mutual distinction— because those whose forms are respectively inclusive (*anugata*) and exclusive (*vyāvṛtti*) would not be joined together.

Nor is there another intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) by which there might be non-difference between those two, because the substratum (*dharmin*), which consists of infinite properties (*anantadharma-ātmaka*), is not perceived.
The connection is that "if things were distinct," [it would be] by means of a non-distinct self (*ātmā*) called the "Primal Matter" (*pradhāna*) or some other [entity].

By virtue of being "real" (*vastutva*) or by virtue of being "gold," those very particulars such as pots would possess that [universal], meaning they would possess an undifferentiated nature; for that which has as its essence (*ātmā*)—that is, its form (*rūpa*)—an undifferentiated nature identical to those primary principles (*pradhāna*, etc. is "that which has an undifferentiated nature as its essence," and it is because of that state [of being so].
From what source could there even be a mutual distinction between differences? By this, absolute non-difference is explained.
Now, that single, common self of that particularity characterized as a jar and so forth does not exist,
because a particularity possesses a manifold nature by virtue of its forms as a jar and the like;

such being the case, it is not logical for that category of generality— consisting of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) and so on— to likewise exist as a universal self through that very nature of particularity.
The meaning is that because the universal is not distinct from its particular instances, the state of being "common" (sāmānyatā) cannot be established.
By this, absolute difference is also explained.

For, if it were as described—that is, if the primary cause (pradhāna) and so forth were admitted to have the nature of a universal—then the essence of the primary cause and so forth would not possess those properties, nor would it possess the property of difference.

The meaning is that [the entity] would not possess that property called "state" (avasthā) because it is non-distinct from it; in other words, there would be a mutual difference between the state and the possessor of the state. Proving this very point, he says:
The connection is as follows: "For this one intrinsic nature, possessing both activity and cessation, is not logical," and so forth;
"abiding" refers to activity.
"Departure" (*vigama*) means cessation (*nivṛtti*).

For instance, while the primary power (*pradhāna-śakti*) remains and the substance-nature of gold (*suvarṇa-dravyatva*) and so forth persists, cessation is intended as the departure from those specific states.
By this, the argument that "there is a mutual difference between the two" and so forth is explained.
With the words "no," etc., he anticipates the opponent's intention;

[the opponent suggests] that it is not the case that there is absolute non-difference between the universal and the particular, but rather that even between those two—the particular and the universal—there might be a difference.
He explains this with the words "if not," and so forth.
The connection is as follows: in any given substance, there is no absolute difference or non-difference between the universal and the particular;
for what reason?
Because they are discerning, and so forth.

The universal (*sāmānya*) is power (*śakti*), goldness (*suvarṇatva*), and substantiality (*dravyatva*); the particular (*viśeṣa*) consists of things such as pots; thus they are established through such distinctions.

By this [the Master Ācārya] means that this distinction between those two—the particular and the universal—is established by way of a nature that is both excluded (*vyāvṛtta*) and inclusive (*anugata*), such that one can designate: "this is the particular" and "this is the universal."
If there were a difference between the universal and the particular by way of that [common] nature, then there would be an absolute difference;
this is what he explains with the words beginning "yadi" (if).
If there is a difference between the universal and the particular because the self is thus understood as both inclusive and exclusive by that very nature— this is the connection [of the sentence].
Clarifying this very point, he says:
Regarding the phrase "because," and so forth:
those two are the selves that establish the distinction; "of those" refers to the universal and the particular; "their own selves" means they constitute their very nature.

"But rather, there is no jar here in this location."
When there is a negation expressed as "this is not the time," the cognition arises that this jar has no connection with this place or this time;
likewise, when it is said "the jar does not exist in this manner," the cognition arises that the jar does not possess this attribute.
When there is such a cognition [of the word] as "tathā" (thus), the Teacher [states] "even so" (*tathāpi*) and so forth;
by means of the passage beginning with "not now" (*nedānīm*), how is the relation negated? It is until the person has the conviction that "this man has neither a relation nor a property."
When there is a negation such as "not here" or "not now," the cognition is that "there is no relation"; when there is a negation such as "not so," the cognition is that "the property does not exist.
But is it not the case that even the negation of a property is indeed the negation of a relation?
Because the relationship between the property and the property-possessor is negated,

it is true that the relationship is stated separately as either the "property" or the "relationship," due to the distinction between types of relationships characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*).
And since it is not the case that this [cognition] lacks a relation, how could there be the possibility of the existence of a relation and so forth if [the object] exists in some way?
Why then [would it apply] to non-entities (*abhāva*)? By the word "tathā" (thus), the meaning of the word "yathā" (as/how) is implied.
Because of the constant connection between "that which" (yat) and "this" (tat),
when places and so forth exist, there is the cognition that "it does not exist," because this is in contradiction with the cognition of existence as their inherent nature.
Similarly, since the operation of cognition with respect to absences is not admitted when [the object] is non-existent, this cognition—
"it is not here," and so forth— does not arise from the apprehension of an absence of relation.

In the absence of that— that is, in the absence of the cognition of the non-existence of the relation— it would not exist; or else, "that" refers to the cognition of the non-existence of the relation,
and "in the absence of that" refers to the absence of that [cognition], namely, the absence of the relation.
For that person who possesses such a cognition of the absence of a relation,

by whom can those words— which arise from it, being born from the cognition of the absence of a relation and having the absence of a relation as their object— not be prevented from occurring according to that cognition?
If it is argued that the absence of a relation is the object of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) but not of words,
he says "that very same [thing]" and so forth:
that which is not the object of discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) is precisely that which is not the object of words.
The meaning is that whatever is the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is necessarily the object of language (*śabda*).
If these [conceptual constructions] have arisen, they are *vitarkas*.
Now, is there not a conceptual construction such as "this is blue" with respect to a blue object situated before one?
He says "not indeed," etc., [to show] that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not the object of words, and that the particular characteristic is not expressible by words;
"the inexpressible object" refers to the particular characteristic.
Because the context concerns conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), "conceptual cognitions" are understood here;

they "strive," meaning they take as their objective support (*ālambante*) only a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*). This is so even for that conceptual cognition which occurs when a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is present.

However, this misconception of the dull-witted—that conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the form of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—arises from the false assumption that conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions occur simultaneously;
this has already been examined by the author of the treatise in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.
Now, if it is argued that because [the object] is made an object of a conceptual cognition, there is an absence of a relation [between the word and the particular], [we reply:]...
In that case, the relation too would have to be expressible, because it is made an object by conceptual cognition.
If it is indeed accepted [that it is expressible], then how is it that Master Dignāga stated its inexpressibility? To this he says:
Regarding the phrase "of the relation," etc.:
"in its own form" means in the form of a relation;
that a related entity is a "relation" is the very nature of the relation, which consists merely of existence characterized by mutual dependence and is not a substantial entity.
And there is no word that denotes that [relation] by its own form;
for a word expressing a relation must be accepted as its denoter, and when such a word is employed, it implies "of which two?

In that case, when it is said, "the relation between the king and the servant," the relation is the cause of the distinction expressed by the phrase "of the king and the servant"; thus, that relation is perceived in the form of the related entities.
Regarding this, he says:
"By means of the designation as being related," and so forth.

When one states, "the relation between the king and the man," the relation itself—abstracted from its specific forms—is presented to the mind as the relatum by way of the king and the man, which are mutually dependent.

Just as the relationship characterized by mutual dependence— expressed as "the king's man"— is intended to be known according to one's purpose, yet is not cognized in that specific form; for this reason, even though this relationship is being perceived, it is [not grasped] through the word "relationship" (*sambandha*).
Since it exists as the very form of the related [entity] according to the stated rule, it is not denoted by means of a relation;

therefore, the same consequence that applies to non-existence does not apply to the relation either. The meaning is this: just as it must be said that the absence of a relation is made an object of cognition, yet it is not so denoted as a relation, so too the relation itself is not denotable.
For the absence of a relation is indeed made an object of cognition in its own right.
The relation is likewise denoted by the word; however, it is apprehended in its own form,
nor is it denoted [by that word].
Because it is only that which has assumed the form of a relation that is made an object [of cognition] and denoted,
so it has been said:
"The relation, being non-substantial (asattvabhūta), its form is not perceived."
A designation cannot in any way express the relationship in its own form;
therefore, it is established that the object of conceptual construction must necessarily be denotable.
Consequently, even if there is no [real] relationship, a word produced from that [conceptualization] certainly functions.
And thus, it follows that the word has non-existence as its object.

Now, if it is argued that this fault must not occur and therefore one does not intend for the relation to be made an object by the cognition "it does not exist," then in the case of "there is no jar here," what is being negated?
This argument— that [the relation] does not exist because its locus and so forth do not exist,
and because neither the relation nor its existence is perceived— is trivial. Furthermore,

when one who asserts that non-existence (abhāva) is denotable speaks against such a person, this proponent of the non-denotability of non-existence, while refuting by stating "non-existence is not denotable," how could he refute [the opponent] without himself speaking?
For one who utters the word "non-existence" cannot possibly establish that non-existence is the referent [of that word];
yet, if one desires the verbal expression of non-existence, then, once this non-existence is admitted to be expressed, how can it be said that non-existence has not been spoken?
It has indeed been spoken.

Since that very word "non-existence" (abhāva) expresses it by stating "non-existence is not expressible," the negation is made by way of restating that which is asserted by the opponent regarding the expressibility of non-existence.
If it is argued that there is no fault because non-existence (*abhāva*) is not what is denoted,
then why is it not the case that non-existence is denoted even in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), such that this [objection] could be raised?
Therefore, it is precisely the intended non-existence that is denoted.
If it is argued that because intrinsic nature does not exist, there is no statement regarding non-existence due to its non-being, he says:
"But rather [it is] non-existence itself," and so forth; by the word "therefore" (tena), he means by virtue of the non-being of non-existence.
If non-existence does not exist at this time, then how could there be the statement "that very non-existence does not exist"?
Furthermore, why would the employment of the word "non-existence" itself—not the statement "non-existence does not exist"—not occur?
And why would it not occur? Because non-existence itself is not admitted.
For its denotation must be non-existence, yet that [non-existence] is not admitted [by you].
If it is argued that this is a negation of a non-existence imagined by another, then at least a word whose object is non-existence is already accepted.
Therefore, by one who in some way initiates the conventional usage of non-existence, cognitions and words that have non-existence as their object must necessarily be admitted.
Furthermore, regarding what was said—
that because a meaningless word cannot be employed when an object is negated, the negative particle (*nañ*) is not used without an object— the answer to this will be stated:
[it is] "established by conceptual construction arising from beginningless latent predispositions."
With the words beginning with "207" and ending with "tasmāt," the conclusion is reached;
and by this much of the text, the Master has established that which was stated: that in those [cases], the application of words must necessarily occur.

On this point, an opponent says: "If words also exist with respect to non-entities (abhāva), then how could there be a distinction of intrinsic nature (svabhāvabheda) among those non-entities that serves as the cause for the application of words, by virtue of which words expressing non-entities would have exclusion (apoha) as their object? To this, the Ācārya provides the following answer:
Regarding the phrase "there too" and so forth:
because of the absence of form— that is, because of the absence of its own nature— words that express the form of non-existence cannot even be suspected of apprehending an intrinsic nature.
Since those words are established as having non-existence as their object and as denoting exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), that is, other-exclusion (*anyāpoha*), this is what is meant:

because words whose objects are non-existence do not grasp the essential nature of an entity, they have exclusion as their object; likewise, even for words whose objects are entities, because they do not grasp the essential nature of an entity, they likewise have exclusion as their object alone.

It may be suspected that while some words are said to have existence as their object because they determine existence, and others are said to have non-existence as their object because they determine non-existence, regarding those words whose operation or function resides in a real entity (*vastu*), what is their denotable form? Is it the entity to be grasped in a positive form (*vidhi-rūpa*), or is it a particularity (*bheda*)—an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) excluded from others—that is determined?

As for non-existence, however, since it is characterized by differentiation (*viveka-lakṣaṇa*), that is, characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature, why should it be made the cause [of verbal cognition] when there is a form belonging to the intrinsic nature of a real entity?

For, since it is impossible for that form to be non-existent while its existence persists, "tadbhāva" (its existence) refers to the presence of that very form; a thing whose characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is precisely that is so described.
This alone is the primary distinction (*viveka*), which is other-exclusion (*anyāpoha*).

But another [type of exclusion], because it has as its cause the exclusion (*apoha*) of the objects of words such as "cow" and so forth, is metaphorically designated as "exclusion" (*apoha*); it is characterized by the absence of all entities. Of that [exclusion], the words are "indicators of such an absence," meaning they express the nature of the distinction; thus, they have the distinction as their object, which is to say, they have the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as their object.
The connection is that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have differentiation (*viveka*) as their object;
those words and conceptual constructions [refer to] a single entity that serves as the basis for exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
Those words and conceptual constructions for which the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the point of reliance (*pratisaraṇa*) are so described;

for indeed, by the exclusion of the unproduced (*akṛtaka*), whatever object is the basis of the word "produced" (*kṛtaka*) and its conceptual construction is precisely that which is the basis of the words "impermanent," "selfless," and so forth, as well as their conceptual constructions.
The connection is that even though they have become such [as described], their objects remain distinct;
why? Because, as expressed by the phrase "according to each" and so forth, that exclusion from which a determination is established is the limit (avadhi) of that [determination].
Just as "non-produced" is the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of that which is called "produced," so too "permanent" is the exclusion of that characterized by "impermanence," and so forth.

By means of those respective limits (*avadhi*), the various distinctions of impermanence and the like are conceptualized—that is, constructed—by those who discern them; these are the mutual differences between them.
When those properties appear as if divided by those various distinctions within the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*),

there occurs a sequential conjunction: through the presentation of the distinctness and differences of those words and the conceptualizations, [the former] by way of being the denotator (*vācakatva*) and [the latter] by way of being the grasper (*grāhakatva*).
But surely, there is no difference in their limits between "produced" (*kṛtaka*) and "impermanent" (*anityatva*), because that which is unproduced is of the nature of being eternal;
and consequently, the reason would be merely a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*).
This is not a fault, because even for that which is unproduced—namely, prior non-existence (*prāgbhāva*)—there is impermanence.
Even for the non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) which is produced, there is indeed a distinction of limits because it is eternal;

or rather, by the exclusion of the superimposition that "sound is not produced by a cause," it is called "produced" (*kṛtaka*), and by the exclusion of the superimposition of persistence in the second and subsequent moments, it is called "impermanent" (*anitya*). Thus, there is indeed a distinction of limits.

Therefore, by means of this aforementioned distinction of exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), even when the essential nature itself functions as both the probandum and the probans in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), there is no conjunction or identity between the probandum and the probans.

And therefore, he says "that is not so" to show that the aforementioned fault— that if an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were the probandum (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*) would be a mere part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*)— does not apply.
