The word "that" (tad) means "therefore";
the connection is that "this very nature" (svabhāva) is the term,
and "nature" (svabhāva) refers to a property that is non-distinct [from the subject].

Sometimes, even though existence resides in what is produced (*kṛtaka*) and producedness resides in existent things (*sat*), nevertheless, when there is the intention to express merely that "this intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is caused by a cause," the "produced" is called the reason (*hetu*),
but not when there is an intention to express its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).

When there is the intention to express merely that "capacity exists," as in the case of [the property] "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth, "existence" (*sattva*) is stated as the reason; however, when there is the intention to express that it is produced by a cause, [the term *sattva* is used in that sense].
Therefore, that which was said—
that existence is found in what is produced and there is no deviation from its impermanence— why then is it qualified by a distinction of conditions? That [objection] is thus refuted.
Because the capacity [of the reason] with respect to "being produced" and so forth is not intended to be expressed,
that which is pointed out or stated as the reason depends upon a distinction of conditions— that is, it depends upon a distinction of qualifiers.

"Kevala" (exclusive) is stated as being independent of any limiting condition (*upādhi*) for the purpose of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*). When "non-eternality" is the probandum, "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) depends on a specific limiting condition, whereas "existence" (*sattva*) does not depend on it.

By the words beginning with "apekṣita" (dependent), he states that the dependence on a distinction of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) belongs to the state of being produced; for the Supreme Being, who is not admitted to be a cause, the very capacity for production is the operation,
and dependence consists precisely in the conformity to positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
When there is the production of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), that entity for which an operation by another is required as the cause of that production is "produced" (*kṛtaka*).
Because the suffix *kan* is prescribed in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), this word "produced" is a technical term (*saṃjñā-śabda*).

For this very reason, although this auditory expression "produced" denotes an intrinsic nature, it implies that this intrinsic nature possesses an external adventitious attribute (*upādhi*) as its ultimate qualifier.

By this— namely, by the demonstration that being produced (kṛtakatva) depends upon a distinction in its limiting conditions (upādhi)— the difference among causes, which is the nature of those cognitions, is established; that which has the habit of being differentiated by that [difference] is so described, and its state (tattva) is such that sound is differentiated according to the distinctions of place (sthāna), articulatory effort (karaṇa), and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), properties such as "being produced immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) and so forth are explained.
The conclusion is made with the words "in this way" (*evam*) and so on;
in some applications, it is independent of any distinction of limiting conditions (*upādhibheda*).
For this very reason, he said:
"When 'impermanent' alone is to be proven in a general sense, existence is both the essential nature and a property of that [subject], by the inclusion of which [the reason is established]."

In some cases, an essential nature (*svabhāva*) is stated as the reason; this is the subject under discussion. For example, when impermanence is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), "arising" (*utpatti*) is the reason.
And arising is not something other than that which possesses arising, because it would follow that non-existence (*abhāva*), being unproduced, lacks arising.

It is merely imagined as if it were a distinct entity by virtue of being a qualification; therefore, "because of arising" means "because of possessing the property of arising. This nature should be understood as being dependent upon an external condition (*upādhi*).

In cases such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), there is this much distinction: [in the former case] the specific property is essentially identical with the subject itself, whereas [in the latter] the external condition is something separate and devoid of that identity.
"By this direction" means by the direction of the classification of causes, whether dependent on conditions or independent of them.
If the reason is an intrinsic nature called "existence"—that is to say, existence itself—then how is it that the existence of *pradhāna* and so forth is not established?

If, on the other hand, what is to be proven is existence in general, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). Therefore, a specific kind of existence must be the probandum; yet if that specific kind is the probandum, because the specific instance lacks concomitance (*anvaya*), the example would be devoid of the probandum. Consequently, existence is not established [as the probandum].

In that case, even if [the property] exists in the reason (*hetu*), because there would be no concomitance (*anvaya*) of the specific qualification, the example would be devoid of the probans (*sādhana*);
thus he says:
"For there would be no concomitance," and so forth.

The "contradiction" (vyāhata) refers to a faulty reason (hetu) regarding the particulars (bhedānām viśeṣāṇām) in relation to the probandum (sādhya) and the reason (hetu)— meaning in both the reason and the probandum—
and "elsewhere" (anyatra) refers to [the case of] non-self (anātman) and so forth.
The word "tat" refers to the *sattva* (being), and the particle "kila" indicates that it is being established as precisely what is intended.

By such statements as "Pradhāna exists," [the opponent] attempts to distinguish it through its possession of the characteristics of Pradhāna; yet a specific distinction cannot be established because of its lack of concomitance (ananvaya),
as the Master Dignāga has said.

Regarding the claim made by the Sāṃkhyas that the statement "Pradhāna exists" establishes the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of Pradhāna itself: this is due to their ignorance of the object of the means of valid cognition, inference (*anumāna*);
for inference has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, and it is contradicted—and thus rendered defective—when applied to a specific characteristic.
Rather, since the same fault applies to the reason as well,
he states that very point:
"Indeed, it is not a reason," and so forth;
"it has no positive concomitance" means it is non-concomitant (*ananvaya*). Why is it not a constituent part of the proof of what is to be proven? Because it is an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason.

Existence (*bhāva*) is being (*sattā*); when that [existence] is the material cause (*upādāna*)— that is, the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)— of a subject (*dharmin*), then if that very subject, in its mere nature as such, were to be established as the probandum (*sādhya*) in the form of a universal (*sāmānya-rūpa*),
nothing at all would be established for the Sāṃkhya.
Since the definition of "consisting of the three qualities" and so forth is unestablished,
such a thing is merely a general category, unrefuted as being "of such and such a nature."
By this, he states that [the object] is established as being meditated upon;
he explains [this] with the words beginning "not in every way" (na sarvathā), etc. (190–91).

The analysis of the compound *sattāsādhana* is as follows: "that which establishes existence" (*sattāsādhana*) means that which has "existence alone" (*sattāmātra*) as its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for the purpose of proving existence (*sattāsiddhi*).
It is a state where no specific nature (*svabhāva*) is specified; such is the grammatical breakdown (*vigraha*).
The negation "not so" is not a refutation of the proof of existence when proving a mere thing;

rather, it means that the proponent does not touch upon— that is, does not take into account— any particular distinction or specific quality of this subject, such as its eternality or the like, asserting instead that "there is nothing whatsoever [distinct] in the universal."
By the word "by this" (anena), the proponent has employed a distinction; thus,

there is an employment of a qualification such as "consisting of the three guṇas," "eternal," and so forth, with respect to this subject (*dharmin*)— primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the like— in which the distinction is not already established.

The reason would be "without positive concomitance" (*ananvaya*); it is called *ananvaya* because there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of this [reason] with the qualified property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Since this is so...
If existence (*sattā*) were the probandum by that [reason], then a specific property (*viśeṣa*) would be proven;

however, others first explain the latter half beginning with "in existence" (*sattāyām*) and so forth regarding the property (*dharma*) and other factors, and subsequently explain the first half beginning with "the difference already mentioned" (*upāttabheda*) and so forth.
He explains [the verse] with the words "For that" (sa hi) and so forth:
it is one because there is no differentiation from the root-primal nature (mūlaprakṛti),
and it is eternal because there is no destruction without residue (niranvaya-vināśa).
Because it consists of the three guṇas, it is composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion;
or else, being endowed with agency and so forth, it is something other [than the Self] in whatever way that may be.
"Qualified by the aforementioned properties, either collectively or individually,
its nature is such"— meaning its nature is characterized by the aforementioned qualifications—
and yet that subject (*dharmin*) does not thus conform to the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) by way of that qualified nature.
Because such a subject of the example (dṛṣṭāntadharmin) is not established,
it cannot be established by that; for there is no dispute regarding mere existence on the basis of mere existence.

"But surely," and so forth—the opponent [objects]: "In this way, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that was stated regarding existence (*sattā*) by means of the alternative between generality (*sāmānya*) and particularity (*viśeṣa*)."
As it has been said:
"There is an absence of a specific concomitance, and [the argument] regarding the universal would be a proof of what is already established.
For even in those cases where fire and so forth are the probanda (*sādhya*), there is no dispute regarding the nature of fire itself, since mere fire is already established.
And nothing is established by that [inference], because it is not a factor for action;
for it is fire qualified by a specific location and so forth that is a factor for action, not mere fire.
To this, he says: "In that case, that very [qualified fire] is what is to be proven."

A "qualified substratum" (viśiṣṭādhāra) is that wherein fire and so forth are established; that which has such a qualified substratum as its qualifier—namely, that fire and so forth which is intended as the probandum (sādhya)—is what is meant by "the qualifier of the qualified substratum.
Of that [probandum], it is intended as the object to be proven.
"Because there is no positive concomitance (anvaya) in the similar class (sapakṣa), [the reason] is unestablished," says the Teacher (Ācārya).
"Indeed, that substratum, even when apprehended as a qualifier, does not qualify that fire."
By which there would be positive concomitance;
what is the reason for that? It is because of its impossibility, and so forth.
By the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) and qualification of that suspected non-connection of the property with that subject,
this has been stated in the [verse] "the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*).
And it will be stated in the fourth chapter [4.149]:
"But surely, at the time of grasping the pervasion (vyāpti), fire as excluded from non-conjunction with the location (pradeśa) is unestablished."
Or, if that [invariable concomitance] were established, what would be the purpose of following the positive concomitance (anvaya)?
How could it be unestablished? For:

When one apprehends the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "wherever there is smoke, there is fire," fire—though already implied as being excluded from non-connection with the intended location by way of generality—is indeed [already] projected; however, the following of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is desired now for the sake of a specific cognition, namely, "fire is in this very place.
Therefore, [the word] "therefore" (*tasmāt*) serves as the conclusion.

In this context, "in that place and so forth" means by way of excluding non-connection with it; that is, by excluding the non-connection of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) with that locus (dharmin), such as the place, one proves the generality of mere fire. Therefore, there is no fault of lack of positive concomitance (anvaya), nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā), because the exclusion of non-connection with the place has not yet been established.
If it is argued that, regarding a subject such as *pradhāna*, what is to be proven is mere existence by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*),
he says "not so," and so forth;
"in some cases" refers to the subject, *pradhāna* and the like.
Why?
Because that existence is indeed without distinction, since there is no object denoted by terms such as "Pradhāna" that is characterized by the three gunas and so forth.
"Since there is no substratum that serves as a qualifier, how [can there be a subject]? and so forth; the opponent asks this, yet he too must explain how the subject (dharmin) [exists].
It is to be cognized;
having been cognized, it is to be expressed by means of words;
having been expressed, it is to be ascertained by means of valid cognition.
Therefore, since that [Pradhāna] is indeed established by means of its knowability and other such properties, existence (sattā) is being proved as a universal (sāmānya) in it;
so now, let the establishment of Pradhāna follow merely from the fact that "the knowable exists" without further qualification?
If it is argued that the primary object of knowledge is the meaning of the word, which consists of the form of the word itself rather than being endowed with qualities such as eternity,

and that while the "Primal Matter" (pradhāna) is thus established, other properties will be established by other means of valid cognition— [the author] replies: even so, what would be established by [the property of] knowability and so forth?
There would be no establishment of the intended primary specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
because this [conceptualized object] has the nature of a word-meaning (*śabdārtha*).
To the objection that, in the inference of fire as well, only "fire" in general would be established and thus it would not be something to be proven (*asādhya*), he says:

In other cases, however, that very same [universal]—which has a fixed substratum determined by fire—is not established in that particular place; thus, it is there that its existence is being proven. Now, one might object: "But even there, it is [proven] as being devoid of non-connection with that. This means: "non-connection" (*ayoga*) is the lack of connection with that specific location; "devoid of that" (*viraha*) means the presence of connection (*yoga*) with that location. That universal which possesses this [property] is described in that way.
He refutes this with the words "not so" and so forth, stating:
"Indeed, no one who knows the rules of logic establishes a pervasion by means of a fire-universal that is related to such a specific location."

Therefore, one who seeks to establish the matter for an opponent must demonstrate that smoke is invariably concomitant with fire—that is, inseparable from fire—by showing the universal pervasion (*sarvopasaṃhāra-vyāpti*) in the form:

"Wherever there is smoke, there is fire; such is this smoke. Thus, being established as pervaded by fire alone, it generates the cognition of fire precisely in that locus which serves as the subject (*dharmin*), where it is itself perceived in its own form.

In this regard, since the object of inference is cognized through the force of the logical mark (*liṅga*), there is no purpose whatsoever in stating the probandum (*sādhya*); for the establishment of the probandum occurs even without it. This very point is stated in the passage beginning with "tatra" and so forth: because the mark is observed in that locus of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*), the desired probandum is established merely by the declaration of the [mark's] relation [to the subject].

And since there is no indication of the probandum as a composite of the property and the property-bearer, then, in the absence of such an indication, how could there be a positive concomitance (anvaya) with the property to be proven in that which is qualified by it?
For this reason, the fallacy of non-concomitance (ananvaya) would indeed occur.

The word "tat" (that) means: because this smoke is established as being invariably concomitant with fire, it excludes by its very force (*sāmarthyāt*) the non-existence [of fire] in that particular location;
therefore, the whole (*samudāya*) is said to be the probandum (*sādhya*).
For if there were no fire there, there would be no smoke at all—this is the force [of the argument].
The positive concomitance (anvaya), however, should be shown by the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) alone, and not by the combination of the property to be proven and the subject (dharmin),
because that combination is unestablished in the example (dṛṣṭānta) and because there is no purpose in demonstrating pervasion (vyāpti) by means of the combination.
For this very reason he says,
"But not so for this," meaning that there is no positive concomitance preceded by the presentation of a specific location;
what is the reason?
Since the statement of the probandum (sādhya) is not an integral part [of the proof] at the time of demonstrating the positive concomitance (anvaya),
or if one were to require the concomitance to be stated prior to the indication of the probandum, no one would ever remove the proposition (pratijñā) from the syllogistic argument;
therefore, this point is established.
Without even indicating the subject (*pakṣa*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the mark (*liṅga*) by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) must be stated;
and thus the Master Dignāga said:
"The non-deviation of the mark—such as smoke and the like—from the property to be proven must be demonstrated elsewhere, in a general case, that is, in a mere locus (*dharmimātra*)."
And since the logical mark (*liṅga*) is ascertained and non-deviant, being well-known in that subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*),
it will cause one to understand the subject of the thesis as being endowed with that pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*); the conclusion is stated by the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth.

Just as the proof for fire is faultless because it apprehends a specific [instance], the proof for existence (*sattā*) is not faultless, because its particulars are unestablished. Thus, since it would result in proving what is already established and because of the lack of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the existence of *pradhāna* and so forth cannot be proven; furthermore, he says this in order to demonstrate that "all means of proof are here left unmentioned."
"Untouched," and so forth:
that in which the distinction [between existence and non-existence] is untouched— that is, ungrasped— is the mere thing, the mere state of being.
When that proof is being performed, the positive concomitance (anvaya) is not obstructed;
for what [is it not obstructed]?
For the probandum (sādhya), which is pervaded by that alone—that is, pervaded by mere existence.
Explaining this very point, he says:

when existence is asserted again with respect to a probandum-property that pervades all things, without grasping any specific nature [of that property], there is no contradiction of the positive concomitance (anvaya).
The meaning is that the example is not devoid of the property to be proven;
for [the reason] "existence" is not present there [in the example].
Why?
Because even though it is based on pure existence (*sanmātra*), that is to say, even though it relies upon mere existence as its cause,
there is nevertheless no reliance on specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) within that existence when it functions as the probandum (*sādhya*).
Why?
Because it is futile.
To provide another fault regarding the probandum being existence (sattā), he says [in verses 192–93]:

Furthermore, since the subject (*dharmin*), such as *pradhāna* and so forth, is unestablished (*asiddha*), there exists no property of existence (*bhāvadharma*) therein; thus, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished.

Moreover, a property that depends on both existence and non-existence is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and deviant (*vyabhicārin*) when existence is the property to be proven (*sādhya*). Furthermore, a property of non-existence is contradictory (*viruddha*) when existence is the property to be proven, because it proves the very opposite of existence.

Whatever reason (*hetu*) is adduced for the sake of proving that existence (*sattā*) which consists of *pradhāna* and so forth, all such reasons fail to transcend the three logical fallacies (*doṣatraya*).
How can that existence be proven?

For here, having admitted the established nature (*siddhatva*) of the reason, the faults of being contradictory (*viruddha*), inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and unestablished (*asiddha*) have been stated; since these two [the last two] are impossible if the reason itself is unestablished.

But surely, even when the existence of an omniscient being and so forth is the probandum, since defects such as the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason (*hetu*) are equally applicable, how can their existence be established?
This is not a fault.
Whatever is taught is preceded by knowledge, just as anything else that is taught [is so];
and since the Four Noble Truths are taught, they too must be preceded by knowledge. He who possesses that knowledge is accepted by us as the Omniscient One.
No harm is done by the fact that "that cause" refers to the cause of existence; thus,
the threefold [reason]— consisting of the three members— does not fail to encompass the various classes of defects.
He said to her: "Unestablished," and so forth; "contradiction" means the state of being contradictory.

In that case, how could a property of an existent (bhāvadharma) be established for something whose existence is unestablished? It might be argued that while the property of the primary cause (pradhāna), etc., is established, the existent itself is not; to this he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "yo hi" and so forth:

for how could that proponent who desires the cause of the property of being an entity (bhāvadharma) in respect to [the categories] such as Pradhāna not accept that Pradhāna and the rest are established entities?
Therefore, the property is indeed the entity itself.

If it is asked, "How then is it said that 'this is a property (dharma) of an entity'?", he replies: "Sometimes by way of relative dependence. By means of a definition characterized by the exclusion of other differences, a property is indicated as if it were distinct, as if it had a separate form from the substratum (dharmin);
for example, when it is said, "its state of being produced" (*kṛtakatvam asya*), the entity is expressed precisely as excluded from what is unproduced (*akṛtaka*).

He states "not indeed" and so forth to show that it is not the case that one thing called "dharma" is expressed by the word *dharma* and another thing called "dharmin" is expressed by the word *dharmin*;
for when a person, independent of the exclusion of others, desires to know the exclusion of a word from just one [thing], such as the unproduced (*akṛtaka*).

It is said that "this [sound] possesses the property of being produced" when, desiring the exclusion of others, one seeks to understand its exclusion from the single instance of non-producedness; at that time, it is stated that "sound is produced.
And this has already been explained previously.
By the statement beginning with "the exclusion or non-exclusion of other distinctions," [it is meant that] if,
on the other hand, one were to state a property (*dharma*) common to both existence and non-existence as the reason (*hetu*),
how could a single property belong to both existence and non-existence?
For dharma is indeed the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of an entity; how then could there be an intrinsic nature for a non-entity? To this he says "anāśrita" and so forth:
that which is a non-dependent thing, in which [there is] mere exclusion (vyatireka).
Since there is no contradiction even in the absence of that mere exclusion— that is, that which is conceptualized as a mere negation— acting as a property (dharma),
he explains how mere exclusion itself occurs: "by way of non-exclusion, that is, by way of a simple negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha)."
A positive injunction (*vidhi*) in which the negated term is subordinate is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), and that is not what is intended here.

For example, "it is not material" (*na bhavati mūrtaḥ*) implies immateriality (*amūrtatva*), which is merely the cessation of materiality; this would apply whether the entity exists—as in the case of consciousness (*vijñāna*)—or is indefinable, or even non-existent. To refute this, the opponent says:

That which is a non-entity (nirupākhya) cannot be the object of a negation; for only that which possesses the capacity to serve as a locus and so forth can be the object of something. Since a non-entity is devoid of all capacities, how could it be an object?

Now, since the status of being an object of negation has been refuted, is there then an object of affirmation? If it is argued that even that which is indefinable (nirupākhya) cannot be an object of affirmation because it is indefinable,
then how is it that non-existence (abhāva) is not an object of negation?
For the very reason that it is excluded from being the object of an injunction, it is indeed the object of a prohibition;
what is the cause?
Because a prohibition consists in the cessation of an injunction.

Therefore, how could this aforementioned mere non-exclusion (*avyavacchedamātra*)—which is possible for both existence and non-existence—appropriate as its own the status of being a prover (*gamakatva*) when "existence" is the probandum (*sādhya*)? Of what specific nature would that prover-status be? [It would be] "in the absence of the dissimilar instance," and so forth.

If there were the possibility of the reason’s occurrence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), then its exclusion from that would also be established; however, since there is no exclusion of the mere property of being present in both [similar and dissimilar instances] from the dissimilar instance, how could that [reason] be made to function as a means of cognition?

Furthermore, that proponent, by his own words and through the statement of another, asserts that the reason which establishes existence possesses the property of being present in both; thus, he declares the occurrence of this reason—possessing the property of being in both—in something other than the existent object to be proven, namely, in the non-existent.

Furthermore, since the capacity to indicate [the probandum] is based on non-deviation (avyabhicāra) when existence (*sattā*) is the property to be proven, how could anyone other than a madman fail to state the non-deviation as the reason?
For a proponent who asserts a reason that is a property of non-existence (*abhāva-dharma*) regarding existence would be contradicting himself,
because he is proving non-existence, which is the opposite of existence.

Furthermore, what is the property of this very non-existence? He says: "What kind of exclusion [is it]? It is that which pervades mere existence and is characterized by capacity; its exclusion occurs necessarily only for non-existence, but not for properties such as corporeality, because those belong to both [existence and non-existence].
Why is it contradictory? He says:

because that exclusion of objects which is pervaded by mere existence is absent in some cases where existence is present, yet present in all cases where existence is absent; therefore, its nature is contradictory.

Consequently, this property—though of three kinds, being related to existence, non-existence, or both—is stated as the definition of a logical reason (hetu) by virtue of its concomitance with existence (*sattā*).

Furthermore, there is no other destiny nor any other mode apart from the threefold unrighteousness; therefore, its existence is not being established as a probans (*sādhana*) or a logical mark (*liṅga*). Since this existence has not been presented with a specific qualification in a general sense, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*) regarding the subject (*dharmin*) whose existence is already established.
When a property of the thing (*vastudharma*) such as impermanence is to be proven, what is its specific qualification? It is that which pervades only that [property];
and by means of that property to be proven, there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*).
If it is ascertained "somehow"— either by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—
then there is neither contradiction nor deviation;
that is, there is neither the fallacy of being contradictory (*viruddha*) nor the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

For this reason, this consequence does not possess the characteristics of being unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). However, when the pervasion of the mark (*liṅga*) by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is uncertain,

or when its subsistence in the subject (*dharmisamāśraya*)— that is, its status as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)— is uncertain, then that reason which is intended to be a prover by virtue of having a nature consisting of the three modes (*trairūpya*) ascertained through its own essential nature (*tatsvabhāvatayā*) is not a prover at all.

For this very reason, the nature of the probans (*hetu*), which is pervaded by its own property—that is, its own form as the probandum (*sādhya*)—and which is established and ascertained in the subject (*sādhyadharmin*), must be stated. Strengthening this point, he says:
"For not... and so forth.

When, while illuminating jars and other objects by means of its luminosity and radiance, it occasionally comes to reside within the interior of a jar or similar object, then—provided that its form is not perceived and its radiance is not perceived—it certainly does not perform its own causal function, which is characterized by the illumination of the jar and so forth.
Having thus stated the nature of the indicator (*gamaka*), he now states the nature of the indicated (*gamya*):
"of that, the pervader... (*vyāpakas tasya*).

That which is the prover (*gamaka*)— the pervaded (*vyāpya*) nature— is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) nature that is ascertained as the provable (*gamya*); he explains this with the words "its property" (*taddharma*) and so forth, meaning that the property of the subject (*dharmin*) is the provable.

"What is the nature of that which is intended as the indicator (*gamaka*) such that it is ascertained as the pervader (*vyāpaka*), and how, moreover, is it ascertained as the pervader? To this he says:
"Precisely from the ascertainment of that property (*taddharmaniścayāt*)," that is, precisely from the ascertainment of the pervaded property (*vyāpyadharmaniścayāt*).
By this much, the essential nature of the signified and the signifier has been shown;
he now states the essential nature of the excluded and the excluder as well,
beginning with "of that," and so forth.
"This" refers to the pervading property (*vyāpaka-dharma*); when it itself ceases, it causes the cessation of that which is pervaded (*vyāpya*). He explains this with the words "of that," etc.
The connection is as follows: "this pervading property, while itself ceasing, is the cause of the cessation of that which is pervaded."
What is the reason?
Because this pervading property (*vyāpaka*) to be proven is established for him only if the pervaded (*vyāpya*) does not exist in the absence of that pervader.
The word "tat" (that) is used here to introduce the statement;

by this demonstration of the relationship between the follower and the followed (*anuvartyānuvarttaka-bhāva*) and the relationship between the thing to be removed and the remover (*nivartyanivarttaka-bhāva*)—which were mentioned immediately prior—it should be understood that the definition of the indicator (*gamaka-lakṣaṇa*), characterized as the capacity to prove the probandum (*sādhyasādhakatva-lakṣaṇa*), has been stated for both types of formal argument: namely, those based on similarity (*sādharmya*) and those based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
He now explains that [definition].
"Indeed, it is of two kinds," and so forth; as some say, namely the Naiyāyikas, "for the anvayin [type of syllogism] is indeed that formulation which possesses positive concomitance (sādharmya)."

But surely, the negative-only inference (*vyatirekin*) possesses only dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*); whereas in the formulation based on similarity (*sādharmya*), there is the property of being present in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and positive concomitance (*anvaya*), so too in the formulation based on dissimilarity, there is the property of being present in the subject and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Thus, it follows that the logical mark (*liṅga*) would have two forms; to this he says:
Regarding the phrase "of these two" and so forth:

"of these two" refers to the two types of reasons—positive-negative (*anvaya-vyatirekin*) and negative-positive (*vyatireka-anvayin*). In reality, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no difference whatsoever between them, because both possess the characteristics of both positive and negative concomitance.

Except for a difference in formulation (*saṃyoga*), those very same positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are sometimes demonstrated through the application of similarity (*sādharmya*) and sometimes through the application of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Thus, only the formulation differs, but not the meaning.
For what reason?

Since, even in an argument formulated by way of similarity (*sādharmya*), the exclusion of the reason from the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyavipakṣa*)— which constitutes its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)— is understood through the force of the meaning (*arthāt sāmarthyāt*), he states that very same force:
"Non-existent," and so forth;
"in that" refers to the dissimilar instance (vaidharmya).
For the reason would indeed be concomitant with the probandum only if it did not exist in the absence of the probandum.

Likewise, regarding "dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya*): in that formulation of dissimilarity, [it is said] "in that [case]" regarding the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). For if there were a positive concomitance of the reason (*hetu*) with the probandum (*sādhya*), then this [reason] would cease upon the cessation of the probandum; and we shall explain this in the investigation of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
194–95 Just as the effect is impermanent when impermanence [is the probandum], so too is "being produced" (kṛtakatva) necessarily impermanent.
And this is an example of the positive concomitance (anvayin); "or, that which is not an effect is imperishable" is an example of the negative concomitance (vyatirekin).
Therefore, this is the meaning:
when there is no destruction— that is, in the absence of destruction—
there is no "unproduced" thing, because it would lack the property of being produced.
He states that very point with the words "by this," etc.;
"of these two" refers to the positive and negative concomitants (anvaya-vyatirekin).

By the statement "whatever [is produced]," through a universal summary that expresses pervasion (*vyāpti*), the exclusion of the permanent from being produced is stated; thus, the cognition of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and the word "produced" constitute the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
To the question, "Why is the subject (*pakṣa*) not explicitly stated? he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "of that which is produced" (*kṛtakasya*), when the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*)—which is pervaded by impermanence—is stated by means of sound, it necessarily brings its own pervader (*vyāpaka*) into proximity; thus, by the very force of this [logical implication], it follows that "sound is impermanent. Therefore, it is not necessary [to state it explicitly], and so forth.

With the words "here" (*iha*), he states an application characterized by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) within the context of an application based on similarity (*sādharmya*), beginning with "even in the case of negative concomitance" (*vyatireke 'pi*).
And this phrase "it is not to be acted upon" is an elaboration of the statement "it is indestructible";
for here too, it is not a mere statement of a thesis, because it functions as a reason by virtue of its established nature, which is determined to be an eternal nature.

When there is an absence of that—meaning when there is an absence of impermanence—the existence of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) in sound is not established; yet, once the statement of its presence—that is, the declaration of its actual existence—is made, then because producedness exists as something whose very nature is impermanent, its existence in sound is established by implication as "sound is impermanent. This is "as before," meaning like the formulation based on similarity (*sādharmya*).

Now, one might object: "In this formulation of the method of difference (*vaidharmya-prayoga*), the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has not been stated. To this he replies with the words "But the positive concomitance... and so forth; for the impossibility of the method of difference without the positive concomitance constitutes an *arthāpatti* (presumption).
What is the reason?
"Not indeed," and so forth;
because that which is not restricted to having that [permanent] nature is unconnected to the nature of impermanence.

Since it is logical that when that [the probandum] ceases—that is, when impermanence ceases—the [probans] must cease, for this reason, one should first establish by means of valid cognition the necessary connection (*niyama*) of the probans with the probandum through identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*); then, for the sake of a deluded person, the cessation of the probans should be stated upon the cessation of the probandum.
Therefore, as for what is said:

If the restriction has already been established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what is the use of a fruitless statement of cessation? Or how could one not understand the restriction [itself]?
But as for the claim that "there is no cessation in the cessation of that," that has been refuted.
Others, however, explain it differently:

having established [the rule], there is a statement of implication from the meaning of the word; thus, the meaning is that after establishing the restriction and implying the restriction through the force of the meaning, the exclusion must be stated—that is, the exclusion must be stated by such a statement.
The statement of exclusion implies a restriction by virtue of its inherent capacity;
for this very reason, he says "And that," and so forth.
The cessation that implies a restriction is established for the opponent;
if it is manifested by such a statement,
then it implies a restriction upon oneself— that is, a restriction upon the subject to be proven— by the force of the statement itself.
For this reason, [the opponent asks] "How is the positive concomitance (anvaya) established? and so forth;
the meaning is that this is said now when it has been determined that the probans is the indicator provided the relationship of pervader and pervaded (vyāpyavyāpakabhāva) is accepted.

"How and by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is it to be understood and ascertained that whatever is produced is necessarily impermanent, such that you yourself say, 'Sound is produced and impermanent; whatever is produced is impermanent'? Being thus questioned, he speaks in order to demonstrate the subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the scope of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Regarding the phrase "because," and so forth:

it means that because destruction—which is characterized by the property of cessation—is invariably concomitant with its own nature, that is, with its mere essence; or alternatively, "bhāva" refers to that from which something comes into being.

Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) means its own being; the meaning is its own cause. Precisely from that [cause] follows the persistence of destruction in the entity, and therefore that which is produced is impermanent. Why? Because it lacks a separate cause; for there is no cause of destruction other than the cause that produces it.
Therefore, there is no connection to that intrinsic nature;
thus, the collective meaning here is this:
immediately after the operation of the hammer, two things are perceived—the cessation of the jar and [the arising of the potsherd].
And likewise, these two— the pot and the skull— are perceived as having the nature of destruction;
for, as he will state later, because the cessation of the pot is formless, it is not an effect.
However, the cognition [of it] as its effect is merely an error;
for if it were truly its effect, it would not consist in the negation of the jar,
since it would be produced in relation to the jar.
Furthermore, there would be no cognition [of the pot] as having the nature of destruction, because the pot still exists;
for he will state that even though the potsherd is the effect of the mallet, the nature of destruction of the pot has not ceased.
And how, then, can there be a cognition of this [jar] as having the nature of destruction?

If destruction were causeless, the jar would cease of its own accord; in that case, the hammer and other auxiliaries would not produce shards, because they would not initiate similar moments [of the jar]. However, since the jar ceases immediately after the operation of the hammer and the shard exists, it is indeed appropriate for those of dull intellect to determine that these two have the nature of destruction, and that destruction has a cause, because the continuity [of the jar] is severed immediately after the operation of the hammer.
How then can an objection regarding contradiction with empirical experience be raised against those who assert that destruction is causeless?
To explain this very point, he says "na hi" (for not... and so forth.
Regarding those produced things for which destruction is observed— those very things that are perishing—
if they possess that nature of being perishable, why would they require a cause other than the producer of their own nature?
For what reason?
Because things that possess the property of cessation exist as perishable precisely due to their own causes,
and because entities are independent with respect to a perishable nature, therefore whatever is produced is perishable by its very nature. (195–96)
If destruction were caused by a cause, it would not be necessarily inevitable; thus he says "of those that depend," etc.,
where "hi" means "because."
For entities that depend on other factors, there is no necessity of occurrence;

therefore, an entity independent [of causes] possesses a perishable nature in its destruction. For if it were dependent on causes, then among things such as jars, some might even be eternal—those for whom the cause of destruction is not present.

If it is argued that because the causes of destruction are numerous, there is no instance where they are not present, he says "by which," etc.; the connection is as follows: "of that cause" means of those very causes of destruction, there is not necessarily a presence [of all of them].
Why?
Because its presence depends upon its own conditions— that is, its presence is contingent upon its own causes—
and because the causes for destruction are not present everywhere.
Furthermore, due to the non-proximity of the cause of destruction, nothing would necessarily perish;
even when the cause of destruction is present, destruction is not certain,
because causes do not invariably produce their effects— that is, they do not invariably produce the effect known as destruction.
Why?
Because deficiency is the non-presence of auxiliary causes,
and obstruction is the onset of opposing factors.
By this, it is stated that there is no deviation [of the reason] due to the non-necessity of that which is dependent;
for among all causes of destruction, those causes which are adduced as indicators (*liṅga*) of destruction [are not necessarily present].
Why?
Because of the non-establishment of the effect;
that is, because there is no fixed rule for the arising of an effect characterized by destruction.
For those who maintain that destruction is caused by a cause— those who say that its destruction possesses a cause—
since destruction is therefore without a cause,
for that reason this entity, being produced, is independent with respect to its state of being perishable by nature.
"Fixed in its existence" means fixed in the state of having the property of cessation;
he states an example with the words "impossible," and so forth.

The meaning is that the causal totality (*kāraṇasāmagrī*) in which [the effect] is not possible is "complete" (*sakalā*), in the sense that it is fulfilled by both the auxiliary conditions (*sahakāripratyaya*) and the transformation of the continuum (*santānapariṇāma*).
The formal argument (*prayoga*), however, is as follows:
Those things which are independent with respect to a certain state are necessarily characterized by the absence of that state;

for example, a causal complex that lacks impediments is independent regarding the production of its effect, and a produced thing is independent regarding its destruction. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

With the words beginning "nanu" (196–97), he raises the objection of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*): he states that even for certain causes which are independent with respect to some effect, that effect does not necessarily arise.
"Earth," and so forth;

for that [collection] is indeed the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) required for the production of an effect, since even when it is absent— such as at the time of an obstruction— the sprout does not arise.
And this [notion] of the continuity's unity, stated by way of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*),
is refuted with the words "no" and so forth;

for in that aforementioned causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is a transformation of the continuity characterized by the arising of a different intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because it is dependent upon those conditions.

Therefore, because the reason "due to independence" does not apply there— since even that which is produced (*kṛtaka*) has a dependence on another time with respect to its destruction— the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). Thus he says,
"Not so," and so forth.
He will state that for a produced entity (*kṛtaka-bhāva*), there is no dependence on any interval of time for its destruction.
It might be argued: "If earth, seeds, and so forth possess only a single intrinsic nature (*ekasvabhāva*), how can they depend upon a transformation of their continuum (*santāna-pariṇāma*)?"
Therefore, he says "tatrāpi" and so forth, [meaning] that there is indeed an inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason; this is what is intended.

The earth, seed, and so forth do not possess a single inherent nature, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence that the effect would be produced even before [the transformation], just as it is afterward;
rather, they are distinct through successive transformations.
Thus, within that causal complex which is differentiated by the transformation of the continuum, there is the final causal complex.
Since that [causal complex] which is unimpeded by any other characteristic in the production of the effect is indeed fruitful, how could there be inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) of the reason?
To this, he says: "Even though the preceding causal complex is productive, it is not necessarily so."
"That very [final] causal complex" refers to the last one among those; no other among them is the cause of the sprout.
To the question, "For what purpose, then, is the preceding causal complex adopted by those seeking the sprout?", he says:
"But others," and so forth.

The prior transformation is a specific prior state; it is sought by those desiring that very object—namely, the final causal complex capable of producing the sprout—and it is determined as being of the nature of that causal complex.
This might be so.

He says "na ca" and so forth, because even for the final causal complex (*sāmagrī*), an obstruction is possible; thus, since there is no necessity regarding the production of the effect, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
[This refers to] that final complex when the effect is about to be produced.

If existence were in one [moment] alone, then upon the arising of a modification in the final moment, that final moment would lose its singularity; for the preceding [moment] would have ceased and a second [moment], called the modification, would have arisen. Consequently, it would not be the final moment.

Now, if it is not admitted that this final [moment] deviates from its nature as a producer, then— since it has not deviated from its own nature as a producer and thus does not incur any deficiency regarding the production of the effect— the obstructing cause would be non-obstructive because it fails to cause any impairment.
Furthermore, he anticipates the objection of deviation:
"In what respect are barley seeds and the like not dependent?"
Why is it that, although the rice sprout is an effect to be produced, the conditions for its production are not sometimes present even in the case of a barley seed and so forth?
"Even though they are independent, they do not produce a rice sprout; thus [the reason] is inconclusive.
To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) replies: "How so?
[The meaning is that] they are indeed dependent."

The connection is as follows: "of these" refers to barley seeds and so forth; that which is the nature (*svabhāva*) of the rice seed for producing that—namely, for producing a rice sprout—that very [nature] does not exist in them.

"Dependent upon that nature" means dependent upon the nature of producing a rice sprout. And when, and how, could there be independence? [The opponent says: "In that case, indeed... [the other replies:]...
Furthermore, among certain produced things, whether they exist or not,
there is no such intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that is perishable;

therefore, because [the reason] depends upon that intrinsic nature— namely, dependence upon a perishable intrinsic nature— the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) insofar as it claims they are not perishable.
He begins to refute this with the words "the rice seed," etc.; by the word "etc.," seeds such as barley and so forth are included.
That which is intended as "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) is the nature of producing or not producing an effect other than [itself]; this is established by its own cause.
Thus, the meaning is that whatever is a barley seed or the like, if it is not the cause of that [other effect], it must be the cause of something else—namely, a rice seed—for which it is not a cause.
Thus, it does not have that nature; that is to say, it lacks the nature of producing a rice sprout.
Now, one might object: "Could it not be both a non-cause of that [sprout] and yet possess that nature?
To this he replies with the words "niyataśaktiśca" (and having a restricted capacity), and so forth.
That which possesses a fixed and specific capacity is such [a cause];
thus, the seed of rice or barley, whose nature is to produce [its respective plant],
is perceived through direct perception by its very own nature as it is differentiated in its essential form.
It might be argued:

"The difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities is not produced by causes; rather, the very nature of one thing is of such a kind, while that of another is of a different kind. To this, he says:
And so forth; "accidental" means being without a cause (*nirhetuka*),
[referring to] that which is independent of a cause in any particular location.
At certain times and in certain substances, such as rice seeds, there would be no restriction on the nature [of producing] a rice sprout;
rather, it would occur for everything, at all times, and in all places, because of the absence of any requirement [for specific conditions].
Therefore, it is understood that the restriction [of destruction] occurring in dependence upon place and other factors must have a cause;

just as there is a restriction of nature (*svabhāva-niyama*) in the case of rice seeds and the like, so too here among produced things (*kṛtaka*) or existent things (*sat*), a restrictive cause must be stated, from which restrictive cause certain produced or existent things are born with a perishable nature while others are not.
This might be the case.
Even if a regulating cause cannot be demonstrated, it is nonetheless possible; thus he says:
"And in this world, there is no regulating cause for a perishable nature, nor is one even conceivable"—that is to say, such a cause does not exist at all.

Since the destruction of all living beings is established through observation, it follows that destruction has no fixed cause; that is to say, if the destruction of all those who are born is thus established, then the reason "because of existence" (*sattvāt*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). To this, he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "janmī" (that which is born) and so forth: the opponent maintains that destruction is the very nature of only those things that possess birth, and not of those that do not possess birth— such as space and the like— even though these latter exist.
And the Master said: "Certainly not birth," for the intrinsic nature of an entity does not arise by virtue of its birth.
Therefore, birth is not the cause of destruction,
nor does existence exist in space and so forth; thus he says "na ca" and so on.

The restriction of nature— that is, the restriction of intrinsic form— does not belong to causeless things such as space, because for that which lacks a cause, there can be no restriction regarding place, time, or inherent disposition.
Since the destruction of all living beings is established and the non-existence of space and so forth is proven,
there is therefore no differentiation of nature among produced things or existent things based on whether a cause generates what is perishable or imperishable.

Because that state exists and because there is no differentiation of causes, there can be no differentiation between perishable and imperishable for a product that already exists; thus, it is not the same as the case of barley seeds and the like.
This independence of destruction—namely, that the existence of destruction at a certain place or time is opposed [to its non-existence]—effects the absence of that [non-existence].

He establishes the absence of destruction for that [entity] at any place and at any time by means of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and existence (*sattā*); that is to say, he establishes its non-existence everywhere and at all times.
What is the reason?
Regarding the passage beginning with "yo hi" and so forth:

"dependent on that time and substance" means that it depends upon whichever time it occurs in or whichever substance it exists within; thus, as was stated previously, it would not be independent at all.
Is it not the case that destruction is independent because it does not depend on a cause of destruction, and not because it is independent of time and so forth?

How then can it be said that "it depends on that [specific] time and substance"? [For if it were so,] destruction would not be independent at all. Furthermore, if destruction were independent of time, there would be no destruction in the second moment either, since it would depend on that [second] time.
And if there were no dependence on a substance, then whose destruction would it be?
He thinks thus, because of the statement: "Since that [destruction] exists for what has been born, it does not depend on anything else."
Destruction occurs in the very second moment and not in any other moment;
thus it happens to everything that is born, not to a specific substance.
Therefore, if destruction were independent of a substance, of what indeed would there be destruction?
Thus, [the objection] is refuted;
for if destruction were to exist at a later time and in a particular substance, then that later time and that particular substance would themselves be the causes of destruction,
since destruction exists only when they exist.
Therefore, if it were dependent on time and substance, it would not be independent at all; thus the opponent says, "In that case," to which the Teacher replies,
"No."
Because that which is the cause of existence arises precisely from that [cause], there is the arising of a perishable nature;
he clarifies this very point by stating "for that which exists," meaning that for something undergoing existence, there is the occurrence of such a perishable nature alone.
If it is argued that the existence or production of an already existent entity does not necessarily arise from some cause—
since some things, such as space and so forth, though existent, are not produced— the opponent maintains that [production] is accidental, meaning it is without a cause.
This existence would never cease for anything, at any time, or in any substance;
but surely, if the existence of jars and so forth is restricted by their own causes, how can there be the unwanted consequence of the existence of space and the like? True.

However, the meaning of "it does not cease for anything" is that there is no entity whose nature this [space] and so forth would not be; otherwise, it would follow that it is the self-nature of everything— so say some,
but that is incorrect.
For if the form of a jar or the like were to exist in space, it would be causeless, because it would exist even without a lump of clay or other such causes;
therefore, this existence of space and so forth would never cease for anything, such as the self, at any time or in any place.
The meaning is that [the cognition] would not be restricted by place, time, or substance;
confirming this very point,
he says "tad dhi" and so forth.
For that entity would have to adhere to or depend upon something else, wherein some [property] such as its arising and so forth is bound up or contingent.
Nor should it be restricted; for that existence which is unbound to anything would, if it were unbound in any respect,
lack restriction with regard to substance and time.
Furthermore, [if this were so], there would be no such distinction as "this existence belongs to space,
not to the self," or "the existence of the self does not belong to time," and so forth; therefore,
this existence is not accidental, even in those things considered eternal.

If the arising of that which is perishable occurs solely from the cause of its existence, how then can it be said that destruction is causeless? [The opponent] states this contradiction with the words "of that which is born," etc., and [the author] answers:
"Of that which is born," meaning produced; "in the absence of that state" means in the absence of perishability; "because of not depending on anything other than the producing cause."

It has been stated that destruction is causeless, and it was also said previously in this regard that what is called "destruction" is not something distinct from the entity; rather, the entity itself is indeed the destruction.
Now, one might ask: "But destruction is non-existence through annihilation (pradhvaṃsābhāva); how can that be of the nature of an entity? To this he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "sa eva hi" and so forth:
since it is from its own cause alone that [the entity] is born as something enduring for a single moment, therefore destruction is said to be the very nature of the entity itself.
That which has the habit of remaining for only that one moment—the very duration of the entity's existence—is described as such.
Furthermore, having arisen, it does not remain for even a single moment;
for we shall explain that if it were to remain, it would never cease.

If an entity that lasts for only a single moment perishes, why is it not determined as such even before the interruption of the stream? And because it is not so determined, he says that it is non-momentary.
Regarding the passage beginning with "tamasya" and so forth:

due to the persistence of ignorance since beginningless saṃsāra, dull-witted people determine that this jar or other object has the nature of destruction only later—at the time when the continuity of its stream is severed—not previously, even though it was perceived during the time of its existence;
thus, although there is perception of that which has a perishable nature, [they fail to recognize it as such].
At the time of seeing, there is no determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*),
because of the power of ignorance and because of the lack of clarity in seeing due to the arising of a similar [moment] immediately following;

and since certainty regarding the nature of destruction occurs at the time when the continuum is interrupted, therefore, by virtue of that— that is, by virtue of that certainty— [the object is established].

"Later" means that at whatever time the determination of the nature of destruction occurs, it is precisely that temporal condition (*kālopādhi*) which is established as the nature of destruction of the entity;
he states an example with the words "transformation," and so forth.

Just as a poisonous substance, though already taken, is not recognized as poison by ignorant persons at first because of the presence of delusion, but is later determined to be poison upon seeing the effects produced by the poison, such as salivation and so forth;
in this same way, this illustration is given merely for that much [purpose], and not on the grounds that the power to kill was grasped and only later determined—that is the illustration.
Therefore, the connection is: "this is destruction."
Since there is no cause of destruction whatsoever apart from the existence of the entity itself, [the opponent asks] how that which pervades existence can be its pervader, and so forth;
the reply is "and because of incapacity."
Regarding the phrase "taddhetoḥ" (from that cause), this refers to the cause of destruction; and by the word "ca" (and), it also implies the state of being a non-agent.
Explaining this very point, he says:

And because there is a negation of the status of being an agent (*kārakatva*)—which is intended [to belong] to that which is considered to be a non-agent (*abhāvakārin*)—due to its being a non-agent; thus, that which is intended to be a non-substantial agent (*avastukārī*) becomes indeed an agent.
To demonstrate this incapacity, he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "siddhe hi" (for when [the thing] is established), the cause of destruction would either produce a destruction that is non-different from the entity or one that is different from it.

First of all, the first position is not tenable: for when an entity is already established, a causal agent that produces destruction does not create that entity, precisely because it is already established.
Nor is the second position tenable,
because for an entity whose action is different [from its state], there is nothing [new] either,
since it remains in that same condition.
Regarding the phrase "having that form or not having that form," etc.:

since destruction—whether it be of the nature of an entity or something other than that—is caused [in either case], the cause of destruction is ineffective; therefore, it is established that it is not required. As for how there is a negation of its causal activity, he says:
For those who maintain that destruction has a cause think that "destruction" is the non-existence of an entity;
however, we have stated that destruction is simply the very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity.
Therefore, it follows that this so-called "cause of destruction" produces destruction—that is, it produces non-existence.

In this regard, when this [objection] has been raised: if non-existence (*abhāva*) were some kind of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that were to be produced as an effect, then, because it is an effect, it would—like a sprout or similar things—be an existence itself and thus could not be non-existence.

Alternatively, just as a jar is produced as a jar-form and a cloth is produced as a cloth-form, yet a jar does not become a cloth simply because it is an effect; [so too must non-existence be understood].
Likewise, an existent (bhāva) should be produced as an existent, and a non-existent (abhāva) should also be produced as a non-existent;
it is not the case that an existent itself becomes [something else].
Therefore, that [position] is untenable. For an existent is "not becoming," and that is non-existence; thus, non-existence is the opposite of existence.
Nor does it follow that [an entity] has the nature of non-existence simply because it appears as having the nature of non-existence;

for if it were to appear as having the nature of non-existence by virtue of being an existent phenomenon (*bhavanadharman*), then its appearance as such would not even occur—this is precisely what is being questioned.
Furthermore, there is no appearance of non-existents as having mutually distinct forms.
Since non-existence (abhāva) is devoid of form and thus lacks the nature of an effect, the statement "one produces non-existence" would mean "one does not produce existence.
Consequently, the cause of destruction would merely be performing a negation of action;
even so, despite this negation of action, this cause of destruction remains ineffective.
"Why is it that a thing does not depend on anything else for its destruction?"—thus is established the independence of a thing with respect to its own destruction.
Now, even if destruction is causeless, how is there such independence of the thing with respect to destruction?
For that is its very nature, by virtue of which it ceases upon encountering a contradictory factor.

Just as for others there is a stream [of existence] that is [stopped] by a hammer or similar object, so too, since there is no cessation of the preceding contradictory [state] in the absence of such an agent, how can there be momentariness?
That is incorrect.

If the nature of a thing consists in its dependence upon a contradictory [factor], then, since there would be a difference between its earlier and later forms, it would follow that it is impermanent. If, on the other hand, that nature exists even previously, then its cessation would have to occur even before;
yet, if it does not cease at that time because the contradictory factor is absent, [then it cannot depend upon it].
How, then, can there be the nature of depending on an opponent?
Because the nature of depending on an opponent exists only when the opponent is present, and not at any other time.
If that which is contradictory does not assist the thing [it opposes], how can it depend upon it?

Or, if there is assistance, then even in the presence of the contradictory, the other entity would arise; consequently, the prior entity would be seen remaining in its former state, because it would not cease as long as the contradiction is not removed due to the absence of [its] presence.
If it then ceases, the cessation of the entity is not due to its dependence on a contradictory factor;
and if it does not destroy the entity, how can it be a contradictory factor?

Furthermore, for those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*), it is not the case that existence (*sattā*) ceases upon the presence of an opposing factor; rather, it simply does not arise.

For instance, as the jar itself undergoes cessation, it depends on auxiliary causes such as a mallet to become a producer of shards, thereby failing to initiate subsequent similar moments. Thus, there is a non-arising of the continuum (*santāna-anutpatti*), but the stream does not cease by depending on an opposing factor.

And because a state that is about to arise through a preceding continuum fails to arise when a contrary factor is present, for this very reason those of dull intellect form the determination that destruction has a cause, and they perceive a contrary nature in things such as a mallet; thus everything is well-established.
Therefore, since it is independent, wherever destruction is observed by you to occur, it happens there solely by way of its own intrinsic nature.

Surely, even if destruction were causeless, it would only be causeless at the very moment the destruction of a jar or the like is perceived, and not prior, because it was not perceived before; for a jar or the like arises with the property of persisting for only a single moment. But surely, just as there is no arising from its own causes with the property of persisting for only a single moment, so too there could be arising with the property of persisting for multiple moments, for causal complexes are seen to possess diverse potencies.
In this regard, it might be argued that there could be some [cause] which produces an imperishable nature;
to this, he says "asmāt" (from this), etc.
And from this, which is a mere existence consisting of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [the effect would follow] even elsewhere, despite being unperceived due to spatial and other obstructions.
In the same way, because of the presence of its opposite when it is perceived, one considers that destruction occurs by its very nature even prior [to that perception].
First, regarding those things whose destruction is observed: if their destruction were not momentary, then the very cognition of destruction would be impossible.
For instance, if an entity were to persist into the second moment, it would have to remain forever, because its nature would be to endure for two moments even during that second moment.

And at that time, the entity must remain for a second moment as well; because its nature is to persist for two moments, it would necessarily remain in the subsequent moment too. This should be understood for each successive moment, whereby the entity would persist until the end of saṃsāra. Alternatively, if the entity’s nature in the first moment were to persist for two moments, then in the second moment, it would persist for only one moment.
Nevertheless, because those two natures are distinct, there would be momentariness;

yet even so, in the first moment, the entity would be non-momentary due to its nature of persisting through multiple moments, as it has been stated that this would entail the consequence of its remaining until the end of saṃsāra.

[The opponent objects: "But surely, even in the second moment, although the entity does not persist into subsequent moments, it still possesses a duration of two moments because it persists in the previous moment as well, since its form remains undifferentiated from before."
For it is not the inherent nature of an entity that it should abide in one moment and then abide in another moment;

if that very same nature persists in the second moment, then since it abides in one moment and will abide in another, it would likewise abide in two moments. This should be understood for each subsequent moment as well, and thus there would be no destruction of the entity.
And since it is observed [that things perish], the inference of momentary destruction follows from the fact that its perception would otherwise be inexplicable.
But then, how can there be an inference of momentary perishability regarding unobserved produced things, given that their very destruction is not perceived?

This is not a fault, because if that very same intrinsic nature (svabhāva) which exists in their first moment also exists in the second and subsequent moments, then there is indeed "coming into being after having not existed" (abhūtvā-bhavana), just as in the first moment. Alternatively, if in the first moment there is only its birth and no duration, and in the second moment there is only its duration and no birth,
even so, momentariness (kṣaṇikatva) would still be established.
Because there is no difference between birth and that which is born, or between duration and that which endures,
it is not logical for duration to exist in the second moment without birth;
yet if there is birth, then there is no duration, because duration occurs only in the second and subsequent moments.
Since it is the same in the second moment and so forth, there is only arising everywhere and no stability; thus, there is momentariness.
Furthermore, because the connection with successive moments—which is distinct from one another—is non-different from the produced entity (*kṛtaka*), there is indeed momentariness.
He states the meaning of this verse with the words "this is that" and so forth.
"This" refers to destruction;
as it occurs in some case, such as a jar, when a hammer or similar object is present, so it is elsewhere too— even prior to the presence of the hammer,
and even when there is an obstruction by space or other factors.

Regarding what was previously proposed— that there are two [types of] means of establishing a factual entity— he says "therefore" (*tataḥ*) to conclude that: for this reason, whatever inference has an existent thing as its object is of only two kinds, by way of the two marks (liṅga) consisting of effect (*kārya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Why? Because only those two—effect and essential nature—are necessarily connected to their own probandum; thus, the analysis of the compound is: "that inference for which the effect is the mark," and likewise, "that [inference] for which the essential nature is the mark."
In each case, that which pervades is the probandum (*sādhya*): for an effect, the cause is the pervader and thus the probandum;

for an essential nature (*svabhāva*), the essential nature itself is the pervader and thus the probandum. This is because there is an invariable connection (*pratibandha*) between those two very marks—the effect and the essential nature—and the subject (*liṅgin*) in which they are to be proven.
With reference to non-apprehension, he says "from activity," and so forth.
From activity...

Since the characteristics of definitive cognition (*sanniścaya*) and linguistic convention (*śabdavyavahāra*) are preceded by intellect and preceded by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), when there is a non-perception of that entity which is the object of activity—that is, when that entity is not perceived through either perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*)—a discerning person should not engage [with it]. By this much, the status of non-perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated even for an imperceptible object; the connection is that the third reason, non-perception, is said to be the indicator (*gamaka*).

"Without distinction" means that, having set aside the qualification "having a perceptible object," he demonstrates that very same point in a general sense regarding any object to be proven by the phrase "ascertainment of existence" (*sanniścaya*), and so forth.
An ascertainment of existence is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of "existent" that arises subsequent to a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The word "sat" (being) is a resonance that follows immediately after that [negation];
likewise, there is the performance of what is "sat" and the conventional usage of "sat.
Indeed, when these are negated, everything—both that which has the visible as its object and that which has the invisible as its object—is negated.
[Objection: But was it not stated in the *kārikā* that "activity" (*pravṛtti*) [is the object]? How then is it explained in the *vṛtti* as "the ascertainment of existence," and so forth?
[Response: He says, "Because of the ascertainment of existence," etc.

Since linguistic conventions proceed from the ascertainment of things that exist (*satām*), therefore those three—existence, ascertainment, and linguistic convention—are called "activity," because they are limbs of activity and because they are the causes for a person's engagement.
Therefore, there is no contradiction between the Sūtra and the Vṛtti.
What, then, is the reason that the conventional usage of "existent" ceases when perception ceases?
For it was stated previously that non-perception itself—both types of it without distinction—is non-existence.
And that non-existence, in the case of remote non-apprehension, is stated from the perspective of the cognizer;
for the cognizer determines that what is not being apprehended does not exist,
not by virtue of the object itself.
For in this way, the existence or non-existence of a remote object is doubtful;
therefore, that remote entity does not exist for the cognizer as long as there is no cognition of it.
Why is that?
Even though that object exists, because it is remote and unperceived, it does not perform its function;
since it does not perform its function for that person, although it exists, it is as if non-existent.
In reality, however, that which is not perceived is neither existent nor non-existent;
why?
Because even among existing things, there are times when they are not perceived due to the remoteness of their nature and so forth, yet this does not result in the certainty of their non-existence.
In some cases there is a determination of existence for that non-apprehension, because it is the same even in the case of non-existent things;
"tad" means "therefore," and the connection is that "this" refers to existence.

Of what nature is that which is characterized by non-apprehension and remote in terms of place and so forth? Since there is an absence of means of valid cognition for the cognizer—due to the absence of perception and inference—it ceases; but what does it do by virtue of the object itself?
Others read "upalabdhilakṣaṇam" [instead of "anupalabdhilakṣaṇam"], meaning that it turns back linguistic conventions based on its own causes;
since "existence" (sattva) is metaphorically [identified with] "perception" itself, the meaning is that such existence has ceased.
