For this very reason, for which things is this non-apprehension [considered] a non-apprehension that has reached the conditions for apprehension?
That which is non-existent even in terms of its objective reality—
by reason of the word "also" (api), it is also [non-existent] by virtue of the cognizer; what is the cause?

Because it is unfit for occurrence and because it is fit for the conventional usage of "non-existent," the non-apprehension of that [non-apprehension] also possesses an equal degree of validity regarding this object— the negation of the conventional usage of "existent"— by virtue of its being a negator of that very usage.

This non-apprehension which has reached the conditions for non-apprehension (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptānupalabdhi*)—even though it has the result of the ascertainment of non-existence—the analysis of the compound is: "that of which the result is the ascertainment of non-existence" (*asanniścayaḥ phalaṃ yasyāḥ*).
He explains [the passage] beginning with "in the case of non-existence" (*asattāyām*) and so forth:
for even in the case of non-existence— that is, even when there is no certainty—
it is simply not possible that an entity which is capable of being perceived should not be perceived while existing (*san*) and all other causes of perception are present.
Furthermore, the non-apprehension of a remote object in the past does not establish its non-existence;
for non-apprehension is characterized solely by the cessation of perception, inference, and scripture.

In this regard, the scope of the treatise is limited to this specific section; therefore, many topics that are irrelevant, not necessarily implied, and remote by nature and so forth are not included in the treatise.
This means that they are not even objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as he says they are "beyond the senses" (*atīndriya*);
nor are they objects of inference (*anumāna*), because they lack any inferential mark (*aliṅga*).
They are called "signless" (aliṅga) because they possess no indicative mark;
how then can there be an absence of those objects that transcend the senses, based on non-perception characterized by the cessation of the three means of valid cognition?
It is not so.

The proponent [states]: "This [is the case] regarding all objects"— that is, regarding those remote in terms of place, time, and intrinsic nature— by means of the cessation of the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely, by the cessation of perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and scripture (*āgama*).

Regarding the word "of that" (tasya), it refers to the scripture; for if the scripture were applied to a subject matter that is not conducive to human goals (*puruṣārtha*)—that is, where there is no *adhikāra* or qualification—it would follow that [the scripture] does not function [as an authority].
This is because of the statement beginning with "for the scripture... and so forth.
"Otherwise" means if the scripture were to function by relying on a subject matter that is not conducive to human goals.
Since a treatise that consists of incoherent chatter and expresses disconnected ideas lacks authority,
one might argue that all things are useful for human ends; to this, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "tatra" and so forth:
"there," that is, in this context, refers to the introduction to the inquiry into the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*);
"restricted to each individual" means restricted to each person.
By this, he states the infinity of mental fluctuations due to the infinity of persons;
the analysis of the compound is: "those whose nature it is to arise from indefinite causes.
By this, [he shows] that even in a single person there is multiplicity [of fluctuations] due to the difference in causes.
Mental states of this kind need not necessarily be described in their entirety at every step, because that would be impossible;

nor need specific substances that are obstructed by time or space, or which are useless for human goals, be described. Therefore, the scripture does not take those as its subject matter. These mental states and those specific objects are referred to here using the masculine gender.
By applying the rule *pumān striyā* (Pāṇini 1.2.67), the masculine form remains as the remainder.
Nor are they the objects of direct perception; thus he says "na ca" and so forth.

Likewise, in the case of remote objects— that is, those remote in terms of space and so forth— there is no capacity to produce cognition due to the lack of proximity of their own form, because of the non-application of its own causal power.
By this, the statement "they are beyond the senses" has been explained; he says "and that [inference] necessarily... and so forth, to show that they are not even the objects of inference.
"Of these" refers to those separated by space and so forth;
"by which" refers to the perception of the effect;
and "not those" refers to those that are remote.
Since even the non-perception of the invisible— namely, "all"—
is the very basis for the certainty of cessation, that is, the certainty of non-existence, therefore...
This non-apprehension of the unperceivable, expressed as "this is not," has the result of determining existence;
it does not have the result of determining non-existence, nor does it serve as a basis for the linguistic convention of existence, because there remains doubt regarding its non-existence.

For this reason, it may be argued that non-apprehension is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) because its fruit is ascertainment (*vyavasāya*). Since the fruits of the means of valid cognition are certainty, even perception is a means of valid cognition only with respect to those aspects for which it brings about ascertainment, even though it grasps all aspects.
One might object: "Could this not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the prohibition of activity?
To this he says "na hi" and so forth;
"this" refers to non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
The analysis of the compound *niḥśaṅkaparicchedam* is as follows: it refers to a mind whose determination (*pariccheda*) is free from doubt (*niḥśaṅka*).
The meaning is that such a mind does not form a certainty in the form, "I must certainly act," when doubt exists;
for even due to doubt, people such as farmers and others do sometimes engage in activity.

If it is asked, "How then is its validity stated to consist in the result of non-engagement? he says, "In that case—this," and so forth. "In that way" means in that form; this cause of non-engagement, called non-perception (*anupalambha*), is "faultless," meaning free from defects, provided that someone were to act upon it preceded by certainty.

By means of this principle—that one should engage in positive linguistic usage (*sadvyavahāra*) and so forth based on valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—this non-perception of the unobservable is said to have the result of non-engagement; that is, it is said to have the result of negating certain positive linguistic usage and the like.
However, since doubtful positive linguistic usage and the like are not negated, human activity may still occur.

"Arising from a specific excellence of the mark" (*liṅgātiśayabhāvinī*): the "mark" (*liṅga*) is non-perception (*anupalabdhi*); its "excellence" (*atiśaya*) is its specific qualification, namely the fulfillment of the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*). That [non-perception] in which this "existence" (*bhāva*), i.e., the actual presence of that [qualification], exists is so described;
the meaning is that it possesses a specific mark.
In other words, it is the non-perception of something that has reached the conditions for perceptibility.
He explains [the verse] with the words "here," etc.;
"here" refers to the ascertainment of cessation,
as was previously illustrated.
Furthermore, as for what was stated [in verse] 202–3: "Some [non-perception] has non-existent cognition as its result, depending on a distinction of causes," and so forth.
"Non-apprehension is non-authoritative"— this should not be understood without qualification;
rather, it refers to a nature (svabhāva) that is remote in terms of location and so forth, as well as an indicative mark (liṅga).
The ignorance of these two [the self and the world] is established by means of knowledge that makes their nature known; this principle has been illustrated [in the preceding verse].
Regarding the proof of non-existence, there is no [need for] a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). 1.203.

The meaning of the whole is this: ignorance of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the cessation of perception (*pratyakṣa*), and ignorance of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is the cessation of inference (*anumāna*); this principle has been illustrated regarding the cessation of both perception and inference with respect to an imperceptible object (*adṛśyaviṣaya*).
He explains by means of the words "of whomsoever" and so forth:
"of whomsoever," such as a piśāca or the like,
"that" refers to its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).

"By the mere non-perception of that" means by the mere non-perception of its object, which consists in the cessation of perception; as was stated previously regarding "that which is called 'non-existent,'" such as:
"because even existing things are sometimes not perceived," and so forth.
By this, the ignorance regarding intrinsic nature has been explained;
now, in order to explain the ignorance regarding the means of cognition, he says "yopi" and so forth.
The explanation of the term "of the indicator" (*jñāpakasya*) is "of the mark" (*liṅgasya*); thus,
an object beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) is rejected,
such as [the claim] that "there is no dispassionate mind," and so forth.

Likewise, due to the absence of a probans (*liṅga*) that indicates it, either a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) is negated here; it is the particularity that is negated, not the mere locus (*dharmimātra*),
as in [the case of the argument] "there is no giving," and so forth.
The term "dānaṃ ca hiṃsā-viratiśca" is a dvandva compound; it refers to the volitions directed toward those objects,
meaning the volitions of giving and the volitions of abstaining from violence.
Regarding the status of being a cause for worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) as a cause for results such as heaven:
here, the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of volitions (*cetanā*) is not rejected, because they are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
rather, it is stated that they lack the specific essential property (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) of being a cause for worldly prosperity.

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: "But since volitions are perceptible, their status as a cause of prosperity is also, by virtue of being identical with them, perceptible itself; so how could there be error?
and so forth—this implies that one who is deluded even regarding a perceptible object might even go so far as to deny it.
To the question "In what way is it perverted?", he says:
"Those which have that fruit," and so forth.
Those specific volitions (*cetanā-viśeṣa*) which are seen to be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and to have that fruit—that is, those whose fruit is not spiritual excellence (*anabhyudaya*).
Because of its similarity to those,
he asks how there can indeed be similarity, and says:
"because there is no immediate succession of the fruit."
As for those other volitions that do not have that result,
and those which do have that result— in both cases, no immediate succession of that result is observed.
"Not for that long" means that the non-existence of the result— that is, the absence of the fruit— does not follow merely from the non-perception of its immediate succession;
why is this so?

Regarding the phrase "of those separated by an interval" and so forth: because effects are observed to be separated from their cause by a lapse of time characterized by a gradual transformation through successive states— just as, for example, the toxic transformation in a rat or a mad dog caused by the *ālarka* (rabid) dog does not occur at the very moment the poison enters, but rather comes about upon the presence of a specific auxiliary time-factor (*sahakāri-kāla-viśeṣa*).
But it cannot be that there is simply another cause;
for this might be argued: since the transformation caused by poison in mice and other animals is observed at a later time, its existence [as a latent cause] is indeed logical.
But since the fruit of giving and so forth is never seen, how can its existence be established? To this he says "that," etc.,
[meaning] "the existence of that."
Since there is no contradiction in the existence of those two— the fruit of giving and other such acts, and the supersensible entity—
mere non-perception is not a means of valid cognition regarding the fruit of giving and so forth, or regarding the existence of the supersensible; thus,
it cannot serve as a subverting proof [to negate them].

Regarding existence—that is, being present—what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? There is no such means of valid cognition; therefore, the ascertainment of existence is not tenable, says the opponent.

To this, the Teacher replies: "Precisely for that reason," because there is an absence of both proving and refuting means of valid cognition regarding an object that is utterly beyond the senses, doubt is appropriate for a discerning person.

Alternatively, regarding an object that cannot be refuted and for which no proving means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) appears, it is appropriate to entertain this possibility: "Perhaps at some time a proving means of valid cognition will appear to someone who perceives it.
Therefore, due to doubt regarding the object or doubt regarding the means of valid cognition, there is no rejection [of the object].

Others, however, explain that since there is an absence of both proving and refuting evidence (*sādhaka-bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding whether a detached mind is a cause of exalted states (*abhyudaya*), there remains a doubt expressed by the phrase "for this very reason"; thus,
they maintain that a detached mind might indeed be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for omniscience,
and this proof will be set forth in the second chapter.
Precisely because the production of an effect occurs even from that which is spatially remote,
for that reason, although the sequence of the reading here is "among some objects and natures" within the context of those things beyond the senses (*atīndriya*),
nevertheless, the connection is to be understood according to what is appropriate.
For some intrinsic natures, such as those that are causes for prosperity and so forth, there might be a failure of proof regarding their indicator; how so?
Because of the absence of clarity in perception.

Because the experience of that object lacks the capacity to produce a determination of its nature as it was apprehended, and because there is no evidence— characterized by perception or inference— of certain things such as a mind free from attachment, [the existence of that object cannot be established].
To the question, "Why is there an absence of such an effect?
he says, "Of the causes," and so forth.
For there is no rule that an effect which necessarily makes itself known through its causes must be produced as something perceivable by all persons.
Others, however, explain it differently:
for certain proponents who claim that the causes of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) are inherent natures (*svabhāva*),

and for those things such as the dispassionate mind (*viraktacitta*) and so forth, there may be a non-establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes them known— that is, the means of ascertainment.
Why?
Because of the absence of clarity in vision;
this is what is meant.
Perception alone is the indicator of some object; however, due to its lack of clarity, it does not produce a certainty regarding all aspects of that object.

Furthermore, because there is no fixed rule that causes must produce their effects, one cannot deny—on the basis of the effect—that [the practice] is a cause for spiritual prosperity (abhyudaya), since the immediate effect is not perceived.
Likewise, because the perception of supersensuous objects—which is characterized by mental consciousness—is not acute, they are not apprehended through direct perception.
Nor can there be a determination of these [objects] by way of their effects, because there is no necessity for causes to produce an effect;
for there is no rule that a cause must necessarily produce an effect that makes itself known within another continuum.
Therefore, there is neither perception nor inference regarding them that could lead to such a conclusion;
thus, the non-existence of those supersensible objects follows merely from the absence of any such evidence as previously described.

For even in the case of certain objects not perceived through perception or inference, they may later be manifested and cognized through perception or inference in due course—for instance, objects situated behind a wall or in an opening.
Thus, in this way, regarding a remote object, the non-perception of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) is not a proof of non-existence,
nor is the non-perception of its effect (*kāryānupalambha*);
however, the non-perception of its cause (*kāraṇānupalambha*) is a proof of its absence even in that case— so he says.

Regarding the passage beginning with "But in the case of an effect" (*kārye tu*), [the author] explains that even when an effect is remote by nature and so forth, the non-cognition of its producer— namely, the non-apprehension of the cause— is indeed a means of proving its absence; this is what he clarifies with the words "by its own nature" (*svabhāva*) and so on.

When the non-existence of a nature whose object is remote (*viprakṛṣṭaviṣaya*) is to be proven, it is said that only the non-perception of its nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) is a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), whereas the non-perception of its cause (*kāraṇānupalambha*) is indeed a means of valid cognition. But surely, in the case of a remote object, the non-perception of the cause itself cannot be ascertained; how then could it establish the absence of the effect?
It can truly be said that,
in the absence of a cause, an effect necessarily does not occur in an unspecified domain; it is with this slight degree of precision that this [principle] is introduced.
For this very reason, he states generally "na hyasti" and so forth;
then the opponent says "nanu" and so forth.
Since smoke is observed in dwellings and other places even when fire has been extinguished, there is a deviation [from the rule];
thus, an effect is seen even when its cause is absent.
By the statement "the effect would not exist if the cause were absent," it is implied that the effect exists only during the time the cause persists.

We do not say that "as long as there is the existence of the cause, so long is there the existence of the effect," for if we did, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) such as [the effect persisting] even upon the destruction of the cause would follow.
Rather, he says "devoid of a cause" and so forth to explain what is actually expressed by this statement.
Thus far, it has been stated assuming stability;
however, if the cause is momentary, there is no persistence of the effect once the cause has perished—so how can there be any suspicion of deviation?
For instance, that moment of smoke produced by fire does not persist at all once the fire has perished.
Because it perishes due to its momentariness,
that smoke which remains later has smoke alone as its cause and not fire;
demonstrating this very point, he says:
"And not thus," and so forth;
"thus remaining" means that even when the initial cause has perished, that which remains for a period of time is its material cause— that is, it has as its material cause a previously ceased cause.
How then is it said that even subsequent smoke has fire as its cause? To this he says "by way of succession," and so forth:
from beginning to end, fire alone produces each moment of smoke.
That moment of smoke [produces] another, and that too another; thus, clarifying this very point through such a succession, he says:
"due to the assistance of the continuum" (santānopakārāt).
Because it is produced at the very beginning of the continuum, it is designated as the "effect" [of that cause];
therefore, even though it occurs later, it is designated as the effect of that specific cause.
If the absence of a particular cause could somehow be established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it is determined that its fruit—the result of that cause—does not exist.
This was stated with the intention of establishing the non-existence of an object that has been specifically indicated; however,
this is not a means of valid cognition regarding an unindicated object, because [proofs such as] essential nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth result from a logical connection (*pratibandha*).

Regarding the phrase "of the object" (*arthasya*), which refers to the pervader (*vyāpaka*): when the non-existence of that [pervader] within the subject (*liṅgin*)—which is not distinct from its own nature—is to be proven, both the non-perception of the nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) and the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) are the means of proving absence (*abhāva*).
This is the topic at hand, which he explains with the words beginning "the absence of the nature" (*svabhāvābhāva*).
The phrase "some [person]" refers to the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).
If the pervading nature of this pervaded entity were established as being unperceived, then it would constitute a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*);

and the non-perception of the cause or the pervader would be a valid means of cognition only if the absence of those two—the cause and the pervader—were apprehended through some logical reason (*hetu*).
He states the meaning of the verse with the words "If" (*yadī*) and so forth, under the heading "non-perception of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvānupalambha*);
the connection is: "if the non-existence of this causal agent (*kāraka*) were established."
And since the absence of a pervasive intrinsic nature is established through some indicative reason— namely, non-perception of that which meets the conditions for perceptibility—
this very [nature], whether as a producer or as a pervader, being thus proven to be non-existent, successively causes the cessation of its effect and its pervaded.

If the non-existence of that [cause] is unestablished— that is, if the absence of the causal factor and the pervader is unestablished— then because there remains doubt regarding both the effect to be averted and the property to be pervaded,
if it is claimed that the mere non-perception of that [cause] is not a valid means of knowledge when its own-nature's absence is to be proven, [then the following applies].
How, then, is the non-existence of an entity such as a jar established when it is not perceived by itself? He provides the answer with the words "of the perceptible," and so forth.

The meaning is that non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) has been stated as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding an object that is remote (*viprakṛṣṭa*), but not regarding an object that is perceptible (*dṛśya*).
The phrase "of the perceptible" refers to an entity whose intrinsic nature and so forth are not remote, which exists yet remains unapprehended.

When is the non-existence of an entity—that is, its non-existence as a presence—perceived? It is perceived when there is no possibility for a cause of non-perception; [in such a case], what is the cause of that non-perception?
The meaning is: "when there is no deficiency of other causes," that is, when all other conditions for perception are present;
this is the explanation beginning with the words "for an entity... and so forth.
If an entity were not remote from its own nature and so forth,
it would be perceived by its respective grasping instrument; that is to say, whatever the sense faculty is that grasps a particular thing, that entity would necessarily be apprehended by it—
such is the entity as previously described.

When the obstacles to perception— such as "obstruction" and so forth (the word "and so forth" including deficiencies, impediments, and the like)— are absent, and the conditions for apprehension are present; that is to say, when they exist.
Furthermore, why is it determined that what is not perceived as existing is non-existent?
Since such a thing, being existent and meeting the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*),

is invariably perceived, this very reason— which was stated as "the non-perception of that which is visible" (*dṛśyasya adarśana*) and so forth for the sake of determining the absence of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)— is to be understood here as well.
In what case [is there fallacy] when, despite the absence of both the reason and its pervader in the probandum, there is also a contradiction with the probandum, and so forth?

When there is the perception of that which is incompatible with the non-existence of the probandum—that is, with that whose absence is to be established—there occurs the ascertainment of the non-existence of the object to be negated. Why is this?
Because when an incompatible entity exists, its presence precludes the existence of that [non-existent].
He states why the explanation beginning with "For he who... does not suffice, because it subverts the existence of that very thing which is intended to be negated.
Regarding the passage beginning with "tad" and so forth:

the meaning is that of those two contradictory [causes], their respective material bases (*upādāna*), there exists a mutual deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) between them; by virtue of being the locus (*āśrayatvena*) of that deficiency, just as the material base of coldness is the locus of the deficiency of the material base of heat, and the other is likewise the locus of the other.
For that reason, because there is a contradiction in the simultaneous commencement of two contradictory things in one place,
when one of those two contradictories is present, there occurs the cognition of the absence of the other,
as was stated previously regarding the varieties of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).

Although the phrase "there is no cold touch here because of fire" and so forth is not explicitly heard as being "non-perception" (*anupalabdhi*) in this context, nevertheless, this logical mark (*liṅga*) called "contradiction of essential nature" (*svabhāvaviruddha*) is not stated separately from non-perception; for what reason?

Thus, let it be granted that the cognition of an absence may indeed arise from such a non-perception of the perceptible, since it proceeds from non-perception itself, and because the understanding of contradiction arises from that very non-perception, which in turn establishes the absence through contradiction.
Furthermore, how could it not be the case that this is not inference at all, but rather a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*)? Thus asks the Teacher.
"Because it requires an example," and so forth—the opponent [argues]; for inference, being characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), requires an example;
thus he states precisely that requirement of an example.
Regarding the phrase "na hi" (for not), the Teacher asks: "Why is it not so? in reference to this non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "that," the opponent asks: by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is it to be understood that such things as a sky-flower are non-existent, such that this could serve as an example?
If it is argued that non-existence, such as that of a sky-flower, is to be understood from the very mark of non-apprehension,
then how can the proof of non-existence regarding that [sky-flower] and so forth be established without an example— that is, devoid of an illustrative instance?

Alternatively, if there were an example, it would entail the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because one would have to posit yet another [example] for that as well; and since such an infinite regress would exist, there would be no comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*),
because the fault of infinite regress arises from the status of being an example.
Therefore, the establishment of the non-existence of that which lacks any designation must be made without an example;

likewise, in other cases as well— such as in the formulation "there is no jar here because it is not perceived despite meeting the conditions for perception"— non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is not an inference (*anumāna*), because it does not depend upon an example.

The Master has stated this repeatedly: even while hearing it, that "beloved of the gods"—meaning a fool—is not clever enough to comprehend that in the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), it is not non-existence (*abhāva*) that is proven, but rather the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*). Thus, despite the presence of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), he raises the objection that it is unestablished (*asiddhi*).
He begins to demonstrate the very example with the words "For the cause," and so forth:
non-apprehension of what is apprehensible— that is, the non-apprehension of the perceptible— is the cause, the reason, for the conventional usages regarding non-existence.
Thus, non-apprehension, by its own presence— that is, by the presence of itself—
establishes these linguistic conventions of non-existence which have as their cause its own nature, namely the form of non-apprehension; this being so, what kind of example is there in every case?

The formulation is as follows: that which possesses a suitable proximity to the totality of its own causes—the totality of its own causes being the collection of its own causal factors—and which has a suitable proximity within that [totality], such as a sprout, is so described. Furthermore, the formal argument is: [the subject] possesses a suitable proximity to the totality of its own causes.
Wherever the complete and unobstructed cause of something exists, that thing must exist there; for example, as with a sprout and so forth.

Furthermore, the state of being the cause for the conventional designation of "non-existent" belongs to the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Why?
He says "non-existence," etc., to show that here it is only the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of non-existence that is being established, and not non-existence itself;
for in this case of the non-perception of the perceptible, non-perception alone is non-existence.

As was stated previously, non-existence itself is not what is being proven; rather, the connection is that precisely because it is the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) that is being proven here, this non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is included within the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

The inference of the conventional designation of non-existence for an effect based on the non-perception of its perceptible cause—that which has this very [non-perception] as its defining characteristic—is shown here as a general compound (anyapadārtha). Subsequently, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied.
Furthermore, in the case of inferring an effect from a complete cause, it is an inference of capacity; thus, it is included within the *svabhāvahetu*.
We shall explain this in the fourth chapter.

While there may be an example for the non-perception of the perceptible, how can there be one for the non-perception of the imperceptible? To this he says, "By the word 'existent' (*sac-chabda*)," and so forth. When the negation of the conventional usage of "existent" is to be proven regarding things remote in space and so on, by means of the cessation of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa-nivṛtti*), the absence of the effect is proven due to the absence of its cause; therefore, in this case, the example is not merely that which is devoid of any nature (*nirupākhyam*), but also sprouts and the like which are absent due to the deficiency of their efficient causes. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

Whatever has its causes incomplete does not come into being, just as a sprout devoid of a seed; and since the conventional usage of "existent" is absent when there is non-perception of the visible, this is the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*).
Furthermore, as for what was stated:

As for how that non-existent, indefinable [object] is to be understood, even in that case, this activity characterized by the conventional usage of ignorance is negated by means of the example of the indefinable through non-apprehension; however,
its absolute non-existence is not being proven.
What is the reason?

[It is because] "non-perception" (*anupalabdhi*) and so forth refers to the perception of the head of a rabbit, for instance, as distinct from horns and the like; it is non-perception by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
That very non-existence of a hare’s horn, which has that [non-perception] as its defining characteristic,
would be established only if this non-existence were established as the object in the case of non-apprehension of the unobservable (*adṛśyānupalabdhi*).
Since the conventional usage of "non-existent" (*asad-vyavahāra*) is already established even by that [absence], what is the purpose of that conventional usage?

Furthermore, since the cause for the conventional usage of "existent" (*sad-vyavahāra*) is absent even in the case of non-perception of the imperceptible (*adṛśyānupalabdhi*), the non-occurrence of such usage is already established; thus, what is the point of establishing it through the negation of the conventional usage of "existent"?
Likewise, there is no purpose whatsoever in an example characterized by the presentation of a previously established object within the context of non-perception. To this, he says:
The phrase "this is it," and so forth,
means that this is being established for the sake of one who is deluded;

that is to say, having accepted non-apprehension of the perceptible as the cause for the conventional usage of "non-existent" in some instances, [the opponent] acts in contradiction to the engagement in that conventional usage of "non-existent," failing to perform it.

Having accepted both the non-existence [of the object] through the non-perception of the imperceptible (*adṛśyānupalabdhi*) and the absence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which is the cause for the conventional usage of "existent," yet subverting and failing to effect the cessation of the conventional usage of "existent" in accordance with that acceptance, you are thus being addressed: "Since the conventional usage of 'non-existent' was established by you elsewhere by means of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*), that same [means] exists here as well;
therefore, apply the conventional usage of 'non-existent'."

Likewise, since you have employed the conventional usage of "existent" (sat) in some cases based on a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and a specific characteristic (*nimitta*), that same usage does not apply here to that which is indefinable (*nirupākhyam*); therefore, it is being demonstrated: "Do not employ the conventional usage of 'existent'. Just as with the indefinable, what is it like? It is like a rabbit's horn.

Just as in the case of a hare’s horn and the like, the conventional usage of "non-existent" occurs because of the non-perception of what is perceptible— which is the cause for such usage— so it is here as well; or else, "otherwise," just as there is the cognition of a sprout and so forth when its causes are present, so too is there the conventional usage of "existent."
Just as the cessation of the conventional usage of "existent" occurs with respect to that which is indefinable due to the absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),

or as the cessation of an effect occurs in another case when its causes are deficient, so too is it established that the cessation of the conventional usage of "existent" occurs with respect to remote objects.
Now, by what means of valid cognition is that very absence of perception— known as non-perception (*anupalabdhi*)— itself established?
It is not [established] by perception, because there is no contradiction with its having non-existence as its object;
nor by inference, because the latter is preceded by perception;
nor is it the non-perception of a connection with a location, because non-existence, being formless, cannot possess the nature of a related term.

Udyotakara and others maintain that since the locus (*pradeśa*) is not perceived, the reason (*hetu*) for establishing the property (*dharma*) suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*); thus, non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) does not possess the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).
To this, he replies:

we shall explain this later—that there is indeed a perception qualified by that [non-existence]; therefore, its non-perception is also established. Consequently, this non-perception is established by perception itself.
Regarding what was further stated—namely, "What is the purpose of showing an example in the case of non-apprehension?
[the author] says: "In other cases as well," and so forth.

Even in an inference that establishes through affirmation (*vidhi-sādhana*), why should the person to be convinced be made to understand by means of an example the probans, such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), which is pervaded by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) that acts as the pervader (*vyāpaka*)?
What is the reason?
Because the property to be proven (sādhya) is established by the very indication of the probans (hetu), which is pervaded by that [sādhya] according to its own nature;
thus, for one who is confused, it serves the purpose of reminding them of the relationship characterized by a certain object.

This very point— that the production of memory for a deluded person occurs here in the case of non-perception— is stated by means of an illustration in the passage beginning with "this is that," and so forth.
"In other cases as well" refers to things such as the horn of a hare (śaśaviṣāṇa).
Now, as for that which was stated by Ācārya Dignāga and others:
Regarding the formulation [of the argument], "The primal matter (pradhāna) and so forth do not exist because they are not perceived," the Teacher asks:
"And why should it not be so?"

The objector says, "tadartha" and so forth, according to his own intention: because when that object— the primary meaning— is negated, the designation expressing the substratum (dharmin), such as "primordial matter" (pradhāna) and so on, is not employed.

For there is no employment of an expressive word without that which is to be expressed; and when words such as "pradhāna" (the primal cause) are not employed, then it follows that they do not exist. In that case, only the word expressing the negation remains. Since a negation without an object of negation is impossible, the word expressing that negation cannot be employed.

And thus, since neither of the two propositions—that "the primal matter (pradhāna) and so forth do not exist"—is employed, where and what could possibly be proven? Consequently, the application of the proof [of non-perception] is futile; furthermore, because the subjects under discussion—the primal matter and so forth—do not exist, the logical reason would fail to be a property of the subject (pakṣadharma).

Alternatively, there is a mutual contradiction between the two terms of the proposition (*pratijñā*); for, by using the expression "the primal matter and so forth" (*pradhānādayaḥ*), their presence is implied, yet by the statement "they do not exist," their absence is asserted;
and these two—presence and absence—are contradictory when occurring simultaneously in one and the same place.
"This is not a fault," is the rebuttal;

for the referent of a word (*śabdārtha*) is established—that is, mounted—upon a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arisen from beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). And that property (*dharma*) is of three kinds, because it rests upon existence, non-existence, or both.

In that case, regarding the meaning of the word [as] "that which has no external primary cause (*pradhāna*) or the like as its material cause" (*bhāvānupādāna*), when this is the probandum (*sādhya*),

the reason (*hetu*) is "non-perception" (*anupalambha*) with respect to the subject (*dharmin*)— namely, the primary cause and so forth— which exists only within the transformation of the intellect (*buddhiparivartin*), insofar as it would possess the property of having an external primary cause and the like as its material cause (*tathā*).
In this context, non-apprehension consists precisely in apprehending [an object] as having its material cause in latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
it is not that the non-existence of that very subject (*dharmin*) established by conceptual construction is being proven.
Why?

He explains [the point] with the words "it has been stated," etc., on the grounds that if there were a negation of things such as *pradhāna* based on the usage of those very terms, then because of the lack of an object, the employment of words would not occur at all.

For if the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) were the denotable object, then upon the negation of that particular characteristic, because the referent of the word would be negated, the word expressing it could not be employed. However, this has already been explained: these words do not have the particular characteristic as their object;
rather, they appropriate as their own object the thing that appears in a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which originates from beginningless mental predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Why is it that these [cognitions] take as their object only that thing which is the domain of conceptual construction? To this he says:

"of the speaker who possesses that conceptual construction. He states the reason for this: [the speaker] is one who possesses a conceptual construction of a universal form based on existence, non-existence, or both.
"Yathā" and so forth:
because of the employment of words through the desire to communicate an object as it appears, without deviating from that appearing object.

Therefore, words take as their objects only those things that appear in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and likewise, they cause the listener to possess such conceptual constructions; this is the connection [between word and object].
What is the reason?
Because they generate conceptualizations of those forms,
and because they generate conceptualizations of general forms based on existence, non-existence, or both, words take as their objects only those things that appear within conceptualization;
this might be so.

Even if this were so, why would words not have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object, given that there is a cognition of the particular characteristic? To this he says, "And not," and so forth:

it is impossible to determine that [the word] has as its object that form which appears therein—that is, in the cognition which is the causal condition consisting of both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the effect (*kārya*).

In this context, the condition consisting of grasping (*upādāna-pratyaya*) is the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the speaker, which takes the form of the desire to communicate; because it is the cause of the word, the conceptual construction arising from the word in the listener is the "condition as effect" (*kārya-pratyaya*). For that which does not appear within the cognition of the word is not the meaning of the word.
And the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear therein, because it is devoid of a clear form;
[if you object: "But how can it be based on the absence of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), given that it would follow that it is non-conceptual by virtue of being produced from an object?"
And how could non-existence be the locus [of another non-existence], given that non-existence is not a cause?
And how could one [non-existence] be the locus of both, since that would entail the consequence of it being causeless?
To this, he says: "But that," and so forth.

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has the form of existence, non-existence, and both; its cognition is of existence, non-existence, and both. The latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) is deposited by that [cognition], and that from which its arising or production proceeds is described as such.
For this reason, it is said to have the nature of existence, non-existence, and both;
thus he states the second cause.
Regarding the phrase beginning with "that" (*tad*):

the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that aspect which appears within that very conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)— by way of its being existent, non-existent, or both— is what is called "having the properties of existence, non-existence, or both," by virtue of that determination.
This is what is meant:

that which arises from the latent impressions (vāsanā) deposited by the cognition of existence, and which appears as if it were a determination of the form of existence, is called a property of the entity (bhāvadharma).

In this same way, it should be understood for both existence and non-existence as well. Because conceptual constructions such as "existent" and so forth arise from the latencies (vāsanā) deposited by preceding cognitions of "existent" and so on, these conceptualizations are beginningless;
therefore, they are not produced by [external] entities and the like. Furthermore, the referent of a word is threefold.

Therefore, in this case, persons established upon the subject (dharmin) which is the referent of the word—standing as the basis for their dispute—deliberate upon the existence or non-existence of the *pradhāna* and so forth.
To the question of how they deliberate, he says:
"Does this object, appearing as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) from the uttered word 'pradhāna', have its basis in an external *pradhāna*, or not?"

When the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is that this appearance of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-pratibhāsa*), such as "primordial matter" (*pradhāna*) and so forth, does not have an external entity as its material cause (*bhāvānupādānatva*), then that very appearance of conceptual construction is the subject (*dharmin*). This is because, being of the nature of cognition (*buddhi-svabhāvatā*) and being personally experienced (*pratyātmavedyatva*), it is established by self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*) and thus cannot be rejected.

[Objection: But is not that very object apprehended by conceptual construction the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), since it is determined (*adhyavasāya*) as having the form of a particular characteristic?

And consequently, would not primordial matter and the like already be established by perception, and would not the word also have the particular characteristic as its object? [Response: He says [the following]:...
Nor can it be said that "it is that very thing," and so forth; for it is impossible to claim that the object appearing in conceptual construction is the external particular (svalakṣaṇa).
What is the reason?
Since that appearance of conceptual construction does not cease even when its own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) has not yet been attained, has not yet arisen, or has already ceased; furthermore,

because there exist those cognitions of other schools which have the habit of adhering to mutually contradictory, erroneous forms— such as permanence, impermanence, and so forth— with respect to real entities like pots, the appearance of the meaning of words [persists].
And that very object is not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); this is connected with the subject at hand.
To summarize this very point, he says:

Ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) consists of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); that in which these have a single locus is their mode of occurrence, and its state is "reality" (*tattva*). When this exists, the operation of words—which lack a basis in ultimate reality and are devoid of a foundation in the ultimate—would not occur with respect to objects that differ according to various philosophical systems (*darśana*) and are distinguished by differences in tenets (*siddhānta*).
Or, regarding the phrase "also for the past and the unborn": if this were so, there would be no application of words toward objects that are past or future;
likewise, no speech whatsoever could possess the quality of being about something non-existent or false.
Therefore, for the reason stated, this speech [is as it is].
It is considered to have as its object the conceptualized appearance of a thing that is the referent of a word.

Regarding the phrase "of that" (*tasya*): when it is to be proven that the appearance of conceptual constructs such as *pradhāna* (primordial matter) lacks an external substrate such as *pradhāna*—that is, possesses a form corresponding to its intended object or its imagined nature—then there is a non-perception of it "in that way.

This means that because there is a non-perception of it as having the intended form as its substrate, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*) nor is it a non-property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*). This is the meaning.
Furthermore, in this context, it is not the case that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which arises from the words "this very word" and so forth is what negates the object appearing therein;
for what reason?

Regarding that object appearing in conceptual construction, [it is presented] in the intellect of the listener... [Note 386-1: The property to be proven (sādhyadharma). Note 386-2: For the purpose of producing (utpādanārtham).]
Because a word is employed for the purpose of establishing [an object],
and in the absence of that [object], it would be impossible to employ the word because it is incompatible with an object that appears only as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, if the negation of the word and its object is being proven, then,

when the negation of the word and its object is the probandum (*sādhya*), the locus (*dharmin*) of that property to be proven— the non-existence— which is characterized by the word and its object, is itself refuted; consequently, the aggregate consisting of both the locus and the property would not be the probandum,
and the property to be proven alone would already be established.
Since the mere non-existence [of a thing] is established in some cases,

the explanation beginning with "if" and so forth refers to that; therefore, this property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is independent of that exclusion or qualification which belongs to its locus, namely, this non-existence.
For this reason, at the time of debate,

one should not indeed propose [an argument] by distinguishing between the positions of existence and non-existence (sadasatpakṣabheda); rather, it is the very entity itself that is investigated through the distinction between the theses of existence and non-existence.
Therefore, by discerning persons who do not deny the referents of words and who seek purposeful action,
because the arising of the result is bound to this [specific] entity (vastu).
Even if this is so, why should the referent of a word (*śabdārtha*) not be investigated?
To this he says "the referent" (*artha*), etc.:

for those who do not seek that [referent], but rather seek purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), what is the use of investigations—namely, investigations into existence and non-existence—concerning the referent of a word which is incapable of purposeful action?
He states an illustration: "Of a eunuch," and so forth.
Regarding the physical form—whether beautiful or deformed—of one who lacks masculinity, what is the use of investigation by a lustful woman desiring sexual union?

The explanation beginning with "na hi" (for not) should be connected as appropriate: for a non-existent word-meaning does not obstruct—that is, turn away from—any human goal, nor does an existent one accomplish—that is, bring about—one; [this is to be understood] according to the context.
What is the reason?
Because a person adheres to and determines that word-meaning as being external according to his adherence, yet it lacks such existence— that is, it does not exist—
either because it is non-existent or because it is not intended in accordance with reality.

— Since the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object as it truly is, or the particular characteristic of cognition, remains unobjectified by a word; for this very reason, a person engaged in the investigation of what exists and what does not exist always takes as his basis and makes as his object the thing-in-itself alone, disregarding and setting aside the appearance of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-pratibhāsa*), in that thing-in-itself where this human purpose is bound up,
such as in fire, meaning in the particular characteristic of fire.
Because of the inclusion of the word "etcetera," there may be burning, cooking, and so forth;
[the author] says this to show that such a purpose is also accomplished by means of the word-meaning (*śabdārtha*).
"Not indeed," and so forth;
"here" refers to the warding off of cold and the like;
why [is it not so] even when that experience is attained?
Even though there is the experience of that word-referent,
because that [referent] is absent— due to the absence of the remedy for cold and so forth— for that reason, this person seeking purposeful action [does not engage].

Therefore, it is not appropriate for one who has applied inquiry toward a word-meaning that is incapable—that is, incapable of purposeful action—to be attentive to it; for a woman desiring sexual union does not fix her attention on examining the beauty or ugliness of a eunuch who is incapable of engaging in intercourse. [The author] asks in order to refute the objections stated by Uddyotakara and others.
Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Ācārya Dignāga beginning with "of that which is imagined" (kalpitasya), what is its meaning?
He states the answer:
"The object of a word," and so forth;
because it is the object of conceptual cognition, the object of a word—such as the object of words like "Pradhāna" and the like—is [the conceptual construct].

By relying on the imagined nature of an external object characterized as *pradhāna* (primordial matter), the Master Dignāga, the proponent of logic, stated that the non-apprehension of this referent of terms such as *pradhāna*— which serves as its logical mark (*liṅga*)— is a property (*dharma*) when proving that it does not have existence as its material cause (*bhāvānupādānatva*).
Therefore, as for what is stated by Udyotakara and others:
"If the *pradhāna* is conceived as existing by means of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how can its non-perception be understood as its property?
Or, if the *pradhāna* is conceived as non-existent, even so, how can its non-perception be its property, given its non-existence?"
That is refuted because, since it is the object of conceptual cognition, it is only the word-meaning that is imagined; however,
the external *pradhāna* is not imagined as existing by means of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The opponent states, "Regarding that," and so forth, referring to the Master Dignāga’s intention, which is that the referent of the word "pradhāna" (the primary cause) cannot be found by relying upon an external, primary entity. 214-15.
The three means of valid cognition— characterized as perception, inference, and scripture—

are [the basis for knowledge] when other means of valid cognition are absent; that is, when perception and inference are absent, there is an absence [of knowledge] regarding things remote in space and so forth,
because those two, perception and inference, are lacking.
It does not pervade anything at all, yet it makes everything its object; the cessation of that [object] is the cessation of attachment.
Thus has it been stated here by the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī).

Because it has not entered into the present context— that is, because it is irrelevant to the investigation of the human goal (puruṣārtha) and because it was stated in this very section [at sūtra 1.2.01] that "many matters are unrelated to the scope of the treatise."
And this was stated while accepting the authority of scripture (*āgama*) regarding outsiders;
now, [the author] says "Moreover," and so forth, to show that there is no authority whatsoever for the objects of outsiders.

Because there is no necessary connection (*avinābhāva*)— that is, no inseparability— between words and real entities (*vastu*) possessing their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), no establishment of an object nor any ascertainment of an external thing arises from those words;
for they merely indicate the intention of the speaker.

Although the word "cloth" (*paṭa*) arises from the intention to speak of a "jar" (*ghaṭa*), it nonetheless lacks the fault of being causeless, because it is produced directly from the impact of the articulatory places (*sthāna*) and the vocal organs (*karaṇa*), and thus there is no deviation [from its causes].

Furthermore, for one who perceives the word "jar" as produced by the intention to speak of a jar, the inference of the intention to speak of a cloth from the word "cloth" occurs; and such perception by people exists indeed through context (*prakaraṇa*) and other means. Thus, there is no lack of invariable concomitance (*avyabhicāra*) in the inference of the intention to speak.

"In accordance with the state of being" (*yathābhāvam*) means according to its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); "from which" (*yataḥ*) refers to the fact that [the cognition] proceeds in accordance with the state of being. Thus, from words, the nature of the object—the intrinsic essence of the object—would be determined;
for those, namely the words, [are the cause].
Those whose occurrence is by virtue of the intention to speak are so described;
therein, "invariably concomitant with the intention" means not invariably concomitant with that very intention.
That very intention to speak does not occur without the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa);
therefore, there is indeed no deviation of words from their objects.
Thus he says, "And not," and so forth.
Those whose nature is to exist in accordance with reality and in accordance with things are so described.
He says that all [these qualities] belong to one whose faults are exhausted and who is compassionate, as they exist in accordance with reality.
If it is argued that even a word not connected to an actual object will convey its meaning, he replies:
"And not," etc.:
that word-characteristic whose nature is not tied to that object,
[is] "other" where it is not tied.

If the word has no authority regarding external objects, then what of this [inference]: "Because of the commonality of non-contradiction in the speech of a reliable person (āptavāda), whatever is the speech of a reliable person is non-contradictory,
just as, for example, 'all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are momentary' and so forth"?

And this is the word of a reliable person (*āptavāda*) even regarding an object that is entirely beyond the senses; therefore, since it is non-contradictory, the scripture is an inference because it possesses the general quality of being non-contradictory due to its non-contradictory nature. Thus, the teacher Dignāga stated that scripture has the nature of inference with respect to external objects.

To the question "How is that so?", [the author] states the contradiction with what has been accepted [by the opponent] with the words beginning "This is not," and so forth, and then provides the rebuttal.
This states that the Teacher, when asserting the ontological validity [of scripture], did not describe scripture as being inferential; rather, he did so with respect to human activity,
because this person, desiring action, is unable to remain without relying on the validity of scripture.
What is the reason?
It is because for some [actions], whose fruits are either perceptible or imperceptible, there is engagement or desistance as appropriate;
for it is heard that desisting from objects of volition such as violence yields great benefits by having heaven and so forth as their fruit.
Because it is heard in scripture that specific volitions of violence lead to results such as rebirth in hell and constitute great sins,
there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here that functions by the force of objective reality (*vastubala*) which could establish [the truth] independently of scripture;
nor is there any subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) from which one might turn away.

He states the very absence of a subverting factor [for the authority of scripture] with the words "the existence of that": because no contradiction is observed in the existence of the desired or undesired fruit through the aforementioned engagement and withdrawal,
and because this person wishes to engage by the power of scripture, it follows that one must engage when there is something to be engaged in.
"It is better to act after having examined such a scripture"—by this, the Master [Dignāga] states that the authority of scripture depends upon its examination;
however, not every treatise is subject to such examination.
However, that scripture and so forth is "connected" because of the mutual relationship between its subject matters;

it is "possessing a suitable means," meaning that within it there is a means for accomplishing the result that is consistent with [the goal]; thus, "connected and possessing a suitable means" is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).
If even such a statement were to express a human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), then it would be subject to investigation;
therefore, he explains that any other statement, distinct from the aforementioned nature, is not subject to investigation, by means of the words beginning with "the connection" (*sambandha*).

The mutual relationship between sentences is their connection through a process of integration (*upasaṃhāra*) or synthesis (*mīlana*), whereby they function as subordinate and principal elements toward a single intended object characterized by what is to be enjoined or prohibited.

He asks, "Of which [sentences] would there otherwise be no such assistance? and answers with the verse beginning "Ten pomegranates," etc.: "Ten pomegranates, six cakes, a bowl, a goat-skin, minced meat"—such are the sentences [in question].
For there is no synthesis of a single purpose among these [statements], because they are not mutually connected.
If one were to claim that this lack of connection constitutes a deficiency in the speaker or the author of the treatise— namely, the quality of speaking what is incoherent—
then those [teachings] whose means are impossible would have infinite results that are impossible to achieve.
Thus, a man seeking results should not take the trouble to examine those treatises which have such [unrealistic] fruits;
this is an explanation by way of contrast (vaidharmyeṇa) to the statement "this is a suitable means."
Those treatises for which the human goal is the fruit are described as such;
one should not, however, take the trouble to investigate those others which have goals other than the human goal as their fruit.

An example of a result whose means are impossible is "poison" and so forth; for instance, it is said that his poison is pacified only if he is adorned with the jewel located on the ear of the serpent-king Takṣaka.
And this is an example of that which cannot be accomplished and whose fruit is not a human goal,
like the examination of a crow’s teeth.
By the opposite of that— that is, by the reverse of those three aforementioned [characteristics]— the inclusion [of the means] is explained; by this [phrase],
"connected with this," it is explained that [the means] is "suitable" (anuguṇa), and by the phrase "capable of being practiced" (śakyopāya), it is explained that [the means] is "feasible."
The word "elsewhere" refers to that which is devoid of the triad beginning with [proper] connection;
"of attention alone" means of respect.
Thus, when there is an investigation, that scripture—which is endowed with the aforementioned three qualities—does not become subject to contradiction.
A person who engages with this scripture, which is free from contradiction, shines.
But what is the non-contradiction of this scripture? To this he says:
"By perception," and so forth; the first term *artha* signifies a real entity (*vastu*).
The second [term] refers to the object (*viṣaya*);
thus, the meaning is as follows:

the non-sublation of this treatise—by means of perception and inference respectively, both of which operate through the power of real entities (*vastubala*) and rely upon scripture—with respect to the two types of objects, seen and unseen, which are the referents of those [two means of knowledge], constitutes its non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*).

He explains [the verse] with the words beginning "pratyakṣa" (216–17): in the treatise, the "state of being perception" (*pratyakṣabhāva*)— that is, the state of being perceived— of those objects which are regarded as perceptions and accepted as such, is their non-sublation by perception.
With the words "Just as... and so forth, he demonstrates that in his own established doctrine, the object intended by direct perception is comprised within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
By the phrase "blue and so forth," he refers to the five objects such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest;
by this, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is stated.
"Pleasure and pain" refers to the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
"The perception of signs" (*nimittopalakṣaṇa*)— where "signs" (*nimitta*) refers to the characteristics of women, men, and so forth—
is by this [term] the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
By the mention of "attachment and so forth" (rāgādi), the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) is indicated;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), hatred, delusion, and the rest are included.
By the mention of "intellect" (buddhi), the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is indicated.
The compound consists of "blue and so forth," "pleasure and pain," "the discernment of signs," "attachment and so forth," and "cognition.

Thus, according to the treatise, those things considered to be perceptible are indeed perceptible, because blue and so forth are perceptible by means of visual consciousness and the other [sensory cognitions].

The connection with the subject at hand is as follows: because pleasure and the like are directly perceived through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), while those things not so intended and those objects not intended to be perceived are not perceived, their non-perception is determined by direct perception.

The word "yathā" (as) indicates the object [of the inference]: those things such as pleasure (*sukha*) which have the nature of being disposed in the form of sound (*śabda*) and so forth; their non-perceptibility follows from the fact that pleasure, pain, and delusion—which possess the intrinsic nature of sound and the rest—are not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This was stated by way of refuting the Sāṃkhya view;
now, by way of refuting the Vaiśeṣika and other views, he says:
"Substance is of two kinds."
A substance that is non-substantial (adravya) is, for example, space and so forth; and a substance that consists of multiple substances (anekadravya) is,
for example, a composite substance (avayavidravya).

Action such as upward throwing and so forth is the universal; "existence" refers to [universals] such as "cowness," and by the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is the inclusion of disjunction and the like.
For there is no perceptibility of anything else apart from the five [sense-faculties] with respect to objects such as blue;
this is because nothing is perceived apart from them.
An inference that proceeds by the force of real entities (*vastubalapravṛttānumāna*) is an inference that does not depend on scripture (*anāgamāpekṣānumāna*).

The fact that those things intended as its objects do not exist in that manner constitutes the state of being an object of inference; furthermore, that [inference] does not contradict the Four Noble Truths,
which will be established later.
The non-existence of those things that are not inferable is their "non-inferability," which means they cannot be sublated by inference,
as is the case with the self (*ātman*) and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), the Lord (*īśvara*), and others is intended.
For these [entities] possess no characteristic mark (*liṅga*) by which they might be inferable;
this too he will demonstrate:

when there are two objects that are extremely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), such as the domain of scripture (*āgama*), and one engages in reflection upon them through the contradiction between earlier and later [statements], then even inference depends upon scripture regarding that object.
"Non-contradiction" is the subject under discussion.
To the question "Of what kind is that non-contradiction?", he says:

having accepted as unrighteousness (adharma) that which consists of passion and so forth—namely, the nature of passion, hatred, and delusion—and having also accepted as unrighteousness the bodily and vocal actions produced by them, that is, those originated by passion and so forth.

For the sake of abandoning that— that is, for the removal of that unrighteousness— there is no instruction regarding bathing, the *agnihotra* sacrifice, and so forth; such as the claim that "the destruction of sin occurs through bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*)," or "the destruction of that sin occurs for which ghee and other substances are offered into the fire."
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), fasting and other such practices are included;
for instance, bathing and the like do not remove sin,
because there is no opposition between them and passion and so forth, which are the causes of sin.

This very [reliability] consists in the non-sublation of the entire range of objects that can be determined and ascertained through the aforementioned two kinds of means of knowledge— perception and inference. Because of this general characteristic of non-contradiction,

just as the word of a reliable person (*āptavāda*) is non-contradictory regarding an object that can be determined, so too is it non-contradictory even with respect to an absolutely imperceptible object, precisely because it is the word of a reliable person.
Furthermore, the teacher Dignāga has stated that the non-contradictory cognition arising from the mark characterized as the word of a reliable person (*āptavāda*) is inferential (vv.

217–18). He states that this [cognition] has as its object even that which is beyond perception (*parokṣa*), meaning even that which is extremely beyond perception (*atyantaparokṣa*), because there is no other way to engage with what is extremely beyond perception.
"If activity is indeed present, it is better that it proceed in this manner"—
this is the explanation of "of that" and so forth,
referring to that scripture whose status as an inference was pointed out by the teacher Dignāga.
The word "of this" (asya) refers to that which has been examined by us through the passage beginning with "the appropriate means" (anuguṇopāyam);
for this very reason, he says "of such a one" (evaṃbhūtasya), meaning "endowed with qualities such as connection" (sambandhādiguṇayuktasya).

Since there is a commonality of non-contradiction regarding that object which is accessible through perception and inference—due to the cause of its being non-contradictory—the non-contradiction of the cognition or understanding that arises from the word of a reliable person (*āptavāda*) concerning an object or domain accessible through perception and inference is inferred, even though deviation has been observed [in other cases].
Why? Because it is an exception [to the general rule of deviation].
Because it has that as its basis, its status as being based on the word of a reliable authority is established through the instruction of the lineage of teachers,
just like the cognition of other [objects].
This is just like the cognition regarding other objects— those within the range of perception or inference— that are not absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*).
Therefore, regarding an object that is absolutely beyond the senses, the cognition based on the aforementioned authoritative scripture— though it arises from words and is thus produced by sound—
is not like other verbal cognitions in that it merely communicates a [speaker's] intention;
rather, this cognition does not communicate an intention alone.
Because the particle *eva* is displaced in its position, [the meaning is as follows]:

rather, since that object which is desired and is accessible neither through perception nor inference is non-contradictory by virtue of the reasoning just stated, there is indeed inference for a person desiring action based on the force of his intention;
however, in reality, it is not inference, because words lack a relationship with their objects.
The word "also" (*api*) is used for the purpose of clarifying this very point; showing the non-contradiction of the authoritative word (*āptavāda*) by way of another method,
[the author] says "or else," etc.,
[meaning that] everything to be abandoned is suffering.
Nirvana, the abandonment of all afflictions, is that which is to be adopted;

its reality is the unerring nature of both the truth of suffering and the truth of cessation. Together with the means, there exists the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, as well as the means for that [reality].
The means for that which is to be abandoned is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), and the means for that which is to be adopted is the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).

This is because these truths— the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted along with their respective means— have been shown by the Blessed One and are established through certainty by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) derived from the power of facts (*vastu-bala-āyāta*).
In the word of the Blessed One, there is no contradiction regarding the primary subject matter characterized by the four truths;
for the subject matter characterized by the four truths is primary because the attainment of nirvana occurs through its realization.
Therefore, it is non-contradictory with respect to the primary subject matter.

Knowledge arising from the words of the Blessed One regarding even objects that are extremely beyond the senses constitutes either inference or verbal testimony; the word "or" (vā) has the sense of an alternative in view of the preceding types [of valid cognition].
The means for those two—what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted—are their "means" (*tadupāyau*).
This is a *dvandva* compound consisting of: "the thing to be abandoned," "the thing to be adopted," and "their means."

The non-erroneousness— that is, the truthfulness and non-contradiction— of those things taught by them, taught by that authoritative person, when examined through inference, is established as being non-false; this is just as, for example, the four noble truths beginning with suffering [are established] through investigation according to the method that will be explained in the second chapter.

Regarding the phrase "of this [treatise]": because that which was previously indicated by the Blessed One has now been analyzed, it refers to this treatise characterized by the fourfold truth. Furthermore, what is its nature? It is "serviceable for the purpose of the person" (*puruṣārthopayogin*);
the "purpose of the person" (*puruṣārtha*) is nirvāṇa, and "serviceability" (*upayoga*) therein means being the cause; that which possesses this is so described.

Therefore, because there is no contradiction with that which is fit for application and fit for cultivation, one accepts the same status even in another object— though inaccessible to perception or inference; thus, the acceptance of non-contradiction serves neither for deception nor for contradiction.
What is the reason?
Because there is no contradiction and because it is not sublated by a valid means of cognition.

And regarding the primary object characterized by the fourfold truth, since the speaker has not deceived the person, there is no purpose for the speaker’s false statement in the third instance; because of its fruitlessness, one might think that such a statement could sometimes arise even from ignorance. To this, he says "that," and so forth.

"In both ways" means that this scriptural authority (*āgama*), being of the nature of inference (*anumāna*) according to the manner indicated by the two verses, has been described as such out of necessity;
it should be understood that it is "inference" because it is the cause of inference.
If activity proceeds from scripture, it is better that it proceed from such a scripture as this, and not from one that is deceptive regarding an object accessible to valid cognition;
for even by the manner just described, knowledge based on scripture is not an inference that is infallible or faultless.
Why?

It has been explained that words do not have an invariable concomitance with objects because they lack correspondence to them; as stated in the passage beginning with "because there is no necessary connection between words and things" (1.213),

other disputants maintain that one must depend upon a person whose excellence consists in the exhaustion of his defects and so forth, for they know— that is, they understand— that whatever word such a person utters is in accordance with reality.

"Seeing things exactly as they are and as they exist is 'seeing according to reality' (*yathārthadarśana*). That which has this as its beginning—namely, compassion, detachment, and so forth—is 'seeing according to reality and the rest' (*yathārthadarśanādi*). A person endowed with that very quality is an *āpta* (a reliable authority). Because [the scripture] is composed by such a person, the non-contradiction of the scripture is the "word of an *āpta*"; thus say others."
"Desired," etc.: This very point just mentioned by the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) is desired by us.

However, it can be known through human necessity that such excellence exists; [the author] explains this with the words "but all [of it] is possible," starting from "characterized by perception and so forth," [implying] that every person who acts with foresight [is capable of it].
Whether it be scripture or non-scripture, one investigates and examines it;
desiring to engage by means of scripture while abandoning what is not scripture,
and not out of addiction or mere attachment.
He says "not even the desire for engagement" and so forth;
