by the word "even" (*api*), he means "how indeed might I..."— that is, having understood from this scripture the object that is to be practiced and directly realized, and having engaged [in it], may I become "possessed of the goal," meaning possessed of the fruit.

A person seeking [truth] is able to perceive and ascertain an object that is accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*); the non-contradiction of that [object], its ascertainment by means of direct perception and inference, is precisely the cognitive support (*ālambana*). For what reason would one proceed toward another object—even one inaccessible through direct perception or inference—on the basis of that?

Because worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*) is generally of such a nature, it is described as "generally" (*prāyaḥ*), meaning for the most part (*bāhulyena*), that which consists in proceeding toward other [objects] by means of observing non-contradiction in one part, expressed as "thus" (*evam*).
Furthermore, if it is admitted that activity proceeds from an examination of the person, then no activity would ever occur;
for what reason?
Because such a person is endowed with qualities such as seeing things as they truly are.
The phrase "there would be no activity at all due to the lack of desire" is to be connected [to the preceding].

Therefore, the meaning is this: it is not the case that for persons endowed with qualities such as seeing things as they truly are, there would be no activity at all due to the lack of desire because of their truthful speech.
What is the reason?
Since such persons—endowed with qualities such as the vision of reality—speak non-erroneously and thus illuminate things exactly as they exist, he asks:
"What, then, is the reason that such a person cannot be known? and says:
"For instance," and so forth;
this person is either possessed of such faults or not.
Others, however, maintain that while [the self] is thus possessed of faults, its being faultless— or even the faultlessness of other things— is difficult to comprehend;
this is indicated by the singular number and the feminine gender in the word *durbodhā* (difficult to understand), which refers back to the term *nirdoṣatā* (faultlessness).
However, with reference to the phrase "other faults," a modification must be made by changing [the gender and number] to the masculine plural— namely, *durbodhāḥ*—
because they are difficult to understand and because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that determine the virtues and faults of others are difficult to obtain.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "from the mental factors" (*caitasebhyaḥ*) and so forth: those persons whose activity— characterized by bodily and vocal action— is correct or false,
for them there exist in the mind (*cetasi*) mental qualities (*caitasāḥ*) consisting of virtues and faults.
From mental qualities (*caitasika-guṇa*) such as compassion, detachment, and awakening, which serve as causes, there arise correct activities—that is, activities in accordance with reality;
and from mental defects (*caitasika-doṣa*) such as attachment and so forth, there arise false activities—that is, perverted activities.
These, namely the mental qualities and defects of others, are beyond the reach of the senses because they are properties of the mind.
Therefore, they are not accessible through direct perception,
nor are they accessible through inference, precisely because they are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) and thus their essential nature as a logical mark (*svabhāva-liṅga*) is unestablished;
rather, they are those bodily and vocal actions whose origin (*prabhava*) or production arises from one's own virtues and faults.
They are to be inferred by that mark which is the effect;
yet that does not exist,
because conventional activities— characterized as actions of body and speech— are for the most part, or in their majority, [absent].
Considering that these are preceded by intention, they can be performed otherwise through analytical discernment;
for instance, even those with passion display themselves as being free from passion,
and those free from passion appear as if they have passion.

What is the reason? Because linguistic conventions (*vyavahāra*) function according to human will; the analysis of the compound is: "those whose functioning or activity (*pravṛtti*) proceeds from human will.
Even if linguistic conventions indeed function according to human will, he asks: "Why then are they not performed otherwise? To which he replies:

And because those persons possess diverse intentions and diverse purposes, worldly transactions proceed from them according to their own whims; thus, there can be no certain discernment regarding transactions arising from virtues or faults.

Therefore, since this inferring person, failing to reach certainty due to the confusion of signs (*liṅga*) and the deviation of signs, is not one whose defects have been exhausted, how could he establish the author of scripture? The conclusion must be: he certainly cannot.

Now, as for the passage beginning with "What then," [the author], demonstrating that there does indeed exist such a person who is faultless— meaning devoid of defects such as passion and so forth— says:

"In all," and so forth: [this refers to] the diminution, that is, the decrease [of afflictions], upon the manifestation of their antidotes. (Note 397-1: The restored text from the first page up to this point.
(Note 397-2: *Bya-ba-daṅ*.)

It is said: [this is] a statement of action (*kriyā-vacana*). Furthermore, those [afflictions] such as attachment (*rāga*) which, when their counteragents (*pratipakṣa*) are not present, resort to excellence and accumulation, are dependent upon decrease and excellence;
for all of them are the objects to be countered (*vipakṣa*).
And it is by the presence or absence of whichever [counteragent] that they undergo decrease or excellence.
That very [state] is their adversary (*vipakṣa*) and its sublater (*bādhaka*); that which exists together with it is "possessing an adversary" (*savipakṣa*).
The state of being so is "the fact of possessing an adversary" (*tattva*); therefore, it is because of that sublativeness—this is the meaning.

And by means of that subduer through which the faults possess their counteragents— due to the cultivation of that subduer, its repeated and uninterrupted production, and the resulting state of being assimilated (*sātmībhāva*), its firmness, and its becoming one's very nature— from that assimilation of the subduer, they would diminish and be exhausted.

The outflows (*āsrava*) are passion, aversion, and so forth; and it will be demonstrated that when the antidote to these faults has become internalized within a certain mental continuum, the knowledge of selflessness (*nairātmyajñāna*) acts as the subduer of those faults.
Therefore, such a person is not denied; however, we say only this: he is one whose outflows are exhausted (*kṣīṇāsrava*) and is difficult to know.
This is the explanation beginning with "for the fault... and so on.
For the defects, such as attachment and so forth, are of a nature characterized by decrease and increase.

Being of the nature of decrease and increase, they establish and demonstrate the increase and decrease of the subjugation caused by the adversary—that is, the subjugation which is the overcoming or disparagement [of the fault].
Therefore, this is the meaning:

those possessing the quality of diminution establish the increase of the subjugation of the adversary through the diminution of faults by means of the increase of the subjugation of the counter-agent; those possessing the quality of excellence establish the decrease of the subjugation of the counter-agent.
Because they possess the quality of excellence due to the weakness of their suppression by obstructing factors—just like flames, for instance;
the word "etc. includes sensations such as cold and heat.

Just as flames and the like possess the properties of diminution and intensification when there is an increase or decrease in their opposing factors such as water, and thus successively establish the overcoming of water and so forth through their own intensification; likewise, [the case of passion and the rest].

Now, one might object: "Passion and the other afflictions are dependent upon external objects, and since external things are always present, how can there be an eradication of passion and the rest? To this, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "te hi" and so forth:
the word "hi" has the sense of "because";
those [afflictions], such as attachment and the rest, arise from conceptual construction.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "their origination" (*prabhava*) or arising is from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is characterized by improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*).

For indeed, even when external objects exist, passion and the like do not arise in the absence of improper mental attention; yet, when that [attention] is present, they arise even without an object. Thus, passion and the like originate from conceptual construction.
Therefore, even though the grasping (*upādāna*) exists as previously defined, [they do not arise].
And this locative case is used here in the sense of disregard;

the meaning is that [the afflictions] become diminished— that is, subject to decrease— due to the cultivation of a certain mental quality characterized by the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*).
This is what is meant:

although there is no total eradication of the cause of the defects at all times because the counteragent lacks absolute intensity, nevertheless, due to the practice of the counteragent, the power of the [defects] that diminish the appropriation is weakened, and thus the defects become increasingly attenuated; by this, the reason has been stated.

But when proficiency arises in that mental quality as described— due to its reaching the ultimate limit of cultivation— then, upon that proficiency of the mental quality, the "concomitant" (anvaya) arises; it is called "concomitant" because the seed of the afflictions follows from it, in the sense that a fault is produced from it.

That destruction in which no continuity remains is "destruction without continuity" (*niranvayavināśa*). Those defects whose nature is such destruction are "possessing the nature of destruction without continuity";
the meaning is that they are of a nature to perish along with their latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Like a flame and so forth;
just as flames and the like possess the nature of absolute destruction when their counteragent— such as water— is increased, so too is the application [of the argument] again.

Those things which, by the application of a certain factor, undergo diminution, possess the property of being destroyed without remainder through the complete increase of that factor due to its overcoming them—
just as flames and the like [diminish] upon the increase of their submergence by water;
and since the defects (doṣas) possess the property of diminution through the application of the vision of selflessness (nairātmyadarśana), this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Since it is so, for that reason, [the opponent asks]: "Could there perhaps be someone who is faultless? and so forth;
here, the particle *yāvat* functions in the sense of *yadā* (when/if).

And as for the statement "like the arising of the antidote to what has become one's nature through the faults": for a person whose faults have become their very nature due to practice since beginningless time, there is the arising of the antidote— the arising of the vision of selflessness—
even though that vision of selflessness, which is the antidote to the faults, has become their nature, it occurs according to the conditions.
The Master [Vasubandhu] states that this is not the case, for even if a fault were to arise due to the presence of its causes,
it is "free from calamity" (*nirupadrava*) because it is devoid of all the afflictions of cyclic existence.

The term *bhūtārtha* (the true object) refers to that whose object (*viṣaya*) is a real thing (*bhūta*) characterized by impermanence and so forth, which is contrary to [false] reality. Furthermore, because it grasps the true object, the path has the mind as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Since this [path] is both free from affliction (*nirupadrava*) and a true object, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound containing within it another *karmadhāraya*: namely, "the intrinsic nature which is that true object. When, through the repeated cultivation of that true object which is free from affliction, it reaches the state of being fully integrated (*sātmībhāva*), [the path becomes stable].

And by this, the meaning is that there is no affliction by defects—namely, those which are contrary to the nature of the mind as the antidote to defects, which differ from the aforementioned triad, and which are accompanied by calamities, are unreal in their objects, and lack intrinsic nature; for the path, having become habitual, overcomes [the defects] so that no defects arise.
What is the reason?
Regarding the phrase "even when there is effort," etc.,
this means that for one who has made the path their very nature (sātmībhūta), no effort whatsoever is possible for the production of faults.
Nevertheless, even granting this for the sake of argument, it is said that because the intellect exerts effort toward producing faults due to its partiality for that [self],
it does not apply itself to that faultless path of selflessness, which serves as the antidote to those faults.

Having set aside the effort toward establishing [the opponent's position], [one acts] through partiality and great respect; this fault does not belong to the base text. (Note 399-1: Seventh Chapter – Saptamamāhnika)
The meaning is that because one applies effort specifically toward the antidote to faults through partiality toward virtues,
he first explains the term "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*):
for the intrinsic nature, characterized by the vision of selflessness, cannot be [overcome] by a person established within a self, which is its very opposite.

Just as the compassion of one who is both a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) and a Kāpālika cannot be removed without effort— meaning that the compassion existing during his state as a Vedic scholar cannot be revoked without exertion— so too,
effort must be applied to turn back from the inherent nature of this path.

The attainment [of the goal] would be effected by perceiving the virtues of that which has the nature of passion and so forth— which is to be abandoned— and by perceiving the defects of that which has the nature of insight— which is to be cultivated. Furthermore, that perception of defects does not arise for a person whose nature is the opposite of the defects— that is, whose nature is the antidote to the defects— [just as] that perception of virtues does not arise for one whose nature is the opposite of the virtues with respect to the defects.
Why, then, is it that the perception of faults in the antidote is not possible? He says "of that" and so forth:
because that antidote is free from affliction (nirupadrava).

For there are three kinds of affliction (*upadrava*), the absence of which makes the path free from affliction (*nirupadrava*). Namely: the affliction of the faults (*doṣa*) which is the cause for the mind to become obstructed, by which the mind, being obstructed, does not engage in the vision of things as they truly are; and the affliction of suffering and mental distress (*duḥkha-daurmanasya*), which is the cause of pain in body and mind.
Because contaminated pleasure is not tranquil, there is a distaste for its enjoyment and agitation;
regarding this, he states the absence of the first calamity by saying "due to the abandonment of all defects."

By stating "due to the abandonment and disappearance of all defects such as passion" (*rāgādidoṣa*), he expresses the absence of the second [category] through the term "outbursts" (*paryavasthāna*) and so forth; for "outburst" (*paryavasthāna*) refers to the manifestation of passion and the like, while "birth" (*janman*) refers to rebirth; thus, these two together are "outburst and birth" (*paryavasthānajanmanī*).
Because suffering is bound to those two, through their discernment [one understands]:

the suffering characterized by the burning of body and mind that arises at the time of the production of passion and so forth is bound to the *paryavasthānas* (obsessions); however, the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and so forth is bound to birth.
Thus, he states the absence of a third calamity.

"Tranquility," and so forth: tranquility is *nirvāṇa*, characterized by the absence of passion and the like; the "taste" (*rasa*) is the savoring of the untainted bliss therein; and because of not being repelled by that—that is, because of making one non-averse to it.
Furthermore, the connection is that passion (*rāga*) and so forth would not have a non-existent object as their domain;
if they have a non-existent object, then how does their arising occur? To this he says:
"Arising through the power of grasping" means arising through the power of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of false conceptualization.

Thus, because the continuum of consciousness—which serves as the substratum for the seeds of passion and so forth—is characterized by a perverted grasping, and because it adopts an antidote characterized by the reversal of passion and so forth, [the latter] would not exist and would not arise;
however, it would not mean that there is no object which is real and non-perverted.
But how could it be so?
For [the cognition] proceeds by the force of the object itself.
Because they arise through the power of the object as it actually exists,
the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) apprehend aspects such as impermanence even while [the object] remains in a state of being habituated to defects.
They bring about the path of the counteragent;
how much more so, then, for one who is established in insight?
Furthermore, defects such as attachment and the like have unreal objects,
because they function with respect to objects superimposed as self and what belongs to the self; therefore,
they do not exist for one who expresses the natural state (*sātmya*)— that is, the essential nature (*svabhāvatva*)— of their antidote, which has a real object.

Since this is so, there is no further arising of defects for those whose defects have been abandoned; even when making an effort to produce a defect, because the intellect has a natural partiality toward virtue, one exerts effort specifically toward the antidotes to passion and the like. Thus, for a discerning person who investigates by means of reasoning—even one who remains for a time in the habitual state of defects—no further arising occurs.
For one of uncorrupted nature who abides in the self through the cultivation of counter-measures, there is the application of effort specifically and preeminently toward virtues alone.
Furthermore, what is the source—the cause of origination—of these defects?
It is called "source" (*prabhava*) because from it they "originate" (*prabhavanti*), that is, arise.
He states the subsequent [verse] beginning with "of all," etc., regarding that cause of the defects which are abandoned through the practice of their antidotes.

Regarding the "origination" (*jāti*)—that is, the arising—of the various types of faults (*doṣa*), [it occurs] from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is the adherence to a self and what belongs to a self (*ātmātmīyābhiniveśa*).
Now, since it is stated in the scriptures (*āgama*) that the afflictions (*kleśa*) have ignorance (*avidyā*) as their cause, how is there no contradiction? To this, he says:
"That is ignorance" means that very view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is ignorance;
therefore, there is no contradiction.
But by what sequence does the arising of the defects from the view of a self-identity occur? To this he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "there," etc.:
therein, attachment is the affection for an object that has been clung to as self and belonging to self.
Attachment to self and what belongs to the self;
from that attachment to self and what belongs to the self, there arises aversion and so forth—this is the sequence.
He explains this with the words "for not," and so on.
"I am not" is the negation of the aspect of a self; "it is not mine" is the negation of the aspect of what belongs to a self—
for the person who perceives by means of the aspect of non-self and the aspect of non-belonging-to-a-self.
"Without grasping" means that apart from the conceptual construction of things as "self" or "belonging to self," or as being "benefactors," there is no attachment toward any object;
and for one who is without affection— that is, one devoid of attachment to self, what belongs to self, and so forth— there is no aversion toward anything whatsoever.
Because that [attachment] does not exist without affection (*anunaya*),
what is the reason?
It is because of [the notions of] "self" and "mine," and so forth.

Because that [hatred] is absent in the case of the neutral party— since [the neutral party] does not obstruct the self or what belongs to the self and does not act in opposition to them, there is an absence of that hatred.
And "obstructing what is opposed":
it refers to that which obstructs— that is, prevents— the harm or suffering of that which has been grasped as "self" or "belonging to the self."
Because that [hatred] is absent in the case of friends,
due to the absence of aversion; rather,
it arises through opposition toward those who have become objects of attachment for oneself or one's own.
Hatred is that which exists toward that very object which stands as an adversary;
therefore, hatred does not exist without the affection for self and what belongs to the self.
The conclusion is stated by the words "therefore" and so forth;
for this very reason, "those two" refers to the view of a self and the grasping at what belongs to a self.
The connection is made by modifying the wording to "they produce affection" (*snehaṃ prasuvāte*);
and that affection produces—that is, generates—hatred and the other [afflictions].
To the question, "What then is the cause of those two, namely the view of self (*ātmadarśana*) and the grasping at 'mine' (*ātmīyagraha*)? he says:

"Similar," and so forth: that very perception of a self which belongs to a similar class; its "practice" is its arising repeatedly over a long period of time, as well as the latent impression (*vāsanā*) thereof.
Therefore, the view of self that has arisen produces the grasping at "mine";
thus, all afflictions are born from the view of a real body (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
In our established doctrine (siddhānta), that very view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) which is ignorance is called "ignorance" (avidyā).

For this very reason—that the view of a self-identity itself is ignorance—it is stated in another Sūtra that delusion (moha) is the source, the primary cause, of the defects such as attachment and the rest: "All afflictions have ignorance as their cause. Why, then, is the view of a self-identity elsewhere in other Sūtras stated to be the source of the defects?
When that is abandoned— that is, when the view of a self-identity is abandoned— because of the abandonment of the faults,
the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, say that delusion is the source of the faults, the cause of the faults; why is this?
Because faults do not arise for one who is undeluded and free from ignorance, they state elsewhere that the cause of the fault of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is something else.

This status of being a cause would apply to delusion (*moha*) and the view of a self-identity when there is an indication of the primary cause, but not when there is merely an indication of a [general] cause.
What is the reason?

Since those defects arise from a multiplicity of causes— the sense faculties, their objects, and improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*)— it would be contradictory for them to arise from a single cause, namely delusion (*moha*) or the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Therefore,
it is understood from the Buddha’s word that although other causes exist, delusion and the view of a self-identity are stated to be the causes by taking their predominance.

If delusion (*moha*) were one thing and the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) another, and if both were [equally] predominant, then—given that predominance of both delusion and the view of a self-identity—it would not be the case that there is a singular designation for each;
that is to say, in some places there would be a designation of delusion alone, and in others a designation of the view of a self-identity alone.
This would not be conducive to excellence (*parabhāgabhāk*), meaning it would result in nothing but a lack of skill on the part of the speaker.
Furthermore, when there is no difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) between these two,

then there is no contradiction in designating a single object by means of both the term "delusion" (*moha*) and the term "view of a self-identity" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as synonyms; for the preeminence [of one over the other] depends on the fact that the view of a self-identity is the primary cause of the defilements, just as it is the primary cause of the [other] faults.
That has been established immediately above and will be established in the second chapter;
and since the faults are abandoned when that view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned, its preeminence [is evident].

Since this is so, birth arises from the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Therefore, the remedy for those defects that arise from that view of a self-existent body is the realization of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*); through the cultivation of that, there is the abandonment [of the defects]. And that person whose defects are exhausted is difficult to follow and difficult to understand—meaning that one who desires to engage [in practice] should rely upon the instruction of that person whose defects are exhausted, and should carry out the purpose taught by him.
Let it not be that scripture is a statement dependent upon a person or caused by a person.
For what reason?
Because, according to the principle just stated, the author of the scripture is difficult to trace and difficult to understand.

This genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) for those defects such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, which are the causes of the falsity— that is, the deceptive nature— of words and speech;
"resort" (*āśrayaṇa*) means the locus (*āśraya*).

The compound "puruṣasyāśrayaḥ" (the support of the person) is formed with the genitive case; furthermore, the genitive case after the word "puruṣa" is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), and there is no restrictive rule stating that when both [agent and object] are possible, the genitive must be used only for the object.
Because of the optionality expressed by the rule *śeṣe vibhāṣā*, the meaning is as follows:
[the Veda is not a valid means of knowledge] because it is accepted by persons who possess defects that serve as causes for error.

Alternatively, the genitive case in "of the defects" (*doṣāṇām*) is used in the sense of the object; some Mīmāṃsakas declare that because the Veda is not of human origin, it has true meaning, since there is an absence of defect— which is the cause of falsity— due to its being grasped or taken as a refuge by a person.
This is what is meant:

the threefold invalidity—characterized by falsity, ignorance, and doubt—does not exist at all in the case of the Veda, because words possess a twofold nature: that which is innate and that which is adventitious; therein, the innate nature is their capacity to convey things as they truly are.
Furthermore, the quality of not representing things as they truly are is a contingent nature (aupādhika-svabhāva), because it is dependent upon the person;
thus he says:
It is established that the arising of defects in words depends upon the speaker;

therefore, their absence in certain cases occurs because the speaker possesses excellence, since it is impossible for those [defects] to be transferred to the word when they have been removed by his excellences. (62)
Or rather, due to the absence of a speaker, there would be no defects, as they would lack a substratum (Ślokavārttika,
Codanā 63). Therefore, upon the removal of the person [as author], there is the removal of falsity.
Nor is invalidity characterized by non-origination, because the understanding of the meaning arises from the Veda;
nor is invalidity characterized by doubt, because no doubt appears when the meaning is cognized from the Veda. Thus he says:
In this way, for such a Veda which produces knowledge,
both its contrary nature and doubt regarding it have been refuted by the Bhāṣya; thus,
Ibid.
Since the three grounds for invalidity have been excluded,

and since the Veda possesses an intrinsic nature characterized by the communication of its meaning as established by its very origin, therefore its validity is inherent (*svataḥ*) because it communicates its meaning;

and since in the case of ordinary speech the defect characterized by sublation or a defective cause can occur through the fault of a speaker, therefore, in the Veda, with the absence of a person, there is an absence of defects, and thus [its validity] is inherent.
Since there is an absence of the two factors that subvert validity—the cognition of a subverting condition and the cognition of a defect in the cause—there is no suspicion of invalidity;
thus he says:
"In that case, freedom from subversion is easier [to achieve] due to the absence of a speaker."
In the Veda, therefore, even the suspicion of invalidity does not arise;
however, in the case of human [utterances], validity depends upon the existence of other means of knowledge.

In its absence, however, that [Vedic injunction] would be corrupted, whereas the Vedic [injunction] is never corrupted. Therefore, the validity of the Vedic injunctions arises precisely through their non-contradiction with other means of knowledge; otherwise, they would be mere restatements (anuvāda).

Furthermore, how can the sublation of an inference by that very knowledge [of the Veda]— which effects a contrary state of the meaning of the injunction— be prevented? If it is argued that there is no sublation because that [inference] is false, then a circular argument (anyonyāśraya) results.
For you, there is no subverting factor other than inference.
Nor is there an absence of the Vedic meaning simply because it is not apprehended by other means of knowledge, as is the case with taste and the like.

If it is argued that the validity of the initial cognition of taste is established because it is subsequently apprehended by another cognition of taste, then the same will apply to the Vedic meaning as well.
To this he says:
"And there would not be an absence of the object because it is not grasped by other [senses], as in the case of taste and so forth;
if the cognition of the object occurs through that very cognition [of the universal], then such a property will exist."
If one says, "This [Veda] is unestablished for me," it is not proper for a speaker of truth, when a cognition has arisen from the Veda, to say so out of mere malice. (91,
92) He explains the meaning of the verse with the words beginning "Certainly not" (*na khalu*).
"All indeed" means that both the human and the non-human [scriptures] may have possible deception— that is, possible contradiction—
but it is only the human [scripture] that has possible deception.
"Because the faults that cause deception—the causes of contradiction—reside in persons;
therefore, some maintain that what is non-personal (apauruṣeya) possesses true meaning. (227)

Regarding those Mīmāṃsakas who argue that because there is an absence of persons who are causes of falsity within the Vedas, the absence of the effect— namely falsity— is established, and thus the Veda is non-human (apauruṣeya) and possesses true meaning— the author of the treatise himself speaks as follows, addressing them through the very mouths of others.

Those qualities which are the causes of the truthfulness of words depend upon a person; therefore, in the case of non-human (apauruṣeya) utterances, since the person is absent, the quality that is the cause of truthfulness ceases to exist. Consequently, the effect—truthfulness—also ceases. Thus, why would a non-human utterance not be false? This is what is meant: since truthfulness and falsity in speech depend upon a person, if one maintains that there is truthfulness when the person is absent, why is it not maintained that there is falsity [when the person is absent]? So it is said.

But from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), since the cessation of the person entails the cessation of both that which has a true object and that which has a false object, [the Veda] would be purposeless; thus, its invalidity is characterized by non-origination.
If you argue that this [non-origination] is not established for me because [knowledge] arises from the Veda, [we reply:]...

It is not proper for a speaker of truth to speak out of mere hatred; this has been refuted [in verses] 92 and 93. Furthermore, because the understanding of the meaning does not arise from the Veda by its own nature...
[2] Moreover—
Since phonemes, whether individually or collectively, lack the nature of being expressive, and since the Veda consists of the form of phonemes, how can there be knowledge of meaning from it?
Indeed, even for one who has not grasped the linguistic convention (*samaya*), when a sentence is uttered, a doubt is observed such as, "What meaning has been expressed by this?
And that [doubt] would occur only if the word possessed an inherent power (*śakti*) for conveying meaning by its very nature.
In that case, its lack of authority would be characterized by doubt,
since the capacity to reveal both a desired and an undesired object is possible;
and if that capacity belongs to it by its very nature, what is the use of convention?
If it is argued that just as a lamp, though capable of illuminating an object, depends upon the sense organ, so too does a word depend upon convention (*saṃketa*), we say no;
for in the absence of either the lamp or the sense organ individually, there is no illumination of the object.
In that case, mutual dependence would be logical;
however, it is not so for the word and its expressive power (*śakti*) or its convention (*saṃketa*), because the cognition of the meaning arises through the convention alone.
Therefore, a word is not inherently capable of conveying meaning; thus, its invalidity is characterized by non-origination (*anutpatti-lakṣaṇa*).

[Objection: But surely, in sentences such as "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra," the fact that the Agnihotra and so forth are the means for attaining heaven and so forth is indeed perceived. How then can there be invalidity characterized by non-origination?
[Reply: This is true.
For it is perception alone that sublates non-perception, but not falsity,
since that too is perceived.

Therefore, by these words, does the Agnihotra and so forth—which are not actually means for achieving heaven—being presented as such means, or are they indeed means? Thus, the suspicion of their falsity does not cease;

for there is an absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) [to prove them false], and because the quality of being authorless (*apauruṣeyatva*) lacks contradiction with the state of having false content.
Moreover, it is observed that even authorless [texts] can be causes of erroneous cognition.

For example, just as moonlight and the like serve as causes for the cognition of yellow in white cloth and so forth, and by that [cognition] the falsity of the object's nature is established through inference, how could there be sublation by that [kind of] cognition? However, in the case of cognitions of taste and so forth, because their validity is first ascertained precisely through the non-contradiction of their effects—such as satiation—it is logical that at other times, through repeated practice and the like, the ascertainment of validity occurs intrinsically (*svataḥ*); thus, no suspicion of falsity arises.
But since no non-contradiction has ever been established for the Veda at any time, how can there be a determination of its intrinsic validity at any other time?

Therefore, even though cognition exists, just as intuition (*pratibhā*) and the like lack the status of valid means of knowledge due to their independence, so too should it be seen in the case of the Veda. Furthermore:
The knowledge of the meaning of an injunction (*codanā*) is false because it consists in the apprehension of what is non-existent;

for the authority of the Veda is held to reside in matters that are to be accomplished (*kārya*), and such an object is precisely that which is to be performed. Since that [object] exists as something yet to come into being, it is non-existent at the time of the cognition of the injunction and therefore does not exist at that time.
How then can there not be falsity in the cognition arising from the Vedic injunction (*codanā*), since its object does not exist?

For it has already been established that all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have non-entities as their objects; therefore, by that very fact, the cognition arising from the injunction is indeed false.
Furthermore:

In both worldly and Vedic usage, phonemes and words are indeed identical; only the difference in sentences is admitted. Furthermore, the meaning of words in the world is determined by convention (*saṃketa*); since the meaning of worldly words is the same as that of Vedic words, the relationship between the word and its meaning is purely human (*pauruṣeya*).
Since the understanding of the meaning of Vedic sentences occurs through the medium of worldly objects, that [Vedic sentence] is indeed dependent on human [agency], just like a worldly sentence.

Furthermore, because words have multiple meanings in the world, it is possible for a Vedic sentence to also have multiple meanings; thus, the doubt regarding a contrary meaning does not cease. Therefore, the Veda possesses the lack of authority characterized by uncertainty.
He explains the meaning of the verse with the words beginning "yathā" (just as).
"Overcome by passion and so forth" means being joined with passion and so forth;
"compassion" (dayā) is pity (karuṇā),
which, when it has become one's very nature, is the true reality (dharmatā).
From the word "etcetera" [in the compound], wisdom, faith, and so forth are included; one who is endowed with these [is not subject to error].
Therefore, just as the falsity of a statement arises from its dependence on a person, [so too does the falsity of the Veda arise if it were dependent on a person].
Likewise, that person also causes that reality-status to cease.
It is not merely that there would be falsity;
rather, upon the cessation of the person, there would follow the cessation of both his qualities—truthfulness and falsity—and thus the Veda would become purposeless.
Alternatively, if truthfulness were maintained even upon the cessation of the person, [then...]
In that case, there would either be a non-reversal of the true meaning or a falsity of the meaning.
Should it be thought that the meaningfulness of words does not depend upon a person but exists by their very nature, he says:
"Not indeed," and so forth;
why is it that they are meaningful by nature, that is, by their own intrinsic essence? What is the reason?
From convention (*samaya*), that is, from agreement (*saṃketa*),
there arises the manifestation of meaning— that is, the cognition of an object— from words,
just as in the case of bodily gestures and the like.

Just as bodily gestures such as the movement of the hands or the contraction of the eyes are designated as "bodily" and convey a meaning in certain cases through convention (*samaya*), so too [is it with words].
Furthermore, if words were by their very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*) illuminators of meaning, they would not depend upon convention.
Therefore, words do not possess an inherent capacity to illuminate their objects;
rather, their capacity consists simply in their functioning in accordance with convention, provided there is no contradiction.
What is the reason for this?

At the time of convention (*samaya*), that is, at the moment of establishing a linguistic agreement, words are produced and employed according to one's will, wherever the person who establishes that convention desires to apply them. If, on the other hand, words were established by nature—that is, established by their own inherent essence—with respect to any particular object, then it would be impossible for those words established by nature to convey meaning through convention according to human will.
Therefore, words are meaningless in themselves; being thus meaningless, they acquire meaning only through the refinement of persons, namely, through the conventions of persons.

Now, if it is maintained that these [words] possess purposefulness by depending on the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of a person— lest they be meaningless— then they would necessarily be of human origin (*pauruṣeya*).
For it is logical that the very fact of these words being refined by him, and indeed their being refined by a person, constitutes their status as being of human origin.
There is no production [of knowledge] from a person;
for what reason?
Precisely because of that, due to the deception regarding the object—that is, due to the contradiction—arising from the conventions of persons.
There is no deception arising from its production by a person,

because even though the word is produced by a person, it is applied [to its object] in accordance with reality— being applied (samita) according to its actual state without contradiction to the true meaning; thus,
it is not obstructive nor deceptive.

"Other than that" means other than the word; it refers to the human attribute such as the opening and closing of eyes, which, though inherently meaningless, does not deceive when conjoined with the person according to its actual state.
Concluding this point, he says "that."

Therefore, when this person desists from his own established convention, he also causes that conceptual appearance of an object—that is, the cognition of an object—whose occurrence or arising [depends on it] to desist;
for that reason, how could there be truthfulness of meaning through the desisting of that person? On the contrary, there would be only meaninglessness.
By this, it is shown that the proponents of the Veda have fulfilled their purpose by refuting whatever proofs are asserted by others regarding the two extremes of the beginning and the end.

The *Ślokavārttika* states: "The prior limit of the Veda is characterized by being composed by a person, and the subsequent limit consists of its destruction; indeed, the absence of these two is eternity."

That [position] is refuted because, even if the Veda were non-human (apauruṣeya) and eternal, it would be purposeless and thus fail to achieve its intended aim. Now, if "human origin" (*pauruṣeyatā*) is defined not as the act of explaining a convention (*samaya*) or establishing a linguistic sign (*saṃketa*), but rather as the very act of production itself—such that the Veda is considered non-human and therefore true to reality—nevertheless, the convention which is the cause for making the meaning known and the cause for manifesting the meaning depends upon persons and follows human will; thus, it does not necessarily correspond to reality. This remains the case even when the non-human origin of words is accepted.
Therefore, because it follows human intention, there is the possibility of falsity [in the Veda]. The explanation of the phrase "how so? and so forth is as follows:

regarding this Veda, since the cognition of meaning—the manifestation of meaning—arises from a convention (*samaya*), that is, from a linguistic agreement (*saṃketa*), and since that convention is of human origin, it could therefore be false or even unreal.
Furthermore, because of its independence,
the Vedic statement regarding that heaven— which has morality as its means and cause,
and which is characterized by the summit of Mount Sumeru— would not be subverted otherwise in the [Buddhist] system.

One might interpret "heaven" as an unsurpassed pleasure in a contrary sense, and one might likewise produce a contrary result through the performance of means such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice; for that reason, since it is possible for [the Veda] to reveal what is not true to fact, the same defect that was stated regarding human compositions applies here:
namely, that because they are of human origin, deception is possible due to human fallibility.
228.8 But surely the relationship between word and meaning is non-human (apauruṣeya);
for in this way, contemporary elders merely teach the relationship between word and meaning as it has already been established from before.
Likewise, since even those who were elders in the past [possessed this knowledge], the relationship is indeed non-human (apauruṣeya) due to its beginninglessness;
as it has been said:
"Apart from the beginninglessness of words and their meanings, there is no other cause for the beginninglessness of the relationship."
"There is nothing other than this; therefore, no [independent] relationship and so forth exists in the Veda," according to the *Ślokavārttika*.
And that relationship is established by three means of valid cognition (*tripramāṇaka*).
For instance,

when a word has been employed by some elder for the sake of a hearer’s comprehension of an object, another observer standing nearby perceives neither the speaker nor the signified object through direct perception; rather,
he understands the hearer’s state of comprehension by means of his subsequent activity.

And because the comprehension of meaning would otherwise be impossible, one understands the expressive power residing in the word and its referent; thus, the relationship is established by three means of valid cognition.
As it has been said:
"In this case, one perceives through direct perception the words, the elders, and the objects denoted."

The establisher of the relationship perceives the listener’s state of comprehension through inference based on his behavior and through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)— since such behavior would otherwise be inexplicable— as well as the capacity of the intellect, which rests upon both [the speaker and the listener]; thus, he understands that the relationship is established by means of valid cognition.
Regarding this, he says:
"If the relationship between word and meaning were non-human-made," and so forth.

If the relationship between word and meaning is accepted as being non-human-made, there would be cognition—that is, the comprehension of the meaning—even for one who lacks [prior] awareness [of that relationship].
Conventional knowledge is consciousness;
for one who lacks that,
there is no connection with those things which are "not produced by men," meaning they are not generated by human beings.
Those words, because they manifest their objects as they truly are when denoted by persons, are not by their very nature inverted; nor are they made causes of false cognition.
Therefore, through this absence of inversion, there is no fault characterized by non-correspondence with reality.
Regarding the phrase "now" (*idānīm*): if the relationship [between word and meaning] is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), what is the purpose of a convention (*saṃketa*)?

For that relationship between word and meaning is the cause for the cognition of the object; if that relationship is not of human origin, then a person understanding the meaning from a word—which possesses a relationship established by nature—would not depend upon a convention, just as one does not depend on a lamp or similar [means of perception].

And since it depends upon convention (*saṃketa*), there is therefore no non-human (*apauruṣeya*) relationship between words and their meanings, like royal insignia and so forth. It might be thought: "The relationship is indeed non-human, but it is independent of convention and serves as the basis for cognition"; to this he says:
How can that which is not perceived as a basis be a basis for the perception of meaning, or how can it be a relation?
It is not so;
for the postulation of a relation occurs precisely because the perception [of meaning] would otherwise be impossible.
If there is no dependent existence, how can there be a relationship? Furthermore,
since a relationship exists by virtue of being indicative, it depends upon the cognition of its own nature.
Therefore, although it exists, that manifestor is not apprehended; thus,
the relationship established by each preceding speaker with all the unmanifested [sounds] is proven, and in this way, no such thing as a "relationship" and so forth exists.
Regarding that,
he says "by convention" and so forth;
[this means] when that relation is manifested by convention.
The postulation of a relation other than convention is both incapable and fruitless;
this is what is meant:

since the cognition of an object arises when there is a convention and does not arise when it is absent, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), convention alone is the cause of the cognition of the object—what, then, is the use of another relation?
He explains by means of the words beginning with "no" (*na*), etc.:
"the cause of the cognition of an object that is unmanifested and not revealed"—this is the connection; "that [connection] then"—this is the connection.
Since the communication of meaning is accomplished through convention alone, why is this "relation"— which has the nature of being present [in the word]— nurtured without cause, that is, fruitlessly?
He states its very fruitlessness with the words beginning with "nanu" (surely).
This [connection] is merely this much:
that the production of a cognition—an understanding—regarding a meaning to be expressed has been brought about by convention; thus, the connection is fruitless.
Convention is not effective with respect to what is unfit;

rather, convention is effective only with respect to that very word which the communicator has understood to be capable because the comprehension of the meaning would otherwise be impossible. If it is argued that fitness is the relationship [between word and meaning], it has been said:

For the relation is indeed a power (śakti), and no difference in it is perceived; since that power is to be inferred from its effects, it conforms to their differences. [Sambandhaparīkṣā 28] Here, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "tatkim" (then why?), it is thought as follows:
a single power does not reside in both the word and its meaning; rather, the expressive power resides in the word, while the expressed power residing in the meaning is indeed distinct.

But when the power of the word (*śabdaśakti*) is the relation, then it follows that whatever is the relation is itself the related entity; therefore, he asks: "In that case, let the word itself be the relation. [The opponent objects: "Is it not the case that fitness (*yogyatā*) is one thing and the word is another? How then can the word be the relation? To this, he replies:
For that which is capable is indeed the form [of the word] with respect to the communication of the meaning of the sound;
it is a fitness, like the fitness between cause and effect,
for the production of the effect, which is the fitness for producing the effect.
Just as [the capacity] is inherent in the cause,

so too, if that [capacity] exists [in the word], then since it is a fitness (*yogyatā*), what relation could there be between the word and its object? In that case, a connection must be stated between the word and its fitness.
Otherwise, it would not be established that "this is the capacity (yogyatā) of the word.
If it is argued that this capacity, which is a distinct entity, is assisted by the word— meaning, to put it another way,
that the word performs an assistance upon the capacity— [we respond as follows].
The point is that because it is produced by sound, the word is said to possess "fitness" (yogyatā); [the opponent asks:
how could there be any assistance to fitness by means of the word?
Since eternal capacity (*yogyatā*) is unsurpassable,

if it is argued that even for this capacity a distinct assistance (*upakāra*) is produced by the word, then it must be explained what the relationship is between that word-produced assistance and the capacity.

Now, if another assistance is produced there [in the first assistance] by way of fitness (*yogyatā*), then, since one must postulate yet further and further assistances in that assistance according to the aforementioned rule, there would be the fault of infinite regress (*atiprasaṅga*).
Consequently, because no assistance would be established due to this lack of finality (*anavasthā*), the very relationship between the word and its fitness remains unestablished.
Furthermore, a word that assists a distinct fitness does so by means of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone, not by means of another form.
Because it would follow that the word is incapable of providing assistance;

and if, at that time, the capacity exists inherently by its own nature, then why is it not accepted that the meaning itself is the very nature of the word, being capable of generating cognition? What is the point of this indirect process? This is the sense.

Therefore, fitness is not the relation, nor is it the cause for the cognition of an object, because the cognition of an object arises from inherence alone. If that is so, how then, for the Buddhist as well, can convention be the relation between word and object?
And how could it not be so?
For the statement of meaning—namely, "this word is the designator of this object"—resides in persons; it does not reside in the word and its object.

Nor is the property of one thing the property of another, just as the property of a horse is not that of a cow; however, the Teacher [Dignāga] says "no" and so forth, asserting that there is not only no convention (*samaya*) or relation (*sambandha*), but also no other real (*bhāvika*) relation.
For instance, the relation between entities must consist either in the fusion of their forms,
or in dependence, or in mutual expectancy;
among those things that are unmixed and mutually distinct, there can be no relation characterized by the fusion of forms.
Because it would follow that they are non-distinct, there would be the consequence of their being one;
likewise, for forms that are established— that is, already produced— there is no relation characterized by dependence.
Since dependence has been established, there is no relation characterized by mutual dependence either; thus he says,
"and because of non-dependence."
Because that which is established is independent of everything else.
If, then, there is no relationship between word and meaning, how is there the cognition of word-meaning,
and how is verbal knowledge included within inference?
To the question, "What is the purpose of that convention at such a time?
he says:
"Because of a specific meaning," and so forth.
That specific object which has been made the focus by the intention to communicate— it is the striving for that, the desire to communicate,
which impels and generates speech; this speech indicates or reveals the object as it appears within its own causal basis.
For one who knows that speech has its own cause— the intention to communicate— and that this [intention] indicates the speaker of it, [the question] "Whose is this? does not arise.

Therefore, for that wise person who understands that "this speech has arisen from the intention to communicate," there exists between the mental cognition characterized as intention and the vocal intimation a relationship defined by the nature of producer and produced; consequently, comprehension arises from that word through invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
Therefore, the comprehension of meaning arises from the sentence through the relation of producer and produced;
thus, as it has been said:

"Even if the cognition of meaning from a word is inference, the comprehension of meaning from a sentence is a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because its connection [with the meaning] is not previously grasped."
And since inseparable connection (avinābhāva) is not useful in this context,
that [position] is rejected; for without inseparable connection, the relationship between the signified and the signifier (vācyavācakabhāva) cannot exist.
As for what was also asked: how is there the comprehension of meaning from a word,
and how does verbal cognition (śābdajñāna) fall within inference?
That has been avoided;
now he states the purpose of the convention,
beginning with the words "the narration of that" (tadākhyāna).
The "explanation of that" is the explanation of inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*); it is called *samaya* (convention) because it is by means of this that [the relation] is explained.

Therefore, from that convention, there is the establishment—that is, the cognition—of the definition of inseparable relation, which is the member of the proof that causes the understanding of the object.
The designation "relation" is applied to the convention because it expresses a relation through metaphorical usage;
however, that convention itself is not the primary relation.
Therefore, as for what is said:
The view that the convention (samaya) is made for each individual person, or with each utterance, or once at the beginning of the world by some single person,
has been refuted.
Is the convention (samaya) made with respect to each individual person, or with each utterance, or was it made once at the beginning of the world by some single being?

Now, if the cognition of the meaning from a word occurs through invariable concomitance (avinābhāva), then the word’s communication of the meaning would not be by way of its being a denoter (vācakatva).
If the relation between word and meaning is called "convention" (samaya) because it expresses the existence of things without a convention— just as smoke indicates fire—
then there would also have to be a convention between fire and smoke.

This is not a fault, because when one intends to convey a meaning, one employs a word while superimposing upon it the status of being denotable (*vācyatva*) for the object and the status of being denotative (*vācakatva*) for the word itself—thinking, "I shall communicate this meaning even by means of a word that has not been previously established as conventional. At that time, the word arises precisely in its form as a denotator.

[Objection: But surely, with the intention of communicating a meaning, only phonemes (*varṇa*) are produced, and phonemes are not accepted as being denotators. So how can it be said that the word, as a denotator, arises from that intention?
It is true that,

because the speaker and the listener have the conceit of denotation only with respect to the phonemes themselves, it is said that the denotative [word] alone arises; therefore, for the sake of the deluded, the communication of this very inseparable relation— characterized as the relationship between signifier and signified, which is the connection between word and meaning— is called "convention" (*samaya*).
However, not every instance of explaining the relationship between cause and effect is a convention (*samaya*);
therefore, the relation in the case of smoke and so forth is not called a convention.

Even though there is a difference in the relation between word and object between the time of the initial agreement (*saṃketa*) and the time of practical usage (*vyavahāra*), people nevertheless proceed by determining them to be one due to their similarity.

And for this very reason, when a speaker communicates a particular relationship between word and meaning that was previously established, the listener understands that very same one; therefore, as it has been said:
"Does that relationship differ with each instance, or is it one?"

If [the relationship] were one, it could not be something produced; if it were distinct, there would be a cognition of that distinction. Regarding the connection (saṃbandha), because the cognitions of the speaker and the listener are distinct, linguistic usage is not impaired; for the connection in the mind of the speaker is indeed one thing, while that in the listener's mind is another.
What relationship does the speaker establish for the listener and the agent?
For that which was previously perceived by him, he does not produce for the listener; and that which he does produce as something new, he has not himself previously perceived as a communicator.
That is refuted,
because in all cases the world proceeds by determining the identity of the various relations between the signified and the signifier, even though they are distinct;
nor is there any beginninglessness for them, since recognition is not a valid means of knowledge.

Or, let there be a distinct, eternal relationship between words and their meanings, other than the relationship of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). If, by virtue of that relationship, words are restricted to a single meaning, then— due to the force of convention (*samaya*)— there would be no comprehension (*gati*) or understanding of another meaning where that word has not been restricted.
What is the reason?
For it is not logical that there should be a cognition of an object that is unrelated through a connection fixed to a single specific object;
why is that?
He says that because it would follow that such a relation is fruitless, there can indeed be no cognition of it.
The phrase beginning with "dṛṣṭaśca" (and seen) refers to that which is established by convention (*samaya*) according to the will of persons; it is an illuminator (*dīpaka*), meaning a revealer,
as indicated by the passage beginning with "aneka" (many).
If it is admitted that a word has a connection with multiple meanings, then even if the author of the convention (samayakāra) brings about its manifestation through a restriction to a single meaning,

he does so only regarding the intended meaning and not regarding another, contradictory one; thus, there is no absolute necessity, and consequently, the manifestation of a contradictory meaning is possible—
the manifestation of even a contradictory sense from [a word] intended [to convey something else] is conceivable.

He explains with the words beginning "atha" [and so forth]: if there were a fixed restriction to a single meaning, then the observation of the expression of multiple meanings by virtue of convention would be contradicted; therefore, so that this observed fact is not contradicted, all words are denoters of every object.
And by the words "and likewise" (*ca tathā*) and so forth, there is the demonstration of a contradictory instance:
just as it is accepted that all [words] are denoters of everything, so too must this necessarily be accepted,
because it follows from logical necessity that not every object is the accomplisher of every effect.
And he states the logical principle:
"Because of confusion," since the relationship between cause and effect is strictly determined.

In this regard, given this principle, for that intended object to be proven— such as heaven or the like— which has a specific, determined entity as its means or cause, what kind of specific word is there with respect to that which constitutes the subject matter?
Regarding the passage beginning with "sarva" and so forth:

since that common word functions as the designator (*vācaka*) of all things to be proven (*sādhya*)—that is, of all effects (*kārya*)—each according to its own specific means of proof (*sādhana*) or causes (*kāraṇa*), the author of the convention (*samayakāra*) brings about the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of that word only in the intended object, which is accepted as having a specific thing to be proven. Why is this so?
This is what is meant: [the convention is established] in such a way that the word manifests only that which is intended.

That very meaning which, by the nature of things, is the means for attaining heaven—does the author of the convention merely manifest that same meaning through words such as *agnihotra*, or does he, due to intellectual dullness, apply it to something else entirely that is contrary to the means for attaining heaven? Such is the doubt itself.
Thus, a word, being unrestricted in its denotative capacity across all objects, acquires a restriction to a specific meaning from a person—that is, from human convention.
And that person might establish a convention even for a meaning that is contradictory [to the true state of affairs].

And thus, not only is there the possibility of a contradictory manifestation, but even this postulated authorlessness of the Veda, which is desired [by you], would be rendered useless; how indeed could that be?

Thinking, "May I understand from non-human (apauruṣeya) words an object that is indeed desirable, unmixed with and uncorrupted by what is undesirable," [one concludes that] the cause of confusion— the intermingling of the desirable and the undesirable— is the human element, which is excluded from Vedic words. This being the case, those words regarded as human-made, when employed by persons for some intended meaning, become confused through the possibility of expressing what is undesirable.
Even those words considered to be non-human (apauruṣeya), being common to all possible meanings, are restricted by men to a particular meaning according to their own whim through convention;
for what reason?
Because those men lack knowledge of the true nature of reality.
If it is argued that Vedic words are by their very nature and inherent essence restricted to their intended meanings,
and therefore no fault arises from human refinement [of those meanings], then, this being the case, they would not require instruction for the manifestation of their meaning.
Furthermore, they depend on convention,
because from them there is no cognition of an object by virtue of their own nature;

and if they were restricted by their very essence, then once they had been assembled for a certain object at some time or place, they could never again manifest a different object through a different convention.
And they illuminate [them] from that;
therefore, it is not due to intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*).
(Note 415-1: Restored from Tibetan. (Note 415-2: *Bsgrub*.)
performing [the ritual]
"Is seen" (*dṛśyate*) means "is realized. [It is] by way of its own nature (*svabhāvena*). Thus, it is called "the certainty of the purpose" (*kāryaniyatā*).
Furthermore, if there were a restriction to a single meaning by virtue of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
then this diversity of interpretation among commentators regarding Vedic sentences— and the differences between successive explanations— would not exist,
because of the fixed determination to a single meaning.
And therefore, unlike human speech, Vedic words are not restricted to a single meaning;
thus it may be argued.
Since their instruction concerns only a fixed meaning, he says "of the instruction," and so forth.

A Vedic sentence in which there is a conceptualization of a plurality of possible meanings due to different interpretations is described as such; in that Vedic sentence where there is a possibility of alternative meanings—[he states: "in that Vedic sentence where there is a possibility of alternative meanings."

Regarding the instruction of commentators, there is no correspondence with what is desired; since there is no rule that "this is its meaning" or "that is another," the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatā*) of such [Vedic texts] is useless,
because even after postulating it, the suspicion of error (*vyabhicāra*) is not removed.

Furthermore, whoever maintains that there is a relationship between word and meaning must also state the reason for the establishment of that relationship; for whom, then, is this establishment of the relationship [intended]?
Regarding words and objects that are distinct and mutually different,
there is first of all no relationship characterized by identity between the word and the object;
for external objects such as pots and cloths are not the form or the intrinsic nature of the word.
For if jars and other objects were of the nature of sound, they would be non-existent;
nor is sound the nature of objects, because if they were of the nature of objects, it would follow that they lose their nature as sound—
by which [identity] there could be an inseparable concomitance through a non-different essence.

Inseparability would exist even when there is a distinction in the formal arrangement; therefore, why should it not be so even when there is a distinction between the probandum and the probans, based on a distinction in their exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*)?

Just as in the case of "being produced" and "impermanence," although there is a difference in their exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), they possess an inseparable connection (*nāntarīyakatā*) due to their single nature, so it is here.
He says "nor even," etc., stating that there is also no relationship characterized by origination from that (tadutpatti).
This is what he means:

For the relationship of words, if it were to exist as characterized by "origination from that" (tadutpatti), would have to be with either an object established in the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) or with an external object. It cannot be the first position,
because these Vedic sounds are not held to be born from a speaker's intention.
The analysis of the compound is: "those whose birth [occurs] from the desire to speak.
Alternatively, because their eternity is accepted, they are either unborn or unproduced, and thus they are not even manifested by the desire to speak.
Because it would entail the loss of their permanence, and because manifestable things are produced, as was stated previously;
nor is the second position tenable, as he says:
The phrase "not dependent on objects" means that they are also not dependent on external objects,
precisely because of their eternity.
Others, however, compose and explain it as a single passage:

"Since [Vedic words] do not arise from the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), nor are they manifested by it, Vedic words are therefore independent of meaning in both ways; that is, they are not bound to external objects."
And since they are not dependent upon the object, therefore—
given the absence of a connection [to that object] at this present time—
how could those words establish its concomitance, that is, the presence or existence of that object?
How could they possibly accomplish anything?
For what kind of thing is that which is to be accomplished through specific determination?
Regarding that external object, the restriction of words based on identity (*tādātmya*) and causal origination (*tadutpatti*) cannot be established by means of them,
because there is an absence of necessity due to the lack of a connection with the external object.
He summarizes the very same point in a verse,
beginning with "asaṃskāryatayā" (by way of being unconditionable), and so forth.
1. Regarding the phrase "by all":

if words were neither created nor conventionally assigned by persons with the intention of conveying meaning, then, on the grounds that they could not be refined by persons, Vedic words would be devoid of meaning.

Since the truthfulness or falsity of words depends upon human refinement (*puruṣasaṃskāra*), in the absence of that [refinement], they would necessarily be meaningless. Furthermore, if one were to resort to human refinement again in order to avoid this meaninglessness, there would also be the possibility of falsity; thus, this would become like "the elephant's bath" (a futile effort).
For it is said that an elephant, having bathed to remove the mud, again covers itself with mud;

thus, [the action] must be either eternal or non-eternal, as there is no other possible state for a real entity (vastu). Alternatively, it may be a function of human desire, produced by the power of human will, like the contraction [of a limb].
Or rather, its non-functioning is not by the will of a person; its functioning is like that of a sprout and so forth.

In that regard, under the view that [words] are impermanent and dependent upon persons, there would be a change of place and so forth due to the alteration of place and other factors— the word "and so forth" (ādi) including time and state—
such that words would not convey things according to the person's intention; the connection is that a person could not convey by means of a word exactly what they intended to convey.
What is the reason?

It means that even when there is a desire to convey a person, because a word is independent [of human intent], it can never be employed by a person; thus, it is impossible for a person ever to apply [the word] arbitrarily, just as one cannot command a mountain and so forth.
Just as mountains and the like, being independent of human beings, cannot be employed at will even when there is a desire to do so,
likewise it is observed that by changing the location and other factors, one can present [the object] according to one's intention.
Therefore, since the relationship is not dependent upon persons,

this very fault that was just mentioned— namely, the fault arising from a non-eternal relationship being independent of persons— applies equally to the case of an eternal relationship as well. Why is this so?

Because that relation, having a stable nature, cannot undergo transformation through the shifting of place and so forth, and because it would otherwise be impossible for it to exist, just like space. 4.
Now, if the word is connected to all objects whatsoever,
he says "equal" and so forth in response to that.

Even if it is postulated that the relationship [of a word] with all objects exists simultaneously at one and the same time, since there would be no restrictive determination regarding the specific object intended, the cognition of that particular intended object—which is common to all objects—would not occur. Therefore, one must admit that although a word is connected to multiple meanings, it attains a restriction to the intended meaning through the mental refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person [who uses it]. In this regard, however, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) as before follows: when there is a connection with multiple meanings, the manifestation of contradictory [meanings] is possible.
By such statements as these, the fault has been stated regarding the relation's dependence on a person— whether that relation is eternal or non-eternal; and,
assuming that the relation functions according to human will, there arises the suspicion of deception, since the relation would then be of human origin (*pauruṣeya*).
Because he accepts that the person is the cause of [scriptural] contradiction, [the author] states another refutation in that very same place, beginning with "and also in the sky," and so forth.
For the object of words is twofold: directly, it is the genus (*jāti*), and indirectly, it is the individual (*vyakti*) characterized by that [genus].
In that regard, if the relation were with the individual instance, he says:
because the objects to be expressed—the related things—are impermanent, when they perish, the relation which depends upon them also perishes; thus, the relation possesses no permanence.
Regarding the term *parāśraya*: it is so called because the other (*para*) is the related entity (*sambandhī*) which serves as its locus (*āśraya*).
Since the relation is not restricted to the related entity, it would be impossible for those two related entities to possess the status of being related;
for indeed, no one can be possessed of something by means of that which is unrelated to them, just as a cow is not possessed of a horse.

And that substratum of the relationship between word and meaning is impermanent because meanings are impermanent; upon the departure— that is, the destruction— of the substratum, the dependent relationship also departs,
just as light, which depends on a lamp, disappears when the lamp is extinguished.

Otherwise, if it were maintained that even when the substratum (āśraya) perishes, the dependent (āśrita) does not perish, then the relation would not be dependent upon that which is intended to be its substratum; consequently, since it would not perish along with the destruction of its substratum, the relation would not be eternal,
and the meaning of its having that as its substratum must be explained.
By what meaning can the two relata of that relation be said to be the "substratum" (āśraya)? The meaning of "substratum" must be stated;
for the meaning of "substratum" is the sense of "benefiting," and that [benefit] does not exist here.
What is the reason?

Because an eternal relation cannot be assisted, as it is incapable of having any excellence added to it; and that which is intended to be the substratum, not assisting [the relation], would not be a substratum.
This might be so.
If the individual were the denotable object, then the fault just mentioned would apply;

however, since it is the eternal genus that is the denotable object, there is no fault. [The opponent objects: "There is no fault of the relation being non-eternal due to the disappearance of its relata.
[The author replies] with the words beginning "No" (na).

Regarding the statement that there is no purpose for denoting a genus (*jāti*), this has already been thoroughly examined in the *Anyāpoha* discussion (PV 3.55): "A person acts only after having recognized those things capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*)."
In this context,
because a universal (jāti) is impossible in every instance of denotation, the application of an injunction based on a universal is untenable.

Just as in the case of arbitrary words denoting individuals— where "arbitrary" (*yādṛcchika*) refers to those words such as *devadatta* and the like, which denote specific individuals and arise from the speaker's whim (*yadṛcchā*), that is, the desire to employ a word without an external cause— so it is here.
According to the view of some, the application of words is fourfold.
According to their view, it has been stated that there are genus-words (*jātiśabda*), quality-words (*guṇaśabda*), action-words (*kriyāśabda*), and arbitrary-words (*yadṛcchāśabda*); however,
even words such as "Devadatta" are held to denote a genus through the distinction of different states.

Furthermore, if it were admitted that a universal (*jāti*) always denotes [its instances], then because it would exclude other particulars and abandon other individuals, it would be impossible for it to function toward any intended specific individual. Moreover, when a cow-owner says, "Bring the cow," we observe that the activity directed toward bringing a cow is restricted precisely by excluding cows belonging to others;
and this would be possible only if the word "cow" (*go-śabda*), through context or other means, were functioning with reference to a specific instance.
