Furthermore, there would be no comprehension of the sentence-meaning such as "the bringing of the cow" either;
therefore, it is not the case that the genus (*jāti*) is always what is denoted.
For this reason, a real relationship between words whose bases (*prakṛti*) are distinct is not tenable.
Therefore, regarding those [reasons] characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekin*), the very presence and absence of the effect— intended as a real entity—

which occur through the presence and absence of the cause— intended as a real entity— is itself the relationship. In other words, for non-distinct things, the relationship is precisely the state of being produced and being producer (*janyajanakabhāva*).

For this reason, therefore, the relationship between words—which are of the nature of effects—and their objects—which serve as the causes—must be established by persons acting as agents through the intellect (*buddhi*). This is because a word is employed when an object exists and is not employed when it does not; thus, relying upon the presence and absence of the word that correspond to the presence and absence of the object, the relationship between word and meaning is established by the intellect. Such is the meaning of the sentence.
He explains this very point with the words "those two indeed," and so forth.

Based on the existence and non-existence of a word through the medium of its object, the word and its referent— though by their own nature unmixed and unrelated— appear to a person as if they were mixed and connected;
why do they appear thus in conceptual cognition?
Due to the cultivation of conventional usage—
that is, due to the habituation to usage from beginningless time— the connection between things and words, which is their association, is a human product.
Because [the relation] is established by the force of the latent impressions of conventional usage (vyavahāra-vāsanā),
he states that this is another fault if one were to admit a relation that exists as a real entity (vastubhūta-sambandha):
Furthermore,
because the substratum intended as the signified perishes, that verbal relationship intended as its signifier would remain even when the relationship itself has not perished.

On the grounds that it has no relation, that [relation] is absent; therefore, because of that lack of relation, it would not again be connected with the new entity (*apūrva*) which is the denotable object.
Consequently, all things as they arise would be non-denotable, since they would be unrelated.
Why indeed would they be unrelated?
Because there is no pre-existing relation:
for those various things that arise, there is no relation established prior to their arising, since it is impossible for that relation—which resides in two things—to exist without its relata;
"there too," and so forth.
Furthermore, if it is imagined that a relationship with each object arises whenever those objects arise,
then a change in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of words is not logical; for that very relationship which subsequently arises with the object [would have to be something new].

The nature of being related to that [object] does not exist previously because of the absence of a relation, but it comes into existence later; thus, there would be a reversal of the inherent nature (*svabhāva-viparyaya*) of words, and since they are eternal, that is not tenable.
This is the explanation beginning with "athā" and so forth.

When the former related object has perished, the relation of a word [to that object] is destroyed. Consequently, there would be a deficiency—namely, a lack of relation—with respect to another object produced later; and for this reason, lest there be an inability to denote subsequently produced objects, it is held that every object as it arises possesses a relation. Even if an object were to arise while its relation remains ungrasped, nevertheless, the relation, though having arisen, would not belong to the word;
thus, by virtue of that relation, the word would not be the possessor of that [object].
For what reason? Because it is impossible for that sound, which by nature lacks a connection with that subsequently arisen [moment], to become connected to it;
and because it is impossible for it to possess a nature connected to it through that connection.
When,
without a reversal of its own nature and without abandoning its prior unrelated nature, does it [arise]? He states another fault as well:

Furthermore, since a relation that arises simultaneously with its object is established through something other than the word, and since the word does not assist that relation, the relation cannot depend upon the word; therefore, it is impossible for the relation to exist [in the word].
Furthermore, if that sound were also assumed to be a cooperative cause for the production of the relation— that is, a cooperative cause for the arising of the connection—
it would follow that the sound, being capable, would produce the relation eternally;
it would follow that the generation of the relation would occur at all times.
What is the reason?
Because it does not depend on auxiliary causes;
furthermore, this independence is due to the fact that an eternal sound cannot be assisted by auxiliary causes.
If it is argued that [the cause], being incapable [of producing the relation] on its own, produces it by depending on auxiliary factors,
then why would it remain powerless even later— at the time when the object is present— even though it was previously incapable of generating the connection?
Because it does not abandon its previously established nature of incapacity,
this fault that exists regarding a relation that is a real entity (*vastubhūta*) does not exist regarding a relation that is conceptualized and displayed by the intellect;
for [the verse says] "not indeed," and so forth— this is the explanation.
In dependence upon that, the mutual dependence of those entities arises from some cause imagined by the intellect;
their characteristic relation has the nature of appearing to the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the person,
because it is so disposed as to appear therein— that is, in the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*) of the person which possesses the habituation of such cultivation.

And this human-made relationship does not depend upon the fusion of entities— that is, their commingling— because all entities remain established in their own essential natures due to the distinctness of their intrinsic forms. Rather, that person, without altering the inherent nature of eternal things, merely removes the stable nature of the related entity and does not assume another related nature.
"From somewhere"— because one observes the existence of something when that [other thing] exists; or else,
through the ripening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for such conventional usage within, one might conceive it by oneself and establish this connection here, thinking, "This is related to that."
Through the repeated practice of human convention, even those things regarded as eternal would likewise become possessed of relations fashioned by humans;
yet, for all that, they do not undergo the property of deviating from their previously established nature of being unrelated.
This is what is meant:
the relation conceptualized by the intellect—the relation imagined by you—is not contradicted even in the case of those [entities] you imagine to be eternal;
therefore, it is proper to rely on that very [relation], and not on a real one.

Regarding what was stated previously— that the relation is impermanent because the supported [relation] perishes due to the cause that is the loss of the substratum— if, in response to this objection, it is argued that the relation does not perish even upon the loss of its substratum because it is eternal, just like a genus (*jāti*); that is, just as a genus does not perish even when its substratum is destroyed because it is eternal, so too it would be with the relation.
To this, he replies:
Even in the case of eternal entities such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which are accepted as substrata, what efficacy does the substratum possess? None at all.

By the phrase "it is heard that the basis [of cognition] which is desired by him is ineffective," and so forth, the commentary— by the words "it is heard"— states that this is merely a conventional renown and is devoid of any real entity (*nirvastuka*).

We do not perceive any assistance produced by the substratum—namely, the capacity of the substratum—residing in universals and the like which are exclusively eternal; for what reason, then, would that which is intended to be the substratum actually be a substratum?
What is the cause?
Because there is no cause for that which is already produced and established by its own nature,
and because a substratum that is not an agent is independent.
If it is argued that the manifestation— that is, the fitness for the appearance— of the universal (*jāti*) and its relation arises from the substratum (*āśraya*),
and that this very [fitness] is the benefit conferred by the substratum, and for that reason the category is called a "substratum," he provides the following answer:
Regarding the passage beginning with *jñāna*:

due to the connection with auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*)—namely, lamps and so forth—which are the causes for the production of cognition, and because they reside in a suitable location, there arises in the objects to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*), such as jars, a capacity to produce a cognition corresponding to themselves by virtue of their fitness for producing that [cognition]. This very arising is what is intended as "manifestation" (*vyakti*) by those who know logic and understand the principles. However, in the case of universals (*jāti*) and so forth, which are to be manifested, because they are eternal and thus immutable, there is no differentiation [in them] on account of the manifestor.
If the capacity for the production of cognition has not arisen, what meaning or what assistance has been rendered to those universals and so forth by their own manifestors?
None at all.
Because those [factors] such as birth and so forth are considered to be manifested by those manifestors,
he explains [this] with the verse beginning "The auxiliary causes... (sahakāriṇa...).

From what kind of cooperative cause, such as a lamp, which depends upon its material cause (*upādāna*), does there arise—out of a prior material cause characterized by a jar or the like that was incapable of producing cognition—the production of a subsequent moment characterized by a jar or the like that is capable? This is because the material cause, being characterized by a jar or the like, depends upon [the lamp] for its capacity.
The "manifestation" (*abhivyakti*) of jars and so forth is precisely the arising of another moment that is fit to produce a cognition of its own object.

Otherwise, if jars and the like did not acquire the fitness to produce cognition from the lamp and so forth, then it would follow that cognition would be produced from jars and the like even without depending upon that assistance—that is, without the assistance provided by the lamp.
In the margin,
the phrase *tadapekṣatvāt* is missing.
Now, it might be argued that a lamp or similar object produces the capacity for a previously incapable suggestible (*vyaṅgya*).
In that case, since things such as lamps, which exercise efficacy, are the producers of things such as jars, what is the reason?
It is because that efficacy has the nature of that [lamp] itself; it does not have a non-manifested nature.
Upon its production, only the jar or similar object would be produced;
now, if it is maintained that this fault shall not arise because the capacity produced by the lamp and so forth is intended to be a different entity from the manifested object, then,
when such a difference between the capacity and the object is admitted—
Because it would follow that entities such as jars would not be assisted by lamps and the like;
for when something is done to one thing, another is not thereby assisted, as this would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Furthermore, if the capacity produced by the lamp were a distinct entity, then since the cognition of the jar and so forth would arise from that [capacity], the capacity itself would have to be perceived at all times. Consequently, it would follow that jars and other objects—which do not produce cognitions of themselves—would never be perceived at all.
And it is accepted that [objects] such as jars are perceived; therefore, at that time too, there would be the undesirable consequence of perception independent of light—
meaning that the perception of jars and so forth would follow even without depending on light.
If it is asked how it is that [the cognition of] jars and so forth is independent of light, he says "independent," etc.

This independence of jars and so forth which has been proposed follows because there is no benefit to their own nature; for since the essence of the jar and so forth is not benefited by lamps and the like, there can be no benefit to the jars and so forth through the production of some capacity distinct [from themselves].
Therefore, for this reason, these manifested objects (vyaṅgya), depending upon external factors such as lamps in order to produce cognition of their own objects,
consequently acquire from that external source a specific excellence of nature (svabhāvātiśaya), namely, a self-nature (svarūpa) capable of generating cognition.
For that reason, those things such as lamps which are considered by him to be manifestors are in fact produced;
if they are produced, why are they designated as "manifested"? To this he says:
"In the form of the object of knowledge," and so forth.

However, because of the acquisition— meaning the obtaining— from a manifestor such as a lamp of the form of the object of knowledge, which is the form of the apprehended, cognition necessarily arises regarding that object;
therefore, by virtue of cognition,
which expresses a specific excellence of the effect.

An effect whose cognition has not yet been grasped is distinguished from other effects whose cognitions have not been grasped by means of a word such as "manifested" (*vyaṅgya*), which denotes a specific excellence of that effect;
when it necessarily possesses a grasped cognition, even though it is something produced (*janya*), it is called "manifested."
The meaning is that those things which are not of such a nature are said to be merely effects; thus, for the sake of establishing this distinction, the manifested (vyaṅgya) objects are explained.
It is not so with the universal (jāti), the relation (sambandha), and so forth—meaning those things of which the universal and the relation are the first.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), other things also considered eternal that are dependent are included;

since they cannot be assisted in any way by that which is considered their support, the connection [of the sentence] is that it is not at all logical for them to be manifested by that which provides no assistance.

And in order to show that a relation is not established by three means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), he says: "If the relation were a real entity (vastu), then because the relation is distinct from the two relata, a third entity called 'relation' would come into being.
And if that [third entity] met the conditions for perception (upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta), then there would be a diversity of cognitions based upon three objects."

And this relation between word and object, if it were a real entity (*vastu*), would necessarily not transcend—nor deviate from—the states of being either different or non-different from the word and the object.

If it is argued that there might be a mode distinct from difference and non-difference, he replies: "For its form... because form (*rūpa*) is intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and it has been stated previously that for an entity, its "non-being as such" (*atattva*)—that is, its very state of not being that—is precisely its "otherness" (*anyattva*).
In this context, [it was stated]: "Because that which has not become form does not deviate from its otherness," and furthermore...
B.
And that which...
And this relation, being perceptible by the senses, [is apprehended] in a cognition that has the relation as its object;
therein, it is "by way of exclusion from what is other than it.

Therefore, how could that which is not manifested in a form distinct from the relatum—that is, as an object different from that relation—be such [as it is claimed]? How could it have a nature that excludes others?
What is the reason?
Because the non-distinction (aviveka) of the object of perception from its perceptual appearance is its non-separation (apṛthagbhāva);
and since non-perception is likewise [non-separation], these two—non-distinction and non-perception—are respectively the basis for the existence of their opposites (distinction and perception).

The opposite of discrimination is the absence of discrimination; its basis is the non-discrimination of the object of sight. The opposite of existence is non-existence; its basis is the non-perception of the object of sight.
Therefore, this is the meaning:
Whatever is not perceived as distinct from something else is not other than that;
whatever is visible yet is not perceived is, in short, non-existent.
B.
If they, having reached [it], O Bhagavat...
"Otherwise" means:

if it is accepted that the object is distinct from its cause, and yet, while there is no differentiation between them and they are not perceived as such, one nevertheless postulates their differentiation and existence,
then it follows that the stability of those two— their persistence and the absence of non-differentiation— would be impossible.

For it is thus: if the non-perception of the non-distinction between the two perceivable objects were the cause of this determination, then since those two—the absence of distinction—are not accepted as the means of proof, that determination would be destroyed;

for the relation is supersensible (*atīndriya*). If it is argued that there is no fault as stated, because even though the distinction does not appear in the cognition, it is like the case of the sense organs and so forth;

The meaning is that just as the sense organs, such as the eye, do not appear in cognition as distinct from their objects, such as visible forms, and yet they exist separately, so too will the relation exist. B.
The Teacher says that it is not so, because the relationship is not beyond the reach of the senses.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the object could not be understood from a connection that transcends the senses;
for what reason?
Because that which is unestablished—that is, not ascertained in its own form—is not a signifier.
For it is not logical that something should be cognized by means of another when their relationship is not apprehended;
otherwise, one might as well claim that an object makes its meaning known even while remaining unknown, like a sense organ.
To this, he says: "By mere proximity," and so forth.

If it were admitted that the relation [of a word] makes its meaning known by mere proximity—that is, by its mere existence—then even those who are unacquainted with the relationship between word and meaning would have the realization: "This is the designator of this meaning.
This might be thought.
There is indeed the apprehension of the relation through its distinction [from the relata], but that is not from perception; rather, it is from inference. To this, he says:
"The cognition of the relation is not from inference."
How so? Because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*);
for there is no logical mark whatsoever that establishes the relationship, nor is the cognition of the object itself a logical mark, because an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) cannot be established.
For nowhere has the cognition of an object through the operation of a relation been observed in an example; why?
Because even in that which is adduced as an example, there is a dependence upon a means of proof, since the relation therein is also beyond the reach of the senses.
If it is argued that there is no proof for that [existence] either because the example is unestablished,
and thus this lack of an example is equal when an inference is being made to prove the existence of supersensible things such as the sense organs;
It is not equal;
why?
Because those [factors] such as the sense faculties are inferred otherwise.
No specific form of the sense organs and so forth, which are not themselves perceptible, is established as "this" such that the same fault would apply;
rather, cognition, being the effect, is perceived, and it exhibits positive and negative concomitance with certain factors such as light.
Just as in states such as the closing of the eyes there is a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and in states such as the opening of the eyes there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*),
so too this kind of cognition is an effect that cannot possibly arise from those [sensory] elements alone.

Even when those [other causes] are present, the fact that [the effect] does not arise establishes from that alone the non-origination of the self; and it establishes the dependence upon something distinct from them,
just as it establishes the dependence upon a cause distinct from the proximate cause.
B.
Regarding the subtle elements of the effects:
there exists some other cause.
Therefore, from the aforementioned positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the sense organs are established by way of their effects;
and here, sprouts and the like—which do not occur due to a deficiency of other causes—serve as the illustration.
However, there is no such inference of the relationship by means of its effect apart from [the senses] themselves, as is the case with the eyes and so forth.
Because it is an inference of a particular;
for that inference which holds that "there is a relation" is indeed an inference of a particular.
Because it has been stated according to the principle [of logic],
that is improper; for what reason?

If it is argued that since that very relationship is unestablished, there is an absence of the cognition which is the effect of that relationship— that is, the effect of the relationship itself— and therefore the word-meaning is the logical mark (liṅga), he replies with the words "For not," and so forth.
For in that case, neither the form of the word nor the object is a logical mark (*liṅga*) with respect to a particular relation;
what is the reason?
Because both the word and the object are capable [of being related] everywhere.

Since every word is capable of denoting every object, and every object is capable of being denoted by every word, the cause for the cognition of a specific object is a specific relation; and since that relation, which is the basis for the cognition of a specific object, is not communicated by means of an indefinite word and object— or if it were communicated, there would be no distinction— then, from the cognition of every relation, there would follow the comprehension of every object.
But this is not the case; therefore, there is no cognition of this relationship from words and meanings that are themselves indeterminate.
Because every object is capable of being expressed by every word;
and if a specific relation between words and objects were established through a [general] relation, then a cognition of that specific relation would occur in some cases.
For, in the absence of the establishment of a relation between words by means of a specific relation, such a cognition of a specific relation would not be logical.

Furthermore, if it is maintained that the cognition of a specific relation arises from a word even without a [pre-existing] relation, or if such a cognition of a relation is desired to be without a cause, then why is it not also accepted that the communication of meaning by words is likewise without a cause?
For that nature of the word and its object is a mark (*liṅga*) that is similar and equal in all relations;
consequently, since there would be no distinction, the word would lead to every possible relation, and thus there would be the cognition of every object without distinction.
Every person, whether they have grasped the convention or not, would have cognition of all objects;

therefore, since the cognition of objects arises through the establishment of the relationship by the aforementioned reasoning, no person would depend upon tradition or the instruction of another for the cognition of objects.
The relation is similar to that which is restricted to the cognition of its specific particulars.
B.
And [the word] "ca" has been added.

If it is argued that it is not the isolated word that possesses the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*) for establishing the relationship, but rather the word together with its traditional transmission (*saṃpradāya*).

So, what is the use of this succession—namely, that from the tradition (*sampradāya*) comes the word’s status as an inferential mark (*liṅga*), from that the cognition of the relation, and from that the communication of the object? What is the purpose of this succession?

Why does that very same word alone—not devoid of a real-world relation and depending solely on tradition—not effect the cognition of the object, such that another relation would have to be postulated?
For this very reason, even the postulation of a relation of power (*śakti*) based on the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the cognition of meaning is refuted;
since the cognition of meaning is possible through the force of convention alone even without a [real] power,
the claim that "the relation is established by three means of valid cognition" is thereby discarded.
B.
Because of its existence:

that word is seen to be employed by persons with a specific intention—that is, with the intention of conveying a particular meaning—at the time of convention; it is not seen otherwise, nor is it seen when employed contrary to the intended meaning.
By this, positive and negative concomitance have been stated; thus,
through the aforementioned observation and non-observation, it produces the cognition of that object, just like smoke and so forth.
That very relationship between word and object, known as "inseparable concomitance" (avinābhāva), is indicated by the terms "perception" and "non-perception.
Furthermore, we do not perceive any capacity in any other real entity for producing cognition apart from this aforementioned inseparable concomitance;
nor do we perceive any means of establishing, or any cause for the establishment, of such a relationship.
Thus, having stated the fault in accepting a distinction between the relation and its two relata, he states the fault even in the case of accepting their non-distinction with the words "Now," etc.;
"by those two" means by the two relata, given that the relation is non-different from them.

If it is argued that the relation will be something distinct from the two related entities— the word and the object— which are themselves merely the relata, being devoid of both identity and difference,
[the author] says "not from this" and so forth.
Therefore, there is no other possible mode of being for a real entity apart from the conceptual alternatives of identity and difference;
the detailed explanation of "form" and so forth refers to the differentiation of form, which is the differentiation of intrinsic nature.
Because it is based on that [connection], there is another determination; that is, the determination of a different intrinsic nature.

However, that entity called "connection," which is not of a distinct form but is intended to be of that very form—the form of the related entities themselves—would be nothing other than those [related entities] themselves.
It would be of the very nature of the related entity and nothing else;
how then is there the cognition that "there is a relation between these two"? To this he says:
"But the distinction of properties (dharma-bheda) would be merely conceptualized."
By means of the previously described method— which establishes the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) and relies upon the distinction between exclusions—
that distinction of exclusions, though produced by conceptual construction, is not contradictory even in a single [entity].

But a difference in reality is not non-contradictory in one and the same thing; rather, it is indeed contradictory, because multiplicity is impossible for a single entity from the perspective of ultimate truth. Apart from difference and non-difference, there is no other way for a real entity to exist.
Whence could there be such a statement? For that entity has the characteristic of form, it has the characteristic of intrinsic nature,
and this [statement] does not transcend the conceptualization of form.

Since the conceptual alternatives of difference and non-difference cannot be transcended, and because the nature of the entity— which is the very nature of the word's referent— is distinct, it was stated previously that the relationship characterized by the fusion of forms is not real, but is produced solely by conceptual construction.

Due to a person's habitual practice of linguistic usage, even though those two [word and meaning] are not actually conjoined, they appear as if conjoined; on account of that, the determination of their relation is established. By such arguments, he states that a relation characterized by "adherence"—defined as the mutual mixing of the two relata—is not possible among things that are unattached or unconjoined.
Rather than this, he asserts that for words and meanings, the relation is a third entity entirely distinct from them, consisting of the "adherence of form" (rūpa-śleṣa).
And so forth:
Since that which is already established cannot be dependent on another entity, how [could it be otherwise]?
How could [a relation] be dependent upon a relation?
For a relation is held to be dependent upon a relation because it resides in two things;
nor is it logical for a relation to be something distinct from those [relata], since a relation consists in the nature of mutual contact. Thus he says:

Furthermore, if substance (*dravya*) were a distinct category (*padārthāntara*), how could it be the relation of one thing that is related to another? By this, both points desired by the opponent—that a relation, being a distinct entity, must reside in its relata and consist in a mutual contact (*paraśleṣarūpa*)—are refuted. To the question, "Even if it were a distinct entity, why would it not be dependent on others? he says:
"Indeed not," and so forth; for that which is already established does not depend upon another,
because that which is fully accomplished has no further need for anything.
Being independent by virtue of being non-contingent, it has no relation to anything else;
nor is it logical for a relation to be a distinct entity,
because "substance" is said to be an intrinsic nature, which is to say it is spoken of as a distinct category of reality.
How could there be a conjunction of that other-nature with its two relata?
It could not be at all,
nor does it serve as a cause for such conjunction.
What is the reason?

Because a third nature, by its existence, does not cause another nature of the two related entities to become "joined" (śliṣṭa)—that is, to become connected; for a state that is unjoined and unrelated cannot be called "joined" merely by being named "relation.
If it is argued that it would indeed be joined by being joined with something already joined:
This is not so;
for what reason?
Because the connection known as "relation" (sambandha) is established through its fusion with those two related entities.
If a relation, once created, were to join those two related entities [as in the case of "this is that" and so forth],
then there would be the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of joining them with a third entity as a different object.
Everything would be connected with any third term whatsoever, because there is no distinction;
for indeed, there is no difference in the fact that both the intended related entity and any other thing are equally connected with another object.
Furthermore,
those phonemes which exist as real entities are nonetheless devoid of meaning; therefore, they are not denoters, and consequently, the relation of denoted and denoter does not operate therein.
To this, he says: "In that case, since the word and so forth possess meaning, the operation of the relation will occur there. [The opponent replies:

"By the word 'and so forth' (ādi), a sentence imagined as a word might be the signifier; and when that [sentence] is imagined, it is a non-entity (avastu) whose nature is non-existent, whether it be a word or a sentence."
How could there be the occurrence of a relation characterized as the signifier-signified relationship— a real entity that is the very nature of things? For,
as the commentary beginning with "the signifier indeed" explains,
a signifier would indeed possess that [relation]— that is, it would be endowed with the relation known as the cause of expression, by virtue of being a constituent part of speech.
Even though phonemes exist and are present, they are not expressive because each one individually does not convey a meaning, because they lack simultaneity,
and because no comprehension of meaning is observed from those uttered by multiple speakers at different times.

If it is argued: "Therefore (*tat*), that relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) does not exist in those phonemes (*varṇa*); for if that relationship were to reside in them—that is, if it were to reside in those phonemes which are the signifiers—there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the loss of the relationship's status as a subordinate factor (*aṅgatva*) to the act of signifying. Consequently, it is the phonemes themselves, when uttered by a single speaker in a specific sequence (*krama-viśeṣa*) or a specific order (*ānupūrvī-viśeṣa*), that are the signifiers; thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply."
As it has been said:
"To whatever extent, of whatever nature, and for the purpose of conveying which meaning the phonemes have their capacities known, they convey that [meaning] in exactly that way."
This very point is clarified [in Sphoṭasiddhi 69]:

"In whatever number, of whatever nature, and whichever letters have their capacity for conveying a particular meaning well-known, they are the conveyors of that meaning in exactly that way. (Sphoṭasiddhi 69)

However, regarding those [phonemes] which have become subordinate [elements], their conjunction (*sāhitya*) with respect to the communication of meaning, as well as their sequence determined by a single agent and so forth, is intended [by the speaker]. And when there is a sequence based on the identity of the agent, there is a regulating factor (*niyāmaka*). *Sphoṭasiddhi* 70.

For one who employs [the phonemes], that sequential observation from the elders which occurred previously is not at all capable in sequence, just as those whose capacity is observed simultaneously are not so when used sequentially. (Sphoṭa 71)

By their very nature, entities are not capable of acting in that manner sequentially; they would likewise be incapable of acting simultaneously. (Sphoṭasiddhi 73) Furthermore, with regard to the communication of meaning...
The proximity of something is always necessarily present;

however, by that alone, other factors do not lose their status as constituent parts simply because they are separated [from it]. Just as, for example, the *visarjanīya* lacks the capacity [to produce its effect] when there is an intervention. (Sphoṭasiddhi 83)

In the same way, the capacity of others does not exist in immediate succession. (Sphoṭasiddhi 85) Nor is it the case that where there is incapacity for each individually, there is incapacity for all together.
There is a lack of capacity in all [the parts],
for it is observed that the wheels and other components possess the capacity for drawing [the chariot] and so forth. (Sphoṭasiddhi 86 B)
He provides the refutation with the words beginning "they are not seen to be capable," stating:
"it is not so."
Since the sequence [of phonemes] must be either non-different from the phonemes or different from them,
in the first case— because the sequence, being non-different, is not a differentiator and thus not a qualifier—
for that which is non-different from something else cannot be a differentiator of the nature of that thing.
Furthermore, since the form of that sequence consisting of phonemes—

which is [the basis for] the word *rasa*— is identical to the form in another sequence such as *sā*, the comprehension of meaning would be the same in both cases, just as it is with the phonemes themselves. B.
If it is then argued that the sequence is distinct from the phonemes, he says:
"Even as a different entity," because the fact that the sequence is a different entity from the phonemes will be refuted later.

Since a sequence is not possible for letters produced simultaneously because such a sequence is not perceived, nor is there a sequence existing as a separate entity for letters produced non-simultaneously— because non-simultaneous production itself constitutes the nature of sequence;
for when people in the world speak of a sequence, they are speaking precisely of non-simultaneous production.
Therefore, sequence is simply non-simultaneous arising;
nor is sequence a property of one among two things that have arisen non-simultaneously, because sequence is not perceived in the cognition of a single [entity];
nor is it a property of both.
Since both [the preceding and succeeding states] do not exist at one and the same time, how can there be a property (*dharma*) of that which is non-existent?

Therefore, it will be stated that "sequence" is merely the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of two entities existing in succession. And even if sequence consists of a preceding and succeeding form, nevertheless, phonemes do not become the cause for the comprehension of meaning through such a sequence.
Because each [letter] individually does not convey the meaning, because there is an absence of simultaneity,
and because it is impossible for those occurring in a fixed sequence to act in combination through non-simultaneity.

It might be argued that just as a seed, though not a causal agent toward a sprout when alone, becomes a causal agent when in proximity with auxiliary factors due to its specific state, so too the phonemes, though individually incapable, become causes for the cognition of meaning when distinguished by a particular sequence.
B.
There is no [distinction] among the phonemes;
that is incorrect.

For regarding the final phoneme—whether it is uttered in conjunction with other phonemes or by itself—what distinction could there be such that the presence or absence of the cognition of meaning would depend upon it? [Objection:
But surely this very fact—that they are either combined or not—is the distinction! [Reply: True.
For indeed, their cooperation exists only when they are performing an action;
however, when they are not present, they do not engage in the cognition of an object, because each one individually is incapable of doing so.
Nor [can it be argued that it does not exist] because it is non-existent at the time of other phonemes;
for then this would be the distinction: that the perception of the preceding phoneme occurs in some cases and not in others.
But even this is not sound.
For the perception of preceding phonemes that have already occurred cannot affect the final phoneme, because they no longer exist;
and if there is no distinction, then just as blind people cannot see the sun, if the phonemes are individually incapable of producing a certain effect, they will remain so even when combined.
By this, the argument beginning with "where there is no power individually" and so forth is refuted;

for it is only when the specific qualities of the chariot parts have arisen that they possess the capacity for drawing [the load] in their state of conjunction. Otherwise, as with each part taken individually, there would be no capacity even in their conjunction.

Furthermore, there is no mutual relationship of cause and effect among the phonemes by which the preceding phonemes could be capable of producing the comprehension of meaning through a traditional succession.

Nor can it be argued that the preceding letters possess efficacy through a causal chain because the final letter, accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by those preceding letters, is the cause of the cognition of the meaning;
for the impression deposited by the experience of the letters is the cause of recollection only with respect to those very letters, not with respect to the meaning.
Indeed, an impression deposited by the experience of a cow does not produce a recollection of a horse.

Nor can it be that syllables are the denoters [of meaning] through a specific sequence, because we observe the cognition of the object when there is the perception of the final syllable accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the preceding syllables;

yet, in the absence of convention (*saṃketa*), there is no cognition of the object, and convention has the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, not the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the syllable. How, then, could syllables be denoters?
Furthermore,
if a single phoneme by itself does not convey meaning, then it would not do so even when accompanied by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*),
because no distinction [in its nature] has arisen.
How then can it be said that one phoneme is capable of conveying the meaning directly while another is so only through a succession?
Furthermore, as for what is said:
"Whether they are grasped in sequence or otherwise, their simultaneous presence [is required]."
Therefore, she (the sphoṭa) must be the eternal cause for our cognition of meaning.
(Śloka-vārttika, Sphoṭa 108)

Thus, it is argued that because the phonemes (*varṇa*) realized in sequence are eternal and all-pervading, their simultaneous existence in the locus of space (*ākāśadeśa*) is the very cause for the cognition of meaning;
however, this is incorrect,
for it is the phoneme as it is being perceived that conveys the meaning, not its mere presence.
Because it would entail the absurd consequence of establishing all categories of objects,
and because neither simultaneity nor eternality and omnipresence are tenable for things produced by a single author— as he will explain later— this [position] is devoid of substance.
And as for what is also said:
"Alternatively, that final cognition of all the phonemes among those known in sequence through direct perception is the cause of the cognition of the meaning."
And in that cognition, the simultaneity of the phonemes is perceived;

it need not necessarily exist as a simultaneous perception, for that which is subsequent arises through the reflection upon the preceding and following [phonemes] as a single cognition whose object is the entire set of phonemes, serving as the cause for the comprehension of the meaning.
The phrase "it would be the representation of the object" means that the representation of the object could occur even by another cognition of simultaneity;

or rather, it means that among those letters previously known in succession through perception, that subsequent cognition of all the letters taken together is the cause of the cognition of the meaning.
And in that cognition, the simultaneity of the phonemes is perceived;
however, it need not necessarily arise through a simultaneity established by direct perception. (Ślokavārttika, Sphoṭavāda)
109–10 This too is incorrect,
for sequence is dependent upon the agent who employs it, whereas simultaneity is not.
Furthermore, since the comprehension of meaning arises from phonemes existing in a state of being employed by an agent, the comprehension of meaning could not result from simultaneity;
for there would be the consequence of error if there were a simultaneous apprehension of phonemes that are actually sequential,
and yet no such simultaneity exists among them because it is impossible for them to be eternal.

Some say that this cognition is multiform (*citrarūpā*) and has both existent and non-existent phonemes as its object—that cognition by which the final phoneme is grasped in each word. Regarding *Sphoṭasiddhi* 11: some say that the cognition by which the final phoneme of each word is grasped is of a dual nature, consisting of both recollection and direct perception, because it has as its objects both proximate and non-proximate phonemes.
That too is incorrect,
because it is contradictory for a single cognition to have both perceptible and imperceptible forms;
nor is perception alone capable of having both existent and non-existent phonemes as its object.

Nor is it of the nature of memory, because that would contradict its having non-existence as its object; nor is it of the nature of perception, because it is not accepted that [perception] has a proximate object.
For this very reason, the cognition grasping words and so forth would have a conceptually constructed object.

Others, however, maintain that when the final phoneme is cognized, memory—produced by the awakening of latent impressions (saṃskāra) deposited by the experience of the preceding phonemes—is what conveys the meaning across all the phonemes; as it has been said:
"For others declare that when the final phoneme is known, memory, produced by all the latent impressions, occurs simultaneously with respect to all [the phonemes]."

If it is asked how there can be simultaneous recollection of things experienced sequentially, he says: "And regarding all such objects, a mental cognition of a collective synthesis (samuccaya-jñāna) is accepted by all theorists, even though the cognitions [of the individual items] occur in succession. (Sphuṭārthā 113)
Therefore, although there may first be a cognition of the phonemes sequentially by means of the ear and the mind, and subsequently a simultaneous recollection [of them],
the phonemes mounted upon that [recollection] are not distant from the comprehension of the meaning.
"The cognition of the object from the word is thus designated by worldly people"— this [statement] from the *Ślokavārttika*, in the section on the *sphoṭa*,
is also untenable.
Since letters are expressive only when employed by a single agent and are expressive only when they do not exist simultaneously,
and since no simultaneity is perceived among the letters that are objects of memory—
because they are remembered precisely in their fixed order.

Nor is there a grasping of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the phonemes by means of memory, because—unlike direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—there is an absence of a clear manifestation; and because it is impossible for a single [cognition] to possess multiple forms, both clear and unclear.

Rather, it is simply because the phonemes, which are indistinct in nature and consist of their own internal forms, are determined (*adhyavasāya*) as non-different from external phonemes by means of recollection, that it is said that the external phonemes themselves are the signifiers.

Furthermore, regarding external [non-Vedic] castes, we certainly accept that which is conceptually constructed as a "word" (*pada*) and so forth through the determination of external phonemes (*varṇa*).
Thus, in the Mīmāṃsaka position, once the expressive capacity of phonemes has been refuted, the word and so forth are likewise refuted,
because there exists no word or such entity apart from the phonemes and the like.
Thus it has been said: "Indeed,
no word exists apart from its phonemes (varṇa),
nor does anything exist apart from phonemes and words."

Now, in order to refute the position of the grammarians that words and so forth exist as entities distinct from the phonemes and other components, he says: "That is non-existent," introducing the point with the word "that" (*tat*).
Therefore, either the meaning does not exist, or if the phonemes lack the capacity to denote, then the word and so forth must be the denoter; yet that word and so forth is nothing at all.
What is the reason?
Because there is a contradiction between the identity and difference of that [word] and its phonemes (varṇa),
if it were different from them, it would have to be perceived as distinct;
and even if it were not perceptible, it could not be expressive, because that which is not apprehended cannot function as a signifier.
Even if there were no distinction [between the letters], the consequence would be that they are non-expressive, just like the individual phonemes themselves.

Therefore, it is a specific auditory cognition— a sensory consciousness capable of grasping the letters in their successive order— which follows upon that [process] and arrives by way of the experience thereof.
That whose material cause (*upādāna*) is the homogeneous latent impression (*sabhāgavāsanā*), which is the capacity for a conceptualization of a similar kind, is described as such.
This conceptualization, having that homogeneous latent impression as its material cause, possesses an appearance-delusion (*pratibhāsavibhrama*);
that is, the very error of appearance is the word and the sentence, which manifest as a single [entity] and are indeed false.
This is what is meant:

the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which arises subsequent to the experience of the letters in their sequential order, determines those letters as having a single nature in the form of a word (*pada*) and so forth; thus, the conceptual construction (*parikalpita*) of a word and so on is indeed false.
Now, one might ask: since the letters themselves are experienced as distinct, how can a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arise that manifests as a single word or the like?
And since [the cognition] arises from that, there must be an experience of a single word and so forth within the phonemes; thus, this is not a fault.

For at the time of establishing a convention, the instructor—who has already understood the sequence of phonemes as having the form of a single word or the like—conveys to another person that "this is one word" or "this is a sentence.
At that time, the other person also develops a cognition that superimposes the status of a single word upon that sequence of phonemes.

Then, for that person whose mental impression (*saṃskāra*) has been instilled by the experience of that single form superimposed upon the word or the like, there arises at the time of linguistic usage a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a single form, such as "this is one word" or "this is a sentence," upon hearing the sequence of phonemes.

Thus, for each preceding listener, there arises a cognition through the superimposition of identity upon the sequences of phonemes received from each preceding speaker; consequently, the conventional usage of words and so forth is beginningless.
For this very reason it is said:
"The delusion of conceptual appearance, conditioned by beginningless homogeneous latencies, manifests as a word or a sentence appearing as a single unit, yet it is entirely false."
Furthermore, falsity [belongs] to distinct phonemes because they appear in the memory-cognition (*smaraṇajñāna*) as having the form of a single word and so forth;
and since it is impossible for that many [phonemes] to possess both unity and plurality due to their contradiction.
Now, it might be argued: "The word and so forth, which is grasped by perception, is indeed one; how then could it be false?"
That is incorrect; for indeed, a single word or the like [cannot be the cause].
What is the reason?
If it is argued that because it is impossible to grasp [the word] sequentially by means of a cognition that apprehends a series of phonemes,
and that if [the word] were a single unit it would be grasped all at once by a single cognition— yet in fact a word or the like is not grasped by a single cognition— the author replies:
"By that alone," and so forth;
that [object], such as a word,
is not to be grasped by a single cognition.
What is the reason?

Because words and sentences are grasped through the sequence of phonemes and the succession of phonemes, one might think that a word consisting of a single phoneme would then be graspable by a single cognition; therefore, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "of a single phoneme" (*ekavarṇa*):
even at the time of the production of a single phoneme, it is not [actually] a single phoneme because it involves multiple moments of cognition.
For instance, when the sound *bhāḥ* is uttered, the letter *ga* is perceived as being without its vowel (*niracka*) for the duration of half a mora (*ardhamātrā*).

But since the duration of a *mātrā* is perceived as belonging to a consonant (*sakta*), how can there exist a word consisting of a single phoneme (*varṇa*) that could be grasped by a single cognition?
Therefore, it is said that [the cognition] grasps the whole [word].
If the intellect does not grasp a sound uttered even with minimal effort, or if it does not clearly perceive the phoneme as a whole,
then the parts of a phoneme are never perceived individually.
That has been refuted in Śloka-vārttika, Sphoṭa section, verses 10 and 11.
According to the reasoning already stated, because a phoneme possesses parts,
and because cognitions are momentary, it would not be possible for a single cognition to grasp the successive parts of a phoneme.
This might be so.

The time required for the completion of a phoneme (*varṇa*) constitutes a single moment (*kṣaṇa*); therefore, it will be possible to grasp a word with a single cognition. To this he says "of a moment," and so forth:
because a moment is of such a duration that a single atom (*paramāṇu*) traverses the space between one atom and another.

Time is indivisible, and it is logically consistent that it consists of exactly the duration required for a single atom to pass by; for if one were to accept a *kṣaṇa* (moment) longer than the aforementioned time, it would be impossible for that divisible *kṣaṇa*, which possesses parts, to constitute the ultimate limit of time.
For what reason is there the production of even a single, highly distinct color in multiple moments?
[The answer begins with] "multiple," and so forth.

In that moment of time (*nimeṣa*) during which there is the displacement—that is, the passing away—of many atoms, there occurs the displacement of many atoms; because [the duration] is equal to that, even the final phoneme, such as a vowel (*ākāra*), is completed. Therefore, a word consisting of multiple phonemes is not grasped by a single cognition.
Nor is a single word apprehended by memory as having multiple natures;
for what reason?
Because remembrance occurs in accordance with the original experience.

Just as the perception of phonemes occurs in a specific sequence, so too does the memory of them arise there in that very same sequence. Since memory belongs to that same time as the perception—meaning it shares the temporal order of the perception—it is said, with reference to another type of activity, that this [memory] is likewise sequential. However, in the case of an activity characterized by repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), although there may be a simultaneous recollection of phonemes even when they were perceived sequentially, nevertheless, because no distinction is perceived between the sequence of perception and the sequence of recollection, a single word or the like does not [arise].
Therefore, this is the meaning:

no distinction or difference is perceived between the sequence of phonemes that appears in direct experience and the sequence of phonemes that appears in memory; consequently, how can it be said that a single word or the like is grasped by a single cognition, nor yet that the word or the like is multiple?
What is the reason?
Because cognition appears without differentiation;

that is, because cognition—in the form of words and sentences—appears as non-different, as a unity. For when a word or a sentence is uttered, the thought occurs to people: "This is one word," or "This is one sentence."
Therefore, what was said in *Sphoṭasiddhi* 121—
that because of the rapidity [of pronunciation] and the smallness of the interval, that [non-difference] might occur in the word "cow" (*go*),
whereas in words such as "Devadatta," a clear difference is perceived— is refuted.

Since a cognition that superimposes a single word arises at a time subsequent to the experience of the individual phonemes, and since their multiplicity— that is, the multiplicity of the constituent parts such as the phonemes— will be refuted later,
such [a cognition] might indeed occur in the case of the word "go" (cow) due to its rapidity and the smallness of the interval between the sounds.
Since a clear distinction is perceived in words such as "Devadatta," it follows that the word and so forth are not manifold; therefore, [the sphoṭa is one]. (Sphoṭasiddhi 121)
The meaning is that because it appears as both one and many, and because oneness and multiplicity are mutually contradictory and thus incompatible, the word and so forth are not a real entity;
or rather, those words and so forth are not a real entity because oneness and multiplicity are impossible for them.
What is the reason?
Because that entity does not transcend these alternatives:
for an entity must be either of a single nature or of a manifold nature at any given time, but it cannot be both, due to contradiction.
Furthermore, the opponent maintains that the relationship between word and meaning is a real entity (*vastu*); how then could it have that [unreal] as its locus?
It would have to have unreal words and sentences as its locus.
The analysis of the compound is: "that which has those words and sentences as its locus."
What is the reason?
Because it is impossible for a locus such as a word to exist as a non-entity;
thus, in the absence of a locus to be resorted to, the relation would be ungrounded.
And thus, because it would be non-dependent, there would be no relation at all, since there would be an absence of dependence upon the relata;
therefore, the relation between word and meaning is neither natural nor non-human (apauruṣeya).
However, the relationship is indeed human-made,

because it consists of the physical movements and so forth occurring at the end of the act of employment, which are intended to convey the speaker's intention— that is, the intention to communicate a particular meaning.
Therefore, "the word is produced" is stated according to our own view,
while "the word is manifested" is stated according to the intention of others; thus,
it is non-deviant [from the truth].
Considering that it is non-deviant in its communication of meaning, the relationship (*sambandha*) of this word is its being an effect produced by the intention to communicate a specific meaning.

Because a word is employed with the intention of communicating meaning, that [intention]—whether as the production or the manifestation of the word—is the basis for its non-deviance regarding the communication of meaning; it is the cause of that non-deviance, being human-made (*pauruṣeyī*), created by a person.
Thus, the relationship between word and meaning is indeed human-made;

and by means of that—that is, by means of the aforementioned relationship—there is no restriction on words in the communication of meaning. Therefore, even if words were not of human origin, that same deception and contradiction would persist.

Thus, the implication is that the postulation of the Veda's lack of human authorship (apauruṣeyatva) is entirely futile. Furthermore, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the Vedic sentences are indeed without human authorship.
Indeed, because there is no recollection of the authors— that is, the composers— of the Veda,
the word "kila" (it is said) is used to indicate the impropriety [of such a claim];
and the explanation beginning with "yāpi" and so forth follows.
The creator of many objects is not remembered,
yet they are not uncreated on that account, just as in the case of ancient wells and the like.

Thus, although this authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatā*) of Vedic sentences is logically untenable due to the fallibility of the reason, it is nevertheless asserted by Jaimini on the grounds that no author is remembered;
for there are those who continue to recite such a matter even in the present day.
What more need be said here? A mere curse upon all-pervading darkness!
For thus it was that the Jaiminiyas, on the grounds of the non-remembrance of an author, asserted the lack of human origin [of the Veda].
Thinking, "How has such a lapse in wisdom occurred even for him at this very stage? our minds are moved by both wonder and compassion; thus it is "with wonder and compassion.
Furthermore, thinking, "Even for one who has heard [the teachings], such is the play of ignorance," it is "with wonder";
and thinking, "Sentient beings are tormented by the tight bonds of ignorance," it is "with compassion."

In this regard, others such as Kumārila and his followers, who consider themselves investigators, now repeat this very thing: "Alas, that pervasive darkness by which the world has been so mercilessly and pitilessly assailed! Here, the expression of reproach (*dhig*) is appropriate toward ignorance alone, not toward living beings;
for what fault is there in a living being who, though speaking thus, has been deceived regarding the desire for welfare—that is, deceived by the wish to attain what is beneficial?
However, this is merely a fault of ignorance;
what then is there to say of the lapse in wisdom of one who speaks thus, since this proof is both unestablished (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)?
Regarding that, with reference to the unestablished (*asiddha*),
he says "for thus" (*tathā hi*) and so forth.
They remember Ṛṣikas and others as the authors of the Veda;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), they remember Vālmīki, Vāmadeva, Viśvāmitra, and others; and the followers of Kaṇāda and Vaiśeṣika remember Hiraṇyagarbha-Brahmā as the author of the Veda.

If it is argued that the non-remembrance of an author for those [Vedic texts] and for the Sugatas is unestablished, and therefore the doctrine of the remembrance of an author for the Veda is a false claim because of that reason for proof;
What other word besides the Veda is now [claimed to be] human-made?
The meaning is that none whatsoever is human-made;
"thus" refers to the falsity of the doctrine that there is a recollection of an author.
Clarifying this very point, he says:

"In works such as the *Kumārasambhava*, etc. This means that if those such as Kālidāsa were to be refuted in this manner while designating themselves or another as the author (*praṇetṛ*) or composer (*kartṛ*) of works like the *Kumārasambhava*.
If they were to reject [the authorship] by saying,
"Your claim is false; you are not the authors," then in that case, there would be a contradiction of what has been accepted regarding the rejection of an author in works such as the *Kumārasambhava*.
If it is argued that [the Vedas] must be human compositions because works such as the *Kumārasambhava* are accepted as being so, we reply:
Is it not this very fact—the non-remembrance of an author—that serves as the proof for accepting their non-human origin?

Since that same proof exists for the *Kumārasambhava* and other such works according to the logic already stated, how can it be that the *Kumārasambhava* and others are desired to be human compositions by you? What, then, sublates what?

Now, if—even though the logic is the same—it is maintained that in works such as the *Kumārasambhava*, the refutation of an author constitutes a contradiction of what has been accepted (*abhyupetabādhana*), then this very same contradiction of what has been accepted applies equally to the opponent, the proponent of the Veda (*vedavādin*), when there is a refutation of an author regarding Vedic statements.
For that proponent of the Veda accepts the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Vedas; therefore, since non-human origin is accepted, there is no fault even in refuting an author.

If it is argued that there is no fault of contradicting what has been accepted (*abhyupetabādhā*), [we reply: from where did this proponent of the Veda derive his acceptance—that "the Veda is not of human origin"—prior to the investigation of the grounds for accepting the scripture? This acceptance was without proof, being devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For, when the non-human origin of the Veda was accepted, the non-remembrance of an author was stated as the proof.
Furthermore, since the fault was just stated immediately prior, this desired position is unauthoritative.

Now, if the proponent of the Veda (Vedavādin) has accepted the non-human origin of the Veda without any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then what kind of Mīmāṃsaka is he—this one who grasps things arbitrarily and accepts them without reasoning? Moreover, why would he require a means of valid cognition as a proof regarding such matters as whether something is human or non-human in origin?
The word "yat" refers to the consideration of whether [the Veda] is of human origin or not; by introducing the proof for its being either human or non-human, he brings himself into this state.

For if one who grasps what is illogical should proceed in that very same way everywhere, why would he trouble himself by introducing means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in some instances? This is the general meaning.

Therefore, since the Mīmāṃsaka maintains that the Veda is of infinite extent and is not of human origin, even when he rejects the existence of a creator for the Veda—desiring thereby to avoid contradicting his own tenets—the same applies to anyone else, such as a Kumārila-advocate, who likewise desires another work (e.g., the *Kumārasambhava*) to be of non-human origin; thus, when he rejects its author, the contradiction of his own unaccepted position is equal. Consequently, there is no valid reproach here, meaning that the reproach "there is a contradiction of what has been accepted" does not apply.
Furthermore, [the phrase] "one who perceives no excellence," etc. [follows].

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: [the Mīmāṃsaka] sees no distinction in the proofs for the lack of human authorship—such as "because there is no recollection of an author of such types"—in those sentences which are considered by some to be of human origin and by others to be of non-human origin.

For instance, just as there is a non-recollection of the author for many human compositions whose authors have passed away long ago, so too, seeing no distinction (i.e., seeing no specific difference) in the proof of the non-recollection of an author and so forth regarding Vedic sentences, the Mīmāṃsaka [asserts their non-human origin].

Alternatively, the "properties of effects" (*kāryadharma*) are the properties of words produced by human effort, such as their conformity to the presence and absence of persons; since one observes no distinction or excellence in these properties of effects within worldly and Vedic sentences, this Vedavādin accepts an excellence—a specific quality characterized by authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*)—only in certain Vedic words and not elsewhere. Since there is no proof for such an acceptance, the conduct of this Vedavādin is either irrational or based on a lack of conviction. Thus, according to the method described, the reason "because the author is not remembered" is unestablished (*asiddha*);
he also states that it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
"Are seen," and so forth.
The tradition of oral instruction (*upadeśa-pāramparyam*) is the *sampradāya*;

the tradition of ritual practice (*kriyā-sampradāya*) and the tradition of human authorship (*puruṣakṛtatva-sampradāya*) [are also absent]. As for those [words] such as "in every banyan tree" (*vaṭe vaṭe vai*), "hearing" (*śravaṇa*), and so on, they are likewise [of human origin].
By this, he states that the author is not remembered;
and since there are both produced and human-authored [texts],
the non-remembrance of the author exists even in the case of human-authored sentences— thus, this reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
"Those [words]" refers to artificial words whose tradition of usage has been interrupted;
diligent persons perceive them as "these were made by this person."
This is not so;
for what reason?
Because there is no necessity that even an agent who exerts effort must remember [the action].
Since even one who exerts effort does not necessarily perceive an agent, there remains doubt; furthermore,
because an agent is not perceived even in other cases where words are claimed to be non-human (apauruṣeya), this constitutes a non-perception [of the agent].
As for the claim that an author of this non-human [Veda] is perceived, there is no ascertainment of such perception through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
rather, it arises from the instruction of another. Since such an instruction is untrustworthy and lacks validity, the perception of an author derived from it is incapable of providing certainty.

The claim that the absence of an author for Vedic sentences is determined because no one is observed to say, "I have composed these Vedic sentences," is also not tenable; for we observe people who deny even words they themselves have created, such that even after composing words themselves, they are seen to repudiate them by saying, "These words were not composed by me."
And in that regard, because it is impossible to reach a definitive conclusion— that is, a certainty— as to whether these [scriptures] were composed by this person or by another,
[the argument fails]. Thus, having refuted the reason "because the author is not remembered," [the author proceeds to] refute another proof as well.

He introduces [the following] in order to refute [the opponent's position]: "All study of the Veda must be preceded by study from a teacher, because it is designated as 'Vedic study,' just like the study performed at present."
"Yathā" and so forth:

just as this present-day student of the Veda, having heard it from another, is not capable of speaking or studying this sequence of the Veda— the sequence of letters and words— without [prior instruction].

Likewise, any other person who is considered an author of the Veda would also require instruction from another, and that person likewise from another; thus, because this process is beginningless, its non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva) is established. Someone might say this, but for one who speaks in such a manner, the same answer applies as was stated previously regarding the "non-remembrance of an author. Even if [the Veda] were non-human in origin according to the method just described, would all human sentences now consequently become non-human?

If it is argued that since the study of any other *Kumārasambhava* is preceded by study, its beginninglessness is established, and thus establishing it [as beginningless] would result in the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*abhyupetabādhā*),
then one must state everything starting with: "But this very point is a constituent of the tenet," and so forth.
The word "etcetera" (ādi) is employed for the purpose of including this very [category].
(Ślokavārttika, Vākya, 366)
Demonstrating this very over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),
he says "For likewise," and so forth:
or else, another text composed by a person, such as the *Kumārasambhava* and others.
Apart from the traditional lineage,
no other work has ever been seen by others to have been composed by someone else without the instruction of another;
for that reason, even that [other work] is nothing but a text derived from the Veda.
"Why is it not inferred that [the Veda] is thus non-human (apauruṣeya)?"—this he explains with the words "Certainly not," and so forth.

Certainly, there is no other ground for establishing non-human authorship than the fact that the recitation of those [Vedic texts] by people of the present day occurs without instruction; for they lack the capacity [to produce such a recitation].
For it is not possible to recite the Veda without the instruction of another; thus, the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Vedic sentences is asserted.

And that inability to recite without instruction is equal in other cases as well—namely, in those works accepted as human compositions, which are composed by some particular person for another student.

By the phrase "following that," it means that whatever follows [the argument] as a proof for non-authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*)— namely, the inability to teach or recite [the text]— by that [proof], every word, whether worldly or Vedic, is to be inferred as being authored by a person;
or rather, no Vedic word [is so inferred], because there is no distinction [between them].
Regarding that worldly statement, because it is not lost due to being non-human (apauruṣeya) by way of [the word] "thus" (tathā), the word "etc.

(ādi) in the phrase "etc. includes the contradiction of what has been accepted (abhyupetabādhā). What was stated there immediately following is: "Because the desired [property] is its locus," meaning because the proof of non-human authorship has that as its locus, and so forth.
B.
Furthermore, [the phrase] "because it is a means" (sādhanatvāt), etc., also [applies].
Whatever is of a certain class and of the same class as a given substance,
and which is established by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) from a certain cause—
that other thing, though not observed to have that cause and being indistinguishable from it in terms of its class, is understood not to arise from that cause.
How is this so? It is like fire and wood:
just as one fire is seen arising from fuel and the like, another fire of an identical nature is likewise understood—even if its cause is unperceived—to have that very same cause.
By this [verse], he states the sublation of the proposition by inference (*anumāna-bādha*) in the proof of the Veda’s lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*). B. 0 *tato bhavati*... [etc.]
He explains with the words "no," etc.:
because no cause is perceived, there is nothing called "causeless," since even those things for which no cause is seen [are not truly causeless].
The analysis of the compound is: "the cause of these has not been seen.

The meaning is that even though these entities exist in such a manner, they possess an identical nature (*svabhāva*) because they experience non-difference from other things whose causes have been observed;
thus, being of such a kind, they are inferred to have similar causes.
This is the collective meaning here:
by means of a worldly word, a Vedic word would possess the same property; thus, like the worldly one, it would either be caused by a person, or else not be anything at all.

Now, even if the cause-form—that is, the causal nature—is absent, it is nevertheless maintained that the form of the Vedic word, which is similar to the form of a word caused by a person, has not ceased to exist.
In that case, there would be a transgression of the nature of an effect (*kāryadharma*).

For this is the nature of an effect: that it ceases when its cause ceases. But if, even though the person has ceased [to exist], the Vedic words were to possess a human form, then by that [fact] the nature of an effect would be transgressed.

Consequently, because of the deviation from the properties of an effect, no statement whatsoever would originate from a person; thus, no worldly word could be designated as "human" (pauruṣeya) on that basis. Alternatively, a specific characteristic of human [utterances] distinct from Vedic ones must be shown—one such specific characteristic that would conform to the reason called "person."
By whatever distinction the Veda— being accepted as non-human-authored— and the worldly [text], which is not so accepted, would not undergo a reversal of their desired status,
such that they would respectively be human-authored or non-human-authored.
Furthermore, it has been stated by B that there is no distinction whatsoever in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of worldly and Vedic [words]; thus,
[your objection] would not hold.
Furthermore, even when there is the cessation of the nature of the cause called "person" (puruṣa), because the sixth and seventh case endings are non-different—

just as in the cases of "the branch on the tree" (*vṛkṣe śākhā*) and "the branch of the tree" (*vṛkṣasya śākhā*)— if it is accepted that Vedic sentences possess a form identical to human sentences through this non-difference;
That distinction among those worldly sentences, being produced by a person, would be accidental and causeless;
for that same distinction would exist even in Vedic sentences in the absence of a person,
and thus it would never cease, as in the case of space and so forth.
And it is not so; therefore, that which is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), that from which its birth arises, and that from which the birth of something occurs—
this analysis applies elsewhere as well, even where no visible cause is perceived, for [intrinsic nature] remains undifferentiated.

When something is not differentiated from its visible cause—the effect—and thus comes to be that effect, it is observed that it does not transcend the state of being that effect by way of its own self, that is, by its own nature;
how so? Like fire and fuel.
"Fire and fuel" refers to fire and its fuel; "like that" means similar to that.
Just as fire, which is seen to have fuel as its cause, undergoes differentiation [from it], so too fire whose cause is unseen does not transcend its state of being an effect of fuel.
B.
"His birth" (janma-asya);
this being the established principle therein.
Without demonstrating the distinction between worldly and Vedic sentences, those reasons which are elaborated— that is, set forth in detail— to prove their lack of human authorship are as follows:
for instance, "because there is no recollection of an author."
The study of the Veda in its entirety is preceded by the study [of the Veda] from a teacher,
because it is denoted by the term "Vedic study," just like the study performed nowadays. (Vākya-paddhati 366) The past and future times are devoid of an author of the Veda.
Because they are temporal beings, just as time is observed to be present;
it should be understood that Brahmā and others are not the authors of the Vedas due to reasons such as their being persons, just like ordinary men.
In the *Ślokavārttika*, it is stated:
"All those reasons are fallacious and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) precisely because one observes only the general nature of the effect."
Because words denoting human effort are observed among Vedic words to be identical to those denoting universals—
what is the reason for this? (added).
B.
He says that because they are equal, the arguments are inconclusive (anaikāntika).
In the formulation "yathā" and so forth, or "tatra," [the meaning is]: "that study of the Veda is preceded by the study of the Veda."
