Without demonstrating a distinction—that is, without showing the difference from a person who is devoid of the manifestation of Vedic activity—[the opponent now argues] that because the study of the Veda is preceded by the study of the Veda, and likewise other [instances], one observes a general effect characterized by the nature of Vedic study; thus, all such reasons are elaborated, yet they are all inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*). For example, another fire produced by a traveler [is also inconclusive] because its cause is unperceived.
It is preceded by another flame, not by the rubbing of wood;
why?
Because it is like the fire of a traveler.
"How is it like fire immediately following [another fire]? means like fire seen when produced by the connection of another flame;
"how" and so forth [is the question].

Because it relies on the capacity for origination from a flame—meaning that it relies on the capacity for arising from a flame—the other cause, the friction of fire-sticks, is rejected for the fire produced by the traveler.
Why?
Because if this fire could exist without a flame, then it would likewise exist even in the case of the traveler’s fire which was preceded by a flame, even in the absence of a flame.

In this regard, the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of this proof is stated: how so? Because between the two origins of a flame—namely, the origin of a flame from another [flame] and the origin from something else, such as the friction of fire-sticks—there is no mutual relationship of sublation (*bādhya-bādhakatva*) within the generality of fire (*agni-sāmānya*).
For what contradiction is there here in the claim that "there may be fire, yet it is not preceded by another flame"?
This being the case, the nature of fire as originating from a flame could exist otherwise; it could also arise from the friction of kindling wood (*araṇi-nirmathana*).

Since these two properties—originating from a flame and originating from something other than a flame—are both possible within the single object of fire-in-general, if that fire on the traveler's path or some other [fire] such as that from study were the case...

The objection is raised that there would be an inconsistency [in the rule] "restricted to one," namely, that it would not be the case that the study of the Veda is preceded only by the flame [of the teacher's instruction], or that the study of the Veda is preceded only by the study of the Veda.
There would be the study of the Veda,
yet it would not be preceded by the study of the Veda;
likewise, there would be the fire of the traveler, yet it would not be preceded by a flame.
It would be so, because there is no contradiction.
Abandoned by the araṇi.
B.
[The objection concerning] the study of the Vedas and so forth:
Now, one might ask, "Since the fire produced from a flame is not the same as that produced by the friction of fire-sticks, how is there no contradiction? To this, he says:
"Even that," and so forth:

even that [pair of properties], which are mutually exclusive and contradictory—namely, the two characteristics of being produced from a flame and being produced from the friction of fire-sticks—is said to be non-contradictory with respect to the general entity (*vastu-sāmānya*), but not with respect to the specific fire (*vahni-viśeṣa*) distinguished by its different states, whether it be produced as a flame or produced from the friction of fire-sticks. It is not said to be non-contradictory in such a case.
But why is it indeed contradictory?
Because it contradicts the reality of the nature of the Self, which is partless and undivided.
For, in the case of fire arising from a flame, its being preceded by a flame and its not being so preceded are contradictory;

and in the case of fire arising from a fire-drill, its being preceded by a fire-drill and its not being so preceded are contradictory; and even in the case of the generality of fire produced by travelers, both [alternatives] are contradictory—thus he says "na ca" and so forth.

Regarding the relationship of sublation and sublated between the birth of a flame and the birth from friction of fire-sticks— both occurring in the case of a traveler’s fire, which is a common instance of traveler’s fire—
what is the reason?
It is because that commonality of traveler’s fire lacks the impossibility [of occurring] apart from the production of a flame, that is, apart from the arising of a flame.
The meaning is that [fire] exists even from the friction of fire-sticks (*araṇi*) without the production of a flame;
for while it may be the case that fire originates from a flame, not all fire is without distinction [of origin].
What is the reason?
In that regard, since it is impossible to deny a specific quality in fire— which is differentiated by its various causes— by rejecting the particularity produced by the friction of fire-sticks,
and because there is no necessity for that fire which possesses a quality produced by the fire-sticks to remain in that same state,
as there is no such necessity in the condition characterized by its arising from a flame.
B.
Form is like fire.
B.
The commonality of fire—added.
B. raṇi0
B.
To this, he says:
B.
The word "jvālo" by Bhāvatā B. has been omitted.
B.
That which is impossible [does not arise] because of its non-existence, even from the friction of fire-sticks—added.
B.
Thus, another such instance has been observed: the origin of a flame.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that if the first fire of a traveler could exist without a flame, it would also exist elsewhere in a place devoid of flames—[that too is refuted].
To this it is replied:
it certainly does occur,
provided that the causal complex consisting of the friction of the fire-drills— by means of which that traveler’s fire comes into being— is present.
If, however, after demonstrating the possibility of this causal complex, one were to state the absence of fire due to the absence of that [complex],
or if one were to point out a flame in a place where the aforementioned causal complex is possible,
then fire would indeed be preceded by a flame; but it is not so.
Therefore, it is not the case that every fire of a traveler is preceded by a flame; thus, there is no deviation [from the rule].
To this, it is said:

Since a traveler's fire indeed occurs even in a place devoid of flames, for this reason, the fact that the study of one person who lacks the power of performing the Vedic rites is preceded by another—that is, preceded by a teacher—is not observed as a universal rule. For how could such a state establish that the study of everyone, including even Hiraṇyagarbha and others, is likewise preceded by another?
What is the reason?
The meaning is that since the occurrence of such study would otherwise be impossible without being preceded by another [source], study could not take place by composing it oneself;
for [it is argued] that Hiraṇyagarbha and others possess the capacity for the composition of the Vedas.

But as for one who is currently devoid of such capacity—who, being unable to compose a Veda himself, is likewise incapable of studying it—the "performance of that" means the performance of the Veda; "devoid of intuition regarding that" means devoid of the intellect capable of composing a Veda.
On the grounds that the study of such a person must likewise be preceded by another study, [the inference follows].

Regarding the phrase "of such a kind": for one who is devoid of the capacity for the act of knowing [the Veda], the very fact of recitation would constitute such a statement; it would have to be said that it is preceded by another recitation, and not without qualification.
Furthermore, since recitation can occur through one's own effort—given the possibility of a superior person—it possesses the potential for such qualification.

The opponent objects: "If it is stated without qualification that all study is preceded by another study, this does not support the intended thesis because it fails to establish the pervasion (*vyāpti*) due to being inconclusive (*vyabhicāritva*). How so? and so forth.
Having established the distinction [of the Veda], how is it possible for those outside the Vedic fold to study it?
The meaning of "yāvat" is "yadā" (when).

Even for those persons who are considered to be the authors of the Veda, there is an incapacity regarding the composition of the Veda because they are human beings, just like people of the present day.
Regarding this as well,
the Master [Vasubandhu] says: "In this application too, it is not [the case] of the capacity and the person."
Since no contradiction whatsoever is observed between the capacity to compose the Vedas and the status of being a person (*puruṣatva*),
the fact that Brahmā and others are described as persons by way of a reason does not, due to its lack of contradiction, remove their capacity to compose the Vedas.
Therefore, there is no formulation of what is non-contradictory;
that is, a non-contradictory formulation within a given application of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*)—such an application of non-perception is not a means of proof.
He asks: "How is it that there is an absence of contradiction? and says:
"Indeed not," and so forth:

regarding Brahman and other such entities that are beyond the senses and utterly imperceptible, there is no cognition of a contradiction characterized by the impossibility of coexistence with the capacity for composing the Veda.
Precisely because they are beyond the senses,
there can be no cognition of a contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion between capacity and incapacity, or between being a man and not being a man, since these are mutually contradictory.

The argument that "the person who [is claimed to be] the author of the Veda is incapable of composing the Veda, like a person of the present day" does not differ from the previous formal argument (prayoga), namely: "Whatever study of the Veda there is, it is preceded by a prior study of the Veda, just like the study of the Veda by people of the present day. Thus, this [new] formulation is distinct from that previous formulation.
Therefore, the intention is that the inclusion of both [the author and the student] is indeed redundant.
Furthermore, as for what is said: "If people of former times, having composed the Veda, were capable of studying it themselves, then those of the present day would also be so."
To this it is replied:
this [objection] would apply immediately after what was just stated only if there were no distinction among persons;
however, because such a distinction among persons does not exist, that which is difficult to accomplish cannot be established.
Because there is no subverting evidence,
even in this proof— namely, that "where one person lacks capacity, all persons lack capacity because they possess the nature of being a person"—
the mark of "personhood" (puruṣatva) is inconstant, just as in the previous case with "being a student" (adhyetṛtva) and so forth.
What is the reason?

Even in the case of the *Bhārata* and other works which are admitted to be of human origin, although present-day persons lack the capacity [to compose them], the power of certain superhuman beings such as Vyāsa and others is established;
for this very reason, one who discriminates the causes of Vedic statements must set aside the operation of the palate and other vocal organs as their cause.
Regarding objects— whether worldly or Vedic— and regarding words, which are of two kinds:

those produced by that [palate and so forth] and those not produced by that, the difference in their intrinsic natures (svabhāvabheda) must be demonstrated with respect to their causes, such as the palate and other organs, or the absence thereof.

The nature of causes such as the palate is of one kind, while the nature of their respective causes is of another kind; thus, this diversity of natures must be demonstrated, by which the distinction between what originates from that and what does not originate from that arises.
In the absence of that—that is, in the absence of a difference in nature—everything would become identical with its essence.
Every word would either be of human origin or none at all, even among worldly ones;
to this, he says that there is indeed a difference in their intrinsic natures.
Regarding the passage beginning with "na cātra" and so forth:
here, in this world, we observe a difference in nature between worldly and Vedic sentences.

In the absence of such a distinction in their essential form (*svarūpa-bheda*), since one perceives only a commonality—a similarity in form characterized by the sequence of phonemes—between those worldly and Vedic sentences, a person who attempts to distinguish some specific property of a single sentence, whether worldly or Vedic, and thereby establishes its status as either human-authored (*pauruṣeya*) or authorless (*apauruṣeya*), is made the subject of a critique regarding the charge of fallibility.
A person for whom a statement might be suspected of deviation is so described;
by whom is it made?
By that [person] in whom the occurrence of such a nature is possible.

The meaning is that by asserting the authorlessness of the Veda—which possesses properties identical to those of human compositions—on the basis of that general characteristic consisting of the arrangement of phonemes and words found in both worldly and Vedic sentences, one commits the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

[Objection: But surely there exists a distinction between the Veda and non-Veda characterized as "being the Veda" and "not being the Veda," namely the specific definition of being the Veda and not being the Veda.

The opponent maintains that, due to this distinction, there will be a state of being authored by a person (*pauruṣeyatva*) for the worldly [texts] and a state of not being authored by a person (*apauruṣeyatva*) for the Vedic [texts], respectively. To this, the Teacher replies: "True. But is such a distinction the sole proof for their being authored or not authored by a person? For it is not only between these two—the worldly and the Vedic—that there is a distinction.
Rather,
it refers to both the ancient and the non-ancient [texts] composed by the naked teachers (nagnācāryas) known as the Ḍiṇḍikas, namely, the Purāṇa and other such works.
Such a distinction exists,

yet by that much alone, a difference in name or designation— conceived through convention and intended for practical usage to illuminate the differences in one's own systems— does not subvert the human origin of the Veda;
what is the reason for this?
Furthermore, because it would follow that other Purāṇas are also non-human (apauruṣeya),
and because there exists a difference in name between the *Ḍiṇḍika* and other Purāṇas;
for if men were unable to produce such an arrangement of letters and words as is seen in the Vedic sentences, [then those Purāṇas would indeed be non-human].

If one who has not previously established a convention could discern, merely by hearing it, that a composition of phonemes and words was either made or produced [by a person], thinking "this was preceded by a human," then the Veda would clearly be non-human (apauruṣeya). Since he does not discern that composition, how could the Veda be non-human?
"Is it not so? and so forth—the opponent [says]:
"We shall examine later that even mantras are indeed composed by persons; moreover, what is called a 'mantra' is nothing other than something else."
Rather,
"truth" (satya) and so forth refers to the proclamation of things as they truly are (yathābhūta).
The subduing of the senses and the mind is austerity;

the power of those two is the capacity for such feats as the immobilization of poison. For those men who possess such true austerity and power, that very [austerity] is the mantra for accomplishing their desired object.
That characteristic of mantra-speech is indeed observed even today among men;
for what reason?
Because we see the power to paralyze poison, fire, and so forth, as well as the impairment of their capacity, through the force of one's own truth-consecration (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*).

Likewise, even today, certain Śabaras who abide by their own traditional rules are indeed able to compose mantras— whether non-Vedic, such as those of the Buddhists and others (the word "others" including the Ārhata, Gāruḍa, Māheśvara, and so forth)— by means of causes endowed with the power to remove poison and the like.
From the observation of mantras and mantra-kalpas:
the syllables of the vidyās are the mantras,
while the instructions for the methods of their accomplishment are the mantra-kalpas.
And because those ritual manuals (mantrakalpa) of the Buddhists and others are "human-made"— that is, composed by persons—
therefore, there is no difference in nature between the worldly [texts] and the Vedic ones;
this is what the opponent [means] in the passage beginning with "tatra" and so forth.
Furthermore, even if the ritual manuals for Buddhist mantras and the like were assumed to be authorless,
how could it be that every authorless statement is now true, when some may even have false content?
By the words "for thus" and so forth, he makes this very point clear:

in the Buddhist mantra-system (*bauddha-mantra-kalpa*), violence, sexual intercourse, the view of a self (*ātma-darśana*), and—by the word "etcetera"—false speech and the like, are described as causes of non-prosperity and causes of suffering;
however, in the other, non-Buddhist mantra-system (*itarasmin tv abauddha-mantra-kalpe*), those very same acts such as violence and the rest are described in a different way as causes of prosperity.

And if all mantra-rituals (*mantrakalpa*) were non-human (*apauruṣeya*), then how could these two mutually contradictory statements be true within a single non-human [text]? It might be argued that in the Buddhist *mantrakalpa*, the words such as "violence" (*hiṃsā*) have entirely different, non-standard meanings that are not in contradiction with the Vedic *mantrakalpa*.
Therefore, he says "therein," and so forth; that is,
when another meaning is being postulated, distinct from the meaning well-established in the Buddhist mantra-ritual (*mantrakalpa*).

Since the postulation of a different meaning for those [Vedic passages] is equal to that of non-Buddhist Vedic mantra-collections, and because it is impossible to determine a specific meaning in all mantra-collections due to the possibility of postulating various alternative meanings, there would be no comprehension or performance of the action based on the meaning they convey. Thus, in the absence of performance due to uncertainty regarding the meaning, even a non-human (apauruṣeya) statement would be useless with respect to human goals.
If it is argued that Buddhist and other [non-Vedic] formulas do not possess the status of *mantra* at all, he says:
"Regarding the non-mantra-status of Buddhist and others.

This means that even elsewhere—namely, in Vedic mantras other than those Buddhist and other formulas—one must undergo the ordeal of drinking from a vessel (*kośapāna*) in order to establish their status as *mantra*.
The intention is that there is no such thing as a specific individual [instance];

furthermore, this contradicts what is observed, for even Buddhists and others are seen to employ mantras when performing acts such as administering poison, as they perform the rites of poisoning and so forth.
Therefore, in that regard, even the claim that the Buddhist and other mantra-rituals lack the status of *mantra* is contradicted,
because the status of *mantra* is established for Vedic utterances as well by means of their employment in rites such as the neutralization of poison (*viṣakarma*).

Nor is it logical to conclude that a Vedic sentence is non-human (authorless) merely because it possesses a superior capacity compared to a worldly sentence due to its power to paralyze poison and so forth.
For instance, a *mudrā* is a particular arrangement of the fingers of the hand;
a *maṇḍala* is a specific configuration of deities and so forth;
and *dhyāna* is the contemplation of the form of a deity or similar object.
By means of those [mantras] which are without syllables and lack the nature of speech, their respective functions—characterized by the removal of poison and so forth—are performed;
yet it would not be logical for those mudrās, maṇḍalas, and meditations to be non-human (apauruṣeya).
This might be argued.
The claim that men possess the capacity for action only in respect of mudrās and the like, but not in respect of mantras consisting of sequences of phonemes—
that is incorrect;

because when those mudrās and other such things can be performed, what obstruction could there be for men who possess truthfulness and so forth in the composition of syllables, since there is no distinction [between the two cases]?
Therefore, there is nothing whatsoever that these persons are incapable of accomplishing,
such that a person, having observed some excellence produced by them, might postulate a difference in nature between worldly and Vedic [mantras],
provided that both the Buddhist and other mantra-systems are human compositions and originate from truth.
Since these two [traditions] originated from a person who speaks what is not false,

how is it now logical that these very same mantra-systems— one Buddhist and the other non-Buddhist— should be mutually contradictory? For in one case, acts such as violence are shown to be causes for the absence of prosperity (*anabhyudaya*), while in the other, they are shown to be causes for prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
He refutes this with the words "No," and so forth:
"Indeed, those two types of mantra and ritual are not in all cases produced by truth, such that this contradiction would arise;
rather, those two types of mantra and ritual also exist as being characterized by the assertions of persons endowed with supernatural power."

"If a person possessing power practices this arrangement of syllables and words and performs its ritual procedure, I shall accomplish for him the purpose as promised"—this is the vow. Even though the mantra and the ritual manual (*mantrakalpa*) possess these characteristics, there is no contradiction in the fact that one might also create mantra and ritual manuals possessing power even if they speak otherwise.
If it is asked, "Since truth (*satya*) is absent, how can there be such power? he says:
That power might also arise from specific attainments (*siddhi*) regarding rebirth (*gati*);
that is, such power comes about through merit (*puṇya*), or through a specific attainment of mantra (*mantra-siddhi-viśeṣa*) acquired by deities and others, which is embraced by them.
If mantras were of human origin, then since all humans are equally human, why would not all men be creators of mantras?
"And they do not perform [them];
therefore, even though they are desired, men did not compose the mantras"—this is the intended meaning.
"Tad" (that), etc., says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*).
Because of the deficiency in those means for accomplishing the rites of those mantras—such as truthfulness, austerity, and spiritual power—not all persons are capable of performing mantras.
However, if persons were endowed with such causes of mantras as truthfulness, austerity, and so forth, then they would certainly compose mantras, and even poetic works;

for if one holds that a person composes poetry because he possesses the creative intuition (*pratibhā*) for that activity, then every person, being equal in their status as a human being, would be a composer of poetry, even if they lack that specific creative intuition for such activity.
Or, if someone else were not to do anything at all when [the first person] does not act,
it would be just like a man incapable of composing poetry.
The meaning is that this unprecedented argument is fallacious;
[this is] the opponent’s response beginning with "True," and so forth.
Men who are deficient in the means for accomplishing mantra-rites do not perform those mantras;

yet we do not perceive such completeness of the means for accomplishing mantra-rites— such as truthfulness and so forth— in any single person, because all men possess these same common characteristics.
"It has been stated" means that the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) has stated the answer to the objection here;
what was stated?

The compound "vacanaṃ ca samayaśca" (speech and convention) refers to speech that accomplishes the desired aims of persons possessing truthfulness and so forth, beginning with the words "na mantra nāma" (there is no such thing as a mantra).
Likewise, because of the convention characterized by the assertions of persons endowed with truthfulness and other virtues, there is nothing else whatsoever apart from mantras;
and those means for accomplishing mantra-rites, characterized by specific results such as truth, austerity, movement, and supernatural powers, are observed only in certain individuals.
This might be so.
Whosoever among men is devoid of the means for performing mantra-rites— just as, for example, a man on the street—
and this person intended as a mantra-author is likewise a man;

in that case, all men are devoid of those [means], being devoid of the means for performing mantra-rites, because there is no contradiction between "being a man" and "the possibility of possessing the means for performing mantra-rites."
"Indecision" means lack of certainty.
If it is argued that the determination of the person's nature arises precisely from the non-perception of the nature of the means for performing the mantra-rites,
he says "And not," and so forth.
Regarding things whose nature transcends the senses— the meaning being those whose nature has passed beyond the senses and are thus absolutely imperceptible—
non-perception is not a cause for the ascertainment of non-existence.

If it is argued that because one does not perceive in oneself the recollections and so forth that are the means for performing mantra-rites, their non-existence in others is also ascertained, [the author] says:
And so forth:
*smṛti* is the recollection of past births and so on;
*mati* is the understanding of the minds of others.
The vision of the true nature of things regarding those not previously seen is penetration;
truthfulness is the state of speaking otherwise than what is; power is majesty.
Those [cognitions] caused by mantras occur in all [persons], occurring in the mental continua of all men;
therefore, because they have not been perceived in oneself, they should not be rejected even in other cases.
Now, he states that memory and the other qualities occur only in certain persons, beginning with the words "the means for that":

the means for those aforementioned qualities such as memory is their cause of production; the transmission—that is, the instruction—of that [means] has a distinction or particularity, in that its occurrence is found only in certain scriptures and not everywhere.
In the same way, the means for accomplishing other qualities may also exist;
they would occur in a particular person,
for accomplishment is the means.

The other qualities in the form of memory and so forth, which are the effects of the causes such as memory, their means of accomplishment—that is, their production—would occur only in a particular person through the practice of the causes of memory and so forth. If it is asked, "If memory and so forth were a [direct] means, why is it not seen? he says:
"Nor even," and so forth:
although it exists—that is, although it is present—the mental quality (manoguṇa) residing in another continuum cannot be perceived by a mere person;
for this very reason, there is no denial or rejection of the mental quality of another continuum, which is unperceived (adṛṣṭa).

Nor is there any obstructer or sublater of the mental quality that is about to arise or desires to arise in persons, by virtue of which it could be said that no one possesses a mental quality superior to others;
for if it is argued that the property of being a person (*puruṣatva*) and so forth is itself the sublater, we say no.
What is the reason?
Because a quality existing in another continuum (*anyasantāna*), which is the object of sublation, is not perceived by a mere person;
therefore, the relationship of sublated and sublater cannot be established on the basis of a property such as "being a person" (*puruṣatva*).
And because it is not sublated, there is no rejection [of our position].
By this which has been stated above, the negation of that cognition of every object is refuted;
by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the negations of those free from passion and so forth are described as having their answers already given.

Just as the omniscience and other qualities are not refuted by the mark of being a speaker and so forth, so too in that case, it is logical to apply the reasoning: "A person of such a kind is not one endowed with qualities such as freedom from passion," which serves to refute freedom from passion and the like.
Of what nature [is he]?

The analysis of the compound *asambhavantatsādhanasaṃpradāya* is as follows: it refers to one for whom there is no tradition (*saṃpradāya*) of the means (*sādhana*) to achieve those qualities; that is, one who lacks the tradition of the means such as freedom from passion (*vītarāgatva*) and so forth.
The meaning is that this is the logical principle: one who is deficient in the means, such as freedom from passion, will certainly not become free from passion and so on.

Nor is it tenable to say that "the indicator is not of that nature because it is not seen," meaning that even though the indicator— such as the mark of being free from passion (*vītarāgatva*) and so forth— is unseen, one cannot claim that by mere observation it is of a nature other than that [of the subject], namely, a nature devoid of qualities such as freedom from passion. This too is not logical to assert.
For it is not logical that the absence of the signified follows merely from the non-perception of the signifier;
why?
Because it is possible for some existing things not to initiate their effect, which would serve as the inferential mark.
Even if it were begun by those supersensuous beings, because these [beings] are remote by their very nature, it is impossible to perceive that "this is their effect.

Therefore, just as for one person there might be a deficiency in mantras, rituals, or means, so it might be for everyone; thus, it remains established that this [deficiency] is impossible to ascertain.
Consequently, when the thesis to be proven is that "study is preceded by another study, like other instances of study," the logical mark (*liṅga*) "because of study" is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*).
In the case of the study of the *Bhārata*, since there exists the property of being a human-authored study,
there is no fault because it is qualified by "Veda.
For the intention is that while mere study may be deviant [with respect to the conclusion], study qualified by "Veda" is not.
"But what [is the excellence]? and so forth—the proponent of the established doctrine asks:
"What excellence does the study of the Veda possess such that it could not be studied otherwise, i.e., by one who has composed it himself? There is no excellence whatsoever."
Therefore, since there is no contradiction in the fact that Vedic study may exist without being preceded by [another] study, that very same [reason] remains inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*).

For the qualification "being Veda" (*vedatva*) is not incompatible with the opposite case (*vipakṣa*), namely, being not preceded by another study; consequently, it does not exclude the reason from that opposite case.
What is the reason?
Because the two [properties]—being a Veda and not being preceded by another study—are possible in a single Vedic sentence;
for what contradiction is there here in that something might be a Vedic study and yet not be preceded by another study?
This has already been answered by the fact that people of the present day do not study [the Vedas] independently, but rather because their study is necessarily preceded by another study [of them].
By extension, this would also apply to the study of the *Bhārata*;
for even now, people study it only through the instruction of others.
Consequently, its initial study—just like that of the Veda—would have to be considered non-human (apauruṣeya), as it would necessarily be preceded by another instance of study.
If it is argued that the study of the Veda must necessarily be preceded by the study of the Veda because no author of such study is observed, this too has already been refuted and rejected;
for we do indeed observe cases where the tradition of a ritual practice has been interrupted.

By the statement beginning with "and being produced" (*kṛtakāś ca*), it is shown that even mere non-perception does not establish non-existence; therefore, there is indeed a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the reason "because of being the study of the Veda.
Consequently, the property of being the Veda (*vedatva*) as a qualification of the reason "study" does not possess any excellence; it does not contribute any specific distinction.

Furthermore, because there is no opposition to the counter-example (vipakṣa), the reason does not exclude itself from the counter-example; thus, even though a qualification has been employed, it is equivalent to one not employed.
Moreover:
Whatever study of the Veda there may be, all of that is preceded by another study; thus, even when the reason is qualified by "Vedic," the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established.

This is because, in the absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for the contrary case, it is not proven that every study of the Veda is of such a nature—that is, that it is necessarily preceded by another study.

However, in the case of a particular kind of study which is observed to be caused by another study—namely, that of one who is unable to perform it himself—it would indeed follow that it is preceded by another study.

For one who, having composed [the work] himself, is unable to study it, whatever observed deficiency characterized by dullness and so forth exists, that is caused by that [inability]; because it is caused by the prior study of another [work],
through the abandonment of that [inability], there is the abandonment of that study which is the cause of the dullness and so forth— just as there is the abandonment of an observed specific quality—
or rather, because it is caused by that, namely, caused by [one's own] capacity.

When a specific instance has been seen and understood— namely, that one’s own Vedic study was preceded by another study— and having abandoned that specific case, one attempts to grasp the universal property of being a Vedic study by abandoning that particularity, asserting that "all Vedic study, whether by the capable or the incapable, is preceded by another study because it possesses the universal property of being Vedic study," such an argument is indeed fallacious;
for what is it like, other than an attempt to prove the existence of fire?

The meaning is as follows: just as in the proof of fire, when smoke—which is to be established by fire—is observed to possess a specific shade of paleness, the abandonment of that specific paleness and the employment of the general property of being a "pale substance" becomes deviant (*vyabhicārin*) regarding the proof of fire; it is exactly like that.
By this demonstration of deviation just mentioned, [the same applies] to speech and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [reasons] such as being a male (*puruṣatva*) and so forth are refuted,
since they too are inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) with respect to whatever is to be proven (*sādhya*).
In the proof of passion and so forth— that is, in the establishment of passion and so forth—
since a specific kind of speech arising from passion and so forth has been observed, the general property of being a speaker would be inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) if that [specificity] were abandoned.
Even granting that it might be so, he says:
"In any case, by doing this, the beginninglessness of the Veda would be established; only its lack of a beginning would be established, not its non-dependence on a person."
But the quality of being authorless (apauruṣeyatva) would not be established;
for if authorlessness is desired on the mere basis of that [Veda] being authorless,
then other worldly conventions as well would be authorless, since they too have proceeded from time immemorial and do not depend upon human beings.

For it is the person alone who, having inferred for himself or having learned from another, studies [the Veda]; yet for those men whose organs are not engaged— that is, whose palates and other vocal organs are not active— the sounds themselves resound and manifest their own nature.

If these Vedic words were manifested by their own inherent resonance (*dhvanana*), they might be considered non-human (*apauruṣeya*); however, since these Vedic words are manifested through human activity, they would indeed possess the status of being human-made (*pauruṣeya*), just like worldly sentences.
Yet, it is possible that they are non-human, provided there were no beginning to humans.
And since study is beginningless, even then, the study of the first person cannot be established as being preceded by another's study or preceded by a different instance of study;
for what reason? Because there would be no other person to act as the teacher.

The first student of that Veda, being the first to study it, would himself have inferred and studied the Veda; thus, he alone would be the author of the Veda. Therefore, this worldly practice characterized by the study of the Veda—where one, having studied from one person, teaches another, and he likewise teaches yet another—is a human convention proceeding from the observation of preceding generations and is thus beginningless. Consequently, it would follow that this practice was composed by humans alone, and not that it is of non-human (apauruṣeya) origin.

How is it like the dust-play of children? Just as the dust-play of children (*ḍimbhaka*)— those who are young— is beginningless because it proceeds from previous observation, so too is human worldly activity (*puruṣavyavahāra*).
By the word "etcetera," worldly practices such as eating and so forth are included.
Regarding the phrase "because of beginninglessness" and so on:

if the Veda is accepted as being authorless (*apauruṣeya*) due to its beginninglessness, then the same would apply to the practices of barbarians (*mleccha*) and others—namely, those customs passed down through their own family lineages characterized by the marriage of mothers and so forth—since they too are beginningless; thus, like the Veda, they would be authorless.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the beginningless noble conventions (*āryavyavahāra*) is intended;

likewise, because the words of nihilists (*nāstikya*)— which proceed by denying *dharma*, *adharma*, and the next world— are also beginningless, they too would possess that same status, namely, being authorless (*apauruṣeyatva*).
If it is asked how they are indeed beginningless, he says:
"Because of the continuity of prior formations," meaning because they proceed as a continuum by the power of prior formations;
thus, the linguistic conventions of barbarians (*mleccha*) are beginningless.
Who, then, are they? He says:
it is the practice of certain Mlecchas that the mother's remarriage should be performed by the son once the father has died.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of conventional expressions such as "the killing of the elderly for the sake of liberating them from saṃsāra," and so forth.
He states what is included by the word "etc. with the words beginning with "madana" (*madana*).
On the thirteenth day of the month of Madana, there is the festival of Madana;

here too, by the word "etcetera," festivals such as the celebration of a son's birth are also understood to be beginningless. [Note 456-1: Restored. This note belongs to the base text, which was not keyboarded.
Thus, what are those words? They are those which deny the unprecedented [factors] such as dharma and adharma, as well as the next world; that is, they are those which reject them.
The connection [of the word] "those too" with the term "beginningless" is made by changing the gender.
Furthermore, how is it that the linguistic conventions of the Mlecchas and others are beginningless?

To this he says, "For not... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "those conventions and those nihilistic utterances," there is a singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) for the neuter gender according to the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccānyatarasyām*.
Therefore, this is the meaning:
contemporary people, whose mental impressions have not been instilled by others and whose intellects are unrefined, do not engage in those conventional practices nor utter those nihilistic words;
rather, it is only those whose intellects have been refined who do so.
"By others [they were produced] by yet others," thus it is established that there is no beginning (*anāditva*).
(Pāṇini 1.4.2)

Even for those who compose original poetry and the like, their activity proceeds by means of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by others; thus, stating that even the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) created by them is beginningless, he says:

Regarding the phrase *svapratibhā* and so forth: for those who have composed a convention (*samaya*)—such as the definitions of poetry and the like—by means of their own intuition (*svapratibhā*), that is, by their own intellect, even for such persons, there is first of all the "withdrawal" (*saṃhāra*) of the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) concerning whatever meaning has been heard from another, whether taken collectively or individually; this means their gathering together in one place, that is to say, their categorization.
In that very same manner, because works such as treatises are produced through the process of [mental] engagement, even a work composed by one's own intuition is in reality preceded by another;
how then can it be called "one's own creation"? To this, he says:
The connection is that such poetry and so forth is said to be "not preceded by another";
it is said to be "composed by someone himself.
What is the reason?
Thinking that some collection of meanings has come from some teacher,
and because there is no single teacher existing as a continuous tradition,
even a treatise composed by one's own intuition is, in the ultimate sense, preceded by another.
How much more so, then, those who act according to what they have seen; that is to say,
those whose engagement and withdrawal from activity proceed exactly as they have perceived it— those who engage correctly or incorrectly.
Those worldly transactions whose engagement and practice are both correct and false are so described;
therein, correct engagements consist of honoring those worthy of honor and the like,
while false engagements consist of those associated with sensual desire and the like.
And these [examples] are clearly preceded by another;
here, one anticipates a deviation [from the rule] with the words "But surely," and so forth.
Those who exist in the first eon are the "beings of the initial eon" (*ādikalpika*).
Among them, linguistic conventions (*vyavahāra*) are held to be unobserved,
for they did not receive linguistic conventions from predecessors, as they themselves were the very first.
He refutes this with the words "teṣām api" and so forth:

even for those men of the first kalpa, whose latent impressions (saṃskāra) were instilled by the linguistic conventions observed in previous successions of births— having had impressions deposited through previously seen usage— there occurs subsequent activity due to awakening [of those impressions] according to conditions and according to the proximity of auxiliary causes.

If it is argued that these [conventions] also do not have a prior origin— meaning that because all conventions, such as those of the Mlecchas and others, are beginningless, they must be non-human (apauruṣeya)— then [the response follows].
Even if the lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) of all conventional transactions were established by such mere beginninglessness alone, what benefit would there be? None at all.
For instance, one might desire that it be non-contradictory, and thus accept its lack of human authorship.

Furthermore, since this quality of being non-human (apauruṣeyatva) exists even in certain worldly conventions that are deceptive, non-human authorship is not a prover of truthfulness due to its deviation; so what is the use of postulating such non-human authorship?

If, on the other hand, it is intended that only Vedic sentences possess non-human authorship, then even though the Vedic sentences themselves are non-human, there remains doubt once again regarding the objects expressed by them. Thus, "again" (bhūyaḥ).
The meaning is that even after postulating the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) [of the Veda], doubt is once again encountered.
What is the reason?
Because various divergent interpretations of the meanings of the Vedas are observed among different teachers.
He explains with the words beginning "yadi" (if): even if the Vedic sentence were non-human in origin, if it were to produce a cognition of its own specific meaning only as determined by itself...

If [the scripture] were to produce such a cognition for one who desires the activity of the intellect based upon the meaning expressed by the Vedas, then there would be consolation due to the absence of the superimposition of a contrary meaning, and that person would become one who has attained consolation; however,
that is not the case,
because:
The meaning is: "at will" refers to [the practice of] superimposition and denial, either by the addition of extra words or by the suppression of other words.
Those who engage in the practice of contradictory scriptures are the *naiyāyikas*;
by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of the *vaiyākaraṇas* and others is intended.
Vedic sentences are seen being dissected by those who produce various [contradictory] meanings;
yet those mutually contradictory meanings brought about by different interpretations do not fail to cohere within those Vedic sentences—they indeed do so.
What is the reason?

Since the application of a word toward an object proceeds by way of denoting that object, it is dependent primarily upon convention (*samaya*) because it is bound to linguistic agreement (*saṃketa*); therefore,
even in the case of a single sentence, since multiple conceptualizations of meanings are possible according to convention, there is indeed doubt.
Furthermore, the claim that because Vedic sentences are explained according to their roots and suffixes,
and because those [roots and suffixes] have fixed meanings, there can be no possibility of alternative interpretations for the Vedic sentences, is also false.
What is the reason?
Because it is possible for both roots and suffixes to be listed with multiple meanings—
indeed, a single root is listed in many senses, and likewise a suffix as well.
In that very state, doubt would arise due to the difference in the mental impressions regarding the meaning according to one's own intention;

furthermore, the claim that there is no doubt even when roots and suffixes are listed with multiple meanings— on the grounds that the meaning of the Vedas is explained by relying on conventional usage— is also incorrect.
What is the reason?
Because even in the case of conventional usage (*ruḍhi*), one does not accept it by oneself with absolute certainty;
why is that so?
Because of the abundance of non-etymological words:
those very words that are non-etymological in common usage are seen in great abundance in the Veda,
such as *jarbhurāṇa* and others.

Therefore, in that case, there can be no determination based on conventional words; for in determining the meaning of a word whose sense is not conventionally established, one must depend upon the instruction of an explanatory person,
and such instruction by a person [is inherently unreliable].
Because they follow his will and do not follow the will of the person, there is indeed no definitive determination regarding the meanings of Vedic sentences.
[This applies] to the Vedic mantras.
Moreover, this [argument] establishing the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Veda must establish it either for the phonemes (*varṇa*) or for the sentence (*vākya*);
by the same logic applied to the sentence, the expression of the word (*pada*) is also to be understood.
With reference to the alternative regarding the phonemes, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "tatra" (therein),
the phrase "because there is no distinction from others" means that there is no distinction between the Vedic phonemes and the worldly phonemes.
What fruit would be obtained by proving that the phonemes are not of human origin?
None at all. He explains this with the words "for it is not," and so forth.
For indeed, there are not different phonemes in worldly and Vedic sentences;
rather,
just as the Vedic *a* and other phonemes are non-distinct, so too are the worldly ones.
Because they are recognized as being identical, even though such recognition exists, if one were to maintain that there is a difference between the Vedic phonemes and those of common worldly usage,
then [the same would apply] even in the case of their difference.
Furthermore, because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), the unity of Vedic phonemes such as 'a' and so forth—which occurs at every utterance—would result in being unestablished;
for what reason?
Because of the distinction in recognition.

The meaning is as follows: since the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) observed regarding the distinction between worldly and Vedic phonemes (*varṇa*) is no different in the case of Vedic phonemes, how can the oneness of Vedic phonemes be established through a recognition that deviates from oneness?
Furthermore, because their difference is not perceived, the distinctness of Vedic phonemes is not established.

Because no distinction is perceived between worldly and Vedic [sounds], it might be argued that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to Vedic phonemes because they are based on identity, whereas in other cases it is invalid because it is an error due to similarity; to this, he says:
"because it would follow that there is no cognition through recognition."
If [recognition] were invalid elsewhere, then it would follow that momentariness could not be established even in the case of a jar and so forth due to recognition; furthermore,
because of this very "otherness," you Mīmāṃsakas do not accept a difference between worldly and Vedic phonemes.

And if the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of those phonemes is accepted on the grounds of their proof, then since those phonemes are identical everywhere—in both the world and the Veda—what has been set aside by this Mīmāṃsaka who thus establishes non-human origin? It would be the entire class of phonemes that might be human-originated. Furthermore, if both worldly and Vedic phonemes were non-human-originated, then all verbal usage, whether worldly or Vedic, would be non-human-originated; yet not all would be non-erroneous, nor would all have true meaning, because even in the case of non-human origin, there is the possibility of erroneous meaning.
For this reason, the effort expended in postulating that [the Veda] is not of human origin is futile. Now, with the words "Or rather" (*atha*), the second position is introduced:
"Or rather, the sentence is held to be not of human origin."
That is incorrect; for indeed, a sentence does not exist as something distinct from its phonemes.
What is the reason?
He explains [the point] with the words "na hi" (for not) and so forth, on the grounds that the visible object is not perceived:
"For we [do not perceive it] in words and sentences such as 'Devadatta' and so on."

In words such as *devadatta* and in sentences, apart from the appearance of the phonemes beginning with the letter *da*, we do not perceive in the intellect any appearance of a word or sentence consisting of other phonemes,
just like the appearance of a second phoneme; for example, when the letter *da* appears, at that very same time a second phoneme does not appear.
In the same way, a word or sentence does not appear [as a distinct entity];

and that which does not appear cannot be determined to exist as something that has met the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*)—that is, as an object of apprehension by the intellect (*buddhi*)—whether it be [the whole] other than the phonemes (*varṇa*). Thus, it is impossible to determine that it exists as something other than the phonemes.
The word "not" (na) is connected [to both].
Since existence has been negated, otherness is also necessarily negated; nevertheless, the mention of both is for the purpose of establishing absolute non-existence.
Just as when one aspect (ākāra) is appearing, there is no other distinct visible aspect not appearing therein, so too [the object] is impossible otherwise, and so forth.

If it is argued that the function of conveying meaning— which is impossible for other phonemes— is a characteristic that indicates the existence of a word or sentence distinct from the individual sounds,
then indeed, such a lack of comprehension is observed in the case of words and sentences such as "Devadatta."

Nor can it be understood that this [cognition of meaning] arises from the individual phonemes, because each of them is individually meaningless, and because they lack totality— since at the time of one phoneme, the other phonemes are absent. Therefore,
he provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "syāt" (it might be), [arguing] that there exists that word or sentence from which this cognition of meaning arises.
The word and so forth might be something distinct from the phonemes if, even when those phonemes are present, the effect characterized by the cognition of that meaning did not occur;

for if the cognition of the meaning did not arise from the entire collection of phonemes as it was conventionally designated for the purpose of conveying that meaning, then this [distinction] would be established.
To the extent that it exists,
it is said to be so;
however, the impossibility of its being otherwise serves as the basis for the cognition of the object's meaning.
"That alone would be its cause, that which arises immediately after it" (Sphoṭasiddhi 95). [The opponent says:
"It does not happen," and so forth;
that is, there is no comprehension of meaning from the phonemes.
What is the reason?
Because, despite there being no difference in the phonemes themselves, the comprehension of meaning is impossible across different words and sentences.

For if the comprehension of meaning were to arise from the phonemes alone, then the comprehension of meaning in the word *sara* would be exactly the same as in *rasa*, since the phonemes are identical in both cases.
The same should be understood regarding sentences consisting of similar phonemes; therefore, the effect characterized by the cognition of meaning does not arise from the phonemes.
He refutes this with the words "no," and so forth,
because those phonemes are not established as being non-distinct across different sentences;
for indeed, the phonemes that exist in one sentence are not the very same ones in other sentences, since phonemes arise as distinct in every sentence due to the difference in human effort.
If it is argued that the non-distinction and non-difference of phonemes in every utterance is established by the recognition "this is that very same phoneme," this is not so;
for what is the reason?
Because that recognition is fallible—
it is observed, for instance, that in the case of hair that has been shaved and grown back again, there is a recognition in one who is deceived by the apprehension of similarity;
and this apprehension of similarity is the apprehension of the very nature of the similar object itself, not the apprehension of it as being "similar to something else."
Furthermore, because it is non-demonstrable and lacks a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*), recognition— which itself lacks a logical mark (*liṅga*)—
is untenable; for there exists no single instance recognized as such that is established for both the proponent and the opponent,
nor is it possible for a perception of recognition to occur at every step that apprehends the identity of a phoneme.
Because the connection with a previous time is not apprehended due to its current non-proximity,
or if it were apprehended, there would be a clear manifestation as in the case of auditory cognition; yet this does not occur.

Therefore, that which perceives the color of a previous time cannot perceive [the same] thing currently being seen, because its present time is different; and how could a nature connected with the present time be connected with a previous time, given the mutual contradiction between prior and posterior times? Thus, how can it be said that reality is grasped by perception?
Furthermore, perception is held to have a proximate object as its domain,
yet proximity is not possible for a phoneme because it possesses parts; moreover, at the time of the final part of a phoneme, the preceding parts of the phoneme do not exist.
Therefore, a perceptual recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) that grasps the identity of phonemes (*varṇa*) at every step is not possible.
Consequently, it is established that the phonemes are indeed distinct in every sentence; their distinction [is known] because the cognition of meaning arises from their very distinction.
But has it not been stated that phonemes are devoid of meaning? How then can it be said that the distinction [of meaning] arises from the distinction of those [phonemes] alone?

It is true that phonemes (*varṇa*) are real; however, those which are objects of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and possess a universal form (*sāmānyarūpa*) are indeed distinct in every sentence. It is held that phonemes, as particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), are the expressive agents when they are superimposed (*adhyasta*) as if distinct.
Therefore, it is said that the distinction in the cognition of meaning arises from the very distinction among the phonemes themselves.

If, however, this difference in the comprehension of meaning is not accepted as being due to the difference in the phonemes, but rather— despite the lack of difference in the phonemes— the difference in the comprehension of meaning is held to arise from the difference in the sentence which is distinct from them,
then that very [sentence] would be the difference in the effect.
And that comprehension of meaning must arise from the sentence;
yet that sentence is beyond the senses, because it does not appear in sensory cognition apart from the phonemes—
how then could this be so?
There would be no cognition from the sentence because the relationship has not been apprehended;
this might be argued.

Even though that sentence is invisible, it produces cognition by its mere presence, like a sense organ; and since such cognition would otherwise be inexplicable, the sentence is postulated. To this, he says:
"If the production of cognition by the sentence through its mere presence is admitted..."
Just as in the case of the sense organs and so forth, even for a person who is unlearned and has not mastered linguistic conventions, there would have to be a cognition of meaning from a sentence;
yet this does not occur.

Therefore, since the cognition of meaning arises from the phonemes solely by virtue of linguistic convention, how can a sentence be postulated on the grounds that its existence is otherwise inexplicable?

Therefore, there is no such thing as a "sentence" distinct from the phonemes for which one might establish non-human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*). Since that [sentence] does not exist, and consequently the sentence itself is absent, only the phonemes remain;
and since they are indistinguishable everywhere, when their non-human authorship is being established, [they are all equally so].
Even for worldly phonemes that are distinguished by their specific sounds, it would have to be proven that they are not of human origin;
and in this regard, under the first position— the position seeking to prove the non-human origin of phonemes— it has already been stated that such an effort is futile.
249–250 Furthermore, etc.:
if it is assumed that a sentence consists of multiple constituent parts, and if those constituent parts are individually meaningless when taken separately;
He explains this with the words beginning with "tepī" (those too).

If the many constituent parts (*avayava*) of that sentence are individually meaningless by their own nature (*prakṛti-svabhāva*), then the sentence—which consists of a collection of multiple parts—would likewise be meaningless. Consequently, since it would not possess that [meaningful] form, there would be a "resemblance to that form" (*tādrūpya*) within the aggregate of parts, which are non-expressive by virtue of being meaningless; that is to say, there would be the state of being meaningful in the form of an expressive sentence.
It would be imagined and superimposed,
like "lion-ness" and so forth,
as in metaphorical expressions such as "the boy is a lion."

In the case of [terms] such as "young brahmin" applied to those who do not possess that form, [the author] explains by means of the passage beginning with "possessing meaning" (*arthavān*) that the self (*ātman*) indeed possesses meaning, just as [the term] "lion" is superimposed upon [a person].
The sentence is nothing other than the expressive nature itself,

yet those parts of the sentence are themselves devoid of meaning; and upon those parts, which are themselves meaningless, that meaningful essence of the sentence would have to be superimposed through conceptual construction.

Just as the term "lion" is applied to a young boy and so forth, the self (ātman) is merely a designator of that [boy] because it is constructed by conceptualization; therefore, it is indeed of human origin.

Now, if it is maintained that each individual member of the sentence possesses meaning with respect to the sentence-meaning—lest this fault [of redundancy] arise—then, since each member would possess meaning individually, there would be the false assumption of multiplicity; for since even a single member would have its purpose fully accomplished, the dependence of the sentence upon other members would not be logical.
And when [the meaning is understood] through the cognition of a single member...
Or, upon grasping even a single member of a sentence, there would arise the cognition of the comprehension of the sentence-meaning;
for it might be argued that through the apprehension of even one member, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning indeed occurs in a general way.
As Bhartṛhari said:
"All [words] possess individual meanings, because the complete sense is fully realized in each word."
Likewise, since the very first word that is employed is understood as encompassing all forms and meanings, the subsequent words are recognized merely as the basis for restriction or restatement;
thus, how can it be said that the postulation of multiplicity is useless? — so says the *Bhāgavṛtti*.

This is not a fault, because this is stated with reference to a specific intended meaning: even though each [word] is meaningful individually, there would otherwise be the false assumption of multiplicity,
and the comprehension of the sentence-meaning would occur through the cognition of only a single constituent part.

Nor is it reasonable for each individual member of a sentence to possess its own distinct meaning and efficacy by having one part denote a specific *kāraka* (participant in action) and another denote a specific *kriyā* (action),
because it is impossible to denote a specific *kāraka* that is not connected to a specific *kriyā*.
On the other hand, if such a connection is denoted, the aforementioned defects— such as the false postulation of multiplicity— remain exactly as they were.
He explains [the passage] with the words "having a completed meaning" (*parisamāptārtha*) and so forth:

that form of speech whose meaning is completed is "thus"; and those components situated within the sentence, being of such a nature, are "of a completed-meaning form" (*parisamāptārtharūpa*), individually and separately.
For this reason, it follows that each individual member [of a sentence] would be a sentence;
and thus, a sentence would not consist of multiple members,
meaning that a single sentence could not be composed of several members.

If each individual component were meaningful on its own, then upon the comprehension of a single component, the entire meaning of the sentence would be comprehended; consequently, the listener would have no need for subsequent components, and there would be no delay.
The meaning is that through such a lapse of time, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning would not occur.
What is the reason for this?
Because that meaning of the sentence, being partless and undivided in nature, is realized in a single moment; why is this so?
Because that sentence-meaning is apprehended in its entirety upon the arising of a single cognition;
others, however, explain it otherwise,
[arguing] that if the sentence-meaning were apprehended through the comprehension of only one constituent part, there would be no lapse of time for that constituent part.
What is the reason for the cognition of that partless entity in a single moment?
What is the cause?
Because, upon the arising of a single cognition, that partless entity is understood in its entirety;
otherwise, if everything were not grasped in a single moment of cognition, there would be a contradiction regarding the oneness of the natures of what is grasped and what is not grasped,
since it is impossible for two contradictory things to be one.
Now, if it is maintained that there is a single hearing [of the word] so that this fault may not occur,
then, when a single hearing of all the constituent parts (avayava) is postulated, a lapse of time is not logical.
He explains [the passage] beginning with "lest it be so" (*mā bhūt*) as follows:

since the meaning of the sentence would be established from a single constituent part alone— without waiting for the other parts— and because the determination of the sentence-meaning would thus result in the loss of the sentence's possession of multiple constituents, it is therefore maintained that all the constituents of the sentence must be heard simultaneously.
Even then, a delay is certainly not appropriate;
for what reason?
Because at the very time one part is perceived, all parts are heard.
Furthermore, sequential hearing is observed;

and if there were sequential hearing, since each individual component possesses its own distinct meaning, the meaning of that [whole] would be established from just one component, thereby rendering the other components useless for the establishment of the sentence-meaning—
this has been stated immediately prior.
Pointing out the fault in the opponent's position regarding the simultaneous hearing of all parts at once, he says:

"If the simultaneous apprehension of all parts upon a single hearing were admitted, then even when combined, the meaningfulness of those parts—which have not been observed to possess the capacity [to signify meaning] individually with respect to their respective objects—would not be established.
It might be argued as follows:

If it is argued that because the meaning is perceived—that is, the cognition of the object—arises when the parts are combined, the parts must possess the capacity to generate the cognition of the meaning even individually, and therefore this is not a fault;
that is not so.
Why? Because...

Since the nature of form—which has the capacity to convey meaning—that does not exist in those individual parts separately cannot possibly exist when they are combined, the form of the parts taken alone is entirely different from the form that arises when they are assembled and is capable of conveying meaning; therefore, he says: "And because no other [new] entity is produced."
The meaning is that because phonemes are eternal, there is no production of a different, capable form from a preceding incapable form;
[the author] asks why this fault does not apply even to the proponent of impermanence.
Regarding the phrase "in the production of sound," etc.:
for those who maintain that sound is produced, this fault just mentioned does not exist at all.
What is the reason?

For that proponent [of the theory of sentences], even though the individual parts are individually incapable, they possess an excellence characterized by the capacity to convey meaning when in a state of conjunction—due to a specific assistance produced by human effort—and thus they are employed for a specific effect, which is the cognition of meaning. However, for the proponent of eternality, since the meaning would be cognized from even a single part if each part were individually capable, the postulation of any other part would be useless.
Thus, the fault has been stated regarding the position that the sentence possesses parts.
Furthermore, if the sentence were indeed a single, partless entity,
then even if the oneness of the sentence were admitted, it would be impossible for that undivided and partless entity to be apprehended sequentially, step by step.
Because apprehension is impossible, a distinction in time is not tenable; for it is not logical that a single [cognition] should be apprehended successively.
What is the reason?
Because there is no difference between what has been grasped and what has not been grasped;
for there is no other nature of it that has not been grasped, distinct from its nature that has already been grasped, which could be apprehended sequentially.
If it is argued that the sentence may indeed be grasped non-sequentially, he says:
Regarding the phrase "gradually" and so forth:
what is the reason?
It is because for every sentence, there is a time of usage for the speaker, and a time of hearing and a time of recollection for the listener.
If it is argued that this sequential apprehension of phonemes occurs because their production follows a sequence consisting of many moments within a single blink of an eye—
where "many-moment-blink" refers to a blink of the eye in which there are many moments— and that the sentence, however, is apprehended without such a sequence, he replies:
Regarding the passage beginning with "varṇa" and so forth:

[the word-sound] does not appear as having the nature of color, nor as something distinct from color and form, because it appears as the essence of sound (*śabdātman*) manifesting in a single moment of cognition.
Why is this so?
Because the sequence of letters is perceived, and because the sentence is perceived precisely through that sequence of letters—

since no other manifestation of sequence occurs in auditory cognition apart from that which is produced by the letters— for this reason as well, there is no manifestation of a sentence devoid of sequence.

Because, even though there is no difference [in the letters] according to your view— even though those letters are not distinct— the cognition of a sentence occurs sequentially rather than simultaneously, since the distinction between sentences is produced by the sequence of the letters; for if the sentence were not to depend on the assistance produced by the sequence of the letters, it would not require that assistance.
In that case, some kind of sentence would be understood even when those phonemes are employed in whatever manner— whether in their proper sequence or in a different sequence;
for instance, when "rasaḥ" is uttered, "saraḥ" might be understood,
because [the sentence] would not depend on the assistance of the phonemes, or the sentence would be understood even without the phonemes.
Nor is the cognition of a sentence dependent upon the assistance of the phonemes;
for what reason? Because it is impossible for those phonemes, which possess a specific sequence, to provide such assistance to this sentence.
If it is argued that a sequential assistance must be produced by sequential [factors], and thus the assisted object would likewise possess sequence,
and this is not what is intended—
namely, that the letters themselves, being non-sequential, will be the assistants of the sentence— the author replies:
Regarding the phrase "and not by way of sequence," and so forth:

because it is impossible to speak or utter phonemes (*varṇa*) without a sequence, and because there is no other mode apart from the assistance provided by either sequence or non-sequence, there is no alternative possibility; thus it is established that phonemes do not assist the sentence.
Neither do phonemes exist within a sentence, nor is a sentence composed of phonemes;
rather, a sentence is a single linguistic form (śabdarūpa) that is a distinct entity from the phonemes.
The manifesting sounds possess a sequence; they manifest [the word] through a specific order, not through a disordered one.
As it has been said:
"Just as there is a fixed rule of succession in the transformation of milk and seeds."
In the same way, there is a fixed sequence in the cognitions of those who practice [the ritual],
according to Kumārila; therefore, there is no fault in the statement beginning with "by those [mantras] employed in whatever manner."

Due to the sequence of its manifestors, that single sentence— though devoid of sequence and the distinction between phonemes in ultimate reality— appears to a person as if possessing sequence and the distinction of phonemes, because the sounds in the form of phonemes are perceived according to the sequence of their manifestation, despite being non-distinct from the nature of the *sphoṭa*.
As it has been said:
"Because the *nāda* is produced through a sequence, it is neither prior nor posterior;
being itself without sequence, it arises as if possessed of differentiation through the form of sequence."

Therefore, Kumārila maintains that among letters, sentences, words, and so forth, which exist at non-distinct times, the nature of the sound and its duration are differentiated by the diversity of the manifesting noise (*nāda*).
To this, he states the following reply beginning with "anukramavatā" and so forth;
he thinks as follows:
Whether manifestation takes the form of determination or the form of non-determination,
that manifestation in the form of determination for a sentence— which is itself devoid of sequence— is refuted and rejected by a manifestor that possesses sequence;
for what reason?
Because there is a contradiction between the manifested and unmanifested forms—the determined and undetermined forms—within a single entity;
for there is no other undetermined form distinct from the determined form belonging to that same thing by which it might later become manifested.
Therefore, as for what is said:
The claim that "the function of the other phonemes is for the sake of ascertainment, because the manifestation produced by the first phoneme is not ascertained" is refuted;
for the manifestation has already been brought about by the first phoneme itself in the form of ascertainment.
He will state the answer later, beginning with the words "in the case of a manifestation in the form of non-ascertainment, [it would require] all the phonemes... and so forth.
Now, it might be argued that the sentence appears as something entirely distinct from the phonemes, and not as merged with the sounds;
as it has been said:
Regarding the claim that "for some, *dhvani* is imperceptible, while for others it is postulated as independent," he says here [the verse] beginning with "a-varṇa" and so forth.

If a sentence is accepted as being composed of parts consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*) that do not [simultaneously] exist, then for a person who hears it incompletely— that is, one who hears the sequence of all the phonemes in fragments—
the comprehension or hearing of the sentence would never be complete.
What is the reason?
Since there is no single sentence apart from its constituent phonemes— due to the absence of parts and the absence of divisions—
and yet in the world, upon hearing only a few phonemes, there arises the cognition of having heard a prior portion of the sentence,
it follows that the sentence must be admitted to possess parts through its phonemes.
It is claimed that upon hearing a few syllables, there must have been a prior hearing of the preceding portion of the sentence;

this is incorrect because a sentence is a single unit. If there were a hearing of the preceding portion, then it would necessarily follow that there was a complete hearing of the entire sentence in its entirety.
Because it is not distinct from its preceding part,
if the whole were not heard, then nothing at all would be heard; or else,
even the preceding part would not be heard, because it too would be distinct from the sentence.
Therefore, what was stated by Maṇḍana—

that because of the similarity between the manifestor and the sentence, there arises the conceit of grasping that [sentence] as the self [of the word], and thus there is neither non-hearing nor hearing of the whole—
is refuted.

Since an indivisible sentence is not heard at the time of perceiving the portions consisting of complete or incomplete phonemes, there can be no similarity between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), because they are dissimilar by virtue of being composed of phonemes or not being composed of phonemes; therefore, the claim that there is a misconception regarding the apprehension of the nature of phonemes within the sentence is trivial. Others, however, explain it otherwise.

Now, if it is argued that— even though it is illogical because there is no relationship of assisted and assister— the sequential conformity to the manifestors is admitted for the non-sequential sentence,
and consequently there is no hearing of it in its entirety, [the author] says "sakaletyādi" and so forth.

If there were hearing of the sentence as a whole by the listener even part by part, whether it be with parts (*sakala*) or without parts (*niṣkala*), then [if that were not accepted], there would be no hearing of the sentence without parts for any person at all, even for one who has heard all the phonemes (*varṇa*). Alternatively, there would be no hearing of the sentence without parts even for one who has not heard all the phonemes.
Even at the final stage, since the phonemes are not heard simultaneously, it is only a portion that is heard.
Now, it might be argued that just as a verse, when revealed once, is not fully grasped, but becomes capable of being grasped when revealed on another occasion; [so too would the word be].
When [the sentence] is manifested again and again, it is then apprehended;
for even though the sentence was not manifested due to the existence of preceding sounds, it was not yet apprehended.

Therefore, by means of the mental impressions (*saṃskāras*) deposited by the manifestation of each preceding word—which serve as causes for the apprehension of the sentence—the sentence is apprehended at the time of hearing the final phoneme.
