Therefore, it is indeed logical that the manifestation of the sentence—which is without sequence—is brought about by the phonemes in their sequential order;
as it has been said:
"Just as an *anuvāka* or a verse attains its complete form [through successive recitation]."
This "return" is not defined as the physical re-reading of the text; rather,
when the word has been manifested by sounds that are themselves inexpressible yet conducive to apprehension, its true nature is then determined through mental cognitions.

Kumārila maintains that the word is apprehended when the intellect— having had the seeds sown by the preceding sounds and having reached full maturity through their repetition— is conjoined with the final sound.
He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "samasta" and so forth:
that cognition in which there exist the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by all the phonemes, either individually or preceded by the manifestation of the sentence, is described as such.

The notion that there is a comprehension of the partless sentence by means of that final cognition—which possesses the refinement of all phonemes and has the final phoneme as its object—is also false;
for what reason?
Because that sentence does not touch upon the form of any phoneme.

The meaning of the verse is that because nothing devoid of color, form, and contact is ever perceived by the auditory cognition of any person at any time, there is no appearance [of such a thing] upon the utterance of each individual phoneme; however, there *is* an appearance upon the utterance of the sentence as a whole.
Now, it might be argued that the sentence consists precisely of the phonemes themselves, and therefore it is indeed an object of sensory cognition; to this, he says:

Since phonemes cannot be apprehended out of sequence and are apprehended only in a specific order, how could there be such a thing as a "sentence" that is grasped by a single cognition and devoid of sequence?

Now, if it should be argued that following the apprehension of the final phoneme, there is indeed the determination of the partless sentence by means of mental cognition (*mānasa-jñāna*), [the author] replies:
And so forth: after the apprehension of the final phoneme, we do not perceive any essence of sound that is distinct from the other phonemes, incomplete, partless, and undivided.
Nor does this speaker himself perceive the word-as-such as it has been described;
for even then, while apprehending the sentence, he apprehends only the sequence of phonemes as having an external form,
and he does not apprehend a partless sentence distinct from the phonemes.
If this speaker were merely one who says, "Just as I have stated, the word, its parts complete, appears in the final cognition," and if he were thus correct,
it would be well for me; yet, with a mind deluded by that desire for welfare— the hope for the attainment of his intended object— he dreams on.
Even though not sleeping, one behaves as if one were situated in sleep;
and because it must be stated "and after a locative," the suffix *kyac* occurs even after a word ending in the seventh case.
Some say that even according to this [other] method, this very thing is what is remembered;
others, however, say that it is merely a dream due to the metaphorical application of non-difference.
Alternatively, since the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is prescribed by way of the *ārśa-ādi* group [of gaṇas],
it is expressed by the word "dream" (*svapna*); thus, the *kyac* suffix is applied because the agent himself is the object of comparison.
"He acts as if asleep" means that he is dreaming; by this [the author] mocks him.
Restored.

If it is argued that words and sentences are grasped in their sequential order by means of recollective cognition (*smaraṇajñāna*), he replies with "not indeed" (*na hi*) and so forth: Even in the case of words and sentences being recollected, the phonemes (*varṇa*) belonging to them do not establish the distinction between those words and sentences without a specific sequence; for they are not manifested within a single, non-sequential cognition. Rather, just like the sequence of experience, recollection also occurs only in a sequence; such is the meaning.

If, however, in the final cognition—which is itself devoid of sequence—the phonemes of a word or a sentence are perceived even without a specific order, then, because there is an absence of priority and posteriority within that non-sequential cognition, the phonemes would be perceived all at once. Consequently, there would be no distinction or difference among those various words or sentences caused by that [sequence], meaning that the difference between words and sentences would not exist, since it is precisely from the perception of a specific sequence of phonemes that the mutual distinction between words and sentences arises; in the absence of that [sequence], it would not occur. This is the sense.

Nor is it without sequence, and so forth; for we do not perceive any form of speech that is "without sequence"— that is, a form of speech in which no sequence of phonemes exists— as something distinct from the phonemes themselves, since it has been stated that nothing whatsoever is apprehended that does not involve contact with the nature of phonemes.
The theory of the *jāti-sphoṭa*, however, is refuted precisely because of the non-existence of a universal (*jāti*);
or, even if such a universal were to exist, that form of the word— consisting of a sequence of phonemes— would have to be either impermanent or permanent.
Since there is no other possible state for an entity,
if it were impermanent, then how could that statement— produced by human effort and thus human in origin— not indeed be of human origin?

For that which is impermanent and produced must necessarily arise from some cause of its own; for it has been stated that if existence were admitted to be accidental— that is, devoid of a cause— there would be no restriction regarding place and so forth,
the word "and so forth" implying that there would likewise be no restriction regarding time or substance.

And that sentence is observed to arise from those persons whose organs are impelled by human effort and are free from defect; however, it is not observed to occur otherwise when there is no desire to speak or when there is a defect in the organs. Since the characteristic of being a cause—consisting of positive and negative concomitance with human activity—is thus observed in relation to the sentence, human activity alone is the cause of the sentence. Therefore, for this reason, even a sentence composed by a person [is authoritative].
Now, if that sentence were eternal, then its eternity being admitted, there would have to be constant perception of the sentence;
for what reason?
Because for that which is eternal, no obscuration is possible.
Because there is no obscuration,
the explanation beginning with "atha" and so forth [is as follows]:
suppose that which consists of the form of the word "atha" were eternal and of a nature capable of being perceived.
The analysis of the compound is: "that which has a perceivable intrinsic nature" (*upalabhya-svabhāva*).
Since that perceivable intrinsic nature of that sentence never departs from it nor diminishes, it would necessarily be perceived at all times;
for if it were so, it would be eternal and could not fall away from any capacity whatsoever, even that characterized by the production of cognition.
What is the reason?
Because that capacity for producing cognition is of the very nature of the word, being the eternal essence of sound;
nor is the capacity for producing cognition from the word a separate entity, since the existence of such a separate entity has already been refuted.
If it is argued that [the atoms] are not perceived constantly because they are obstructed by still air— lest it follow that [the air] would fail to assist the entities—
the author says "nor also," and so forth.
For that external object of perception, which is of the nature of the visible, no obscuration whatsoever is possible,
because there is a lack of evidence to establish its existence;
or even if such an obscuration were present, it could not prevent that [object] from remaining as its own undivided self, which is by nature the eternal word.
Because it is impossible for there to be a subversion of capacity—
that is, because it is impossible for there to be a suppression of the power to produce cognition—
for that which is considered an "obscuration" cannot be said to perform any function at all if it does not produce some excellence (*atiśaya*) within the nature of the sound itself.
Furthermore, what object that is ineffective could be an obscuration, or what else could be an impediment to knowledge? In other words, it cannot be anything that causes harm in any other way;
this has been thoroughly examined and essentially already investigated above.
The opponent, stating that even that which is ineffective is observed to be an obscuration, says:
"Walls and so forth," etc.;
[he asks] what excellence do walls and so forth produce in jars and the like?
The intention is this: since they do not destroy the excellence of capacity by which they would be considered obstructions,
therefore, just as they are considered obstructions for jars and the like without producing any [further] excellence in them,
so too there will be some obstruction even for the eternal word.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "We do not say," and so forth:
we do not say that those things such as walls surpass some object like a jar or produce a specific nature for it;
rather, he asks, "In what sense, then, are they called 'obstructions'? and provides the answer.
However, "not all," and so forth;
not every moment of a jar is the cause of sensory cognition for every person;
rather, what then?
However, when the object, the sense faculty, and the light are conjoined with one another,
they become causes for consciousness because they produce a distinct subsequent moment through mutual differentiation;
what is the reason for this?

Since that which cannot be assisted by others—being incapable of having any excellence (atiśaya) imparted to it by others—is logically independent of others, it must either have a nature that is capable [of producing an effect] or a nature that is incapable.

In this regard, it has been stated previously that for that which has a capable nature, there would be the constant production of the effect; whereas for the other, which has an incapable nature, there would be non-production.
And when those objects, sense faculties,
and so forth are not obstructed by that resistant [substance] such as a wall, they then become mutual benefactors;
what is the reason for this?

Regarding the phrase "without obstruction" (*avyavadhāna*) and so forth: that location for which no obstruction exists is an "unobstructed location. Its "fitness" (*yogyatā*) is its capacity; because of its being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*), there arises a mutual excellence among those [factors] such as the object and so forth.
However, when there is an obstruction caused by walls and the like for those [factors] such as light and so forth...

Because of the absence of the cause characterized by the suitability of being in an unobstructed location—and because of the non-arising of another capable moment—there is no production of cognition of a jar or similar object.

Since, in this way, there is no persistence of a single nature at all times among momentary things, the previously arisen and capable moment of the sense organ and so forth ceases by its own inherent nature (*svarasataḥ*). Furthermore, when there is an obstructing wall, another capable moment that is about to arise does not come into existence due to the absence of the aforementioned causes; thus, there is a deficiency in the causes of cognition. Therefore, it is due to this deficiency of causes [that cognition does not arise].
Since cognition does not arise with respect to jars and other objects when they are obstructed by walls and the like, walls and such are called "obstructions" (āvaraṇa);
it is not, however, because they prevent a jar or similar object—which was previously capable of producing cognition—from doing so.
What is the reason for this?
Since that jar or other object, while remaining in its capable nature, does not deviate from that nature even when in proximity to a wall or other obstacles,
whatever is capable remains indeed capable;
it is impossible to effect any alteration in its state.
Thus, since objects are momentary, an obscuration is said to exist even if it does not produce an excellence (*atiśaya*) according to the aforementioned method;
now, he says "or else" (*athavā*) and so forth, to show that obscuration occurs precisely by means of producing an excellence.

Even though momentary entities such as jars and the like can indeed receive mutual assistance—even assistance provided by walls and so forth—there is no dispute regarding the assistance rendered by auxiliary causes;
however, an obstruction is distant from both the sense faculty and its object.
To the question of how that [obstruction] could assist the sense faculty and the object, he says:
"Because it is inconceivable," and so forth—it is not possible to conceive [it] in this way: how can an obscuration situated at a distance be beneficial to the object?
[For we observe that] even by means of a magnet situated at a distance, iron is attracted.

The cause (*hetu*) is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), and the condition (*pratyaya*) is the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*); because the efficacy of these two is inconceivable, it cannot be known by one who is not omniscient.
For that reason, whatever obstruction exists between the sense faculty and its object— [...is not perceived.]
In what manner, then, could one surpass even the sense organs and their objects?
By means of the degree of deficiency in the production of consciousness.
The word "api" (even/also) is used here in the sense of possibility, implying that this matter is conceivable because there is no subverting evidence to the contrary.
[Objection: Surely, by means of the immediately present obstruction, that substance is rendered incapable of producing cognition in the second and subsequent moments;
it is not produced [as such] at the very moment of contact, since [the obstruction] provides no assistance [at that time].
Consequently, in the first moment, that substance would be visible even in the presence of an obstruction,
because its capacity to produce cognition remains unimpeded;
this is not a fault.

For whatever is observed to be the producer of an obscuring moment is observed to be the producer of the very same [moment] being obscured, even though that moment is incapable [of producing its effect], as is the case with the second and subsequent moments; therefore, the producer of the obscuring moment at the beginning must likewise produce the obscured moment as something incapable.
For this very reason it is said:
Because the efficacy of causes and conditions is inconceivable, how could there be perception of a substance in the first moment when an obstruction is present? Furthermore,
this point has been demonstrated in the context of the apprehension of degrees of intensity.

It might be argued that although the defect was produced by the obstructing cause of the object at the first moment, it produces an excellence (atiśaya) in that obstruction during the second and subsequent moments.
The capacity of an obscuration to produce a defect must be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); however, since such concomitance does not exist, he says:
"By means of the distinction of obscurations," and so forth.
The mention of "hearing" (*śruti*) regarding sound, smell, and touch— distinguished by obstructions such as rags, cloth, or walls— is intended as an illustration; thus,
from the observation of the dullness or acuity of hearing, sight, and so forth, the capacity of an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) is inferred.
Otherwise, if no distinction were produced by the obscuration,
then that proximity of the obscuration— which would be ineffective— would be equivalent to non-proximity; consequently,
the attribution "this is the obscuration of this sound," as well as the relationship between them, would be merely a construction of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) and not based on reality.
If it is argued that [causal efficiency] will be the basis for the object projected by conceptual construction,
he says "and not," etc.:
and causal efficiencies do not follow conceptual superimposition, nor do they have as their basis objects projected by conceptual construction, because they have real entities as their basis.

Because a young boy is not employed—that is, appointed—for the purpose of cooking on the basis of the metaphorical designation "the boy is fire" due to his proximity to fire; therefore, even though such conceptual construction exists, entities do not have their exclusion [of others] effected by that conceptual construction. Those whose exclusion is effected by that conceptual construction are "those whose exclusion is effected by it."
In the absence of that [object], mental modifications would not be directed toward it; rather, they would function solely according to their own inherent nature.
The analysis of the compound is: "those whose functioning is according to their own inherent nature" (*yathāsvabhāva-vṛtti*).
"That" (*tat*) means "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

If no specific quality were imparted by the obstruction, then even when an obstruction is present, the sense faculties and so forth would still cause cognition— that is, they would indeed produce knowledge—
and yet this is not the case. Therefore, it is understood that the sense faculties and so forth possess specific qualities and specific modes of arising which are produced by that obstruction.
Indeed, for eternal sounds, there can be no loss of excellence or production of excellence when some particular obstruction exists;
therefore, if those eternal sounds possess the inherent nature of producing cognition, [they must do so at all times].
All objects of their own respective domains should produce all cognitions for every person at all times.
If it were not the inherent nature [of things] to produce cognition, then no cognition would ever be produced for any person whatsoever; this is an absolute certainty.
If you argue that even though sound is eternal, it is not heard at all times because of the deficiency of certain auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), [we reply:]...
He explains [the objection] with the words "It might be so," and so forth:
"However, for the apprehension of some of these eternal words, there exists a specific, fixed object that serves as a cooperative cause for their apprehension, determined by its very nature."

Since the auxiliary cause for a particular sound occurs only at a certain time, it is due to this— namely, what is produced by the auxiliary cause— that these sounds are heard only occasionally and in certain locations.
Regarding the passage beginning with "kāmam" (be it so), the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) means: "Be it so.
Let there be the waiting for another auxiliary cause; that is not being prevented.
However, the restriction alone is contradicted;
for if the word remained in its very prior nature, this restriction would not exist, because something that provides assistance must be depended upon.
With the words "Indeed, we do not [deny] this," and so forth, he explains this very point: "We certainly do not reject the auxiliary causes of the primary causes;
rather, the causes indeed depend upon the auxiliaries—[auxiliaries] that are of what nature? Those which provide assistance to that state."

For what reason [is it not so]? Because of the utility— that is, the operation— of the excellence (*atiśaya*) obtained from those auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), which is applied toward the production of the effect that is to be produced, [an excellence] which consists in the state of having the nature of producing the desired effect.
Likewise, if even a Vedic word, depending upon some auxiliary cause, were to produce an effect in the form of a cognition having itself as its object, let it do so;
who is there to prevent it?
It would simply not be the case that it remains restricted to its previous nature—that is, it remains fixed in that very same prior nature.
What is the reason?
Because that previous nature has ceased,
and because another, previously non-existent, nature is acquired from the presence of auxiliary causes.
Because there can be no dependence in the absence of the attainment of some excellence,
for it has been stated previously that one does not depend on what is not superior.
Now, if the word receives an assistance (*upakāra*) from its auxiliary causes that is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), then, since that assistance is also a distinct entity,
it has already been stated that there would be an absence of a relationship— such as "this assistance belongs to that"— between them.

By the word "etcetera," if for the sake of establishing a relationship, a sound-produced assistance is postulated for the assistance provided by auxiliary factors, then the faults already mentioned—such as infinite regress (anavasthā) because another [assistance] would be required there, and yet another there as well—apply.
Furthermore, it follows that this sound itself would be unknowable;
for what reason?
Since the production of cognition arises from an assistance produced by auxiliary factors that is distinct from [the object] itself,
for this very reason, this word is not the sense organ known as the ear.
There is neither contact between the sense organ and its object, nor [contact] with the self;
and this has been stated according to what is established for the opponent.
"And what else?"—it refers to effort and so forth; what is its nature?
It is that which serves as the basis for the arising of cognition and acts as a cooperative condition for the arising of cognition, and which is required for the production of its own cognition.
What is the reason? Because, in that case, sound would be useless for everyone since it would be eternal; "moreover," and so forth.
If they were non-pervasive, then those sounds would not be perceived in all locations;
for how could a person situated in a place devoid of them perceive a sound existing in another location?
If it is argued that this fault does not apply under the view that perception occurs without contact (*aprāptagrahaṇapakṣa*), [we reply:]...

If sound were perceived by the auditory faculty even without reaching the location of the ear, then one situated in a place devoid of sound would also perceive it; therefore, the fault of non-perception everywhere does not arise.
This is not so;
for what reason?
Even there, under the view that [the sense organ] grasps what it has not reached, the grasping of an obstructed object is not possible;
for what reason?
Because the sense organ depends on the degree of proximity of that sound as it remains within its suitable range.
How is this so? It is like the magnet and similar objects;
for instance, although a magnet attracts without reaching its object, it does not attract iron situated in an unsuitable location, and it is just like that.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), things such as venomous snakes that cause damage to lamps and the like are included.

"Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means: if the sense faculty did not disregard the sound's presence in a suitable location, then there would be no distinction between clear and unclear cognitions based on the varying degrees of the sound's presence in a suitable location.
And therefore, because it depends on a suitable location,
he says that even if sound— which is not actually reached— is perceived while situated in a suitable location, there would be no distinction between clear and unclear manifestations.

Furthermore, if the condition for perception— characterized by the activity of the palate and other organs— were present, sounds would be perceived equally in all locations, whether near or far; but since this is not the case,
they are not non-pervasive.

But the Buddhists do not maintain that sound is perceived by the sense organ without having reached the location of that organ; for how else could there be the distinction between clear and indistinct hearing?
As it has been said:
"For those [who hold] that this sound is perceived by the ear without even reaching it..."

Since their non-attainment is equal in the case of objects that are distant, obstructed, and so forth, then in that situation, the apprehension and non-apprehension by those situated far and near would be identical;
furthermore, there could be no sequence [of perception], nor the possibility of degrees such as intense or faint.
Kumārila thinks as follows:

this fault applies only to one for whom all cognitions—whether their manifestations are clear or unclear—are non-erroneous; it does not apply to the Buddhist, because he accepts that a cognition with an unclear manifestation is erroneous.

Since sound is perceived as it arrives through its production in successive locations, a sequence is apprehended; and because sound arises in the region of the ear as either intense or faint, the occurrence of intensity, faintness, and so forth is possible—thus there would be no inconsistency. This is just as a form is perceived as blurred when far away due to contact with dust, mist, and the like, but clearly when nearby because of the absence of such [obscuring factors].
Likewise, it is incorrect to claim that sound is also perceived as clear or indistinct according to distinctions such as distance and proximity.

Since there is the apprehension of the mixture of form with dust, mist, and so forth—if, first of all, those two are apprehended separately, then the appearance of the form would be the same for two persons situated at a distance and nearby, because it would be apprehended according to its actual nature.

If, on the other hand, their apprehension is as one, which constitutes the apprehension of mixture, how could a cognition with an unclear appearance not be erroneous? For it would be the apprehension of distinct things as one. Furthermore, how can there be an appearance of multiple forms for a single form?
As it has been said:
"Since the substrata of cognitions regarding that single object are indeed distinct from one another,
how can its form appear in diverse aspects?"
Kumārila:
But surely words do not pervade space and time,
since the permanence of a word is established by auditory recognition.
And who could determine the pervasiveness of that [Self], or its contrary—
namely, its distinctness due to spatial differentiation? This [notion of distinction] is inferential,
whereas the cognition "it is that very same one" is perceptual and thus sublates it.
Just as in the world Devadatta does not become divided even when traveling to different places in succession, so too the word is not divided;
therefore, its oneness persists across all times and all places.
"That [permanence] is established by perceptual recognition and serves as its sublater;
therefore, sounds are all-pervading. — Ibid.
Regarding this, it is further argued:
there would be the simultaneous perception of all sounds by all persons, if those sounds were omnipresent;
for indeed, no sound exists in any particular place that is not present elsewhere, since every sound exists everywhere due to its omnipresence.
For this reason,
all sounds would be perceived simultaneously and would be perceived by persons situated in all locations;
what is the cause?
Because men possess fit sense faculties, and because the eternal object characterized as sound is always present everywhere due to its pervasiveness, and because,
precisely due to its eternity, it is incapable of having any excellence added to it, and because of its continuity.
In the phrase "of the conditioned" (*saṃskṛtasya*) and so forth,
the genitive case is used either in the sense of the object (*karman*) or the agent (*kartṛ*);
therefore, this is the meaning [of the passage].

He offers the following reply: "If it is accepted that sound, which has been refined by air struck by effort, is perceived by a sense organ that has likewise been refined, then the aforementioned fault does not apply."
He explains [the objection] with the words "Who would be the modifier of a changing sound? No one at all," and so forth.
Even though sound exists at all times, it is not perceived by every person;
for what reason?
Because a manifested sound is perceived only when the sense organ has been similarly manifested by the air struck by effort.
In that regard, between those two, there is first of all no perception of a conditioned sound;
for what reason?
Because a sound, being incapable of undergoing modification, cannot be joined with a refinement (*saṃskāra*).
However, because the sense organ is impermanent, there may be an embellishment (*saṃskāra*) of it by means of the air impelled by effort toward the specific object to be produced;
as it is said:
"The air within the body, impelled by effort, goes forth"—this is certain (Ślokavārttika, Śabdanityatā, 122).

Having reached the space of the ear, it imparts its power to the auditory organ (Śloka-vārttika, Śabdanityatā 124). Furthermore, the power of the sense organ is postulated because the perception of the form of sound would otherwise be impossible; thus, this refinement (saṃskāra) is accepted as being of the nature of a power.
Regarding that,
he explains with the words "there" and so forth that even that conditioned sense organ would hear every sound there without exception or remainder.

If it is argued that because sound is perceived only by a sense-organ that has been refined (*saṃskṛta*), a person whose sense-organ is not so refined does not perceive it, then the previous undesirable consequence— that one for whom the refinement of the sense-organ has been performed would hear all sounds simultaneously— remains unrefuted. Now, suppose it were argued as follows:

Just as the postulation of a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sense organ follows from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the cognition of sound, so too does the postulation of a specific refinement follow from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the cognition of a specific sound; as it has been said:
In the same way, its specific quality would also arise from hearing that specific quality;
therefore, due to the difference in mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and because the sense organ is distinct for each respective object, there is a restriction to a single object— namely,
the apprehension of only one particular sound.
This being so, how could there not be auditory perception of a tumultuous sound (*kalakala*), which consists of a collection of many words and is composed of a multitude of diverse sounds?
He explains [the verse] with the words "And it is seen even... and so forth:

those refinements (*saṃskāra*) of the sense faculty are specific to particular sounds; in that case, due to this specificity of refinement, a sense faculty refined by a certain [refinement] is the perceiver of only a certain sound, and thus there is no simultaneous hearing of all sounds.

Thus, if it is admitted that there is a restriction of auditory perception for the sense organs due to a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*), then the hearing of a "tumultuous sound" (*kalakala*) consisting of a multitude of various sounds would not occur;
for the reason that a single sound is not what is called a "tumultuous sound.
Why is this so?

Because there is a simultaneous hearing of a cacophony of sounds from flutes, drums, poetic recitations, and songs—which possess distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*)—there is no non-difference even when distinct intrinsic natures are apprehended; for the establishment of difference is based precisely upon the difference of intrinsic natures.
Now, it may be argued that this occurs when multiple sounds are heard.

Furthermore, since the hearing of multiple sounds cannot otherwise be accounted for, it is postulated that there is a multiple refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sense organ; thus, the hearing of multiple sounds is entirely uncontradicted. This is the view held by those who maintain that refinements are imparted to the organ by means of the winds impelled by effort.
If they [the impressions] are non-different from the sense faculty, then how can there be a multiplicity of impressions,
given that the sense faculty is one? On the other hand, if they are different, then how is the sense faculty conditioned?

Furthermore, the relationship expressed as "the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras) of that [mind]" is not established; for how could those [phenomena] which arise once [the mind] is already produced possess its own nature? Because of the superimposition of contradictory properties, it is illogical for the conditioned phenomena to be either identical to or different from it—thus, this argument is trivial.
It is not the case that multiple sounds are perceived simultaneously in a cacophony; rather, they are perceived only in succession, and therein each individual sound is heard one by one.

If it is argued that those auditory cognitions are of rapid occurrence (*laghuvṛtti*), and therefore, due to that rapid occurrence, there is an illusion of simultaneous hearing even though they are apprehended sequentially—

then, in the case of a continuous stream of notes such as a flute, because the constituent parts of those specific notes (the *gamaka*s) would also be merged through their rapid occurrence, there would result a confused perception due to their unification.
However, it should not be such that its constituent parts, which lead to comprehension, are unconnected or disordered; and a refutation of this will be stated here in the third chapter,
beginning with the words "it would occur upon the utterance of two short vowels," and so forth.
Therefore, because the capacity for the apprehension of a single word is restricted, the cacophony— which consists of multiple sounds and possesses a manifold nature— is not heard by the sense organ.
Moreover, it is heard that there is no refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sense organ; rather, sound is produced by the palate and other such organs.
Therefore, as many sounds as are produced are exactly as many as are heard; thus, there is the perception of a cacophony (*kalakala*).
He explains [the verse] with the words "If it were not so that only sounds are heard there, and not expressive words," and so forth;
for in a confused clamor, expressive phonemes, words, and sentences are not perceived.
What is the reason?
Because there, one hears mere sounds that are not expressive [of meaning].
If it is asked, "How can there be simultaneous hearing of sounds when their power to convey a single object is restricted?", he says "vācaka" and so forth:
we maintain that the sense organ has a restricted power with respect to the expressive word.
But he refutes [the objection] regarding non-expressive sounds with the words "In that case," and so forth;
for it is specifically particularized sounds in the form of phonemes (*varṇa*) that are expressive.

The claim that there exists a form of speech (*śabdarūpa*) distinct from those [articulations] which denotes a different object is something to be believed with great difficulty, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend its existence.
For what reason?

Because we do not perceive any nature distinct from the articulated sounds (*dhvani*), such that the sound (*dhvani*) would be non-denotative while the word (*śabda*) would be the denotative in a separate form.
However, at one time, during the process of hearing the sequence of phonemes, we determine that there is only a single essence of sound characterized by that sequence of phonemes.

How then, while determining and discerning this essence of sound as distinct from the sounds themselves, can we— based on that determination and preceded by that certainty— proceed toward a form of sound that is separate from the sounds and lacks any [phonemic] basis?

Therefore, it is a specific sound itself that exists in the form of *a*, *ā*, and so forth; the analysis of the compound is: "that which has the name 'syllable' (*varṇa*)," and by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), words, sentences, and the like are also encompassed.
Furthermore:
If, when a tumultuous noise is heard, the individual words are not discernible—
because many speakers remain silent while other sounds persist— then how can that which is uttered by a single person be heard as a meaningful word?
Now, it might be argued that in that case the sound (dhvani) would also be perceived; to this he says:
"The sound is not different from the expressive word (vācaka), for its form is not heard separately from that expressive word."
If it is argued that [the sphoṭa] is indeed heard from the sounds (dhvani), he replies:
"For instruction by another does not carry more weight than what is perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa),
such that one who does not himself hear it through discernment could nevertheless understand the hearing of a distinct [sphoṭa] merely from your word."

Therefore, while other speakers remain silent, this listener hears the word of a single speaker as something entirely distinct from the sounds of other meanings; he perceives the incapacity of the conditions for perceiving that word—namely, the conditions for perceiving sound residing in the speakers, such as the integrity of their vocal organs—to produce their effect, which is the perception of the word. In what respect does he perceive this? In the matter of what ought to be produced.
Regarding the production of something other than that:

if there were a cause for the production of another sound from the very same auditory conditions by which the [original] sound is perceived, then the form of sound produced by those auditory conditions that produce it would be perceived.
And yet they are not perceived;
now, if it should be argued that those tumultuous sounds are the initiators of the resonance, he says:
"Having that as their intrinsic nature," and so forth:

if the conditions for the perception of sound possess only the nature of producing sound devoid of resonance (*dhvani*), then even when many people are speaking in a clamor, how could they produce another effect, namely resonance, while abandoning their own effect, which is sound?
They certainly could not.
For since it is not logical for there to be a difference in the effect when there is no difference in the cause,
it is not logical that a difference in effects— characterized by sound and resonance— should occur within that very same cause.
What is the reason?
As was stated previously, it would follow that a difference in effects independent of a difference in causes would be causeless;
therefore, in a cacophony (*kalakala*), only expressive words (*vācaka*) are heard, not mere sounds (*dhvani*).
Now, if it is accepted that only expressive words exist in a cacophony...

How then is it that those at a distance hear only the sounds (*dhvani*), while those nearby hear the expressive sounds (*vācaka*)? It is true that those very expressive sounds produced by effort are themselves the initiators of the [perceptible] sounds (*dhvani*) through their mutual friction.
Therefore, there is no fault in the fact that for some, in a tumultuous noise, there is the perception of mere sound (*dhvani*), while for others, there is the perception of both;
this is because, even when a tumultuous noise is present nearby, only the sounds (*dhvanayaḥ*) are heard, and not the expressive words (*vācaka-śabdāḥ*). This is what was stated.
That too is incorrect,
because it is not the case that the expressive word is not heard amidst a cacophony; rather, it is indeed heard.
What is the reason?
Because it serves as an indicator for the divisions of words and sentences;
furthermore, how could there be a perception of distinct sounds if the sense organ were restricted to a single capacity?
He explains [the objection] with the words "there would be the apprehension of many sounds" and so forth, [stating that] it could not be so.
Even though those sense faculties possess specific capacities, they simultaneously hear various forms of sounds— of what kind?
Those determined by their respective echoes.
Since these sense organs are restricted to manifesting one sound after another,
yet do not hear all sounds simultaneously, what aversion or disinclination could the senses have toward sounds that they do not hear them?
Nor can it be said that such is the nature of their inherent power.
"Because even when many speakers are heard," as was stated [in verse 260],
the opponent argues that it has been said by the Buddhist that sounds (*dhvani*) are not established as distinct from the letters, words, and sentences that serve as the expressive agents.
How is it that they are not perfected?
They are indeed perfected;
what is the reason?
Since the comprehension of meaning arises from speech— that is,
since the understanding of the expressed object results from the uttered sound—
this comprehension of meaning cannot possibly arise from mere sounds (*dhvani*).
What is the reason?
For indeed, there is no cognition of meaning from a portion of sound smaller than that which manifests a phoneme;
moreover, even a single phoneme is generally devoid of meaning.
If it is argued that even more so the manifesting portion of sound (*dhvani*) is minute, and thus the [phonemes] in combination are the conveyors [of meaning], he replies:
"And that [combination] does not come together."

Since one part of the sound, due to its momentariness, cannot meet— that is, join with— another part of the sound occurring at a subsequent time, therefore this comprehension of meaning, which is accomplished by that expressive [word] in which all parts are complete in the form of words and sentences, is not possible within the sounds themselves.

In what kind [of sounds] are the parts "uncombined" (*asamasta*) and "unconnected" (*asaṃśliṣṭa*), such that because each produced sound-part is momentary, a second sound-part does not persist? It is in those [sounds] that the existence of non-sequentiality is established by the fact that the comprehension of meaning would otherwise be impossible.
That sound-form which possesses non-sequential existence is thus "undivided" (nirvibhāga); that is to say,
sequential and divided sound is distinct from the signifier (vācaka).
The analysis of the compound is "that which has parts possessing a sequence";
he refutes this with the words "that is not," etc.,
meaning that what was just stated is not possible.
Why?

Because it has already been refuted [previously] by such arguments as: "The sequence does not exist as something distinct from the phonemes that possess the sequence; for in words and sentences such as 'Devadatta,' we do not perceive any manifestation other than the manifestation of the letter *da* and so forth."

Furthermore, if it is postulated that the nature of the word exists without succession because the comprehension of meaning is impossible if the sounds were incomplete parts, then such a postulation leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For instance, regarding the actions of the hands and so forth which indicate going, coming, and the like according to convention: since those parts [of the action] are momentary, the preceding part of the action cannot connect with or produce the subsequent part of the action, as they do not coalesce.
And because there is no comprehension from a single part:
since one does not comprehend the meaning characterized by going, coming, and so forth, according to convention, from even a very small portion of the action,
it is distinct from that [action].
Other than the components of action are things such as hand gestures according to convention;
by the word "etcetera," head-shaking and so forth are included when there is the comprehension of meaning.
In those cases, one would have to admit that the cause of the comprehension of meaning possesses the nature of all forms and functions,
just as in the case of sound itself, where there is the postulation of a "sound" distinct from the audible resonance (*dhvani*).
Furthermore, as Maṇḍana has stated:

"When those learned in the three Vedas accept that objects such as hand-gestures consist of generalities and particularities expressible by words like 'upward-thrusting' (*utkṣepaṇatva*) and so forth, then what is the logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) that one must accept a single self of action (*karmātmā*)?"
Sphoṭasiddhi 33, pp.
That is incorrect.
For if a single action in the form of upward motion (*utkṣepaṇa*) were established,
and likewise if subsequent [actions] were also established, then the universal of upwardness (*utkṣepaṇatva-sāmānya*) would reside in each of those many upward motions;
however, that very [universal] is not established, because there is no continuity (*ananvaya*) among the preceding and succeeding parts of the action.
Nor does the existence of a universal follow from the absence of particulars;
nor is there a cognition of each part of an action as having the specific form of upward throwing and so forth—
what then?
If that universal of "throwing upward" (utkṣepaṇatva) were admitted to exist in those parts by virtue of being a form belonging to them,

then upon such admission, the object characterized as "going" and so forth would be understood even from a single part of the action, because the universal denoting that object would be present; therefore, this [objection] is trivial.
And just as there is no self of action (karmātman) distinct from the constituent parts of the action, so too there is no self of sound (śabdātman) distinct from the constituent parts of the phonemes;
how then does the cognition of meaning occur? To this he says:
"It is precisely those [phonemes] that arise in succession," and so forth.

Just as each has its own respective instrument, such as the palate and so forth, the employment— that is, the activity— of those [instruments] results in distinct portions of phonemes or portions of actions,
according to the employment of their respective instruments.
It should also be connected here that [the parts] are distinct because they arise sequentially due to the application of karma;

for those aforementioned portions of phonemes or portions of action, having entered the domain of conceptual cognitions—which follow the sequence of direct experience and conform to the sequence of conceptual objects—in succession, produce the cognition of an object exactly according to convention. This is logical, as it is not devoid of reasoning.
Furthermore, he states another defect:

by means of whatever defects— such as the fact that each preceding portion of the sound (dhvani) is not connected with each succeeding portion of the sound— and so forth, those very sounds are observed to be non-expressive of the [phonemes] such as *ka*, *ra*, *ṇa*, *a*, and *ya*.
If this denoter—which is distinct from the sounds—is manifested by those sounds occurring in succession, why do those defects inherent in the sounds not affect it? Indeed, they certainly do;
for whether the sounds are taken individually or collectively, according to the reasoning previously stated, they are not the conveyors of the meaning.
However, you maintain that each [articulation] is a manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*) of the expressive word (*vācaka*).

Since the expressive word manifested by a single sound (*dhvani*) is not definitively apprehended, it is apprehended through the awakening of varying degrees of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the manifestations of other sounds. Thus, even when the expressive word is manifested by the sounds, how could those defects [of indistinctness] apply to it?
As it has been stated by Maṇḍana:
It is incorrect [to claim] that for the proponents of *sphoṭa*, a sentence or a word does not consist of multiple parts;
for even if there is unity, the manifestation of the undivided [entity] is shown to occur sequentially.
Thus, that [position] is untenable.
For manifestation is indeed cognition,
and cognition is not admitted by you to exist without the accompaniment of a word;
therefore, what is called "manifestation" is nothing other than certainty.
Furthermore, since the determination of the expressive word does not appear immediately after the first sound,
how can its manifestation occur?

Therefore, it is established that just as sounds— whether individually or collectively— are incapable of conveying meaning, so too are they incapable of manifesting the expressive word (*vācaka*). Thus,

the explanation beginning with "succession" (*krama*) and so forth means that the non-sequential essence of the word (*śabdātmā*), which is the expressive agent, reveals or manifests its meaning when manifested by the sequentially arising portions of sound.
Merely by virtue of their presence,
those sounds do not reveal that essence of speech— which is distinct from the sounds themselves— all at once;
what is the reason for this?
Because those parts of the sound occur sequentially,
not even a single part of the sound manifests— that is, determines— the word.
What is the reason?
Because it would follow that the other portion of the sound (*dhvani*), which is intended to be the manifestor, would be rendered useless.
Furthermore, a single portion of the sound is not the manifestor of the entire word, because at the time of a single phonemic portion, the form of the entire expressive [word] is not perceived.
*Sphoṭasiddhi* (by Maṇḍana) 29: Therefore, for this reason, this essence of the word (*śabdātmā*),
because it is manifested in succession by the successive parts of the sound (*dhvani*), [is eternal].

That nature of sound which is not connected [to its parts] and whose apprehension is not complete— how could such a nature of sound establish its own denoted object, characterized by manifestation, which is to be accomplished through the completeness of apprehension? It could not establish it at all.
How is it like sound?
Just as, according to your view, the parts of a sound do not manifest meaning because they are not connected with what precedes and follows, so too [is the case here].
With the words "Who indeed," etc., he supports this very point:
regarding objects that are to be established through perception, what indeed is the difference between existence and non-existence when there is absolute non-perception? None at all.

For just as momentary parts of sound are incapable because they do not possess complete perception—due to their non-existence at the time of the succeeding parts—likewise, even if the nature of sound were non-sequential, it would be equally incapable if it did not admit of complete perception.
Furthermore, this nature of sound does not establish the cognition of an object by its mere presence, independent of apprehension;
for what reason?
Because of its dependence upon that [manifestation],
this manifestation occurs in a temporal sequence; it belongs to both the existent and the non-existent, and it pertains to the existent nature of the Word-soul (śabdātman).

And since the successive occurrence of the non-existent parts of the sound is of equal utility and yields an equal result, it is likewise [ineffective] even with respect to that effect characterized by the comprehension of meaning— which cannot be accomplished by the sounds and is impossible to achieve through them.

Even if the nature of the word is manifested by the sounds (dhvani), it remains impossible to establish [its eternity] in that way; therefore, there is no need for another imagined word distinct from the sounds. Consequently, the letters do not possess the quality of being uncreated (apauruṣeya).
Nor is it the case that [the Veda] is a sentence; this is the conclusion:

if it is argued that a sentence is not something distinct from the phonemes, but rather that the sequence of phonemes constitutes a sentence, and that this [sequence] is of non-human (apauruṣeya) origin.
What is the reason for that? Because there is no difference [in the cognition] from the sequential order of the phonemes.
The sentence is not an eternal entity distinct from the phonemes, nor is it the form of the word itself;
rather,
for us Mīmāṃsakas, the sentence is characterized by the specific sequence of the phonemes.
If it is argued that its being non-human (apauruṣeya) is what is to be proven, we say no,
because there is no difference [in the Veda] from the sequential order of the phonemes.
This sequence is not something distinct from the phonemes.
Why?

Because if this sequence were admitted to exist as something perceptible yet failing to meet the conditions for perception (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), it would follow that its difference [from the phonemes] could not be perceived as distinct from them.

And since it is not perceived, when its non-existence is to be established, the non-perception of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) must be stated; or, if it is a sequence of imperceptible [parts],
then, regarding that imperceptible sequence—
Consequently, because it would follow that there is no comprehension of the meaning due to the sequence,
perception cannot be the apprehender of a sequence that is visible, precisely because such a sequence is not visible;
nor can it be inference, because of the absence of a logical mark (liṅga).

Furthermore, if there were no sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), then mere phonemes would be indistinguishable everywhere—in all worldly and Vedic sentences—and the aforementioned undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would follow, as stated in the passage beginning with "What would be eliminated by this? and so forth.
Now, it might be argued:
"The sequence of phonemes is merely a property (*dharma-mātra*) and not a separate entity; therefore, there is no fault."
Thus it has been said:
"This [cognition] is merely a property (dharma) of those [phonemes]; it is not held to be a distinct entity.
Therefore, the phonemes, when cognized in succession, become the means of comprehension."
Nor is the sequence something produced, because it is adopted from what was previously established;
for no speaker adopts a sequence independently, but rather intends to speak it exactly as it has been stated by others.
Kumārila [argues] that even for another person, since this [word] exists as something related, it is beginningless; therefore,
he says that the sequence of phonemes, having come down from the observation of successive elders, is indeed non-human (apauruṣeya).
And there is no fixed arrangement for those phonemes;
they do not possess a fixed order.
What is the reason?
He explains [the verse] with the words "If... and so forth, because it is contradictory for there to be another sequence from a single fixed [source].

If the sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) of the phonemes were something produced, and if those phonemes were not many and of the same kind—such that the Vedic phonemes could have a fixed sequence through some [specific arrangement]—[then the objection would hold].

Others, however, are worldly [sounds] whose transformations are according to one's will; the analysis of the compound is: those whose application consists of a transformation according to one's will through a different sequence.
What then? In the three worlds, the form of the letter 'a' is one and the same, as is the letter 'ga'.
Thus it has been said:
"Even though there is a difference in place, time, and speaker, the phoneme *ga* and others are not distinct, since the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of them therein is perfectly clear."
Kumārila:
And when this is so, since the sequence of phonemes is fixed, why is it that one says "agni" (fire) and not "gagana" (sky)?
What is the reason?

The meaning is that because the prior-posterior relationship between the phonemes *a* and *ga* is fixed— such that the *a* is established as preceding the *ga*, and the *ga* is established as following the *a*—
in the word "gagana," the *a* would necessarily follow the *ga*, and no other sequence would be possible.
Confirming this very point, he says:
"Even of produced things," and so forth; let alone for those that are unproduced, let this consideration stand aside.
Since it is impossible for anything to undergo change in any way whatsoever,
what kind of transformation of the cause could there be even for conditioned entities that possess a fixed sequence of causal transformation— that is,
the attainment of successive states?
Therefore, the restriction is that existence [occurs] immediately after the cause; those things for which this is found are so described.
Even for these, it is impossible to reverse the sequence;
just as in the case of the seed, sprout, and so forth, where the sprout follows the seed, the stalk follows the sprout, and the flowers and so on follow that, there can be no reversal.
Likewise, there is a fixed order for the seasons, the years, and so forth— namely,
the seasons characterized by the winter solstice (*hemanta*) and others,
and the years such as those presided over by Śukra and Bṛhaspati.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), planets, constellations, and so forth are included;
however, what [need is there to mention] those phonemes which are unconditioned (*akṛtaka*) and whose nature is an immovable state?
The analysis of the compound is: "those unconditioned things whose nature is an immovable state such as sequence and so forth."
For things established in any particular way,
it is impossible for them to undergo alteration without abandoning their prior state according to a fixed sequence, and it is likewise impossible for them to remain in a different sequence.
Or, if the abandonment of their previous state is admitted for the phonemes (*varṇa*), it follows that they must perish;
for even in the case of phonemes, a reversal of sequence cannot occur without abandoning their previous state, especially since the sequence is eternal.
Thus, this alteration of sequence would only occur if there were a difference in the phonemes at each word, on the grounds that even though the phonemes are eternal, they are distinct in every word.
Because new phonemes would be produced at every single word, there would be an abundance of phonemes;
or else, there would be a difference in their sequence. Yet both of these consequences are unacceptable to the Mīmāṃsakas, because they maintain that phonemes are unitary and eternal.
Furthermore, with the words "api ca" and so forth, he states another refutation:
how can that sequence which is produced by space and time be absent from the phonemes?
Because pervasion and eternality have been described, it has been stated that,
moreover, the eternality of sound is established by auditory recognition.
"Since its omnipresence is established, who could determine its contrary?"—
so says Kumārila.
Because it is described as being all-pervasive like space, there is no sequence [of phonemes] produced by location.
He explains that it is not produced by time because of its eternal nature,
using the words "And this [is] that," and so forth;
and this is the sequential order of the phonemes.
Or it may be produced by place,
such as the sequence of ants and so forth standing in a row while mutually excluding one another's positions;
or it may be produced by time.
Just as in the case of seeds, sprouts, and so forth—

where when there is the seed there is no sprout, and when there is the sprout there are no leaves and so on— this sequence occurs in two ways, produced by space and time; however, it is not possible for such a sequence to exist among phonemes.
Why? Because of pervasion and because of eternality;
in that case, first of all, a spatial sequence of phonemes is not possible.
Because the spatial priority and posteriority of entities consists in their existence by way of mutual exclusion of location, such a priority and posteriority is not possible among phonemes;
for what reason?
Because of its pervasiveness, every color occupies the same location as all other colors; thus,
the worldly example of wind and sunlight is given.
He states the scriptural authority: "And like the self, etc.";
by the word "etc.," there is the inclusion of space and so forth.
Likewise, a temporal sequence of phonemes is not possible because they function by mutually excluding one another's time; this very [sequence] consists in their temporal priority and posteriority.
Why is this so?
Regarding the passage beginning with "yadā" and so forth: at the time when one [letter] does not exist, because another exists,
that temporal sequence (kālapaurvāparya) is also impossible in the case of eternal phonemes (varṇa).
Since all phonemes exist at all times,

there is no way for the sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*) to be anything other than that produced by space and time; how then could you establish that a sentence is non-human (*apauruṣeya*), given that a sentence is nothing but the priority and posteriority of phonemes?
Furthermore, a sequence produced by sounds for letters that arise simultaneously is not logical, because it would entail their impermanence;
as it has been said:
"Because it is an effect of impermanent sounds, sequence is therefore perishable."
And its dependence on a person would arise from the power of his intention to speak, according to Kumārila;
thus, this is the meaning that results.
Because phonemes are all-pervasive, they must exist simultaneously; therefore, succession contradicts their pervasiveness, and pervasiveness contradicts succession.
If succession is asserted for phonemes, then the recognition that apprehends their pervasiveness would be erroneous.
And likewise, since phonemes are distinct according to differences in place, time, and speaker, they must be produced; how then can the sequence be beginningless?
To this, it is said:
"Nor is the sequence a product, because it is adopted from what was previously established."
For no speaker adopts a sequence independently; rather, he intends to speak it exactly as it has been stated by others.
And since others do likewise, its connection, like that of other things, is beginningless.
That [objection] is refuted because,

given the existence of sequence, the recognition of the identity of phonemes lacks authority; for at each utterance the phonemes are produced anew, and since sequence is not something distinct from them,
sequence cannot be a property of the things that possess it.
Since the property (*dharma*) is also distinct from the substratum (*dharmin*), it should appear as something separate in auditory cognition; however, it does not so appear.

Therefore, entities arise only non-simultaneously, and this is what constitutes "sequence" (*krama*). Consequently, because there is a difference in the arising of phonemes at each utterance, there is also a difference in their sequence.

It will be demonstrated that this recognition is based on similarity— namely, the realization that "this is the very same sequence seen previously"— and thus recognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

How then can the sequence [of the Veda] be considered authorless on the grounds of its beginninglessness? (263) Now, if the Vedavādins should desire that this fault not arise, they would have to accept that phonemes are both impermanent and all-pervasive.
At that time, the fault regarding impermanence and non-pervasiveness has already been proclaimed;
now, with the words "atheti" and so forth, he explains [the opponent's position]:
"Let this fault of the absence of sequential order among the phonemes not arise"—thus the Vedavādin would not accept that the phonemes are impermanent and non-pervasive.

Thinking that "this [Veda] is characterized by temporal sequence due to its impermanence, and by spatial sequence due to its non-pervasiveness," those two positions— impermanence and non-pervasiveness— are already established;
how then could that which is impermanent, produced through effort, and of human origin not be so?
by such statements as "it would follow that there is non-perception everywhere," and so forth, [the opponent's position] has been refuted in due order; thus, this is not a valid rebuttal.
The manifestation (*vyakti*) or disclosure (*abhivyakti*) of phonemes (*varṇa*), or even their sequence, does not constitute a sentence.

The meaning is that when the action resides in the object (*karmasthā kriyā*), then neither the manifestation of the phonemes nor the sequence of the objects of that manifestation constitutes a sentence.
He explains [the reason] with the words "Because of the refutation of eternal manifestation," starting with "not" (na), and so forth.
A sentence is not a sequence of phonemes or a sequence of their individual forms, by which this fault would arise;
rather,
it is the manifestation of them.
That sequence which belongs to the manifestation of phonemes and forms, characterized by their being manifest, is the sentence;
showing that very thing,
he says "no," and so forth.

That manifestation is also false—namely, the claim that a sentence is the sequence of those manifested phonemes, on the grounds that the manifestation of each phoneme occurs in a specific order because the causal conditions for its manifestation, such as the operations of the palate and other articulators, arise sequentially. Thus, the sequence of those manifested phonemes constitutes the sentence.
This too is incorrect.
For what reason?
Because that individual manifestation has already been refuted in the context of the discussion on individuals among eternal things;
reminding [the opponent] of that very point, he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "kāryatā" (being an effect), it has been explained that for objects such as jars, which are incapable of producing cognition by themselves, their "manifestation" (vyakti) is nothing other than a specific effect produced by the manifestor through the imposition of a capacity for direct production.
Furthermore, because those phonemes are perceived solely through the activity of the organs such as the palate and so forth, it follows that those phonemes possess the nature of being effects;
for the connection is this: whatever form is perceived from a particular source, people designate that form as an effect.

The word "yataḥ" (from which) refers to that which was indicated by the relative pronoun "yaḥ"; "tadupalabdhiḥ" means the perception of that [phoneme], which relies upon a perception that is invariably concomitant with it—the particle "eva" (only/just) being placed out of its logical order.
That aforementioned perception exists even in the case of phonemes, precisely because the perception of phonemes is invariably concomitant with the perception of the operation of effort (*prayatna*).
And that perception, which is the basis for the designation of "being an effect" even in other things well-known as effects, is the basis for the conceptualization of effect-ness;
there is no further distinction beyond this.
Therefore, how is it that, given that the basis for accepting their status as effects is equal, the phonemes are not effects?
To this, the opponent replies: "No, etc.";
nor is this [status] based on perception.
The establishment of the state of being an effect is based on the fact that the perception of one thing is invariably concomitant with the perception of another;
rather,
it is that which occurs only when [the other] exists.
The status of being an effect is established as depending on existence, in the sense that "only when X exists does Y come to be";
however, it is held that for phonemes, existence does not arise from their instruments, but rather only their perception [arises].
The Teacher [Dignāga] says, "That is existence.
[The opponent replies: This is false, for it is merely a designation that the locus of existence itself possesses the status of being an effect.
From what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is that existence established, by which it could prove this status of being an effect?
For as long as this existence (sattā) is not established, it does not occur that "this being present,
that comes to be";
thus, the establishment of existence is the means of proving that [causal relation].
The proof that establishes that [effect-ness] is precisely apprehension (*upalabdhi*),
because proof has the nature of cognition.
Therefore, it is established that whatever existence is invariably concomitant with the apprehension of something is the effect of that thing.

"And since that [reason] is equal even in the case of phonemes (*varṇa*), why are the phonemes not considered effects? To this, the opponent replies: "True; indeed, if the word were perceived solely through the operation of the articulatory organs, they would be its effects."

If the existence of that sound were not established by the operation of the palate and other articulatory organs, but rather were already established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it would be as follows:

for a person who previously heard the word "cow" and hears the word "cow" at another time, there arises a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) apprehending its identity, namely, "This is that very same word 'cow'."

The apprehension of reality itself would not be possible otherwise if the sound did not exist in the interval between the times of hearing the preceding and succeeding [sounds]; thus, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the existence of the prior sound is indeed established,
and an establishment preceded by another establishment cannot serve as a proof for its being an effect.
"But that establishment of existence (*sattāsiddhi*) which is the cause for the conceptualization of being an effect (*kāryatva-prajñapti*)— that which is preceded by an [actual] establishment,
such as the subsequent establishment of a jar that was previously non-existent, occurring precisely through the activity of the potter and so forth"—
thus says the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*), beginning with "nanu" and so on.
This states that recognition is not yet established as a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa); since this will be demonstrated later, how then can the existence [of the word] be established?
Indeed, the existence of the word was already established previously.
Nevertheless, since that form of the word is unestablished,
he asks, "Which is that form? and replies with the words beginning "that which is of such a kind," and so forth.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "one whose morality (*śīla*) has been employed through the mediation of such a cognition in which the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound appears.
For if such a form were established beforehand, then there would be a constant perception of sound.

If it is argued: "That aforementioned form of the sound is indeed established; it is simply not employed as a cause for auditory consciousness due to the deficiency of another auxiliary factor (*sahakārin*)."
If this is so, then that state which is subsequently employed in its own cognition when the auxiliary causes are present,
and that state prior to the exertion which was not so employed,
are mutually contradictory.
How, then, can there be non-difference between these two contradictory states—the one in which [the sound] has been employed and the one in which it has not?
On the contrary, there is indeed difference; and since there is thus multiplicity, that nature of the word would have been produced, whereby the word would necessarily be something created (*kārya*).
Furthermore, it might be argued:

That excellence (*atiśaya*) which occurs is not the very essence (*ātmabhūta*) of the word, but rather a distinct entity (*arthāntara*); thus, it remains entirely unaltered from its prior nature. Therefore, he says: "Nor is there a difference characterized by the state of being a causal factor (*kāraka-avasthā*) from the state of being a non-causal factor; the excellence does not touch the nature of the word, meaning it is not distinct from the nature of the word. For if it were distinct, then since that very excellence would be established as the means for the cognition of the word, its status as the cause would be established, and consequently, it would follow that the word itself is not the cause.

For indeed, that alone is useful for the probandum (*sādhya*) in a given case, in whose presence the establishment of the probandum occurs, and nothing else; excellence (*atiśaya*) is directly useful for cognition, whereas the word is useful for excellence. Thus, even the word is indirectly useful for cognition. To this, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "tadatiśaya," even if one assumes that the word functions as a qualifier (*atiśaya*) for that [object], the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) follows.
The consequence is that it would be like cognition:
just as when cognition is to be produced, sound is not employed as something distinct from the excellence [itself],
so too, when excellence is to be produced, an excellence distinct from it must be postulated.
And thus there would be an infinite regress; since the excellence (*atiśaya*) is non-different from the sound, and because it is non-different [from it],
it must indeed surpass the nature of the sound which produces the cognition of its own object, being distinct from that [sound].

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "an *avasthābheda* (distinction of states) whose application of unmediated capacity is by way of a difference in its own nature (*svarūpa*). Now, it might be argued:
A state that produces consciousness does not arise at all because it is eternal;
rather, it produces cognition in dependence upon the palate and other such factors.
Therefore, he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "of the excellence" (*atiśayasya*), it has already been refuted that there is no excellence produced by auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) for this [permanent entity], and thus its dependence upon auxiliaries is precluded. Furthermore,
since that sound-nature which is the producer is established solely through the operation of the instrument (*karaṇavyāpāra*), it possesses properties identical to all other effects.
The analysis of the compound is: "that whose properties are equal to those of all effects.

For such a word, whose properties are equal to all effects, if manifestation were intended, then everything—even a sprout and so forth—would be manifested; or else, nothing at all would be manifested.
Sound, too, would be an effect, because there is no distinction;
for in this way, an object is considered a manifestor when, by means of its own cognition as an instrument, it becomes the cause of the cognition of another.
When,
for the sake of accomplishment,
does that which is to be manifested (vyaṅgya) come to possess its existence by means of a cause?

Just as a lamp is a manifestor that serves as the cause for the cognition of a jar already produced by a potter and others— or even otherwise— if the object to be manifested were unestablished prior [to its manifestation],
then what distinction would there be between this manifestor and a productive cause?
He explains [the verse] with the words "one's own cognition" (*svapratipatti*) and so forth:

one's own cognition itself is the door, that is, the means; by means of that instrument, it is established in the world that the cause for the cognition of another thing, such as a jar, is a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), like a lamp and so forth.
If that which is manifested were already established prior to the operation of the manifestor,
then surely even a lamp or similar object produces a momentary jar that was previously unestablished yet capable of being perceived;
so why is it said, "if it were already established prior"?
Therefore, he says "of the same kind," and so forth:

the preceding moment of a jar or the like, which is capable of being perceived, is of the same kind as its material cause; because it would have been established prior to the operation of the manifestor, it is said that "if it were already established beforehand."
It is not said that the excellence of that very cause of cognition—which is obtained from its manifestor—is established prior to [the manifestation];
for what reason?
Because of that aforementioned excellence.
Because it has that causal complex as its condition, the analysis of the compound is: "that [causal complex] which is the manifesting cause (pratyaya) of that [perception].
Furthermore, those which bring about the apprehension of what was previously unestablished through their own operation are indeed producers (kārakas).
Just as in the case of a pot and other such objects, the causes for the perception of sound— being similar to a potter and the like— are equal to those of a potter;
therefore, sound, like a pot and so forth, is indeed an effect.
Now, when a word heard at one time is heard again at another time, its identity—that "this is that very same [word]"—is apprehended through perceptual recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

Furthermore, since such an apprehension of identity would otherwise be impossible, it is certain that the word exists prior to the activity of the palate and other articulatory organs. Therefore, how could the palate and so forth be considered "perceivers of what is already established"?
Consequently, it is logical that they are merely manifesters (*vyañjaka*).
He thinks as follows:

in the first moment there is the apprehension of the sound; in the second moment there is the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the previously apprehended sound; then in the next moment there is the recollection of the sound;

and then, in the fourth moment, when that sound has vanished, how could the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)—"this is that same word 'ghaṭa'"—be perceptual (*pratyakṣa*), since its object is no longer present?
Nor is recognition of a phoneme possible for a person who has already awakened from [sleep] due to latent impressions (*saṃskāra*),
because it has been stated that a phoneme possesses parts;
furthermore, at the time of the final part of a phoneme, the preceding parts of the phoneme do not exist, and thus even the final phoneme itself is not present.

For this very reason, direct perception as a means of recognizing words and sentences is also impossible, because words and the like are aggregates of phonemes; furthermore, at the time of the final phoneme, the preceding phonemes no longer exist, and direct perception is held to have only present objects as its domain.
Therefore, direct perception cannot possibly grasp the identity of phonemes, words, or sentences.
For this same reason, it was not put forward by the Teacher (Ācārya).

Or, let us grant that there is a perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) regarding them; even so, it is not logical to postulate the existence of sound prior to the operation of the palate and other articulators on the grounds that such perception could not otherwise be explained. This is because the perception of identity is possible even through the apprehension of another similar [sound].
