If you argue that the apprehension of another similar [sound] is itself unestablished (*avyāpyasiddha*), then we reply: in that case, unity (*ekatva*) is likewise not established at all.

If it is argued that [the prior existence of the object] is established by the apprehension of its identity (*tattvagrahaṇa*), we say no; for such apprehension of identity is observed even in the case of severed hairs that have grown back again. Therefore, since there remains doubt, how can one postulate prior existence through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)?
Now, because sound is recognized [as the same], it is eternal;
for if it were non-eternal, it would be manifold, and consequently, there could be no recognition at all.
Thus it is.
That which is employed for the sake of another exists prior to its employment, just as an axe exists prior to the act of cutting;
and since sound is employed for the purpose of communicating to others,
it too must certainly exist prior [to its utterance].
Therefore, he says "recognition" and so forth,
[meaning] the reasons for establishing the constant existence of sound.
These also do not support the definition of a logical reason;
for indeed, recognition is observed even in the case of impermanent things such as lamps;
therefore, this [reason] is inconclusive.
Likewise, even in the case of an action that is momentary, it is observed in its application;
therefore, the reason "because it is being applied" is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, whatever mark (*liṅga*) may be adduced to prove the oneness of sound—
The subsequent cognition of the letter *a* has the same object as the preceding one; that is, it has the same object as the previous cognition of the letter *a*.
By this means, through the proof of the identity of words, their eternity is established—so he thinks.
The reason is the cognition of the letter *a*;
"like that" means like the previous cognition of the letter *a*, and so forth.

By the word "and so forth," it is meant that in the states of fast, medium, and slow [utterance], there is the cognition: "this very same phoneme *ga* and so on is indeed this phoneme *ga* and so on, though distinguished by the differences of fast and so forth."

The formal argument (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: whatever cognition of the letter *a* there may be has an object non-different from the previous cognition of the letter *a*, just like the previous cognition of the letter *a*; and the subsequent cognition of the letter *a* is indeed a cognition of the letter *a*. This is a fallacy that resembles a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetupratirūpaka*).
Furthermore, that proof is not capable of establishing the non-difference between the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the two preceding and succeeding *a*-sounds;

for this reason— "because of the cognition of the letter *a*"— must be stated either specifically as "because it has the nature of the cognition of the preceding *a*-sound," or generally as "because it is merely the cognition of the letter *a*."
In the first position, the reason is unestablished;
for what reason?
Because its being of that nature is unestablished, and because its being perceived as having a prior form is unestablished.
Alternatively, if it is argued that the specific reason is "because it consists in the cognition of a subsequent form," even that is not a proof;
for what is the reason?
The meaning is that because its being of that same nature is not established— that is, because its being of the nature of the probandum is not established—
there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) due to the non-establishment of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Alternatively, if the logical mark (*liṅga*) is stated in a general sense, there is no contradiction even if it has a different object-domain.
And if there is a cognition of the letter *a*, and it has an object distinct from the object of the previous cognition of the letter *a*, what contradiction is there?
Others, however, explain that just as "being a cognition of the letter *a*" is a universal (*sāmānya*) common to those two cognitions, so too is having the letter *a* as its object not contradictory.
Furthermore:

Furthermore, regarding two cognitions directed toward the same object—two cognitions occurring at earlier and later times that have as their object a single form established previously—their relation of priority and posteriority (earlier and later) is contradicted if they exist [simultaneously] before and after.
Why?
Because the effect arises or does not arise according to the sequence of the cause being present or absent.
And if those two causes were present simultaneously, they would have to exist at once;
furthermore, if the former cognition of the form were to arise and not the latter even when the cause is present, then the latter would never arise even subsequently.
What is the reason?
Even when the causes for the cognition of the preceding and succeeding [moments] are present, the specific cognition of the subsequent form that has not yet arisen lacks those as its cause;
the meaning is that the cause of the cognition of the preceding form is not its cause.

Therefore, regarding those two perceptions occurring in prior and posterior succession, the analysis [of the compound] would be: "having entirely different causes," meaning that all their causes are distinct from one another;
such might be the opinion.
Since sound alone is the single cause for those two perceptions of the letter ‘a’, while the sequence of their arising is due solely to the sequence of the proximity of auxiliary conditions,
he says "therein," and so forth.

In that case, at the time when the posterior and anterior forms arise through dependent origination, even though there is no difference in the intrinsic nature of the single cause, the two cognitions would necessarily exist simultaneously;
what is the reason for this?
Since that single, potent cause does not require an auxiliary,
it follows that the identity of object between the preceding and succeeding cognitions is contradicted by reason;
and by all of this, it has been stated that the thesis— that the cognition of the subsequent form has an object non-different from the cognition of the preceding form— is sublated by inference.
The inference is as follows:
that which arises sequentially does not have a single object,
just like the visual and auditory cognitions that arise in succession.

Furthermore, the two successive cognitions of the letter *a*, namely the preceding and the succeeding, are pervaded by non-successiveness in their having a single object; and since succession is the opposite of that [non-successiveness], it is indeed contrary to the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddha*).
If it is argued that, because this is sublated by perceptual recognition (*pratyakṣa-pratyabhijñā*), the inference does not even arise as a formal proposition (*pratijñā*):
The cognition "this is that very same [thing]" has as its object the relation to both prior and subsequent times; therefore, it has difference as its object,
for the state of being related to a prior time is indeed one thing, and the state of being related to a subsequent time is another.

Otherwise, because of the non-difference between its connection with a prior time and its connection with a subsequent time, since the entity exists now, there would be no manifestation of the entity as "this is that," nor would there arise the cognition "this is that very same thing."

Alternatively, because its connection with a prior time is distinct from its connection with a subsequent time, there would be no appearance of it as "prior," nor would there arise the cognition "this is that very same one," but rather [the cognition] "this is it."

Therefore, that which is related to a prior time is not related to a subsequent time, and that which is related to a subsequent time is not related to a prior time; since recognition has as its object the relation to prior and subsequent times, it has as its object difference. Thus, how could there be a subversion of the thesis by means of recognition?
To this, Umbeka says:

Even if there is a single experience in the form "this is that very same thing," it is nevertheless perceived as apprehending both the past status of being an object of cognition and present immediacy within a single substratum;
or even if this consists of two cognitions in the form of perception and recollection,

it is nonetheless distinct from the case of the uninterrupted arising of the recollection of a jar and the perception of a cloth, because this [present experience] manifests through the mutual relation of its own object and the other's object.
For in recollection, the object itself appears as qualified by a past cognition,
and that which was the object of the past cognition appears with immediacy in perception,
because it appears [in the form]: "I remember this."

Therefore, it is incorrect to claim that the conviction of a person with unblinking vision regarding the continuous persistence of something devoid of arising and destruction constitutes a sublation of the inference proving momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

This is because each subsequent perception has as its object a successive difference in the state of the thing; thus, the superimposition of identity—thinking "this is that very same thing"—is an error.
For instance, in the perception of one seeing for the first time, the state of the object appears as something immediate, not as the state that was the object of a past cognition;
likewise, even for one who sees repeatedly,
the object exists in its present form, not in its former one.

And when form remains constant, the non-continuance of the previous form is itself its destruction; just as, for example, the form of childhood [is destroyed] in the state of old age. Furthermore, the previous form is an object of past cognition and action, whereas the present form is directly perceived (*aparokṣa*). Yet, a person seen in the state of childhood and so forth is recognized (*pratyabhijñāyate*) in the state of old age and so forth. How, then, can the status of being an object of past cognition and action and the state of direct perception appear as co-located within a single substratum?
Or how can it be said that an object which is actually present appears in memory as qualified by a past cognition?

Even in cases where one who has been gazing with unblinking eyes perceives a continuous determination over a very long period of time, the object’s state of being directly perceived arises through its connection with the present perceptual cognition. Since the past cognition no longer exists, the status of being the object of that past cognition is likewise absent right now; this is what constitutes its "destruction. How, then, can you say [otherwise]?
As for the claim that the very determination of continuity—which is devoid of arising and destruction—is the sublater of the inference of momentariness:

this objection applies only to one who asserts a difference at every moment; for if non-difference were established merely by recognition, then even for what has perished, its identity would be understood.
The argument that it is "like the recognition of a dead person" is also refuted,
because there is no such thing as non-difference [between the two states].
Nor can there be non-difference between the destroyed and the undestroyed, because of their mutual contradiction;
nor can non-difference be established by the fact that the cognition of identity would otherwise be inexplicable, since the cognition of identity is possible even through similarity;
furthermore, the aspect "that" (the past object) is not perceptible, as its object is not present.

If this [cognition] were of the nature of recollection, it would not grasp an object previously perceived, because of the absence of a clear manifestation. However, if it were of the nature of recollection by way of determining a perceived object, it would be erroneous,
because it determines the perceived object as non-different from its own [present] form.
The aspect "this" is held to be perceptual;
however, the identity between memory and perception is contradictory.

Therefore, with respect to an object standing before one that is devoid of being the object of a previous cognition, the mind grasps it through the mental cognition "this is that very same [object]," having superimposed the status of being the object of a previous cognition upon it by way of similarity.
Through the power of superimposition (āropa), the state of being an object of past cognition and direct perceptibility appear as having a single substratum,
just as in the recognition of water in a mirage;
however, in the absence of superimposition, these two appear as having distinct substrata.

Therefore, just as in the case of the recollection of water and the grasping of a mirage, it is established that because recognition is erroneous and not a form of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no sublation of the inference of momentariness by recognition.
Therefore, the cognitions of the letter *a* [produced] earlier and later have distinct objects;

likewise, the cognitions of the letter *ga* produced at fast, medium, and slow speeds have distinct objects, because they take as their objective support a *ga* that is differentiated by the distinctions of speed and so forth.
The cognition that "the letter *ga* itself is rapid" and "the letter *ga* itself is slow" is based solely on similarity;
therefore, it is said that [the universal] is not perceived as established even when there is a difference in speed and so forth.

One cow-individual is clearly distinct from another cow-individual; therefore, due to the oneness of the phoneme, a single cognition arises. The existence of cognitions of difference would be due to the difference in the manifestors.
Kumārila [replies]: That is refuted,
because it is precisely a particular sound (*dhvani*) that is called a phoneme (*varṇa*).
Therefore, specific sounds uttered rapidly are called rapid articulation (*drutā gavyakti*); those uttered at a medium speed are medium articulation (*madhyā gavyakti*);
and specific sounds uttered slowly are slow articulation (*vilambitā gavyakti*).
However, no *ga*-sound distinct from the manifesting sounds (*vyañjaka-dhvani*) appears;
rather, in those [sounds], one perceives only a commonality of name, namely "the *ga*-sound, the *ga*-sound. Likewise, among the short, long, and protracted [vowels], there is no single uniform form.

Since it is specific sounds (*dhvani-viśeṣa*) themselves, when employed for the duration of one *mātrā*, that becomes the short *u*; likewise, other specific sounds, when employed for the duration of two *mātrās*, become the long *ā*; and specific sounds, when employed for the duration of three *mātrās*, become the protracted (*pluta*).
Therefore, it is only the difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the short, long, and protracted vowels that appears;

the letter *a* does not appear as undifferentiated among them. Rather, it is the letter *a* itself, when uttered for a duration of one, two, or three morae (*mātrā*), that is perceived respectively as short, long, and protracted; thus, it is merely the sound (*śabda*) alone.
Therefore, as it is said:
"In the doctrine of eternality, the distinction between short vowels and so forth is contradicted;
for how can that which exists at all times be itself measured by a specific duration?"
Therefore, let its duration be understood as lasting for one *mātrā*, or two *mātrās*, or three *mātrās* according to its pronunciation; the word itself is not inherently possessed of a *mātrā*.
(Śloka-Sphoṭavāda 50, 51)
That too is refuted,
because the cognition and designation that follow [the notion] "the letter *a* and the letter *u*" do not apply to the short, long, and protracted [vowels].
Nevertheless, it might be argued as follows:
Because the two cognitions occurring at the earlier and later times share the same name, they have the same object;
therefore,
he says "pratīti" and so forth.
Even though there is a difference in the cognition and appearance of the two [sounds] "a" occurring in succession—
namely, a difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) by way of being prior and posterior, and a difference in speed such as fast, medium, or slow— nevertheless, [the object remains the same].
It is incorrect to claim that the cognition of the letter *a* and the cognition of the word "non-existence" (*akāra*) have the same object simply because their names are identical;
for what reason?
Because this would lead to the absurd consequence [of identity] even in the case of jars and other such things.
The cognition of a jar that occurs previously and the cognition of another jar that occurs later would both have the same object simply because they share the common name "cognition of a jar.
Consequently, it would follow that there is one single jar everywhere.
In that case, attempting to prove the oneness of jars and so forth contradicts what is observed, since jars and other such things are seen to be many.

If it is argued that, therefore, there is no proof for oneness in that case, then here too— in the proof of oneness among the phonemes— by what means of valid cognition is the absence of contradiction with observed facts established?
For here too, the difference [of the organs] is already established by their distinction according to each person.

The point is that, just as in the case of hair that has been shaved and grown back, there is an apprehension of identity due to similarity; he states "up to" (*yāvat*) and so forth to show that this reason— namely, "because of the identity of name"— is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Likewise, regarding "denotability": the denotability [of a term] through similarity of name—such as the cognition of the letter *e* following the cognition of the letter *a*—is not established by pervasion (*vyāpti*) through non-difference of meaning or identity of object; thus, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) remains doubtful, for there may be similarity of name even where there is difference.
Furthermore,

since sound possesses distinct natures with respect to each difference in its counter-correlates (pratikaraṇa) and each difference in its instruments (karaṇa) according to the difference in persons, when it is established as one while entering and ascending into hearing— that is, auditory consciousness— why are jars and other objects not also established as having a single form?
Let them too be established as such.
Alternatively, even a distinction must be stated;
for if it is argued that although the word is one, there is a difference in appearance due to a difference in the manifestors,
he says "In that case also," and so forth.
Even in that case, when a jar or similar object is broken, one might still object that the difference in appearance is due to a difference in the manifesting conditions;
furthermore:
Since sound is invariably perceived through the operation—characterized by vibration and so forth—of a complete set of causes, it follows that sound is an effect;
for what reason?
Because such [operation] is impossible in the case of a manifesting cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*).
He explains with the words "for not," etc., that because it is impossible to perceive the suggested meaning by necessity;
for when the sense organs are functioning, there is never a non-perception of the word, but rather its perception alone.
Furthermore, the operation of a manifestor does not necessarily cause an object to be perceived or grasped;
for what reason?
Because in some places devoid of jars and the like, even when illumination characterized by lamps and so forth exists, jars and the like are not perceived.
Therefore, for a person who possesses the auxiliary causes for the production of an unimpaired cognition,
this perception of sound would necessarily occur through its operation— that is, through the operation of its cause—
provided that the sound has arisen from the operation of the instrument [of its production].
Consequently, sound is indeed produced (*janya*) and not manifested (*vyaṅgya*).

Now, it was previously stated that a *kāraka* (productive cause) is defined merely by its capacity to generate [an effect], whereas a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is that which produces [an object] through its fitness for generating cognition;
therefore, it is logical that the palate and other such organs are merely manifestors.
This is not a fault,
because it was stated that [the cause] is a producer merely by producing the effect,
whereas it is a manifestor by virtue of its fitness for generating cognition.
But this is not so with respect to the effect that is visible;

for, in the case of a person whose auxiliary causes are complete, that which produces a lamp or the like is necessarily its perceiver, and thus it is a producer (*kāraka*) rather than a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), so there is no fault.
Furthermore, the word "instrument" (*karaṇa*) does not denote an agent (*kartṛ*).
Since it is impossible for that which is not an agent to be established through the operation of an instrument, and since it is impossible for sound to be so established,
sounds are all-pervading and eternal.
Therefore, because sounds are pervasive and eternal, they are perceived everywhere due to the operation of their manifesting instrument;
however, jars and the like are neither pervasive nor eternal.
If it is thus the case that they are not necessarily perceived due to that operation of the manifestor,
then what confidence or certainty can there now be regarding jars and other such objects?
If it is argued: "Just as they are neither eternal nor all-pervasive, let them likewise be eternal and all-pervasive;
why then are they not perceived at all times?"
If it is argued that this is the same regarding words as well,
and that the refutation applicable there will also apply to jars and so forth—
since those jars and so forth are not accepted as being all-pervasive and eternal— then [we reply]: [this objection is invalid].
Is sound desired to be all-pervading and eternal?
Why is it so desired? [It is not, for] it possesses the same properties as a jar and other such things.
Since pervasive eternity has been refuted, the argument that "prior [to manifestation]" and so forth regarding jars and the like is trivial;
for there is no fault, as other manifestors exist apart from the causal factors.
There is no fault of the consequence of [the word] being identical to the sound; demonstrating that it is indeed another manifestor, he says "For illumination," and so forth.
For in the world, light is established as the manifestor of these things such as jars, whereas potters and the like are not;
if potters and the like were manifestors, they would be exactly like that [light].

Just as lamps and the like do not invariably cause a jar to be perceived— since in some instances of illumination the jar may still be absent— in the same way, potters and other such agents might also be [invariably necessary].
Nor do potters and the like exceed this [principle],
because a jar and so forth exist at all times during the activity of the potter and others.
Therefore, because they function as distinct from the manifesting agent due to the excellence of that manifestation, potters and the like are indeed producers.
What is the reason?
Because there is no other mode of being for that which is beneficial; for apart from being either a producer (*kāraka*) or a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), there exists no other category.
In that regard, since its status as a manifestor has been refuted, it follows by elimination that the potter and others possess the nature of producers (*kāraka*).
However, no other manifestor of sound is established apart from the instrument (*karaṇa*), such that the instrument itself could be postulated as the producer of sound.
Therefore, because of its difference from objects like a jar, sound is indeed a manifested entity (*vyaṅgya*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "that," the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) states that this possibility of other manifesting agents is equal even in the case of sound; for in that case as well, [manifestation occurs] due to the word's being in a location suitable for the sense organ, that is, its abiding in a location suitable for the auditory faculty.
From the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [it follows] from attention (*manaskāra*) and from the excellence of the instruments (*karaṇa*).
If it is asked how there is indeed excellence, he says:
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "hi" (for/indeed) in the phrase "ghaṭādi" and so forth;

for one observes in the instruments that which is the property of the complete causal factors— such as the potter and others— of a jar and so forth, namely their necessity in initiating their own effects.
For those [causes] as well, being engaged in activity, invariably produce sound;
therefore, like a potter and others, they too are indeed *kārakas* (efficient causes).
Moreover, since there is no other manifestor (*vyañjaka*) for sound, if manifestors are intended [to be called] instruments (*karaṇas*), [then these causes must be the instruments].

In that case, since there would be no other manifestor— such as a lamp— for that very [object] being manifested, nor for any other object such as flavor (*rasa*) and so forth, then, due to the absence of another manifestor,
their causes— the causes of those lamps and so forth— would themselves become the manifestors of these lamps and the like.
Since this is so, the manifestation (*vyakti*) of sound does not arise from the instruments; rather, it is its very production that occurs.
Or, if manifestation were to occur from the instruments, it would be of three kinds:
(1) manifestation would consist in the sound abandoning its prior state and possessing an excellence (*atiśaya*).
Alternatively, manifestation (*vyakti*) is either the removal of the veil of perception (*upalambhāvaraṇavigama*), or consciousness having sound as its object (*śabdālambanaṃ vijñāna*);
for there is no other possible way [to define it] apart from these three modes.
In this regard, the manifestation of sound is not the production of an excellence, because that would entail its impermanence.
If it is asked, "Granted that there is the production of an excellence, how does that entail impermanence? [the author] replies:
because that production of excellence is characterized by the loss of its prior form and the arising of another, subsequent form.
2. He states the second position with the words "atha" and so forth:
the obstructions of that sound—which consist of the conjunctions of the particles of stagnant air—are of a nature that obstruct its perception; these are the forms of that sound which produce it.
If their disappearance— that is, their separation by means of air impelled by effort—
is what you consider to be the manifestation (*vyakti*) of sound, then according to your [Mīmāṃsaka] view, of what [nature] would that be?
As it has been said:
The air within the abdomen, struck by effort, undoubtedly moves;
it follows the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other [articulatory organs],
and because it possesses velocity, it necessarily persists for as long as that velocity lasts.
"Because of its movement, conjunctions and disjunctions certainly arise between it [the air] and the parts of the self through the still air. (Śloka-vārttika, Śabdanityatā, verses 122–24).
How is that manifestation produced?
Since the removal of obstructions is a non-existence, how could the collection of instruments—the aggregate of organs—possess any efficacy toward that non-existence, which is in no way an effect?
[The author] explains this with the words "for not," and so forth, meaning: "it certainly could not."
This is what he says:
when the nature of the obscuration is established, the instruments (karaṇa) are indeed incapable of acting;
for they possess no efficacy even regarding the removal of the obscuration.
Since it has been explained in the investigation of causal capacity that departure is non-existence, and yet non-existence is not an effect,
he says that this very thing does not exist, even having provisionally accepted this for the sake of argument.
"Nor indeed," and so forth:
because an eternal word cannot have any excellence added to it, there is no obscuration whatsoever by which the removal of an obscuration could constitute its manifestation.
What is the reason?
It has also been stated that because that obscuration lacks efficacy with respect to an eternal entity,
for this very reason there is no application of instruments toward the obscuration;
the meaning is that one should not propose that "the instruments effect the removal of the obscuration of sound."
Nor is it the case that the causes lack capacity with respect to sound;
for what reason?
Because when there is an absence of their activity—that is, an absence of the activity of the instruments—there is no perception of sound.
Therefore, it is logical that these operations of the instruments should produce sounds;
otherwise, if the instruments were not *kārakas* (productive agents) but merely *vyañjakas* (manifesters),

then, since there would be no distinction regarding the sound, it would follow as an absurd consequence (*prasajyate*) that other things such as jars and the like would also be manifested by potters and other such agents.
Furthermore, if it is maintained that even those things such as jars are indeed manifested by potters and the like,
then by accepting that position, all causes would be rendered purposeless; for instance:

Regarding the suggested object (*vyaṅgya*), the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) would have to be either a producer of an excellence (*atiśaya*), a producer of the absence of an obstruction (*āvaraṇābhāva*), or a producer of cognition (*jñāna*). However, since an excellence and so forth, as well as the very nature of manifestation (*vyakti-svarūpa*), are not effects, all [theories of] manifestors that produce these, as well as those that produce the essential nature itself, are rendered purposeless.
The explanation beginning with "yadi" [is as follows]:
if the instruments (karaṇāni) are manifestors (vyañjakāni), what are they like?
[The compound] "sarvakāraṇasamānadharmāṇi" is analyzed as: those instruments which possess all the common properties (samānā dharmāḥ) that belong to all causes (kāraṇānām).
In that case, not even a jar or similar object would now be the effect of anyone, such as a potter, because there is no distinction in the word [used];
for if it is claimed that everything is intended to be manifested [by the word],
this is not tenable.
What is the reason?
Because it would follow that all causal agents (kāraka), which are considered to be manifestors (vyañjaka), would be rendered purposeless;
for there are three possible alternatives regarding manifestors.

A manifestor (*vyañjaka*) might be so called because it produces an excellence (*atiśaya*), or because it effects the removal of an obscuration (*āvaraṇābhāva*), or because it brings about knowledge (*jñāna*) of the object to be manifested;
however, a manifestor does not first of all produce an excellence in the object to be manifested.
What is the reason?
Because an entity that possesses a fixed nature cannot have any excellence added to it,
nor can [knowledge] arise from the removal of an obscuration,
since the absence of an obscuration is not something produced as an effect.
Nor is it a manifester by virtue of being the instrument of cognition;
for what reason?

Because, according to the view of the proponents of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), the cognition whose object is that [manifested thing] is established as existing just like the thing itself.
Now, if cognition is produced as something previously non-existent,
then, if some factor is desired to be the causal agent (*kāraka*) with respect to that cognition,
it would follow by extension that other factors such as the potter— who possess the same characteristics as those [factors] acting upon the cognition— would also be so.
Otherwise, by the consequence that [the universal] would be a causal factor (*kāraka*) with respect to jars and the like, it would follow that every entity is an effect;
or else, some distinction must be stated whereby [the universal] is a causal factor with respect to cognition but not with respect to jars and the like,
for no other mode of manifestation than the individual (*vyakti*) is possible.
Therefore, this collection of factors intended as agents is not useful for the manifestation of any object such as a jar,
because manifestation has already been refuted on the grounds that a real entity cannot possess an added attribute;
nor is it useful for the action itself.
Because the status of being an agent (*kāryaka*) is not admitted, [the argument] would be entirely futile;
and if that were so, then in the event of the deficiency of causal factors (*kāraka*), this world would be devoid of impulse (*nirīha*) and devoid of activity (*nirvyāpāra*).
What is it that has come to be which is neither assisted nor assisting?
The analysis of the compound is: that in which there exists neither an object of assistance (upakārya) nor an agent of assistance (upakāraka).
Furthermore,
when the permanence of sound is to be proven,
the means of proof intended and accepted [by the opponent] is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), such as non-application (*aprayoga*) and so forth.
Just as sound is eternal because it is recognized as being one and the same,
so it has been said:
"Because of the absence of number."
For they say, "The word 'cow' has been uttered eight times," and not,
"There are eight 'cow' words"; by this it is understood that they recognize [the same word] because of its repeated use while existing.
Whatever is employed [as an instrument] exists prior [to its operation], just as an axe and so forth exist prior to the act of cutting;
and since a word is employed for the purpose of conveying a meaning, it too must exist prior to that employment.
By the word "etcetera," phrases such as "because it is uttered for the sake of another" are included;
as it has been said:
"But [the Veda] must be eternal, because its perception is for the sake of another."
Perception is utterance;
it is for the sake of another, in order to convey meaning,
since the word perishes as soon as it has been uttered.

Since one would not be able to convey the meaning from that [mere word], it should not be uttered for the sake of another; thus, "not being an example" means it is without an illustration (*adṛṣṭānta*),
for there is nothing eternal upon which this proof could operate.
For what reason?
Because all entities are subject to momentary destruction;
explaining this very point, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "for [things] subject to momentary destruction," it was stated previously that destruction is uncaused,
and this will be explained further below.
Having demonstrated impermanence by way of destruction, he says "arising," etc., demonstrating it also by way of arising:
entities possess arising from an external cause; therefore, they are not eternal either.
From where does it follow that things arise from another?
Because existence cannot be accidental;
for it has already been stated that if existence were accidental, there would be no restriction regarding place and so forth.
Therefore, recognition— characterized by such factors as the application of the existent—
is not found to follow in any instance with respect to a stable, unitary entity that serves as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).

Transformation is the arising [of something] through successive, distinct intrinsic natures, just as in the case of lamps and the like; for in those very cases, the mark of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and so forth is observed to be pervaded by difference. Thus, [the opponent's argument] is indeed contradictory.
Furthermore, the recognition here is not caused by a universal such as "lamp-ness" (*dīpatva*), because the existence of a universal has already been refuted.
"No," and so forth, says the opponent.
Recognition is not contradictory;
for what reason?
Because recognition—which has its origin in that which is non-different, stable, and of a single form—is observed even in the case of lamps and the like due to delusion.
If it is asked, "How is there delusion? [the answer is:
because of deception by similarity; that is, because one is deceived—meaning led astray—by the resemblance between the preceding and succeeding moments. This is what he states.
Non-erroneous recognition is adduced as a logical mark (*liṅga*), yet that does not exist at all in the case of lamps and the like;
thus the Master [Dignāga] says, "it has an undifferentiated birth.
On what basis, on what authority, is it said that recognition has an undifferentiated birth?
If it is argued that because a permanent entity lacks causal efficacy,
this same refutation should also be seen to apply to direct perception in the form of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), on the grounds that what is being recognized appears as non-different;
This is not so, because that very non-difference must be considered in all cases, even regarding diamonds, stones, and the like, in terms of their temporal sequence.

For instance, one must consider whether the nature [of a diamond] at the beginning is exactly the same as it is later, or whether it is indeed different, such that the impression of oneness arises merely due to similarity—as is the case with lamps and similar objects. This is what must be investigated.

If it is argued that just as non-difference is conceivable in the case of diamonds and the like, so too is difference conceivable, the Master [Dharmakīrti] replies: "In that very same way, it must also be investigated how this difference appears in a temporal sequence of before and after. Thus, even this point remains to be examined by him alone.

Since neither difference nor non-difference can be determined with absolute certainty, let there be uncertainty due to that very lack of determination; let there be a doubt regarding difference and non-difference in objects being recognized.
If it is argued that because they are recognized, there is a certainty of difference precisely because of that doubt, [the author] says:
Nor can the oneness of sound be established from a mark of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that is itself doubtful and whose object is subject to doubt.

If it is argued that "the oneness of an entity across preceding and succeeding times is established because no distinction is seen between the preceding moment and the subsequent moment, and because no distinction appears," the reply begins with "No" (*na*), and so forth.
Therefore, the meaning is this: for an entity, its manifestation at present is precisely a momentary manifestation, because it does not manifest as connected to prior or subsequent times;

and the manifestation of the moment itself is precisely its manifestation in its own nature, which is a manifestation as distinct from prior and other moments. Thus, it possesses a distinct manifestation, and not a manifestation [of identity] through invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with the manifesting prior and other moments.
Since that distinction alone is not apprehended, inference is employed for that purpose; thus he says:
"There is no non-perception of the lack of distinction in the case of diamonds and the like."
What is the reason?

Because the existence or non-existence of the vajra and so forth is established through the prior and posterior state—that is, by way of the preceding and succeeding nature—of the cognitions of the vajra and so forth;
for it is thus:

The subsequent cognition having the diamond and so forth as its object establishes that the specific cause of the diamond and so forth was previously non-existent and later existent; thus, through the temporal sequence of cognitions, the existence and non-existence of the diamond and so forth are established,
because of the presence of distinction and the presence of difference.
Clarifying this very point,

he says "yadi" and so forth: if other cognitions arising at a later time were to have their causes present at the time of the preceding cognition, they would indeed be produced just like that preceding cognition.
But since this is not the case, those cognitions, being unarisen, indicate beforehand a deficiency in their own causes.
Otherwise, if their cause existed even previously,
it would have to be either capable or incapable; if it were capable, it would have produced them even previously.
What is the reason?
Because [the cause] produces [the effect] when it is capable,
or when it is incapable?
Nor could it produce [the effect] later; for why would that which is incapable— being incapable of having any excellence added to it— ever acquire capacity from anything else?
If, on the other hand, it were to acquire capacity from some source, then upon that acquisition of capacity, because stability would be impossible,
its prior nature of incapacity would be lost and another, which is capable, would arise.
Therefore, since successive cognitions establish the succession of their own objects, the distinctness of all things is proven; consequently, the impermanence [of all things] is established.

As for the cognition "this is that very same thing," it is caused by the perception of similarity. Since this is so, even this second reason which is stated—namely, that "this is a connection with an existing object"—is likewise [refuted].
By that [word], too, only the production of the sound is expressed;
for what reason? Because of the capacity of the sound [to arise] from the speaker.
The meaning is that a word acquires its capacity for performing the intended action;

otherwise, if tools such as an axe or a word were already capable of their respective effects prior to the agent's operation, then, since the agent would be of no use given their inherent capacity, these tools and words would function by themselves independently of persons,
yet this does not occur.

Therefore, even the term "application" (*prayoga*) refers to the accomplishment or proof of a desired or intended object, such as cutting; specifically, it is said to be the production of an axe or similar tool that possesses a nature capable of that task.
What kind of production is it?

It depends on a homogeneous and similar material cause (*upādāna*) that exists as a preceding moment; thus, it is "dependent on a homogeneous material cause," like the application of an axe and so forth, because axes and such tools employed for cutting depend upon their own preceding moments of a similar nature.
Alternatively, it may be independent of a material cause.
And it is like the employment [of the term] "action" (*karman*) and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of sounds such as those of the lute (*vīṇā*) is intended.
For when actions and the like are first employed, there is no dependence upon a preceding similar moment.
Furthermore, there is one who thinks:

"Let it be that recognition is not inference because of its fallibility; rather, that recognition which occurs with respect to an object situated directly before one's eyes is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) consisting of perception.
Therefore, the stability of entities is established from that very means of valid cognition, namely perception."

We shall refute that as well later on. By this same method, the fallacious reason (kuhetu) adduced to prove stability is to be understood; for there exists no such probans for establishing stability that follows after an object which is of the same class and possesses a stable, unitary nature.
Why?
Because all phenomena abide in this state,
having the nature of the cessation and arising of successive intrinsic natures.
And since all recognition of stability is contradicted by reasoning and contradicted by inference, how can it be as described?
Just as the proof of momentariness has been stated and will be stated in this treatise,
so too, due to the reason of contradiction with logic (*yuktivirodha*), other reasons for proving stability (*sthairya*) imagined by others are likewise subject to verbal faults (*vācyadoṣa*).
Thus, having begun with the premise that "the sequence of manifestation (*vyaktikrama*) is not the sentence," manifestation was conceived as being of three kinds.
The production of excellence in sound,
the removal of its obscuration,
and knowledge.
In this regard, since sound is eternal, there can be no production of an excellence (*atiśaya*) within it;

and since the absence of an obstruction is not something produced, the removal of an obstruction cannot be its manifestation. Thus, when these two alternatives have been rejected, it remains that cognition (*jñāna*) is the manifestation.
And at that time, the sequence of individuals would constitute the sentence,
or the succession of cognitions would become the sentence;
and this is not tenable.
Alternatively, because a sentence does not have cognition as its intrinsic nature,
even so it is stated [for the sake of argument]:
if the non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva) of a sentence consisting of a sequence of manifestations were to be proven, then the non-human origin of cognition itself would be what must be proven.
In that context, regarding the thesis to be proven— that cognition does not have the person as its locus, meaning it does not depend upon the person—
there is a sublation of the proposition by means of what is accepted, perceived, and inferred, all occurring simultaneously with what has been accepted and admitted.
Since the sequence of that [Veda]— whether perceived directly or inferred— is the sequence of cognitions,
and that sequence is not something distinct from the cognitions themselves, its status as non-human (apauruṣeya) is established by proving the non-human origin of that very sequence.
In that case, it would be established that the Buddha alone is not of human origin;
and therein, the convention—that is, the tenet—of this Mīmāṃsaka is contradicted.
What is the reason?

Since [the opponent] accepts in their own established doctrine that cognitions are qualities of the person (*puruṣaguṇatva*), [the author], demonstrating the contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣabādha*), says:
"Indeed, this is directly perceived: if those cognitions arise from mental attention (*manaskāra*) and so forth..."

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are also included. From what kind of mental attentions (*manaskāra*) and so forth? From those for which a convention has been established for the sake of linguistic brevity, such as [the designation] "person.
This has been stated according to his own view.

Or, having bypassed the phrase "from the qualities of the person" (*puruṣaguṇebhyaḥ*), [the opponent] says "from the qualities of the person"; this, however, is stated according to the view of another.

Therefore, since the fact that cognition (*buddhi*) arising from mental attention (*manaskāra*) and other factors is an effect is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*) when its lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) is being proved.
If it should be thought that,
because the state of being an effect is not perceived, there is no sublation by perception, he says "nanu" and so forth.

The very existence of that which is considered the cause when [the effect] exists, and its non-existence when that [cause] is absent—these two specific instances of existence and non-existence constitute the causality of the entity;
there is no other causality than these.
That aforementioned existence is established by direct perception.
If it is asked, "In the absence of that [object], how can its non-existence be established by perception? he says:

"Non-existence also has non-apprehension as its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)," which is a compound analysis meaning "that non-existence whose very nature (*svabhāva*) is non-apprehension. We shall explain later that this too is established through the power of perception.

Perception, by establishing the very existence of an entity as distinct from others, leads to the cognition of non-existence through its own force; thus, the term "force" (*sāmarthya*) has been employed.

Furthermore, since the presence and absence of cognition follow from the presence and absence of mental attention (*manaskāra*) and other factors, the fact that cognitions are produced by human effort is to be inferred precisely from that fact of their occurring when those factors are present.
What is the reason?
Because this status as an effect has positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as its logical mark (*liṅga*);
by this, the sublation by inference (*anumāna-bādha*) has been stated.

Now, it might be argued that the sequence of individual manifestations (*vyakti*) is not the sentence, but rather the sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*) is the sentence; to this, he says "Furthermore," and so forth.
The distinction of the *sphoṭa* from the phonemes (*varṇa*) in their sequential order has already been refuted by the previous investigation into the *sphoṭa*;
for apart from difference and non-difference, there is no other possible mode of existence for a real entity.

And in that case, the sequential order of all-pervading phonemes would be something superimposed by conceptual construction; or else, how could it be that what is not based on a person at that time becomes based on a person?

He explains [the verse] beginning with "varṇebhyaḥ" and so forth: the *ānupūrvī* (sequential order), which is distinct (*vyatirekiṇī*)— that is, of a different nature— from the phonemes (*varṇebhyaḥ*),
has already been refuted by the very sequence of the investigation into the *sphoṭa* mentioned previously.
By the refutation beginning with "A sentence is not distinct from its phonemes, because it is not perceived [separately]," even the sequential order is rejected;
nor is that [order] of the same nature as the phonemes.
Because it would follow that there is no distinction between the cognition of "lake" and "water," nor can it be inexpressible in terms of identity or difference,
since the nature of a real entity cannot transcend these two alternatives.

Because it does not transcend the conceptual alternatives of identity or difference, this is an error of the cognition that manifests as a superimposition of that form—namely, a superimposition of sequence—upon phonemes which lack that form and are devoid of any real, distinct sequence.
How could that sequence be non-human (apauruṣeyī)? It is indeed human (pauruṣeyī).
For what reason?
Because it has been demonstrated by the presence of this activity through the expansion of the intellect.
Furthermore, since there is no such thing as an absolutely eternal intrinsic nature, that sound (*dhvani*) which exists for you must necessarily be non-absolute and unstable;
moreover, that sound would have to be without a cause.
Or else, if it has another cause— that is, a cause other than the person— it would be "caused by another.
In that case, if it were causeless, it would be eternal,
because it would not depend on anything else.
If it were caused by something else, it would not arise from human activity;
yet it does arise from human activity,
therefore it is understood to be of human origin.
"How so? and so forth;
the opponent asks, "How is it understood that sound or something else, such as the absence of earth and so on, is not ultimate? To this, the Master [Dharmakīrti] replies, "Because of existence."
Because destruction is invariably concomitant with mere existence, sound is impermanent by virtue of its very existence as something that exists;
it undergoes destruction and does not depend on any other cause.
The meaning of the whole [statement] is that sound is existent; therefore, it is not eternal.
Why? He says: because destruction is necessarily concomitant with mere existence.
"Not indeed," and so forth;
because there is no separate entity called "destruction" that arises for things from any cause of destruction,
it is for this very reason [that the argument holds].
Therefore, destruction must be the very nature of the entity;
why is this so?
Because the entity itself arises from its own causes as possessing that property—that is, as possessing the property of destruction.
Destruction is simply the property of existing for only a single moment,
and since that arises from causes alone, it follows that destruction belongs only to those things that are produced, and not to other things that exist.
As it has been said:
"That which exists and is without cause is eternal," and so forth.
Furthermore, destruction is not the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of any particular entity;
for what reason? Because that [destruction] will be refuted later on.
Therefore, destruction would have existence as its sole intrinsic nature;
it would have mere being as its sole intrinsic nature.
For that reason, sound or any other entity whatsoever is a vessel for existence, a substratum of existence—that is to say, it is "existent."
It is established that it is not ultimate;
why does the opponent say it is not established?
Since that very destruction has no subsequent birth,
there is no "other birth" (parajanma) from another; thus, it is not a "non-other birth" (apara-janma).
Because that is unestablished;
that is to say, because it is not established that destruction is causeless.
For instance, wood is burned by fire.
In the case of "the jar is broken by a stick," causes of destruction such as fire and so forth are observed for entities like wood;

for indeed, when fire and the like are present, there is the destruction of the wood and the like, whereas in their absence there is no destruction. Thus, the destruction follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). And they say that this is the defining characteristic of the cause and the effect, or of that which possesses the cause.
As it has been said:
"Without the presence of causes such as a blow, contact with fire, or destruction, destruction does not enter into a state of conjunction with jars and other objects."
"No footnote on this page!"—

with these words and others, he refutes [the opponent's view]: "In the world, fire and other such things are not perceived to be causes of destruction for wood and the like without the presence of an instrument."

However, when each preceding moment of wood and so forth ceases by its own inherent nature—that is, ceases spontaneously—another subsequent moment, in the form of ashes or the like, arises; thus, fire and other factors are recognized as the causes for the destruction of the wood and so forth, not because they perform an act of destruction.
To the question, "How then does that modified state arise? he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "viśiṣṭa" (distinguished): even if we were to admit that a distinguished cognition, such as that of fire and so forth, is the auxiliary cause, we shall speak on the basis of that assumption.
Or let fire be the cause of the destruction of the wood; that destruction is "born from fire," according to the analysis of the compound: "that whose birth is from fire."

Is it the wood itself, or rather something distinct from the wood that is the destroyer of the fire? If the destruction were produced as a distinct entity from the cause [the wood], what would be the reason for the continued perception of the wood?

Because the wood does not perish, what [is gained] by the production of destruction as something distinct from the wood? When there is the arising of destruction as something other than the wood, the wood would be called "non-existent" or "destroyed";
however, it is not at all non-existent. This is the meaning.
If it is argued that even though [the object] has not perished, its perception occurs through the arising of a different entity, he says:
"Or it is not seen.
Why is it not seen?
If it is indeed perceived that one thing perishes through the arising of another thing, yet it is not perceived,
then there would be an over-extension of the principle (*atiprasaṅga*).
If, by the arising of some other entity whatsoever, everything were to become non-existent or would no longer be perceived,
then that very object must have fire as its cause of birth.
It means that not every destruction of this wood is perceived in the world as having the nature of destruction;
he explains this very statement of summary (*grahaṇaka-vākya*) with the words beginning "if," and so forth.
If that very fire-born non-existence were the destruction of the wood, then—
on that account— it would follow that this wood is not seen because it has ceased to be, because it has been destroyed; [the opponent] objects to this with the words "let it be so," and so forth.
Let it be that this object born from fire has the designation or name "non-existence" (*abhāva*);
nevertheless, how can there be mutual destruction by means of a mere name?
For it is not reasonable that simply by giving the name "destruction" to some object born from fire, the wood should cease to be perceived.

Now, one might object: "Since this is well-known in the world as destruction itself, it is merely a matter of giving that [entity] the name 'destruction,' rather than [the entity] being destroyed. To this he says:
"Nor is one entity the destruction of another, because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga); for then all entities would be the destruction of a piece of wood."
This recalls exactly what was stated immediately prior;
he thinks as follows:

just as there is no cognition of wood in the form of its destruction because [destruction] is a distinct entity from all other things, so too, since that which is produced by fire is a distinct entity, there would be no cognition of it in the form of the destruction of the wood.
It might be argued that if, because it is a different entity, the effect produced by fire does not have the nature of destruction,
then smoke likewise would not be an effect of fire, since it too is a different entity, like a jar.
And since there is no difference in its being a distinct entity from that [fire], one might think that the destruction of the wood will take the form of something produced by fire;
therefore, he says:
"because there is no distinction."

The point is this: since that which is produced by fire and consists of a real entity—such as wood—is not distinct from other things like jars and so forth, how could it possess the nature of destruction? For destruction is, by definition, a state of cessation.
However, in the case of smoke, even though it is a separate entity, its being an effect of fire is entirely logical.
This argument— that because there is no contradiction between another entity and being the effect of fire— is trivial.
If you claim that the destruction produced by fire in wood is not its inherent nature (svabhāva) and thus does not apply to all things such as jars, thereby avoiding over-extension (atiprasaṅga),
then what is the relationship between this destruction produced by fire in the wood and the wood itself?
Because there is no mutual assistance between them, no relationship exists at all;
[it is like saying] "the wood is the support" and "this has a support," where the supported [entity] perishes without [the support].
If it is argued that there is, therefore, a relationship of substratum and dependent,
this is not so,
because that relationship of substratum and dependent is yet to be refuted.
If destruction is something produced and wood is its producer,
then there would be a relationship of produced-to-producer between destruction and the wood.
Regarding the phrase "from that fire": is it being asked whether destruction occurs from the presence of fire,
and what is the reason for this?
If it is argued that there is no fault because the destruction arises from the wood itself— that is, because destruction arises from the wood in dependence upon fire,
and thus the previously stated objection that "destruction could not be produced by fire" does not apply— then [we reply]:
If the wood gains no excellence from the fire, what expectation could it have regarding the fire?
There would be none at all.
Alternatively, if the wood were to gain an excellence from the fire, there would arise a second thing, namely that which is designated as "excellence."
And likewise, the analysis of the compound is: "the eastern quarter is the cause of non-falling for this [object], and there is no cause for its falling";
thus it is seen just as before.

It might be argued that since the birth of a second piece of wood occurs from fire possessing a specific excellence, for that very reason the destruction of the previous piece of wood occurs from that same fire.
What is the connection between this wood and the destruction produced by fire? That very same difficulty was just stated: "What is the connection with the wood?
Even if one were to resort to a relationship such as that of substratum and superstratum (āśrayāśrayibhāva), [the problem remains].
In that case, because [the wood] would be subject to negation, all of this [argument] would recur, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Therefore, fire, while assisting the subsequent excellence of the wood—which is necessarily fit for connection with destruction—produces an entirely new wood; otherwise, the previous wood would be seen remaining in its former state. This is the conclusion.
Furthermore:
The "destruction of wood" is said to be the absence of wood;
and an absence is not an effect, because if it were accepted as an effect through a positive injunction, it would follow that it is an existent entity (*bhāva*).
Therefore, the statement "it produces non-existence" means that it does not produce existence; it is merely a negation of action.

Consequently, that which performs this [act]—being a producer of non-existence—is indeed a non-producer, since it consists solely in the negation of action. Thus, it has been stated in the section on the consideration of the locus and the located regarding the universal and its instances (*sāmānyatadvat*), that fire and so forth do not depend upon the destruction of the wood.
Furthermore,
if the non-existence— that is, the destruction— of the intrinsic nature of wood and so forth is admitted to be distinct from that intrinsic nature of wood and so forth,
then the entity such as the wood would cease to exist due to that non-existence being a separate thing (arthāntara) from it.
Therefore, for wood and the like, which are turning away from that non-existence, their very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) would be established;

and for that which is turning away from non-existence, existence itself would be established. Given this, how could wood and the like be "non-existent" through a destruction produced by fire and so forth?
For this reason, there is no mutual destruction.
The meaning is that one entity does not cause the destruction of another entity; even granting this for the sake of argument, we say:
let there be another destruction produced by fire, yet why is the wood not seen to remain in its very same state within that other entity?
Establishing this very point, he says:
"What is this contradiction?
It is the existence of a distinct entity (arthāntara) consisting of the destruction produced by fire."
Furthermore, the perception of the wood occurs at those two [times],
and thus the wood would be seen remaining in that same state; for that which is a distinct entity produced by fire is what constitutes the destruction of the wood.
Because it is perceived as having the nature of destruction,
and since destruction is non-existence, that which is the non-existence of the wood is produced precisely as a form opposed to the wood.
Nor is this [destruction] impossible to produce because it is a distinct entity (arthāntara) like a jar, by virtue of having a contradictory nature;
for smoke does not fail to be an effect of fire simply because it is a distinct entity like a jar.
Therefore, just as smoke, though being a distinct entity, is produced by fire, so too is destruction, which has a contradictory nature, produced.

Śaṅkara objects: "How can it be said that when there is a contradiction between two things by way of mutual exclusion—wherein the non-perception of one occurs precisely when the other exists—there could be the perception of wood when its contradictory, namely the destruction designated as something distinct from fire, is present?
This is incorrect.
Since there is no contradiction between another object (arthāntara) and being an effect of fire,
the fact of being an effect of fire remains entirely uncontradicted even if smoke were another object;
for that other object produced by fire possesses the nature of becoming and is thus of a positive (bhāva) character.
And how can that which is an entity be, for you, a non-entity?
Since destruction is held to be a non-entity,
destruction is therefore contradictory to existence as a distinct entity.
Nor does it follow that even a distinct entity [such as destruction] possesses the nature of the destruction of wood and so forth simply because it appears as such;
for the cause of the appearance of destruction is indeed the spontaneous cessation [of the entity itself].

But if one does not accept that destruction occurs through its own inherent nature (*svarasa-nirodha*), how can it be said— as was stated at the very beginning— that even a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) appears in the form of destruction because it is of the nature of an existent?
How then can it be asserted that the wood is no longer perceived because of the presence of a contrary entity called "destruction," which is produced [by causes]?
If destruction were formless (nīrūpa), there would be no contradiction between it and the entity [it destroys];
however, even in that case, because it is formless, it could not be a distinct entity (arthāntara) nor could it be produced by a cause.
Therefore, if fire were to produce something other than the wood, the wood would be seen remaining in its original state.

If it is argued that the wood is not seen because it is encompassed— that is, appropriated— by that other entity produced by fire, then it follows that this other entity is an obstruction of the wood;
and that is not tenable.
Since an obstruction of the wood by that other entity is not possible,
he explains this with the words "if" and so forth,
[meaning] by that other entity produced by fire.
Therefore, it is not logical that this "tat" refers to a distinct entity produced by fire, nor is it appropriate for this to be imagined as a covering;
for indeed, the covering—
If the perception of objects were obstructed by being covered,
it would not obstruct the capacities of substances such as striking;
for we observe striking and other effects in jars and similar objects even when they are enveloped in darkness.
In that regard, "obstruction" (*abhighāta*) is the hindrance to the arising of another in its own location;
by the word "etc. (*ādi*), odors, tastes, and so forth are included.
Now, as for "covering" (*āvaraṇa*): it would bind all the capacities of the wood.
Furthermore, if it were admitted that all obstacles [to combustion] are present,
then the wood would not be destroyed by this very [obscuring] covering, nor by fire;
what is the reason?
Because that very [fire] would cause the loss of all the capacities of this wood,
such being the case, there would follow the same undesirable consequence as when fire is the cause of destruction: namely,
that the fault already stated in detail regarding fire in relation to the destruction of wood would apply even when the destruction of the wood is brought about by another entity produced by fire.
And likewise, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*);

for by that other entity, namely the destruction produced by fire, yet another distinct entity called "destruction" must be produced, and by that [second] one yet another, and so on, resulting in an infinite regress.
Now, if [it is argued] that this fault must not occur, then the capacities of the wood for being struck and so forth would remain entirely unimpaired.
Even then, since the wood’s capacity to be struck and so forth remains unimpaired,
what has been destroyed by that fire produced by another such that the wood would be thus obscured and no longer visible? And if [it were so], etc.
The analysis of the compound is "that whose origin is from fire" (agnisamudbhava);
the meaning is "because of being grasped by the object called destruction, which originates from fire.
In that case, destruction itself would be destructible.
What is the reason?
Because it possesses origination, destruction would also be destructible—just like wood; such is the meaning.
He explains this with the words "then, from the destruction of the destruction, there would necessarily be the seeing of the wood again," and so forth;
[he means that] since it possesses the quality of arising, the destruction of the wood must necessarily itself be destroyed.
If that destruction of the wood were to perish, then there would again be the emergence— that is, the reappearance— of the wood and so forth; thus,
with the words "the killer [would be] the slain," and so on, the opponent raises a further objection.
If it is argued: "Just as when there is the killing of the killer of Caitra—whoever he may be—the killed Caitra does not come back into existence, yet this is not a case of his non-arising;
likewise, even when wood is destroyed, the wood does not come back into existence."
He refutes this with the words beginning "hanta" (alas), [stating]:
"This solution is not tenable;
for what reason?"
Because the killer is not subject to death;
for the killer of Caitra does not have the nature of death, but rather—
Therefore, it is logical that upon the destruction of the killer, Caitra does not come into being again; however,
if death has not ceased, his rebirth must necessarily occur.
He explains by means of the passage beginning with "vināśa" [destruction]: even if destruction itself were destroyed, there would be no restoration of the entity, nor a return to its former state;
for when a killer has been killed, one who was killed by that killer does not come back to life on account of that killer having been slain.
This rebuttal is not tenable;
why?
Because the person who kills is the cause of that killing.
Because that death of Caitra has him as its cause, he is not the killer; for death is not of the nature of an agent.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"No," and so forth:

we do not say that when the causes of destruction, such as fire or a staff, have ceased to function, the entity that has already perished must come into being again; if one were to assert this, then this [objection] would indeed be a valid rebuttal.
Rather,
what kind of non-existence of an entity, such as wood and so forth, is produced by fire and the like?
The characteristic of absolute non-apprehension is as follows:
here, action residing in an object is apprehended;
by the negation of that [action], absolute non-apprehension is said to be the absence of all causal capacity.
When there is the cessation of such a non-existence,
what other course remains for an entity than its abiding in its own nature?
That is to say, its course is nothing other than abiding in its own nature.
But when the killer has perished, it is not logical for [the victim] to come into being again; for the killer of Caitra is not identical to his destruction, but rather—
The analogy of the staff and so forth means that it is similar to a staff and the like because it is a cause of destruction; for Caitra’s death is indeed comparable to his destruction,
and upon the cessation of that death— which is equivalent to his destruction— there would necessarily be the renewed existence of this Caitra.
Thus far, the fault has been stated regarding the case where destruction is a distinct entity; now, concerning the case where it is not a distinct entity, he says:
"Even in the case of non-difference," and so forth.
Even if destruction were non-different from the entity itself, destruction would simply be the wood;
and since that wood has already arisen from its own causes,
nothing further needs to be done to it by fire and so forth— thus, destruction, being of that very nature, is causeless.
Since there is no other possibility for the destruction of a real entity apart from the conceptual alternatives of being identical to or different from it,

he explains this with the words "not a different thing" (*anarthāntara*) and so forth: when destruction is not a different thing from the wood, then that very wood itself becomes the entity designated as its destruction.
And since that wood and so forth already exist prior to the proximity of fire and so forth,
one should consider what efficacy fire and the like possess with respect to the wood and such things that are to be destroyed.
In some places, the reading is "of the staff and so forth," but that should be explained as referring to [the causes of destruction] with respect to jars and the like.

Therefore, because they merely imitate those [jars], the causes of destruction do not provide any assistance to the wood and so forth; thus, by that wood and so forth, the causes of destruction are not required in any way whatsoever or in any form.
Nor can this fire and so forth be said to possess a relationship with the wood and so forth such that it is their cause of destruction;
for what reason?
Because such a relationship is based upon a prior benefit (upakāra).
Otherwise, if one were to postulate a relationship in the absence of any benefit, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),
whereby everything would become related to everything else.
This might be argued:
Fire and so forth do not assist wood and so forth directly, but rather by producing assistance through that which is related to them;
therefore,
he says "indirectly," and so on.
Fire and other factors perform a service for wood and other objects by becoming their related entities, not directly;
thus, even when such a mediated service is postulated, this dilemma necessarily follows:
is that mediated service a distinct entity (arthāntara), or is it that very same wood and so forth?
In that case, even if the assistance is a distinct entity from the wood and so forth, one must inquire as to what the connection is such that "this is the assistance of that wood";
for in that regard, the fact that the assistance produced by fire acts as an assistance toward that wood must be accounted for.

Because there would be no relation without that [intermediary], the phrase "and so forth" includes the fault of infinite regress (anavasthā) due to the necessity of postulating further assistance in those cases as well;

likewise, even if the assistance were non-different [from the entity], the same objection would apply—namely, that which was stated starting with "destruction would be the wood itself. Therefore, because an existing form cannot transcend being either identical to or different from [the cause].

It might be argued that since an existing entity cannot transcend being either identical to or different from itself, the production of an assistance effected by a cause of destruction must be non-existent;
therefore, he says:
"Upakāra," and so forth,
because it has the characteristic of producing form, that is,
the characteristic of producing the nature of existence.
Furthermore, that object must either be produced by that destroyer or something else;
and since the aforementioned fault applies to both cases,
a cause of destruction that is devoid of performing either that [action] or its opposite cannot be a producer at all, and thus it is not the cause of anything.
Furthermore, a cause such as a staff or the like is not required by a perishable entity such as a jar;
therefore, this entity possesses its respective nature—namely, a perishable nature—by virtue of its own mere existence.
Having thus apprehended destruction as the non-existence following cessation (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), he anticipates the objection of another.

Regarding the phrase "even if there were no cause," and so forth: if [destruction] were causeless, it would have to be eternal; and because of its eternality, destruction would occur even at the time of the entity's existence. If you argue that this leads to the undesirable consequence of the coexistence of the entity and its destruction, this is not a fault.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "How could there be eternality for a destruction that is non-existent and characterized by annihilation? and so forth, asking what the reason for this might be.

Even though for the proponent of momentariness destruction is causeless, it must necessarily be eternal; therefore, existence— characterized by the absence of that [destruction] and consisting in the non-cessation of destruction—
and destruction— characterized by the absence of that [existence] and consisting in the cessation of existence—
would coexist in a single entity.
This is not so;
why?
Because that non-existence, being a non-entity, cannot be associated with properties such as permanence and so forth.
For indeed, the conceptual distinction between the eternal and the non-eternal is not possible when [the object] is absent,
because those two [categories] are properties of real entities (*vastu*),
and because destruction— characterized as the cessation of existence— is a mere nothingness.
Furthermore, since that which is arising for you exists eternally, it would have coexistence with something [else],
and yet there is no destruction.

Since an entity whose nature is to exist for only a single moment does not exist by itself, this [statement] is merely a negation of activity; therefore, the fault just mentioned does not apply. Thus, he again anticipates the opponent's intention.
If destruction were non-existent, then since destruction would be non-existent, it would follow that existence is indestructible;
thus, the consequence that "existence would not be destructible" is also untenable,
because we do not maintain that the destruction of an entity is brought about by a separate entity called destruction.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "How? [The question is: How could a non-existent destruction destroy an entity? Because it is impossible for that which is non-existent to possess causal activity.
For this reason, the entity would be indestructible; thus, the undesirable consequence (aprasaṅga) does not arise at all.
What is the reason?
Because the destruction of an entity is not admitted to be something distinct from its destruction;
he supports this very point with the words "For whoever," and so forth.
For how could a proponent who asserts that "destruction" is nothing at all desire the destruction of an entity by means of that destruction which lacks intrinsic nature, or not desire it?
"How so? and so forth—the opponent asks: if destruction (*vināśa*) does not exist—that is, if it is non-existent—how can there be the state of having perished?
[One] would simply not have perished at all.
For it is thus: in the present state, there are non-existent destructions; the analysis of the compound is "those whose destructions are non-existent.
