Indeed, they are not reckoned as having perished.
And when there is no destruction of an entity, how can it be designated as "possessing destruction"?
For an object that does not possess a certain nature— that is, one that lacks a connection with it— is not designated by that unrelated property in such a manner.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "tadvān" (possessing that), "is designated by a word," or "is cognized by a cognition," and so forth.
Indeed, it is not that the destruction of an entity does not exist; rather, destruction certainly exists. How then is it said that it does not exist?
It is because that destruction which belongs to the entity does not [itself] come into being.
If destruction does not exist, how then is it said that "destruction exists"? To this he replies:
"But existence itself has the property of lasting for only a moment."
If destruction lasts for only a single moment and is indeed the very same as the entity itself, how then does the world designate it as "the destruction of the entity"? To this, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "tamasītyādi":

one perceives this entity’s nature of abiding for a single moment— characterized by the deception of the arising of a similar [moment]— through its non-perception at a later time when the continuum has been interrupted, which leads to the realization of its non-abiding.

As was stated previously, people engaged in worldly transaction (*vyavahārin*), while discerning and determining that "the destruction of this entity has occurred," designate it according to their cognition;
for indeed, no other form whatsoever called "destruction" ever arises in an entity once it has been established.
That very entity, having arisen from its own causes as such, exists for only a single moment;
therefore, it is not the case that some entity called "destruction" destroys that entity.
Rather, it is the very nature of this entity that it has the character of persisting for only a single moment,
by virtue of which that entity is said to have "perished."
Otherwise, since it would not possess that nature by itself, it could not perish even in the absence of another cause; if destruction is nothing at all,
then why do you now say that destruction occurs without a cause?

For how could one refute— by means of the argument beginning with "how could that which is perishing be permanent," etc.— the claim that "the destruction of an entity [occurs] through the thought of whether it is causeless or caused," when for that [entity] there is no intrinsic nature at all? Thus he provides the counter-argument (*vyatireka*).
Since an entity perishing independently does not depend on another cause of destruction,
it is not for the sake of making known— that is, not for the sake of making known its independence from another.

That state of destruction has been described by us as being causeless; having superimposed a distinction— that is, a difference— between that state of destruction and its existence as conceived by the mind through conceptual cognition,
this was stated.
The meaning is that the destruction of an entity occurs without a cause, and thus its destruction does not possess a cause;
he explains this with the words "no," and so forth:
an entity, once arisen, does not obtain destruction from another cause of destruction.
For what reason?
Because that which has become thus—namely, that which possesses the very nature of perishing—is produced from its own cause of existence, i.e., from birth itself;
therefore, it does not depend on any other imagined cause of destruction, and is thus "independent of another" (*aparāpekṣa*).
And that phenomenon called destruction, being of such a nature, is a property independent of anything else; the purpose of [the statement] "for the sake of its negation" is,
in other words, for the sake of negating destruction that possesses a cause.

The phrase "by making known its intrinsic nature" is connected with the statement "its very intrinsic nature is so described," meaning by making known that the entity has a perishable intrinsic nature; thus,
it is said that "its destruction occurs without a cause."
If there is a desire to know that alone—
namely, whether the destruction of an entity arises from something other than itself or not— then in what manner is this mere point of inquiry explained?

Having mentally distinguished—through the intellect—as if it were a separate entity from the substratum (dharmin) a property called "destruction," and having made the division that "this is the destruction of this entity," [the author] connects [the following]: although this very destructibility has been established in reality as non-distinct from non-existence in the manner described, those of dull intellect, by superimposing destruction as a quality or property, cause themselves to be bewildered.
To the question, "Why, then, do they thus bewilder themselves? he says:
"In some cases," and so forth;
for in expressions such as "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), where a case ending denoting separation (*vyatireka-vibhakti*) is employed, one observes such [usage],
because a distinction between the two related entities is perceived.

Here too, those who are deceived by the mere proclamation that "the destruction of an entity occurs" superimpose upon the entity a destruction that is a distinct quality or attribute; and having superimposed existence— that is, being— upon that imagined quality, [they proceed].

Having superimposed that quality called "destruction"— whether it be with cause or without cause— through various philosophical views, by means of a conceptualization of existence, that is, a conceptualization of a real entity characterized by a lack of established reality;
He anticipates the opponent's intention with the words "even from their own side," etc., [referring to those] who, by means of that reflection in which reality is non-abiding, agitate themselves.
Even for one who maintains that destruction occurs spontaneously and without cause, if the existence of that very non-existence— namely, destruction— is admitted,
there arises this conceptual dichotomy in the mind characterized by "is it identical" or "is it different."
He explains with the words "nanu" and so forth:
the meaning is that even in the absence of a cause, there is neither posteriority nor anteriority for the destruction of an entity—
that is, for the destruction of a real thing— which occurs by its own nature alone.
The conceptualization of identity or difference is the same:
is destruction a distinct entity from the thing, or is it the thing itself?
In that regard, if it were a distinct entity, then why is the thing not perceived when the destruction—that distinct entity—exists (i.e., possesses being)?

Now, if destruction is not a different entity [from the object], then even though it is not a different entity, that very same thing—the jar or whatever it may be—becomes what is called its "destruction. Therefore, since nothing at all has happened to this object, how can it be said to have "perished"?
He answers this with the words beginning with "nanu" (but surely).
In this context, it was said; what was said?
There is no property called "destruction" that exists as something distinct from that entity;
rather, how then can an entity be said to be perishable?
It was stated previously that it simply does not exist at all.
Clarifying this very point, he says "na hi" and so forth:

for this proponent of causeless destruction does not assert that for an entity produced from its own causes, there exists some property such as destruction— which might be of the nature of an entity, of the nature of a non-entity, or something else such as alteration while persisting.
Rather, he says that it is simply the cessation of the entity— that the entity itself does not exist;
therefore, the meaning is that in the first moment, the entity comes into being as something previously non-existent.
In the second moment, for that [entity], there is neither existence nor non-existence, nor even a loss of its own inherent nature; it simply ceases of its own accord.

If, however, by the term "destruction" one were to speak of the existence or arising of some phenomenon, then existence would not have been negated by this proponent; that is to say, the cessation of existence would not have been stated.
And thus, while the cessation of existence was the subject at hand, because another distinct thing would have been established instead, something entirely irrelevant would have been said.
What is the reason?

For there is no entity called "destruction," nor any non-existence consisting of the cessation of an entity, which— by its arising as an entity— could cause that entity to become non-existent, such that by the production of that [non-existence] the entity itself would undergo its own cessation.
This is what is meant:
just as when an entity exists within the state of consciousness, the entity itself does not cease, but rather that consciousness alone becomes related to it;

likewise, if one accepts that the cessation of an entity occurs, then that very property called "cessation" would be related to it, but the entity itself would not cease. How, then, could there be its cessation?
Therefore, at that time, that entity would not have come into being and would not have ceased if it did not exist by itself;
for this reason, it is said: "But surely, even non-existence does not occur for an entity [if it does not exist]?"

In that case, its imperishability would either be distinct from it or non-distinct; and under either of these two positions, there would be the perception of the entity at all times, because of its imperishability.
Therefore, it is not the case that there is a destruction of non-existence;
rather, how is it that existence is not perceived at all times? [The objection] that this is due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has thus been refuted.
For the existence of a perceptible object is pervaded by its being an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);

therefore, in the absence of that [means of cognition], there is non-existence, or if it does exist, it must necessarily be an object of a means of valid cognition— so how can there be a lack of apprehension?
Now, if its state consists in being invisible, then there must be a cessation of its visible form;
and that [cessation] must be either different from or non-different from the entity itself.
In either of these two positions, the fault remains exactly as it was: the entity would still be perceived.
Therefore, there is neither the non-occurrence of an entity,
nor the fault of its being indestructible, because it ceases by way of its own nature.
If it is argued that because the cessation of an entity is formless, it must be distinct from the formal entity, [we reply]:
how can there be distinctness for that which possesses no form at all? Should it then be considered identical?
That too does not exist because it lacks form;
therefore, its identity with or difference from an entity is merely negated,
like that of a hare's horn.
But even so, how is it maintained that an entity does not exist in the second moment?
For if the entity exists in the second moment, then how can it be maintained that it does not exist there, given the contradiction?
On the other hand, if it does not exist, then how can it be said that "the entity does not exist," since it is non-existent?
That is incorrect because,
even regarding the first moment, it is said in common worldly usage that "an entity comes into being"; and in that case, if there is already an entity, how can it be said that "it comes into being"?
Therefore, the claim that the conventional practice of affirmation and negation occurs by taking an entity as it exists solely within the intellect is trivial;
thus, it remains established that at that time, the entity would not have come into being if it did not exist of its own accord.

One might object: "By this sentence, 'it is not self-existent' (nanu svayambhāvo na bhavati), it is stated that the non-existence of an entity occurs by itself; and if that were so, the same fault would apply. To this, he says:
"And [the phrase] 'it does not exist,' etc."
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "because";
thus, since existence does not occur, this is a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*),
not an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*).
When there is a mere cessation of what was engaged in, without any contact with a portion of a real entity, that is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (non-implicative negation);
whereas when the negation of one thing entails the affirmation of another, that is a *paryudāsa* (implicative negation).
Otherwise, even here in the case of *prasajya-pratiṣedha*, if some real entity were to exist...
If such a distinction were made, there would be no difference in form or essential nature between a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) and an exclusion (*paryudāsa*); thus,
what is called a "prohibition" is merely a term for a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).
What is the reason?
Because in both cases— whether it is a prasajya-pratiṣedha or a paryudāsa— the affirmation (vidhi) is predominant.
And if there were a positive injunction even in the case of a non-implicative negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), then negation itself would not exist;
and since there would be no negation of anything, there could likewise be no exclusion (*paryudāsa*) anywhere.
What is the reason for this?
For if some entity were to be excluded from something else, then that which is distinct from it would come into contact with the entity from which it is being excluded.
By means of that exclusion (*paryudāsa*), through the exclusion of what is being negated—
just as in the command "bring a non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*), where by the exclusion of the Brahmin there is contact with the Kṣatriya and so forth— that is not at all a negation of anything.
What is the reason?

Even when it is stated that "in every case there is the cessation of something," no exclusion of an entity (*bhāvavyavaccheda*) is perceived; rather, even by the word "cessation" (*nivṛtti*), only some kind of entity is perceived.
Furthermore, although this proponent speaks of the cessation of an entity, he has not actually stated a cessation at all, but would instead have stated the existence of a different entity.

And thus, when one thing is said to be distinct from another through exclusion (*paryudāsa*), their mutual distinction is not established; and in the absence of such distinction, there can be no exclusion,
because exclusion is characterized by the appropriation of one thing through its distinction from another.

Thus, in the manner described, because there is an absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), there would also be no positive concomitance (*anvaya*); the meaning is that there would be no "concomitance," which is to say, no following after or affirmation of any object.
What is the reason?
Because that lineage is characterized by the state of having a single intrinsic nature (*ekasvabhāva*),
its stability and that state of having a single intrinsic nature would exist only if there were the exclusion or removal of anything other than it; yet,
according to your own view, that exclusion of what is other than it does not exist.
Thus, if it were so, the world would be devoid of engagement and withdrawal based on words; there would be an absence of verbal activity consisting of injunctions and prohibitions.
Since this is not the case, one must necessarily admit that the denotation of a word consists solely in the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of something.
And since this is so, when it is said that "the destruction of a thing occurs," what is meant is that the thing itself does not exist;
it is not that some other distinct property called "destruction" is predicated of it.

For just as there is a real distinction in the expression "Caitra’s son," so too there must be one here in the case of "the destruction of a thing," because the use of the ablative case (indicating separation) is identical in both instances. To this, he says:
"No," and so forth. Indeed,
because of the similarity with the mere sound of the words "Caitra’s son," a rule observed in another context— namely,
that which is seen as real in the case of "Caitra’s son"— does not deserve to be applied everywhere, even here in the case of "the destruction of an entity."
Because it is impossible to establish a connection with a real entity based on the mere application of a word,
he states this very point with the words "for indeed" (*na hi*) and so forth:
because a certain person has given a man the name "donkey," the qualities of a donkey— the qualities of a *bāleya*— need not be attributed to that human being as well.
Likewise, just as in the sentence "Caitra’s son exists," the positive injunction (vidhi) seen therein—the prescription of another entity, namely the son—is to be applied here too;
for in the case of "the destruction of an entity occurs" (*bhāvasya nāśo bhavati*), destruction must also be prescribed as distinct from the entity.
What is the reason?
Because destruction is of the nature of non-existence, and because non-existence is opposed to being, it has been stated [that there is no contradiction].
If destruction is not a distinct entity, why is it said that "the destruction of an entity occurs"? [This is asked] because of the apparent contradiction.
Therefore, he says "And thus," etc.;
even though it is designated as "the destruction of an entity," the purpose [of this designation] has already been explained.

Because it has been explained [by us] that— having mentally distinguished the property from the property-bearer as if they were different entities— one speaks of the very nature [of the bearer] in that way when there is a desire to know that alone;
therefore, since non-existence is nothing at all, the dilemma of its being either identical to or different from [the entity] is not comparable.
Therefore, if an entity were to exist as a real thing, this conceptual distinction between identity and difference would arise;
for what reason?
Because existence, being an affirmation, must conform to a real entity.
But surely, even when an excellence arises, that very thing has produced that excellence; so how can it be said to have perished?
Therefore, it is not in that same state that it is called "perished," since it does not cease to exist by its own nature.
Therefore, it was stated that [an entity] does not perish through the production of a different thing;
for it is not the case that something which has not itself come into being is called "non-existent" merely by the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*).
This is because non-existence is characterized by the exclusion of all properties of existence, through the cessation of every description of excellence.
And because existence (*bhāva*) is characterized by the entry into arising, he explains it with the words "existence" and so forth;
"existence" means becoming, that is to say, origination.
Thus, that which is necessarily occurring depends upon that which will come to be, because without that which will come to be, there can be no occurrence.
And that entity, in its operation, is indeed its own nature and a real thing;
for what reason?
Because that which is devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) cannot have any involvement in such things as "existing somewhere" and so forth.
Because there is no relation [between them], there is no such thing as an "operation" (vyāpāra) that is a distinct entity;
rather, what is called "operation" is simply the arising of a specific nature, which is the arising of a nature as it actually is.

And how could there be the arising of that which is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), if there is no engagement with activity for that which lacks intrinsic nature? How, then, does conventional usage such as "the non-existence of a rabbit’s horn" occur? The meaning is that the conventional usage "the rabbit’s horn becomes a non-existence" occurs through an activity characterized by the process of becoming (*bhavana*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of such expressions as "the son of a barren woman becomes a non-existence" is intended.
He refutes this with the words "No," and so forth:
"It is certainly not stated by way of affirmation that 'the hare's horn is something—either a non-entity or something else';
rather, by the sentence 'thus the hare's horn becomes a non-entity,' it is shown that the non-existence of this hare's horn occurs."
The statement "an entity does not exist" performs merely a negation of the entity; furthermore, persons engaged in worldly discourse,
having superimposed this [negation] as if it were an active process, demonstrate that things such as a hare's horn are "non-existent."
Based on some particular context or occasion, one may inquire whether things such as a rabbit’s horn are non-existent or not; however,
that rabbit’s horn and so forth do not, by mere conventional usage alone, become engaged in such activity.
Since the discernment of all objects and the absence of an intrinsic nature in all objects constitutes reality in cases such as a rabbit's horn,

and there is no inclusion of any non-existent thing such as arising and so forth— even if it were caused— [the opponent] might argue that destruction will likewise occur in this manner; to this, he says:
"No," and so forth; for what reason is it that destruction, characterized by the absence of all objects like the horn of a hare, is desired by others?
Since that destruction exists as a positive entity (bhāva) within the object, how could that which comes into being be a non-entity (abhāva)? This would involve a contradiction.
Furthermore, if this destruction itself is indeed devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), it is merely described by speakers as if it possessed activity, saying "it occurs in this way."
But it is not the case that [the entity] itself possesses the property of becoming thus; for since this [non-existence] is formless (*nīrūpa*),
even one who asserts that "at that very time, non-existence comes to be" must indeed accept that "nothing at all comes to be."

Since this statement consists merely in the negation of activity, an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) existing in some entity in its own non-superimposed form cannot transcend two conceptual alternatives— namely, identity and otherness— because there is no other possible mode. (0.280)

If it is argued that the person (pudgala) does not have the nature of the aggregates such as form, yet is not other than form and so forth, and therefore its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) indeed transcends both identity and difference—
that is not so.
Since non-reality is precisely the lack of that nature, which constitutes the "otherness" of a nature—

if the person (*pudgala*) does not have the aggregates (*skandha*) as its nature, then it must be something other than the aggregates; for indeed, even in the case of form (*rūpa*) and taste (*rasa*), which are established as distinct, their mutual otherness is not anything other [than the very fact of their being different].

However, since the state of not having that nature is itself "otherness," and this state exists in the person (*pudgala*) as well, the person too must be accepted as being other than the aggregates (*skandhas*).

If it is argued that "otherness" consists in the absence of a mutual essential connection even when there is no identity of nature, and that such a lack of connection exists between the person and the aggregates, then even though they do not have the same nature, there would be no "otherness" of the person from the aggregates.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "What is this," etc.:

"What indeed is this so-called 'bond' of the person (pudgala) to the aggregates (skandhas), by virtue of which bond that [person] would not exist, and yet the person would not be of the same nature as the aggregates?"
And "not having another nature" means that its nature is not other than the aggregates; this is the analysis of the compound.
If it is argued that the birth of the person from the aggregates is itself the connection [to those aggregates], then:
This being the case, since the person (pudgala) is an effect, it is accepted that it cannot be described as either identical to or different from the aggregates (skandhas).
If that were so, then all causes would likewise be indescribable in relation to one another; and thus, if [the person] were indescribable because it is an effect...

Everything is somehow useful for everything—whether directly or through a succession of causes; thus, because of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) existing everywhere, nothing whatsoever could be distinct from anything else.

And so, even by one who asserts "ineffability" (*avācyatā*) on the basis of the definition of ineffability just mentioned, it would simply be the causal relationship itself that has been stated in different words, with no difference in meaning whatsoever. Furthermore, the absolute otherness (*anyatva*) of things has not at all been negated.

Because we define "otherness" as the mutual non-concomitance and non-mixture of two intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), and since this non-concomitance of intrinsic nature exists indeed among all things that possess such natures, there is only mutual otherness between the person (*pudgala*) and the aggregates (*skandha*), and no other kind of necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

For there is no connection other than the essential nature of birth—that is, the necessary connection consisting in the very nature of arising—because what is not dependent [on another] cannot be connected to it through the process of origination.
What is the reason?
Because that which is not reliant [on another] is not bound to it by way of its production.
Because there is no contradiction in the deviation [of the person] from that [the aggregates],
and because there is no necessary connection, the person is distinct from the aggregates;
and it is distinct due to the difference in their defining characteristics (dharma).
For thus there is a difference between the phenomena (*dharma*): the person (*pudgala*) is inexpressible, whereas the aggregates (*skandha*) are mutually expressible.
Even if there is no causal connection (*pratibandha*) based on birth, it might be argued that there is nonetheless a connection between the person and the aggregates based on cognition;
this [objection] is explained by the words beginning with "syāt" (it might be).

The cognition of a person is "invariably concomitant" (*nāntarīyaka*)—that is, inseparable—from the cognition of form and so forth; thus, when there is the apprehension of that [person], it necessarily appears [simultaneously] with the apprehension of form and so forth. Therefore, there is a connection established by cognition, for it is maintained that the apprehension of the person occurs precisely through the apprehension of form, sound, and the rest.
Because the person (*pudgala*) is cognizable by the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth,

that entity called "person" is— in virtue of that connection established by cognition— indescribable as being other than the aggregates (*skandha*), even though it does not possess their form and does not have the nature of the aggregates.
He refutes this with the words "no," and so forth:
the cognition of a person is not invariably concomitant with the apprehension of form and the other [sensory objects];
for what reason?
Since that person, having abandoned the intrinsic nature of form and so forth, is devoid of intrinsic nature,
it is precisely that which appears in the form of form and so forth which constitutes his own intrinsic nature; otherwise, the person would not have the intrinsic nature of form and so forth.

In that case, if this *pudgala* were by nature devoid of form and so forth, it would follow that it must appear as something separate from them—just as form and the rest do not appear as such [in themselves];
yet it does not so appear. Therefore, the *pudgala* simply does not exist, because that which is perceptible yet does not appear is non-existent.

Now, if it is maintained that the person (*pudgala*) is imperceptible, then even while the person is held to be imperceptible, there is no cognition of its form—that is, no cognition having the aspect of the person. Thus, for whom does what depend upon what for its apprehension?
The meaning is that the cognition of the person is not invariably concomitant with the cognition of form and so forth.
And thus, the sense is that there is no obstruction caused by cognition.
If it is argued that the person (pudgala) does not appear as a separate entity precisely because its perception is dependent upon [the perception of] form and so forth, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "na ca" (nor), the connection is as follows:
when a thing whose cognition is dependent upon another has its perception necessarily bound to that other, the manifestation of its own nature does not fail to occur;
to illustrate this, he asks, "What is it like? and says:
"Light," and so forth:
just as for blue and other objects whose cognition is dependent upon light, even when the light appears, their own appearance does not perish,
because they appear as distinct from the light.
In the same way, it would also apply to the person (pudgala). Furthermore,

what kind of proximity or connection does that person have with those aggregates, such that— by virtue of that cause of proximity— the person presents itself spontaneously when those aggregates, which are non-self in nature and lack the essence of a person, appear?
This amounts to saying that it causes one to grasp a self;
for in this way there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga),
if the person (pudgala) were necessarily to appear whenever something unrelated appears.
The meaning is that, at that time, even in the appearance of anything whatsoever, an absolute lack of connection is perceived.

If it is argued that there is a proximity consisting in the person being perceived having matter (*rūpa*) and so forth as its material cause (*upādāna*), then what is this meaning of "material cause"?
First of all, there is no causal relationship between the person (*pudgala*) and form (*rūpa*) and so forth, respectively,
because such a relationship is not admitted; or, even if a causal relationship were admitted, there would be no necessary perception of the person upon the perception of form and so forth.
For what reason? Because cause and effect do not bring about the mutual presentation of their respective cognitions.
The meaning is that just as there is cognition of a cause from an effect, there is no such cognition of an effect from a cause;

it is not that the person (*pudgala*) is invariably concomitant with form and so forth, but rather that the cognition of the person is invariably concomitant with them— that is, it is invariably concomitant with form and so forth.
If it is argued that this very [perception] constitutes the proximity,

we reply: surely it has been stated that such a perception is not tenable for a person (pudgala) with respect to form and so forth, unless there is an inseparable connection (nāntarīyakatā) between them, provided no obstruction exists.
One might argue that even for a person (*pudgala*) and form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are neither cause nor effect, there will be a necessary connection (*pratibandha*);
therefore, he says:

"It has been stated more than once that there is no real (*vāstava*) necessary connection between things that are neither cause nor effect. Furthermore, as for what is said—that the cognition of one thing is inseparable from the apprehension of another—[that too is rejected].
That knowledge— namely, the knowledge of the person (pudgala) occurring when there is the discernment of form and so forth— would exist;
however, that does not exist.

The connection is as follows: since that which does not appear in a person (*pudgala*) or in consciousness (*vijñāna*) by way of its own nature—that is, by way of a non-connection with others that is not connected to its own nature—there is no cognition of it whatsoever.

Due to the absence of such [cognition], that is, due to the absence of the aforementioned cognition, the characteristic of inexpressibility (*avācyatā*) of the object-entity called "person" is not established.

Therefore, in reality and from the perspective of ultimate truth, that entity must exist somewhere as something possessing either identity with or difference from [the cause], because there is no other possible mode for a thing to exist. However,
for the proponent of momentariness who holds the view that when a perishing entity ceases, nothing at all happens, but rather that the entity simply ceases to exist by itself—
Therefore, even by one who says "it becomes non-existence," only a negation—that "existence does not become [something]"—is expressed, and there is no affirmation of anything whatsoever.
Consequently, he considers that for the proponent of momentariness, there is no room for the conceptual alternatives of identity or difference regarding non-existence;
this he explains with the words beginning "yadapi" (even what...).

Furthermore, when this proponent of momentariness says, by means of a word that appears to involve a positive injunction, "the non-existence of an entity comes into being," what he actually says is "it does not become an entity";
for in this way, that entity is negated if nothing at all is positively enjoined.
What is the reason?
Because in a negation that consists merely in the exclusion of an entity, a positive injunction is impossible;
and because for an entity that is perishing, there exists no property whatsoever that is a real thing.
Therefore, there is no cause whatsoever for the destruction of this entity;
for a separate cause of destruction would only be required by a perishing entity if it had some effect to be produced by that cause.
But there is no effect whatsoever; therefore, the cause of destruction is ineffective,
and that which is an ineffective thing [cannot be a cause].
He explains [this] with the words "Is that dependent on anything? It is not dependent at all," and so forth, because it already exists.
For a causal factor (kāraka) exists only when there is something to be produced;

it has been stated that there is no effect whatsoever for an entity that is perishing. Therefore, whatever is called a cause of destruction does nothing to the entity; since it is thus ineffective, the cause of destruction is not to be relied upon.
"How is that so? and so forth—the opponent asks:
"If no excellence whatsoever arises in that which is perishing, how then can there be [destruction] when no excellence has arisen?"

The analysis [of the compound] is: "one whose excellence has not arisen. The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) objects: "Is it not the case that an entity, while remaining in that very state—that is, while remaining in its prior state—is what is called 'destroyed'? and so forth.
Even if it is admitted that a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) arises in an entity from the cause of its destruction, since that very excellence called "destruction" has arisen,
how can that entity be said to have perished?
For the destruction of one thing does not occur through the existence of another.
For this reason, that entity remains in its very same state and is not what is called "destroyed";
rather, it is called "destroyed" because it does not exist of itself, and not because of the arising of some other distinct thing called "destruction," as was stated immediately prior.
For indeed, by the arising of an excellence (atiśaya) called destruction, the entity itself does not become non-existent.
What is the reason?
Because all excellences are characterized by the capacity of non-existence.
And by the cessation of those designations and expressions— meaning the cessation of all expressions of capacity—

the meaning is that it is characterized by the distinction (*viveka*), that is, the absence (*viraha*), of every property of existence (*bhāvadharma*) which consists in the nature of becoming (*bhavanarūpa*).
And because existence (bhāva) is characterized by the occurrence of arising,
it is called "existence" (bhāva) in the sense that "it comes into being" (bhavati); therefore, existence is that which is connected with arising.
And because it is thus, there is no occurrence of some other entity in the non-existence or destruction of an entity; the meaning is that there is no arising of anything whatsoever.
By this, namely by the demonstration of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Even if destruction is accepted as being causeless, since that destruction first does not exist and then comes to be— thus, because destruction exists after having not existed— it would follow that this destruction possesses existence (*sattā*) like a sprout or similar things, and would therefore be subject to perishability (*naśitva*). By this very [argument], the objection regarding the faults of existence and perishability has been refuted.

He explains with the words "yopi" and so forth: even if destruction were causeless, since this destruction comes into being after not having existed (*abhūtvā bhāvāt*), its existence and impermanence would be unavoidable;

furthermore, it is contradictory to say that something which comes into being after not having existed is causeless, because that which occurs only occasionally (*kādācitka*) is necessarily in contradiction with being causeless.
That objection regarding the fault has also been refuted by this very demonstration that destruction is formless;
for what reason?
Because it is not admitted that any property exists at the time of destruction.

Just as, despite the equality of their status as real entities (*vastutva*), only certain produced beings (*janmin*)— those possessing the quality of origination (*utpattimat*)— are held to possess what is called "resistance" (*pratigha*), characterized by the obstruction of another's origination in one's own location, and not all [entities]; so too, let the nature of destruction belong only to those things that possess origination, and not to non-originating things such as space (*ākāśa*) and the like.
And thus, [the opponent argues that] the statement "whatever exists is momentary" is subject to deviation;
this he explains with the words beginning with "atha," saying: "Let it be so."
This is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of entities; what is this intrinsic nature? He says:
it is that which has the property of existing for only a single moment (kṣaṇasthitidharma).
The analysis of the compound is: "those things whose nature (*dharma*) is momentary duration.
However, that nature of momentary duration will belong only to those entities (*bhāva*) that possess origination, and not to non-originated things such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.

The meaning is that it is not simply because something has an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that everything becomes the intrinsic nature of everything; rather, just as the quality of resistance (pratighātmatā), despite being an intrinsic nature of a thing, does not belong to everything, so it is in this case as well.
The Master says: "It is true that everything is not the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of everything; this is indeed true.

Nevertheless, because there is a restriction of intrinsic nature based on the cause—namely, that 'this is the producer of that which possesses resistance, while this is not'—there is a restriction of intrinsic nature regarding the effect: 'this is resistant, this is not.'"

But in the case of the impermanent—that is, regarding that which has impermanence as its object—there is no difference in the nature of produced things by which one might have a non-eternal intrinsic nature while another does not.
What is the reason?
Because there is an absence of causes that could differentiate the intrinsic nature of impermanence.
This means that all things arise with a perishable nature;
for indeed, the objection raised—that "the nature of entities is destruction, but not for those that do not arise"—is relevant to the present context.
Furthermore, the resolution offered—that "there is no difference in form regarding impermanence because there are no differentiating factors"—is also logical.
For space and so forth do not possess a perishable nature produced by their own causes, because they are unproduced;
therefore, how could it be said that "it is true" and so on? This is what [the author] intends.

Just as "existence" (*sattva*) was stated to be inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*), so too one might suspect that even among "produced things" (*kṛtaka*), some are perishable while others are not; therefore, there is no fault in stating "existence" (*satyam*) and so forth at the very beginning in order to first eliminate the inconclusiveness of "being produced. He explains this with the words beginning with "no" (*na*).

"Other" refers to that which is visible and so forth; "without cause" means that it would occur by chance, being restricted such that it exists in some cases and not in others, even in the absence of a cause.

However, since the result arises in accordance with the causal power— namely, the established capacity and restriction of power belonging to a cause that produces specific properties such as resistance— it is accepted that there is a restriction on the nature of the result based on the restriction on the nature of the cause.
If, however, it were accidental—that is, causeless—then the fault already stated regarding the necessity of the nature of the fruit would apply:
namely, that a restriction by place, time, and intrinsic nature would not be possible.
Therefore, its nature is the cause of its resistance-essence, and that [nature] possesses its own specific restriction.

We do not perceive any entity that possesses a specific nature as its cause for producing perishability—such that it would produce only some perishable thing and not all others; this is the analysis of the compound: "that entity which has a specific nature (svabhāva) regarding the production of perishability.
By means of which causal restriction...

That which has its birth from that cause—namely, from a perishable birth—is likewise perishable; it cannot be otherwise, for nothing else can arise from a cause possessing characteristics different from those.
What is the reason?
Because all things born in any form whatsoever are observed to perish.
The analysis of the compound is: "those whose birth arises from causes in all their aspects.

To this, the opponent replies with "But surely," and so forth: "Is it not the case that even this—that those entities which have birth from causes in all their aspects perish—is itself indeterminate?"
What is the reason?

Because those causal complexes (*hetu-sāmagrī*) cannot be seen in their entirety by those of limited vision (*arvāgdarśin*), since they are not perceived exhaustively; and because, having observed that a certain complex produces perishable things, even those [complexes] not yet observed are determined to be of such a nature by virtue of belonging to that same class. If this is argued:
He said: "Variegated," and so forth;
the analysis of the compound is "those causal complexes whose power is variegated" (vicitra-śaktayaḥ), and such causal complexes are observed.
Among those various causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) possessing diverse powers, there might be some complex that could produce an entity whose nature is imperishable;
[the author] refutes this with the words "no" and so forth.
Furthermore, this refutation applies to the fact that destruction is the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of entities, not of those that are unproduced.
The word "yadi" (if) should also be understood here in this objection because it is common [to both cases];
why is this not a fault?
In accordance with the section on the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), he clarifies this very point, saying:

"We maintain that when objects, having been known at some time, in some place, by some person, are no longer known, there is a destruction (*nāśa*) that persists as a continuity (*santānānubandhin*)."
Those things which, being previously unknown, come to be known, or having been known, are no longer known—
these alone are established as produced and impermanent;
and by this [argument], it is stated that the pervasion of "producedness" by "momentariness" is ascertained through the reason "existence."
But surely, even if they are not perceived despite being knowable, how can their impermanence be established?
To this he says:

for it is impossible that those things which possess the nature of producing cognition, having previously existed and later not perished, should remain in that very same nature and yet fail to produce [cognition].
If it is argued that they do not produce [the effect] due to the absence of auxiliary causes,
he says:
"They would require nothing else."
For there is no possibility of this; such is the connection.
What is the reason?
Because its nature of producing that has already been established.
Now, it might be argued that even if those [causes] are independent, knowledge will nevertheless arise for someone at some time;
therefore, he says:

Furthermore, if those [senses] were established as having an inherent nature of producing cognition and were independent of auxiliary causes, then for some person at any time, no cognition whatsoever would ever cease;
rather, they would produce cognitions of their respective objects for everyone at all times.
And since this is never observed from the perspective of knowledge and vision,
it is understood that those [causes] which do not produce knowledge have deviated from their nature as producers.
If it is argued that what is unknowable— whether produced or unproduced— will not be like this,
he says "no," and so forth.
And there is nothing of such a nature that is unknowable;
for what reason?
Because every object is known by some person at some time.
Furthermore, if that [entity] were not to produce even cognition,
then, being incapable even of the causal efficiency consisting in mere cognition, it would not be a real entity at all,
for we shall state that the defining characteristic of a real entity is its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*).

Furthermore, since that entity capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) which performs such efficiency sequentially is invariably subject to destruction, and since destruction is itself causeless, it is established that destruction is inherent to existence (*sattā*). For this very reason— namely, from the proof of the momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) of all entities just mentioned— the eternity of the relationship between word and meaning must also be rejected and refuted.
He explains [the point] with the words beginning "not," etc.:
for this very reason, because destruction— as previously described— is invariably concomitant with any entity whatsoever,
just like sound.
Just as the eternity of sound has been refuted, so too must the eternity of the relationship be rejected.
Thus far, the fault has been stated by assuming the relationship to be distinct; now it is said that the relationship is not tenable even if it is non-distinct.
Furthermore, that power of words known as "fitness" (*yogyatā*), which the followers of Jaimini describe as the basis for the comprehension of a meaning designated by that fitness,
is not actually something distinct from the word's meaning.

For it has already been explained previously that fitness is simply a specific excellence of the nature (*svabhāva*) of entities, which consists in their capacity to perform the intended purposeful action.
For [the author] states, "Indeed, form is capable," and "fitness [belongs] to the word," and so forth;
the meaning is that since the word is impermanent, its fitness is also impermanent because there is no distinction between them.
Alternatively, let fitness be something other than the word.
Nevertheless, it should be understood that the power of the word is also refuted by those previously mentioned defects of the relationship.
He explains with the words "For it has been said," and so forth;
for in the discourse that the relation is an entity distinct from the related terms, many kinds of faults have been stated, such as:
"Because the related terms are impermanent, the relation cannot possess permanence."
Since the power of words, which is also postulated in the form of a relationship, has already been refuted by that same previously mentioned defect, the fault is not stated separately once again.
Thus, the Veda is not authorless;
even if it were authorless, its truthfulness could not be ascertained.
Because, simply by virtue of being non-human (apauruṣeya), a Vedic statement is not a means for the knowledge of things as they are— that is,
a cause for the knowledge of an object without error—
since it is not rendered defective by human faults (puruṣāgasā), such as those of fire and so forth.
The word "etcetera" (ādi) refers to moonlight and so forth;
the meaning is that even otherwise, such things are observed to be causes of false cognition.
He explains this with the words beginning "let it be," and so on.

Granted that Vedic words may be non-human (apauruṣeya), nevertheless, it is quite possible for these Vedic words to be a cause of false cognition; for it is not only through the imposition of human defects— namely,
the imposition of human defects such as passion and the like— that [error arises].
Regarding objects to be made known, there occurs a delusion of knowledge— a perversion of knowledge— on the part of the words that serve as the means of making them known,
because it is possible for such words to generate false cognition even by their very nature.
Because even for things such as lamps— which are devoid of that [defect] and also free from the imposition of human defects— there arises knowledge of an unreal object;
and by the word "etcetera," [this includes] moonlight and so forth—
in what [case does this occur]?
For instance, among blue lotuses and the like,
at night a lamp is the cause of a cognition appearing as red in the blue lotus,
while moonlight is the cause of a cognition of white in a yellow garment.

The connection is as follows: "Therefore" (*tad*), these Vedic words would be independent of human refinement; and by their "nature" (*prakṛti*) and "intrinsic character" (*svabhāva*), they would be the causes of cognition—the causes of knowledge—regarding their objects.
Why?
Because of a specific nature, that is, a specific essential form.
And why would false manifestations necessarily arise in the same manner as fire and other such things?
If it is argued: "The analysis of the compound is 'those words from which the cognitions of objects are false' (*vitathā vyaktayo ’rthapratipattayo yebhyaḥ*).
There is no reason for the rule that Vedic words are always characterized by false manifestations;
therefore, because of the absence of such a restrictive cause, the conceptual construction that 'Vedic words are indeed characterized by false manifestations' is untenable."
For you as well, what is the cause for this rule of non-erroneous manifestation—that Vedic words are the cause of non-erroneous knowledge? None at all.

Therefore, according to your own view, since there is a rule of manifesting things as they truly are, why is it not postulated that by nature—that is, by its very essence—there is a rule of manifesting things as they are not?

Alternatively, just as fire and other such things serve as causes for both true and false cognitions regarding objects such as jars and blue lotuses respectively— as is appropriate— so too would Vedic words possess the capacity to cause both types of cognition by being causes for both false and non-false cognitions regarding their objects; for even non-human-made things like forest fires or moonlight, while being causes for correct cognition in one instance such as a jar during the day, are not necessarily so in all instances, such as a blue lotus at night.
In such a way that they become causes of true knowledge,
so too— even if Vedic words are not of human origin— both would occur:
they would be both causes of true knowledge and causes of false knowledge.
"Let it be so," and so forth—the opponent [argues]:

because fire and other such things are produced (*kṛtakatvāt*), they appear according to their respective conditions (*yathāpratyayam*); that is, by virtue of whatever cause of error pertains to each, they appear as such in other cases, such as the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*).

"Alteration" means being the cause of false cognition; however, this quality of being a cause of erroneous cognition does not exist in eternal sounds by virtue of the power of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*), because it is impossible for eternal things to function otherwise through the power of auxiliaries.
[The opponent asks: "But surely... and so forth—this is the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*).
"Of such a kind" means that by the power of auxiliary factors (sahakārin), there is indeed a property (dharma) characterized by transformation into another state within objects;
"there too" refers even to Vedic words— what is the reason for this?

The meaning is that even for those Vedic words, there is a deviation from their [inherent] function due to the power of convention (*saṃketa*), because they produce a different cognition through the power of conventions that conform to human will. Now, if it is maintained that there is no deviation of those [Vedic words] from their objects due to the power of convention, but rather that— because of their eternity— the Vedic words possess by their very nature the inherent capacity to generate cognitions of their own objects;

In that case, since these Vedic words possess the inherent nature of producing a cognition whose object is themselves, and since there is an absence of anything else to be depended upon— such as convention (*samaya*) or, by the word "etcetera," other causal operations and so forth— therefore, from those Vedic words, cognition or knowledge regarding objects would arise for every person at all times.
Furthermore, there is no cognition of meaning for everyone at all times;
therefore, Vedic words do not have a nature established in the cognition of meaning, but rather depend upon convention (*samaya*) and so forth.
Thus, they too are causes of false cognition, and the aforementioned fault remains as it was.
Moreover,
if that word is accepted as being uncreated, it could not even be the cause of cognition;
for nothing whatsoever arises from eternal entities by virtue of their objective capacity— that is, through the capacity of imparting their own nature.
He explains by means of the passage beginning with "If [knowledge] or something else were unproduced":
if the Vedic word were unproduced, then there would be no cognition at all regarding its meanings.
What is the reason for saying "is perceived," and so forth?
The analysis of the compound is: "the other" (referring to non-arising) and "non-arising" (referring to arising), thus "the other and non-arising."

Regarding the time of those two—the time of cognition and the time other than it—since that which is of a uniform nature is eternal, it is impossible for there to be the capacity for cognition at the time of its production;

furthermore, because it would be contradictory for that which remains in the very same nature which was its producer at the time when cognition had not yet arisen to still be a producer [at a later time].
What is the reason?

If it is argued that, because there is no distinction in form or distinction in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) such that this [entity] which is considered eternal is a producer in one form but not a producer in another form—
since the eternal is always of a single form and thus possesses a single intrinsic nature— it might nonetheless become a producer later, having previously been a non-producer.
He says "no," and so forth: it is not logical that this eternal [entity], which is a non-producer, should have the very same nature as a producer,
because it possesses a single, uniform form.
The claim that [an eternal entity] produces [an effect] later only after obtaining an additional auxiliary cause is false;
for the dependence on another—namely, dependence on an auxiliary cause—is already precluded in the case of what is eternal.
Therefore, eternal words possess the capacity to generate knowledge in a person regarding certain objects.
What is the reason?
If there were a time when cognition was not produced, then because it would possess that same nature even subsequently, it would follow that it would never produce it at all.
Alternatively, if one maintains that this fault shall not occur and thus [the causes] always perform their own effect, [then...]
That too does not exist;

and because their effect, which is the cognition of their own object, is not observed to be continuous, those sounds are in no way whatsoever the agents [of that cognition]. This has already been stated previously.
It might be argued that cognitions indeed arise from eternal entities such as space (ākāśa) and so forth for someone at some time;
therefore, he says:

Even those cognitions or understandings that are held to arise with respect to space and other things considered to be eternal— these too do not possess the nature of those [entities], nor is their production dependent upon the nature of space and so forth;
for in the case of eternal things, causal efficiency is contradicted by both succession and simultaneity.
What, then, is the cause for their arising?
To this he says: "For not," and so forth.

They arise with respect to those things— space and so forth— which are imagined as external; they are produced solely as manifestations of that very object, having for their domain a superimposed form such as space that has arisen from a potency (śakti), which is a latent impression (vāsanā) deposited by beginningless conceptualization of a similar kind, and which accords with traditional scripture.
But those cognitions do not have objects as their domain, nor do they have the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of space and so forth as their objects;
this he explains by the words "the specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*), etc.

For a cognition whose object is a specific characteristic necessarily follows the capacity, the efficacy, the presence, and the proximity of that specific characteristic; that is, it exists only when that [specific characteristic] exists. Thus he considers it.
Whatever is the cause of this cognition—the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—is that which is fit and capable; when that capable cause is present, that cognition necessarily arises.

Such being the logical state of affairs, if there were to be knowledge of the specific characteristics of eternal entities for some person, then because the cause would be eternally present, it would occur for every person at all times.

Nor can it be argued that eternal things produce knowledge at some time or place due to dependence on auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). For an effect is produced by those individuals through a specific excellence (*viśeṣa*) brought about by auxiliaries; such individuals, being employed in a certain effect according to the constraints of place, time, and state, attain the status of a cause. Thus, an "auxiliary" is a particular entity that serves as the cause for obtaining that excellence which is the very nature of the capacity for producing that effect—just as [the capacity] is non-eternal.

An eternal entity, being a specific effect that cannot have any excellence (*atiśaya*) imparted to it by anyone, would— if it were to produce a perception for a person while depending on that person’s perception as a cooperative cause— logically be perceived by that person alone and not by another, due to the restriction of the cooperative causes; however, such production by an eternal entity through dependence on a cooperative cause is impossible.
What is the reason?
Because that which is eternal has a fixed nature; therefore, no excellence can be imparted to it by an auxiliary cause. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, because it would always abide in its nature of being produced, it would be perceived by every person at the same time; or else, because it would not be a producer for anyone, it would not be perceived by anyone.

In that case, since that very nature belongs to it, it would never be perceived by any person whatsoever. Therefore, if an existent, permanent entity were seen by some yogi, then nothing at all would be permanent or beyond the senses, because everyone would necessarily perceive it.
And thus, this [object] would have to be eternally perceptible by the senses of all persons, because there is no difference in its capacity to produce cognition with respect to every person;
yet this universal perceptibility does not belong to an eternal entity.

Therefore, [cognitions] that do not depend on the causal efficiency of an object—that is, those that do not depend on the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of space and so forth—have superimposed objects as their domain.
The meaning is that they appear in the forms of space and so forth as superimposed according to scripture.
Relying solely upon an internal material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), what kind of awakening of conceptual latencies (*vikalpa-vāsanā*) is there?
It is the beginninglessness of the conceptualization of space and so forth.

The awakening of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) that has been deposited is its orientation toward the production of an effect; since it does not depend on the causal efficiency of an external object, it follows that for everyone, these are indeed errors devoid of external objects, occurring in relation to space and so forth—
this is established.
It is not the case that the production of an effect from eternal things is impossible;
for it is observed that at times the effect of cognition [arises] from sound. Therefore, sounds do not possess the property of being non-reversible.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: those whose property is precisely non-reversibility when they possess a single form.
But if every cognition has a distinct object and each cognition functions differently,

or if they are instead eternally of a single uniform nature— whether one accepts their reality or their uniformity— then on what basis can it be said that Vedic words produce cognitions of non-erroneous objects?
The analysis of the compound might be thought to be "those from which the comprehension of meaning is non-false"; thus,
because Vedic sentences such as "Fire is the remedy for cold" are non-false, it might be argued that all [Vedic statements] are non-false.
Therefore, he says "na hi" and so forth:
for in such Vedic statements as "fire is not the remedy— that is, the counteragent— of cold," the capacity of fire to ward off cold is known from the Vedic statement itself.

Since even prior [to the Veda], that which is well-known in the world is proclaimed according to convention, all Vedic sentences— even those whose objects are not perceived— become such [i.e., true] and are non-false; for it is observed that regarding an object well-known in the world, worldly usage proceeds in accordance with convention.
Therefore, because of the convention established by people's own will, at the time of linguistic usage following upon that convention,
there arises precisely a doubt regarding usage: "Is this person conforming to, or following, his own convention?"

From such sentences as "Fire is the remedy for cold," one understands that fire possesses the capacity to dispel cold; yet, does one understand this because of a fixed capacity inherent in the very nature (*svabhāva*) or essence (*prakṛti*) of the word?

The point is that when the Vedic word's power to convey meaning even regarding a perceptible object is itself doubtful, it is all the more impossible to conceive of such power regarding an entirely imperceptible object.
Now, one might argue that the meaningfulness of Vedic words is established simply by conforming to the beginningless worldly convention, and no doubt appears there;
to this he replies:

Words are seen to be subject to change according to the will of the world, being applied to objects as determined by convention, yet when there is a reversal of place and so forth, they are changed again—being diverted through the application of a different meaning.
Thus, even if one accepts conformity with worldly consensus for this reason, a change in nature— that is, falsity— of these Vedic words is indeed possible,

because such consensus itself is not fixed. Therefore, even though no contradiction is observed in some Vedic statements such as "Fire is the remedy for cold," it is not established that all Vedic sentences possess such a character of being true in meaning.

If it is argued that the Veda possesses true meaning precisely because it is uncreated, [the author] replies: "For if these Vedic words possessed an uncreated nature, then some word among them might even be restricted to false meaning."

For this reason, because the nature of words cannot be ascertained through such a distinction as "this has a true meaning" or "this has a false meaning" based on a thorough knowledge of their intrinsic nature (svabhāva), there would be doubt regarding every word. Thus,
when the argument is formulated as "The Vedic sentence has a true meaning because it is uncreated," since there is no positive concomitance (anvaya),
he states the negative formulation (vyatireka).

The connection with the phrase beginning "falsehood" (*mithyātva*) is as follows: since falsehood is observed only in things that are produced, if the word [of the Buddha], being unproduced, were to have a true meaning—
what is the reason for this?
Because its exclusion pervades the contradictory:

the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of the reason "non-produced" is its state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*); since this pervades the falsity (*mithyātva*), which is the contradictory of the probandum (*sādhyadharma*)—namely, truthfulness (*satyārthatva*)—the genitive case in "of the exclusion" (*vyatirekasya*) is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).

He explains [the argument] with the words "just as," and so forth, because falsehood— which contradicts the quality of having true meaning— is pervaded by being produced, which is absent from the cause [of truth]; thus, since the Vedic word is unproduced, upon the cessation of being produced, falsehood ceases, and its having true meaning is indeed established.

Whatever speech has a false meaning, all of that is entirely produced; thus, by means of the production (kṛtakatva) which is the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of the reason’s non-producedness (akṛtakatva), one establishes the negative concomitance of the probandum. The probandum is truthfulness, and its negative concomitance is falsity. Because of the pervasion—that falsity cannot exist elsewhere than in the non-produced—falsity is impossible in what is non-produced. For this reason, it follows that what is non-produced is truthful, even without a positive concomitance (anvaya).
In the formal argument (prayoga) "The Vedic word has truth as its object because it is produced," although there is no positive concomitance (anvaya),

the meaning is that it is nevertheless established even without anvaya. For, regarding an object characterized by falsity which is not pervaded by "being produced" (kṛtakatva), one might suspect the absence of that [pervader]— namely, the property characterized by being produced— to exist in that falsity as well.
That [truthfulness] does not exist here, because being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is pervaded by falsity;

nor is there the possibility of a contradictory [property] existing where its opposite is pervaded, since it is impossible for two contradictories—producedness and non-producedness—to coexist in a single instance of falsity. Therefore, when the non-produced possesses truthfulness, the presence of the heterogeneous falsity is precluded.

Since there is no other possible mode besides being either true in meaning or false in meaning, and because there is no alternative mode, it must be true in meaning by virtue of its being uncreated (*akṛtaka*). Thus, since the desired object—characterized by being true in meaning—is established through its being uncreated, what is the use of showing positive concomitance (*anvaya*)?
Furthermore, because the logical mark (*liṅga*) is the means of establishing the desired object, the demonstration of positive concomitance is useless;
why is this so?

The Master [Dharmakīrti] states, "This is true," meaning that it is indeed true that the probandum is established by the mere absence [of the reason] from the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) according to the method already described;
for when the exclusion of the reason from the dissimilar instance is established, the probandum is established.
If the relationship of pervaded and pervader between falsity and being produced— which are the opposites of truthfulness and being unproduced— were established, then,
because being unproduced would exclude falsity which is pervaded by being produced, it [the unproduced] would be excluded from it; however,
that relationship of pervaded and pervader is not established for the two opposites.

What is the reason? Because, when the impossibility of "uncreatedness" (akṛtakatva) in the case of falsity [is established], and no subverting reason (bādhaka-hetu) has been stated as the cause for that impossibility,
the existence (bhāva)— that is, the reality— of that very uncreatedness can still be maintained even if it were false.
And it would be both uncreated and false in meaning (290ab).
But surely, falsity is observed to be concomitant with being created?
And since where there is "producedness" (kṛtakatva), how could there be "unproducedness" (akṛtakatva)? To this he says:
"Of contradictory [properties]," and so forth.

Because even contradictory categories of entities can be seen to share a single pervader— just as impermanent things, whether produced by effort or not produced by effort, are pervaded by the single property of being "produced" (kṛtakatva)—
he explains this with the words beginning "yadi."

If the absence of the reason called "uncreatedness" in the opposite of the probandum— namely, in falsity— were established, then the negation of the probandum (truthfulness) would be falsity, and the negation of the reason (uncreatedness)— namely, what is called "createness"— would pervade it. However, we do not perceive any subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for that uncreatedness being impossible in the case of falsity.
If it is argued that because the Veda is uncreated, it cannot function as having false meaning, he says:
"And not," and so forth.
It is logical that the prescription of "uncreatedness," which is not contradicted by its being false, serves as a proof for the negation of falsity;
why?
Because otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For in this way, by the presence of one thing, the absence of another would be perceived.
If it is asked, "How can falsity, which is observed in what is produced, apply to what is unproduced?", he says:
Nor is it the case that falsity, which is observed in one instance of something produced, cannot possibly occur again elsewhere in something unproduced; rather, it is indeed possible.
What is the reason?

Regarding "separately" (*pṛthak*) in the case of those that are contradictory or co-existent: it is used because one observes that even among things that are contradictory or co-existent, there is a distinction between their individual instances (*vyakti-bheda*). For example, just as impermanence (*anityatva*) is observed, so too between the two—being produced immediately after effort (*prayatnānantarīyaka*) and its opposite—one is the opposite of the other;
namely, impermanence is observed together with being produced immediately after effort, and it is also observed together with not being produced immediately after effort.
If it is argued that, because falsity is not observed in what is uncreated (*akṛtaka*), it must therefore be non-existent, to this he replies:
"And not so for such a thing," meaning that it is not the case that the uncreated, being existent, is non-existent simply because falsity is not observed in it.

Since it was stated previously that the non-existence of the reason (*hetu*) in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is not established because of its non-perception everywhere, he explains with the words "for [it is] not" (*na hi*) and so forth that, when the non-existence of the reason in the counter-example is unestablished, there is no exclusion from the counter-example due to doubt regarding it.

This person, being merely human and seeing only what is near, would not be capable of seeing every object such that, through the cessation of his vision, he would not exist in that way or would not be unseen;
for this reason:

For that person whose cognition does not deviate from the existence of the object of cognition—meaning, one for whom cognition proceeds toward every object of cognition simply by virtue of its being "existent"—his cognition pervades the object of cognition; thus, when [that cognition] ceases, it also causes the object of cognition to cease. Therefore, he who says "it does not exist because it is not perceived" would be justified.
Therefore, it is not the case that all of that [is so].
If these entities exist yet are unperceivable, how could they be excluded when they are separated by nature, place, and time?
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "nature," "place," and "time"—the remoteness or intervention by these [factors] constitutes the meaning.
Even though something exists, it may be remote from place, time, and nature, like a *piśāca* or similar being.
Objection: Since past and future things, being separated by time, are not perceived, their non-existence is logical; for they simply do not exist.
Response: True, but even though past and future things are not perceived at present, they have existed at some time or will exist at some time; thus, there is no absolute non-perception of them.
By the words "for thus," and so forth, this very point is made clear:
for who, being not all-seeing, could verify the correspondence of an unauthored statement regarding a matter that is absolutely beyond perception?
One is not at all capable of producing or ascertaining the non-correspondence of another, artificial statement regarding an object that is entirely beyond the senses.
It might be argued that since it is accepted that what is composed by another lacks consistency, this two-fold [criterion] has been stated;
however, because consistency is observed in one Vedic sentence, there would be consistency throughout the entire Veda.
Therefore, he says:
"And this has already been established previously in the investigation of *śeṣavat* inference.
To the question, "What was established? he says:
"In some places," and so forth:
in certain locations or times,
there is a change into another state of things that were previously perceived in such a manner.

The reversal from the previously perceived form is expressed by the words "just as" and so forth; it arises from a specific conditioning (*saṃskāra*), characterized by the preparation of milk, honey, and the like.
And the connection is that in some regions *āmalaka* fruits are sweet;
this is not [known] by one who does not see them, namely, one who has not seen the sweetness of *nimba* fruits and the like.
Just as those sweet neem fruits must indeed be rejected,
so too, even if the falsity of Vedic statements were observed, it could not be rejected; therefore,
we see no contradiction between being uncreated and having false content.
Now, one might object that because the state of being unauthored is not perceived in the case of false objects, its absence [in true objects] follows; to this he says:
"For this non-perception was stated previously to be incapable of proving the absence of a thing when that thing is of an invisible nature or possesses a nature that is not perceptible.
Consequently, the absence of the state of being unauthored in the case of falsity is not established.
Therefore, since whatever is false is all of human origin, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) between falsity and being produced;
for what reason? Because of certainty.

The meaning is that if that which has not been produced were false in its object-referent, there would be no certainty regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Furthermore, the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) does not follow from a reason whose negative concomitance is uncertain;
for instance, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of a reason consists in its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with its own probandum.

The meaning is that "presence" (sattva) refers to either the exclusion from the dissimilar instances (vyatireka), or the exclusion from the counter-examples (vipakṣa), or the presence of the reason in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin), which is called the property of the subject (pakṣadharma).

And if these three aspects are established by means of cognitions that are valid measures (*pramāṇa*), then—provided that those cognitions have the ascertainment of those three aspects as their result (the analysis being:
"those whose fruit is the ascertainment of that triad of aspects")—those three aspects become the proof for the intended probandum (*sādhya*).
As it was stated by the Master Dignāga:

For indeed, that very word which expresses a meaning determined by both [the proponent and the opponent]— a meaning that possesses the characteristics of a valid reason— is a proof; whereas a word that expresses a meaning possessing characteristics such as being unestablished (*asiddha*) is a refutation when it is employed by the opponent with the intention of refuting.

A statement based on what is established for only one of the two parties, or a doubtful statement, is neither a proof nor a refutation; that is, a word which expresses something established for only one of the proponent or the opponent, or something that is doubtful for both or for either one of them, is not a means of proof nor a means of refutation.
For what reason?
Because it depends upon further proof.
Because that which is not yet ascertained requires further reliance on a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of its ascertainment,

and because the contradiction between "uncreatedness" (*akṛtakatva*) and "falsity" (*mithyārthatva*) is not yet established— such that the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of falsity from the uncreated could be proven—
it might then be argued:
If it is argued that falsehood does not exist in the Veda precisely because it is uncreated,
he says "For who," and so forth.
For what reason? Because what conscious person would deny the possibility of falsity—which is contradicted by its very nature—in Vedic statements, simply because they are unauthored (*akṛtaka*)?
Therefore, this aforementioned negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason "being unauthored" is not a valid proof.
Why is that?
