Furthermore, demonstrating that there is no reason (*hetu*) that is a negative-only (*vyatirekin*) because of doubt, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*), and so forth.
In a given case, where the negative concomitance (vyatirekitā) of the counter-example to the probandum— namely, falsity— is described as being the opposite of truthfulness,
[the formulation is]: "whatever is not produced is not false."
Whatever is the object of the exclusion of falsity is precisely the similar instance (sapakṣa) for this reason of being produced;
for this reason, every reason is positive (anvayin).
The meaning is that it is both positive and negative (anvayavyatirekī), because the negative (vyatireka) is the subject under discussion, and not merely negative (vyatirekī).

Now, it might be objected: "A similar instance (sapakṣa) is defined as an object that is similar by virtue of possessing the general property to be proven (sādhyadharma), and such an object does not exist here; how then can it be said that this very [object] is its similar instance? To this it is replied:
True; it is precisely that which possesses the concomitance with the probandum as its similar instance (sapakṣa) that is called a "similar instance" (sapakṣa);
for this very reason, he says:
He explains that "every reason is thus concomitant" with the words beginning with "whatever," [stating]:
"Whatever has false content, all that is of human origin."

Thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason’s opposite (*vipakṣa*), namely "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), by the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyavipakṣa*), namely "falsity" (*mithyātva*), would only be established if there were the absence of falsity when there is the absence of being produced. Why? Because it is impossible for that which is false to exist in the absence of being produced while still being pervaded by that "being produced."

Therefore, one who desires pervasion must accept that the absence of falsity follows from the absence of being produced; and this very establishment of the exclusion of falsity and being produced— which belong to different classes from the probandum and the probans— is what constitutes pervasion.

The establishment of the positive concomitance (anvaya-vyavasthiti) of that very same reason—namely, the non-produced—is the fact that through the cessation of being produced, falsity ceases; that is, the non-produced is established as having truthfulness.
What is the reason for this?
Because the probandum— truthfulness— is characterized by the exclusion of its opposite,
and since its opposite is falsity, it is characterized by the exclusion, that is, the exclusion (vyāvṛtti), of "being produced" from that which is unproduced; furthermore:
The negation of truthfulness is falsity;
and when that falsity is negated in the uncreated, then a double negation has occurred.

Because of this double negation, which consists in the exclusion of truthfulness, there is the establishment of the affirmation of truthfulness; for this reason, it is devoid of both non-connection and connection.

The establishment of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of falsity—the negation of the probandum—by means of the negation of the probans, namely "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), is not at all an establishment of pervasion through non-concomitance (*ananvaya*).
Therefore, there is no such thing as a "non-concomitant" reason;
rather, every [valid] reason possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
What is the reason? Because, in the case of an uncreated [thing], the exclusion of falsity— which is a single exclusion— is inseparable from the establishment of its opposite.
Because the establishment of falsity— which is of a different class from truth— is invariably concomitant with it:

if the exclusion of one thing is invariably concomitant with the establishment of its opposite, then even when there is the exclusion of "non-eternal," "selfless," and so forth, there would likewise be [the establishment of] eternality, selfhood, and— by the force of the word "and so forth"— suffering and the rest,
whenever an exclusion is made of these in some instance such as a rabbit's horn.

The opponent maintains that, just as the establishment of "truth" occurs through the exclusion of "falsity," there would likewise follow the establishment of properties such as permanence, selfhood, and happiness— which belong to a different genus from impermanence and so forth;
however, this is not desired,
and thus it should not be the case here either.
He refutes this with the words "No," and so forth: "This fault does not apply;
for what reason?"
Because the exclusion of the contrary (*vyatirekavyavaccheda*) is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*), and because the contrary is non-existence (*abhāva*),
while the exclusion or cessation of that non-existence is likewise of a positive nature.
The point is that the establishment of existence occurs through the cessation of non-existence; by this, the definition of existence has been stated.
From this very statement, the following is also implied by implication:
Because the exclusion of an entity (bhāva-vyavaccheda) is of the nature of non-existence (abhāva).
Thus, by this, the definition of both existence and non-existence has been stated;
therein, when that [entity] is being excluded—
There is no attachment to existence; and showing that in which, when excluded, there would be an attachment to existence, he says "na bhāva" and so forth.

When there is the exclusion of the intrinsic nature of an entity (*bhāva-svabhāva*), there is neither an attachment to an entity nor an implication of an entity, because only the negation of that [nature]— in the sense that "an entity does not exist"— is possible. However,

the exclusion of that which is the exclusion of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāva-vyavaccheda-svabhāva*)— that is, mere absence— is necessarily the presentation of an entity and thus implies an entity.
What is the reason?
Because it has the nature of, that is to say, the essential character of, the distinction— that is, the separation— between existence and non-existence, which are mutually exclusive.
The meaning is that since the exclusion of existence (*bhāvaviveka*) is of the nature of non-existence, and the exclusion of non-existence (*abhāvaviveka*) is of the nature of existence.

Having thus stated that the exclusions of existence and non-existence do not imply or exclude [the other], he applies this to the subject at hand with the words "But that which is of the nature of non-existence," etc.,
referring to the exclusion of truthfulness, which is characterized by falsity.

That [non-truthfulness], being of the nature of an absence, when it is excluded by the exclusion of "being produced," brings about the presence of existence characterized as truthfulness; for [the reason] does not imply the presence of existence in that which is unproduced,
as has already been stated.

If, however, the opponent accepts that "falsity" (mithyārthatva) is the opposite of "truthfulness" (satyārthatva), then, upon the exclusion of the quality of being produced (kṛtakatva) from Vedic statements, falsity itself would not exist, and truthfulness would consequently not exist either; thus, they would result in meaninglessness (anarthakya), as he will state later.
Therefore, truthfulness must necessarily be a positive entity (bhāvarūpā).
A phenomenon characterized by falsity must be admitted;
and that, being distinct from truthfulness, establishes the existence [of its opposite].
This is not the case for selflessness and the like, which are of the nature of absence.
What is the reason?
Because of the distinction of intrinsic nature;
for the distinction of intrinsic nature is indeed selflessness.
He explains that very point:
action is the performance of what is auspicious and inauspicious;

enjoyment is the experience of pleasure and pain; and their substratum is the appropriation [of them]. In this regard, the self (ātman) is indeed not independent but subject to another; its own nature is without a self (nirātman).
The word "self" (ātman) is a synonym for intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
But what is the reason that such an intrinsic nature is "selfless" (nirātman)? He says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "tatsvātantrya" (its sovereignty): because it possesses the characteristic of that sovereignty which exists within that substratum of action and experience,
the Self— though imagined by others as something else— is of that very nature.
Therefore, the intention is that by contrast with that [self], that which lacks independence as its intrinsic nature is "selfless" (nirātman);
this is precisely what constitutes being false in its object.
B. is form. B. is form.
Since it is so, therefore "form" (*rūpa*) is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and not merely the cessation of a self (*ātman*).
Otherwise, if *nairātmya* (selflessness) were merely a cessation, then, due to its lack of intrinsic nature, it would be utterly indefinable (*nirupākhya*);
and in that which is indefinable, [logical reasons] such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) would have no application.

Because, due to the word "and so forth" (ādi), properties of things such as being produced immediately after effort would be unsuitable as reasons, there would consequently be no comprehension of selflessness— that is, no establishment of selflessness— from reasons such as being produced;
yet this is [indeed] accepted.
If it is argued: "Therefore, for a Buddhist, *nairātmya* (selflessness) is intended neither as the mere absence of a self nor as a mere negation;

rather, because the term *nirātman* refers to and denotes a real entity (*vastu*) that is devoid of a self through the exclusion of a self, the consequence that the realization of selflessness would not follow from [the reason] 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth does not constitute a fault."

Even so, because there is contact with a real entity through the exclusion of a self, that very thing we have described— the nature of the entity— results in the selflessness (*nairātmya*) of the intrinsic nature of existence;
and yet, when existence is excluded, there is no implication of another existent.
Therefore, for Buddhists, even though there is an exclusion of selflessness (*nairātmya*) in the case of a rabbit's horn and the like, this does not establish the existence of a self;
thus, what was stated— that the same would apply to the exclusion of impermanence and selflessness— is refuted.
Not merely the exclusion of self—
[this is] autonomy.
Even for the Naiyāyikas and others, for whom the self (*ātman*) as a non-existence (*abhāva*) is not the exclusion (*vyatireka*),

but rather the very absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvābhāva*), there would be no establishment of the existence of a self through the exclusion of that non-self (*nairātmya*) which is of the nature of an entity (*bhāvarūpa*).

For this reason, even though the exclusion of selflessness (*nairātmyavyavaccheda*) occurs in cases such as a rabbit’s horn, there is no consequence of the persistence of a self; that is to say, there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or following along with a self. And just as there is no positive concomitance or following along with a self despite the exclusion of selflessness in the case of a rabbit’s horn, so too, in the case of a living body, even if there were non-selflessness—that is, even if there were an absence of selflessness—there would still be no establishment of the existence of a self.
Alternatively, it is explained otherwise:

in the context of refuting the negative-only (vyatirekin) inference as stated by the Mīmāṃsakas, he says "yasyāpi" and so forth in order to refute the negative-only inference as stated by the Naiyāyikas.

For those such as the Naiyāyikas, for whom the self (ātman) is not of the nature of non-existence (abhāva)— that is, for whom it is not a negative concomitance (vyatireka)— but rather selflessness (nairātmya) is itself of the nature of existence (bhāvasvabhāva).

For this Naiyāyika who speaks thus, there would be no establishment of the existence of a self (*ātman*) through the exclusion of a self that is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva-rūpa*), because when a positive entity is excluded, there is no implication of another positive entity; for this reason, there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) such that "wherever there is possession of breath and so forth, there is a self."

And just as there would be no unwanted consequence [of proving the self], so too, even when selflessness is absent in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), the existence of the self would not be established upon the cessation of selflessness.
Demonstrating this very point by means of a formal argument (*prayoga*),
he says "yathā" and so forth.
"This living body is not soulless, because it possesses breath and so forth"— here, "breath" (prāṇa) refers to inhalation,
and by the word "and so forth" (ādi), exhalation and other such functions are included.

In this formal argument (*prayoga*), the possession of a self (*sātmakatva*) in a living body is the property to be proven (*sādhya*). Since that self, which constitutes the subject (*pakṣa*), is not established for both [the proponent and the opponent], a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not considered. Rather, when one examines the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between the two counter-examples (*vipakṣa*)—namely, the absence of a self (*nairātmya*) and the absence of breath and so forth (*aprāṇādimattva*) corresponding respectively to the property to be proven (the self) and the reason (*hetu*) (the possession of breath and so forth)—one finds that the absence of a self exists only where there is the absence of breath and so forth; and in the absence of the pervader, the absence of breath and so forth, the pervaded, the absence of a self, is also absent.

According to the principle that [a property] does not exist in that which possesses breath and so forth, even though selflessness (*nairātmya*) itself does not exist [therein], it does not establish proof for the breath and so forth— which are intended as reasons— within the "similar class" (*sapakṣa*), namely the self; for although there is an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of selflessness as a positive entity (*bhāva-rūpa*), this does not entail (*anākṣepāt*) a positive entity characterized by non-selfhood.

Therefore, since there is no concomitance (anvaya) even when there is exclusion (vyatireka), the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are indeed only negative reasons (*vyatireki-hetu*); thus, by this much of the text, it has been shown that the opponent’s desired conclusion regarding the definition of the self (*ātman*) is not established.
Regarding this acceptance, he states the fault with the words "tathā" and so forth:
even though selflessness is being excluded from breath and the like by the exclusion of the absence of breath and the like, [it does not follow that it is excluded from the subject].

Just as [the reason] does not establish the existence of breath and so forth in the self, which serves as a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), so too, even in the subject— the living body— when non-selfhood (*nairātmya*) is excluded by reasons such as breath, it would merely be a negation;
it would not, however, establish the self.
Clarifying this very statement of the formal agreement (*grahaṇaka-vākya*), he says:
"Because of their absence in selflessness," and so forth.

Since vital breaths and the like are absent in selflessness, the vital breaths and so forth—by excluding that [selflessness]—are exclusions of mere selflessness (*nairātmya-mātra-vyavacchedaka*) and are not presenters of a self (*ātma-upasthāpaka*).
What is the reason?
Because in that case, where there is a self (sātman), the existence of breath and so forth is not established;
nor is there an establishment of the self through the exclusion of selflessness (nairātmya), which is the opposite of the self, in a living body.
What is the reason?

Because even if one demonstrates the exclusion of breath and so forth from the heterologue (*vipakṣa*)—namely, selflessness (*nairātmya*)—there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that breath and so forth are established in the homologue (*sapakṣa*), namely, the self (*ātman*).
Since this is the case...
Therefore, there is no pervasion by the contrary;
the meaning is that since there is no self in the counter-examples (vipakṣa) of both "possessing a self" and "possessing breath and so forth," the pervasion between these two is not established.
When? At any time.
Since the exclusion of selflessness from [the presence of] breath and so forth is not established,

the pervasion of the probandum's counter-example— selflessness— by the reason's counter-example— the state of lacking breath and so forth— would only be established if selflessness were excluded from breath and so forth.
And that cessation would occur only if there were a positive concomitance (anvaya);
thus he says:
"And the establishment of that [is as follows]," and so forth.
The establishment of that very absence (vyatireka) is itself the establishment of the positive concomitance (anvaya), because the latter is invariably dependent upon the former; thus,
the establishment of absence has been described as the establishment of positive concomitance.

Now, if the establishment of positive concomitance (anvaya) is not accepted, then even if the occurrence of its absence (vyatireka) were established upon that non-establishment of the positive concomitance, [the probans would remain unproven].

Even if the exclusion of that self (*ātman*)—namely, its non-existence (*nairātmya*)—is established in relation to [the subject] such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), there is still no establishment of it; for, given that the self, which would constitute the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), is unestablished, it follows that even in the case of the probandum—the living body—there would be the undesirable consequence of the self remaining unestablished despite the exclusion of non-selfhood.

Therefore, "that" means that there is no negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) devoid of positive concomitance (*anvaya*); the meaning is that there is no pervasion between the opposite of the probandum and the opposite of the probans.
Even granting this, we say:

let it be that there is a negative pervasion (vyatireka-vyāpti) lacking positive concomitance (anvaya); nevertheless, since no other alternative is possible, the absence of selflessness in a living body entails the possession of a self for that living body.
However, this method is not possible when "being uncreated" is the reason for proving "having true meaning";
thus he says, "But as for having false meaning," and so forth.

For even if "having false meaning"—which constitutes the opposite of the probandum—is excluded from the non-human (apauruṣeya) word by means of the reason consisting in its pervasion by "being human-made" (pauruṣeyatva), the fact that the uncreated possesses true meaning would still not be established.
What is the reason?
Because, apart from being true in meaning, there exists another possibility, namely being meaningless;
for this twofold classification of words—into those that are true in meaning and those that are false in meaning—would only hold if such were the case.
When falsity is removed, truthfulness must follow;
for what reason?
Because when one is removed—namely, the removal of falsity—there is no other possible state apart from truthfulness.
But there is no such thing as a duality of categories because other possibilities for their status exist;
therefore, those words might even be meaningless, so that your desired conclusion is not established—namely, the establishment of their having real objects.
If it is argued that they are not meaningless because meanings are cognized from words, [we reply:]...
This cognition of meaning is not inherent; rather, it must be a human activity, namely convention (*saṃketa*).
It is called a "human activity" by way of identity because it is the result of human activity. The meaning is that [the cognition] arises from human activity.
Like what?
This very point is explained by the words "just as," and so forth, like the conceptualization of one object from a well-known object.
If it is argued that the story of Bharata, the story of Urvaśī,

and so forth (the word "ādi" including the stories of others such as Purūravas) do not constitute the primary meaning [of the Vedas], even though they are included; and if, by the second use of the word "ādi," other Mimāṃsakas explain the meaning to be something other than the stories of Bharata and the rest— namely, specific states of being and so on, which differ from the meanings well-known in the world.
"Bharata is the sacrificial post, Urvaśī is the vessel, and Araṇi is the fire-drill," and so forth.
If it is argued that the comprehension of the meaning does not occur at all from an object conceptualized by the commentator,
he says: "In accordance with that," and so forth.
Just as in the case of the etymological explanations of words such as *bharata*, comprehension indeed occurs for certain listeners in accordance with the meanings conceptualized by commentators.
Even regarding Vedic sentences that are inherently devoid of meaning, the conceptualization of meaning would be human-made rather than produced by the nature of the words themselves. Why is this?
Because, in the case of understanding the meaning of Vedic texts, a person such as Jaimini and others must depend upon instruction.
The meaning is: "Like what? Just like words such as 'Bharata' or 'Urvaśī,' which possess alternative referents; that is, they possess alternative conceptualizations of meaning."
It is also false to claim that [words], even while manifesting their meaning by their very nature (*svabhāva*), would depend upon human instruction;
for fire and other such things do not depend on human instruction when they illuminate an object by their inherent nature (*prakṛti*).
A person, however, instructs another by expressing his own [intention] through the power of convention (*samaya*), operation, and linguistic agreement (*saṃketa*).

It is logical that one should know, "This word has been employed by me in this meaning," but it is not logical that there should be instruction from a person regarding the manifestation of meaning through the word's own nature (*prakṛti*).
Furthermore, even if the Veda were established by its very nature like an object perceived by a person, it would still require instruction from a person regarding its meanings.

At that time, since there is no distinction between these two— the object established by human convention and the object established by nature or inherent essence— insofar as both equally depend upon human instruction,
there is no other difference whatsoever by which one could be recognized as "established by man" and the other as "established by nature."

For this reason, one [type of word], the Vedic, has a natural meaning— derived from the sense of "existing in nature" (nisarga) by the suffix *ṭhak* according to the rule for words beginning with *adhyātma*—
while the other, the worldly word, has a human-made meaning; thus, [the latter] is difficult to determine.
It is difficult to understand because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes its distinction;
however, there is some correspondence with valid cognition regarding that which is natural and Vedic.
If it is argued that whatever does not follow from other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not of human origin,
we shall refute this later in the passage beginning with, "Just as there is no operation of other means of valid cognition regarding an object that is entirely beyond the senses."

Furthermore, since worldly and Vedic [utterances] share common characteristics such as the dependence upon human instruction, and differ only in their conformity with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇasaṃvāda*), if one were to postulate the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Vedic alone,
then now many more worldly utterances that conform with valid means of knowledge would have to be postulated as being authorless.

This is because there exist certain sentences composed by humans, such as "Alas, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent," and so forth, which likewise conform with valid means of knowledge.

Thinking that "of such a kind" means "consistent with valid cognition," it follows that those [Vedic words] would be non-human (apauruṣeya). Now, if even worldly speech that is consistent with valid cognition is human-made, then likewise, these intended meanings of Vedic words would also be human-made and yet consistent with valid cognition; we see no difference between Vedic words and worldly ones in this regard.
Demonstrating that Vedic words are non-human (apauruṣeya) precisely because they are mantras, he says "api ca" and so forth;
"contradictory" means mutually opposed.

For instance, since mantras are established by a certain person’s convention—that is, they are fixed by a formal agreement—it is logical that they accomplish their purpose; that is, it is logical that the accomplishment of the desired goal results from the application of the mantra.
This is the explanation provided by the passage beginning with "If these... and so forth.

If these mantras were to have a powerful author who established them as a convention (*samaya*), they would be called "conventions" because they were established by such a convention; this is the connection with what will be said hereafter.
To explain how that convention was indeed established, he says:
"Parārtha," and so forth: "devotion to the welfare of others" means being primarily concerned with the welfare of others; that is to say, it is compassion.
Out of consideration for her, or for some other reason such as fame and so forth, he might have made [this agreement];
what kind of agreement was it? To this, he says:
"Yathā" and so forth: how is this sentence composed by me? What is its nature?

"Connected with the intended purpose" means that the specific ritual procedure— characterized by such acts as invocation (*āvāhana*) and dismissal (*visarjana*)— which is intended by the author of the mantra, is the "connection" (*nibandhana*); that sentence in which this connection exists, being a factor for engagement (*pravṛtty-aṅga*), is described as such.
If there were an agreement such that "I shall join the person who employs [the rite] by employing it in this sequence with this result intended by the person," then,
through the application of the mantra, the desired object might occasionally be accomplished upon the completion of the procedure.
Just as if by some poetic convention (*kavisamaya*), someone, having composed a poem, established this rule:
"Whoever reads the poem composed by me..."
Thinking, "I must give this to him," just as there is the accomplishment of the promised object for those who recite the poetry composed by that person,
so too is the power of *bhāva* (intentional state); it is a specific power inherent in the very nature of the word by which the desired result arises,
and not from a human convention according to one's mere preference.
In that case, why would it not also occur elsewhere, even from a mantra that has been applied in some manner whatsoever?
The explanation beginning with "not so" regarding the mantra consisting of phonemes without distinction—
that the accomplishment of the purpose from mantras does not indeed arise from the convention of men— is [incorrect].
Rather,
this is the inherent nature of the mantra as a phenomenon consisting of phonemes:
that if mantras are not applied according to the prescribed rules, they do not yield results for anyone.
"Then in that case," and so forth— the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntavādī*) says:
"In that case, the nature of phonemes called 'mantras' exists everywhere, even at times devoid of injunction."
Or, if there were no distinction even when used with reversed syllables and so forth,
then the desired result would arise even from a mantra employed in any way whatsoever— transgressing the sequence of the text and the prescribed rule—
because the mantra is nothing other than the phonemes themselves; there is nothing at all distinct from the phonemes.
If it is argued that the sequence is the word-order and not the phonemes themselves,
that is incorrect;

for the distinctness of the sequence from the phonemes, as well as the claim that the sentence is the succession of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*), has already been refuted previously in this very context.
The explanation beginning with "no" [is as follows]:

even if the sequence is not distinct from the phonemes, the phonemes themselves would be the mantras; and since those phonemes are indistinguishable everywhere—in forward recitation, reverse recitation, and so forth—they would yield results whenever they are employed in any manner whatsoever.
Yet, in reality, they do not yield results.

He says "upaplava" and so forth to show that not only do [rites] fail to yield results when there is a deviation from the prescribed rules, but on the contrary, they become sources of harm (*anarthakārin*).
"Upaplava" means an affliction or calamity.
However, an excess of sound is observed even from a very slight deviation from the prescribed order of procedure.
And that [reliability] is appropriate for mantras being based on a human convention (*samaya*), but not for them being authorless (*apauruṣeya*).
If it is asked: "Even if something is based on a convention, how can there be error (*upaplava*)?", he says:

Among the injunctions prescribed by the author of the mantra beginning with "of someone" (*kasyacit*), through the performance of one particular injunction, the presence (*sannidhi*) of the deity occurs; thereafter,
due to that presence, because another specific injunction has not been fully accomplished (*asākalyena-asampādanena*).
From the displeasure and vexation of the deity, there will be calamity; in that case, the deity who has not yet abandoned passion,
being offended, brings misfortune upon oneself.
However, it should be understood that those who are free from passion do not perform it themselves; rather, other deities and so forth, being well-disposed toward them, perform it.
As for the question of how this occurs in cases where no ritual injunction whatsoever is prescribed in the mantra: [it is as follows].
He says "all," and so forth: however,

in the case of a failure in all the prescribed rules, there is neither benefit nor harm [resulting] from the non-proximity of the deity, because one has performed the ritual procedure of some particular *samaya* (convention) established by the author of the mantra.
With the words "Furthermore," etc., he states another fault:
the distinctness of the sequence from the phonemes has been refuted;
however, let it be that the sequence is either distinct from the phonemes or not distinct from them.

In that regard, if the sequence is not a distinct entity, then the mantra is of the very nature of the phonemes— that is, its essence is the phonemes themselves; however, if it were a distinct entity, then the mantra would consist of that sequence—
that is, it would consist of the sequence of phonemes.

Since that mantra—whether consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*) or consisting of their sequence—is eternal because it is not produced by causes, and because its presence is eternal, there would be the constant accomplishment of its purpose;
that is, from those mantras, the fulfillment of the aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*) would occur.
What is the reason?

For when the result to be accomplished by the mantra arises from a particular power of disposition (*bhāva-śakti*) or power of mantra (*mantra-śakti*), that power of disposition is unimpaired; thus, there can be no deficiency in the result.
This is because it is not logical for an effect to be deficient or non-existent when its cause is complete.
Why is this so?
Because it would follow that even an unimpaired cause would not be a cause if it did not produce its effect; therefore,
although mantras are eternal, the desired result does not arise from the mere employment of the mantra alone, but rather from the connection with the mantra— what is the reason for this?
If it is argued that this is because the mantra depends upon its ritual procedure (*vidhāna*), that is incorrect;

for if it is admitted that the mantra depends upon the ritual procedure and so forth, then that which is depended upon—the procedure and the rest—would lack efficacy with respect to the mantra, since no excellence (*atiśaya*) can be imparted to the mantra by them.
He explains this as follows:

If, through the ritual procedures and so forth, the mantra’s efficacy were to obtain or acquire some excellence of its own nature from something else— namely, from a certain auxiliary cause such as a particular location—
then that auxiliary, being capable of producing that excellence of the mantra’s nature, would have to be disregarded [as irrelevant].
Furthermore, it has already been stated that such production of an excellence does not occur in eternal things.

Therefore, if [the cause] were of the nature of an agent, why would it depend on mantras for the sake of producing an excellence through auxiliary factors? Consequently, the mantras would either never produce the effect at all, or they would always produce it.
If not, they would never produce an effect, because their nature, being without any increase, remains identical at all times.
Furthermore,

if such were the inherent power of mantras, then those mantras would not be the means for the attainment of results even for every person, including one joined with sins and the like, provided they were independent of the ritual observances (samaya).
Now, it might be argued that [the mantras] bestow their fruit only when employed by the sacrificer himself; to this he says:
"The distinction of the employer" means the specific quality of being the sacrificer and the dependence upon that.
It is not logical for a mantra that is unconditioned (*asaṃskārya*) [to grant results];

for if mantras were to yield results solely through their own inherent power (*bhāvaśakti*) without depending on ritual observances (*samaya*), they would not exclude any person from granting those results, nor would they exclude others such as *śūdras* and the like.
For it is not the case that the intrinsic nature of mantras—their capacity to perform an action—becomes a non-intrinsic nature or a non-productive nature with respect to one who is not a sacrificer;
why?
Because that productive nature cannot be diminished by that non-Brahmin.
Because it is not interrupted and because it is not surpassed by another, such as a sacrificer (yajamāna) or the like,
for this reason, there is a connection between the mantras and a certain person in the form of a cause-and-effect relationship.

Furthermore, because of that lack of connection, since there would be no distinction between proximity and remoteness for the mantras—whether recited by a Brāhmaṇa or by another—everyone would be able to accomplish [the ritual].

For this very reason, since this mantra is eternal and thus not subject to refinement (*asaṃskārya*), there is no one, whether a Brāhmaṇa or anyone else, who is an agent (*prayoktā*) or an instigator (*niyoktā*) regarding the action; consequently, there would be no one through whom the performer might obtain or attain the fruit to be accomplished by the mantra, [and] only a Brāhmaṇa, and no other.

For instance, just as a Śūdra or others who do not study [the Veda] perform nothing and thus are not "users" [of the ritual], so too is the Brāhmaṇa, because he does not acquire the [Vedic] refinement (*saṃskāra*) from that source.

Furthermore, even for an entity that is to be refined and in which an excellence is produced, it is indeed a difference in the substance—namely, a difference in the cause—that acts as the differentiator; yet, in the ultimate sense, there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of Brāhmaṇas, Śūdras, and the like.

The distinction between Brahmins, Śūdras, and so forth is created solely by worldly convention; therefore, because there is no inherent difference among the users— such as Brahmins and others— who are distinct from worldly conventions, no restriction regarding the power of the mantra is possible,
whereby only a Brahmin would attain the fruit and not a Śūdra.
To the question, "Where then would this restriction apply?
he says:
"It would apply at the time [of the convention]."
When the commitment (*samaya*) is the mantra, then the agent of the commitment performs the commitment without regard for the intrinsic nature of things;
there would be a restriction such as, "I shall grant the fruit only to those well-known Brahmins who are the practitioners, and not to others.
This is the explanation beginning with the word *ādheya*.
Those entities (*bhāva*) for which there is a produced (*janya*) or superadded (*ādheya*) particularity (*viśeṣa*),
when there is a difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) due to that cause of particularity—

that is, because they have acquired a specific excellence from that cause of particularity— then, having been of one nature in one place, they would be otherwise in another place due to a different cause; however, there can be no alteration of the nature of a cause when there is no such difference.
What is the reason? Because if there were no distinction in the cause, there would be no distinction in the effect.

Alternatively, if there were a distinction in the effect despite the lack of distinction in the cause, then, since that distinction in the effect is being admitted, it would follow—as has already been largely stated—that such a distinction is causeless.

Therefore, for this reason, these mantras—though they are effects and though they are impermanent—do not fail to yield their fruits due to a difference in nature produced by causes; even when employed by Śūdras and others, they would not otherwise become fruitless.
What is the reason?

If it is argued that although there is no difference in nature among the intellect, senses, and bodies of those two persons designated by the names "śūdra" and "brāhmaṇa" or "vipra," there nevertheless exists a distinction of specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) in each individual, we say:
no.
Since that [quality] exists even among Brahmins in every individual,
it is said that there is no distinction based on caste;
yet, is it not the case that in the world there is a difference in names, such as "this is a Brahmin" and "this is a Śūdra"?
If it is argued that, likewise, a distinction in conventional practices such as honor and so forth leads to the inference of a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
He said:
"No," and so forth.

Because there are distinctions in names such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so on which conform to human desire, and because there are distinctions in conventional usage such as "respectful treatment" and so on, there would be a change in the nature of things that are followed by a distinction in intrinsic nature (svabhāva) produced according to their causes—that is, things that are accompanied by a distinction in intrinsic nature arising from their respective causes.
For there is no difference in intrinsic nature; this is the connection [of the sentence].
If it is argued that there is a difference in caste between those two persons, the Brāhmaṇa and the Śūdra, that is not so.
Since that [universal] has indeed been refuted by the general negation beginning with "yasmāt sa khalu" and so forth, it is merely stated here while assuming its existence for the sake of argument.
Indeed, that very distinction of genus, though existing even in the case of an entity, is held to be threefold when there is a difference in configuration, quality, and capacity,
as in the case of a cow and a horse.

Like "cow-and-horse," the term *gavāśva* refers to the distinction of form— that is, a specific configuration— which exists as a recurring feature even among individual cows that differ from one another, but does not exist among individual horses.

The differentiation of qualities in substances such as milk and the like— consisting in the distinction of their taste, potency, post-digestive transformation, and so forth— is observed to follow along with individuals of the same class,
and not with those of a different class;
it is characterized by the capacity for an effect corresponding to a specific difference in power.
Just as the capacity for milking cows and so forth does not belong to horses,

so too, since one perceives differences in form and other characteristics that follow after individuals of the same genus, let there indeed be a difference of genus in the case of cows, horses, and the like; however, such a fixed difference in form and other characteristics does not exist among Brāhmaṇas and others by which a difference of genus could be postulated.

Furthermore, once a person has acquired proficiency regarding cows and the like, people recognize this distinction of genus— such as "this is a cow" or "this is a horse"— without instruction even when there are differences of place, time, and so forth; however,
they do not recognize the distinction between Brahmins and others in the same way without instruction.
"In the same way"— that is, like a cow and a horse—
we do not perceive even a single fixed quality in these two, the Brāhmaṇa and the Śūdra, that resides exclusively within individuals of the same genus;
the mention of "quality" (guṇa) here is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa).
Thus, we do not perceive any fixed distinction in form or distinction in capacity;
and not perceiving such a distinction in form and so forth, how could we establish a difference in caste between a Śūdra and a Brāhmaṇa?
The meaning is: "We certainly could not."

For indeed, every distinction such as study, purity, and conduct is subject to deviation; and as for the difference in physical form that is postulated— characterized by being fair-skinned, reddish-brown, or having reddish hair— that does not exist even among some Brāhmaṇas,
yet it is found among some Śūdras.
If there is no difference in caste between a Brahmin and a Śūdra, how then does this distinct cognition arise upon hearing words such as "Brahmin" and so forth? To this, he says:
"And even that which... and so on.

The association with different names is caused by specific designations such as "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth; this distinction in cognition, this difference in mental apprehension— such as the cognitions "this is a Brāhmaṇa" and "this is a Śūdra"— may arise even in the absence of a real difference in birth (jāti) due to the performance of specific activities, that is, the performance of specific rites such as recitation (*japa*) and fire-offerings (*homa*), and also due to lineage, meaning birth from a family that has performed such activities.
It is like the designations "physician" or "merchant," and so forth;
just as among Śūdras of the same genus, the designations "physician" and so on arise from the performance of specific occupations and from lineage,
yet there is no difference in their caste (jāti) by that much.
In the same way, it would also apply to the Brāhmaṇas and others.

The word "tat" (therefore) means that these mantras, when employed by an undistinguished person such as a Brāhmaṇa or a Śūdra, attain a nature that is likewise undistinguished from that of the Brāhmaṇa and others;

for that reason, they would yield results without distinction even among Śūdras and the like—this is the conclusion. Thus, this fault arises because the production of results occurs through the inherent power (*bhāva-śakti*) of the mantras; however, when a result is desired from these Vedic mantras or from other mantras based on the aforementioned human convention (*puruṣa-samaya*), [the fault does not apply].

In that case, these [mantras] would grant results without distinction; this is not a fault, because the production of results is restricted by the inclination (*ruci*) of the author of the convention (*samayakāra*), who is the composer of the mantra.
What is the reason?
Because the production of results is determined by the intention of the one who established the convention.

The author of the system (samayakāra) has expressed this preference: "I appear for the sake of the connection with the fruit only for one who possesses such a designation as 'Brāhmaṇa' and performs such a rule, and not for others. Such is the inquiry regarding the regulator of the fruit for one who has such a preference;
for it is thus: [text continues].

The meaning is that entities whose functioning consists of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) act as effects by the very state of things, independent of human activity; they deserve to be brought into a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) through that—that is, by way of their intrinsic nature—just as [one might argue]: "Since this occurs due to a specific intrinsic nature, why does it not happen here in this case as well?"
Entities do not deserve to function according to human will;
for what reason?
Because those persons, who act according to their own whims, function in whatever way [they please].
As for the claim that a distinguished practitioner obtains the fruit of the mantra,
even there we observe that the application has this very characteristic:
namely, the production of that essential nature of the mantra which is capable of achieving the human goal desired.

Even for that which has already arisen, there must be either a transformation of the continuum through the production of successive distinctions, or a change [in its state]; both of these—either production or transformation—would occur only when a distinction arises, that is, when a specific excellence is produced.
Otherwise, if no distinction were produced, what could the mantra possibly do to act as an instigator for those things (the mantras) in which no further excellence can be imparted?
He explains by means of the passage beginning with "naiva yena":
for which reason, from that application of the mantra, a certain practitioner who is a Brāhmaṇa enjoys the fruit, while another, such as a Śūdra, does not enjoy it.

The application of mantras is not their production, but rather their manifestation; if this manifestation is what is intended by "application," then that has already been refuted in the *Mānyacintā*. *In the margin:* [This refers to the discussion] regarding the nature of sound (*śabda*). If it is argued that the manifestation of a mantra is its application, we reply: no, because that manifestation was already rejected in the *Mānyacintā*. This is because manifestation is merely the removal of an obstruction, and since the mantra is eternal, there can be no such obstruction to its manifestation. Furthermore, if manifestation were a new quality produced, it would contradict the doctrine of the eternity of sound. Thus, the theory of manifestation as application is untenable.
He explains this:
for it has been stated that there is no manifestation whatsoever of eternal categories,
on account of which the speaker could be the manifester of sound.
Or let there be manifestation; and since that manifestation consists in the arising of fitness— which is eternal—
nevertheless, if the person who is the speaker of the cognition whose object is the word is joined with the fruits of the mantra through that manifestation, then that person [is the one affected].
There might also be a connection with the fruit for the listener; if one merely hears a mantra being recited by another,
there would be a conjunction with the fruit of that mantra for him as well, and not for the speaker alone.
Because the speaker is indeed the cause of manifestation and, as such, the cause of knowledge, he is connected with the result;

and since that quality of being the cause of knowledge regarding the subject matter of the mantra is equal for the listener as well, why is it that he too is not the speaker, and thus why is he not connected with the result?
He explains this with the words "For not... and so forth.
For an eternal sound, manifestation is neither a transformation of its own nature— a change in its essential form— due to some other cause, nor is it the removal of an obscuration,
since an obscuration of an eternal entity is logically impossible.
However, the cognition, intellect, or manifestation regarding that [sound]— namely, the cognition regarding sound—
is due to what cause?
Because even when the sound is not being heard, it is designated as "unmanifest."

For a sound that is not being perceived is not said to be manifested; this being the established case, if the speaker were the cause of the cognition regarding the object that is the sound, then since that nature of the speaker— which is the cause of the cognition regarding the object that is the sound— would also exist in the listener, the listener too would obtain the desired result arising from the employment of the mantra, just like the speaker.

For there is no state of being other than that of the speaker; the state of being a speaker is nothing other than the cause of the cognition of that [word], which is to say, the cause of the cognition of the word.
Therefore, since there is no difference between the speaker and the listener in their being the cause of the knowledge of the word, the connection with the result would be equal for both.
The cognition whose condition (*upādhi*) is the speaker who is another is "cognition conditioned by another" (*paropādhibuddhi*);
it belongs to the listener, not to the speaker; it is not the cognition conditioned by another belonging to the speaker.

If it is argued that there is a distinction between the speaker and the listener for this reason, what, then, is the utility [of the speaker]? What is the capacity of the speaker toward the generation of cognition in the listener,
by virtue of which capacity the speaker is accepted as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)?
If it is argued that the hearing of sound—that is, the perception of sound—occurs for the listener from the presence of the speaker, and therefore that speaker is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*);
[we reply: is this not precisely what is being questioned? How is it that the hearing of sound occurs for the listener from the presence of that speaker?
And how could it not arise from that?
Because of the absence of a relationship,
due to the absence of the state of being the beneficiary and the benefactor.
Demonstrating that very absence, he says:
"Due to the presentation of the object—that is, due to the bringing near of the object—this speaker would become a hearer of this listener; he would be one who causes [the meaning] to be heard."
Furthermore, that manifestation is not possible for that sound because,
being eternal, it cannot undergo transformation in any way and lacks any change of state.
If it is argued that the speaker would be of service by effecting a refinement of the listener’s sense organ or by bringing about the removal of an obscuration of the sound,
that is not so;
for the refinement of the sense organ and the other such factors have already been mentioned and refuted.

If it is argued that there is a distinction between the speaker and the listener based on two types of cognition (*pratyaya*), as follows: by the statement "the sense organ would be conditioned; he would hear all of that," the listener has the cognition, "This speaker is making me hear," and the speaker has the corresponding cognition, "I am making this listener hear"; therefore, from these two cognitions, there is a distinction between the speaker and the listener according to their respective roles.
In *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.258,
he refutes [the opponent's position] with the verse beginning "anupakārya" (that which cannot be assisted).
The notions "he makes me hear" and "I hear" are mere delusions;
for what kind of relationship could there be between one who is not benefited and one who benefits?
The beneficiary is the listener.
A speaker who provides assistance does not exist in that which is mere error; thus it has been stated.

Furthermore, since there is in every respect an absence of human activity toward the production of cognition regarding an eternal word, the relationship between the assisted and the assister has been established as non-existent.
Therefore, if that [cognition] were to exist from such mere error...

In the absence of a distinction between speaker and listener, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga); for it would follow that this would apply to everyone, even to those who do not cause others to hear and those who do not hear.
What is the reason?
Furthermore, since even in cases such as those of the insane, one observes the occurrence of cognitions like "I hear" through delusion even without hearing a sound,
and since such a cognition occurs even when there is no assistance whatsoever, the cognition "I am causing [the sound] to be heard" and so forth is not tenable.
What is the reason?

Since there would be the undesirable consequence that for all things—which are neither mutually assisted nor assisters—one could say, "I hear this from him," and so forth, [the opponent] might argue: "Just as cognitions arise through delusion regarding those who are insane, let it be the same with respect to eternal things. To this, he says:
"Delusion," and so on.

Even the delusion that occurs to a person who is insane arises— when, in a state of sanity, some benefit has been received from another person and a corresponding cognition has been produced— by virtue of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by that [cognition], so that it occurs again during the state of insanity even toward something else, through some proximity or similarity, even though [the object] is not being spoken of.
Furthermore, that error would not occur even through an extremely remote lineage if there were no assistance [provided] toward the eternal mantras.

With the words "Therefore," etc., he concludes the subject at hand: since there is no distinction between the speaker and the listener in being the cause of manifestation or the cause of the cognition of the word according to the aforementioned rule, their connection with the fruit of the mantra would be equal.
Even the status of being a cause for manifestation does not exist at all in eternal things; this is stated merely by way of concession.
Furthermore, with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth, he states another refutation.

"Unmanifested" means that those vocal organs, such as the palate and so forth, by which sound has not been brought within the range of the sense of hearing are "organs with unmanifested sound. The connection [of the sentence] is made by changing the gender: "the employment, that is, the operation, of those organs would be useless," where silent recitation (*upāṃśujapa*) is performed merely by the movement of the lips and other parts.
The meaning of the sentence is that [the latter] would be useless;
where there is not even the movement of the lips and so forth, but merely the mental contemplation of the mantra, that is *manojapa*.
The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Furthermore, mental recitation would be useless because sound is within the range of the ear; indeed, sound is that which is grasped by the ear,
and a mantra has the nature of sound.
Furthermore, because the two types of recitation—the whispered (*upāṃśu*) and the mental (*mānasa*)—are not perceived by the ear, they lack the quality of being "sound" (*śabda*);
and due to this lack of sound, they lack the status of being "mantra. How, then, could one who performs such recitation be successful in obtaining the fruit?
"Grasping" (*grahaṇa*) means that which is grasped (*gṛhyate*).
The meaning is "that which is perceivable by the ear"; that sound which has that very quality as its defining characteristic is described as such,
because otherwise there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If, setting aside sound as that which is grasped by the ear, one maintains that things such as mental recitation—which are of the nature of cognition—are "sound," then taste and other [sensory objects] would also have to be "sound. To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) replies: "No; for even if that which is within the range of the ear has the nature of sound, it does not follow that the universal 'soundness' (śabdatva-sāmānya) must possess the nature of sound."
We do not say that sound is exclusively the object of the auditory faculty;
rather, we say that sound necessarily has that as its characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being apprehended by the ear.
Why?
Since there is no other definition for sound apart from its being perceivable by the sense of hearing,

if— within this very definition of the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of sound— one posits a person as the cause of the manifestation of mantras, which possess the nature of sound, and as the cause of the cognition that grasps the essential form of sound— and if that person is intended to have a connection with the fruit [of the ritual],
then [this would apply] to those sounds whose objects have not yet been manifested to the ear.

The analysis of the compound is: "that sound which is the object of hearing (śruti-viṣaya) is that which is unmanifested by certain causes"; the "agent" (prayoktā) of those causes is the one who sets them in motion merely by the movement of the lips and so forth.
One who mutters [the mantra] in a whisper is not joined with the fruit of the mantra, nor is one joined with the fruit of the mantra by muttering it mentally;
for at that time—during the period of silent muttering—one does not perceive or grasp any object called sound with the ear.
He says that mental muttering, too, is a mantra.
Nor is mental conceptualization (mānasa-vikalpa) the mantra, because mantra is non-verbal in nature; for sound is admitted to be perceptible by the ear, to be non-human (apauruṣeya), and eternal,
whereas conceptualization is the opposite of these.
With the words "pāramparye" and so forth, he anticipates the opponent's objection:
even that mental cognition which appears as a mantra at the time of silent or mental recitation is a manifestation (*tadvyakti*), that is,
a cognition of the manifestation of that sound.
Why?
Because it is produced through a succession,
that is, because it is born from sound.

For instance, since the knowledge of the word arises for him beforehand, and because the appearance of the word gradually arises during mental recitation (*manojapa*) for one who has been infused with a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) by that prior knowledge,
[the author] explains this with the words "not so" and so forth:
"Indeed, even for a reciter who meditates with the mind, the cognition in which the mantra appears does not arise without [prior] hearing."

Since that cognition arises from a word produced by a word even without hearing the sound, that cognition at the time of mental recitation (*manojapa*) is indeed a manifestation of sound, which is to say, it is the very knowledge of the word; therefore,
because mental recitation and so forth have the nature of mantra, the practitioner of such recitation shall obtain the fruit— this is the intended meaning.
If it were thus, there would be an infinite regress regarding the nature of mantra through a continuous succession.
He states this very point in the passage beginning with "śabda" (sound), etc.:
from the sound that is the definition of mantra, there arise conceptual constructions of meaning—namely, conceptual constructions of the meaning of the sound.
For instance, when it is said, "Svāhā to Agni," [the following occurs].

Conceptual constructions (vikalpa) such as "fire has a blazing, radiant form" and so forth sometimes arise; since these too have their origin in words through a traditional lineage, those conceptual constructions would likewise be applications characterized by the manifestation of mantras.
Even though [the mantra] originates from words, that which has them as its purpose—that is, that whose object (viṣaya) is the meaning—is the word. This is the analysis of the compound.
If that very cognition is the manifestation of the word and not the conceptual constructions regarding objects which have words as their domain,

then the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) states: "It is unestablished," meaning that it is unestablished that the conceptual construction of a word has the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the word as its object.
What is the reason?
Because it follows from conceptual construction, that is,
because it has conceptualizations of a similar kind as its cause.
He explains [the objection] with the words "mental conceptualizations have as their objects only superimposed forms, not [real things]," and so forth:
"We do not say that every cognition arising from a word is a manifestation of that [object], nor that it is a manifestation of the word."
However, the claim that the conceptual cognition regarding that [object], which has sound as its object,
is the manifestation (vyakti) of that sound, is incorrect.
Since it is unestablished that mental consciousness has sound as its object—

because we shall demonstrate that words do not function with respect to specific individualities (*svalakṣaṇa*)— if external objects are not the cause of conceptual constructions, how then do they arise? He says:
"Those indeed," and so forth:
for those conceptual constructions (vikalpas), "according to their own" means that whatever awakening of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) is their cause,
they exist internally by virtue of being established within consciousness.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: it refers to those by whom there is the presence—meaning the proximity—of external objects, which occurs independently [of such objects] due to the awakening of the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Why is this so?
Regarding the phrase beginning with "external" and so forth:
*apāya* means cessation;
*anāgama* means non-arising.
Since conceptual constructions cease to exist when external objects are suppressed or do not arise,
and because they occur even in the absence of an object, they are therefore not caused by objects.
For what reason?

For that which does not depend upon the proximity of existence (*sattopadhāna*)—that is, the presence of being—for its own existence, being independent, is neither a cause nor a non-cause for that [existence].

Since it is thus, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not the object of words; therefore, mental conceptual construction characterized by "mental joy" (*manojalpa*) and so forth is not the manifestation of a word, by virtue of which it would possess that [word].
A person possessing mental recitation (*manojapa*) would be the performer of the mantra, or rather, he would not be so at all— this is the sense.
In the margin:
Even while accepting the manifestation of sound (*śabdābhivyakti*), he states the fault:

"The cognition produced by the sound has that [sound] as its object; the manifestation of the sound is its locus, since the person is the locus of that manifestation, therefore he is the 'user' (*prayoktṛ*). This is stated even in this position.

What is meant by the consequence that the listener would also be the performer? For the listener, too, is the substratum (*āśraya*) for the cognition arising within his own continuum which is produced by the sound and has that [sound] as its object; and thus, he too would be joined with the fruit of the mantra.

Furthermore, the application (*prayoga*) of eternal mantras does not consist in the production of some excellence; rather, the application is the knowledge regarding them. And if that knowledge is accepted as the application, how could the word (*śabda*) be active with respect to a person?
Because knowledge is produced for that person,
the person does not exert effort toward the word;
why is this so?
Since no benefit whatsoever can be conferred upon the eternal self, which is of the nature of sound, by the person,
yet it is said that "the person is the user of words"— this is an extraordinary convention;
for in the world, he who exerts effort toward something is called its "user."
The conclusion is stated with the words "in every way" and so forth:
whether the cognition produced directly from the word is the "word-cognition," or [the cognition] through a succession of steps.

If the attainment of the desired result is sought through the employment of mantras, which by their very nature consist of sound, by generating knowledge regarding that object, then mental recitation (manojapa) is useless.
Why?
Because the conceptual construction characterized as mental recitation does not touch upon the actual form of the sound.
To the question, "Even for one who [accepts] that the fruit arises from convention (*samaya*), how could mental recitation (*manojapa*) not be useless?

he says: The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound is its own intrinsic nature (*svasvabhāva*); the form appearing in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is their common nature (*sāmānyasvabhāva*). When there is the intention to express these—intrinsic and common natures—as a single entity, by unifying the perceived (*dṛśya*) and the conceptualized (*vikalpita*), the author of the convention speaks; because of the formulation of the mantra, mental recitation would otherwise be useless. Thus, there is no contradiction.
Because the result is accomplished by fulfilling the intention of the author of the convention, there is no lack of contradiction regarding the actual entity; rather, there is indeed a contradiction.
For it is thus:

When the attainment of the fruit [arises] from the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the entity that is the word, mental recitation (*manojapa*) is useless because it does not touch upon the real entity; this he explains with the words "by convention" (*samayena*), and so forth.

One should, by means of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), synthesize according to worldly usage—that is, without overstepping common worldly practice—the particular characteristic of the word, which is the object of the auditory faculty, and the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which is the appearance in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Having unified, through the conceptualizing intellect, the visible and the conceptualized—the particular characteristic of the word and the form of the universal—one should announce the convention.

"Whoever performs the recitation of the mantra composed by me with both speech and mind, for him this mantra shall accomplish its purpose according to the prescribed time. Therefore, there is no fault in reciting this mantra with the mind or through mental repetition (*manojapa*), and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), practices such as whispered recitation (*upāṃśu*) are also encompassed.
For one who recites this mantra with speech and mind, it shall accomplish its purpose at the appropriate time; thus, there is no defect in mental recitation and the like.
The use of the term "etcetera" includes the employment of whispered recitation and other such methods.

However, if it is maintained that the result arises from a mantra whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is that of a real entity (*vastu*), then when there is contact with that which lacks such an intrinsic nature—as in the case of mental recitation (*manojapa*) and so forth—there would be no result.
With the words "as has been stated," etc., he anticipates the opponent's intention.
As has been stated:
If it is argued that since a mantra is nothing but the phonemes themselves,
there is no sequence distinct from the phonemes,
and therefore, in the absence of such a sequence, there would be no difference in effect— characterized by a difference in cognition— between hearing the word *sara* and hearing the word *rasa*.
For indeed, there is no difference whatsoever in the phonemes between words such as *sara* and *rasa*; for the very same phonemes that occur in the word *sara* are present in the word *rasa*.
Nor is there any other distinct word from which the difference in effect— characterized by a difference in cognition— could arise;
yet a difference in effect does exist,
since we observe a distinct manifestation of cognition (*pratibhā*) for those two words, "sara" and "rasa."
We observe that the sequence itself is incomparable and distinct in its two ends, yet the phonemes remain the same;
and it is not logical for there to be a difference in the effect—characterized by a difference in cognition—when there is no difference in the cause, which is the phoneme.
Therefore, even though the phonemes are non-different, there exists a distinct cognition for each word that possesses differentiation.

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) maintains that this sequence is real, because there is a difference in cognition— a difference in the intellect— regarding words such as "sara" and so forth, due to a sequential order consisting of distinct steps.
It is true that there is a sequential order in the various paths leading to truth; however, that sequence is dependent upon persons, is human in origin,
and is not distinct from the phonemes themselves.
Furthermore, different phonemes arise at every step, and others arise as well, due to a difference in their causes;
it is solely because of the similarity among them that those of dull intellect determine them to be one and the same. Demonstrating this very point, he says:
Regarding the phrase "for thus" (*tathā hi*) and so forth, the collective meaning here is as follows:

by means of the mind that gives rise to each preceding phoneme, residing in the speaker, the mind that gives rise to each subsequent phoneme is produced; thus, [the sequence of phonemes arises] from the sequence of the producing minds.

The process of the arising of the phonemes produced by that [cognition] is as follows: auditory cognitions, which have their respective objects as domain, are produced directly by the phonemes arising in succession;
and likewise, memories having those phonemes as their objective support arise in succession.
Therefore, from the sequence of the cognition that originates the phonemes, there is a causal sequence in the effect.
And that which is the causal sequence in the cognitions of their respective objects is established as "succession" (anupūrvī); thus it is now [said]:
"the sound which is produced"—this is the connection [of the words].
Just as in the word "sara," the vowel *a* following the letter *sa* arises from the cognition produced by the knowledge of the origination of that specific phoneme.

The letter *sa* occurs at an earlier time; and that which is the letter [itself] is "the letter" (*yadvarṇaḥ*). It is the origination (*samutthāna*)—that is, the cause (*kāraṇa*)—of that letter, because it is by means of this that [the letter] originates (*samuttiṣṭhati*).
The term *yadvarṇṇasamutthāna* is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which has the arising of a particular phoneme," and the knowledge that arises from that is [the knowledge of phonemes].

The meaning is this: from that knowledge which arises from the knowledge of the origination of the phoneme, there arises the knowledge that originates the letter *sa*; from that knowledge which originates the letter *a*, the letter *a* is produced once it has arisen.
In the same way, it should be applied that each subsequent phoneme arises from the knowledge of the origination of each preceding phoneme.
Thus far, it has been explained that the phonemes are effects because they arise sequentially from the sequential origination-knowledge residing within the continuum of the speaker.

Now, demonstrating that these phonemes—having arisen sequentially—become the causes for the sequential cognitions of their own objects residing in the continuum of the hearer, and are thus known, he says:
Regarding the phrase "having that as its adjunct" and so forth: that subsequent phoneme, which has the preceding phoneme as its specific adjunct, is thus described;
that [subsequent] phoneme is apprehended—that is, grasped—by *śruti*, which is auditory cognition.
In the margin:

But surely, the preceding phoneme does not exist at the time of the succeeding phoneme; how then can the succeeding phoneme be perceived as having that [preceding] phoneme as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)?
He said:
"The cognition produced by that cognition.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: it is that which has a cognition of its own object produced by that previous cognition whose object was the preceding phoneme.
This is what is meant:

when the auditory consciousness has the letter *sa* as its object, at that very moment, the letter *a* is produced by a mind that brings about the *a*. Thus, the letter *a* and the condition consisting of the letter *sa* as its object are simultaneous.

In this context, the meaning is that the letter *a*, while producing a cognition of its own object in conjunction with the auditory consciousness which has the letter *sa* as its object, is said to be "perceived" as qualified by the preceding phoneme (*pūrvavarṇopādhi*).
Thus, being produced by that preceding cognition acting as a cooperative cause,
what kind of subsequent phoneme is it at the time of hearing?

When a phoneme is uttered slowly and not hurriedly, it is called *apaṭuśruti*. In that state, the auditory cognition (*śrotravijñāna*) is "not acute" (*apaṭu*), meaning it is slow-moving and perceives the phonemes as clearly distinguished;
that is to say, it is the state in which the distinct phonemes are discerned.

When [the word] is pronounced too rapidly, because the individual phonemes cannot be distinguished, how can there be the production of memory in a sequential order? It is for the purpose of demonstrating this that the term "imperfect hearing" (*apaṭuśruti*) is employed;
for what function does such a phoneme perform?
In the margin:
He says,
"depending on the memory of that, [namely] the memory of the preceding phoneme."
Afterwards, it produces and generates a memory within itself regarding its own object.
It should be understood as being "by way of succession.
By this, it is stated that phonemes are the causes of cognitions regarding their own objects in a sequential manner;
thus, by the sequence already mentioned, this relationship of cause and effect is established.
Regarding the phrase "in the phonemes" (*varṇeṣu*), it means that [the sequence] has the phonemes as its substratum; that is to say,
even in the case of human [speech],
it is said in the world that the succession is indeed produced by a person.
In response to the question, "With respect to what do the phonemes possess the state of being an effect and the state of being a cause? he says:
"of the cognitions that grasp their causes.
This is a *dvandva* compound meaning "the causes and the graspers."
The compound *varṇānāṃ hetugrāhiṇī* is a genitive tatpuruṣa;

subsequently, it forms a descriptive (karmadhāraya) compound with the word *cetas*. If the cognitions (*cetāṃsi*) are the causes of the phonemes (*varṇa*) in successive order, then by virtue of their connection, the phonemes possess a sequential status as effects (*kāryatā*).
Since phonemes are produced by those cognitions,
the causal status of the phonemes occurs sequentially through their connection with those cognitions which apprehend them.
Because those vocal expressions are produced by minds that grasp at colors, he explains them with the words "mind" (*citta*) and so forth;
that vocal intimation for which mind is the motivating cause (*samutthāna-kāraṇa*) is described in that way.
Speech itself is communication because it makes others understand;

and that is threefold in the world, as he says beginning with "phonemes" (*varṇa*). The analysis of the compound is: that of which the designations are phonemes, words (*pada*), and sentences (*vākya*).
In this context, "syllables" (akṣara) are phonemes (varṇa); a collection of phonemes delimited by meaning is a "word" (pada);
and a collection of words is a "sentence" (vākya).

Regarding the passage beginning with "therein" (*tatra*) and ending with "the lake" (*sara*): in the word *sara*, there is the letter *sa*; after that is the vowel *a*; after that is the letter *ra*; after that is the vowel *a*; and after that is the *visarjanīya*.
In this context, the cause for the arising of the letter *sa* is the mind; by means of that mind acting as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

The inclusion of the term "immediately following" (*samanantara*) is for the purpose of excluding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); it refers to that mind by which the letter *a* is raised— that is, the letter *a* is produced or generated.

It is produced in that manner according to the sequence already described; the letter *r*, the vowel *ā*, and the *visarjanīya* are raised up by those mental states (*citta*). The analysis of the compound is as follows: "those for which each preceding mental state is the condition (*pratyaya*), that is, the cause. Thus, each preceding mind serves as the causal condition for the subsequent ones.

In that case, the vowel *a* arises through a mind that originates the vowel *a*; immediately after that, the consonant *r* arises through a mind that originates the consonant *r*, acting as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*);
and finally, the visarga arises through a mind that originates the visarga.

Now, if a word is uttered with the intention, "I shall utter this word," then the sequence of phonemes is uttered by that very same intention; it is not the case that each individual phoneme is preceded by a separate intention, because such is not perceived.
How then can it be said that the mind which originates the letter *sa* produces the mind that originates the letter *ā*?
It is thought thus: [the former serves as a condition for the latter].
In the pronunciation of phonemes, this is indeed the sequence;
likewise, in the pronunciation of words as well, this is the very same sequence at the outset.
For instance:
One utters the letter *sa* with the intention of uttering the letter *sa*; likewise, one utters each subsequent letter with the intention of uttering each subsequent letter.
However, some maintain that when a word is uttered through practice, the sole cause is the intention to utter the word as a whole;
others, however, hold a different view.
It is true that, upon the utterance of a word, there is only a single intention [to speak] as the cause.
At the very time of the utterance of the letter *sa*, the mind necessarily exists; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of death.

That very mind is said to be the originator (*samutthāpaka*) of the letter *sa*, because the letter arises immediately thereafter. In this same manner, the status of being the originator of the mind should be understood for each subsequent phoneme.
