And here, by the passage beginning with "by the mind that originates the letter *sa* as its immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*), it is stated that the sequence of phonemes has a single agent as its cause for the cognition of meaning, and not different agents; therefore, what is said by Maṇḍana— that if sequence is the causal relation, then it belongs to the cognitions that grasp it— [is refuted].
"Or, even when there is a difference in speakers, the cognition [of the word] would arise from the identity of its cause, which is the self; thus the *sphoṭa* is established.
(Verse 31) This is refuted because it is not admitted that the identity of the cognitions apprehending phonemes produced by different agents is the cause for the comprehension of meaning.
And as for what was said by Maṇḍana—

that even if the comprehension of meaning occurs through the sequence of phonemes via the sequence of the mind that produces them, nevertheless, that sequence, being indicative (*jñāpaka*), depends upon cognition;
and it is observed that the knowledge of meaning arises from words uttered by a speaker who is hidden or obstructed—
Furthermore, no one is able to ascertain the causal relationship between the motivating mind and its effect in that case;
for such a relationship could only be ascertained if there were oneness of the eye, independent of the cognition of sound—
and there is no proof for the oneness of a speaker who is either concealed or obstructed.
That is incorrect,
because even in a state where [the speaker] is hidden or obstructed, the oneness of the speaker is indeed ascertained by some;
for instance:

In the world, activity is observed to be preceded by the cognition that "Devadatta is calling me, not Yajñadatta"; where there is no such ascertainment, there is no activity. Thus, our desired conclusion is indeed established. Furthermore, even for the proponent of *sphoṭa*, how can there be a manifestation of the *sphoṭa* in cases such as when it is in a concealed state, since there is no ascertainment of the manifesting phonemes (*varṇa*) being produced by a single agent?
Furthermore, some maintain that the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* must necessarily be accepted there; otherwise, the comprehension of meaning would not occur—
but this is merely something trivial.
In the margin:
"Therefore, these phonemes have different causes" means that for each [phoneme], there is a distinct, successive mind that serves as its cause— that is, the originator.
Their own causes are precisely the cognitions that produce them; those whose birth occurs according to their sequence—that is, their order—are so described.
The meaning is that phonemes arise sequentially due to the sequence of their causes.
And by this much...
Explaining the statement, "That sound which is known through the cognition arising from the knowledge of the origin of its specific color (articulation) is determined by audition," he says:

Regarding the phrase "at the time of hearing" (*śrutikāle*) and so forth: even at the time of hearing—that is, at the time of listening—when they are "moving slowly," meaning when they are pronounced not too rapidly;
those phonemes which depend upon that very cognition having the preceding phoneme as its object as a cooperative condition (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) are described in that way.
What do those things of such a nature do?
They produce their own cognition, namely, auditory consciousness, which has themselves as its object.

For instance, at the very moment that auditory consciousness has *sa* as its object, the phoneme *a* is likewise produced by a mind that brings about the manifestation of *a*; thus, the phoneme *a* and the cognition having *sa* as its object exist simultaneously. Therefore, the phoneme *a*, together with the cognition having *sa* as its object acting as its concomitant cause (*sahakārin*), produces a cognition of its own object.
This same principle should be applied to the other phonemes as well.

The word *tadā* means: when they have produced the cognition of experience regarding their own objects, then—depending precisely upon that recollection whose object is the preceding phoneme—they merge into recollection; that is, they ascend into recollection.
The meaning is that they are remembered in the very same sequence in which they were experienced.
This is the connection: "this very nature of the phonemes is characterized by non-simultaneity."
To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says "distinct," and so forth;
because it is produced by preceding preceding cognitions, its state as an effect is distinct.

Because they serve as the causes for each subsequent cognition, there is a distinct causal relationship among those cognitions that give rise to [the letters] *sa* and so forth; these very things, having a distinct causal relationship, are the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the causes (*hetu*).
The analysis of the compound is as follows: that which has as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) a characteristic (*dharma*) whose very essence is the production—that is, the arising—from them.
By this, it has been stated that phonemes possess the nature of being effects in relation to the cognitions that cause them;
now he states their nature as causes in relation to the cognitions that apprehend them.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that which has as its characteristic (lakṣaṇa) or intrinsic nature (svabhāva) the very act of producing—that is, bringing about—the effect, which is a distinct cognition."

Such a sequence, which is of the nature of the phonemes (*varṇa*) and differentiated by the distinctions of human articulation (*puruṣasaṃskāra*) as well as by the distinctions of human effort (*puruṣaprayatna*), is called "sequence" (*krama*).
Now, since sequence is a property (*dharma*) of the phonemes, how can that which is of the nature of the phonemes itself be called "sequence"?
It is thought thus [in response].
There is no sequence for those [phonemes] that arise simultaneously, because such a sequence is not perceived; therefore, sequence belongs only to phonemes that arise non-simultaneously.
If phonemes are held to arise non-simultaneously, then that very [sequence] is what is found in the world, for it is not perceived as something distinct from the phonemes themselves.
Nor is their sequence a single entity, because they do not exist simultaneously; nor is each individual [phoneme] the sequence, because the sequence is not perceived in them individually.
Therefore, it has been stated that phonemes produced non-simultaneously are themselves called "sequence."
This convention of "sequence" for these [phonemes] is merely imagined;
for the very sequence that is perceived in the world in the word *sara* is not the same as that in the word *rasa*,
nor does the nature of the preceding and following phonemes exist apart from their sequence.
Therefore, the intrinsic nature of phonemes in each individual word is indeed distinct;
and the world itself perceives the difference between the word *sara* and the word *rasa*.
Thus, as it has been stated by Maṇḍana:
Let it be granted that the phonemes (*varṇa*) are distinct according to those who maintain they are produced;

however, their specific distinction is not the cause of the cognition of meaning. This is because the *sphoṭa* has been established [as the cause], since that [distinction] cannot be determined, and because it is not perceived at the time of the convention (*saṃketa*). (Sphoṭasiddhi 30)
That is refuted because the sequence of phonemes *rasa* is perceived as entirely distinct from the sequence of phonemes *sara*; furthermore,
phonemes do not appear apart from their sequence.

Therefore, the determination of the difference between letters is simply the determination of the difference in their sequence; because of their similarity, the difference between one word for "rasa" and another word for "rasa" is not perceived.
For this very reason, it is logical that [the word] conveys the meaning of the word "rasa," since it was observed as such at the time of the convention.
The same applies to any other term; thus, this [objection] is trivial.
Demonstrating this very point, he says "something else indeed," and so forth.
Since the nature of the phonemes is as previously described and is called "sequence," for that reason,
although that form— which is determined as a unity due to similarity— is [actually] distinct from the phonemes, every single word (*pada*) is indeed different. What is the reason?

Since the motivating mind alone is the agent, it is distinct from the mental formation [of the action] because of the difference in its capacity; thus, it is said to be "distinct" and "conjoined," uttered according to the sequence of prior and subsequent.
"By the phrase 'producing a difference in the effect,' it means that it produces a difference in cognition; and it is not the case that the phonemes are themselves devoid of meaning."
Since this has already been established previously, how can it be said that the nature of the phonemes (*varṇa*), when combined, produces a distinction in the effect?
On this point, some hold the following view:
Regarding what was said: "The specific form of each individual phoneme is distinct and is a human-made denoter, not something non-human-made."
It is true that she exists, but it is incorrect [to say] that she has the person as her locus.
Since phonemes, whether combined or uncombined, do not convey meaning, this is the intended sense:
if the sequence of phonemes were real in the ultimate sense, then that [sequence], being conceptualized as the form of a single word and so forth, would be the conveyor of meaning.

And since the sequential phonemes, having been made objects by a single conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*), are expressive, it follows that because they appear within a single conceptual cognition, the combined form of these sequential phonemes is said to produce a distinct effect; thus there is no fault.
Furthermore, their difference [from other words] arises from the difference in their producers (*samutthāpaka*).
Therefore, there is certainly not just a single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) for phonemes in words such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*;
what is the reason?
Because they differ according to the distinction in the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the agent's mind.

And that is the agent of the cognition of the object; it is the differentiation of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) through the differentiation of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), which results in a differentiation of capacity. Because of this, there is a differentiation in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the phonemes.

And that differentiated intrinsic nature of the phonemes, which consists in their sequential form, becomes associated with a single conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); thus, it is the cause of the differentiation of the effect, namely, the differentiation of the cognition whose object is the meaning.

And this causal relationship characterized by a specific sequence—that sequence of phonemes has come into operation; it is produced from a person who creates the composition, for he "creates the composition" (racanākṛt). From whom [did it arise]? He says: from that [person].

With the words "icchetyādi" and so forth, he explains that for those phonemes whose establishment is not contradicted by human desire, [the sequence] must be produced due to the contradiction of an established order,
as indicated by the phrase "kāryetyādinā."
The analysis of the compound is: "those conditions which have become cause and effect.
Thus, the minds that give rise to the phonemes are so called;
for they are effects in relation to the preceding consciousness and causes in relation to the subsequent consciousness.
The specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) produced from those [phonemes] is called "succession" (*ānupūrvī*).
And since that succession is brought about by the initial mental application (*vitarka*) and sustained investigation (*vicāra*) of a person, the phonemes do not have a fixed order.
Initial mental application (*vitarka*) is a conceptualization (*vikalpa*) in the form of deliberation, such as "Is this it, or is that it?"
Why is it that the form of the certainty "this is indeed [it]" is *vicāra* (investigation), while the desire and so forth do not abide in that sequence?
The sequence in which accomplishment is not contradicted by one's will is "icchā’viruddhasiddhiḥ"; those [beings] for whom such a sequence exists are so described,
and the state of being that is what is meant by "tasmāt" (therefore).
For instance,
just as the sequence of phonemes is established according to one's desire, what is there to wonder at?
Just as there is a sequence following the specific order of particular actions—
just as there is a sequence established by the desire for particular actions such as contraction and so forth—
[the author] states the dissimilarity (vaidharmya) with the words "for it is not," and so on.
Regarding "of place and time," it means situated in a place...
[text fragment]...
The connection is that it is not possible to do so;

for indeed, it cannot be made by human will that "let the Vindhya be in the place of the Malaya, and let the Malaya be in the place of the Vindhya," nor can it be made that "first let there be the sprout, and afterwards let that which produces it arise from the seed.
However, phonemes (*varṇa*) can indeed be reversed according to one's desire.
Therefore, phonemes do not possess a fixed order; for that very reason...

because the sequence of phonemes exists when there is a sequence of conceptual constructions standing in a cause-and-effect relationship, and because the sequence of phonemes does not exist when the sequence of conceptual constructions is absent.

In worldly sentences, the causal relationship between the sequence of phonemes and persons is established: the person is the cause and the sequence of phonemes is the effect. From that establishment of the causal relationship, it follows that all other Vedic phonemes...
thus, just as it is logical that every instance of burning is preceded by fuel, so too is this case.

One side of the leaf is torn, with approximately thirty-two letters missing in each line. He explains [the verse] beginning with *sati*: "When fuel exists, that which functions as burning (*dāha-vṛtti*) is called 'burning' (*dāha*)," meaning it is the act of burning itself.
Since there is no fire in the absence of fuel,

once the causal relationship between fire and fuel has been established in some instances, then even that fire for which fuel is not observed— indeed, for which no fuel is seen at all— is likewise [established].
...then, because that fire would lack a cause for its restriction to a specific place and a specific time,
it would exist everywhere and at all times.
Now, if it is maintained that [fire] occurs in a certain place and so forth by way of necessity,
then, since that very place and so forth is desired to be the fuel for the fire when there is such a restriction of place, what is the cause?
"Conflagration," and so forth;
[this refers to] the material cause of the conflagration...

because if there were no dependence [on causes], a restriction by place and time would be impossible; likewise, if this sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) did not depend on the effort of a person acting as its cause, then—being without support, without basis, and independent of human effort—it would manifest of itself. Even when a person exerts the effort thinking, "I am pronouncing this sequence of phonemes," it would be impossible for that sequence of phonemes to be manifested.
Why is that?
Because...
[the text is incomplete]...
If the sequence [of the Veda] were dependent on the power of a person, then, when some such power is postulated, the entire sequence of phonemes in the Veda would likewise be human-made;
why so?
Since there is no difference between the sequences of letters in worldly [texts] and Vedic [texts],
and since a specific effect characterized by the removal of poison and so forth is observed even in worldly cases; furthermore,
because [the result] occurs when that [knowledge] exists, it depends on the person...

...and since the Vedic sequence of phonemes is not distinguished from the worldly sequence of phonemes— such as that used for removing poison and so forth— if it were produced by someone other than [the Lord], then in every case where human authorship is accepted, the relationship of cause and effect would also be refuted.
Why [is it called] "positive concomitance" (anvaya), and so forth?
Positive concomitance (anvaya) is the presence [of the effect] when that [cause] is present.
In the absence of that [cause], there is an absence [of the effect]; this is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), because it is defined by that [characteristic]. Thus, [it is] the effect...
If [the relation of] being an effect is not accepted [in this case],
then another definition of the causal relation, distinct from "arising when that exists," must be stated,
such that in its absence the causal relation between human effort and the Vedic [mantras] would not exist.
And there is no other characteristic of the causal relationship [than this]. Now,
if the worldly sequence of phonemes is accepted as artificial, even though the characteristic of the causal relationship is the same...
[these] logical fallacies follow.
What is the reason?
Because even in the case of jars and the like, such a conceptual construction is possible— just as in the case of the sequence of Vedic words—
wherein there is the conceptual construction that "that very Vedic sequence is manifested by human activity."
Likewise, since there is no distinction in the case of jars and so forth,
it is not [the case that they are produced] from the jar and so on by virtue of their conforming to human activity.
If it is asked what the distinction of that [state] is, he says:
"Those," and so forth;
even those [objects] such as pots were previously seen by others— the preceding potters and so forth— in the construction of those pots and other things.
"Upon merely seeing them"— that is to say,
even another person such as a potter who acts later does not do so without instruction.
And for those whose practice is preceded by the instruction of others, if [the scripture] were not of human origin...
...then indeed,
just as the sequence [of the Veda] is held to be non-human (apauruṣeya) because its author is not remembered,
so too are certain things such as jars whose authors are unknown.
Objects such as jars are seen in places that have been covered for a long time,
yet no creator of them is remembered;
therefore, since the dependence upon human activity is equal in both cases, if the Vedic sequence were not of human origin, then [there would be] no creation of all things such as jars.
Just as the Vedic sequence might not be performed because its author is not remembered,
so too let there be the insistence on the non-performance of certain things such as jars, which at some time have no remembered maker.
And since this is not the case, therefore, neither this worldly nor the Vedic sequence of phonemes is man-made; such is the connection [of the argument].
Why? Because...
He said:
"Established," and so forth;
"establishment" refers to the relationship of cause and effect...
[This is] a descriptive compound (viśeṣaṇasamāsa):
their nature (dharma) is the conformity to the presence and absence of their own causes; [it is so called] because of not overstepping that [conformity].
Precisely because these mantras are of human origin, the excellence and distinction of certain men who perform the sequence known as *mantra* over ordinary persons is established.
For those who arrange the sequence of syllables designated as mantras, by what [means]... [is it accomplished]?
What is the cause of this thorough knowledge— the power that accomplishes the desired object— which is called "majesty"?
He states that it is uncommon to others:
because of the absence of those two— knowledge and power— in other persons such as the *prākṛtas* and so forth.
He explains [the meaning] with the words "this" and so forth:

if even an ordinary person were to know, through such a distinction, that "this sequence of phonemes is capable of destroying poison and so on, but no other," then he would likewise understand and practice that sequence of phonemes according to that very distinction;
however, he does not understand it in this way.

Therefore, even if this sequence of syllables called a *mantra* is accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas as being effective by its very nature, nevertheless, some person endowed with a particular supersensuous power must have known it; thus, there exists a person who perceives imperceptible objects and who knows the *mantra*, its efficacy, and its ritual application.

Although it has been stated that a *mantra* is a statement that accomplishes a desired object through the power of truth and austerity, it is spoken here while provisionally accepting that definition.

Since a mantra is a producer of effects even by its very nature, it follows that either through the production of effects by a mantra, or through the knowledge of the power of the fruit of a mantra, there is a preeminent person (puruṣātiśaya); this is what has been stated.
Regarding the claim that there is no one who perceives the imperceptible because of the inability to distinguish between a mantra and a non-mantra through inference, he says:
"Not indeed," and so forth;
the meaning is this:
while a particular sequence of syllables is capable of removing poison and the like, this specific sequence of syllables is not so capable.
Thus, it is indeed not possible to understand [the distinction] from a formal indicative mark (liṅga);
for what reason?
Because a specific indicative mark that is unmixed with the division between mantra and non-mantra is unestablished.

But surely, since both mantra and non-mantra consist of the nature of phonemes (varṇa), their capacity to bestow a fruit is also apprehended through direct perception when those phonemes are perceived, because that capacity is not distinct from them;
to this he replies with the words "pratyakṣayoḥ" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of those not taught": because there is no instruction such as "this is a mantra" or "this is not a mantra," there is a lack of recognition;
and because there is no certainty such as "this is capable of removing poison and the like" or "this is incapable," even when an instruction is given.

Even if it were taught by someone that "this mantra performs such-and-such an action," nevertheless, because the specific nature (*svabhāva*) of the mantra is not perceived— that is, because it is not ascertained in any manner whatsoever—
and because the instruction lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*).
Otherwise, it would be impossible to ascertain that "this is a mantra" except through the correspondence with its effect— that is, by attaining the result to be accomplished by the mantra—
and because that result to be accomplished cannot be perceived prior to the performance of the mantra, since it is only through the production of that result by the mantra that such certainty arises.
The sense is that [the mantra] exists at that time;
furthermore, the performance of a mantra that has not been ascertained is impossible.
Therefore, one must necessarily accept a person who perceives supersensuous objects—an expert in Mīmāṃsā—who distinguishes between what is a mantra and what is not a mantra.
Otherwise, there would be no performance of mantras;
nor does this sequence of syllables called a mantra produce effects such as the removal of poison by its own nature, but rather through human convention.
What is the reason?

For one person practicing a mantra, there may be swift accomplishment (*siddhi*), while for another who performs the same identical ritual application of the mantra, accomplishment occurs only after a long time.
This difference in time regarding the granting of results cannot be due to the mantra itself, as no excellence or deficiency can be produced in the mantra by anyone else.
Furthermore, since another person requires the observance of vows (*vrata*) and other practices for the production of results from the mantra, the mantra is not an agent (*kāraka*) by its own nature.
A *vrata* is a restrictive observance prescribed by the ritual manuals (*mantrakalpa*); its performance (*caraṇa*) means its execution,
and by the word "also" (*api*), the inclusion of fire-offerings (*homa*) and so forth is intended,
for [the rite] bestows fruit by its very nature.
What is the use of performing observances such as vows and the like, since no excellence arises from them?

Likewise, even when two persons perform the same ritual procedure based on a single mantra—such as recitation (*japa*) or burnt offerings (*homa*)—one may observe success while the other observes failure; therefore, the fruit does not arise from the intrinsic nature [of the action].

But in terms of yielding results by their own nature, the application of purpose would be equal even for those [mantras] that are currently effective; for even in the case of mantras that remove poison and the like, when they are employed again at a later time by that same person, there is sometimes a failure or non-performance of the intended effect.
For this manner of occurrence is not tenable regarding the intrinsic nature of things; why?
Because intrinsic nature is identical everywhere, whether in persons or other entities.
For that which is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of something does not become its intrinsic nature by depending on anything else;
however, when the fruit is held to result from a convention (samaya) established by human agency, then this fault does not apply,
for it is as follows:
But since the Person (Puruṣa) is the creator of the mantra-samaya and acts according to his own will, for what reason is it logical that he favors one person and not another?

Due to a specific similarity of being (*sattvasabhāgatāviśeṣāt*), there is a commonality (*sabhāgatā*) between the practitioner of the mantra and the originator of the mantra, by virtue of having similar ethical conduct, behavior,
and so forth; the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the offering of gifts and other such factors.
Due to that [power], through devotion to that,
or through a specific form of service— namely,
the worship of the deity by means of recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth, which constitutes a specific form of service— or because of that [service].

He raises a supreme objection with the words "by means of a vow, etc.," [suggesting that] it favors a certain person and not another who is devoid of the commonality of sentient beings (*sattvasabhāgatā*) and so forth.
The performance of the rules (*niyama*),
the practice of vows (*vratacaryā*), and the violation of the practice of vows (*vratacaryābhraṅśa*) constitute a *virūpaikaśeṣa* (an elliptical compound of dissimilar members);
the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is connected with each [member].
The meaning is: "by means of the practice of vows" and "by means of the failure in the practice of vows.
The connection is that success (*siddhi*) occurs when there is an accumulation of merit through the practice of vows and so forth;
likewise, success comes about for a person who is by nature (*prakṛtyā*) righteous by their very essence (*svabhāvena*).

However, when there is an accumulation of demerit (*adharma*) due to the violation of vows and so forth, or for a person who is by nature unrighteous (*adharmātman*), there is no success; this is how the meaning of the sentence should be construed.
Even if the fruit is produced from the mantra by its very nature, the opponent maintains that the distinction between success and failure will occur according to the manner already described.
He refutes this with the words "no," etc.:
the accomplishment of the fruit does not arise from a mantra that depends upon ritual duties;
what is the reason?

Because vows that are contrary to the Dharma yet serve as causes for the accomplishment of mantras are seen in the *Ḍākinī-bhaginī-tantra* and others; specifically, in the *Ḍākinī-tantra* and the *Caturbhaginī-tantra*.
And because of the word "etcetera," since they are seen among the causes of theft such as conch-shells, lutes, and so forth, he asks:
"Which, then, are those things contrary to dharma? and says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "cruelty" (*kraurya*): cruelty is the killing of living beings, and theft is robbery.
Sexual intercourse through the union of two organs is a base act; this includes [acts such as] the offering of smoke by cats and other impurities.
By the word "etcetera," other actions contrary to the Dharma are also included.
Those vows which have cruelty and other such qualities as their predominant features are described as "those characterized by cruelty and so forth";
and by means of those aforementioned vows, through the specific power of mantra-attainment,
it is thus:
In the *Ḍākinītantra*, the rule regarding the observance (*samaya*) is that when one kills and eats a living being, one attains the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of mantra;
likewise, in the *Kambukinītantra*, it is stated that accomplishment is attained through the practice of theft.
If it is argued that, according to certain other *bhaginītantras*, there is a rule stating that some deity bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*) through the practice of sexual union,
and that cruelty and the like will therefore be the very nature of dharma,
he says:
And as for the passage beginning with "na ca" and so forth:
we shall explain later, at the appropriate occasion, that such a nature of dharma is characterized by cruelty and the like;
thus, in this way, it is observed that accomplishment is achieved even through non-dharma.
Success is not seen even through [the practice of] Dharma; thus he says "loving-kindness" (maitrī) and so forth.
Loving-kindness is the contemplation of the welfare and happiness of sentient beings.
Purity is of two kinds:
external and internal;
the external consists of bathing and so forth.
The internal [dharma] consists of the cessation of theft and so forth;
dharma is the favoring of others through giving and so forth;
those for whom the supreme gifts are the dharmas of friendliness and purity are described as such.

For such persons, taking precisely that [state] as the cause— namely, the cause consisting of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth— for the sake of some accomplishment; for there is the non-accomplishment of that which is obtainable through the reversal of loving-kindness,
and there is accomplishment again through the reversal of that, namely through hatred and so forth.
Since the accomplishment of the fruit does not depend on the accumulation of merit from a mantra,
even cruelty and the like arising from hatred and so forth, when performed according to the ritual injunctions of a mantra, would be merit itself;
therefore, he says:

And so forth: from a single-natured action characterized by [the presence of] *sa* (compassion) and so on, it is not logical that there should be both a dharma which is opposed to that opposing non-dharma (*adharmavirodhī*), and a non-dharma;
for, apart from the injunction of a mantra, it is likewise not logical that non-dharma should arise from that very same [action], such as violence (*hiṃsā*) and the like.
For dharma does not arise from a cause that is non-dharma, because of their contradiction;
for instance, by that very same disposition of hatred and so forth, one incurs non-dharma when performing acts such as violence elsewhere through the application of mantras.
If it is argued that even when performing the application of mantras with that very same intention, acts such as violence are committed, how then can those acts be limbs of dharma?

If, because they are produced by hatred and so forth, cruelty and the like are indeed non-dharma even when performed through the application of mantras, then how can there be vows and the like whose nature is non-dharma? [This refers to] the vow characterized by cruelty and so forth mentioned previously.

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) asks: "How can the practitioner of recitation (*jāpī*) experience—that is, partake in—the fruit of the Dharma, characterized by the enjoyment of desired objects and so forth, [arising] from other inferior causes such as the offering of impure incense and the like? And so on.
And for one whose nature is unrighteousness, the desired fruit—that is, the ripening which is the result of action—does not arise from vows and the like;
rather, it is the ripening of previously performed virtuous karma.
How so? Just as [in the case of the previous examples].
He said:
"It is like the acquisition of a village resulting from the instruction regarding the killing of a Brahmin and the subsequent performance or accomplishment thereof."
Just as someone might employ another man,
saying, "Kill this brahmin; I will give you a village," and that man obtains the village by carrying out that command.
And that is not the fruit of the killing of a Brahmin;
rather, having obtained as a cooperative agent the person propitiated by the performance of that killing of a Brahmin, his previous auspicious karma alone bears fruit in that manner.
To the question, "What then is the fruit of that vow for one whose nature is unrighteousness? he says:

If it is argued: "Since the desired fruit of that unrighteous vow—characterized by cruelty and so forth—is its future result, which will occur in a future birth, such as rebirth in hell, then what is the use of that unrighteous application of mantras and the like, which is sought after?
To this, he says:
But he, being unrighteous in nature,
employed the *ḍākinī* mantra and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the employment of vows such as cruelty and the like is intended.
Regarding that auspicious action which has a desirable fruit—
the analysis of the compound being "that action whose fruit is desirable"— it is, by some manner or means, through its assistance, the ripener, the giver of the fruit.
But how can the unwholesome be beneficial to the wholesome? He says: because of the diversity of the power of assistance.

For the nature of auxiliary conditions is manifold: sometimes an unwholesome factor is an auxiliary condition for a wholesome one, and likewise, a wholesome factor is an auxiliary condition for an unwholesome one.

Just as for one who performs exceedingly noble wholesome deeds, unwholesome karma— which has the suffering of hell and so forth as its fruit— is exhausted by obtaining a wholesome co-operative condition and yielding merely the suffering of illness and the like in this very life; such is the case with an unrighteous application of mantras and the like.

It has been stated that [the mantra] is somehow beneficial to an action that yields a desired result; showing the manner in which it is beneficial in a particular case, he says: "The specific person who is the author of the mantra is himself the basis (*āśraya*); by him [is determined] the ripening (*vipāka*), which is the yielding of the fruit; that which has this as its nature (*dharma*)—its very essence—is 'that which has the person as its basis for ripening' (*puruṣāśrayavipākadharmā*)."
"Dharma" refers to a specific kind of merit;
"by him" means performed by that person in a previous birth; "he is such" [means he becomes so] through the propitiation of that [dharma].
That dharma bears fruit through the practice of cruelty and so forth, as well as through its propitiation— that is, the propitiation of the person who composed the mantra;
explaining this very point, he says:
"By that," and so forth:
by that person who composed the mantra, an assistance was provided through the application of rites such as vows associated with cruelty; this constitutes the nourishment of the action.

Because of the performance of that karma which has ripening as its nature— meaning its characteristic is the giving of a fruit— for that very karma possessing such a nature, namely the karma of desirable fruit.
If it is argued that the fruit results from propitiating him [the deity],

and thus even without a person who composes the mantra, the fruit arises from the mantra because the mere recitation (japa) and other activities of that very ritual device (yantra) provide assistance;

Furthermore, the opponent considers the statement that "the fruit results through the propitiation of the Person" to be incorrect; to this, the proponent of the final doctrine (siddhāntavādin) replies:
"No, it is not so."
"What is the reason?"—
the phrase beginning with "puruṣa" refers to the form, color, configuration, and so forth, of the person who composed the mantra.
Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of [states] such as peaceful or wrathful;

conduct (*caryā*) is characterized by the activity of body and speech; and resolve (*adhimukti*) is the mental conviction regarding those forms and so forth—[the latter is mentioned] because otherwise there would be the consequence of such resolve being rendered futile.
If there is no person who is the empowerer (*adhiṣṭhātā*) of the mantra, for what purpose would one have faith in its form, letters, and so forth? On the other hand,

if it is accepted that such a person is indeed a benefactor (*upakāraka*), then, by admitting that this very person— the author of the mantra— is a benefactor with respect to the accomplishment of the fruit from the mantra, it is established that there exists a specific person possessing extraordinary qualities (*asādhāraṇa-guṇa*).
The analysis of the compound is: "one whose qualities are uncommon.
What is the reason?

Because it is precisely through the inclination toward that [Buddha]—that is, through the inclination toward the specific forms, nature, and conduct of a particular person—that one performs such acts as the administration of poison.

Therefore, even though mantras are composed by persons, they do not yield results by their own nature or by their very essence independently of the application of that person, nor independently of the application of a specific person; rather,
they depend precisely upon the application of a specific person,
provided that the person who composes the mantra possesses extraordinary qualities.
How is it that even those who know the tantras recite mantras that are devoid of specific powers and so forth?
To this, he says:
"Even those who... and so on.

The treatises (*śāstra*) and tantras are bound to mantras; those who know them are called "knowers of the tantras" (*tantravid*). Even today, some among them compose certain unprecedented mantras. This is not due to their own solitary lack of capacity, but rather it is the power and efficacy of that preeminent person—the Lord and Master—who is the author of the tantra upon which they rely.
Why?
Because they act according to the principles taught by him; that is, because they follow the system of rules, such as the agreements and so forth, which was instructed to them by the Lord.
The meaning is that the Lord, being pleased, presides even over the mantras composed by them.
With the words "Even the men on the street," etc., he explains the meaning of the verse by first presenting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):

"Even the men on the street" means that even certain ordinary persons, such as snake-charmers (*gāruḍika*) and others who know the characteristics of mantras and tantras, perform some action characterized by the pacification of poison and so forth.

Nor would he be distinguished from others by virtue of performing such acts as drinking liquor; thus, the author of the mantra— who is intended to be possessed of power— would be devoid of excellence, just like an ordinary man on the street, and would be one lacking any superlative quality as the creator of the mantras.
And thus, regarding the view that a person lacking supernatural power (*prabhāva*) cannot achieve success,
he refutes it with the words "no," and so forth;
for there is no composition of mantras by those devoid of such power.
But as for those even among the men of the streets who compose mantras, their capacity to do so is due solely to the empowerment by the author of the tantra, who possesses great power;
demonstrating this very point, he says:
"For that which is made by him," and so forth.

By following the agreement made by that person endowed with such extraordinary power, and by acting according to his instructions—that is, according to the instructions of the person possessed of power—they become capable of performing mantra-rites. Why is this so?
It is because of his power, [specifically] the agreement (*samaya*) which belongs to him.

Furthermore, as for the instruction [concerning the *samaya*], since men who are independent [of such instruction] lack the capacity to compose mantras, there is a commitment (*samaya*) whose transgression necessitates re-entry into the mandala and so forth; therefore, the instruction regarding other procedures is distinct from this— such is the difference between these two.
"In that case too" means even in the case of mantras composed by ordinary people on the street, [the result arises] solely from meditating on their form,
and for a person possessing power, [it arises] solely from such meditation on the form.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the meditation on intrinsic nature (*svabhāvacaryādhyāna*) is intended.
Therefore, because it proceeds from the application of the mantra,

for that very reason, its empowerment (*tadadhiṣṭhānam*)— that is, the empowerment by a person possessing supernatural power (*prabhāvavatpuruṣa*)— must be inferred and understood as being of such a kind.
Furthermore, by asserting that some who know the tantras perform mantras with mantras composed by themselves, it would actually be the excellence of a person (puruṣātiśaya) that is established.
Because he too, being such an expert in tantra, is indeed a powerful author of mantras— since he possesses powers not shared by other men who are unacquainted with tantra—
and because the fruit of mantras occurs only when they are presided over by a person.
Therefore, one who desires results and seeks fruit from mantras should declare that mantras are produced and human-made (*pauruṣeya*) in order to grant results;

mantras are not eternal, but rather produced. Even though they are produced, they are not independent of persons in the granting of results. To demonstrate these two points, both "produced" (*kṛtaka*) and "human-made" (*pauruṣeya*) are employed.
He explains this with the words beginning with "for not" (*na hi*).
For the employment— that is, the utterance— of eternal Vedic mantras is impossible, because they cannot have any excellence added to them;
and since no fruit arises from mantras that are not employed, one who desires a fruit through their employment must assert that mantras are produced and are of human origin.
And it must be stated that [the mantras] yield results when presided over by a person;
for what reason?

Because, apart from the presiding of a person, the results of mantras—which could not otherwise arise from the power of entities and so forth—are observed to come about solely through the presiding of a person.
And how it is not through the power of an intrinsic entity that results arise from mantras has already been established in the passage beginning with,
"If such were the power of an entity, for everyone... (1.297).
And he provides an illustration:

just as in a poem or similar work where a convention (*samaya*) has been established—such as "I shall provide this particular meaning for whoever recites my poetry in this manner"—where "similar work" (*ādi*) includes fields of craftsmanship (*śilpasthāna*) and so forth; in that very case, such as in the poetry or the like where the convention was made, it is just like that.

The meaning is that just as in that case [of poetry], for those who recite poems and the like, there is a result due to being presided over by a person (*puruṣādhiṣṭhāna*), so it is with mantras as well. Whatever proof of incapacity—that is, whatever proof of inability—regarding the capacity of men to perceive supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha*) is asserted by the Mīmāṃsakas, all of that is refuted by this very proof of the excellence of knowledge and power in mantra-makers;
he explains this with the words beginning "pratipāditā hi" (for it has been established).
For it has been established that mantras are created by persons, and it has also been established that mantras yield results through their presiding authority;
yet not all persons are capable of either composing or presiding over mantras. Therefore, there exists a certain person of superior excellence who is the creator of the mantra.
The arguments for refuting that person who possesses excellence have also been countered and rejected.
By this, it is not being suggested that the opponent’s argument for refuting excellence suffers from the fallacy of "contradictory non-deviation" (*viruddhāvyabhicāritva*);
rather, it is stated under this pretext that arguments for refuting a person’s excellence—which are derived from the force of reality (*vastubala*)—simply do not exist.
Indeed, there is no means of proof that can refute a superior person who has attained excellence through the power of reality;

yet, is it not the case that such a proof exists: "The person intended [as an object of dispute] does not possess excellence, because he possesses intelligence, and because he possesses sense organs"?
Because of the statement [of gender], [the argument] "because of masculinity, like a man on the street" is therefore addressed:
Regarding the phrase "intellect, sense organs," and so forth:
it is a *dvandva* compound consisting of intellect (*buddhi*), sense organs (*indriya*), speech (*ukti*), and masculinity (*puṃstva*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), qualities such as possessing vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the like are included.
As for that proof which is described as refuting the excellence of a person (*puruṣātiśaya*), all of it is a fallacy of proof (*pramāṇābhāsa*)— that is to say, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
What is the reason?
Because there is doubt regarding its occurrence in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), everything is like the "remainder" (*śeṣavat*);
for since the "remainder" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*),
there is no non-erroneous understanding of the object to be inferred, which constitutes a cognition of the inferable as it truly is.

He explains with the words "As for that which... and so forth; the connection is that the proof which serves to reject the excellence of a person (*puruṣātiśaya*) is indeed a means of knowing reality (*tattvagamaka*).
Furthermore, that proof...
To the question, "Why is [the statement] beginning with 'due to the conjunction of the intellect and the sense organs' non-informative? he says:
"Because of the rejection," and so forth.
And because there is both rejection and generality— since those two, namely rejection and generality, are not possible when proving those [two properties],
for instance:
Either a negation—that there is no superior person—would be established by means of a proof such as "possessing intelligence" and so forth;
or else, that which is a superior person would be established as being identical to persons on the street, thereby proving his commonality with other ordinary persons.
Regarding these two cases, [the author] states the absence of a proof for negation with the words beginning "for not," and so on.
For it is not possible for one who does not perceive those things—that is, one who does not see objects beyond the senses—to refute objects that transcend the senses;
why?
Because even though these objects beyond the senses exist, they are unknown to one of limited vision.
Therefore, the point is that there can be no rejection [of the possibility of such a person] based merely on non-perception,

nor can there be a rejection of the excellence of a person based on the affirmation of its opposite; for precisely because of this very fact of being beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), neither of the two types of contradiction is established by the reason of "being an intellect" (*buddhitva*) and so forth.

And it was stated previously—by the words "nor even... and so forth—that there is no absence of a general proof, because there is no contradiction in the possibility of a person's excellence existing in one instance along with such qualities as being a speaker, which are not contradictory;
nor is there a proof of generality, that is, a proof of equality, with another person who possesses limited vision (arvāgdarśin) regarding that person of excellence.
For what reason?
Because it is impossible to know the occurrence of such a distinction characterized by the perception of supersensible objects and so forth—
distinctions that exist within the mental continua of others and are imperceptible to ordinary persons regarding such supersensible matters.

Furthermore, whatever non-apprehension characterized by the absence of possibility and the presence of valid cognition is adduced, since the status of that non-apprehension as a reason has already been rejected,
what more is there to say?

Just as, despite the equality of their masculinity and other such traits, one observes an excellence in the wisdom and so forth of some due to their respective mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), so too the possibility of excellence in others can be conceived.

Therefore, persons in whom such distinctions are possible [are distinct]; for if no distinction were possible, the commonality with other persons could not be established—this was also stated previously.
Consequently, this is an inference *a posteriori* (*śeṣavat*) intended to demonstrate the impossibility of the excellence of a person who possesses the capacity for speech and other such qualities.

Even if the presence [of the reason] in the counter-example is not observed— that is, even if the occurrence of "being a speaker" and so forth in the counter-example, namely a person of superior capacity, is not seen— nevertheless, because there is doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) due to the absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*), [the reason] is incapable [of proving the thesis].

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "those who speak thus": the followers of Jaimini (the Mīmāṃsakas), by speaking thus—that there is no person who perceives objects beyond the senses—contradict and subvert their own position. For they claim that the understanding of the meaning of the Vedas arises from someone like Jaimini himself, who possesses some degree of excellence; yet, by asserting that "there is no person whatsoever who knows objects beyond the senses," they undermine this very claim through their own words. This is because, if one rejects the existence of a person possessing such excellence, the comprehension of the Vedic meaning becomes impossible. Indeed, the Vedic words themselves do not say, "This is our meaning," or "This is not our meaning."
Therefore, whatever meaning of the term *agnihotra* is desired by the Mīmāṃsakas must be postulated by those persons; yet that is not possible,
because those persons are indeed possessed of passion and other such afflictions.
Therefore, that object imagined by him is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Now, if someone such as Jaimini or another were to imagine that meaning of the Veda, then in that case, a single person would be considered a knower of reality (*tattvavid*).
The notion that no person other than Mīmāṃsaka knows the true meaning of the Vedas is based on what?
There is no reason for this here, because there is no difference in their being human beings; the implication is that either everyone knows it, or no one at all does.

Now, even though there is equality in terms of being human and so forth, if someone like Jaimini is postulated as a knower of the relationship between Vedic words and supersensuous objects because he possesses extraordinary powers, then— just like him—
how could another person who is equal in terms of being human (puruṣatva) and male (puṃstva) also somehow, without any basis, become a knower possessed of superior knowledge?
"Why is it not accepted by you?"—meaning, why does it not follow that there would be another person possessing knowledge [other than the Veda], just as in the case of Jaimini?
He explains this with the words beginning with "no" (*na*).

"Come here, sirs, O Brahmins! This matter of ours must be accepted by you, and no other"—Vedic words do not cry out or speak in such a manner, whereby one might derive the understanding of the meaning from them.
The word *kevalam* is used for emphasis; [the analysis of the compound is as follows:

"those whose connection (*saṃsarga*), that is, relation (*sambandha*), with the auditory cognition (*śruti*)—which is the consciousness of the ear—is such that the specific objects (*arthaviśeṣa*) are not manifested. Thus, it is these very [words] whose connection with the specific objects remains unmanifested that "attack" or "ascend" the audition. This is the grammatical analysis (*vigraha*).

In that regard, when words whose connection to their meanings is unknown are heard, one person imagines some meaning according to his own whim, while another person imagines a different meaning; thus, there is simply no certainty regarding the word-meaning. Therefore, he says "no," [refuting the claim] that the relationship between words and their meanings is inherent, by which a restriction to a single meaning would be established.

Furthermore, there is no inherent restriction of nature among words such that they possess a natural or innate connection with their meanings; for if that were so, even when multiple meanings are postulated, it would not be logical that some of these Vedic words—while being seen to apply to a particular meaning and adopt it as their denotation solely by virtue of convention (*samaya*)—should express the true reality while others do not. This is because [the words] have no fixed rule regarding their meanings.
The analysis of the compound is "those for whom there is no restriction regarding the objects of knowledge.
What is the reason?
Because of the penetration into that which is beyond the senses.
Because it brings under its own control as its object a matter beyond the senses— such as the means for attaining heaven and so forth—

it is indeed the ignorant person who is unable to know the fixed meaning of a word concerning such supersensible matters; for one with limited vision is not capable of knowing the restriction of the meaning of a word regarding that which transcends the senses.
Someone— whether Jaimini or Śabarasvāmin— who is overwhelmed by defects such as passion,
declares the true nature of those words.

"The meaning of this [scripture] is precisely this and no other," and "no other person, such as Jaimini and others who are not distinct [from the author], teaches the truth"— such an establishment of distinction is not logical, because it lacks justification. Now, [if it is argued that the distinction arises] from some indefinable form of the intellect, the sense organs, and so forth...

If, on account of the excellence of practice (implied by the word "etc."), it is maintained that Jaimini and others alone understand the meaning of the Veda and no other ordinary person does, then from what source does this Jaimini and his peers derive such an excellence of knowledge regarding that which transcends the senses—
an excellence of knowledge concerning the reality of the Vedic meaning that is indistinguishable [from the state] of those whose true nature remains unknown to others?
Or let it be that Jaimini and others are knowers of objects beyond the senses;

nevertheless, is it impossible that there might be another superior person— such as those favored by the Buddhists and others— who perceives objects remote in space, time, and nature, just like Jaimini and the rest?
Why is that which does not exist seen by him such that it is rejected?
Let it be accepted that he too is a seer of supersensible objects;
otherwise, let even those such as Jaimini and others who are favored [by you] not be so.

For there are no arguments for refuting him— such as "being a human being" (puruṣatva) and so forth— which are intended to refute the excellence of a person as accepted by Buddhists and others, that do not also apply to Jaimini and others who discern the meaning of the Veda.
They do not take [them] as objects,
but rather they dissolve into them as well, because of their connection with the nature of being a person (puruṣatva) and so forth.

Now, even if the means of establishing [his] status as a human being and so forth are possible, if a distinction is nevertheless sought for Jaimini and others, then just as this distinction— characterized by the discernment of the meaning of the supersensible Veda— is desired for this Jaimini and his peers despite the possibility of other means for it; [so too must it be for the Buddha].

Even if the grounds for rejecting a person who perceives supersensuous objects—such as being a human being and so forth—are possible in his case, it would follow that other persons might likewise perceive supersensuous objects; therefore, it is more reasonable for you Mīmāṃsakas to refrain from such dogmatic insistence.
It is not because he is a perceiver of supersensuous objects that the knowledge of the Vedic meaning by Jaimini and others is accepted; rather, [it is accepted] because...
If it is maintained that a person whose speech accords with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇasaṃvādin*) is one who knows the meaning of the Veda,
then the opponent considers that only those such as Jaimini— who perform the discernment of the Veda’s meaning— possess speech that accords with valid means of knowledge.
"No," says the Master [Ācārya].

This subsequent [objection] is not tenable, because there is no possibility of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the objects of the Vedas—which are absolutely beyond the senses—such as the fact that [rites] are the means for attaining heaven and so forth.
He explains this with the words beginning "It might be thus."
We do not adhere to the interpretation of the Veda by anyone such as Jaimini on the grounds of that person's authority;
rather,
we adhere to the interpretation because it accords with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This very point is clarified by the fact that, even among many commentators on the Veda,
he who is the commentator of the Veda [is preeminent].

One who harmonizes— that is, correlates— the means of valid cognition, such as perception and so forth, with the meaning as it has been explained, is accepted and acknowledged as such an interpreter, and no other;
this [position] he refutes with the words "that is not so," etc.,
[arguing that] merit and demerit constitute the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
Because of the word "and so forth" (ādi), since other means of valid cognition such as perception do not operate regarding supersensuous matters that establish [results] such as heaven,
there is no statement by anyone regarding the meaning of the Veda that is corroborated by another means of valid cognition; for it is precisely because of that impossibility [of corroboration].

For it is precisely because perception and other means of valid cognition are impossible regarding that which is absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*) that scripture (*āgama*) is invoked— meaning it is requested— for the sake of cognizing that which is supersensuous (*atīndriya*). Otherwise, if the ascertainment of an object were to occur solely through corroboration by another means of valid cognition even with respect to an object accessible to scripture, then, even though that scripture exists, if there were no operation of another means of valid cognition regarding the object cognized by it, [ascertainment would not occur].
In that case, since there would be no comprehension from scripture alone when other means of knowledge are not operative—
and for this reason, because comprehension of the object occurs only through other means of knowledge when devoid of scripture— scripture itself would be a non-prover,
since the presence or absence of the comprehension of the object depends solely upon the presence or absence of other means of knowledge.

If it is argued that the cognition of supersensible objects arises not only from scripture independent of other means, but rather that the cognition of supersensible objects arises from perception and the like when accompanied by scripture—how is this so? The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) asks: how can that which is indeed supersensible, such as the means for attaining heaven and so forth, also be an object of perception and the like? For there is a contradiction.
It might be thought:

"Perception and the other means of knowledge do not establish an object that is absolutely beyond the senses; rather, those very perceptions and so forth establish even their own respective objects only by depending upon scripture (āgama). Thus, it is scripture alone that possesses authority"—this is what the opponent believes.
To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) replies with the words beginning "anāgama... [and so on].
"Since there is no scripture regarding this [fire], the cognition of fire and so forth would not arise from a mark such as smoke; this is the opponent's objection.
"No," [the author] replies:
"Indeed, when one proceeds toward objects that are beyond the senses, it is not the case that the means of valid cognition, such as perception, are sought within the domain of scripture."
If this fault were to arise from that alone, then scripture would not even be a means of valid cognition (*sādhana*) for comprehension.
But if it is argued that the very operation of scripture regarding supersensible objects is not known,

and therefore the operation of scripture depends upon perception and the other means of knowledge— then the rebuttal beginning with "by itself" (*svayam*) follows: since perception and the rest are themselves capable of establishing supersensible objects, what excellence does the proximity (*upadhāna*) of that scripture provide to perception and the rest, by virtue of which the operation of scripture makes known an object that is supersensible?

Now, since perception and the other means of knowledge are incapable regarding that which transcends the senses (*atīndriya*), and it is precisely perception and the others that would have to establish the operation of scripture, how could that operation of scripture—which is itself beyond the senses because it is connected with an object that transcends the senses, such as heaven—be established by another means, namely perception and the rest? For just as the means that accomplish heaven and so forth transcend the senses, so too does that operation of scripture in relation to such an object transcend the senses; how, then, could it be proven by something else?
It is not at all established that perception and the other means of knowledge are sought for its sake; therefore, this [objection] is trivial.

Furthermore, among many commentators, one who harmonizes the means of knowledge such as perception with [the subject matter] would have his explanation accepted; however, since this is not of human origin, the definition of scripture (*āgama*) would be something other than the standard definition of scripture.
He says this very thing with the words "For thus," and so forth:
for that person whose speech is in agreement with valid cognition...
It follows that "Agama" is the word refined (saṃskṛta) by that person;
and the refinement of the word is the manifestation that its meaning is supported by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). This is another definition of Agama.

And thus, he explains with the words "tulyā" (equal) and so forth that authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatā*), which is intended as the defining characteristic of scripture, is equally useless and redundant.

For when there is a claim of authorlessness regarding scripture, even though the objects postulated by a person whose speech accords with valid cognition and those postulated by another are equal, if one desires that a scripture— though authorless— be considered a scripture in some matters due to its accord with valid cognition by the force of evidence, then the accord with valid cognition would be the defining characteristic of scripture for sentences such as "The Agnihotra [is to be performed]," and so on.
If there were no human activity,
the characteristic of scripture as being "not of human origin" (apauruṣeya) would not exist; what is the reason for this?

Although that non-human agency is equal with respect to all objects taught by humans—whether they are desired or undesired—it is nonetheless accepted as a means of cognition because it is not sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
What is meant is this:
the meaning is that the comprehension of the content of scripture is accepted precisely because it is in conformity with valid cognition.

Even if that [authorlessness] were present— that is, even if authorlessness were equally established— since comprehension regarding an object that lacks corroboration by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is undesirable, the characteristic of scripture (*āgama*) for verbal statements would have to be their corroboration by a means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, if it were possible to have knowledge of an absolutely imperceptible object without scripture— that is, if knowledge independent of scripture were possible— then one’s own intended position, namely that "there exists someone who knows supersensuous objects," would be established.

If it is maintained that a person such as Jaimini— who explains the meaning of the Veda— possesses, regarding supersensible matters such as the means for attaining heaven and so forth, a knowledge of reality that does not depend on scripture and is free from error, then it would follow that one must accept that other persons besides Jaimini are also perceivers of supersensible objects.
This might be argued.
That he does not know an object beyond the senses through direct perception, but rather teaches it after having known it through inference—
that is not so, because:
Since inference and the other means of knowledge are impossible without being preceded by perception,
[the author] clarifies this very point with the words "at that time, when there is no seeing of that," meaning when the supersensuous object is not seen by that perception.

Because perception does not function with respect to those objects that transcend the senses, and because other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are preceded by perception and thus cannot apply there, it is understood that [the object] has something other than that as its objective support (*ālambana*).

That is to say, the objective support or domain of perception and the like is not its objective support; rather, it is understood that what is not the objective support of perception and the like is apprehended. For the purpose of certain determination (*niścaya*), scripture (*āgama*) is sought—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

However, since the operation of other means of valid cognition, such as inference, regarding supersensible objects depends upon and establishes perception— because inference and the like are preceded by perception— for this reason,
the Mīmāṃsakas could not avoid [accepting] a person of superior excellence who perceives supersensible things.
And since that [independent operation] has been refuted, there is no operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding objects beyond the senses;

for this very reason— that is, precisely because of the absence of such an operation— there is no certainty regarding the specific function of the scripture, namely the Veda, with respect to its particular object characterized as the means to attaining heaven and so forth, which are beyond the senses.
"This person here,
whether myself or another, is *svayaṃ* (self-existent)," thus [he is] independent of instruction from another.
Since one who possesses passion and the like does not understand the meaning of the Veda,
the state of possessing passion and the like is the cause of non-comprehension.
One does not know the meaning of the Veda from anything else either, because that person [who would know it] is likewise possessed of passion and other defects;
nor does the Veda itself make known or reveal its own meaning.
Therefore, how can there be any comprehension of the Veda's meaning?
Since there is no such course [of knowledge], for every person indeed has not transcended the confusion and delusion produced by defects such as passion; this is the analysis of the compound.
Regarding that [Veda], he does not himself know that "this alone is its meaning, and not this," because it consists of the determination of supersensuous objects.
Nor does one person perceive another person who possesses passion and so forth, because that other person would be subject to the same logical consequence;
that is to say, by virtue of possessing passion and so forth, that [second] person would likewise be ignorant.
For a blind man, being led by another blind man who himself does not know the path, does not reach the path.
Nor does the Veda reveal its own meaning independently of instruction;
why? Because it would follow that instruction is rendered useless.
If it were otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the exposition of the meaning is fruitless;

therefore, this thing called the Veda, whose meaning is not understood, is a "goitre" (gaḍu) among words— a goitre being defined as a lump of flesh between the chin and the head due to its fruitlessness.

In the same way, even a Vedic word, because its meaning is unknown and thus rendered fruitless, is like a goitre (gaḍu); for, due to the doubt—"Is this its meaning, or rather that?"—it becomes a thorn to one who has faith in it, a cause of pain; therefore, it brings suffering and establishes it in that person who has accepted the Veda.
What kind of thing is this? It is like a sinew or a tendon;

bound by that very [sinew], even one who wishes to remove it out of compassion finds it difficult to extract—thus he mocks [the opponent] with the word "by that. Since the meaning is not understood, what proof is there regarding the Vedic statement in the *agnihotra-juhoti* injunction—"one desiring heaven should perform the fire-sacrifice"—that its meaning is not "one should eat dog-meat," but rather some other intended meaning?

He explains [this] with the words "not at all any means of valid cognition anywhere," and so forth; for, by refuting a real relationship— whether characterized by proximity in the sense intended as the expressed meaning of a sentence such as "one desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra" or by non-proximity in the sense not so intended— there is an absence of both [proximity and non-proximity].

We do not perceive any significant difference between the meaning "one should cast clarified butter and the like, purified by mantras and so forth, into the fire which is a particular element according to one's desire" and the meaning "one should eat dog-meat. Indeed,
this same objection applies equally everywhere, even in the case of human-authored scriptures.
Showing that very point, he says:
those words or scriptures whose speaker or teacher is absent are so described.
Regarding the phrase "their meaning according to intention":

it is uncertain whether contemporary persons who have not seen the teacher follow and understand the meaning as intended by the teacher, or rather, through error, they understand it contrary to the teacher's intention; because there is no fixed rule, doubt arises in every case.
[The author] refutes this with the words beginning with "no" (na).

This undesirable consequence does not apply everywhere, because the teacher reveals the intention of the author of the scripture. By revealing [it] first, he declares his own intention to the listeners present at that time, saying, "This is the meaning of this statement.
Those listeners, in turn, reveal it to others, and they to others as well; thus, since a tradition of succession is possible through the teacher's instruction, there is no such fault.

For this characteristic of expressing an intended meaning is not possible for Vedic words that are non-instructive and thus authorless (*apauruṣeya*), because of the absence of an instructor. Furthermore, in the case of human compositions, the possibility of a well-known meaning exists because the author of the scripture intends to inform the world, thinking, "The world must be enlightened by me. Speaking with the intention of communicating to the world, he maintains and protects the established usage of a word regarding whatever meaning it has a convention for; otherwise, its communication would be fruitless.
Furthermore, from the adherence to conventions well-known in the world, the establishment of that meaning would occur— that is, the establishment of the meaning of a scripture composed by a person;
this is so because of the word "also" (api), which implies the previously mentioned possibility of an unbroken tradition (sampradāya).
The establishment of meaning for non-human (apauruṣeya) words does not occur in the manner described; why?
Because, in the case of Vedic words, there is an absence of any person's intentional effort (*samīhā*).

Since there is no intention to speak for the sake of mere verbal expression, it has been stated that there is no parity of consequence regarding the possibility of understanding the meaning of a human-authored scripture, given the existence of tradition and other factors; now,
he says that the determination of the meaning of human-authored works occurs precisely through the application of logic (*nyāya*).
Moreover,
following precisely this principle and this very reasoning, the wise Buddhists— who act with foresight— engage themselves in the process of what is to be abandoned and so forth,
for the sake of relinquishing that which is to be abandoned along with its basis.
They proceed toward the appropriation of that which is to be appropriated along with its basis;
therein, what is to be abandoned is suffering and what is to be appropriated is liberation,
while their respective bases are karma and the afflictions, and the knowledge of reality.
This is what is meant:

although words may have multiple meanings, the followers of the Sugata determine the meaning of the scriptures to be that which is logically consistent and conducive to the goals of human beings, rather than accepting it based on mere instruction from others; therefore, this is not a fault.
He says that very thing:
"not by mere report," meaning not by mere report from the elders; thus, the [alleged] parallel consequence does not apply.
And we shall later demonstrate, as the occasion arises, that this engagement with scripture must indeed be preceded by the adherence to logic;

for if the determination of the meaning of scripture were dependent on the adherence to logic regarding that which is absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), then there would be no certainty regarding the meaning of scripture— thus he says, "But surely," and so forth.
"The arrangement of the world and so forth" refers to the arrangement of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), such as the earth and other elements, as it has been stated therein:
"They desire the arrangement of the receptacle world below."
"The wind mandala is sixteen hundred thousand [yojanas] in depth, or it is incalculable," and so forth—
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Chapter 3.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), you Buddhists also accept as objects of cognition those things that are beyond the scope of logical reasoning, such as the granting of desirable or undesirable fruits by volitions like giving or harming, which are remote due to factors such as place and intrinsic nature.
How so?
Because the word of a person who is capable [of being reliable] is non-contradictory regarding those objects that are accessible through perception and inference.
His statement in the third position is considered plausible because it possesses a true meaning;
therefore, the object is understood from that plausible human statement.
Thus, he considers that there is no engagement with the meaning of scripture preceded by the observance of logic, and so the same undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) applies equally.
He refutes this with the words "No," and so forth:
an object that is absolutely beyond the senses is not understood from the word of a person;
what is the reason?

It is also false to claim that because there is no lack of certainty regarding the objects of perception and so forth—due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) directed toward them—and because there is correspondence (*saṃvāda*) regarding those objects, correspondence is therefore ascertained even for things that are extremely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*). For it is not the case that, on the grounds that a non-deviating [cognition] has been observed in some instances through the correspondence of a means of valid cognition regarding the objects of perception and so forth, everything taught by him—even that which is not accessible through reasoning—is likewise [true]. What is the reason?
Regarding the phrase "from its occurrence" and so forth:

because the occurrence of the speech of that person of superior excellence (*puruṣātiśaya*) is established through pervasion by non-contradiction, and because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhakapramāṇa*) for the contrary case, [one might ask]:
"But is this not also [the case] for you?"

By the statement beginning with "Non-sublation by both types of [valid cognition], perception and inference" (1.218), it is intended that the definition of scripture consists in its non-contradiction regarding at least one part [of its content].
Therefore, he says "and because there is no other way," and so forth.

The definition of scripture (*āgama*) is that it is a statement that is non-contradictory even regarding extremely remote objects, by virtue of its non-contradiction with objects accessible through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is accepted as the definition of scripture because, when one must act on the basis of scripture due to the lack of any other way, it is better to act in this manner.
Therefore, the determination of supersensuous objects does not arise from the aforementioned scripture, because that [scripture] lacks authority;
thus, it was stated previously that scripture is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Consequently, the knowledge of the meaning of words that are not of human origin does not derive from the tradition of teachers.

Because there is no teacher, and because a means of valid cognition does not operate regarding an object that is entirely beyond the senses through the power of reasoning, nor is there comprehension of the meaning from common worldly usage— since there is an absence of formal application for the purpose of instructing the world, it is impossible to follow worldly conventions.
