In that regard, it is logical that there would be no comprehension of meaning at all from words that are not of human origin; even so, regarding Vedic speech, there is a well-known worldly convention, such as the worldly practice that people proceed toward objects capable of burning, cooking, and so forth upon hearing words like "fire" (agni) and the like—
if this [convention] were the cause for comprehending the meaning of the Veda.
He states the reply beginning with "In that case" (*tatra*):
In that regard, who among men in this world is a seer of supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*) when it comes to the nature of ignorance (*avidyātva*)?

He explains with the words "na hi" and so forth that there is no such person as one who, by means of a vision of supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha-dṛś*),— given that among words which have multiple meanings there is an absence of restriction to a single meaning— could distinguish and specify the supersensuous meaning among those Vedic words whose specific meanings are being suspected, determining: "this is its meaning, not that."
For this worldly convention does not arise from a non-human, uncreated connection between words and their referents; rather,
what then?
From the convention characterized by the expression of one's intention,
how could there be [an objection] such as "by the author of his own treatise," and so forth?
This is because of the convention (*samaya*) of the authors of their own treatises, such as Pāṇini and others;

for those who follow that convention, such as the followers of Pāṇini, there is the linguistic usage of designations like "vṛddhi" and "guṇa," just as there is [the usage of terms like] "father" and "son. What is the reason?
It is because of the dependence upon instruction (*upadeśāpekṣaṇāt*).

For if even worldly convention were established by nature (*nisargasiddha*), it would not depend upon instruction from others. Furthermore, just as the comprehension of meaning from a conventional relationship depends upon instruction, so too the comprehension of the Vedic meaning from an impersonal relationship would depend solely upon instruction; however, such instruction is not appropriate for that impersonal Vedic relationship between word and meaning.
What is the reason?
Because that meaning of the Veda is unknown by any person whatsoever, and because the meaning of the Veda is beyond the reach of the senses for those who do not know it.
As it has been said:

For this [dharma] is understood from the Veda as the means to the highest good (*śreyaḥ-sādhanatā*), and its nature as dharma is established by that very fact; therefore, it is not within the range of the senses. (Ślokavārttika 1.1.2.2, verse 14) For the highest good is the pleasure of the person, and that [pleasure] is produced by substances, qualities, and actions.
"Therefore, since [Dharma] is to be established by means of those [means of knowledge] characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*), Dharma-ness resides in them alone. (Śloka-vārttika 1.1.2, v.

191). For if it were admitted that the object of the Veda is perceptible by the senses, it would follow that the meaning of the Veda could be understood even without its own instruction, just like color and other such objects.
Just as form and other such objects are perceived without instruction because they are perceptible by the senses, so too,
if instruction is accepted for the sake of certainty regarding the supersensible meaning of the Veda,
then [regarding] that instruction...

Regarding those independent men who teach the meaning of the Vedas, because they lack perfect knowledge due to being overcome by passion and other defects, they act according to their own whims; thus, since it is impossible to establish non-contradiction through their instruction on the true nature of reality, there can be no trust—that is, no certainty—regarding the meaning of the Vedas.
For those who are ignorant are not capable of teaching according to the true nature of reality, and therefore such persons do not teach out of their own free will.
But if it is argued that, like the Veda itself, the commentary on the Veda is also authorless— having come down through an unbroken tradition characterized by a succession of instruction—
and therefore the meaning of the Veda is established from such a Vedic commentary, he states the following reply:
Regarding the phrase "of that too" and so forth:
even for this commentary on the Veda, if it consists of words—that is, if its nature is verbal—it is subject to the same inquiry as the Veda itself:
namely, "How is the meaning of this non-human (apauruṣeya) Vedic commentary known? From what, then, could the determination of the Veda's meaning arise from it?

However, this fault does not apply to scripture that is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), because a person can personally establish the meaning of words—whether they are conventional or technical—by pointing them out directly, saying, "This is the meaning of this word. Thus, there exists a means for understanding the meaning and for the cognition of the object in the case of human words; such a means does not exist for those that are not of human origin.
For a non-human word does not act in this way, [saying]: "This is my meaning, and it must be grasped by one possessed of passion and so forth."

Furthermore, since this non-human (apauruṣeya) word has no author such as Jaimini or others who possess passion and other defects, no one is capable of knowing the fixed relationship [of words] to supersensuous objects;
thus, there is simply a lack of comprehension regarding its meaning, including the meaning of the Veda.

Granted that the Veda and its commentary are indeed not of human origin, nevertheless, there is no evidence that what was taught by a person possessed of passion and other defects to another person continues to the present day without the tradition being lost. Since there is no proof for this, [the opponent] resorts to conventions, oaths, and so forth; however, by stating "for those who cause the ruin of the scripture," he actually supports the possibility of a different composition through the interruption of the tradition, as is the case with men who cause the ruin of the scripture.
The connection is that [this] is because a composition is seen that is the reverse of previous compositions;
otherwise, he states the reason for the composition with the words "by way of self-aggrandizement," and so forth.
"By way of self-aggrandizement" means through the pride of "I-ness," as for instance when Mādhava, a destroyer of Sāṃkhya, composed a distorted version of the Sāṃkhya tenets;
for such a distortion could not have been made out of hatred for that system [without the underlying conceit].

Just as it is impossible for those who do not hate the Mahāyāna to compose sūtras that are counterfeits of the Mahāyāna in order to disparage those who have entered it— since such a person who has entered that view could not possibly compose them otherwise.
How indeed is it that this very humiliation of one who has entered upon that [path] constitutes the vice of rogues—
the vice of rogues being that another must be humiliated?
Or from any other source such as gain and so forth; moreover, in this matter of determining the meaning of the Vedas, you are indeed a Vedic scholar.
Because of the reason of attachment to his own doctrine,
he describes— that is, adorns— his very own facial color; thus, he is "mukhavarṇṇa."
He has surely forgotten his own admission when,
by stating "the determination of the meaning of the Veda [is sought] from persons defiled by passion and other faults," he describes the very complexion of his own position.
Since it is held that a person, being overwhelmed by passion and other defects and thus deluded, might speak even what is false, and therefore the word of such a person is not authoritative—

why then is it not considered here whether or not it is possible that this same quality of speaking falsely could apply to persons such as Jaimini and others who are performing the transmission of the Vedic meaning?

Because that very person, such as Jaimini and others, who possesses passion and other defects while teaching the Veda or the meaning of the Veda, might teach otherwise due to the cause of being afflicted by passion and so forth; thus, the suspicion of falsehood is not at all removed.
Demonstrating the very causes for such suspicion, he says:
"For it is heard," and so on—that [Vedas] which were recovered from what had been lost by certain persons, such as Jñānavalkya and others.
There are other branches of the Veda that have been lost and eclipsed;
they were recovered by being remembered again and again and reconstituted.
But what is the proof here that they were recovered by being remembered exactly as they truly were?
Even now, certain other recensions such as the Āhūraka and others are seen to have few readers and very few students;
what proof is there that those few students do not teach them by superimposing [their own interpretations]?
Just as other recensions (*śākhāntara*) are seen to have few students,

so too it is possible that even those other recensions which once had many or very many students may, at some point in the past— given the nature of cyclic existence— have come to have only a few students.
Since there is no evidence that those [scriptures] were widely studied even previously,
one might ask how they could be widely studied now; therefore,
he says "furthermore," and so on.

Furthermore, there is uncertainty because it is possible that those students who have preserved [the texts]— in contrast to the study by other persons not so considered— may have become numerous or prevalent due to the conviction in the authority of a person deemed trustworthy after a lapse of time;
moreover, there is a connection [to the argument] that for those persons who became rare— the propagators of the various branches— it is possible that they gave instructions otherwise.
And thus, the intention is that there would be no confidence;
for what kind of propagators? Those who have forgotten their studies—those by whom the study, once learned, has been forgotten.
The meaning is that, having forgotten what they have studied, they might even propagate it otherwise;
he asks "for what reason? and says:
"because of other students who are devoted to that teacher."
If, out of fear of losing the high reputation I have acquired, I were to teach otherwise than [the truth], [it would be a fault].

Thinking, "Surely these people are abandoning their conviction in me," and so forth— by the word "etcetera" (ādi) being included— there is the possibility of instruction otherwise, such as through vanity (*āhopuruṣikā*) and the like;
let them indeed propagate [the teaching] in another way.
Nevertheless, lest students should not understand it in that way,
he says "that," and so forth;
[this refers] to the conviction regarding that person who is considered [authoritative], and to the things spoken by him.

For those who, having gained faith in the author as one worthy of esteem, engage in the study of the Veda without critical inquiry, there arises the possibility of a distorted tradition; for he states that activity [in this regard] is established precisely by the authority of the person, since it is observed in the world that among many students, activity generally proceeds from a person who is esteemed.
[Objection: But surely, if one acts based on what is considered reliable, there will be agreement [with the facts]. To this he says:
because even from such a person who is considered reliable, deception—that is, contradiction—can somehow arise due to some cause, such as the fear of losing that reputation.
He states the cause for this accumulation with the words "Furthermore," and so forth:
we hear from you Mīmāṃsakas that there is indeed a succession of those limited human commentators here in the exposition of the Veda.
Among them, one might be a commentator on the Veda who is one of those characterized by hatred and so forth;
another might be hostile toward the vision of the Veda and thus teach otherwise;
and yet another might be ignorant or a rogue.
And thus, there is a lack of confidence in the interpretation of the Veda;
for this very reason, the meaning of the Veda is not established through an authorless (apauruṣeya) commentary on the Veda,
nor is the meaning of the Veda established through conventional or symbolic worldly usage.
Since the world is afflicted by passion and other defects,
let it be that Vedic words are established by nature and independent of convention;
even so, if their independence from convention were admitted, [the following would ensue].

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: because words such as "cow" (go) are seen to have multiple meanings in common usage (vyavahāra), there is no cessation of that suspicion regarding every Vedic word as well;
the meaning is that the suspicion of multiple meanings has not been removed.
If it is argued that only worldly words possess multiple meanings and not Vedic ones, he replies with the words "of some," etc.;

this refers even to certain Vedic words whose meaning is not well-known— namely, those words for which the word itself is well-known but the meaning is not, or to the word in its own form when its meaning is unknown.
Furthermore, since the meaning must be inferred by persons through the demonstration of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*),
and this being the case, there remains everywhere an unavoidable suspicion of multiple meanings— namely, whether a person teaches the meaning of Vedic words exactly as it exists or otherwise—
and thus it is also illogical to claim that Vedic words do not produce comprehension even when employed for an unintended meaning.
For, even when all words— both worldly and Vedic— are employed according to their actual referents, there is an *avyayībhāva* compound with *yathārtham*; because,

although the application or convention (*niyoga*) pertains to this or that specific meaning, it generates a cognition in each respective meaning according to the occasion and according to the convention, without any deficiency.
Nor can it produce a cognition of something unintended,
because there is no distinction in the production of cognition regarding desired and undesired objects due to the absence of proximity or distance;
therefore, since Vedic words are indistinguishable with respect to all objects, what specific single object— characterized by an imperceptible connection— could they denote?
One who has a connection with the word is so described;
for what ordinary person, lacking transcendental vision and seeing only what is proximate, could discern [the relationship]?
Nor indeed could anyone distinguish [it] from that world from which [our] cognition arises;
moreover...
This person here, who himself does not follow established usage even regarding the Veda—
by whom could the understanding of the Vedic meaning be derived from popular worldly parlance?
What is the reason for this?

For it is observed that by this proponent of the Vedas, words such as "heaven" (*svarga*), "Urvaśī," and others— indicated by the word "etcetera"— such as "Nandanavana" and so forth, which denote either well-known or unfamiliar meanings, are being described and explained.
For it is thus: it is the abode, the place, of those qualities that distinguish a person from ordinary men;
it is a happiness transcending humanity, superhuman; it is the foundation and the support for that superhuman happiness;
and it is that in which there are various kinds of implements and articles of enjoyment.

"It is a popular worldly saying that heaven consists of various enjoyments; it is a popular worldly saying that there dwells among its inhabitants a celestial nymph named Urvaśī. Disregarding that popular worldly saying, [the sage concluded that] heaven is simply unsurpassed pleasure among human beings, and Urvaśī is the means for attaining it."

By proposing an interpretation of the meaning entirely different from that which is well-known in the world through such words as "pātrī" (a vessel), how could this Jaimini and others rely upon common usage as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for determining the meaning of other terms such as "agnihotra"?

The opponent maintains that one should not accept [the conventional meaning] at all; for while there is no contradiction in assuming meanings well-known in the world for words such as *agnihotra* and so on,

and thus the very meaning already understood is accepted, in the case of words such as *svarga* (heaven) and *urvaśī* (Urvaśī), the conventional meaning is not accepted because it contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
With the words "No," and so forth, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) refutes the distinction just mentioned,

because even here, in the case of words such as "heaven" (svarga) and "Urvaśī," if one were to accept objects that are not supersensuous (atīndriya) as they are well-known in the world, [it would lead to absurdity].

Because no contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established— since there is no subverting *pramāṇa*, whether perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), in this case as in any other— it is difficult to maintain that there is no contradiction even in the case of words such as "Agnihotra" when one assumes their meanings are those well-known in the world; for, in the absence of a supporting *pramāṇa*, such a meaning is difficult to ascertain.
Establishing this very point, he says:
there is doubt that even someone like Jaimini might, due to dullness of intellect, perhaps fail to perceive that the attainment of heaven from the Agnihotra is contrary to what is commonly known;
and furthermore—
Furthermore, contradiction and non-contradiction are not something other than this; rather,
they are the operations of subverting and establishing pramāṇas.

The occurrence of the subverting means of valid cognition called non-apprehension as previously described is contradiction; the occurrence of the establishing means of valid cognition, namely inferential cognition, is non-contradiction;
and these two have the nature of contradiction and non-contradiction respectively.
The operation of subverting or establishing means of valid cognition does not apply to an object that is imperceptible,
beyond the senses, and not intended [as an object of knowledge];
for indeed, neither a subverting nor an establishing means of valid cognition operates with respect to things remote in space and so forth, such as the means for attaining heaven and the like.
And if this is so, how can it be said that "it is not by virtue of that"? This is because of the presence or absence of contradiction:

by virtue of contradiction, there is the cognition of the conventional meaning in words such as *svarga*; and by virtue of the absence of contradiction, there is the cognition of the conventional meaning in words such as *agnihotra*.
Now, if it is thought [that this is the case]...

Non-contradiction does not consist in the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) established by the practitioner regarding supersensible objects; rather, non-contradiction is simply the operation of that which is termed "scripture"—namely, the injunctions concerning the *agnihotra* and so forth—by way of expressing meanings well-known in the world.
Therefore, he says:
"And not," and so on.
The absence of contradiction consists simply in the application of words such as "agnihotra" by virtue of their denoting meanings well-known in the world; nor is there any reason [to restrict this],
for otherwise it would follow that there is no contradiction even in the case of other words such as "svarga" and "urvaśī," since they too function by denoting heaven and so forth.
For instance,
words such as "svarga" (heaven) and "urvaśī" (Urvaśī) are seen in common usage to denote specifically a place and a particular celestial nymph;
therefore, since there is no distinction [between the two senses], let both well-known meanings be accepted.
Furthermore, even in a single case,

the scripture known as the Veda is not of human origin; yet it does not manifest its own meaning by itself, but rather the establishment of that scripture's meaning is accepted based on worldly consensus.

Furthermore, even if one accepts what is established by worldly consensus, if one proceeds to investigate contradictions, there would be a lack of confidence in all scriptures, because it is impossible to determine whether a contradiction exists or not regarding matters beyond the senses. Demonstrating this very lack of confidence, he says:
"Even though," and so forth.
Even though that non-human (apauruṣeya) scripture exists,
since the object denoted by words such as "heaven" (svarga)— namely, heaven itself— does not exist in that way,
its being so is its "suchness" (tathātva).

Just as there is a grasping of the meaning of "heaven" (svarga) as it is well-known in the world because its nature is not otherwise [than thus], yet there is also a grasping of an unknown meaning—since even other terms such as "agnihotra" might be suspected [of having a different meaning]—one must ask:
is the meaning of this [term] exactly as it is well-known in the world, or is it something else entirely, like the word "heaven"? Why is this so?
The opponent says: "For it has been stated that in this case, when grasping a meaning well-known in the world, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not operate," and so forth.

As for what was said— that in the sentence "one should perform the Agnihotra," there might be the fault of imagining an option (vikalpa) by asserting that it enjoins the eating of dog-flesh— that fault does not apply.
What is the reason?

Because in another part of the Veda itself it is stated thus: "One should pour ghee and so forth into such-and-such a specific substance"—this being the consideration and explanation of the meaning of this sentence concerning the Agnihotra and other rites.
"No," and so forth; this reply is not appropriate for the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī),
because he has failed to understand the meaning of that statement which occurs in another section and serves as its explanation.
Furthermore, since the assumption of such a meaning would be unavoidable even in other explanatory passages,
the phrase beginning with "yadi" (if) serves precisely as its justification.

For if this collection of words called the Veda were non-human (apauruṣeya) and its meaning were known in some other portion, then from that known portion one could understand the meaning of the remainder;

however, since those Vedic words—even in their abundance—are entirely blind because their meaning is not understood, they are composed and explained by persons according to their own whims. Therefore, it is the same with other such words.

He states what kind of such interpretation should be applied to those sentences that serve as explanations for injunctions such as "one should perform the Agnihotra": "Let there be an interpretation of that very same kind for the sentences that constitute the explanations of [injunctions] such as 'one should offer the Agnihotra.'"
Just as the interpretation has been made for the statement, "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra," so too might the interpretation of eating dog meat be made in another context;
furthermore, common renown is not something else at all, but rather this very thing.
The discourse of men— that is, of persons— is not accepted by you as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because all persons are further (*bhūyaḥ*) afflicted by passion and other defects.
"Further" means again.

Furthermore, since worldly report was previously established as being non-authoritative, how can it now be that the meaning of the Veda is derived from it? Is this not simultaneously both hated and desired—that very same thing which was hated for being non-authoritative is now desired and longed for as a cause of valid cognition? Thus, there is a mutual contradiction.
Notoriety is nothing other than public rumor;
rather, public rumor itself is notoriety.
And all those people are speakers whose words cannot be relied upon for their factual accuracy—that is, whose speech lacks that factual accuracy which consists in being non-erroneous.
The analysis of the compound is: "those whose words possess an inconceivable state of reality.
What is the reason?
Because they are enveloped by passion and ignorance.
Because it is pervaded by passion and ignorance,
that [popular saying] is not an authoritative means of knowledge for these people;
furthermore, the claim that "the popular saying of the majority of people is an authoritative means of knowledge" is also false.
For,
when there is an absence of correct practice even among a single person in the midst of many people, the mere multitude of the world does not become meaningful or purposeful; how so?
Regarding the passage beginning with "pārasīka" and so forth:

just as the practice of sexual intercourse with one's mother by many Persians does not thereby become valid, so too, even if it were common, the word of those possessed of passion and other defects regarding supersensuous objects is simply not a means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, if the understanding of an imperceptible object denoted by words such as *agnihotra* arises from the speech of those very persons possessed of passion and other defects,

how can it be logical for that same word to simultaneously denote both what is loathsome and what is desirable? This is because it would involve transgressing and abandoning the meaning in which the word *agnihotra* is established by worldly convention.

Furthermore, the claim that there is no basis or cause for postulating another meaning, such as the eating of dog-meat, and therefore only the conventional usage (*prasiddhi*) is accepted—this too is incorrect;
because since conventional usage is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), what would be the basis for accepting it? What is the ground for grasping that conventional usage?

He first explains the first half-verse with the words "by means of attainment" (*prāptyā*) and so forth, so that there might not even be a grasping [of the object] based on its being well-known (*prasiddhi*).

When one perceives the merits and defects [of an object], it is logical to engage with another object that is not well-known by means of the reversal— that is, the abandonment— of an object already attained through common renown.
If it is argued that "there is a perception of defects in what is already established and a perception of virtues in what is not yet established,

and since there is no perception of defects in the well-known meaning of words such as *agnihotra* nor a perception of virtues in what is not well-known, therefore the connection [of the injunction] follows from the well-known meaning alone," [the author] refutes this with the words beginning with "no" (*na*).
And this is an explanation of the second half [of the verse];
it is not thus,
for what is the reason?

Since attainment (*prāpti*) is characterized by the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for it is by means of a validating cognition that the attainment of an object is ascertained; thus, attainment is said to be characterized by the operation of a *pramāṇa*. Furthermore, renown (*prasiddhi*) is not a *pramāṇa*, such that an object established by it would be established through logical necessity (*nyāya*).

Consequently, for the Mīmāṃsaka who does not accept this well-known worldly consensus as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), any comprehension of the object denoted by words such as *agnihotra* through that consensus is a mere "grasping of anything whatsoever" (*yatkiñcanagrahaṇa*), because it lacks a basis in valid cognition; the meaning is that such grasping is arbitrary. Therefore, since the worldly meaning of words like *agnihotra* is not established by logical necessity (*nyāya*), and because the attainment of the worldly meaning is thus precluded by logic, the meaning of words such as *agnihotra* must be postulated according to one's own will.

In this regard, concerning the meaning of words such as *agnihotra* that is postulated by the Mīmāṃsakas—characterized by fire, substances, and so forth—and that which is postulated by the opponent—characterized by the eating of dog-meat: whether one follows established usage (*prasiddhi*) or does not follow it, in either case, since there is an absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the operation [of accepting a meaning] based on mere whim is equal. Thus, what adherence to established usage is there, by virtue of which the postulation of a meaning would be made from established usage?
Moreover, if the determination of the meaning of all words were achieved through established usage alone...

This doubt has been raised because of the word's multiple meanings; for it is observed that the quality of having multiple referents is well-established in the case of words such as "fire" (agni) and others.
He explains by means of the words "no," and so forth:
there is no determination of a single meaning for Vedic words based on common usage;
what is the reason?
For doubt arises precisely from that very well-known usage;
for instance, words such as "fire" (*agni*) are seen in common worldly usage to have multiple meanings.

This observation of multiple meanings is a worldly convention (*lokavāda*), a popular tradition (*lokapravāda*), and a matter of common understanding. Since there is multiplicity of meaning due to this worldly convention, it is therefore not logical to restrict Vedic words to a single meaning based on that worldly convention.
Strengthening the very point that the meaning is indeterminate,
he says "otherwise" and so forth;
for there is no possibility of it being otherwise, since speech— namely, sound— is by its own nature possessed of manifold capacities and thus capable of conveying multiple meanings.

The occurrence [of the reason] in another object than the intended one is "otherwise-occurrence" (*anyathā-vṛtti*); otherwise, such occurrence in another object would be impossible. "Otherwise-impossibility" (*anyathā-asambhava*) is the absence of that [otherwise-occurrence];
because of this double negation, an affirmation is accepted. This means that [the reason] could also occur otherwise [i.e., in the dissimilar class].

Consequently, regarding Vedic words that function with respect to supersensuous objects, there must necessarily be doubt as to their having multiple meanings for those men who perceive no restrictive factor— those who perceive no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a specific, fixed object. 326
Therefore, the analysis [of the compound] is as follows: those words for which the distinction of meaning is unknown;
among such words whose distinctions of meaning are unknown, a single intended meaning [is established].
"What is the meaning of *atyakṣasaṃyogam*?

The analysis of the compound is as follows: that which has a connection (*saṃyoga*)—that is, a relation (*sambandha*)—with sound, wherein that connection is *atyakṣa*, meaning beyond the senses (*atīndriya*)."

The object of cognition (*ālambana*) is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); because that [object] does not exist, [the view] is without an object and without a means of valid knowledge. Having thus ascertained such a matter, Jaimini, while explaining it, says "by way of that" (*tadvyājena*), meaning that by attributing it to the Veda—thinking that he is stating his own opinion under the guise of the Veda saying so—he, being a heretic (*tīrthakara*), speaks thus without any pretext.
"I myself speak [this]"—
therefore, we see no distinction between this Jaimini and other non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthakara); indeed,
he speaks while establishing precisely their lack of distinction.
Regarding the phrase "tathā hi" and so forth:
"tadartha" means that which is both "that" (the Veda) and "its object"; its "prakāśana" is the expression or verbalization;
the "vyāpāra" therein is the capacity or efficacy; [the Veda] is "śūnya," meaning devoid, of that [capacity].
"By superimposing that" means by superimposing the operation of manifesting the meaning...
such that the expression "it speaks thus" occurs.
that very statement of his is what constitutes it; such is the meaning.
By Jaimini— who, while performing that [act], falsely attributes to the Veda, which is devoid of verbal activity, the activity of manifesting meaning— only his own false modesty would be illuminated,
but there would be no distinction between this [Veda] and a human statement.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "tathā hi" and so forth:

when asked, "Which is the path that goes to Pāṭaliputra?", a certain man says, "I do not know; I myself merely say that this post is the path. In this way, one person, devoid of the capacity to instruct on the path, indicates the way under the pretext of a post.
But another says: "The post has no capacity for speech; I myself, having known it, say 'this is the path'.
Regarding these two who speak thus, let their difference in speech be examined—whether it exists or indeed does not exist; such is the intended meaning.

He explains by means of the passage beginning with "without intention" (*nirabhiprāya*): "intention" (*abhiprāya*) is the volition (*cetanā*) [thinking] "I shall do this and that," and the activity (*vyāpāra*) is the effort (*prayatna*) preceded by that.
The connection is as follows: "intent," "activity," and "speech"—that in which these do not exist is so described;

in such a post (*sthāṇu*), having superimposed the quality of being a path-indicator, one instructs either a single person who is independent (or) another person who is independent of the post, instructing him regarding the path.

Between these two persons, there is no distinction whatsoever in their acceptance of the words as their own, except for the dull-wittedness of the fool; it is precisely the dull-wittedness of the listener, the fool, that is distinguished, because he understands the speech of a post—which is devoid of intention and so forth—to mean "the post itself is speaking.
In this way, when Jaimini expresses his own view under the pretext of the Veda, the fool, due to his dull-wittedness, understands it to mean "the Veda itself speaks thus."
Furthermore, if the Vedic word were restricted to a single meaning, Jaimini might recognize that restriction to a single meaning;
however, since a denotative word is capable of denoting all objects as its potential signifier, why would there not be a restriction regarding the illumination of a single object?
Indeed, no object is restricted to a word by its very nature or by way of innate establishment.
What is the reason?
Because a word is capable of expressing every possible meaning;

or, if on the other hand the word lacks the capacity for every meaning, even then—since that incapacity does not depart from it, and because an eternal word cannot deviate from its inherent nature of incapacity—it is impossible to enjoin or appoint a person to apply such a word as an expressive signifier to any particular meaning against its will or dependence.
Even for one who has been appointed [to a task], there is removal;
for it is impossible [for him] to think, "This word is not expressive now," and yet [removal] does occur.
Therefore, since words are capable of [denoting] everything, there is no illumination of a single specific meaning;
or, even if there were a restriction of the Vedic words to a single meaning, a person would still be unable to know that supersensuous restriction of meaning.
He says this very thing:
For by what person could objects beyond the senses be known? Indeed,
Mīmāṃsā does not accept anyone as a seer of supersensuous objects,
except for one who intends to speak [of them].

The expression "the statement of the intention to speak" (*vivakṣāvacana*) means the manifestation of the intention to speak; the meaning is that without this—without the speaker’s communication of his own intention—supersensible things (*atīndriya*) would never be known by anyone.
He explains this with the words beginning with "by a person" (*puruṣa*).

When a word is composed and uttered by a person with a certain intention (*vivakṣā*), that person might at some time communicate that intention to a listener, saying, "This was intended by me as the meaning to be expressed. Thus, for words preceded by intention, a restriction regarding their meaning might indeed be perceived. However, in the case of a non-human (Vedic) word, which is not employed by anyone based on an intention, how could a restriction of meaning be known, even if it were present?
Not at all in any way;
for what reason?
Because there is no difference in intrinsic nature (svabhāva).

For there is no distinct intrinsic nature (svabhāva) whatsoever belonging to a Vedic word that is fixed to a single intended object, such that from the perception of it there would arise the cognition of the desired meaning;
or, even if there were a difference in intrinsic nature, that difference in intrinsic nature would have to be either perceptible or imperceptible— it cannot, first of all, be perceptible.
What is the reason?
Because it would follow that the nature of direct perception, being independent of instruction, would be self-evident.

Now, [if it is argued that] it is imperceptible— even though it is imperceptible, because there is an absence of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it cannot be known by anyone who perceives only the immediate; this was stated having provisionally accepted [that position].
Nor is there any specific distinction such that [a word] is restricted to a single meaning;
for all words are devoid of proximity or remoteness with respect to all objects.

Indeed, some words are not inherently proximate or remote toward any particular object; rather, those words being equal by nature with respect to all objects, the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) is the cause for their restriction to a single meaning.
"Convention is the manifestation of that": convention is the manifestation of that intention to speak;
for it is understood from convention that "this is the meaning intended by him.
Since that intention to speak does not exist in a non-human (apauruṣeya) word, how could such a word—being non-human—possess the aforementioned singleness of meaning?
He explains [this] with the words "not indeed by intention" (*naiva vivakṣā hi*), and so forth:
by means of intention acting as the cause, a word is restricted to its objects, such that it is determined that "this [word] is the designator of this very object."
But it is not by way of intrinsic nature;
for what reason?
Because that word lacks a connection due to its lack of restriction to any particular object, and thus, by virtue of that cause, it is equivalent to all objects everywhere.
Even where there is a connection between sound and the articulatory places and organs, because sounds arise from or are manifested by them,
it follows that those organs themselves cannot be designated by all sounds;
for indeed, not all sounds are denotative of the organs alone.
Furthermore, since a word denoting an instrument might also convey the instruments themselves, the term "all" is used; for this reason, a convention is established to reveal the speaker's intention—
of what nature is it?
It is characterized by the communication of intention,
specifically the manifestation of the speaker's intention;
however, in the case of non-human (apauruṣeya) speech, the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*) is not the regulating factor.
Nor can convention reveal that [meaning],
because there is no intention on the part of any person to exclude [other meanings]; thus, there is no restriction to a single meaning for Vedic words.
Or, even if there were such a restriction, that knowledge would not exist; there is no knowledge for anyone of a restriction to a single object.
By their very nature, Vedic words are restricted to a single object, not by the speaker's intention.

Then, when an essential nature (*svabhāva*) is accepted as being fixed, he explains with the words "if...": if that word were naturally attached to objects independently of convention (*saṃketa*), it would not be separated from that intended meaning by another object.
The answer to this has already been stated:
because there is no necessary connection with any given object, [the reason] is not certain;
moreover—
If the relationship between the signifier and the signified is accepted as being intrinsic and established by nature,
then a word cannot be further employed at will for another meaning according to one's desire;
for the eye, which is naturally restricted to the manifestation of form, cannot be employed for the manifestation of sound.
And a word is employed according to one's will;
therefore, it is not restricted by its own inherent nature,
just like a hand gesture or other such signs.
If the restriction of objects to words were due to their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) would be purposeless and fruitless;

for a distinction of intrinsic nature or a specific characteristic of intrinsic nature is not accessible to the senses in its own cognition, nor does it depend on technical terminology or convention— where "convention" (*paribhāṣā*) means linguistic agreement (*saṃketa*).
By the word "etcetera," the inclusion of conventional memory and so forth is intended;
how is this not like the distinction between blue and other colors?

Just as specific qualities such as blue and so forth do not depend upon convention and the like for their own cognition, those cognitions which do depend upon them— namely, those cognitions that depend upon convention—
are not the intrinsic nature of the thing itself.
The specific qualities of an object are not established by its very nature;
rather,
they are conventional and produced by linguistic convention.
What is it like?
Like royal insignia and so forth;
for example, the various types of insignia such as banners and the like, which are assembled by a king for his own recognition.
By the word "etcetera," gestures such as those of the hand are included; and that which is conventional is properly determined by its own nature,
whereas that which is established by mere nature is not proper.
What is the reason for this?

If it is argued that the activity of that conventional person proceeds according to human will, whereas for a Vedic word a specific inherent nature is fixed by its very origin regarding its meaning, and that [nature] is merely manifested through convention;
He says, "For this very reason," and so forth;
because convention (*saṅketa*) functions according to one's will, for that very reason...
How could there be a restriction [of the word] to the manifestation of a specific nature fixed upon a single object by convention? He explains that it is not so at all.

Regarding a convention (*saṃketa*) that functions according to one's own will, it can be established here for a desired object but not elsewhere; thus, there is no obstruction, nor is there any expressive power [inherent in the word].

Consequently, when such a convention is made by persons according to their own will, it manifests only that specific nature restricted to a single object and not any other; therefore, there is no fixed rule.
In a convention where there is freedom of will, what so-called restriction can exist?
The meaning is that there is no restriction at all.
For that reason—namely, because of this lack of restriction—the intended object of this Vedic word is indeed restricted solely to its desired meaning.
It has been established that convention cannot manifest fitness;

thus, it has been demonstrated that being non-human (apauruṣeyatva) is not the definition of scripture (āgama). Now, he introduces [the following] to refute the position that the non-contradiction of a single part is the definition of scripture.
Regarding the phrase beginning with "yasmāt" (because), the word "kila" indicates the speaker's intention; [the statement] "fire is the dispeller of cold" means it is the remover of cold.

By this [example], another elder Mīmāṃsaka spoke thus: "Just as the statement 'Fire is the remedy for cold' is true, so too another statement such as 'One should offer the Agnihotra' is not false; this is the probandum, because it is a part of the Veda—this is the reason."
He explains [the objection] beginning with "But another," namely,
another Mīmāṃsaka.
Because it is afflicted by the aforementioned defects,
[the opponent], wishing to establish the authority of the Veda in another way by abandoning the definition of scripture as being authorless (apauruṣeya), says:
"They are not false," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "where there is no comprehension": since those Vedic sentences in which the Buddhist lacks comprehension due to their non-falsity are taken as the subject (*pakṣa*) by the statement "those [sentences] are non-false," and since the reason (*hetu*) "because they are a part of the Veda" is presented as a general property (*sāmānya*), the reason does not suffer from the fallacy of being a mere part of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*).
Just as in the sentence "Fire is the remedy and the antidote for cold," and so forth—
the word "and so forth" (ādi) including sentences such as "Twelve months constitute a year."
He states the reply beginning with "of that," etc.: for that proponent, this proof is *śeṣavat*.
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: because of its fallibility,
such an inference was rejected by the master Dignāga, the knower of logic, in his *Pramāṇasamuccaya*.
To explain what "like the remainder" (śeṣavat) is like,
he says "rasavat," etc., as follows:
Because it possesses a form identical to the fruit already tasted, the fruit that has not yet been tasted is also identical; this inference is "with remainder" (*śeṣavat*).
Similarly, even those rice grains that have not been seen [to be cooked] are cooked, because they were cooked in the same vessel.

"Just like rice observed to be cooked," and "just as cooking occurs in a single vessel"— in this way, the explanation beginning with the words "by oneself" (*svayam*) and so forth is that the inference described by the Mīmāṃsakas is of the *śeṣavat* type.
The connection is that such an inference was stated by the Teacher himself to be non-probative (*asādhana*) in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*,
where he pointed out the fallibility (*vyabhicāra*) of the *śeṣavat* inference among the Naiyāyikas.
How is this so?
It is just as when, by virtue of their identical form acting as the cause, even fruits that have not been tasted are established as having a taste equal to that of a fruit already tasted.

And by the reason "because of being contained within the same vessel," there is the principle that unperceived rice grains do not possess the capacity for cooking, just as there is no such capacity in the case of rice grains already seen to be cooked;
this is the principle of the non-probative nature of that inference known as *śeṣavat*.
For it has already been stated previously [in the verse beginning] "Because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is demonstrated by mere non-perception," etc.

[Objection: But surely, its status as inference (*anumānatā*) follows from the general fact that the word of a reliable person (*āptavāda*) is non-discrepant (*avisamvāda*), [as stated in] *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.218.
By such statements, the teacher Dignāga has also stated that the definition of scripture (*āgama*) is simply non-contradiction with respect to one part [of its subject matter]. Thus he says:
"And this has been stated," etc. And this definition of scripture, which consists in non-contradiction with respect to one part, has indeed been stated.

"In this context, we are not able to remain without relying on the authority of scripture (*āgama-prāmāṇya*). Within this interval, the definition of scripture does not consist merely in non-contradiction regarding a single part, nor does it rely on truthfulness concerning a single object that is extremely well-known; rather, the definition of a true scripture is as follows: with respect to every object that can be determined through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by one of limited vision, and which is capable of being investigated, [the scripture must be non-contradictory].

The analysis of this [term] is as follows: it is possible [to establish] by means of its respective valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) the establishment of what is accepted through affirmation or negation, just like [the establishment of] purity in a treatise. For example, in the Buddhist tenet system, the status of being perceived (*pratyakṣatva*) is attributed to those things intended as objects of direct perception, such as cognitions (*buddhi*) and so forth.

Likewise, just as those things intended to be the objects of inference based on the power of facts (vastubalānumāna)— such as the truth of suffering and so forth— are indeed the objects of inference based on the power of facts,
so too is the status of those things intended to be the objects of inference dependent upon scripture (āgama).

The establishment of the three types of objects by their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the establishment of affirmation through the means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The establishment of negation by their respective means of valid cognition is what is called "being the object of direct perception and so forth."

Thus, when injunctions and prohibitions have been established, regarding the remaining objects that are entirely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), even though words lack an internal correspondence and there is an absence of a [perceptible] relationship, it is better—due to the lack of any other recourse—that a person who is in doubt should act toward them. This is because, since no deviation has been observed in any object within the scripture (*āgama*), there is the possibility of non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*) in some instances;
whereas in other cases, where the scripture concerns objects as previously described...

...even in a case where there is sublation by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding an object such as direct perception, the activity of that person is not appropriate; it is for this reason that we have stated the definition of scripture (*āgama*). Furthermore, the statement "Fire is the remedy for cold," which is a portion of the Veda and expresses the capacity of fire—the object of ordinary persons—to counteract cold, is true in its meaning.
Having presented this as an illustration, he states that the entire treatise characterized by the Vedas has truth as its object:

"What kind of treatise? Even regarding a subject that is determinable and accessible through means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), if it contains much that is illogical due to contradiction with those very means of valid cognition—then a Mīmāṃsaka or similar proponent who asserts such a treatise would, out of audacity, 'conquer a harlot' (as will be stated later); this is the connection.
Having said "even though it contains much that is illogical," he speaks next to demonstrate what that is.
The phrase "saying 'of the eternal,' etc. is to be connected with every instance;
thus, the scripture saying "there exists an eternal agent, the Person" speaks of the agency of the eternal Person.
Likewise, he speaks of entities as eternal;
he speaks of objects that are beyond the senses as being perceptible by the senses;
and he speaks of causes for entities that are inconsistent and illogical.
Likewise,
he spoke of the unstable state and the cessation of phenomena;
we shall clarify this in the commentary.
Or else, an object other than what has been stated is "one whose scope is excluded" (*vyastagocara*); that is, it is so described because its scope or range (*gocara*) has been excluded or rejected.
To the question "By whom is its scope excluded?", he says:
That scripture which speaks of such a thing— which is impossible, as it has been refuted by the two means of valid cognition, namely perception and inference—
and which speaks in contradiction to the inference that depends upon such scripture [itself].
Thus, would a proponent who, out of sheer audacity, claims that a treatise expressing many irrational meanings possesses true meaning,
succeed? To the question of what he succeeds in claiming, [the author] says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "virodham" (contradiction), [the author] explains by means of the words "apracyuteḥ" (due to non-decline) and so forth, one who makes a formal proposition (*pratijānānaḥ*) without resolving— that is, without removing— the contradiction of a treatise regarding a subject matter that is capable of investigation, and without demonstrating the cause for the engagement of a person with the treatise and the purpose of the treatise, which consists of the relationship, the appropriate means, and the human goal.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: it refers to a person whose prior form has not fallen away and whose subsequent form has not yet arisen;
such a person, they say, is the sequential agent of good and evil deeds.
Regarding the manner in which one is the enjoyer of the fruits of actions,
and how one is both the agent and the enjoyer, it is said:
the self is the enjoyer of the fruits of actions by virtue of being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth, produced by prior karma.
Thus it has been said:
"The inherence of the cognition of pleasure, pain, and so forth is 'being an enjoyer' (bhoktṛtā).
In the performance of auspicious and inauspicious actions, the self is the agent through its role as the substrate for knowledge, effort, and the like.
As it has been said:
"The connection with knowledge and effort is declared to be its agency," by virtue of the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi).
Even though the self is insentient by nature, its status as an enjoyer is apprehended through its association with consciousness;
as it has been said:
"The enjoyer is conscious due to the association with consciousness, not by virtue of its own essential nature."
Thus, the Veda speaks of [the Lord] as the substratum of the inherent cause and so forth; however,
this is largely untenable, as has already been made clear by the author of the treatise himself while demonstrating the impossibility of a causal relationship between eternal entities.
And one must connect this with the statement, "The Veda declares that some entities are eternal.
Why is it illogical?

Because for that which is non-momentary, there is a contradiction regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)—whether occurring successively or simultaneously—which entails a transgression of the essential nature of things.
For a real entity is that which is capable of causal efficiency,
and such causal efficiency is not possible for a non-momentary thing; therefore, that [non-momentary thing] is simply non-existent— how then could it possess the property of being a real entity?
Generalities (*sāmānya*) and so forth are indeed imperceptible;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the author] means that the Veda declares that action (*kriyā*), quality (*guṇa*), and the like are perceptible.
Furthermore, the Veda proclaims the birth, the duration, and the cessation of entities, which are manifold.
In the Sūtra, it was stated that the cause of entities is an object [of cognition] through the disparity of their births;
he now states that very same disparate cause,
beginning with the words "of that which cannot be augmented," and so forth.

Because it is eternal and incapable of having any excellence added to it, the Veda asserts that what was previously a non-producer— during its prior state of causal efficiency— becomes a producer later through dependence on others, namely, dependence on auxiliary causes; however,
this has been demonstrated in detail to be untenable.
With the words "because of its production" (*niṣpatter*), etc., he states that the Veda expresses an irregular state of existence.

Because it is produced from its own cause—that is, because it is already established as an entity whose nature is not something to be produced—the Veda asserts that [the Veda] exists by virtue of a substratum. However, this is incorrect; for it has been previously established that that which is entirely independent cannot exist through the power of another.
Demonstrating an inconsistent position, he says: "The Veda states that the destruction of entities occurs from a cause, namely the cause of destruction; and that is incorrect..."
...of the destruction of duality; thus it has been demonstrated.
He says that the Veda also [teaches] other such things as "existent" (sat).
Of what nature is it?
For non-existence is the reversal of existence; that is,
it is that whose reversal is well-known.
The meaning is: by what means does the Veda state its existence through perception and inference?
The Veda declares that the Agnihotra and other rites— by the word "and others," bathing at sacred fords and so forth— possess the capacity to purify sin;
here too, by the word "and others," the accumulation of merit and so forth [is intended].
...is sublated by an inference based on the three marks of a valid reason;
for it is as follows:
The established position of the scriptures is that unrighteousness (*adharma*) consists of passion and the like, as well as the karma produced from them;
yet, since neither of these two is contradicted by the *agnihotra* sacrifice and other such rites, how could there be purification of unrighteousness through it,
or how could there be an increase of righteousness (*dharma*) from it?
Because dharma has as its intrinsic nature actions originating from non-greed and so forth,
whereas bathing at sacred fords and the like do not have that as their intrinsic nature;
by the word "etcetera," other similar improper assertions of this kind are also to be understood.

For that very proponent of the Veda, in all cases— whether regarding objects of perception and so forth, or within the threefold body of the scripture, or the entity to be established by the scripture— [the Veda is authoritative].
Without resolving or avoiding contradictions with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
and without demonstrating those factors that constitute the limbs for engaging with the treatise—
those very factors being what?— he says:
"Connection," and so forth: connection is the mutual coherence of the meanings of the words; it is the means by which the goal can be accomplished.
A suitable means is that which is declared in the scripture as a means for achieving the goals of human life;
the meaning is that such a means, being perceived, can be accomplished by a person.
The compound *abhyudayaniḥśreyasapuruṣārthasambandhānuguṇopāyapuruṣārthāḥ* is a *dvandva*; these are the designations for those [categories].

Now, it might be argued that the scripture’s unacceptability was already stated simply because its internal contradictions were not resolved; so what is the point of stating this failure to demonstrate the properties of the scripture?
It is thought thus:
having demonstrated that [the scripture] is pure regarding the objects of perception and inference, one might perhaps say something else regarding other matters that lack such a connection.
for that purpose, the exposition of the dharma of the treatise has been stated.

Thus, having demonstrated the characteristics of a treatise (*śāstra*) by stating the connection (*sambandha*) and so forth, [the author] proceeds merely by stating the truthfulness of the subject matter, which is extremely well-known. The "extremely well-known subject" is the capacity of fire to dispel cold; the "statement" regarding that is a statement of truth.
Because it is difficult to fathom even with superior wisdom due to its being merely a statement of truth, it is "difficult to grasp through superior wisdom.
For that very reason, it is "profound" (*gahana*); that is to say, even in such a subject, which is otherwise entirely beyond the senses (*atyanta-parokṣa*).
Desiring to establish his own faultlessness and the truth of his purpose, this Mīmāṃsaka boldly and impudently triumphs even over a *bandhakī*;
and as to what kind of *bandhakī* he triumphs over, he demonstrates her with the words beginning "a certain..."—
a *bandhakī* being a woman of ill-conduct.
Having been seen by her own husband at the very place of the transgression, and having been reproached by him— having been told, "You have consorted with another man"—
she replied to that husband.
...how he replied,
[the author] says: "Behold," and so forth.
The women standing nearby are addressed with the word "Mother" (*mātaḥ*);
this is the second-person plural form of the imperative (*loṭ*) meaning, "O Mothers, behold! Indeed, look at the perversity of my husband, this man!"

Consequently, even from the word *mātṛ*, the plural form *mātaraḥ* alone is appropriate; regarding this, some maintain that there exists a word *mātaḥ* which has the same meaning as the vocative singular form *mātṛ*.

...by the maxim that "particles are imitations of sounds," and because it is an indeclinable (avyaya), it maintains the same form in all cases; thus, even when connected with the word *paśyata* in the plural, it is employed as *mātari* alone.
Others, however, read "paśyata mātaraḥ puruṣasya" (behold the mothers of the man).
[In this view,] "dharmapatnī" is a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyapadalopī samāsaḥ*), meaning a wife who is an instrument for the performance of dharma.
Without placing trust in me, your lawful wife, [you have gone to those] water-bubbles of your own...
The phrase "he forms a conviction regarding the two, namely the *ddhāñjala* and the bubble, which are designated as 'eyes'" is the context;
the analysis of the compound is: "those two whose designations are 'eye' (*netra*).
He states the reason why [the woman] does not unite with another man:
"Teneti" and so forth:
"jaratkāṇaḥ" means one who is both decrepit and one-eyed; the sense is "by an old, one-eyed man."
In this context, by the mention of "old," the deficiency of age is expressed;
by the mention of "blind," the deformity resulting from the deficiency of the eye—the supreme locus of form—is expressed;
and by the mention of "village-dweller," the deficiency of qualities such as elegance and the like is expressed.
By the mention of "wood-gatherers," poverty is indicated because their livelihood is one of hardship;
thus, although she was previously requested for marriage by a man endowed with qualities such as old age, she did not unite with him.
Through attachment to the qualities of form,
"form" refers to physical beauty,
while "quality" refers to attributes such as cleverness and so forth.

"Anurāga" means longing or desire for beauty and virtue; by that cause, [he approached] the son of the chief minister— the analysis of the compound being "the child who is both the chief minister and a boy," specifically a young son of the preeminent minister.

"How can it be possible that I should desire such a boy?"—in response to this, the four qualities of the chief minister's son are stated as the opposites of the four defects beginning with "old age" (vṛddha).
By the mention of "form" (rūpa), his comeliness is indicated; by the mention of "qualities" (guṇa), his wit and other virtues are meant.
By mentioning the chief minister, [she implies] sovereignty;
by mentioning the child, [she implies] the quality of youth.
And this is merely her own speech prompted by the audacity of a harlot, not something consistent with reason.
Since only form (*rūpa*) and the other [aggregates] are the cause of desire, and not old age and so forth,
he applies the example to the case at hand with the words "of such a kind" (*evaṃjātīyaka*) and so on;
"of such a kind" means it is equivalent to the reply given by the unchaste woman.
Regarding this inference of the Veda’s non-contradiction with respect to objects that are absolutely beyond the senses:

of what kind of Veda? It is of a Veda whose contradiction with perceived means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been observed in a matter that is capable of investigation; such is the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound *dṛṣṭapramāṇavirodhasya*.
By means of the example of fire removing cold, there is an inference;
through the statement that fire is the remedy for cold— such as the sentence "fire is the medicine for frost"— it is non-contradictory.
Likewise, another Vedic statement is also non-contradictory;
therein, the Veda stands in the place of a lawful wife, while the assertion of the agency and other attributes of the eternal Person is equivalent to a disagreement.
Direct perception and inference are equal to the eyes;
and the word of a wife whose veracity has been observed to deviate is not more authoritative than that of a man for whom... [it is].

Even upon seeing such a contradiction, one should not treat one's own view as authoritative but should instead accept her word as it truly is; for, having rendered invalid those two means of knowledge that contradict the meaning stated in the Veda, we should not understand what is entirely beyond the senses based on the words of the Veda’s wife-like [perception], which is seen to be fallible.
Right here he states another fault,
beginning with "sidhyet" (it would be established):
"evam" (in this way) means that if the entire Veda were [established] merely by stating one perceived truth.
...if validity were established [in this way], then every person would be an authority in every matter;
for among the many statements made by a person, there is not even a single one that possesses a true meaning.
However, it indeed exists;
he explains this with the words "as follows" (*yathā*) and so forth, [showing] how this extreme capacity for denotation exists.
Considering that speaking the truth with absolute consistency is extremely difficult and is performed only through extreme hardship,
[he acted] in such an absolutely... manner.
Since speaking the truth is extremely difficult given this established principle, how could there be any correspondence—
even by the *kākatālīya* logic— with the truthful meaning of even a single word? For that reason, [it is not possible].

Therefore, if it is accepted that the entire collection of words belonging to a person— just like that single non-contradictory statement— is likewise non-contradictory, then no person whatsoever would fail to be an authoritative source (*āpta*). This is because the entire mass of speech of that individual, whose one particular utterance has been observed to be non-contradictory, would be established as being of such a nature— that is, non-contradictory.
But everyone would be authoritative;
however, this is not the case,
therefore [authoritativeness] does not follow from non-contradiction in one respect alone.
...validity. Furthermore, whatever indeed serves as the indicator of something must indicate it by being either of the same nature as it or produced from it; it cannot do so otherwise.
And this sound is not of the same nature as those things intended to be expressed.
What is the reason?
Because sound resides in the speaker; for the nature of one thing does not exist elsewhere, nor does the effect of things [exist elsewhere].
This is not sound;
for what reason?
Because in the speaker, there occurs the cognition of sound.
Therefore, this is the meaning:
because [the word] is dependent solely upon the speaker’s intention and not upon an external object...
This is the meaning.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and not of that which is distinct from those," he explains by means of the words beginning with "there exists no non-deviation" (*avyabhicāritā*) that there is no such non-deviation for an object distinct from both essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*).
The word "first" (tāvat) refers to sequence;
this statement resides in the speaker and is neither the intrinsic nature of the objects to be expressed nor the effect of those objects to be expressed.
What is the reason?

Because even in the absence of that—that is, even in the absence of the thing itself—it arises through mere intention (*vivakṣā*); furthermore, there is no cause other than the effect or its own nature that is invariably concomitant (*avyabhicārī*) with anything whatsoever.
Or...
since there is deviation [of the reason], the word [could] be otherwise than that.
Therefore, "otherwise" means even in the absence of an external object;
because that [word] is possible— that is, because that word can occur— for that reason, the cognition of that [object], namely the cognition of an external object, is untenable.
This might be so:
even though the expression is a different entity from the expressed object, it is nevertheless the effect of that expressed object and is therefore necessarily indicative;
for the activity of expressive words—whether their production or their manifestation—is brought about by the perception of the expressed object.
The perception of the expressed meaning is produced by that [perception];
for when the expressed object exists, there is the perception of it, and from that perception arises the intention to express it.
"The utterance arises from the intention to speak"; thus, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the utterance is, through a causal chain, the effect of the object.
He explains this with the words "this might be so," and so forth, [concluding] with:
"therefore, because the expressive word functions by means of the perception of the expressed object."
He provides the rebuttal with the words "In this way," and so forth:
"If that were so"— meaning, if every instance of verbal activity were true because verbal activity proceeds solely on the basis of an existing object—
then how could there be such a verbal activity regarding a single referent that, due to differences in scriptural tradition (*āgama*), conveys mutually contradictory meanings?
He explains with the words "if," etc., that it would not be the case at all [that they differ], but rather that there would be a single identical meaning in all doctrines.

If this rule were to hold— that a word does not function without another denotable object— then, because they express mutually contradictory meanings regarding a single object, there would be [conflict] among diverse doctrines and systems concerning such things as permanence and impermanence.
...there would be no application of speech through the imposition or attribution of a contradictory nature;
for it is not possible that a single word could be both eternal and non-eternal without distinction— that is to say, without another mode [of expression].
The mention of "sound" is for the sake of illustration;
therefore, even a jar or similar object cannot possibly be both eternal in its absolute sense and eternal [in a relative sense] simultaneously.

Furthermore, there arises for some the claim that "sound is eternal," while for another it is "impermanent"; likewise, [there are claims such as] "it possesses a self" or "it is selfless. Therefore, there is no connection between words and external objects.

For this reason, since for a person who is an apprehender, verbal communications (āgama) that are invariably concomitant with— i.e., inseparable from— real entities (vastu) are not established in any way whatsoever, therefore, from those communications which are not inseparable from real entities, there can be either no ascertainment of the object or [an ascertainment that is not certain].
Furthermore, it is not everyone who seeks the authority of scripture, but rather only an ignorant person.
He investigates for what purpose:
for the sake of understanding the meaning indicated by that scripture,
that is, for the sake of comprehending the meaning shown by that authoritative teaching.

For what reason does only the ignorant person seek [the truth] and not another? To this he says: because those who have realized the suchness (*yāthātathya*)—that is, the non-erroneous nature of things—and have thus attained the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), do not depend upon the instruction of others;
whereas for that ignorant person by whom [the truth] must be sought...
...one whose qualities (*guṇa*) are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) is "one with qualities beyond the senses" (*atīndriyaguṇa*);
subsequently, a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) is formed with the word *puruṣa*. Of that person (*puruṣa*), [there is] discernment (*viveka*). (Note 616-1: Not knowing how to see.)

Since one lacks the capacity to make such a distinction as "this person is omniscient and not another" or "this speaker speaks falsely," how could one proceed by determining that a statement composed by such a person is authoritative scripture (*āgama*)?
Furthermore, not all statements of everyone function in accordance with reality... [para...]
Furthermore,
for a person who perceives the occurrence of an object that is desired and sought after even in the absence of its actual existence, there must necessarily arise a doubt regarding their speech:
"Is this speech true to reality, or is it not?"

In the speech of those whose words have never been observed to deviate from the truth, even regarding matters that are capable of investigation; that is, in the speech of those whose words have not been seen to be erroneous even concerning objects that can be analyzed.
Because of the word "also" (*api*), there is even greater suspicion regarding the speech of those whose words have been observed to deviate from the truth;
for that reason of suspicion, it is not proper for this ignorant cognizer to determine any object whatsoever based on the word of any person.

And because there is no certainty, therefore, even through the cessation of this cognition— that is, through the cessation of the means of knowledge— the non-existence of the entity intended as the object of negation is not established.
He explains this with the words "as was stated" and so forth, referring to what was said previously.
Because scripture has all things as its object, it functions by way of non-contradiction with respect to existing entities.

Non-apprehension characterized by the cessation of that [object], which is characterized by the cessation of verbal testimony, will establish the non-existence of even an object remote in terms of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth;
thus, this [non-apprehension] possesses the capacity to determine non-existence. Consequently, this verbal testimony does not have universal scope.
Because it does not take as its object things that are unrelated to human goals, even if one were to grant that scripture has all things as its object, it is said: "even if..."

...if this [term] *vṛttiḥ* were part of the original text— which has not been keyboarded— then, when there is an obstruction by another object (*vastvantara*), non-perception characterized by the cessation of arrival would possess the capacity to determine non-existence.
And that [non-existence] does not exist, because scripture functions even with respect to other entities.
This being the case, for a person desiring to understand from such scripture—which deviates from the object—the intended object is not established.
For that reason, it is said that regarding remote things, it has the result of determining non-existence; thus, it is the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent."
does not succeed.

Therefore, the conclusion is that even when the three means of valid cognition—designated as perception, inference, and scripture—are absent, there is no certainty regarding objects remote in terms of place, time, and nature.
To show merely a direction regarding the improper assertions of the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika), he says:
"The Veda," and so forth.
The words "iti" and "vāda" here are to be connected with what is to be stated later;
therefore, the meaning is: [the refutation of] the authority of the Veda...

...is it not true that in the case of dullness (*jāḍya*), the indicator (*liṅga*) [is used] with a quality; however, because of the prohibition of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) [in such cases], it ought to be "the authority of the Veda" (*vedasya prāmāṇyam*).

This is not a fault, because only those qualities that are well-known in the world are grasped therein; and the indication for this is the designation beginning with "the [number] of the categories" (*adhikaraṇaitāvatva*) and so forth. Furthermore, the claim of certain Naiyāyikas and others that God is the creator of the principles (*tattva*) and so on is also a sign of their dullness.
The desire for dharma through bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha) is another sign of dull-wittedness...

Delusion and the like, as well as the bodily and vocal actions produced by them, constitute *adharma*; their opposite, characterized merely by contact with water, is bathing (*snāna*). How, then, could *dharma* be obtained from that?
Furthermore, this doctrine of bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) has been refuted in detail by teachers such as Vasubandhu and others, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.

(4) Even in the absence of virtues such as moral conduct (*śīla*), the arrogance and pride arising from the claim of belonging to a caste, thinking "I am a Brāhmaṇa," is a sign of dull-wittedness, because it is irrational.
For instance,
having grasped [this], there might be the arrogance of claiming birth (jāti-vāda-avalepa),
whether based on that which is produced by a Brāhmaṇa father in the womb of a Brāhmaṇī mother, or by relying upon that very [fact].

In this regard, because a real, ontological universal (*vastubhūtasāmānya*) is denied, the former position is not tenable, nor is the latter; for the bodies of a Brāhmaṇa and a Brāhmaṇī are by nature impure, and thus there is no distinction between them and other bodies.

The "undertaking" (*ārambha*) refers to the performance of the practice of "torment" (*santāpa*), which is the affliction of the body through fasting and other means, for the purpose of destroying evil.
Of evil...
[text missing] ...of evil.
For thus, dullness is the sign;
indeed, greed, hatred, and delusion are the cause of all evil.
Since the onset of distress is not inconsistent with those [five signs], how could there be purification of sin through it?
These are the five signs regarding what kind of dullness— what characterized dullness?

"Where wisdom is destroyed" means that in which dullness has destroyed that wisdom which relies upon valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); the meaning is that it is devoid of knowledge that conforms to logic (*nyāya*).
It is said that there are five [aggregates] because they are taken up according to their respective locations...
[omitted]...
"Regarding the *liṅgas* (logical marks):
[this refers to] those such as Bhaṭṭa Uddyotakara and others, in whom there exists great analytical discernment."
My mind is submerged within the ocean of Dharmakīrti, which is the source of all that is real;
my memory is fully capable of reflecting upon what precedes and follows, and my wisdom is likewise preeminent. Whatever little I have spoken here will be understood by those who are truly skilled.
In the successive excavations of its meaning, one perceives a great clarity of speech,
the excellence of other well-spoken words within it,
and the destruction of the doctrines of all the haughty non-Buddhist teachers.
How could this commentary not be accepted by those whose intellects have arisen from [the study of] the *Suvilakṣaṇa*?
Thus ends the *Pramāṇavārttika-vṛtti* composed by Karṇakagomin.
...the means of valid cognition...
